title: London mayoral contenders limber up for a race that is Sadiq Khan’s to lose
summary: Tories and Reform hope to unseat the incumbent by tempting some Labour voters to shift to the right
text: The bicycles have been brought out and eager fists are getting ready to knock on hundreds of doors as the race for one of the most sought-after jobs in British politics springs into action. Sadiq Khan has had a vice-like grip on London, but a range of candidates hoping to unseat him in 2028 have announced themselves. The three-time mayor has been coy about whether he will stand again, and said he would make a decision next year. At the weekend, the former home secretary James Cleverly was seen riding a wobbly Lime bike through London, declaring that “London Bridge has got its mojo back” and that he has a “soft spot for Ealing”, where he met his wife, Susie. Cleverly, the MP for Braintree in Essex, has declared he will seek to be the Conservative mayoral candidate. “I’m going to run as an aspirational, entrepreneurial, forward-thinking Conservative candidate that is in tune with the city,” he said, adding that he thought he could beat Khan even though London is a left-leaning city: “London is a much more pragmatic city when it comes to voting.” Also standing in the contest to become the Tory mayoral candidate is Festus Akinbusoye, a Westminster councillor and Britain’s first ever black police commissioner. He says he is the right candidate because he is a “fresh face”, adding: “I’ve not been part of a government in the past, but I come with solid private sector experience.” But the contest appears to be Khan’s to lose, at the moment. A recent poll by Savanta UK for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, put Labour’s candidate in the mayoral race on 33%, the Tories 18%, Reform UK 18%, Green party 17% and Liberal Democrats 9%,. The Conservatives’ bid to unseat Khan is complicated by the presence of Reform. Laila Cunningham, a former Crown Prosecution Service prosecutor, is Reform’s candidate. She has been pounding the streets of London since the beginning of this year trying to drum up support. “I’m not stepping aside for the Tories,” she told the Guardian. “How many times have they tried to unseat Khan? They have failed.” Cleverly, she says, is “literally the establishment and he’s gone from one ministerial job from another”. She thinks he will be picked as the Tory mayoral candidate and said: “It will be two Sirs versus a woman. Sir Khan and Sir Cleverly.” Though the rightwing vote looks evenly divided between Tories and Reform, she is confident she can charm some of Khan’s voters: “It is not a left or right divide either, we won nine seats in Barking and Dagenham in the local elections, where the Tories wouldn’t dream of winning one.” Cunningham, the daughter of Egyptian immigrants, said she was “not your typical Reform person. People often see me and say they are surprised I am in Reform.” Akinbusoye is on the licensing committee of Westminster council, which is consulting to restrict “vertical drinking” in pubs – standing and drinking. Cunningham said: “That says it all. The fact they even call it vertical drinking is a joke.” The Labour MP Dawn Butler hinted at her intention to run this week: a video of herself walking past a sign reading “a new Dawn for London”, captioned: “When London puts up signs saying ‘A New Dawn’ … what else was I supposed to do?” She first floated her mayoral ambitions in 2023, and has since confirmed to the Guardian that she would run as soon as Khan confirmed he would not seek a fourth term. Khan did not respond to a request for comment. There are no obvious contenders in sight for the Greens, with the party’s attention focused on its leader Zack Polanksi’s plan to fight the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. A Green party source said: “We do have a number of people who’d be incredible candidates but no firm name. We feel confident after our latest local election results that Londoners will be excited by our vision for London.” Would Cunningham rather fight Butler or Khan? “[Khan’s] got incumbency. He may do better. It doesn’t make a difference because it’s what the party represents, she seems to think he was a great mayor so she seemingly wants more of the same.” • This article was amended on 6 September 2026. If Sadiq Khan ran in the next election, he would be seeking his fourth term, not his third as an earlier version said.

title: Online bookies accused of UK privacy breaches with use of cookie banners
summary: Most gambling websites nudge users towards accepting tracking data and harvest it before consent is given, study shows
text: Online bookmakers and casinos have been accused of widespread non-compliance of information privacy requirements, including “data surveillance” of customers, according to a study. Nearly nine out of 10 (86%) licensed British gambling websites appear to be flouting the general data protection regulation (GDPR), the strict rules governing how organisations can collect, store and process personal data, according to the research. The findings relate to the “cookie” banners that appear on a website when a user first navigates to it, asking which information they are willing to share. Britain’s data privacy regulator, the Information Commissioner’s Office, is in the midst of a multi-year project to force websites to comply with GDPR rules governing the banners. It claims to have forced 95% of the top 1,000 websites in the country to comply with the cookie and tracking regulations. But a study by researchers at the Swansea University’s GREAT Centre found that big operators in the gambling industry appear to lag far behind. Nearly a quarter (24%) of 624 gambling websites tested did not offer the option to turn off tracking software, which allows advertisers to follow users around the web and target them with marketing tailored to their interests. Operators that did not provide an option to turn off tracking included the Brentford FC sponsor Hollywood Bets, and Admiral Casino, owned by the high-street slot machine firm of the same name. Two-thirds of operators began harvesting users’ data before they had given their consent for it to be collected, the study found. They included well-known operators such as Ladbrokes and William Hill. Operators are allowed to do this for legitimate reasons, such as ensuring a customer is logging on from the UK, but researchers found that data was sent to third-party analytics platforms used for marketing. Of the websites studied, 2% offered no consent choice at all, including Dafabet, the sponsor of Celtic FC. Researchers also found that the vast majority of bookies and online casinos use “dark patterns” to nudge people towards accepting data sharing. These nudges include visual emphasis of the least privacy-friendly option (60%), default pre-selection of privacy-unfriendly settings (29%), and the reject option being hidden behind a second layer (47%). Such patterns do not necessarily constitute breaches in themselves. But the same proportion of websites that feature them, 86%, appear to have committed at least one breach of GDPR, the study found. This proportion is significantly higher than has been reflected in analysis of the wider internet. A previous study that examined all types of website, not just gambling, placed the figure at 54%. Ravi Naik, legal director at the data protection specialist AWO, said the report’s findings “paint a picture of widespread and systemic non-compliance”. He added: “It is sadly no surprise to see the findings in this report, yet the consequences of non-compliance are no less damaging. “The most striking thing to arise from this report is the light it casts on the failure of the Information Commissioner’s Office to take meaningful enforcement action against the online gambling sector.” AWO has previously acted for the campaign group Clean Up Gambling, which raised concerns with the ICO about gambling firms’ compliance. In 2024, SkyBet was reprimanded by the ICO for unlawfully sharing users’ data with advertising companies, after the campaign raised concerns, through AWO, about an operator that treated a customer’s gambling during early-morning hours as a sign of harm and as a cue to send personalised inducements at those times. SkyBet was not among those claimed to have breached GDPR in the University of Swansea report. The study’s authors said the goal of collecting users’ data was “maintaining engagement and consumer losses”. “The particular risk posed by data surveillance in online gambling, given the structural overlap between profitable behavioural patterns and harmful gambling behaviours, underscores the importance of data consent design as a consumer protection issue.” An ICO spokesperson said the data regulator was committed to “monitoring compliance across the UK’s most visited websites and driving long-term adherence to lawful cookie practices”. They added: “We will take action where necessary to protect people’s information rights.” Evoke, the owner of William Hill, declined to comment. Entain, the owner of Ladbrokes, said any data it collected prior to consent being given was not used for advertising or marketing. Hollywood Bets and Admiral Casino did not return a request for comment.

title: Falklands row shows urgent need to commit to 3% target, says Labour defence committee chair
summary: Exclusive: Tan Dhesi says Argentinian threats make it more crucial than ever that PM increase defence spending
text: Javier Milei’s threats to the Falkland Islands make it even more important that Andy Burnham increase defence spending immediately, according to the Labour chair of the defence committee. Tan Dhesi said the comments by the Argentinian president this week show why the government should raise military spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. But he said Burnham’s plans remain mired in confusion after the prime minister appeared to reassure him that the 2030 target would be hit, only for Downing Street to later retreat. “It’s important the prime minister and the chancellor don’t defer those decisions to next year,” Dhesi told the Guardian. “We’ve seen Germany publicly expose Russia for the drone incident [in Leipzig]. Now we’ve got a threat from Argentina saying they are looking to take over the Falklands. We owe it to the Falklands – they say it’s their right to self-determination. It’s important that we also defend them from this threat.” Dhesi was speaking after a turbulent week in geopolitics and defence policy. The Labour MP appeared to have secured a promise by the prime minister on Wednesday that the UK would spend 3% of its economic output on defence by 2030, at an estimated additional cost of £10bn a year. During Burnham’s first prime minister’s questions since taking office in July, Dhesi asked him whether he backed the 2030 commitment, warning “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”. He was speaking soon after the chancellor, John Healey, declined to sign up to the 2030 target, even though he resigned from Keir Starmer’s government over the issue. Burnham replied that he had “made that commitment”, only for No 10 to say the prime minister was not making a firm commitment. The government instead has signed up to a longer-term Nato target of spending 3.5% on defence by 2035. “There was no clarity [on the government’s defence policy], that’s why I asked the question,” Dhesi said. “There was a clarification post-PMQs that there isn’t an agreement to reach 3% by 2030. I wasn’t aware of [any] clarity [on this question], and that’s what was reconfirmed afterwards. We’re still in a similar situation. My question is valid and important for the country.” Later in the week, Donald Trump appeared to call American support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands into question. The US has traditionally remained neutral on the islands’ ownership, while accepting Britain’s de facto control, but the president suggested this could be changed in retaliation for the UK’s lack of support for his war in Iran. “Don’t forget, you get a big percentage of your oil from the strait of Hormuz, and you weren’t there to help me,” he told GB News. “Your country was not there to help me.” His comments about the islands have emboldened Milei, who said on Thursday night “winds of change” favourable to his country’s claim to the islands were “blowing around the world”. He added: “The US is considering this change of position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come.” He also said companies developing oil “behind the back of the Argentine government” would be barred from doing business in Argentina. Ministers in the UK condemned Milei’s comments on Friday, saying the Falklands would remain British for as long as the people who live there wanted them to.

title: Broken feet, ripped-out hair and now a death sentence: the fate of twin sisters jailed over Iran protests
summary: Taraneh Rahimi was told prison guards would rape her sister, Romina, if she did not sign a confession
text: The twins were 19 and still in high school when they were taken from their beds in the dead of night by masked men later identified as being sent by the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. After four months of desperately seeking news from hospitals and state institutions, their mother, Marzieh Nourmohammadi, finally learned their fate. Taraneh and Romina Rahimi had been seized over their decision to join millions on the streets of Iranian cities during the January protests against the regime. The twins were unrecognisable by the time of their mother’s prison visit in May. The women’s scalps were patchy from being dragged around by their hair, and their faces were bruised, according to their US-based cousin. It is claimed that Taraneh, who dreams of running her own horse stable one day, had been told the prison guards would rape Romina in front of her unless a confession was signed. The visit by their mother to Dowlatabad prison, in Isfahan, the main city in central Iran, was five months ago. It has now emerged from the Iranian courts that Taraneh has been sentenced to death for her participation in the January protests, and that Romina has been given a 25-year prison sentence. Neither of the women have been seen by their family since the sentencing. The difference in the sentences remains a mystery, but the twins’ cousin, Masoud Nourmohammadi, who lives in the US state of Utah, said he struggled to understand anything done by the regime. “They do not follow their own law,” said Nourmohammadi. “There is an 18-day period that lawyers can go and appeal but in a lot of [execution] cases recently that has not happened. They just sentence and take the kids and execute them and hang them. So I mean, nothing, nothing really makes sense.” Nourmohammadi, 43, said he believed Taraneh was sentenced to death by hanging because of her obvious innocence. “You can see her eyes and you know right away that she is a kind person,” he said. “My sense is like they’re looking to put fear within the people, to say: ‘Look, no matter how fine you are, no matter how innocent you are, we can get you, and don’t come to the streets any more.’” Despite the logistical difficulties presented by the war with the US and Israel that began in February, Iran has executed more than 500 people this year, including at least 29 people in connection with the anti-government protests in January. At least 16 women have been among those executed. Hundreds more protesters have either been sentenced to death or are facing charges which could carry the death penalty, including more than 70 in Isfahan. Last month, the UK and 30 other countries signed a joint statement condemning the executions of the January protesters and describing them as an attempt to silence dissent. Nourmohammadi, a healthcare IT specialist who arrived in the US from Iran 22 years ago, is speaking out despite receiving death threats via text messages and social media from people who say they know his home address. His cousins’ case, he said, should instil a determination to end the Islamic regime. The two women joined the protests on 8 and 9 January in Istafan, along with 18 million others. The men who came for them a month later dragged them out with bags over their heads and offered no explanation. “The family didn’t know where they were,” Nourmohammadi said. “They had no idea. They were searching for them everywhere, different courts, hospitals. Then my aunt received a call saying: ‘We have your girls, come to see them at the prison.’” Seeing her daughters was heartbreaking for his aunt, Nourmohammadi said. “She did not recognise her own children: they were beaten up, badly swollen faces, bruises all over their body, broken elbows, knuckles, feet, and they basically had no hair because they would pull their hair and drag them from one cell to another cell. She found out that they had been in solitary confinement.” Marzieh Nourmohammadi, who raised her daughters, now 20, on her own, was not allowed to attend their trial. Their lawyers said Taraneh told the court that any admissions had been secured through torture. No evidence of the sisters’ involvement in violence was provided, it is claimed. They had never been involved in protests before. “My mum lives with me,” he said. “There’s not a single second that I pass her and she’s not crying.”

title: Memory of water: the women reshaping Venice – in pictures
summary: Women – including gondoliers, a maestra d’ascia building gondolas, the city’s only female sandolista, and a teacher for lagoon navigation – are not only preserving Venice’s traditions, but actively transforming them
text: Venice is a city of tradition and projection, a place feeding the imagination of millions of people arriving from elsewhere. The “impossible city”, suspended on water, often appears unchanged, fixed in time. Yet, like the water that carries it, the city is in constant, subtle transformation. Beatrice, 28, has been working as a gondolier for one year, pictured during a shift operating the traghetto public-ferry gondola that crosses the Grand Canal We often speak of Venice as if it were immobile. We call it timeless, suspended outside history, untouched by change. But Venice is changing. It is fragile, exposed, under pressure. On one side, rising sea levels and increasingly unpredictable tides are reshaping the lagoon and threatening a delicate equilibrium. On the other, mass tourism continues to transform the city from within. Homes become short-term rentals, local businesses give way to visitor-oriented commerce, and residents leave the historic centre in steadily increasing numbers. The spaces left empty by those who move away are often filled by tourism itself, both a cause and a consequence of this transformation. Agnese Tegon, 31, works at a Murano glass furnace alongside her maestro, Giancarlo Signoretto. She aims to become the first female master glassmaker in a field that remains physically demanding and largely male-dominated Yet beyond the dominant narratives of overtourism and climate breakdown, another, quieter transformation is taking place. Venice lies on contradictions – appearance and structure, illusion and rootedness. One of these tensions emerges in the role of women in shaping the city’s identity. While many Venetian traditions are historically grounded in women’s labour, from lace-making to textile work and other forms of craftsmanship, women have long been excluded from what in Venice constitutes public space: water. Participants gather along the canal before the Women’s Regata delle Caorline, which was held as a time trial due to heavy fog and safety concerns Above: teams prepare for the Women’s Regata delle Caorline held on 8 March for International Women’s Day. Thirteen teams – made up of professional and amateur rowers of different ages – compete in the 26th edition of the event. During the regatta, Gabriella wears a brooch shaped like mimosa – the symbol of International Women’s Day – made by Luisa Conventi, one of the last remaining impiraresse (traditional bead stringers) In Venice, water functions as the street. The city is crossed by about 150 navigable canals, which remain its main routes for movement, work and social exchange. For centuries, these waterways have been spaces governed by explicit rules and implicit codes that largely excluded women. As in many other cities where women have historically been marginalised from the street, in Venice they have been marginalised from the water. From navigating boats, from professions such as gondoliera and sandolista, from boatbuilding and competitive rowing. Today, these boundaries are beginning to shift. A woman aboard a vaporetto. In Venice, waterways function as streets, and the vaporetto is the city’s public transport system A woman reflected in the rearview mirror of a vaporetto The journalist Anna Toniolo has lived with Venice her entire life, having been born and raised only a few kilometres from the city. This project grew from years of observing Venice and from a shared awareness, with photographer Daniela Sala, that some of the city’s most vital spaces remain inaccessible to women – not through formal prohibition, but through traditions deeply embedded in everyday life. Between November 2025 and March 2026, they spent weeks documenting the experiences of women whose work and lives are closely connected to the lagoon, through field reporting, interviews and observation, seeking stories that challenge the dominant image of Venice. Birds fly over the Giudecca canal The stories gathered in this project reveal how women are reclaiming space precisely through tradition, carrying forward skills and professions that have long defined Venetian identity while simultaneously reshaping them. In 2010, Giorgia Boscolo became the first woman to obtain a gondolier licence, breaking a centuries-old barrier and opening the way for others. Today, women practising the profession are still few. According to fellow gondoliers, those actively working can be counted on the fingers of two hands, although more women have passed the qualification exam in recent years. There are about 440 licensed gondoliers in Venice, alongside approximately 200 substitutes – qualified gondoliers who have passed the exam but do not yet hold their own licence. Chiara Curto is the only female sandolista in Venice (about 20 sandoli operate in the city). Smaller than gondolas, sandoli are ancient boats traditionally used by Venetians for everyday transport A similar profession is that of the sandolista, who rows a sandolo, a traditional flat-bottomed Venetian boat once widely used for everyday transport across the lagoon. Today, there are only about 20 sandolisti left, and just one of them is a woman: Chiara Curto. Silvia Scaramuzza – the only female maestra d’ascia in Venice – works on the construction of a gondola. After a decade of apprenticeship at another boatyard, Scaramuzza opened her own workshop with her business partner, Francesco Stenghel, in 2022. A new gondola costs about €30,000–35,000 (£26,000-£30,000), excluding decorations, carvings, upholstery and other custom work Top left: during the launch celebration of a newly built gondola at Squero Tramontin (where Silvia Scaramuzza works) family and friends gather as a retired gondolier points to Isabella, the two-year-old daughter of the owner, to whom the boat is dedicated. A modern gondola, if well maintained, can last about 30 years. Top right: the launch of Fabio’s gondola: once the boat is placed in the water, Silvia Scaramuzza and her partner Francesco Stenghel check that everything is working perfectly. It takes about two months of work to build a new gondola from scratch. Bottom: a decorative element depicting the Lion of St Mark, ready to be installed on a new gondola In the city’s remaining squeri – the traditional boatyards where wooden boats are built and repaired – Silvia Scaramuzza is the only female maestra d’ascia, or master boatbuilder. Other women are creating new paths into these spaces. In 2020, Marta Canino founded “Fie a Manetta”, a name that roughly translates as “Girls at Full Speed”, while also evoking the image of women taking the helm. It is the first, and still the only, motorboat navigation school in Venice run by women and open to everyone. Marta Canino leads a practical boat-driving lesson on the Grand Canal. Through her association Fie a Manetta, she teaches women how to navigate Venice by motorboat The idea grew from the awareness that navigation remains a predominantly male environment. “Girls, we need to start recognising each other and giving social value and political weight to our role in this city,” Canino said. Slowly, and often without proclamation, women are entering and inhabiting Venice’s public spaces through practice. Their presence does not simply occupy the water, but begins to redefine it.

title: ‘Britain’s Yellowstone’: restoration project aims to take the greed out of land acquisition
summary: Investors in Emblehope Moor will get their financial returns – and then it will be given to community or charity owners
text: It is difficult to find the most remote place in England. There is no public transport, no roads and no sign of any human habitation. Online route finders mistakenly direct cars up a grassy track. But miles along gravel forest roads in the far north of Northumberland is the largest contiguous rewilding site under single ownership in the country. The vast glacial bowl of 7,500-acre Emblehope Moor has been bought for £8.5m by Restore, a nature restoration company that works with landowners across Britain. The aim is to bring golden eagles, curlews, black grouse and beavers back to the moor which in former guises was a traditional grouse shooting and sheep farming estate and a dog-training ground. But the restoration project, which is still seeking to raise £4m to fund its 20-year scheme, also has a unique proposition: after delivering new biodiversity and abundance alongside financial returns for investors and repaying the crucial £4.5m Triodos Bank loan that enabled the purchase, it will hand over the site to local community or charitable ownership. “We want to prove that the bank is paid back, investors get their two-times return but we don’t need to become the next for ever laird,” said Benedict Macdonald, an environmental writer and the founder and director of Restore. “We’re keen to leave a well-funded community project for the future. It’s not an aggressive land-holding model; it’s both a capitalist and community model and I want it to become the national model for the uplands – we’ve got to take the greed out of it for it to work.” The environmentalist Ben Goldsmith hails the burgeoning mosaic of increasingly wild estates in Northumberland as Britain’s Yellowstone. Close to Emblehope in the north of Northumberland is Rothbury, the largest estate to come on the market for 30 years, which the Wildlife Trusts are seeking to buy with an unprecedented £30m fundraising appeal that is nearing its target. Other private estates in the area, including 12,000-acre College Valley and 4,000-acre Hepple Wilds, are accelerating nature restoration while the vast 148,000-acre Kielder Forest is increasingly managed by Forestry England for biodiversity. “We’re not the size of Yellowstone but we’re in England’s largest wild landscape by a long factor,” said Macdonald. Emblehope, a site of special scientific interest (SSSI) which was managed for biodiversity by former owners the Royal Kennel Club for a number of years, already has exciting numbers of raptors, including merlin and prospecting golden eagles. The site’s streams still have trout and salmon, and there are red squirrels and pine martens in the area. But Restore’s first tasks will be to return water to desiccated peat moorland and remove swaths of non-native sitka spruce. A hidden network of land drains have left what should be water-soaked peatland completely parched. Patches of sphagnum moss that are usually water-filled sponges even in summer are dry. Modelling suggests Emblehope’s rewetted peat could store an additional 100,000 cubic metres of water, equivalent to about 40 Olympic swimming pools. “It’s going to be a massive exercise to identify the exits of water from the land,” said Macdonald. In the future, they will call on beavers to help hold back more water. There are promising patches of birch and willow growing beside one stream – beaver food – but Macdonald has witnessed beavers making dams out of heather on even more treeless moors in Norway and is confident they will thrive. Before that, there is a more urgent task for the ponies that are to be introduced on to the site. The cattle- and sheep-grazing on the estate’s moorland was reduced by the previous owners on the advice of conservationists but Macdonald is alarmed by dry “thatch” beneath the thick tussocks of moorland grass. “It’s quite dangerous from a fire point of view,” he said. His priority is to get Exmoor ponies on to the site, because they will eat down the grassy thatch and reduce the fire risk. Opening up the site to more diverse grazing animals will reduce aggressive grass species and increase the diversity of the sward. The grass is also currently too thick and long for curlew chicks to survive and find food, and so other species will benefit from the grazing animals. Destined for the chop are dense sitka plantations, which harbour little life and raise predation to unnaturally high levels because goshawks lurk in them. On Emblehope, the removal of the trees will hit a few species, such as long-eared owls and crossbills. But these will remain in the wider landscape because there are huge tracts of plantation forestry across neighbouring Kielder. Restore plans to leave patches of a few older trees but admits the problem with retaining any sitka – and the problem with its Forestry England neighbours – are what Macdonald calls the “little shitkas”, the baby trees that pop up all over the wilding moors from wind-blown seed. The solution is to plant broadleaved screens around the edge of the site to stop wind-blown sitka seed. While Restore’s promotional videos have tantalised people with glimpses of lynx, Macdonald is wary of being seen to endorse moves to bring back the lost predator, which many rewilders view as an ideal solution to Britain’s overpopulation of wild deer. While a survey suggests 72% of local people are in favour of reintroducing lynx, many sheep farmers in the area are vehemently opposed to an animal that could make their working lives harder. “We have no funded plans for lynx, and we have no wish to be in the reintroduction party,” said Macdonald, although he conceded “the economic argument [in favour] is compelling”. Research to be published next year will quantify the potential tourism bonanza to Northumberland. Although there are proposals to release lynx into surrounding Kielder, one was blocked by Natural England and a second, the Wildlife Trusts-backed Missing Lynx project, is still consulting. Emblehope is unlikely to be a key habitat for the forest-dwelling animal. Despite Restore’s wilding manifesto, it is retaining the estate’s farmer and gamekeeper. “What surprises me is how surprised people are that we’ve retained staff who know so much about the land,” said Macdonald. “The farmer is a real student of the history of grazing here and he’s very open-minded. The gamekeeper has been looking after some of Britain’s highest densities of birds of prey. These guys work 18-hour days, they live and breathe the area.” Restore will fund the transformation of Emblehope via conventional income from forestry (removing the sitkas) and cattle, sheep and, in the future, education and carefully limited eco-tourism – as well as government environmental land management payments. But it expects most of its income to come from natural capital payments. These include carbon credits for the sequestration in restored blanket bog and “30x30 Restore units” whereby corporations pay for the restoration of 30-metre by 30-metre patches of habitat. Restore’s vision is that corporations pay not for biodiversity outcomes but for conservation action on the land which provides more wildlife. Macdonald said: “It’s perfectly natural for large corporates to sponsor big sporting events across the world. In nature, in England, this is a big event.”

title: Travellers to EU face renewed queues as border-check flexibility rules expire
summary: Sources indicate some members states will not enforce EES biometric controls after 6 September deadline
text: Travellers to the EU could face renewed border queues as flexibility measures for the bloc’s entry-exit system officially come to an end – although numerous sources have indicated that some member states will not enforce biometric checks. Airlines last week called on the European Commission to extend discretionary powers to pause EES controls when necessary until the end of 2026, with the deadline for “flexibility” passing on 6 September. Peak holiday season has not resulted in a repeat of the long queues seen at some European airports in early summer, which at worst led to numerous passengers missing flights. But the aviation and travel industry believes further chaos was averted only through relaxation of the rules demanding biometric information, including fingerprinting of non-EU-citizens. While Brussels has not extended the discretionary period, it appears that cross-Channel travellers to France will not face changes next week because of technical problems with the EES software commissioned by French authorities. The fingerprinting kiosks expensively procured by Eurotunnel, Port of Dover and Eurostar at London St Pancras are still not operational. Dover said it was not expecting any changes next week, with car drivers yet to be subject to EES checks. A Eurotunnel spokesperson said it was “awaiting confirmation from the French authorities on the timing of this next phase” but was “ready to implement full biometric checks as soon as formal clearance is granted”. A Eurostar spokesperson said: “The phased rollout of EES continues. EES enrolments will continue to be completed manually by border officers.” A senior airline source said that while they would be monitoring closely, they did not expect to see full enforcement at the busiest European airports. Border officials in main foreign tourist destinations, most notably Greece, appeared to have unofficially exempted UK passengers from EES checks to avoid queues. The source said they expected the practice to continue. Luke Petherbridge, the director of public affairs at the UK travel industry trade body Abta, said it was continuing to push the European Commission to allow discretionary suspension of border checks beyond September, “recognising that there is still some way to go until EES is fully and consistently operational across all participating countries”. The airlines trade body Iata has called for an official extension, saying last week that EES-related delays had resulted in people missing flights and connections. Thomas Reynaert, the head of external affairs at Iata, said: “These are real impacts being felt by passengers. It gives Europe a bad reputation. When systems fail, passengers lose the trust in the system and when people are late, airlines pay a high cost.” The European Commission declined to provide further comment. A spokesperson said early last week: “We are in close and constructive contact with those few member states where some adjustments are needed at certain border crossing points. “And during an additional period of operational adjustment that is needed at these few operational border crossing points, the commission stands ready to provide additional support to these member states.”

title: ‘Nobody will win’: Zelenskyy adviser warns of mutual destruction if war with Russia continues
summary: Serhii Beskrestnov says deadlock on frontline and increasing use of deep strikes is placing civilians and infrastructure at greater risk
text: Russia and Ukraine are locked in an escalating war of long-range strikes with a growing risk to civilians in which neither side can entirely prevail, according to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s defence technology adviser. Serhii Beskrestnov, widely known by his call sign, Flash, said he was worried about the prospects for Kyiv this winter, and suggested elderly people should be evacuated in case Russian bombing were to knock out the capital’s energy supply. However, the rapid wartime evolution also gave Ukraine the means to strike back, with plans to launch 1,000 drones a night to strike economic and military targets in Russia and halt its commercial air traffic, he said. “Now, this is a war of cities, a war of infrastructure,” Beskrestnov told the Guardian, describing a conflict that is essentially deadlocked on the frontline, with civilians at increasing risk hundreds of miles away. “In this war, nobody will win this game, because both countries, after the war, will have destroyed economics, infrastructures. So it’s stupid. We should stop this war. We proposed to Russia to stop this war, but Russia does not want to stop,” he said. Beskrestnov, 51, a radio specialist, was first appointed by the former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as a technology adviser in January, before being taken on directly in July, after the latter’s dismissal. The adviser, who survived a drone attack on his home in April, agreed that “attack had become more powerful than defence”, because both sides’ air defences could not keep up with the number of missiles and drones available. Russia could engage in a sustained bombing of electricity, water and heating systems in Kyiv this winter with the high-speed ballistic missiles it was producing at a rate of more than 100 a month, Beskrestnov said. Earlier this week, Vladimir Putin said Russia’s military had been “ordered to prepare and carry out mass strikes” on Ukraine’s energy facilities, showing no sign of halting the war. “For me, it’s horrible,” Beskrestnov said. “We are talking about 2 to 3 million people, and Russia understands it can create a disaster in Kyiv.” City authorities should think about evacuating civilians in advance, particularly elderly people, he added, while emphasising he was not making an official statement. Ukraine is desperately short of US Patriot air defence interceptors, the main weapon capable of halting ballistic missiles, and Beskrestnov said he was “not sure” that Zelenskyy could obtain enough from abroad to prevent a crisis. Last month, the president said he wanted to secure 300 Patriot interceptors for the winter. Beskrestnov predicted Ukraine would “attack Russia more and more with deep strikes”, continuing a campaign that has resulted in factories, warehouses and oil refineries being bombed. “We have a target from our president to increase the quantity of attacks to 1,000 a day,” he said, rising from its current level of about 300. Addressing Zelenskyy’s announcement this week that there would be a sustained attempt by Ukraine to halt civil aviation inside Russia with the drones, Beskrestnov said: “I think it’s very simple: it’s not necessary for us to attack an airport, it’s just enough for us to fly at the airport and the airport will be closed.” Russia has also made a series of advances that have boosted its attack potential, including its first suspected use of artificial intelligence. Ukrainian investigators concluded that a simple Molniya drone that killed a person near a Zaporizhzhia gas station in July was being guided not by radio but by AI. “I’m just afraid what happens in the future because I think it’s just a question of time before Russia installs this technology in a Shahed,” he said, referring to the country’s standard long-range drone. It could render Ukraine’s “huge jamming network” obsolete without any radio communication to jam. Beskrestnov said Ukraine was working on its own autonomous drones – “We have a prototype” – but that he believed Russia appeared to have more scale right now. Russia has also developed a new wave of drones and missiles powered by Chinese-made jet engines that can fly at more than 200mph (320km/h), faster than the first generation of cheap Shahed interceptors that Ukraine has developed. Moscow fired 2,500 jet-powered Shahed drones into Ukraine in August, up from 1,500 in July, and was planning to make “about 36,000 in 2027”, Beskrestnov said. It also planned to build another 30,000 of the slower piston-engine type next year. Jet-powered Shaheds are already being used to threaten Kyiv and other big cities for hours at a time, but they will be complemented by another 10,000 cheap Banderol cruise missiles during 2027, plus a further 10,000 Dan-T missiles, boosting Russia’s ability to bomb Ukraine’s infrastructure. Four to six Ukrainian companies were working on jet interceptors, Beskrestnov said, but they were “not ready for final production”, giving Moscow a window of advantage. The adviser would not give a timeframe for when the interceptors would be ready. At present, fighter jets take the lead in shooting down jet drones. Civilian casualties have been rising as long-range attacks increase. According to the UN, 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July (the last month for which figures are available), the highest since March 2022. Accurate figures for Russia are not readily available. Beskrestnov said the dismissal of Fedorov as defence minister after a clash with Zelenskyy was “a pity”, though the change in his own role meant the scope of his work had expanded beyond the armed forces to include the national guard and across government. His role, he said, was technical and advisory and he sought to avoid becoming embroiled in personality clashes. “Don’t mix me with politics. Politics always has a part of garbage, rubbish,” he said.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy links Russian strikes on Kyiv airports to US envoys’ visit
summary: Moscow attacked Kyiv and Boryspil international airports as US talks yielded no evident change in Russia’s war demands. What we know on day 1,656
text: Russian attacks on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports were “clearly” a reaction to the possibility of the US negotiators flying to Kyiv after talks in Moscow, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said. On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had “taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side.” Both airports service the Ukrainian capital. There was no comment from the US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and were ‌due to meet Zelenskyy in Kyiv ‌on Sunday. The Kremlin’s tone appeared unchanged. After three hours of talks, an aide to Vladimir Putin, Yuri Ushakov, said the Russian president had told the US pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield, was confident of achieving ⁠its goals, and stressed the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict”. Ushakov said the Americans had “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement”, but he did not say what those ideas were. The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250km (775-mile) frontline. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv. Kremlin spokesperson ‌Dmitry Peskov posted online that Putin had ordered the military not to strike Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight on Saturday. However, he said Russia had not yet agreed to a broader three-day ceasefire. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through to Monday. Russian attacks killed five employees and wounded five others at an industrial facility in the Dnipropetrovsk region, said the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha. “A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. People of peaceful professions. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives.” Russia’s defence ministry said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants that it claimed were sites for military production. A 62-year-old man was wounded, and several homes and an apartment building damaged, in a separate attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said. The city of Dnipro and the nearby Pidhorodne community were among the areas hit. One person died and five other were injured, including two men who were hospitalised in serious condition. A sixth civilian was injured in an attack on the Nikopol district. Other deadly Russian attacks took place in Chuhuiv in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region, on the Bucha district of Ukraine’s Kyiv region, and on a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region. In Russia’s Belrogod region on the border with Ukraine, two people were killed and three others wounded by Ukrainian attacks on Saturday, local authorities said. Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones, Ukraine’s air force said on Saturday.

title: Falling ceiling debris at Kennedy Center may mire debate over renovations
summary: Preservationists worry board may seize on incident ‘to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down’
text: Falling debris from a ceiling in the grand foyer of the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts may have complicated a battle over renovations of the Washington DC arts center that could result in the building being demolished. A portion of the ceiling collapsed on Friday evening after heavy rain swept through the area, prompting officials to temporarily close the Edward Durell Stone-designed building. No one was injured by the debris. Kennedy Center officials posted online on Saturday that the incident showed renovations to the building were urgently needed – an argument that Donald Trump has made in concert with a broader second-term agenda to reshape Washington. “Another warning we can’t ignore,” the Kennedy Center said in the post. “A section of the Grand Foyer ceiling collapsed after this week’s storms. Thankfully no one was hurt. Decades of deferred maintenance made this inevitable.” Roma Daravi, the center’s vice-president for public relations, said in a statement that the collapse was “another example of the urgent need to close for renovation and revitalization, as our Chairman President Trump has championed”. Hands Off the Arts, an activist group fighting Trump’s plans for the Kennedy Center, released a video on Sunday disputing the center’s claims. “The reality is President Trump and his loyalist board are happy today,” said Chris Raleigh, of Hands Off the Arts. “They are happy that their neglect has produced an exploitable image to advance their false claim that the Center needs to be remade in Trump’s image or turned into rubble like the East Wing.” Raleigh pointed out that the center has been under the Trump administration’s stewardship since February 2025, but no repairs have been done to the building since that time. Alongside the White House ballroom, a proposed triumphal arch, fitful renovations to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool and a remodeled golf course on the banks of the Potomac, the Kennedy Center has become a significant project for the president. The Trump-aligned board has proposed adding Trump’s name to the building’s facade and to close the center for two years as it undergoes $250m in renovations. Last month, a federal judge expressed doubts about the Kennedy Center’s stated intention to return Trump’s name to the building after a district court blocked the renovations and said Trump’s name had been added to the center illegally and ordered it to be removed. The board voted earlier this month to inscribe “The John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J Trump” on the facade by 8 September. If a fund for the renovations reaches $100m, another inscription would be added, reading: “Endowed by the Trump Kennedy Center Fund.” Congress has approved $257m for the project, and the Trump administration wants to raise an additional $500m through private donations. Administration attorneys have argued that without Trump’s name on the building it would struggle to raise money for renovations. Without the Trump-backed funding, they argue, the building “will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down, with a determination to follow on what to build on the site, such as a large outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac River that has been proposed, by some, for many years”. Last week a sculpture titled Blue by American post-minimalist Joel Shapiro was taken down. The Kennedy Center offered no reason for its removal, but said in a statement “we are honored to have been stewards” of the work. Friday’s debris shower may strengthen the center’s position that the building needs a complete overhaul. Grace Terpstra of Keep the KC, a group fighting the center’s closure, told the Associated Press that the board may seize on the incident “to make the point that the whole thing needs to be shut down, that it’s going to fall on everybody”. “I think they’ll try to make it into a bigger thing and show that they’ve found a lot of other things,” said Terpstra.

title: Trump’s pique with UK could lead to favor to acolyte Milei over Falklands
summary: US president suggests he might support his Argentinian ally’s drive to reclaim sovereignty of disputed islands
text: Donald Trump has long embraced vengeance. “I am your retribution,” he declared to an admiring audience at the 2023 Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) as he commenced his march back to the White House. It is unlikely Argentina, and far-flung holdovers of the former British empire, were on the US president’s mind at the time. But the tide of international events in the past three and a half years have turned Trump’s vindictive mindset to the advantage of Javier Milei, the boisterous rightwing Argentinian president. Trump’s notorious fixation with payback was almost entirely the trigger for Milei’s televised address to his fellow Argentinians on Thursday, as he stated his intention to reopen his country’s claim to a set of windswept islands in the south Atlantic – known to Britain as the Falklands, and to Argentina as the Malvinas. The centuries-old dispute over the islands’ sovereignty has lain dormant since 1982, when the two countries fought a brief, but bloody, conflict that began after Argentina’s ruling military dictatorship invaded the territory. Britain reclaimed it after troops in a naval taskforce dispatched by the then prime minister, Margaret Thatcher – ironically lionized by Milei as a political exemplar and inspiration – stormed the territory and eventually forced Argentina’s surrender. An uneasy peace has reigned in the generation since, although Argentina, which returned to democracy the year after the conflict, has never renounced its claim to the isles – despite the adamant insistence of their fewer than 2,000 inhabitants that they remain British. This week, however, Trump suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands. Why would the president go out on a limb to threaten this fragile peace? And why now? Milei jumped on Trump’s comment that he was “reviewing” the US’s longstanding neutral stance on the territory’s sovereignty, which amounts to a de facto recognition of Britain’s control. Fueling Trump’s animus is grievance that Britain, under former prime minister Keir Starmer, declined to support the US president’s decision to go to war on Iran, another irony given that country’s deep-rooted suspicions of Britain and its imperial past. The president’s obsession that allies declined to help him in a war he never consulted them on runs deep and wide – from Westminster to Seoul – and has the potential to upend US relationships around the globe, if unchecked. And Milei’s attempt to capitalize on Trump’s vengeance underlines the potential for ripple effects of this war to reach waters far beyond the Gulf. In what has become a repetitive refrain, Trump laid bare his sense of wounded affront in an interview with a rightwing British cable channel on Thursday. “Your country was not there to help me,” he told GB News. “We didn’t need help, but I did ask Nato, and I asked your former leader: ‘Why don’t you send a couple of ships?’ He said: ‘We don’t have any.’ It was pretty sad, the whole thing.” Milei’s opportunism could also be used by Trump as a bargaining chip – to lever more money from the cash-strapped UK treasury for defense spending and Nato contributions, after the new British chancellor of the exchequer, John Healey, recently suggested that it might not reach increased spending targets. It is a sorry pass for the “special relationship”, fostered through alliances in two worlds wars and deepened during the cold war and subsequent conflicts. Yet Britain is hardly alone in feeling the heat of a wrathful Trump. Vengeance has been targeted in recent months at numerous other allies, now regarded with more hostility by the White House than traditional adversaries such as Russia and China. Annual joint military exercises with South Korea – a vital ally of Washington since the Korean war broke out in 1950 – were suddenly scaled down and cut short by six days last month, on Trump’s orders, because of his irritation that the Seoul government declined to join the fight against Iran. He has repeatedly threatened to bomb or “blow up” the tiny Gulf kingdom of Oman, which has had friendly ties with the US for 200 years, if it impedes his efforts to reopen the strait of Hormuz, which Iran has closed to most commercial shipping. The White House also announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US troops from Germany after the country’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, rebuffed pressure to get involved in the Iran conflict and said Trump had been “humiliated” in the conflict. Threats of retribution have also been aimed at Spain, which has resisted pressure to boost defense spending, and Italy, whose prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, was a former Trump ally. Turbulence under Trump But Milei, a self-styled “anarcho-capitalist” who has paraded with a chainsaw to signify his attitude to public spending and attended Trump’s 2025 inauguration, remains on the US president’s good side. Last year, the administration extended his troubled government a $20bn loan guarantee to stabilize the infamously shaky Argentinian economy – but premised the money on Milei’s party defeating the leftist opposition in forthcoming congressional elections, which it duly did. This time there are no guarantees, other than that of never-ending turbulence at the hands of Trump. Such rough currents may be the “winds of change” Milei referenced in Thursday’s speech, delivered – Trump-style – with his cabinet members flanking him. But he may have been aware the phrase had other, historical connotations – evoking the words of a famous speech in 1960 by then British prime minister Harold Macmillan in Cape Town, heralding independence for Britain’s former colonial possession in Africa. “The wind of change is blowing through this continent,” Macmillan said then. “Whether we like it or not, this growth of national consciousness is a political fact.” In his address, Milei suggested the sun was setting on Britain, just as it once did on its empire, citing multiple crises of a migratory, demographic and economic nature that are unlikely to be resolved. “It is clear that they are on a path of decline,” he pronounced. He did not mention his own falling political popularity – a factor that may also have played a key role in the former military junta’s decision to seize the islands in 1982, as opposition grew against the backdrop of mass disappearances of political dissidents and multiple human rights abuses. Then, too, Britain was grappling with tensions over immigration and race riots, soaring unemployment and long-term economic decline that Thatcher had been elected pledging to reverse. In the late winter of 1982, there was little sign that she was capable of doing so – until the Falklands conflict sparked a sudden upturn in her political fortunes. But she had the solid backing of the special relationship, and her ideological soulmate, Ronald Reagan, in the White House. Andy Burnham, Britain’s newly installed Labour prime minister, must contend with the chill wind emanating from the menacing and destabilizing presence of Trump.

title: London Paddington fire causes rail chaos as Heathrow trains cancelled
summary: Blaze causes electricity supply failure and disruption of services to airport and Reading
text: Hundreds of passengers were evacuated from a train, and services to Heathrow airport were cancelled, after a fire near tracks in the London Paddington area caused major disruptions to London’s rail network. The fire caused an electricity supply failure which left all lines between Paddington and the airport blocked, National Rail said on Saturday afternoon. Photographs on social media showed large plumes of smoke rising from the Paddington area. London fire brigade was called to the grass fire near Scrubs Lane, North Kensington, just after 4pm on Saturday, with six fire engines and 40 crew tackling the blaze. Fire crews were also called upon to help evacuate 380 passengers left stranded on an Elizabeth line train. The Elizabeth line was suspended between Paddington and Heathrow Terminals 4 and 5, and between Paddington and Reading, while the line to Abbey Wood also experienced severe delays. Passengers travelling to the airport were advised to use the Piccadilly line, although that line also experienced severe delays between Heathrow and Acton Town. There were minor delays along the rest of the line due to an earlier trespasser at Hammersmith, Transport for London (TfL) said. Heathrow airport advised passengers to leave extra time for their journeys. Great Western Railway (GWR) services to Reading were cancelled, and disruptions were expected until the end of Saturday.

title: More voters identifying as Democrats and not calling themselves Republican
summary: Latest data from Gallup, showing 49% leaning Democrat and 39% Republican, marks sharp reversal from 2024
text: More voters are identifying as Democrats and shying away from calling themselves Republican, according to the latest quarterly data published by Gallup. Some 49% of voters surveyed leaned Democrat, including independent voters asked to pick one party or the other. Only 39% of respondents leaned Republican. That 10-point spread marks a sharp reversal from the four-point advantage that Republicans held over Democrats in the fourth quarter of 2024, when voters sent Donald Trump back to the White House and Republicans swept both houses of Congress. Democrats are seeing their most sizable advantage since 2008, when Barack Obama was elected president, according to the New York Times. The data offers the latest evidence that Trump’s second term has proved unpopular with voters, driving a potential backlash. Trump’s approval rating stood at 52% at the time of his second inauguration in January of 2025, according to an average of polls published by the New York Times. But his popularity dwindled immediately, as he cleaved the federal workforce, imposed price-inflating tariffs, passed a profligate spending bill and launched a rudderless war with Iran. Some 58% of voters now disapprove of his performance, with only 38% approving, according to the Times. Democrats are hoping to take advantage of Trump’s tanking popularity. Liberals are likely to retake the US House of Representatives in midterm elections this November. The party is much less certain to retake the US Senate, though polling is giving Democrats reasons to feel optimistic. A growing share of American voters have not identified with either party in recent years. Back in 2002, roughly a third of voters surveyed by Gallup identified as either Republican, Democrat or independent. By last year, 45% of respondents called themselves independents, with only 27% identifying as either Democrat or Republican.

title: Thousands of jobs to be cut at Jaguar Land Rover after slump in profits
summary: As many as 4,000 positions could go over two years after cyber-attack and US tariffs take toll
text: Thousands of workers at Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) will be offered redundancies after Britain’s largest car manufacturer had its revenues slashed by falling sales, a cyber-attack and Donald Trump’s tariffs. JLR informed workers and their union on Saturday that the company would be opening a voluntary redundancy programme for salaried and management team members, the BBC and Sunday Times reported. As many as 4,000 jobs would be cut over two years, the Times reported. JLR told the BBC it was yet to confirm the number but the company, which is owned by the Indian conglomerate Tata Motors, needed to save about £1.7bn over the next two years. Unite’s general secretary, Sharon Graham, told the BBC she and the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, would meet JLR’s chief executive, PB Balaji, next week, after a weekend of intensive talks to mitigate job losses. About 30,000 of the company’s 44,000 employees are based in the UK. Most of them work at 14 plants across the West Midlands, where the company is one of the region’s largest employers. The job cuts will be unwelcome news for the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who has pledged to “safeguard sovereign manufacturing” and reindustrialise Britain. Under his predecessor, Keir Starmer, Labour said it would underwrite a £1.5bn loan guarantee to JLR after it halted production for several weeks last year in response to a cyber-attack. The attack led to a 27% drop in overall production and cost the company about £200m. It was one of several factors contributing to JLR posting a profit before tax of just £14m – down from £2.5bn the year before. Tariffs on vehicles imported into the US – which Trump raised to 25% before agreeing a deal for 10% for the UK – also caused turmoil for the carmaker, which is attempting to push more luxury cars to the US market. This contributed to the company’s retail and wholesale volumes – sales via dealerships – falling by about 70,000 and 90,000 respectively. “These challenges arrived with the global automotive industry already under continued pressure from cost inflation, slower-than-expected uptake of electric vehicles, and the deterioration of market conditions in China,” Balaji said in the company’s annual report published in May. The carmaker this week launched its first electric Range Rover in an effort to appeal to climate-conscious fans of the luxury SUV – at a starting price of £154,070.

title: Possums in the roof, koalas in bed: study shows how animals resort to Australian homes after habitat loss
summary: Microbats and wombats among the most common species found in buildings, with some discovered in letterboxes or air conditioning systems
text: Possums in the roof, bats in the curtains and ducks on the balcony: new research has revealed how native animals are making themselves at home in our houses. Researchers have analysed a decade of wildlife rescue reports and found brushtail and ringtail possums make up half of all cases of animals in buildings, followed by microbats and bare-nosed wombats. The study in People and Nature included 2,400 cases of animals using buildings as habitat. Most were found in roof spaces, walls, garages and under the house, although some preferred more unusual locations such as letterboxes or air conditioning systems. About 10% were found in indoor rooms such as bedrooms and kitchens. Bethany Kiss, a University of Melbourne architect and the lead author of the study, said animals were seeking out buildings as substitute habitats as their natural homes and hollows disappeared. “We found native wildlife using almost every part of the house imaginable,” Kiss said. “People often think these are unusual incidents, but they’re actually very common.” Wildlife Victoria, which provided the data for the study, said one recent caller to its emergency response service discovered juvenile sugar gliders in her kitchen. “She had reached under the sink for a dishwashing tablet and instead her hand landed on something furry,” said Aleisha Hall, a spokesperson for the rescue organisation. Investigating further, they found two gliders curled up together in a small jar. When a volunteer was dispatched to collect the gliders, they found five more. In another recent case, an echidna found its way into a house and headed straight for the pantry. “The homeowner found him pulling items off the shelves, including a heavy food processor,” Hall said. Luckily, the homeowner was also a wildlife rescuer and was able to safely return it back outside. Microbats often featured in calls to Wildlife Victoria’s hotline. Recently, while renovating, a homeowner found eight little forest bats roosting in a wall. Ericka Tudhope, a rehabilitation specialist from Microbats of Melbourne, said bats living in the roof was common and nothing to be concerned about – so long as people left them alone and didn’t touch them. “They make great housemates by keeping bug numbers down and rarely do any damage to the house. They don’t chew cables or wires,” she said. In New South Wales, the Wires rescue service said animals often sought shelter during cold or extreme weather. Last year a member of the public rang when a koala scampered down her hallway. By the time the rescue volunteer arrived, the animal was sitting calmly on her bed. While such cohabiting in Australian houses was mostly accidental, in the United Kingdom buildings were being intentionally designed for habitat, Kiss said, such as the requirement to include “swift nesting bricks” in new builds. “We’re in a biodiversity crisis and a housing crisis,” she said. While architecture often focused on ways to keep nature out, there were opportunities to design buildings that were better for both people and wildlife. That could include wildlife-friendly lighting and noise reduction measures, as well as habitat features, such as swallow shelves or possum boxes. “One of the things that I would really like to see in Australia, is that we think about embedding the ecologist in the design process like you would with, say, an engineer,” Kiss said. Prof Sarah Bekessy, a co-author of the paper and Biodiversity Council lead councillor, said research consistently showed that people benefited from everyday interactions with wildlife. “Wildlife in our neighbourhoods can improve our mental wellbeing, strengthen people’s connection with nature and make cities healthier, more resilient places to live,” she said. Wildlife Victoria said it advocated for peaceful coexistence where possible, but anyone concerned about an animal in their home was encouraged to contact their local wildlife rescue.

title: Black-clad protesters in balaclavas block road at port of Dover in Kent
summary: Port authorities say access roads ‘free flowing’ again after large group forces road closures in both directions
text: Dozens of people dressed in black and wearing balaclavas blocked the road at the port of Dover in Kent, forcing closures in both directions on Saturday morning. Kent police said they were were in attendance and engaging with the protest, which the Port of Dover described as a “public order incident”. No arrests were made during the incident. Responsibility for the demonstration appears to have been claimed by an anti-immigration group with links to the far right. The behaviour of the participants and the travel disruption they have caused has been condemned by the government. Traffic in and out of the port on the A20 was stopped, causing delays of up to 30 minutes and four miles of congestion, according to National Highways. Videos shared online showed a large number of masked people in black marching on the road in a large group as lorries waited in traffic next to police cars. By lunchtime, the protesters had dispersed and access roads to the port were “free flowing”, according to the Port of Dover. Ferry operators pledged to put those who had been delayed by the disruption on to the next available sailings. The number of people involved was not immediately clear. One livestreamer estimated he was marching with hundreds of people but police did not give an official estimate. Social media videos showed demonstrators linking arms in a blockade across the A20 and chanting “stop the boats”and “England till I die.” A group called Patriot Platform, which styles itself as having “a fierce love for our homeland”, claimed responsibility for the blockade. The far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, reposted videos of the blockade, highlighting a live stream of the protest that directed viewers towards Patriot Platform. In his post, Robinson encouraged more to join, saying: “Get there to support them.” In another post, he wrote: “Simultaneously at different locations across Dover patriots have mobilised to close down the port. There are 3 plus locations that patriots have shut down so far with many more planned to be closed. People wanted action I’m guessing there are 100,000s of men willing to fill their shoes.” The founder of Patriot Platform, Danny Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, wrote on social media “live Dover somethings [sic] happening” and posted a live stream. In a video posted on 2 September, he told his followers he was meeting with “a huge group [of] top, proper patriots” to prepare for a message he was planning to send to the government. “Very, very soon, we are going to send a message that will make sure they understand that we will not go down without a fight. We will not allow our nation to be plagued in the way that it is. “And when you see it and when you feel it, I guarantee the whole thing will change for the better. Because once the message is sent once, imagine the sheer numbers that will be sent on the second, the third, the fourth message.” In further comments, he said: “From the hills of Scotland to the fields of Wales to the streets of Northern Ireland and to the towns and cities of England, we are building something that’s never been built before. “And when you’re part of it and you see what’s about to go down, you will understand … we’re about to show you what can be done when men and women of this country, who have the blood that runs through them like their grandfathers, get off their asses and do something about it.” On Saturday morning, the Port of Dover confirmed in a statement that the disruption was affecting “all routes” in and out, as well as around the town. Nathan Ditchburn, who was on his way to work when he saw the group arrive at about 6.45am, told KentOnline: “I would say there are around 300 men, maybe more. Nobody will speak; they just handed me a piece of paper to look at. They have blocked off every entrance and exit of the Dover port area.” One woman, who asked to remain anonymous, said: “I was at Dover port this morning, trying to get on a ferry to France. In the end we left and returned home – it wasn’t worth our while, we were only going to Lille for the day. “But the headlines calling it a ‘protest’ suggest something very different to what took place – which looked like a highly organised event. “Masked teenagers in black clothes were coordinated by walkie-talkie and I directly witnessed an older man, not in black, on an electric bike – coordinating in plain sight and being applauded by the masked teenagers as he gave them the thumbs up for their ‘good work’. “The guy on the bike then went to the nearest police stop, [he was] obviously monitoring and reporting police activity. “There were no banners and no slogans, just pure intimidation. It was a demonstration only in the sense that they wanted to demonstrate their power and to intimidate.” Mike Tapp, the Labour MP for Dover and Deal, criticised what he described as “idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption”. In a post on Facebook, he said: “Parkrun cancelled and port access disrupted. I am fed up with idiots coming to Dover to cause disruption. “I bet if you asked any one of those ‘protesters’ they wouldn’t know small boat crossings are down by 40% and we are working hard to fix the mess. Go home, enjoy your weekend/get a job.” Chris Vinson, the leader of the Conservative group on Dover district council, said the protest appeared to be “illegal migration-related”, but said the demonstrators did not appear to have placards or banners. “I’m not aware that there’s been any violence, although clearly, having the path of your vehicle blocked by men wearing black paramilitary gear and balaclavas is extremely intimidating, especially when it’s not clear why they’re there, and the police weren’t aware and so haven’t been able to warn people in advance and make sure that they are made to feel safe.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behaviour in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused. “We appreciate the frustration of those who have been impacted today. Access to the port is now restored and traffic is flowing. Those travelling to the port are advised to allow for extra travel time and to follow guidance from providers.” The shipping company DFDS and P&O Ferries said they would offer customers whose journeys were disrupted access to the next available departure.

title: Police seize £200k Lamborghini under tightened antisocial driving laws
summary: Officers seize supercar in Southend after reports of it being driven at up to twice speed limit
text: Police have seized a Lamborghini potentially worth more than £200,000 under tightened laws introduced to crack down on dangerous driving. Essex police confiscated the Lamborghini Huracan on Saturday afternoon after receiving reports of the supercar being driven dangerously in Southend. The car was travelling at speeds suspected to be more than twice the limit, police said. “Antisocial driving can pose a danger to other people using the road and cause misery to residents,” a force spokesperson said. “The safety of our communities will always be our priority and we’ll take action against those who risk the safety of others.” The online marketplace Autotrader estimates the total retail value of the Lamborghini Huracan at £238,195, depending on the model. The vehicle was seized under section 59 of the Police Reform Act, which was strengthened earlier this year to allow police to immediately confiscate a vehicle causing – or likely to cause – alarm, distress or annoyance to the public. Previously, drivers received a warning under which their vehicle could only be seized if they were involved in another antisocial driving incident within 12 months. Officers can still choose to give a warning at their discretion. The law allows officers to stop and seize vehicles, or enter premises where they believe the vehicle is being held – and “use reasonable force where necessary”. Wheelspins and burnouts, drifting in public places, racing in residential areas and repeated revving “causing nuisance” were all reasons for which vehicles could be seized, the Essex police spokesperson said. The Metropolitan police last year seized 72 luxury cars worth more than £6m in a crackdown on antisocial driving in London. The vehicles – which included Ferraris, Lamborghinis and Bentleys – were either unroadworthy or being driven illegally, the Met said. Last month, a police officer drove a Ferrari Monza SP2 worth £3.7m after the open-top limited-edition supercar was seized in a separate, record-breaking crackdown.
