title: ‘I wasn’t even listening,’ Farage says of donations scandal meeting
summary: Reform UK leader maintains innocence in overseas funding controversy on last day of party conference
text: Nigel Farage has claimed that he “wasn’t even listening” during a meeting at the centre of a controversy about whether his party considered evading the law on accepting donations from overseas. The Reform UK leader also claimed he knew donation law “better than anybody” during interviews as he sought to salvage the final day of his party conference from the fallout that has already cost him two of his closest aides. Farage was forced to suspend his close aide Dan Jukes and Reform’s head of policy, James Orr, on Friday after they were filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations. The undercover reporters from a group called Verbatim posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers. The Reform leader himself remains under pressure over a separate clip in which he was heard saying “it’s all above board” after one of the reporters who was posing as the UK-based son of a wealthy US backer told Farage he had been in discussions with Jukes and Orr for some time. “I’ll be the registered donor,” the son says. “But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that’s done and all those conversations are had the money is available.” In an interview on Saturday, Farage told the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg that “of course” he knew it was illegal for foreign firms to donate to UK parties, adding he was told the money was being given via a UK family office. When challenged by Kuenssberg that while in Farage’s presence, one of the undercover reporters had said they “run an American family office”, the Reform leader said: “I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton byelection. I turn up. I frankly wasn’t even listening.” He added: “I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore. The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have come from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.” Farage’s party had been hoping to move the focus to policy announcements, including on tax cuts, as Reform’s conference closed in Birmingham on Saturday. Its Treasury spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, gave a keynote speech in which he pledged to increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 within the first 100 days if the party were to take office. The threshold has been set at £12,570 since 2021 and is due to remain there until 2031. But in interviews given earlier in the day to trail the policy, he also found himself forced to deflect from the donations controversy. “That’s been dealt with,” he told GB News. “The two individuals concerned have gone, and we’re here today moving forward. The language that they used was clearly inappropriate, that was very disappointing.” In an interview with Times Radio he said Orr and Jukes had been “permanently suspended”, appearing to differ from the latest party line that they had “stepped down pending outcome of an investigation”, indicating a possible way back. Farage meanwhile accused “the establishment” of trying to derail Reform UK, when challenged by ITV’s Robert Peston on the string of allegations related to his and the party’s finances. “And it will go on. You come back and see me in six months, there’ll be five more investigations. It won’t end. This won’t end,” he said. Farage said he had some “thoughtful” moments over the summer, claiming his family had been asking him to “walk away” from politics amid pressure on them and him. Despite Reform’s efforts to insulate Farage, the Met police are now assessing evidence after a complaint that the Reform leader, as well as Orr and Jukes, may have broken political funding laws. They all deny wrongdoing. The final day of the conference also coincided with an appeal by West Midlands police for a woman, who was among climate activists who were removed from the hall on Friday as they heckled Farage’s speech, to come forward after footage emerged over her allegedly being assaulted. The police initially responded on X to a clip that appeared to show audience members pulling her hair and grabbing her head as she was carried out of the conference hall. West Midlands police later said in a statement that they were aware of a video circulating from the Reform UK conference showing an incident with a protester, and had asked the woman to come forward. The activist group Climate Resistance, which claimed responsibility for the protest during Farage’s speech , said the protester was considering whether to speak to police. Nadine Dorries, a former Conservative MP who has joined Reform, said sensitivities were “heightened” in the aftermath of the killing of the Reform spokesperson Ann Widdecombe in July. “They tried to completely derail the speech. It was an organised sting again,” she said in an interview with LBC when asked about the incident. Also speaking on Saturday was Suella Braverman, the party’s education spokesperson who, like Jenrick, is another defector from the Conservatives. Her speech announced a planned cut of 20% to the number of student loans given, with funds only granted to university courses that can demonstrate good economic returns, with exceptions for some courses “of strategic or cultural importance”. Farage ended the conference with closing comments to the main hall, where sections of seating were unoccupied and the mood was more subdued than earlier in the event, by telling the Reform faithful that “there would be good days and bad days”. “Sometimes we will get things wrong and get a bit of a kicking, but what this conference has shown is that whatever you throw at the leadership, whatever you throw at you, the people’s army, we immediately stop, pick ourselves up and start all over again,” he said.

title: US military says it struck three Iranian tankers after American warships came under missile attack
summary: Officials said US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided attacks before three Iranian tankers were struck by the US
text: The US military said Saturday it struck three Iranian oil tankers after US navy warships came under missile attack, further escalating tensions in the region and warning it would “if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet”. According to the military, a US aircraft carrier and destroyer avoided “multiple unprovoked Iranian attacks” while patrolling the region. No US personnel were injured. Two of the Iranian oil carriers were “permanently disabled”, the Pentagon said, while a third tanker, which was unladen, was destroyed. The US said the vessels were part of a shadow network that helped finance Iran’s powerful Revolutionary Guards and armed proxy groups operating across the region. “We will not hesitate to defend American forces, and if necessary, destroy Iran’s limited and exposed oil fleet,” the head of US Central Command, Adm Brad Cooper, said in the statement. The announcement followed an earlier report from Iran that the US had attacked an Iranian tanker near Kharg Island in the Gulf. Tasnim, a semiofficial news outlet affiliated with Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, reported the strike happened on Saturday morning. It said the tanker’s crew survived and was being evacuated. The US said one tanker was struck off Kharg Island, while another was hit near Jask. The unladen tanker was struck in the Gulf of Oman. The US statement also shared what it described as video footage of the strikes. Iran’s state broadcaster said later Sunday that Iran targeted three oil tankers and three American vessels in response to the US strikes. This could not be immediately confirmed. The latest attacks came nearly a week after the US and Iran resumed strikes after about a month of relative calm in the on-again, off-again war that began with US and Israeli attacks in February. Attempts at negotiations have collapsed. One of the strikes hit a wedding in southern Iran on Tuesday, killing four people, including a child, and injuring dozens, according to Iranian officials. The US vice-president, JD Vance, said “sometimes things happen” when asked on Thursday whether an US strike was responsible for killing people at the wedding celebration. The renewed strikes have also brought fresh scrutiny to a 28 February US attack in Minab that struck a school compound and killed at least 156 people, most of them schoolchildren. A preliminary US military inquiry reportedly found that the attack resulted from a targeting error after outdated coordinates identified the school as part of a nearby Revolutionary Guards naval base. The Pentagon said at the time that it was investigating. A full report has not been made public. Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Judge orders Trump administration to reveal who set up $1.8bn ‘anti-weaponization fund’
summary: Judge issues order as part of discovery process in lawsuit brought by non-profit into now defunct compensation fund
text: A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to reveal who set up the structure of a controversial $1.8bn “anti-weaponization fund” to recompense victims of so-called political lawfare that was reportedly dropped by the justice department last month. Ivan Davis, the US magistrate judge for the eastern district of Virginia, issued the order compelling discovery materials from the government as part of a lawsuit brought by the Democracy Forward non-profit on behalf of plaintiffs including a fired prosecutor and a college professor acquitted of assaulting federal agents at a protest against an immigration raid in California. “Today’s order granting discovery is a significant step in getting to the bottom of the slush fund,” said Aman George, senior counsel at the non-profit. “We will continue to meet the government in court until our investigation is complete and the slush fund is permanently halted.” Last month, Todd Blanche said the fund he proposed before he was confirmed “is dead”. The US attorney general told Fox News Sunday: “The fund is dead or whatever word you want to use. It never started. So, it’s not as if the fund is coming back.” Democrats maintain that the proposed fund would have been used to compensate prosecuted and since-pardoned January 6 rioters, among others. Blanche said that Trump “believes the justice department was weaponized against a lot of Americans” under the Biden administration, adding: “It really hurt them financially.” The proposed compensation scheme was set up as part of the settlement Trump reached with the IRS regarding a lawsuit over the leak of his tax returns. The agreement shielded the president and his family from future tax audits. In July, another federal judge found that the parties had never truly been in conflict and Trump’s $10bn lawsuit against the IRS had only ever been a pretense for setting up the fund. “There was never adverseness between the parties; there was never a case or controversy; and there was never a question as to who would prevail,” the US district judge Kathleen Williams said in a ruling, adding that the lawsuit had been brought “for an improper purpose – to gain the imprimatur of judicial legitimacy for a ‘settlement’ that had no viable basis in law or fact”. The proposed fund drew bipartisan criticism in Washington, including opposition from two Republican senators, John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and it put Blanche’s confirmation for attorney general at risk. Critics of the program have noted that the document demanded by lawmakers did not include signatories to the initial agreement, suggesting that it could be revived. Blanche has said that “there were never commissioners” in charge of the “payout pot”. But Senate Democrat Cory Booker said the agreement guaranteed “nothing … no guarantees whatsoever that this slush fund still can’t go forward”. Trump has rued the abandonment of the fund and has not ruled out another avenue to compensation. “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t,” he said of the fund at a cabinet meeting in July. “To be honest with you, I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused.”

title: Catastrophic dangers await Burnham’s push for English devolution | Phillip Inman
summary: Like France, the UK has always been centralised – and imposing a new political structure brings huge risks
text: Devolution in England is going to be messy and slow, and brings with it huge risks that Andy Burnham ignores at his peril. The prime minister’s devolution push will be messy because Whitehall’s ingrained anxiety about handing over money and power will lead to piecemeal deals, starting with a deal for Cornwall that will lack the much-promised driving force of a newly minted mayor. And there is every prospect that it will be slow now that the reappointed housing secretary Angela Rayner’s reorganisation of local government, creating hundreds of unitary authorities where counties and districts once ruled, is mired in judicial reviews. Some councils have run up huge debts in the last decade and it’s not clear how these debts will be divided among the new entities. There are claims that plans to divide some existing county councils into three, four or even five unitary authorities is politically motivated and that Labour has become seduced by the prospect of retaining a presence in local government through gerrymandering. Last week, Hertfordshire county council and Newcastle-under-Lyme borough council became the latest local authorities to send letters to Rayner, seeking clarity on how the government reached its decision in their areas. A week earlier, Lincolnshire county council did the same. Farther south, Essex county, which is to be divided into five unitary authorities, found that the recommendation of Whitehall officials for just three new authorities was overruled by Rayner. Supposedly, all this infighting will be resolved by Christmas and England will be ready for an entirely new map of local authorities by next May when fresh elections will be held. Surely these councils and combined authorities, many of which are also embryonic, will struggle to become public institutions with verve, drive, knowledge and experience, able to make good decisions in time for the next election in 2029. When devolution is the prime minister’s big idea, one that will energise Britain’s spirit of enterprise, how it works is going to be crucial. He cannot risk Reform UK and the Tories crowing about another broken promise; or how it shows the British state is clogged with officials waiting for their generous pension, and in need of a Trumpian deep clean. Rayner’s plan is rooted in a belief that local government has failed to work properly and that structural reform is the answer, saving much more over the longer term than the estimated £2bn initial cost. It is a belief that has no basis in academic study. It would be a relief to all of those involved in local government and devolution to know that somewhere in the world there was data illustrating how this kind of structural change improves services, saves money and, as Burnham would have it, supercharges economic growth. Unfortunately there isn’t any such evidence. It is, to use a well-worn cliche, just re-arranging deckchairs. And it is not just because the same people will be taking up the same roles in new offices (and yes, there will need to be five head offices instead of one in Essex). As the Institute for Government says: “Structural reforms can be necessary, and useful. But there is nothing inherently valuable about them.” What improves services are reforms to the way public officials work, and that means difficult discussions with trade unions. There needs to be a level of accountability that is absent in significant areas of the public sector. And it will be crucial to change how public organisations relate to each other, how they work together, breaking down old silos and protective practices. It involves giving more information to local people and including them in decision making going forward. Geoff Mulgan, a University College London professor and the former boss of the Nesta thinktank, says devolution must answer basic questions people should know, such as how private and public services are delivered and who determines the outcome, from broadband to banking. “Otherwise it will remain entirely legitimate for populist politicians to say that people have lost control and to claim that they are the answer,” he says. In most countries where devolution works well, the establishment of local structures was organic, not imposed. Germany grew out of mini-kingdoms. The US started as a collection of states. The Länder in Germany, and US states, agreed to a federal government while retaining a good deal of power for themselves. The UK is more like France. It has always been centralised, and gained in many ways from that and lost out in others. So we should not underestimate how difficult it will be to impose a new political structure on England that devolves money and power to brand new councils and mayors, or in the case of Cornwall, a cabinet committee. The public will rightly be sceptical when so many councils under the current system have fallen for the idea that they can raise themselves up if only they borrow lots of money and “invest it” in new stuff. A new high street with hotels and leisure facilities was Woking borough council’s dream until it crashed, £2bn in debt. To say there are huge dangers in the world of finance when local council leaders are let loose, armed with a mission to generate growth, is to understate the situation. There are catastrophic dangers waiting.

title: Raise the Colours leader given access to Reform UK conference while on bail
summary: Ryan Bridge, arrested this year on suspicion of religiously and racially aggravated harassment, says party invited him
text: The leader of a flag campaign group who was arrested on suspicion of causing religiously and racially aggravated harassment was given access to Reform UK’s annual conference. Ryan Bridge, whose Raise the Colours group has put up hundreds of union and St George flags across England, told the Guardian he was invited to the conference. Raise the Colours has argued the campaign displays flags as a sign of patriotism, but it has been accused of using them to spread anti-immigrant sentiment. Bridge’s attendance at the event comes as Reform UK has been attempting to attract more wavering centre-ground voters who have been reluctant to support the party. But a threat from its hard-right rival Restore Britain has given the party reason to pull rightwards. At a conference event on Saturday, Nigel Farage paid tribute to the flag campaign and told Bridge personally that Reform UK would offer legal support. “What your campaign has done is wake up vast parts of this country,” Farage told Bridge from a stage inside the conference after the activist was among three people selected to ask questions of the Reform leader during a discussion hosted by Jeremy Kyle. “If we can help you legally, we will,” said Farage, after Bridge told him he had an injunction against him putting up flags in Oxfordshire and was also facing one from Birmingham city council. Bridge was among 10 activists who were banned from France this year after they travelled there to take part in actions intended to stop migrant boats embarking across the Channel. He is also named along with six other people in action pursued by Birmingham city council as it seeks a high court injunction to stop activists from Raise the Colours putting flags up. The first hearing of that application will be on Tuesday. Bridge has been on bail since Thames Valley police confirmed earlier this year that a 44-year-old male from Bromsgrove, Worcestershire, was arrested after reports of incidents of public order offences on Abingdon Road, Oxford. The force said he was arrested “on suspicion of causing racially and religiously aggravated harassment, alarm or distress” and that he had been released on police bail. Bridge denies all wrongdoing. He is also facing a trial in East Sussex. He entered a not guilty plea at Brighton magistrates court last month after being charged with common assault in relation to an incident in the city in June and was granted bail. Bridge told the Guardian at the Reform conference on the outskirts of Birmingham on Friday: “We have come to the event today in light of it’s in my home city of Birmingham and with what’s going on with Raise the Colours … what we are doing.” “We got an invite, so we thought we would come along,” he added, saying he was not a member of Reform. There are no general admission tickets to the Reform conference for members of the public. Conference attenders are almost entirely members, with the addition of some lobbyists, people with business interests, diplomatic representatives and members of the press. Commercial passes can be bought for £650 and “platinum” tickets can cost thousands. Asked if his arrests posed a problem with him being at the event, Bridge said: “Being accused of a criminal act of raising a flag of your country in your country, I think is lesser than the actual criminal act that is going on on a daily basis from the far-left ultra NGOs.” Reform UK did not respond when contacted about Bridge being at its conference. His attendance was criticised by the anti-fascist campaign group Hope Not Hate, which said: “That someone as extreme as Ryan Bridge was inside the Reform conference with a pass is genuinely shocking.”

title: ‘The chancellor is in a bind’: is No 11 at odds with Burnham’s big vision?
summary: MPs applaud PM’s ambition and optimism but John Healey has yet to show he can match leader’s radical perspective
text: Until now, Andy Burnham has been a lucky prime minister. In office for just over six weeks, no major domestic crisis derailed his plans over the summer, Reform has been on the back foot, and he arrived back at Westminster with his personal approval ratings soaring and optimism undampened. But underneath the sense of relief that many Labour MPs are feeling that their high-stakes gamble of ousting Keir Starmer appears – for now – to have paid off, there is an unease that Burnham’s premiership is yet to make contact with economic reality. In their early weeks in office, his team were able to point to some inherited green shoots: below-forecast inflation figures, sustained growth, signs that sluggish productivity could be starting to turn around. All despite the economic turmoil unleashed by the Iran conflict. This week, all that changed. With the end of summer recess came a global bond sell-off amid anxiety over oil prices, sticky inflation and pressure to ramp up defence spending, which pushed government borrowing costs to their highest since the 2008 financial crash. It makes the backdrop to John Healey’s first budget as chancellor a difficult one. Economists reckon about half of the £24bn fiscal breathing space his predecessor Rachel Reeves had built up at her spring forecast has since been wiped out by higher inflation and interest rates, severely limiting Healey’s room for manoeuvre. Among the more experienced hands in government, there is a firm view that the new administration cannot return to the days of slim headroom given Reeves’s experience last year, which led to more brutal proposed welfare cuts and ultimately a backbench rebellion last summer. Healey has just returned from the G20 finance ministers’ meeting in North Carolina and is acutely conscious of factors beyond his control that will hit the Office for Budget Responsibility’s forecasts, including the rising cost of oil after bombing resumed in Iran. It is little surprise, then, that he has repeatedly stressed that fiscal responsibility is the “bedrock” of his approach and he will stick to Reeves’s fiscal rules. But his cautious tone jars uncomfortably with the prime minister’s large – and costly – policy vision: more public control of utilities, reform of the broken social care system and a mass social home building programme. “[Healey] is in a bind,” one Treasury source said. “His instinct is to keep things steady, especially while the OBR does its snapshot, but that’s not Andy’s gameplan for his first week back.” Indeed, Downing Street has been eager to ensure Burnham’s vision stays front and centre. In a mammoth three-and-a-half-hour Commons session on Tuesday, he repeatedly promised to deliver the “much more substantial change” the country was crying out for. Among Burnham’s closest allies, there have been some mutterings that Healey could, like chancellors before him, be in danger of being “captured” by the Treasury and its more orthodox arguments. “John did not exactly show in the Ministry of Defence that he was good at questioning internal departmental wisdom and pressures,” one government aide said. The friction between the two operations burst into the open last week when Healey suggested in a television interview that Burnham was running a “continuity” government. No 10 insiders pushed back hard. “Nobody listening to Andy and his plans for growth could think he is just about continuity,” said one senior figure. “He’s going to change things.” A timely report that suggests Manchester’s economic success – one of Burnham’s biggest legacies – could be replicated across England to unlock untapped growth potential of up to £80bn is released this weekend. Mandala Partners, a global economic research consultancy that was led by Nick Williams – a former Downing Street economic adviser who is now working for the first secretary, Louise Haigh – found that housing, transport and health devolution would be crucial to achieving the prime minister’s aim of “growth in every postcode”. Of these, the impact of following Manchester’s housing investment model is most striking. The report found that an £8.5bn programme of revolving public risk capital across mayoral strategic authorities could unlock almost 100,000 additional homes, crowd in more than £20bn of private investment and support more than 70,000 jobs. While not commissioned by No 10, Mandala’s study nevertheless bolsters Burnham’s central growth argument that learning from the success of Manchester’s devolution model could deliver far-reaching economic benefits and release the country from its low-growth chokehold. The chancellor has privately acknowledged there is room for modest additional borrowing to fund investment given Reeves’s rule change in 2024, which allowed the Treasury to offset financial assets against government debt. However, there is little sense of a radical new perspective emerging from the new regime at No 11. On Monday, Healey will give a speech on the government’s mission for growth, which is expected to stress the importance of devolution and public investment – both themes Reeves repeatedly returned to. The chancellor will emphasise the need to give the private sector the confidence to invest – raising doubts about whether he is likely to go ahead with one of the big revenue raisers that progressive economists and the TUC have called for: a windfall tax on banks. Treasury sources have declined to say whether Healey will stick to Reeves’s intention of holding only one major “fiscal event” each year, with the spring forecast a much more low-key affair. That would leave open the possibility of using his 28 October statement to fund the gaps in the defence investment plan and make more progress on tax devolution, while leaving the weightier tax and spending decisions until the spring. Labour MPs are anxious for change as quickly as the government can deliver it. They applaud Burnham’s ambition and the sense of hope he fosters but worry that the economic realities will drag him down. Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the Commons defence committee, summed up the mood when he suggested at PMQs that “vibes alone just will not be enough”. While he was referring to military spending, the sentiment is shared across the backbenches. Burnham has repeatedly said he will be relentless in fulfilling his priorities. But some of his MPs are already worried that his promise to repair the crumbling state and offer “breathing space” on the cost of living could be hard to reconcile with promises of fiscal responsibility. Downing Street sources argue, however, that it is only by improving infrastructure and devolving power that the British economy can grow as fast as Manchester’s. They cite Burnham’s visit to Cornwall this summer, where businesses told him it was taking them a year to connect to the grid. Healey’s economic instincts are less clear. When asked what would be the main difference between him and his instinctively prudent predecessor, one adviser said: “To be honest, I think he will actually be more cautious.” Despite his apparent wariness, government aides insist the chancellor is fully onboard with Burnham’s vision. One said: “There will always be tensions between the different parts of government, but John is aligned with Andy’s agenda. And he knows who is boss.”

title: Cut the cameras: Flock surveillance cameras spur rare bipartisan backlash
summary: Politicians on the right and left are pushing back against Flock as more Americans voice opposition to the tech
text: Growing factions from both sides of the political aisle in the US are pushing back against surveillance cameras made by a single company, a rare response in a sharply divided country with a president pushing an unwaveringly pro-tech agenda. The bipartisan backlash against Flock Safety cameras resembles nationwide rage toward the construction of large datacenters that power artificial intelligence. Polling shows roughly 75% of Americans oppose new datacenter construction in their areas. Flock’s cameras are automated license plate readers (ALPRs), which take pictures of vehicle license plates so police and security companies can log the movement of cars in a given area. There are about 120,000 Flock cameras across the US, which conduct roughly 2bn scans per month. The company is staring down controversy after reports of abuses of its cameras by police officers in multiple states, who have used them to stalk ex-lovers and track people seeking abortions. The network the cameras feed into is also frequently utilized by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Data and polling from the Washington Post show that social media posts about Flock have increased since July, and about 46% of Americans oppose ALPRs being used in their community – up 13 points from the previous year. Vigilantes are posting videos of themselves destroying the cameras to digital applause. According to privacy and surveillance experts, hatred of Flock cameras has become bipartisan. “In my 20-plus years at the ACLU, I’ve never really seen such a grassroots uprising against surveillance technology like this,” said Jay Stanley, a senior policy analyst at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). “On the left, there’s a historical memory of law enforcement spying on and interfering with advocates for social change … On the right, there’s a long tradition of ‘don’t tread on me’ – keep the government out of my life, keep it from looking over my shoulder.” Both liberal and conservative politicians are pushing back against Flock cameras. Greg Abbott, Texas’s Republican governor, blocked state agencies from procuring Flock products. On the other side of the political spectrum, Bernie Sanders, the progressive US senator, is promising to introduce legislation to restrict the use of Flock cameras. Republican senator Josh Hawley has launched an investigation into potential Flock privacy abuses, and Democratic congressman Ro Khanna is cosponsoring a bill with Republican congressman Thomas Massie to prevent federal funds from being used to purchase Flock cameras. Municipal leaders of all political stripes are dropping contracts with Flock, though sometimes they replace the license plate readers with another brand of camera and continue the surveillance. We reached out to Flock Safety for a statement and did not receive a response before publishing. Surveillance hasn’t always been a unifying topic in US politics. Debates over the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (Fisa), the Patriot Act and other surveillance issues have often been divisive. This appears to be an unusual case where politicians are getting on the same side of a hot-button issue. “Privacy, to some extent, is bipartisan,” said Matthew Guariglia, a senior policy analyst at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. “When you put up these cameras, they last longer than the current administration. You might trust the people in power now who put them up – but are you going to trust the next people who get access to that equipment?” Americans have been showing up at town hall meetings by the dozen over the past six months or so, and there have been numerous protests to show opposition to Flock surveillance cameras around the country. More than 100 jurisdictions have canceled their contracts so far, according to data from the non-profit Institute for Justice. An organization called DeFlock, founded in 2024, hopes to increase the numbers by compiling a map of the cameras’ locations. While ALPRs aren’t new, Flock, founded in 2017, has made them far more prevalent than they used to be. The company’s software allows disparate law enforcement agencies to share data with one another, meaning a license plate scan by a police department in one state could easily and quickly be used in another. “Flock represents tech companies in bed with governments, doing the exact stuff people have become distrustful of and resentful about for the past few decades. It feels like it’s finally hit the boiling-over point,” said Woodrow Hartzog, a professor of law and computer science at Boston University. Hartzog predicts the actions against Flock Safety will continue at the state and local level amid this growing popular outrage. He expects people are going to stay angry about the issue, and politicians will have to respond. “The pushback we’re seeing against Flock cameras is one of the most vivid illustrations I can think of that surveillance is not inevitable – that these tools aren’t inevitable,” Hartzog says. “It’s up to all of us to stop them.”

title: Civilians among at least 60 killed in Yemen as ground fighting escalates
summary: Houthi rebel offensive against government forces on west coast leads to some of deadliest clashes in years
text: Clashes between Yemen’s Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel movement have killed more than 60 people, including civilians, as the Houthis pushed forward with a military offensive on Yemen’s western coast. Twenty-six government troops and 31 Houthi fighters were killed during several hours of fighting in the country’s south-west on Saturday, medical and military sources told Agence France-Presse (AFP). A missile strike also killed six civilians and injured seven others travelling by bus in the city of Taiz. The killings were the latest in a series of bloody clashes in recent days as the Houthis continued an offensive in western Taiz and southern Hodeidah along the Red Sea coast. On Friday, 129 were killed in fighting between rebel and government forces, according to an AFP tally. The fighting is some of the deadliest in years, after the collapse in July of the 2022 ceasefire. The truce fell apart after an Iranian plane attempted to land in Houthi-controlled Sana’a, triggering attacks by the Yemeni government on the airport. The Houthis are trying to beat back governmental troops to capture strategic hills overlooking Bab al-Mandeb in order to advance towards port cities on the coast. So far, they have managed to capture areas in western Taiz. In Taiz, a government military officer said the “coming hours will be decisive” as the Houthis had taken positions near the city a day before. They added that reinforcements had been arriving from Aden to try to stem the Houthi advance. On Friday, government forces said that they had recaptured the al-Khazan and al-Makahna hills west of Taiz, two strategically important areas for controlling the region. The Houthis had previously controlled the port city of al-Makha overlooking Bab al-Mandeb, before being pushed out by government forces backed by the Saudi-led coalition. The Bab al-Mandeb strait is a crucial maritime chokepoint for ships heading to the Suez canal. About 10% of global maritime trade passes through the strait. Saudi Arabia has been using the strait to export oil for months after the start of the US-Iran war. If shipping is disrupted in Bab al-Mandeb, it will only further raise the cost of global goods, which has already rocketed as a result of the virtual closure of the strait of Hormuz since March 2026. If the Houthis manage to recapture the port city and take key areas along the Red Sea coast, it will help them control naval traffic in the Red Sea. In July, the Houthis declared a naval blockade against Saudi Arabia, and they have repeatedly disrupted traffic in solidarity with Gaza since the start of the war there in October 2023. Yemen has been embroiled in a civil war since 2014, when the Houthis and allied forces took the capital city of Sana’a and pushed the then government out of power. A Saudi-led coalition then began a military intervention to support the Yemeni government and fight the Houthis, a strategic ally of Iran. At least 150,000 people in Yemen have been killed in the fighting, and hundreds of thousands more have died from related causes such as hunger and diseases. About 4.5 million people have been displaced by the fighting and more than 18.2 million are in dire need of humanitarian assistance, according to the UN.

title: After overtourism besieged Big Sur, the worst finally happened: ‘People kept saying someone is going to die’
summary: The coastal community in California had already been devastated by landslides and wildfires before a fatal crash
text: California’s rugged Big Sur coastline is often called a slice of heaven, 120 miles (195km) of unspoiled rocky promontories, sandy beaches and redwood forests at the foot of the Santa Lucia mountains. This year, it has endured a long summer of hell. Wildfires, road closures and repeated disruptions to the local hotel, restaurant and campsite businesses all have posed significant challenges in an era of climate change and unpredictable weather patterns. One large fire broke out in the highlands east of Big Sur in early August and is still less than 25% contained. A second fire erupted 30 miles to the south two weeks later and is so inaccessible to firefighters that it has grown bigger than the first and is barely contained at all. Residents of the area have long known that the threat of natural catastrophe is part of what it means to live in a remote and beautiful place. But for many, the events of this summer have renewed questions about the sustainability of mass tourism in the area, particularly in the age of Instagram. The tourist industry accounts for about 90% of the local economy, so visitors are certainly welcome. But nobody feels comfortable with chaos on the roads, tourists who leave their messes behind or a pair of recent traffic deaths that have plunged the community into mourning. Like other global hotspots, from Italy to the Galápagos, Big Sur is asking: how many is too many? Henry Miller once described this coast as a place imbued with “the peace of God, and the serene security created by a handful of good neighbors living at one with the creature world”. But many coastal residents worry that sort of peace is rapidly eluding their grasp. *** A reopening marred by selfie-snappers The disruptions began at the beginning of the year with the long-awaited reopening of Highway 1, a two-lane road that provides the only vehicle access to Big Sur from the Monterey peninsula in the north to Cambria in the south. For three years, the route had been cut in two by extensive repair work in the wake of heavy landslides, another abiding natural threat. The region lost about 20% of its tourists over that time, at a cost of millions of dollars a month. Hearst Castle, on the southern end of the route, lost as many as 40%. The reopening immediately caused visitor numbers to shoot back up, but residents and local officials noticed that along with the nature lovers and the hikers came many more tourists interested almost exclusively in snapping selfies at a handful of well-advertised locations before moving swiftly on. Such visitors weren’t shy about stopping in the middle of the road to take pictures at the spectacular, arched Bixby Bridge, even if it meant snarling traffic for miles in each direction. Local media was filled with stories of visitors trampling on plants, camping illegally and tossing their trash in all directions. In July, a selfie-ruining banner appeared on the Bixby Bridge that read: “Overtourism is killing Big Sur.” But it made little difference. “Visitor behavior has changed so much,” said Kate Daniels, who represents Big Sur on the Monterey county council and successfully pressed for a parking moratorium at the Bixby Bridge that went into effect last month. “This is one of the most beautiful places you’ve ever seen, yet people have decided their goal is to take a picture of themselves on a bridge … It’s really difficult and dangerous, and that road cannot handle it.” ‘It was a nightmare’ For many residents, the low point came in mid-August, when Monterey county hosted its annual Car Week extravaganza, featuring thousands of vintage and exotic cars and a lineup of events in and around the city of Monterey and the golf courses of Pebble Beach. Some of the event’s 100,000 visitors repurposed the Big Sur coastline as a playground for their souped-up coupes and convertibles. They had done much the same the previous year, but now the Timber fire was raging, every change in the wind was apt to carry the smell of burning forest and the community had no patience for it. Even as fire trucks were trying to set up defensive lines in an effort to save buildings and people, car aficionados were filmed making high-speed dashes down the straightest stretches of Highway 1, doing doughnuts at traffic intersections and gathering dozens of vehicles for group photographs. Photos and videos posted online showed fire trucks struggling at times to move on a highway clogged with brightly painted sports cars. “It was a nightmare,” Daniels said. “Car Week has been going on for decades and it never used to be like this, but now it’s this hyper-masculine racing culture thing. People kept saying that someone is going to die.” By the end, people did die. On the final weekend, a 20-year-old out-of-towner at the wheel of a Dodge Challenger coupe plowed into Brian Roberts, a popular figure in Big Sur who went by the nickname Brewski and, according to his friends, had spent many of the previous days railing against the behavior of the Car Week attenders. Accounts differ about how the accident happened – some of Roberts’s friends say he was crossing Highway 1 to admire the sunset, while others say he was in the road yelling at cars after he found them blocking the turn-off to Palo Colorado Road, where he lived. Days later, an 80ft skid mark was still plainly visible, along with circular burn marks where vehicles appear to have been doing doughnuts. One of Roberts’s friends, Brendon Shave, arrived on the scene shortly after the accident and found bloodstains smeared across the median line and on the tarmac. The following day, another 20-year-old visitor from outside San Francisco smashed a silver BMW convertible into a tree a few miles north of Big Sur, killing one of his passengers and injuring himself and two other friends. Police said the driver recorded a blood alcohol level of 0.13, well above the legal limit, and they were investigating the death as gross vehicular manslaughter. Traffic deaths are a fact of life in Big Sur, with news reports suggesting that one occurs every few months, either because drivers go too fast along the windy, narrow road or because they become distracted by the natural beauty and plunge off the side. Still, Roberts’s death has moved people to particular outrage. “The community felt disrespected because the land was on fire,” said Lindsey Kirk, a friend of Roberts’s from the San Francisco Bay Area who spends as much time as she can spare in Big Sur. “It’s crazy that the fire services couldn’t get through because of all the cars they brought in.” Shave, who runs a hair salon in Carmel, a 20-minute drive from where Roberts died, blamed authorities in Monterey county who, he said, used the beauty of Big Sur as a draw for big events – marathons and golf tournaments as well as the annual car show – but did little to look out for its residents. “People live here,” he said, “to get away from all the stuff that Monterey county keeps sending our way.” See Monterey, which promotes tourism in the region, has repeatedly urged visitors to Big Sur to stick to the speed limit and park legally and put out one statement headlined: “Big Sur Deserves Big Respect.” But the organization also encouraged Car Week attenders to explore far and wide, including the Big Sur coast. Eleven days after Roberts’s death, See Monterey put out a statement proclaiming “a banner year”, with hotel revenue up, visitor spending exceeding $100m and more than $4m raised for charity. Left unmentioned were the many area businesses that closed for the week or threw up metal fences and hired security guards so their parking lots would not turn into impromptu, days-long motor sports rallies. The visitors noticed. The driver of a McLaren supercar denied entry to an In-N-Out Burger attracted national attention when his brother protested on his behalf: “That’s profiling! That’s racism towards cars.” ‘We lost a good human being’ Days after the last Lamborghinis and Porsches left town, a flare-up in the Timber fire sent cascades of sparks and ash down from Mount Manuel and prompted what many Big Sur residents felt should have happened much sooner: a comprehensive closure of Highway 1 encompassing most of the hotels and restaurants and some of the most heavily visited spots, including Pfeiffer Beach and McWay Falls. Authorities gave residents 24 hours either to stock up on essentials or leave town. Roberts’s mourners cheered – “Tourism is a problem, not a boon,” said Ivy La Velle, who described herself as his best friend – but others acknowledged it was never easy to make such a call. When the community shuts down, many of the hourly workers at the restaurants and hotels lose their source of income. If the fires force them to evacuate – dozens of them are housed by the resorts and campsites that employ them – their problems are compounded by unexpected housing and other expenses. Ryne Leuzinger, board chair of the Community Association of Big Sur, said his organization had been cutting $300 checks to help the neediest community members get by, and another group, the Big Sur Big Share, had spent the last several weeks making sure that people temporarily without an income had enough to eat. Big Sur prides itself on its communal spirit, which was on vivid display the night before the closure, when 200 mourners crowded on to the back patio of the River Inn resort to pay homage to Roberts’s life, surrounded by flowers and crystals. Roberts worked as a maintenance worker and gardener at the Alila Ventana resort but also helped with firefighting efforts in the final weeks of his life and enjoyed a wide circle of friends. “Brian was a big member of the community,” Shave said. “We lost a good human being.” Speakers recalled how he would park a motorbike in the same spot at the River Inn, one of his favorite haunts, and spend his nights smoking and drinking rum and Cokes. “He had terrible taste in cocktails,” La Velle said afterwards, laughing. “It wasn’t even good rum.” Roberts’s parents, who had driven out from the midwest, did not pay for anything because his friends raised money to pay for their lodging, meals, funeral expenses and a $1,200 bill incurred when police towed his parked truck after the fatal accident. The next day, even as a bedraggled parade of dirt- and ash-covered cars and trucks made their way north before the closure deadline, mourners gathered at the makeshift memorial on the side of Highway 1 near the spot where Roberts was hit. Kirk, the friend from the San Francisco area, laid some lapis stones and a bouquet at a shrine that also featured a pack of American Spirit cigarettes, Roberts’s favorite brand, and an empty bottle of Sailor Jerry rum. “He was always around for anyone who needed anything,” she said. “He was a wonderful guy.” Sarah Sweeney, who in less uncertain times sells sushi from a truck, said Roberts embodied a certain Big Sur ethos now under threat, because he was passionate about a community that rejects the ordinary rhythms of modern life and, perhaps, wants to run away from them. “I call this place Neverland,” she said, “and we’re all Peter Pan. Or the lost boys. There are a lot of lost boys around here.”

title: Lindsay Clancy murder trial ends in dramatic deadlock – what comes next?
summary: District attorney must decide whether to retry case after jury’s failure to reach verdict despite hours of deliberation
text: Lindsay Clancy, prosecutors, defense lawyers, the judge and millions watching on are back where they started after her five-week trial over the murder of her three children ended in a mistrial. America’s saddest case has ceased for the moment, but the legal wrangling is not over, and a second trial could now be on the horizon, prolonging and repeating an agonizing spectacle that has gripped America and the world. The trial lurched to its conclusion on Friday as jurors in Massachusetts failed to come to a unanimous verdict. A lone male juror holdout appeared to be preventing a conclusion to the case. That meant the trial ended as it had begun: with no legal certainty about what was in Clancy’s mind when on 24 January 2023 she killed five-year-old Cora, three-year-old Dawson, and eight-month-old Callan, and later cut her wrists and jumped from a bedroom window, sustaining injuries that paralyzed her. Clancy, a 36-year-old former labor and delivery nurse, did not deny the killings but pleaded not guilty to the murders. Defense attorney Kevin Reddington blamed postpartum psychosis coupled with overmedication. Prosecutors said she knew what she was doing. The jury deliberated for six days and over 30 hours, coming back three times in total in a deadlock. The jury foreperson said in a note to the judge on Thursday that a single juror had expressed reasonable doubt but would “not follow the law”. The mistrial finally came after a nail-biting delay when the judge allowed Clancy’s defense to petition the Massachusetts supreme court to replace the outlying juror with an alternate. Massachusetts justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt took the matter under advisement and soon after issued a decision not to intervene in the proceedings, forcing Judge William Sullivan to declare a mistrial. Reddington stared at the ground and let out a sigh as the judge made the ruling. At the back of the courtroom, largely occupied by supporters, people could be seen wiping away tears. And now it starts again. Reddington said he would file a motion for a directed finding of not guilty within days – a ruling that Sullivan could make on grounds that the prosecution failed to present enough evidence to prove the case. A status hearing is set for 29 September when a new trail date could be set. “This whole case has been unbelievable,” said victims’ rights attorney and survivor advocate Shari Karney. “Eleven jurors believed that Lindsay Clancy did not have criminal intent to commit this crime, understood the consequences of her act, and could not conform her conduct to the law.” The decision to try Clancy again rests with Plymouth county district attorney Tim Cruz, a prosecutor since 1985 who has served as district attorney for more than 20 years. Before Cruz’s most recent re-election, in 2022, he took aim at progressive district attorneys, saying they have been causing “anarchy and chaos” across the US. “I am against getting rid of life without parole for first-degree homicide people,” said in a debate. “I am against having a list of cases that will not be prosecuted because it does not work.” Outside court on Thursday, Reddington said he was ready to retry the case. “Bring it on,” he told reporters. But he did not rule out the possibility of a plea deal. “We’ll see what Mr Cruz wants to do, and then we’ll talk about our options,” he said. For now, Clancy returns to Tewksbury hospital, where she has been held since the killings. According to Karney, the complexity of the Massachusetts law on proving “criminal responsibility” – or what in other states would rest on the defense showing the defendant was insane – is a double standard. “It’s very complicated,” she says. Part of the difficulty jurors may have had is that mental health issues are not as a transparent as physical issues, and under criminal law there is a bias against them, she says. Karney said: “Clancy was basically having a mental health stroke, and mental health is the stepsister of the healthcare system. It’s not right. But because we cant see it, that doesn’t mean it doesn’t exist. And the medical healthcare system doesn’t want to recognize and pay for mental healthcare apart from giving out drugs to make them go away.” During the trial, jurors heard from mental health experts who clashed over Clancy’s medical records. But it was her mother and step mother who may have provided the most powerful testimony when they testified about the steps Clancy had taken to seek help. Paula Musgrove, Clancy’s mother, testified that she often stayed with her daughter in the months leading up to the killings because Clancy was afraid of sleeping alone, was increasingly paranoid and believed the medications she was taking “were destroying her mind”. Susan Clancy, Lindsay Clancy’s former mother-in-law, said she was “begging for help” and “was struggling – we were all concerned”. Forensic psychiatrist Phillip Resnick, for the defense, testified near the end of the trial testimony that that Clancy was “frankly psychotic” the day of the killings, and supported her claim that she heard a voice that ordered her to kill the children and herself. Resnick said he believed Clancy had experienced “command hallucinations … almost like she was a puppet and someone else was pulling the strings”. Avram Mack, a forensic psychiatrist, said he did not believe Clancy was showing signs of psychosis but suffered from a major depressive episode and retained the ability to know right from wrong. “There was the ability to act normally,” he testified. In theory, prosecutors and defense attorneys could agree on voluntary manslaughter, a lesser charge. “The problem with a jail sentence for this woman is that she’s paraplegic,” said Karney. “How would you incarcerate a woman in a wheelchair with tremendous mental health problems in a woman’s prison, and ensure her safety?” One takeaway from the Lindsay Clancy trial, says Karney, is the job of getting inside the head of a woman suffering postpartum psychosis is a tough task and that diagnosis and treatment is woefully insufficient. “Telehealth is good for a sprained ankle or a cold, but not for postpartum depression or psychosis. And then you prescribe more psychotropic drugs via telehealth appointment? It’s crazy and it’s not responsible,” she said.

title: ‘I could watch her for hours’: the woman who rescued a bee and created a buzz
summary: After bringing queen Phoebee home, Gilly McArthur expected her to die within a day or two, but she’s bumbling on
text: Fifty-two days ago, Phoebee was lying by the side of a road in the blistering sun with a broken wing. Today, she’s clambering up the arm of Gilly McArthur, around the nape of her neck and disappearing into her hair. “I couldn’t leave her by the roadside,” McArthur says. “So I bought her home and made her a bed of flowers. I thought she’d be dead in a day or so.” Instead of dying, Phoebee did something McArthur didn’t expect: she went viral. McArthur says: “A few days after I rescued her, I was due to go on a sailing trip for a week. I couldn’t leave her here, so I took Phoebee with me – and put a post on my Instagram account of her enjoying the trip.” The following morning, McArthur woke to find messages from around the world. “It was amazing: there were so many posts from people across the globe telling me their lovely stories of capturing bumblebees or helping butterflies with broken wings – and the stories kept coming.” McArthur, an author, is touched but slightly baffled by the furore. “I think it might be because the world is in such a polycrisis at the moment, and everyone is wanting to pull back to something authentic and kind,” she says. “Perhaps Phoebee reminds people of a time when bumblebees were more prolific, in a world that isn’t on fire: lots of the messages said the videos helped them feel more grounded in a world where the algorithms are usually so grounded in clickbait and violence.” Britain has 24 species of bumblebee and more than 240 species of solitary bee. Most bumblebees live for just one year. New mated queens have a bit more of a lifeline: they hibernate in the autumn and emerge in spring to establish colonies of their own. Phoebee has not mated. While McArthur does not know what that will mean for her, she is stalwart in the face of possible tragedy. “If I check on her one day and she’s not moving, I’ll check her bum. When she sleeps, her bum goes up and down very slightly,” she says. “If her bum is still, I won’t give up – I’ll put her in a quiet room and hope she’s hibernating. But her lifespan is her lifespan.” For now, McArthur spends a lot of time watching her. “She’s fascinating: she spends a lot of time cleaning herself like a cat. And I could watch her putting her long tongue out and getting the nectar out of the flowers for hours.” Andy Benson, of the Bumblebee Conservation Trust, has watched the brouhaha with similar bemusement. He thinks passions would have been cooler had Phoebee not been a buff-tailed bumblebee, the biggest and fluffiest bee, and a queen, “the biggest and fluffiest of them all”. Benson says that while McArthur’s heroic salvation of a single bumblebee is heartwarming, the advice is to gently place lost bees on a flower and let nature take its course. “A third of British wild bees and hoverflies are in decline and a quarter of European species are at risk of extinction because of the loss of their natural habitat, climate change and bee-killing pesticides,” he says. This matters because one in three mouthfuls of our food depend on pollinators such as bees, with the crops that depend on pollination – including apples, beans, squashes and almonds – being five times more valuable than those that do not. Benson says if people want to help bees, they don’t have to take them into their home, or on a sailing trip, or let them nestle in their hair. “We can instantly help hundreds of bees in the smallest of spaces by simply planting a few flowers in their garden,” he says. McArthur knows she hasn’t stayed the plummeting bee numbers by prolonging Phoebee’s short lifespan. But she hopes she may have made a difference in another way. “Maybe this is something nice that people can pull back to and just go: ‘Oh, maybe I won’t blow my leaves away this winter – maybe I might plant more plants for pollinators – maybe I might just stop and look at the smaller things with more curiosity’,” she says. “And maybe Phoebee’s videos will help people realise that looking at the smaller things in more detail can make the bigger things feel more manageable.”

title: Even in safe-haven Massachusetts, trans care is at risk. Young people are fighting to protect it
summary: Activists are calling on the state attorney general to take action against hospitals that have ended gender-affirming care programs after Trump retook office
text: A group of trans activists from across Massachusetts brought their needles, hormone gels, pills and sharps containers to Boston on Wednesday to send a message to state attorney general Andrea Campbell. Organizers with the youth-led group Protect Trans Futures (PTF) took their hormone replacement therapy (HRT) in the lobby of her office building, then occupied the space, refusing to leave without a commitment to protect civil rights for trans kids. While Massachusetts is considered one of the legally “safest” places for trans people, some local hospitals are still dropping youth gender-affirming care and canceling surgery appointments amid an expansive legal fight across the US. Gender-affirming care remains legal for all in Massachusetts, but the Trump administration’s attempt to undermine state laws has still created barriers to care, and a chilling effect. So organizers came asking Campbell to order those hospitals to reinstate care, or investigate or launch litigation against them for failing to do so. Some advocates – who share Protect Trans Futures’ outrage at the hospitals for pre-emptively complying with Donald Trump’s agenda – fear undermining a sympathetic attorney general and eventually ending up with a less friendly replacement. But many trans organizers see the action as simply holding the government to its own standards. “Massachusetts politicians at the local, state and federal level are very naive in thinking and hoping that there’s not this massive loss of care, but that’s not the reality of patients and families,” said Teddy Walker, a 21-year-old with Protect Trans Futures. “The Trump administration’s policies are working exactly as intended.” A majority of American medical experts support access to trans youth care, which demonstrably reduces suicide and mental health risks. Nonetheless, in 27 states, such as Texas and Missouri, youth gender-affirming care is now restricted or banned; in some, doctors can be prosecuted for providing it, and parents have been investigated for seeking it out for their children. Fifty percent of trans youth ages 13 to 17 live in one of those states. Even hospitals in blue states, like New York’s NYU Langone, which ended care last year, have been subpoenaed for the medical records of their former minor clients. After the state attorney general’s building had closed for the day, organizers were handed a phone: An assistant attorney general offered them a meeting – a step organizers had taken months before, with no results. So they refused. After a few hours, nine organizers, including Walker, were arrested by state troopers. (The attorney general’s office told the Guardian they were not involved in the decision to arrest the protesters.) He screamed a message to supporters witnessing his arrest – a chant from LGBTQ+ activists who held die-ins and other protests to force a change in the Aids epidemic: “Act up! Fight back!” The ‘trans great migration’ Over the last few years, hundreds of thousands of trans people and families with trans kids have fled home states with anti-trans laws, relocating to states like Massachusetts in hopes of maintaining access to gender-affirming care and other trans civil rights. Massachusetts is one of a handful of US states with shield laws to protect LGBTQ+ residents from lawsuits and penalties from states where gender affirming care is criminalized. In addition, elected officials in the state are vocal supporters of their trans constituents, including Gov Maura Healey, the state’s first woman and lesbian governor, and Senator Edward Markey, who won the Democratic primary this week in a race that was largely defined by trans rights. But the Trump administration attacked these state-level protections for trans youth healthcare soon after taking office in January 2025. In the first weeks of his second term, the president signed an executive order threatening to cut off federal funding for hospitals that provide gender-affirming medical care to trans youth. Later that year, health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr sought to target Medicaid funding to hospitals providing youth gender affirming care. Many of those efforts have been tossed; there are no reports of hospitals losing federal funding for providing this care. Still, in response to the administration’s directives, at least three local hospitals or healthcare systems in Massachusetts have ended gender-affirming care programs for patients under 19. (This means that 18-year-olds, who are legally adults, are impacted.) A fourth Massachusetts hospital canceled all appointments for a gender-affirming surgery for adult trans women, even though adults aren’t the subject of Trump’s executive order. Initially, organizers protested outside these hospitals in an effort to pressure them to reinstate the care. They later shifted their focus to pressuring state officials to enforce existing civil rights laws. In April, Campbell’s office met with a group of trans youth advocates after some hospitals ended care for youth. She has repeatedly expressed support for trans youth, saying that trans healthcare “remains legal and protected” in Massachusetts, and warning hospitals that ending youth gender-affirming care “may amount to discrimination” under state law. And on 2 September, the same day as the protest at her office, Campbell joined 21 other state attorneys general in suing the Trump administration over its attempt to block Medicaid coverage for youth gender affirming care. In August, Walker publicly confronted Campbell at an event at the Boston public library over her inaction. She stated she will not litigate against hospitals that have ended care, and has not ordered them to reinstate it, as attorneys general in blue states like New York and California, as well as Colorado’s supreme court, have done. After Wednesday’s protest, the attorney general’s office shared with the Guardian the email it sent to Protect Trans Futures. In it, the attorney general’s office argued that what’s been done in California and New York were imperfect comparisons and would not result in care being reinstated in Massachusetts. The office reiterated that youth gender affirming care remains legal in the state, and wrote, “The cessation of gender-affirming care for minors by Fenway Health, Outer Cape Health Services and Baystate Health has not resulted in a wave of hospitals or clinics ceasing to provide care in the Commonwealth.” The email added, “The AGO and PTF share a common goal: maintaining access to gender-affirming care.” Campbell’s office has said it is unaware of any youth who has lost care, but Walker, of the group Protect Trans Futures, says he knows dozens of youth and their families who have. In its email, the attorney general’s office asked PTF to connect with those families. Walker said that the group has previously brought those families to meetings with the office, but nothing came of it. Shattered trust Last October, Fenway Health, Massachusetts’ largest LGBTQ+ healthcare provider, stopped providing youth hormone care and puberty blockers, routine medical care to prevent the major physical changes that come during puberty. Fenway was a particular blow: from its founding as a community health drop-in location in the early 1970s, it centered gay clients and made the first Aids diagnosis in New England. Other providers, including Outer Cape Health Services, which runs three facilities on Cape Cod, and Baystate Health, which services western Massachusetts, followed suit. Other hospitals and clinics have taken in those who’ve lost care. Transhealth in Northampton, the country’s only independent clinic focused solely on trans and gender-nonconforming patients, has shouldered an avalanche of referrals. Josh, who asked to use a pseudonym for privacy reasons, 18, was born at Fenway to lesbian parents, and still sees his primary care physician there. Following the typical medical routine for youth who transition in childhood, he started going to Fenway for hormone replacement therapy in middle school. After two years on puberty blockers, he then started taking testosterone. That process is intentionally slow, requiring letters from therapists and evaluations, often taking at least a year. When Fenway halted care last year, Josh was able to get a referral to Boston Children’s hospital, which has vocally refused to close its trans healthcare program. Restarting the intake process, however, took over a year, he said. It shattered his trust that his home state would be able to protect him. He’s just one case of young people abruptly stripped of care. Safara Malone, a senior at Harvard University, moved to Massachusetts from Texas, which has extreme anti-trans laws, in 2024. Malone was a strident advocate for trans rights in her home state and intentionally chose a college where she would face fewer barriers and find more explicit support. But with graduation less than a year away, Malone says she’s not sure where she’ll feel safe living next, amid what she called the trans “great migration”. It was difficult for her to realize that had she arrived in Boston just one year later – after the changes at Fenway – she would have been refused her care. Malone is now considering leaving the country. Fighting for change Now, trans people of all ages are fighting to protect the very civil rights that brought many of them to Massachusetts in the first place. Fenway’s cessation of care spurred the creation of Protect Trans Futures, a group of trans youth that has been fighting the state government and hospitals themselves to reinstate care. PTF has held a series of actions this summer pushing Campbell to consider their demands, including coordinating a letter campaign which now has more than 3,000 signatures. After Baystate cut off youth gender affirming care, another group, Western Massachusetts Trans Alliance (WMTA), emerged to push back. These nascent grassroots efforts join the existing fabric of LGBTQ+ and trans advocacy organizations across the state, including the Massachusetts Transgender Political Coalition. Other organizations like the Boston chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America have signed on to PTF’s efforts. Many of these groups, as well as the national Gender Liberation Movement, joined PTF outside Campbell’s offices. A grassroots group of parents and other adults from western Massachusetts also came in to support and set up a large banner depicting a blue bus labeled “Baystate Health”. Around the banner, people held smaller signs that read “throws trans kids under the bus”. Under the banner, fabric legs with children’s sneakers poked out. “Unlike Boston, western Mass does not have as many choices for healthcare,” Ali Wicks-Lim, one of the grassroots organizers protesting Baystate, said outside the attorney general’s office Wednesday. “So for them to end this gender-affirming care means that people have to travel further, and search harder, to find any kind of gender affirming care for their youth.” Wicks-Lim says that they’ve heard of many families who have not been able to find another provider. “Once we let the government start making decisions about what we do with our bodies, and what our children are able to do with our bodies, and the decisions that parents and grandparents and caregivers need to be able to make for their children”, they said, “we’re in a really dangerous territory.”

title: John Healey warns of tough first budget as Middle East war puts pressure on economy
summary: Chancellor says he wants to ensure country has ‘buffer’ against uncertainty as global bond yields hit 18-year high
text: The chancellor has indicated that the UK will face a tough budget next month due to Trump’s war in the Middle East. In an interview with the Financial Times, John Healey said the conflict in Iran would probably have a strong influence on his first budget on 28 October. Healey, who succeeded Rachel Reeves when Andy Burnham became prime minister in July, told the newspaper he wanted to ensure the country had a robust “buffer against uncertainty” amid increasing global instability. However, economists have predicted that Healey will need to raise taxes or implement significant cost-cutting measures to protect the £24bn fiscal headroom that Reeves had after her March statement. “What’s happening in the Middle East is hitting inflation, it’s hitting growth, it’s hitting borrowing costs,” Healey said. “It’s part of a more dangerous world that is more uncertain and it’s one of the challenges we have to meet in this country, but have to meet with other [countries].” Healey declined to say how much headroom he aimed to have, but insisted he and Burnham were “in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules”. The newspaper said he planned to stick to Labour’s 2024 manifesto pledges not to raise taxes on “working people”, such as income tax, national insurance contributions or VAT, and was also not expected to raise the rate of corporation tax. The public finances are under pressure from soaring global bond yields , which hit an 18-year high earlier this week. Bond yields have a significant impact on government spending plans, as higher yields drive up borrowing costs. Healey has faced criticism for failing to commit to the goal of raising defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030. In June, he resigned as defence secretary because he was unable to get the Treasury to commit to the target, in what was seen as a fatal blow to Keir Starmer’s government. Acknowledging tough economic conditions, Healey said: “The country’s under pressure. People are under pressure with the cost of living. Households are feeling that. We’re concerned about the cost of living, and we’re concerned about the cost of business.” He also said he was committed to cutting the welfare bill. “We must cut the cost of welfare, we have to get more people back into work,” he said. “I know that some of the decisions I must take – and will take – will show the benefits in years to come.” Jim O’Neill, the cross-bench peer and economist who advised Burnham as he prepared to enter Downing Street, has suggested that the prime minister could reassure the bond markets by taking “credible actions” to rein in the “excesses” of welfare spending and the pensions triple lock. Speaking to Times Radio earlier this week, he said: “If you have the markets carrying on doing what they’re doing globally … eventually they’re going to have absolutely no choice [but to cut spending] because the penalty of the debt servicing cost and the knock-on effect to other markets including mortgage rates will be too severe for a government to resist.” The triple lock, introduced in 2010, means that state pension increases annually in line with inflation, average wage growth or 2.5% – whichever is highest. It has led to an increase of about £16bn in the state pension bill. On Saturday morning, Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that the government could consider an Australian-style system. He suggested that the state pension could increase in line with workers’ earnings, with an inbuilt “temporary lock” to safeguard against a decline in average wages due to recession or high inflation. “It’s a reasonable way to increase the state pension over the long run that’s not as expensive but still generates increases,” he said. Reform UK has said it would cut £80bn of public spending within five years by reducing welfare payments, net zero investment and overseas aid. Speaking at the party’s annual conference in Birmingham, its economic spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, also pledged to reduce the number of civil servants.

title: Rescuers in Nepal find two more people alive after flash flood disaster
summary: Chinese man at Trishuli hydropower project and Nepali woman in Nuwakot found 10 days into rescue operation
text: Emergency responders have rescued a Chinese man and a Nepali woman in two separate operations as authorities continued to search for thousands of people missing 10 days after massive floods hit Nepal. The Nepali military said on Saturday a joint team comprising personnel from its army and South Korean disaster experts rescued the man from a 225-metre (740ft) tunnel in the Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project, and that he was undergoing a health assessment. Pictures showed him being evacuated by helicopter after being carried out of the tunnel. Rescue efforts have focused on a dozen hydropower projects across Nepal, where about 900 workers are missing, 500 of whom are thought to be trapped in huge tunnels. International rescue teams from India, China, South Korea and the US have been searching through debris and damaged structures at the projects to try to find survivors. Two Nepali workers were rescued from another tunnel in a hydro-station on the Trishuli River on Friday. Experts have said the possibility of finding missing people alive in the tunnels is diminishing. The Nepali woman, 64, was rescued from a damaged house in the devastated town of Nuwakot. Photos published by the Nepali army showed rescuers discovering the woman submerged in mud before she was pulled to safety and airlifted to Kathmandu for treatment. Members of Nepal’s police force cheered as she was pulled from the home, the lower half of which was buried in thick sludge. Emergency responders have been working to find survivors from the devastating floods in Nepal, which were triggered by a glacial and rock collapse on 26 August. Their work has been complicated by the massive infrastructural damage caused by the floods, with more than 40 bridges having collapsed and rivers swelling unpredictably. At least 1,375 people have been killed in the floods, with more than 5,000 missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency.

title: ‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrike
summary: Exclusive: Guardian investigation reveals targeting of World Central Kitchen convoy was result of widely used military tactic
text: Seven aid workers killed in an airstrike in Gaza were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishing guilt by association, a Guardian investigation shows. A top Israeli military prosecutor announced last month that he would not pursue criminal proceedings for the April 2024 incident in which drones fired missiles at three clearly marked World Central Kitchen (WCK) cars soon after they had escorted a food aid delivery to Gaza. Three British humanitarian workers along with an Australian, a Palestinian, a Pole and a dual US-Canadian national were killed. The official Israel Defense Forces (IDF) version of events pointed to specific mistakes made by a handful of officers. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect a food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route.
