title: Captain calamity: Pete Hegseth under fire for ‘inept’ leadership of US military
summary: The US defense secretary faces internal dissent and discord at the Pentagon, accused of focusing on culture war issues and his own political ambitions as the Iran war drags on
text: In a different Washington, under a different president, a return to the well-worn playbook of all-out sanctions to counter Iran might have been the signal for a publicity-hungry US secretary of defense to adopt a lower profile. But these are no ordinary times. And Pete Hegseth is no ordinary defense secretary. Barely a week after the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, unleashed a supposed “economic D-day” aimed at crushing the regime in Tehran under the weight of commercial pressures, Hegseth once again returned to the limelight – and the center of controversy. The former Fox News host usurped Bessent from center stage as the conflict with Iran reverted to open warfare and discontent at the Pentagon was laid bare once more. Turf wars within Hegseth’s own fiefdom resurfaced with the resignation of the army secretary, fresh revelations of blocked promotions and leaked disclosures of resistance from military top brass of extended deployments to the Middle East. While the Pentagon insists that any suggestion the defense department is in disarray under Hegseth is “completely baseless”, alarm over his conduct in the role – and the implications – has not merely been expressed by Hegseth’s political opponents. “The secretary of defense is a clear and present danger to the national security of the United States and the world,” said Randy Manner, a retired major general in the US national guard – in which Hegseth also served – and member of National Security Leaders for America (NSL4A), a group of former military leaders. “He has done more harm to the national security of the United States than any secretary of defense since the country was created.” Thom Tillis, the Republican senator from North Carolina, who is stepping down from the US Senate after clashes with Donald Trump, bluntly urged the US president this week to fire his defense secretary. “I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country,” Tillis wrote on social media. “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defense and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.” After a month-long lull, the resumption of strikes on Iranian targets near the strait of Hormuz meanwhile renewed questions over just what the US wants to achieve in its war with the Islamic regime, which Trump and his defense secretary once loudly vowed to topple. The strikes, on mainland Iran as well as Iranian islands in the Gulf, caused multiple casualties. In one incident, Iranian media reported that five people, including a six-year-old child, were killed in the southern city of Kuhestak when a missile struck a wedding party. Iranian authorities labelled the deaths a war crime. The episode had echoes of strikes in the city of Minab on the first day of the war on 28 February, when more than 150 people, including 120 children, were killed when missiles hit an elementary school. The US has not formally admitted responsibility, although officials have said the incident is under military investigation. The latest strikes were quickly followed by disclosures that Hegseth had extended military deployments in the Middle East, where the US currently maintains 50,000 troops and 19 warships – partly to enforce a naval blockade on Iran – into the middle of next year. The extensions were ordered even after several commanders in other sectors voiced objections, formally known as “non-concurs”, to the deployments, arguing that they could leave the US at risk of being unable to meet its commitments in other areas, while subjecting forces to the additional strain of being at sea for too long. The non-concurs were recorded in the Secretary of Defense Orders Book of 14 August, a classified document whose contents were leaked and reported by the Washington Post. The Pentagon reached out to the Guardian after publication of this story. Hegseth “has been a transformative leader for the Department of War and, at President Trump’s direction, has ushered in a new era of Peace Through Strength”, press secretary Kingsley Wilson said in a statement. “Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all time highs. “Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way. The entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision and will continue working to put our warfighters and America first.” ‘The past six months has failed’ “I’m not sure what the strategy is here,” Kevin Carroll, a former army colonel and military intelligence officer who served in the offices of the defense secretary and joint chiefs of staff, said of the war on Iran. “What’s the enemy’s center of gravity that we’re going after? “We tried decapitating their leadership. That didn’t work. We tried going after their missile program. We were not able to destroy it. Tried sinking the navy, but they still maintain a mining capability. “We could easily take out their energy infrastructure. But that would drive the price of oil much, much higher, and lead to retaliatory attacks on the energy infrastructure of our Gulf allies. It’s not clear what this target set is intended to do.” Nate Swanson, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and a former White House and state department adviser on Iran, said Hegseth’s long-term deployment orders reflected the administration’s decision to embrace a policy of long-term economic blockade. “It’s a recognition of the fact that the past six months has failed, but they don’t know what to do,” argued Swanson, who suggested that Trump was attracted by the idea of abandoning the conflict, but wanted to do so in way that enabled him to project strength. As the war drags on, Hegseth stands accused of being insufficiently engaged with such grave policy matters, preferring instead to focus on “cultural” issues – sacrificing the careers of talented career officers in the process – and his future political ambitions. The defense secretary, who has evaded awkward questions or scrutiny by not holding a formal Pentagon briefing since 5 May, has reportedly told associates that he is considering a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. In the midst of a burgeoning trade war between the US and Canada, Hegseth – who has previously railed against “fat” generals and instituted testosterone tests for service personnel – found time to wade in by apparently “body shaming” two Canadian female teenage cadets. The social media post attracted a storm of criticism. In a podcast, Joe Walsh, a former Republican congressman who is now a Democrat, accused Hegseth of “fucking online harassment” and denounced the defense secretary as a “punk”. Tensions over Hegseth’s priorities reached a head this week when the army secretary, Dan Driscoll – a friend and ally of Vice-President JD Vance – resigned after repeatedly clashing with Hegseth over blocked promotions and purges of senior commanders on flimsy pretexts. A large proportion of those blocked or fired have been black or female, in line with Hegseth’s vocal crusade against “woke” DEI (diversity, equity and inclusiveness) initiatives. In the latest of a series of purges, the New York Times reported that Hegseth had blocked the promotions of seven officers to the two-star general rank. In submitting his resignation, Driscoll – who has spearheaded efforts to modernize the army, including through embracing drone warfare – voiced concerns “surrounding Army transformation and readiness and Hegseth’s blocking those efforts specifically by firing the generals who were responsible”, a source told CNN. Driscoll’s departure – and the reasons for it – aroused anger even among Republicans, most notably Tillis, the outgoing GOP senator. “Dan was the right man at the right moment to lead our Soldiers and Army civilians,” wrote Tillis. The withering verdict is seconded by some retired generals, who say misgivings over Hegseth’s leadership are quietly shared by many serving officers who remain. Manner said Hegseth was depriving other parts of the armed forces to fund the Iran war out of “readiness accounts”. “These are for training the rest of the force,” he said. “So the rest of the force is losing training hours, equipment and money for maintenance and operations. The rest of the military is significantly degraded.” Manner also said his conversations with serving officers bore out the leaked concerns voiced in the Secretary of Defence’s Orders Book. “I have firsthand knowledge of people who are serving on active duty who echo the exact same concerns that we are headed to a situation where we can no longer defend Taiwan, that we are very unlikely to be able to defend even, quite frankly, South Korea,” he said. ‘Infinitely worse’ than Rumsfeld Hegseth, who has drawn accusations of war crimes for ordering a succession of strikes on alleged drug-ferrying boats off the coasts of South America, is not the first US defense secretary to come under a harsh spotlight over the conduct of a far-off American war. Robert McNamara, defense secretary under Lyndon Johnson, became a lightning rod for criticism during the Vietnam war before eventually undergoing a crisis of conscience and being moved to a new role as head of the World Bank. During George W Bush’s administration, Donald Rumsfeld became the target of fierce criticism after failing as defense secretary to plan adequately for the occupation of Iraq after the initial invasion to topple Saddam Hussein. But Paul Eaton, a retired major general who trained Iraqi troops after the invasion and is now an adviser to VoteVets – an advocacy group for progressive military veterans – said Rumsfeld’s failings paled in comparison with Hegseth. “Rumsfeld had ‘next war-itis’, which was a contributing factor to Bush firing him after the shellacking that the Republican party had in the [2006] midterms,” Eaton said. “All this sounds faintly familiar with what we’re going through right now. “But this is infinitely worse because we had a lot of other very smart people to corral the bad ideas coming out of Rumsfeld. [This time] we’ve had the whole removal of seasoned men and women who have learned things the hard way most of the time in combat. “If you fail to plan, plan to fail, and what we’re seeing in the Iran war is just evidence. The frustration is, we’re better than this in the uniformed military but we got handed a terrible set of guidance from our civilian leadership.” Michael O’Hanlon, a defense and strategy expert at the Brookings Institution, argued that the armed forces had enough “bench strength” to survive Hegseth’s purges without imminent collapse, but lamented the loss of certain key individuals who could not be easily replaced. He singled out Gen Chris Donahue, who recently stepped down from his post as head of the US land command in Europe and Africa. “We haven’t had a TV talkshow star with a strong partisan and cultural agenda wind up as secretary of defense,” said O’Hanlon. “There may be some echoes of previous secretaries, but the political and culture stuff is Pete Hegseth through and through.” Hegseth was “not going to wind up leaving a major mark”, O’Hanlon predicted. “He’s going to wind up being known as the guy who fought Trump’s culture wars for him – and maybe failed to help Trump stay out of trouble in the Iran war, depending on how bad that gets.” • This article was amended on 5 September 2026. An earlier version erred in saying that Robert McNamara became head of the International Monetary Fund; he was head (as its president from 1968 to 1981) of the World Bank, the IMF’s sister organization. • This article was amended on 6 September 2026 to include a statement from the Pentagon.

title: ICE given permission to force-feed Cuban hunger striker with gastric tube
summary: Exclusive: court orders seen by Guardian show agency given approval to fit Texas detainee with tube without his consent
text: Federal immigration officials quietly received permission from a judge in recent weeks to force-feed a detained Cuban hunger striker inside a Texas detention center, including with the use of a rare, nonconsensual surgical procedure, court records reveal. The man is likely the 19th hunger striker in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention where the agency has had an application approved to conduct “involuntary medical procedures” since January 2025. The rising number of cases under the second Trump administration has alarmed advocates amid wide-ranging accusations of mistreatment inside facilities nationwide. Court orders from the southern district of Texas federal court seen by the Guardian suggest ICE followed through with force-feeding via a nasal tube on the Cuban man in August, since agency officials successfully requested this week that the court order be extended. He is currently detained at the Montgomery ICE processing center, a privately-run detention facility near Houston. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, said on Thursday evening the man had “resumed eating and drinking again” and was not being force-fed. The DHS did not answer whether the man had broken his hunger strike this week after the latest court order, or how many times he had been force-fed prior. The new order had given ICE permission to operate on him to fit a surgical feeding tube without his consent. The Guardian is not naming the man because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. Like in all force-feeding cases, the majority of his court records are sealed, concealing many details from the public. The secretive practice of force-feeding inside detention centers has been widely condemned by human rights organizations as torture. Involuntary medical procedures in response to hunger strikes in detention are often painful and traumatizing. During a prolonged hunger strike, ICE will request permission from a federal judge to conduct force-feeding, forced hydration and other measures. Typically, after a judge approves the request, detention center guards hold down a hunger striker while medical staff forcibly insert a tube through the person’s nose and down their throat, and pump nutritional liquid into their stomach. But in this latest case in Texas, ICE also received permission to force-feed the Cuban hunger striker through a “percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy” tube insertion. This is a surgery in which medical staff make an incision in a person’s abdomen, insert a tube that remains in place indefinitely until it is surgically removed again and pump liquid directly into the stomach. This procedure has not been previously identified in other force-feeding cases reviewed by the Guardian. “The cruelty of the extreme tactics at ICE’s disposal to end lawful protest, including forcibly cutting into a protester’s body to insert a tube in their stomach, underscores the horrors happening outside our view in ICE detention centers,” said Savannah Kumar, a staff attorney at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Texas. “ICE’s brutal use of involuntary medical procedures on hunger strikers demonstrates how degrading conditions have gotten in these hidden places, which is often exactly what hunger strikers are protesting in the first place.” Last month, the Guardian published a series of stories about the extent of ICE’s force-feeding practices under the second Trump administration, with the agency getting the green light to perform involuntary medical procedures in 18 hunger strike cases – and the latest being the 19th. “The high number of verified court orders since January 2025 raises serious concern,” said Eunice Cho, an immigrant and civil rights attorney who has extensively documented forced treatment on hunger strikers in ICE detention. Cho added that the high number “suggests several possibilities, none of which are positive”, including that conditions are so bad that more people are hunger striking in protest, and that officials “are more frequently failing to attempt to resolve the issue in a less confrontational and dangerous manner, instead resorting to forced medical intervention”. The Cuban man was arrested by ICE on 22 July and was declared a hunger striker three days later, court records show. The Montgomery facilityholding him is run by the private prison company GEO Group. A GEO Group spokesperson referred all questions to ICE. The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which is representing ICE in the latest court proceedings, did not respond to a request for comment. An ICE official and a doctor at the facility requested permission to force-feed the Cuban hunger striker in August, filings show. On 19 August, federal judge Andrew Hanen gave permission for ICE to force-feed the hunger striker. And on 1 September, ICE requested the judge extend his order. This Wednesday, Hanen extended the order, which is set to expire in mid-September. It includes the option for ICE touse the surgical tube insertion. Like in many cases reviewed by the Guardian, the Cuban hunger striker does not have any current legal representation. “The fact that this person lacks legal representation in a process where the government seeks to subject him to an invasive, involuntary medical procedure performed without consent is a tragedy, and a clear failure of our justice system,” Cho said. “The secretive nature of these cases, and the opacity of the legal process by which the government brings these motions, should concern us all.” According to a DHS spokesperson, the Cuban hunger striker entered the US unlawfully in 1980 and was ordered deported in 2004. The DHS claims he was previously convicted of “aggravated assault with a weapon, aggravated battery, drug possession, and carrying a concealed firearm”. The spokesperson added that he “received due process and will remain in ICE custody until removed from the United States”. The DHS also said facilities distribute proper food, hygiene, phone and other basic services, and that “during hunger strikes, ICE continues to provide three meals a day, delivered to the detained alien’s room”. The Trump administration had previously refused to acknowledge the force-feeding of hunger strikers in ICE detention, until later into the Guardian’s investigation confirming the practice.

title: ‘It cost me many friendships’: former Brazil military chief reveals inside struggle to stop Bolsonaro’s coup
summary: Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior describes 2022 meeting in new book as ex-leader’s son vies with Lula for presidency
text: The far-right populist Jair Bolsonaro was in his final days as Brazil’s president when, six weeks after losing the election and still refusing to recognise the result, he summoned the heads of the armed forces to a meeting. The defence minister, Gen Paulo Sérgio Nogueira de Oliveira, took out a document from a plastic folder and handed copies to the commanders of the navy, army and air force. It was a draft decree proposing to invalidate Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s election in October 2022 and keep Bolsonaro in power. “The draft coup decree – which some people still insist to this day never existed – was there, awaiting approval or rejection; consensus or a majority,” writes the then head of the air force, Lt Brig Carlos de Almeida Baptista Júnior, in a new book coming out this month. After learning that the document would prevent Lula from taking office, Baptista Júnior told the defence minister he refused even to receive it: “The air force will not take part in this.” He then stood up and left the room. The extensive investigation and trial that convicted Bolsonaro of attempting a coup concluded that the plot failed to move forward mainly because the heads of two of the three armed forces – Baptista Júnior and the army commander, Gen Marco Antônio Freire Gomes – refused to take part. The navy commander, Adm Almir Garnier Santos, was convicted, as was Nogueira. Both are serving their sentences at military facilities, while Bolsonaro is under house arrest. Freire Gomes has kept a low profile, but Baptista Júnior, speaking to the Guardian by video call, said he had decided to write a book to help prevent history from repeating itself. In the book, the 65-year-old former fighter pilot gives a detailed, first-hand account of the various ways in which Bolsonaro tried to cling to power. Baptista Júnior said he was motivated by the fact that, despite the abundance of evidence presented during the former president’s trial, opinion polls still showed that about a third of the population did not believe there had been an attempted coup. “Keeping in power someone who lost an election is a coup d’état,” he said, speaking from his home in Brasília, where he was dressed in civilian clothes – having recently retired – and about to pick up his grandson from school. The book, the Portuguese title of which translates as I Said No! – An Anti-Coup Bulwark, is due to be published on 15 September, about two weeks before the first round of the presidential election, in which Lula will face one of Bolsonaro’s sons, the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro. Some Bolsonaro supporters have accused Baptista Júnior of trying to influence the vote, although he makes clear that he will vote for neither Lula nor Flávio, and criticises both in the book. He said the timing of the book was simply the result of the writing and editing process. Despite writing that he voted for the far-right populist in the 2018 and 2022 elections, and even recounting a lighthearted moment at a barbecue when he saw the first lady reprimand the president for drinking beer, Baptista Júnior is critical of Bolsonaro, a former army captain who spent 30 largely undistinguished years as a city councillor and then congressman before reaching the presidency. He describes his former boss as someone with “significant limitations in political, institutional and administrative experience” and an “almost total imperviousness to outside opinions or information that did not conform to the ‘truths’ he had already established as his own” – citing his refusal to accept facts such as the scientific evidence supporting Covid-19 vaccination. During the election, Bolsonaro became “entirely consumed by his own efforts to remain in office”, writes Baptista Júnior. After repeatedly casting doubt on the vote, the president ordered the armed forces to investigate the electronic voting system, but refused to accept their reports when they found no irregularities. “He may still not believe the election result even today. Whether that is a matter of character, personality or something pathological, I don’t know,” said Baptista Júnior. The book touches on, but does not go into detail about, one of the most shocking revelations from the coup investigation: a plan drawn up by army special forces to kidnap or assassinate Lula, the newly elected vice-president and a supreme court justice. Baptista Júnior writes that he was not summoned to those meetings and only learned about them through the press. He does, however, recount more than a dozen meetings in which Bolsonaro summoned the heads of the armed forces to discuss ways to remain in power. At one of them, he witnessed the army chief tell the president, after hearing a proposal for an institutional rupture: “If you do that, I’ll have to arrest you.” Baptista Júnior had already given that account in testimony, and during the trial both Freire Gomes and Bolsonaro denied it. But he stands by his account in the book, writing that it was not something anyone present would forget. Saying no to the coup cost the pilot “many friendships”, he said. Even some military personnel still call him a “traitor” or a “watermelon”, a slur for soldiers seen as green on the outside because of their uniforms, but communist red within. The attacks started soon after the air force chief refused to join the plot, when the army general Walter Souza Braga Netto, whom Baptista Júnior considered a friend, ordered other military officers to attack him on social media and “make his life and his family’s hell”. Braga Netto, Bolsonaro’s running mate, was also convicted over the attempted coup. Most of Baptista Júnior’s revelations in the book initially emerged in 2024, when he was summoned to testify to federal police and only then, more than a year after leaving office, revealed that he had witnessed an attempted coup. Juliano da Silva Cortinhas, who worked on the civilian side of the defence ministry between 2013 and 2016, before the Bolsonaro administration, said: “It’s positive that he [Baptista Júnior] and the army chief said no to the coup, but as a matter of duty they should have reported it to the police as soon as it happened.” Cortinhas, who heads a security research group at the University of Brasília, said the armed forces could not present themselves as the “saviours” of democracy because that would be like “tripping society up and then holding out a hand to help it back to its feet”. “It was the commanders who allowed active-duty officers to take part in politics,” he said, noting that the Bolsonaro administration had by far the largest number of military personnel serving in civilian posts since the end of the brutal 1964–85 military dictatorship. Cortinhas sees as positive the fact that high-ranking officers were convicted of an attempted coup for the first time, but noted that others involved in the plot escaped justice, and many were not even identified. “The risk of a new coup is even greater today,” he said. The new factor, he said, was the US president, Donald Trump, who has sought to influence elections across Latin America in support of far-right candidates such as Flávio Bolsonaro. In 2022, when Joe Biden was in the White House, Bolsonaro’s vice-president acknowledged that attempting a coup would leave Brazil in a “difficult position before the international community”. Cortinhas said he feared that if Lula was re-elected and Trump refused to recognise the result, some members of Brazil’s military could feel emboldened. “Coup-supporting groups remain within the armed forces,” he said. Baptista Júnior confirmed that, although it was difficult to know how many, there remained active-duty military personnel who believed a coup d’état would be justified under certain circumstances. “That’s why eternal vigilance is the best path,” he said.

title: Gaza refugee says sister-in-law ‘would be alive’ if Home Office had let her come to UK
summary: Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, says Home Office refused visa application despite Maryam having cancer
text: A man living in the UK has said he believes his sister-in-law who died from cancer in Gaza would still be alive today if the Home Office had agreed to bring her and her family to Britain. Anwar, who lives in Glasgow, fled Gaza in 2020 and was granted refugee status in the UK in 2021. After the destruction of large areas of Gaza by Israeli forces following the Hamas attacks on Israel in October 2023, he applied to bring his brother Hassan, Hassan’s wife, Maryam, their two young children and other family members to the UK in October 2025. He said the Home Office rejected their application. The process required them to travel to a visa application centre (VAC) for biometric checks, but there was not, and still is not, a VAC in Gaza. It is difficult for Palestinians to leave the territory to access a VAC elsewhere. In April this year the family asked the Home Office to waive this requirement and grant permission for “predetermination” of their application and “biometric excusal”. The Home Office is understood to have rejected this request, so the family launched a legal challenge. The Home Office agreed to reconsider its decision but issued a new refusal in July. Prior to the second Home Office refusal, and shortly after Maryam gave birth to Ismail, who is now seven months old, she was diagnosed with renal cell carcinoma, which had spread to her lungs. Doctors in Gaza said they did not have the facilities to treat her. The family provided the Home Office with medical evidence concerning Maryam’s condition, including cancer test results and medical referral reports. They also provided evidence of their living conditions in Gaza, which involved sleeping in tents and shortages of food, medicine and clean water. Anwar said the Home Office again refused the family’s request for predetermination and biometric excusal but that it accepted the evidence of Maryam’s cancer. In the Home Office’s letter refusing the visa application on 31 July, seen by the Guardian, officials stated: “Given the current situation in Gaza, reliable healthcare may not be accessible.” They accepted that Maryam was facing a significant risk of harm because she was in a conflict zone and could not travel to a VAC. Although the Home Office officials found the circumstances relating to travel to a VAC “somewhat compelling”, they concluded that owing to the difficulty in travelling to the VAC, it was “in the best interests of the children to stay with their parents and delay travel to the UK” for the time being. They concluded the family’s situation did not meet the threshold for “compelling circumstances” and said that pre-entry checks needed to be carried out because the family came from “a territory where terrorists operate”. In the legal challenge, the family’s lawyers stated: “It is difficult to understand what circumstances would ever qualify as compelling if the present circumstances do not.” Maryam died from cancer on 28 August. Gordon McKee, the Labour MP for Glasgow South, raised the family’s case with ministers in June. He warned about Maryam’s deteriorating health and the consequences of the collapse of reliable healthcare in Gaza. In his letter to Mike Tapp, then a Home Office minister, McKee said the case involved “exceptional humanitarian circumstances”. He asked Tapp to consider reviewing the case personally. Anwar said: “We believe Maryam’s case raises serious questions about how the UK government deals with Palestinian families in Gaza who are trying to reunite with their families in Britain, particularly when a family member becomes seriously ill while trapped in a conflict zone and unable to safely reach a VAC. “I believe that if the Home Office had agreed to bring Maryam and her family from Gaza to the UK when we first applied last October, Maryam would still be alive today. “Maryam is now gone, but her family remains in Gaza. We are now urgently asking the UK government to intervene to protect Maryam’s surviving family members and to find a way to bring them to safety and reunite them with their family in the UK.” Speaking from Gaza, Maryam’s husband, Hassan, said: “I am struggling to come to terms with losing my wife while I remain trapped in Gaza with our children, including our seven-month-old baby. “Throughout Maryam’s illness, we were trying to find a way for our family to overcome the biometric requirement and move forward with our applications. The Home Office accepted that Maryam had cancer and acknowledged the evidence, but decided that our circumstances were still not compelling enough to justify biometric deferral or predetermination. “Now I have lost my wife, and I am left trying to protect our children and find a way to get them out of Gaza and to safety.” Home Office sources said they did not routinely comment on individual cases.

title: Sweden confirms 458 Britons deported or forcibly removed since Brexit
summary: Scale of deportations made public for first time amid criticism of hardline approach to UK citizens
text: Sweden has confirmed 458 British citizens have been deported or forcibly removed by police since Brexit. It is the first time the scale of the deportations of citizens who failed to secure residency in Sweden post-Brexit has been made public and comes amid mounting criticism of a cruel and hardline approach to Britons who had chosen to make the country their home before Brexit. Some have been told to go after more than 25 years in the country and even vulnerable elderly people with dementia have been affected. One man was deported even though he had lived in the country since he was 10 years old. Susanna Fonsell, a unit manager and legal expert at the Swedish Migration Agency, told Sverige Radio: “A rejected application does not necessarily result in deportation… and according to the agency statistics, the agency’s rejections of an application for resident status has been accomplished by a deportation decision in only approximately 400 cases,” she told Sweden Radio. The Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, confirmed to the Guardian that 458 British citizens had been deported since Brexit. “According to the agency’s statistics, the Swedish Migration Agency’s rejection of an application for residence status has been accompanied by a deportation decision in only 458 cases,” a spokesperson said. David Milstead, who heads up the 9,000-strong activist group Brits in Sweden, said it was important for Sweden to release full and transparent figures in relation to removals and deportations and their circumstances. “We need to understand exactly what the 458 represents. Does it capture people who gave up and left when they realised their withdrawal agreement application was unlikely to succeed? Does it include people who were refused withdrawal agreement status, subsequently obtained a permit under national law and were only later ordered to leave? “It certainly does not capture people who are currently managing to remain in Sweden on temporary permits, with little certainty about their long-term future.” He said the figures illustrated a “broader problem” in that the data was issued piecemeal and sometimes in an opaque manner. “We still do not have basic published figures showing how many people submitted a missed-deadline application and the fraction of these which succeeded,” he said. The last available data shows that there were 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency, which included family members joining British citizens after the deadline by 2024. Of those, just under 4,000 were rejected, a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3% and 4%, according to Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) analysis. Deportations are still happening. This week, the Swedish wife of a former business director from Cambridge told how her husband was detained in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a forced removal. She said they had been fighting to overturn the decision by the migration authorities for five years and felt that they had been “hunted”. Earlier this week, the Guardian revealed a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, who had lived in Sweden since he was 10, had been deported, separating him from his wife, Caroline, in Gothenburg, who said people needed to know how Brexit had “crushed families”. Another woman, 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, has been told to remove herself from the country before next Wednesday. Friends are trying to get an injunction and have appealed to the European Commission for help. If she fails to comply, not only will she face a forced deportation, but the court of appeal has told her she could face a “re-entry ban” and be “registered on a watchlist” preventing potential entry into a Schengen country, which includes Sweden “as long as the re-entry ban remains in effect”. The Swedish Migration Agency told the Guardian it had “no indication that Sweden has in any way interpreted the withdrawal agreement in an extreme manner or differently from other member states. The Swedish Migration Agency has applied applicable law, and there has been an opportunity to appeal rejection decisions.” Late applications for post-Brexit residency are allowed under the Brexit withdrawal agreement, both in the EU and the UK, but applicants have to show “reasonable grounds” for missing the deadline. The FCDO has said that “in practice” late applicants in Sweden “are not likely to have their reasonable grounds accepted”. Earlier this week, Sweden’s migration minister, Johan Forssell, said his government had followed the rules but that it was willing to look into the matter. “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future,” he said. A spokesperson for the FCDO said: “We continue to raise this with the Swedish authorities and welcome their statement that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so.” Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for Sweden’s opposition Centre party, said the government needed to go much further. He pledged to bring in new laws if his party won power at the next general election to allow British to reapply for post-Brexit residence, saying “a touch of humanity” was needed.

title: ‘Sinn Féin traitors!’: how far-right rhetoric derailed party’s path to power in Ireland
summary: Party insider reveals how election campaign was blindsided by rise of anti-immigrant feeling in new book
text: For Siobhán Fenton, the dream of Sinn Féin winning power and leading a progressive leftwing government evaporated the day she was canvassing in Dublin and felt a cold, sharp sting on her neck. She was in the passageway of a block of flats in the inner city, knocking on doors, and looked around for the source. Fenton, a media adviser to the party leader, Mary Lou McDonald, felt another sting on her shoulder, then another on her forearm. They were coins, thrown from a balcony above, where a man’s voice was shouting. “Sinn Féin traitors!” he roared. “Mary Lou Mohammad! Ireland is full!” It was May 2024, and instead of steaming towards victory in local and European elections – widely deemed a foregone conclusion, to be followed by a historic triumph in a general election – the party was experiencing a backlash fuelled by anti-immigrant sentiment in what was usually a bastion of working-class support. The coins left Fenton with gashes and bruises that augured an electoral hammering. “By the time the party realised how bad things had gotten it was almost too late,” she said. “The far right had infiltrated lots of Sinn Féin strongholds and we hadn’t picked up on it.” In a rupture to the party’s reputation for secrecy and discipline, Fenton has written a rare insider’s account, titled Ourselves Alone: Sinn Féin Behind Closed Doors. It lifts the lid on a debacle that ambushed the party on the path to power. Instead of winning a general election and turbo-charging the campaign for Irish unification by ratcheting up pressure for a referendum, the party stumbled and today remains in opposition. It is a cautionary tale for progressive movements across Europe and elsewhere that struggle to reconcile tolerance for immigrants and refugees with clamours for crackdowns on new arrivals. A surge in xenophobia among grassroots supporters had blind-sided and, for a time, paralysed party leaders, Fenton said in an interview. “There was a moment of genuine sheer panic and just not knowing what to do. We were struggling to adapt because it was a sense that things had started to spiral out of control.” The book, published this week, depicts a largely well-intentioned but hapless party, and is also an account from a member of an organisation that many perceive as secretive and still in thrall to former IRA leaders on both sides of the Irish border, a perception Fenton disputes. Fenton, 34, was an atypical “Shinner”, the informal name for party adherents. She came from a middle-class Belfast family that abhorred the violence of the Troubles and favoured constitutional nationalism, not flinty republicanism. Fenton briefly worked for the Social Democratic and Labour party (SDLP) before studying English literature at Oxford, researching gender-based violence at Cambridge and becoming a London-based journalist for the Independent before returning to Northern Ireland in 2016, where she freelanced for the BBC and other outlets, including the Guardian, and wrote a book on the Good Friday agreement. In early 2020, Sinn Féin offered Fenton a job in Dublin. The party was on a high. It had just won 24.5% of first preference votes in the Irish general election, overtaking Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael, two centrist parties that had alternated in power for a century. As successor to Gerry Adams, McDonald, a Dubliner universally known as Mary Lou, offered a fresh alternative, especially to young voters who blamed the political establishment for a housing crisis. Sinn Féin had run too few candidates to capitalise on the breakthrough, so Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael mustered enough seats to form a coalition, leaving Sinn Féin in opposition. Analysts expected it to win power after the next election. After Sinn Féin became the biggest party in Northern Ireland in 2022, which paved the way for Michelle O’Neill to become first minister at Stormont, the onus was on the party’s southern branch to ensure McDonald became taoiseach at Leinster House. “Don’t fuck it up,” a Belfast colleague half-jokingly told Fenton. For three years, Fenton, having relocated to Dublin, experienced the giddy nervousness of a party soaring in the polls while the ruling coalition slumped. The republican mantra – “tiocfaidh ár lá”, our day will come – seemed apt. A section titled “the long fall” chronicles the unravelling amid missteps and a volatile public mood. McDonald appeared to blame police for a riot that rocked Dublin in November 2023, and alarmed middle-class property owners by suggesting average Dublin house prices should fall to €300,000. More damagingly, the party failed to navigate growing xenophobia, the result of a housing shortage, a cost of living crisis, an influx of migrants and refugees, and far-right activism on social media and the streets. “It was a blind spot,” said Fenton. Covid-19 restrictions and a focus on the parliamentary party withered grassroots networking, leaving leaders unaware of the extent to which conspiracy theories and hostility to Muslims had taken hold, she said. The party should have tried to combat racist narratives by peeling people away from smartphones and having “really difficult conversations”, said Fenton. “Go door to door, talk about community concerns but be very, very clear that scapegoating immigrants and refugees is the wrong response.” Instead of gains in the May 2024 local and European elections, the cascade of coins on to Fenton foretold haemorrhaging support, especially in working-class strongholds that branded McDonald a “traitor” for not seeking greater curbs on migration. Months later the party limped into a general election that kept Fianna Fáil and Fine Gael in power. Fenton’s contract was not renewed and she returned to her native Belfast, where she now works as a writer and analyst. She is no longer a member of Sinn Féin. Immigration remains a fraught issue for a party squeezed between those wanting a harder line and those who favour solidarity, said Fenton. Leaders may be tempted to sidestep the issue until the next election, then take a stance, she said. “It will be dependent on what the political environment looks like then.”

title: Leftist insurgents are storming the midterms – just don’t call them all democratic socialists
summary: Progressive candidates navigate their ties to the DSA as the group faces historic growth and mounting pressure
text: Days before he won the Democratic primary for a US Senate seat in Michigan, insurgent newcomer Abdul El-Sayed was asked whether he was concerned about being labeled a “socialist”. “I’d rather think of myself as a capitalist who has actually read about capitalism,” El-Sayed told CBS News anchor Ed O’Keefe. “I’m not a socialist.” While El-Sayed might take pains to distance himself from the label in the swing state of Michigan, O’Keefe noted that the candidate has been linked to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the ascendant leftist group whose meteoric rise has captured the enthusiasm of voters desperate for bold change and whose recent wins have stoked the anxieties of both conservatives and the party’s establishment. “I’m not DSA,” El-Sayed stressed in the interview, though he made clear there is room for the DSA in the “big tent” he said he’s seeking to build. El-Sayed is just one of a number of progressive candidates and elected officials across the country who are navigating their relationship and differences with the DSA, which has come under increasing pressure as its candidates have won one race after the other in Democratic primaries mostly in blue states. But as other progressive candidates to the left of the Democratic establishment have mounted bids for office, there has at times been confusion about who is a “DSA candidate” – a confusion some Republicans have been eager to exploit. Some, like El-Sayed, espouse many of the group’s political priorities – fighting fascism, instating universal healthcare, getting money out of politics and boosting labor rights, to name a few – but are not members, nor have they been endorsed by the DSA. Others, like New York’s Claire Valdez, have been organizing with the group for years. Then there are those like Colorado’s Melat Kiros and Pennsylvania’s Chris Rabb who have long identified as socialists but only recently joined the organization. (All three are DSA-endorsed.) Brad Lander was once a member but left the group over its response to the 7 October 2023 attacks in Israel. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the national figure most often associated with the DSA, rejoined the New York City chapter last month after letting her membership lapse for seven years, as speculation mounts about her intention to run for president. But DSA membership doesn’t guarantee endorsement, and intense debates have roiled the organization in recent months about which candidates to endorse and how to best ride the current momentum. In Los Angeles, for example, the local DSA chapter voted to endorse mayoral candidate Nithya Raman this week after weeks of discussions on whether she was too centrist to earn their backing. Pragmatism v purism A decade into Trumpism and the Democrats’ failure to stop it, and buoyed up by the popularity of longtime member Zohran Mamdani, the DSA has helped popularize positions once viewed as radical – from taxing the rich to ending support for Israel. The DSA has become a “shorthand for this rebellion against Democratic party leadership”, said Peter Sterne, an editor at City & State New York who has extensively covered the DSA and a former member of the group. In recent months, the group has seen its membership soar to 120,000, its leaders are getting prime time on cable news and a recent poll found that one-third of Democrats now openly identify as “socialist”, a term not long ago viewed as a slur. The backlash has been swift. After DSA candidates won nine out of 10 races in which the group had fielded candidates in New York City in June, party establishment figures issued a string of hostile statements. Third Way, a centrist Democratic group, announced a $15m effort to go to “war” against them. DSA leaders and members have become tabloid fodder. And this week, House Republicans – joined by eight Democrats – adopted a resolution condemning “socialism” and specifically naming the DSA. The organization’s critics point to some of its more radical stances, from eliminating the Senate to abolishing borders and defunding the police, as a sign of its unseriousness. But many DSA members view those as aspirational and consistent with the group’s fundamental values, while calling for a more realistic approach. Even some more moderate Democrats recognize that the DSA’s message is resonating because the rest of the party has failed to present a satisfying vision of its own. “You can’t beat something with nothing,” said Bill Galston, a senior fellow in governance studies at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington. “The more moderate wing of the Democratic party is going to have to raise its game substantially.” The DSA’s popularity and campaigning capacity on the one hand, and the animosity from more conservative corners on the other, has left some candidates, particularly in swing states, navigating a balancing act. In Florida, Angie Nixon, who recently won the Democratic Senate primary in one of the biggest upsets of the primary season, joined the DSA only in June but has not been endorsed by the group. When asked whether she identified as a democratic socialist, she equivocated. “I don’t agree with everything that they agree with, but they’re fighting hard to ensure we have access to universal healthcare, access to free college and fully funded public schools,” she said in an interview with the Guardian. “I’ve always been a lifelong Democrat but I’m more of [a] social democrat who believes in strong safety nets.” Some of the most popular politicians associated with the DSA have broken with the group on some issues. The group has for months been debating how to respond to a possible presidential run by Ocasio-Cortez. Some factions, and particularly many NYC-DSA members, have openly encouraged it, while others are suspicious of what they view as her willingness to compromise on DSA priorities. Mamdani has also broken with the group over policing. Ultimately, the decision will be made democratically – DSA members report often excruciatingly deliberative processes and stress that the “democratic” element of the group’s identity is just as fundamental as its socialist one. Endorsements, Sterne noted, can power a campaign with an “army” of canvassers and phone bank volunteers – the DSA’s New York City chapter says that its 50,000 volunteers knocked on doors 1.6m times in support of Mamdani’s candidacy. But the “DSA doesn’t just want to help get people into office and then let them do whatever they want”, he added, noting that there was some concern within the organization that candidates may opportunistically hitch their wagon to the group but not work with it after getting elected. The tension between the pragmatists and the purists, he argued, is healthy, and a sign of the organization’s strength. “More people are joining,” he said. “More people are identifying as socialists, which was once seen as a taboo term.”

title: A Glitz-Free Place Named for Trump? Welcome to the Golan Heights.

title: ‘We’re plausibly close to crossing the line’: are warnings of uncontrollable AI coming true?
summary: A spate of serious safety incidents have increased fears about the power and impenetrability of the most advanced models
text: Picture humanity in a boat being swept down a raging river, praying there is no Niagara Falls ahead. Or imagine standing with the pioneering physicists in 1942 before they triggered the first self-sustaining nuclear fission chain reaction beneath a Chicago stadium. These were two of the analogies used this week by Prof Robert Trager, an expert in the nascent field of AI governance, to describe the perilous but potential-filled moment the world stands at with accelerating artificial intelligence. Trager, the director of the Oxford Martin AI Governance Initiative, was speaking in the week OpenAI claimed the technology had crossed the threshold known as AGI – artificial general intelligence – with its newest model, GPT-6 Astra. That claim came as the company prepared for a potential $850bn (£630bn) stock flotation, so included a dose of marketing spin, but if true it may be significant. The San Francisco company defines AGI as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. The tasks it claims Astra can automate include designing circuit boards, filling out tax returns, building video games, financial modelling, engineering design and helping assemble legal documents. The threat to some white-collar jobs is implicit. Yet, the AGI claim coincides with rising fears about AI risks among safety experts and political leaders, whose nerves have been jangled by the increasing power and impenetrability of AI models this summer and a spate of serious safety accidents viewed by some as possible final warning shots. “We’re heading through the rapids and we’re really hoping there isn’t some kind of drop in front of us and we don’t really know,” said Trager. “We’re plausibly close to crossing the line to what’s called recursive self-improvement, where [AI] systems improve themselves. That kind of recursivity is actually the definition of an explosion.” The latest worry came on Friday, just hours after Astra’s launch, with reports that a swarm of AI agents had repurposed a German website as a message board to share tactics to cheat on tasks, according to Reuters. OpenAI said it was reviewing the matter but would not characterise it as a hack. There is a sense of an awakening among politicians. On Thursday, the US senator Bernie Sanders cited this summer’s alarming breakout of a swarm of rogue OpenAI agents which hacked into Hugging Face, a third-party software store, when he called for “an immediate pause on advanced AI development, and a permanent ban on superintelligence”. He said countries around the world must “work together to prevent this nightmare scenario”, which he defined as “an artificial mind smarter than any human, capable of operating independently beyond our control”. Concerns currently focus on AIs mounting cyber-attacks that could cripple real-world social and economic infrastructure, but future concerns include their ability to create biohazards and control military hardware. Across the Atlantic, a cross-party group of UK parliamentarians has called for AI “kill switches” to be required by law to prevent disastrous loss of control, citing “a recent spree of rogue AI incidents”. Darren Jones, an MP and former chief secretary to Keir Starmer, is also urgently attempting to set up a body to help legislators grapple with the technology. “AI is developing at such a pace that neither government nor parliament can keep up,” he warned. And next week a bill will be proposed by the Labour MP Alex Sobel to prohibit superintelligent AI development in the UK. The increasing anxiety comes amid a torrent of new AI models. Already this year, 67 have been released by the leading US companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, and their Chinese rivals Moonshot, Z.ai and Qwen, according to one count. With every increase in power, there is a potential increase in risk. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which is targeting a $2tn stock exchange listing, this week admitted its own AIs were “not perfectly aligned” with human values and said there had been a “failure of operational security” in July hacks by its own model, Claude. It said the incidents had “stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defences is even higher than we previously believed”. AI’s double edge – opportunity and risk – was on show when OpenAI launched Astra on Thursday. Its marketing video focused not on the risks but on the breezy convenience that AI could offer to a certain kind of customer. It showed an upmarket San Francisco woman simultaneously booking a tennis court and designing a presentation for her high-end rainwear collection; a thirtysomething man being helped to build his dream space invaders game and order a takeaway; a law firm executive being helped to draft some contracts. Yet only weeks ago, this was a model whose training had to be partly paused because of safety concerns after the Hugging Face incident. An independent safety researcher drafted in to investigate, Ajeya Cotra, said it was “more than 50% of the way to full-blown AI takeover”. Astra also has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability – the first time it has given a model such a label. It means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. The company’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, insisted the model was properly aligned not to do that, but added that “as these models become more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder”. The ability to monitor what AI models are “thinking” as they advance is another growing source of safety fears. This week it was reported that OpenAI had been training Astra to reason not only in natural language, but in a more opaque manner that is faster and more efficient – and can make models’ chains of reasoning harder to follow. It means a model’s internal calculations may not always be written out as directly readable words – as if it was thinking in its head, rather than showing its working. Some experts fear this could help AIs covertly conspire against their human overseers. OpenAI confirmed Astra “shows a substantial decrease in chain-of-thought monitorability compared to previous models” and Pachocki said “as model capabilities are increasing, monitorability is getting more challenging”. The company played down the development, but the increase in opaque reasoning sparked concern from AI safety researchers. Ryan Greenblatt, the chief scientist at Redwood Research, a nonprofit examining AI safety and security, called it “extremely concerning”. Gary Marcus, an influential AI sceptic, compared it to kicking away an already “rickety scaffolding before we have something better”. OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, said this week he felt conflicted about the advances of AI models. He admitted OpenAI’s security had “failed” in the Hugging Face incident and called it “a legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure”. “We have been living with the tension between being excited and anxious about progress for some time, and it is still discordant for us,” he said in a tweet. “We know it is much more discordant for other people.” His rationale for releasing OpenAI’s most powerful model so soon after a safety crisis appears to be that the world needs to see how AIs perform in the real world to understand where AI is heading. He said: “An iterative loop where society and this technology evolve together is what will lead to the highest chance of getting this right.” And yet he can see the risks. On Tuesday he addressed the G20 ministerial summit in North Carolina in the US and told politicians that “some things are going to go very wrong with cybersecurity unless people act quite urgently”. He added: “There will be other challenges in the next five years. People talk about biosecurity and the things we are going to face there. There will be bigger ones yet to come.”

title: The two-year trail of financial controversy dogging Reform and Farage
summary: Six claims the party has faced – from an undisclosed £5m gift to an alleged plot to bypass election laws
text: As Reform UK’s annual conference unfolded in Birmingham, the party was once again facing heightened scrutiny over its finances. Two senior officials have been suspended after they were filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations. Here we look at the various allegations related to finances levelled at the party and its leader, Nigel Farage, in recent years. Farage said he had ‘bought a house’ in Clacton – it’s actually owned by his girlfriend In 2025, it emerged that Farage had not – as he had claimed – bought a property in his parliamentary constituency of Clacton, in Essex: it had in fact been bought by his girlfriend, Laure Ferrari. The Reform leader said he had “exchanged contracts” to buy the house in Essex in November 2024, saying it should deal with criticism that he does not spend enough time in the constituency. But it emerged the detached property in an upmarket part of Clacton-on-Sea was solely bought by Ferrari. It was alleged that this allowed him legally to avoid higher-rate stamp duty on the purchase of an additional residential house, given that he already owns other properties. Farage’s solicitors provided a statement to say they had received advice from a leading tax barrister, which concluded the stamp duty was properly calculated and there was no improper tax evasion. Farage was given an undisclosed £5m gift by crypto billionaire in 2024 The Guardian revealed in April 2026 that Farage was given £5m by the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne shortly before announcing he would stand in the 2024 UK general election. Farage had stated he did not intend to stand as a prospective MP but made a U-turn in June 2024, within weeks of receiving the personal gift from the Thailand-based businessman. In July 2024, Farage became an MP for the first time and has since stated he aspires to become prime minister at the next general election. The Reform leader maintains the gift was accepted in a personal and non-political capacity, and therefore did not need to be declared to parliamentary authorities. While his explanations for receiving the money have changed, he has most consistently stuck with “security” as the reason behind taking the cash. Lawyers for Harborne have said he “expected nothing in return” for the gift and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”. Harborne’s gift is the subject of an inquiry by parliament’s standards commissioner, which resumed last month after Farage won a byelection in Clacton. Police investigate £500,000 donations from mother of fraudster who backed Farage In July it emerged that the Met police are investigating donations worth £500,000 made to Reform UK by Fiona Cottrell, whose son George is a longtime aide to Farage and a convicted fraudster in the US. The donations, in May 2024, are under investigation over whether they were intended to conceal a donation by an impermissible donor. They appear to be separate to a deposit of about £1m that Fiona Cottrell made in June 2024 to a company run by Richard Tice, Reform’s deputy leader. Later in July, the Guardian revealed George Cottrell transferred a total of more than $2m (£1.5m) to his mother in the days before her 2024 donations to the party. Earlier that month, the Sunday Times revealed that Cottrell had provided funding for Farage’s operation, including for staffing, security and housing, and had recruited and paid three staff to work on Farage’s social media before the general election, and offered Farage the use of a five-storey Georgian townhouse he rented near Buckingham Palace. Under rules in place at the time, new MPs were required to register any gifts worth more than £300 they had received in the previous 12 months, except where the gift “could not be reasonably thought by others” to relate to their political activities. Fiona Cottrell has not responded to detailed questions from the Guardian about her financial involvement with Reform, while lawyers acting for George Cottrell refused to answer detailed questions from the Guardian about his financial ties to his mother. Farage and Reform have said they have done nothing wrong. Reform UK transactions worth millions reported to National Crime Agency A host of transactions involving Reform UK’s most senior figures and donations to the party caused bankers to report potential money-laundering concerns to the National Crime Agency. The Guardian revealed in July that the undisclosed £5m gift provided by Harborne shortly before the 2024 general election was reported to the NCA as well as transfers of funds between Tice, Fiona and George Cottrell. Suspicious activity reports raised by bankers were passed to the NCA for examination. Reform declined to comment. Fiona Cottrell has not responded to attempts to contact her. George Cottrell’s lawyers refused to respond to detailed questions. Crypto billionaire pardoned by Trump gives Reform another £4m It was reported in the Guardian this month that the British crypto billionaire Ben Delo – who was formerly based in Hong Kong – donated £4m to the party earlier in 2026. Delo, who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business, before being pardoned by Donald Trump, has previously given Reform another £4m, bringing the total to £8m. It makes him the party’s second biggest contributor after Harborne, who has given £15m to the party since the last election, as well as £5m to Farage personally before May 2024. In March, a rule was introduced that states donors must be on the UK domestic electoral register for at least 12 months to avoid being subject to a £100,000-a-year annual cap. A Reform source said the party was confident it would not have to return any of Delo’s latest £4m, raising the prospect that he may have been on the UK domestic electoral register for longer than previously thought. Reform officials ‘plotted to break law on foreign donations’ in undercover film Reform suspended two senior officials on 4 September after they were filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations. In a blow to Farage hours before his conference speech, the party said it had launched an investigation into the actions of James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Farage, after the broadcast by Channel 4 News. Jukes and Orr were filmed by a group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, allegedly helping to orchestrate a plot apparently to bypass election laws. Farage said the party had done nothing wrong and no rules were broken, saying on LBC that polls were funded by foreign sources all the time.

title: UK subsidence claims surge after hottest summer on record
summary: Insurers in England and Wales tell of busy August with one reporting near-140% jump in claims
text: UK insurers are experiencing a surge in the number of homeowners making claims for subsidence after the hottest summer on record, with Hastings Direct reporting a near 140% jump to an all-time high for August. Insurance firms have been overrun by calls and online queries, as well as a rise in claims during the five heatwaves that followed the warmest spring ever recorded in England and Wales. Subsidence claims typically peak during late summer and autumn, but this year they jumped in number during the summer. Millions of homes are at risk of subsidence because of the worsening climate crisis, the British Geological Survey has said. As hotter, drier summers become more frequent, the ground under houses can shrink and drag down a property’s foundations. Older properties are more at risk. The most vulnerable areas for subsidence include London, Essex, Kent and a tranche of land from Oxford up to the Wash on England’s east coast, according to scientists. Hastings Direct, which has 4.8 million home and motor insurance customers, said it had had a significant increase in subsidence claims over the summer and received a record number in August, almost 140% more than in the same month last year. After two unusually dry summers, subsidence activity has increased significantly, the company said. Hastings predicted the large volume of claims would continue into the autumn even though temperatures had returned to more normal levels and there had been some rainfall in recent weeks. “We expect claim volumes to remain higher than normal through to around October unless sustained rainfall helps restore soil moisture levels,” the insurer added. Signs of subsidence range from diagonal cracks around doors and windows that often widen over time; windows or doors that stick or will not close properly and uneven or sloping floors. Wallpaper creasing or rippling can also be a sign of subsidence, as well as damp. The average subsidence claim in the UK hit a record £20,000 between April and June, more than £2,000 higher than a year earlier, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). Insurers paid out £72m for domestic subsidence claims, up from £60m in the same period last year. About £297m in total was paid out on claims in 2025, up 6% from the year before, and 89% higher than in 2022, the ABI said. Charlie Inwood, the general insurance policy adviser at the ABI, said: “Following this summer’s hot weather, it’s likely we’ll see more subsidence claims over the coming months.” Aviva, which completed a £3.7bn acquisition of its rival Direct Line in July, and dominates the UK home insurance market, has also reported subsidence claim numbers had increased in recent months. “This is likely to continue unless there is significant rainfall,” it said. Amanda Blanc, the chief executive of Aviva, said last month that the company was reviewing the reserves it had set aside for subsidence claims, and would also look at its pricing models and exposure management. The insurer is also investigating what homeowners can do to prevent property damage from subsidence and flooding. Small shrinkage and movement cracks were normal after hot dry weather, Aviva said, while diagonal cracks that were more than 2.5cm wide, roughly the diameter of a £1 coin, could be a sign of subsidence. Axa, another home insurer, said it expected a “surge year” but could not say whether it would be a record year for subsidence claims. Adam Holland, the head of retail underwriting, fraud and pricing governance at the French company’s UK arm, said: “The Met Office’s announcement about summer 2026 being the hottest on record in the UK puts the impact of climate change into sharp focus … and we expect to see an increase in weather-related property damage this year.”

title: Food delivery riders call on platforms to open up AI ‘black box’ they say has cut pay
summary: Workers who blame algorithms for lowering their earnings are getting help from academics to find out how the system works
text: Gig economy workers are urging delivery platforms to open up the “black box” of computer-driven algorithms that determine the jobs they are offered and how much they are paid, blaming increased use of AI for lowering wages. A group of food delivery riders in Edinburgh say their rates of pay have fallen and their working conditions have deteriorated at the same time as Deliveroo, Uber Eats and Just Eat, the three dominant gig economy platforms in the UK and Ireland, have increased their use of automation. “I am making half the money I was making four years ago, for the same amount of hours. It makes no sense,” said David, a food delivery rider in Edinburgh for the past seven years who did not want to share his surname. On a weekday afternoon in the Scottish capital, David and other food delivery riders are sharing their experiences of worsening pay and conditions before they go their separate ways to carry food and groceries to customers’ doorsteps during the dinnertime rush. Standing next to their bikes and insulated food delivery bags in central Edinburgh’s Bristo Square, many have cycled the city streets for several years and tracked a gradual decline in the amount they are paid, even though they continue to deliver similar numbers of orders. The group has come together through the Workers’ Observatory, a charity founded by gig economy workers alongside academics at St Andrews and Edinburgh universities. Its aim is to help riders research the parts of their working experience that are mostly concealed by the companies that operate delivery platforms, to help them to challenge their working conditions. David’s experience is echoed by Xabier Villares, who has been riding for eight years and is now the observatory’s lead organiser. “There has been a dramatic change in the last three years,” he said. “I used to work four or five days a week, especially evenings and some lunchtimes, and was able to pay my rent and bills and make a decent living with that. But that’s not an option any more.” The observatory, which has just gained research funding for the next decade, has previously carried out experiments to monitor the variable levels of pay offered to different workers by algorithms, a system known as “dynamic pricing” that purports to match real-time supply and demand. Trades unions are campaigning to ban the practice, saying it leaves workers uncertain about their earnings. The introduction of a dynamic pricing algorithm in 2023 resulted in Uber drivers earning “substantially less” an hour, according to research from the University of Oxford and New York’s Columbia business school. This week drivers from the UK, the Netherlands and other countries launched a landmark class action against the ride-hailing app claiming they live in “constant fear” of the “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs. The legal case lodged in Amsterdam, which could run into billions of dollars, alleges the AI-powered system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings based on what each driver is willing to take. Uber denies adjusting trip prices based on an individual driver’s behaviour and has put discrepancies down to other features of its system such as GPS. Cailean Gallagher, director of the observatory and a lecturer at St Andrews university business school, said “there is so much infrastructure of knowledge and data that’s concealed” by the platforms, leaving gig economy riders “working in the dark”. He added: “What we are trying to do with the observatory is to get on the ground floor in terms of understanding how the whole apparatus works.” In one Workers’ Observatory test, a group of riders in Dunfermline, Fife, logged on to a delivery platform at the same time, with some rejecting job offers below a certain rate. This boosted the rate for some workers in the short term, while others were penalised – with one deactivated from the platform shortly afterwards, although it was unclear why – in a way that Gallagher says “seemed very arbitrary”. The major delivery platforms insist riders are not deactivated for rejecting job offers. Dylan* has notched up more than five years riding for Deliveroo in Scotland. Since mid-2023, he has kept meticulous records tracking his monthly income, number of orders delivered and what the average pay per order is. The number of orders Dylan delivers each hour has remained constant between 3.6 and 3.8 for the past three years. However, his records highlight how the average fee paid for each order has steadily declined over that period, from £3.67 in 2023, to £3.63 in 2024, £3.51 in 2025 and to £3.42 in the first half of 2026. “I like to keep a close eye on everything, normally just to make paying my taxes easier,” he said. “I started noticing a couple of years ago there was actually a big drop-off in my earnings. If you are doing the same amount of work, that equates to getting paid quite a lot less for the same work.” Dylan blames the algorithm for constantly undercutting rates, along with the introduction of what Deliveroo calls “stacked orders”, where riders can accept two or three orders from restaurants located close to each other, but not receive the level of fees they would get for delivering these separately. “Some of the offers they give you view you as a clown,” he said. Rider Graeme Frances believes the delivery platforms “rely on [the work] being opaque”. He said: “You don’t know what is in the black box of how they work out what to pay to whom.” Deliveroo has named its algorithm Frank and has previously described it as “super smart” and able to decide “which rider to offer which order”. The company, which was taken over by its US rival DoorDash in 2025, said Frank was “made up of machine-learning technology, which predicts the timings of every order”, allowing food to be delivered “in the most efficient and reliable way”. Frances also blames increased use of AI by the platforms for more log-on difficulties. After ending up with a black eye following an accident outside work in August 2025, the facial recognition technology did not allow him to log-on to the Deliveroo app, preventing him from working. He was unable to get help from human support staff. Deliveroo acknowledged Frances failed the facial recognition checks multiple times, stopping him from working, which it said was due to a blurry picture. Frances says he requested a manual review of his facial recognition check and was not aware he had passed this until the next time he logged in, leading him to believe he could not work until his injury had healed. Deliveroo says Frances would have been able to work after the manual review. Deliveroo, Uber Eats and Just Eat all say their riders earn more than the national living wage while they are on an order, but this does not include time waiting for job offers. A Deliveroo spokesperson said: “Riders are guaranteed to earn a minimum hourly fee while on an order, which … rose by 3.8% this year – an above inflation increase. “The vast majority of riders are satisfied working with us, and we continue to partner with the GMB Union to raise the bar on security and wellbeing standards. Information on our algorithm and fees are set out on our rider website. “We have a dedicated team in place to support riders, and any significant decision over a rider account is not automated, but reviewed by our team.” An Uber spokesperson said: “Our matching tools follow a process that balances a number of different factors, such as time and distance, to provide the best possible experience for everyone using the app.” A Just Eat spokesperson said: “As a delivery platform we use technology, overseen by a human team, to match deliveries with available couriers.” * Name has been changed
