title: How posh are you? Do you have a therapist? What would you say to Trump at a party? Marina Hyde answers readers’ questions
summary: We asked you what you most wanted to put to our Guardian columnist. You responded in droves, querying her ‘beef’ with Burnham, who she thinks is this generation’s Hugh Grant, and what she really thinks about Richard Osman ...
text: What are your bunker plans? James, Portugal Masses of things to read, incredible food and an unethical doctor with an insane war chest of interesting pills. The second that bunker door closes, the doors of perception are opening. Will Restore gain more traction by the next election and genuinely split the rightwing vote? Natasha, London They won’t split it in some 50‑50 way, but they could peel off a bit more from Reform’s right flank. Nigel Farage is looking vulnerable. In the Woody Allen film Deconstructing Harry, Robin Williams plays an actor who literally goes out of focus. Having once been sharp and clear, his nervous system is so shot that he becomes a physically blurred and imprecise distortion of himself. Metaphorically, something similar has happened to Farage in recent months. Who do you think is this generation’s young Hugh Grant (ie witty, funny, sexy, intelligent and gorgeous)? Anna, New Zealand It’s being done as a job share between Jude Bellingham and Cole Palmer. Are the men of the manosphere right about anything? Kate, London I saw Clavicular say, “My life is a horror story”, which feels about right. I have noticed a more serious tone in your columns this year. In light of recent events, here and abroad, are you finding it increasingly difficult to maintain your humorous disposition? Tim, London No. I’m sorry, I must have been tired when I wrote those ones. It’s always more effort to be funny than serious. If you met Andrew Tate, Elon Musk and Donald Trump at a hideous dinner party, how would you greet and say goodbye to each of them? Becky, Bristol “You must try the beef bourguignon. I hear our hostess foraged the mushrooms herself.” What would you have said to Margaret Thatcher’s face if you’d had a whole two minutes alone with her? Eamon, Ireland So much is known and has been written about her that new lines of inquiry can feel hard to come by. But I would have liked to find a way of getting her to reveal how she felt about being the object of so many men’s crushes. Both those who worked around her and what Norma Desmond called “all those wonderful people out there in the dark”. She knew, of course, and would most certainly have had Inner Thoughts about the phenomenon. However, I have to say, it would be quite difficult to build the rapport required to get them out of her in two minutes Why are journalists failing to make the case to the public that rightwingers such as Nigel Farage, Richard Tice and Stephen Yaxley‑Lennon are dishonest, self‑serving and not terribly bright? Alexis, Kent I really don’t think the vast majority of people pay the slightest direct attention to journalists at all. There are still some heavily invested continuity Corbynites out there who will imply that two or three critical columns I wrote about their absolute boy had something to do with him losing his second general election on the bounce in 2019. To which my reply would be: “Yes, dear, I’m sure they talked of little else but my columns on the doorsteps of the ‘red wall’. Yet, if we were to humour your notion that the whimsical musings of some silly cow in London make one nanoparticle of difference, how come I wrote 937 critical articles about Boris Johnson and he still won a landslide?” On the rightwingers front, however, I would point out that it is journalists and not anyone else who have been exposing, for example, Farage, Tice and Yaxley‑Lennon’s financial arrangements, and I’m very grateful to them for their work. The citations in your columns have taken me down some scurrilous rabbit holes I would not otherwise have encountered. How much of your research is spent in corners of the web you would rather not be? And do you have a therapist?! Ian, Aylesbury, Buckinghamshire Hahahahaha. Someone once told me they found out about edging videos from something I wrote about Theresa May’s endlessly inconclusive Brexit votes in the Commons. I can only apologise. Personally, I love the fact that I can spend my days wading through the more recherche bits of contemporary culture, and if anyone sees me, just say, “It’s for my WORK????” As far as the last part of the question goes, I don’t have a therapist. It’s so unfashionable, of course, but I have to say I’m a big, big believer in pushing it all down. I know, I know – I consistently note people’s looks of distaste when I tell them that. But I’m just putting the counterpoint out there. Your articles usually speak to power. Have you ever felt fear of the potential consequences? Chris, near Brighton, East Sussex The most credible politically motivated threats I have faced have been from the far right and the far left – and always from supporters rather than any publicly known figures. But – so far! – I’ve always found the bigger danger to be lone men who develop obsessions of one kind or another. Do you work on resilience? Mary, Dublin Not particularly consciously. But I valorise it. The older I get, the more I see that it is an endlessly useful kind of freedom. But that’s easy for me to say, because I’m so lucky. The resilience it takes to be, say, a woman in Afghanistan or a little girl in Congo is quite simply utterly inconceivable to me. I basically think that everything I have, and everything that I have achieved, is overwhelmingly the result of luck and good fortune, and not remotely to do with any kind of exceptionalist skill. If you had to spend a month on a desert island with a group of footballers, politicians or celebs, which would you choose and why? Charlie, Switzerland Hot footballers, let’s face it. Will Andy Burnham’s plan for a No 10 North in Manchester be a stroke of genius or his undoing? Patrick, LaSalle, Canada Neither (the most versatile answer in politics). Clearly, politicians are worse than useless. Who would you pick as prime minister? Eric, Newton Abbot, Devon JK Rowling. What’s always off-limits to critique? And what would feel important enough to make you reconsider your own boundaries? Josh, Palm Springs, US In general, I think everything can and should be written about, as long as you get the right tone. Anything involving children is always what I’d be most cautious about. Do you have a writing routine? Michael, Gijón, Spain I try to be at my desk at 5am, because I’m definitely a lark. Something that takes me five minutes at 5am will take me an hour at 5pm. So the morning is definitely my best writing time. As far as column-writing goes, I tend never to start with the first sentence. I just put a few things down in a Word document and move them all round till some kind of column starts to stagger out of the primordial soup. I mostly don’t know what I think until I’ve gone through the act of writing about it, so the conclusion can often be as much of a surprise to me as to anyone kind enough to read it. Which ludicrous situation involving a UK PM has made you laugh the most during your career? Richard, NSW, Australia Tony Blair having someone at the Foreign Office during the Iraq war whose official, ask-at-reception job title was “head of story development”. That was quite a mirthless laugh, obviously. David Cameron? Either leaving his daughter in the pub during a “troubled families” initiative week, or the shagging-the-pig’s-head thing. Theresa May calling a general election and the exit poll coming out at 10pm showing she’d lost her majority. Boris Johnson hiding from the media in a big fridge. Liz Truss spending her entire career wanging on about the infallibility of free markets, then getting her arse handed to her by them in about 10 minutes. Rishi Sunak calling the election in the driving rain, and then not realising that binning off Normandy D-day celebrations for a media interview would play badly. Keir Starmer calling for the return of the Gaza sausages. Andy Burnham: TBC, but it’s coming, I assure you. The 1970s was a time of revolution, with so many groups up in arms. I sensed the same energy at June’s Dublin Dyke March: outrage, we’ve had enough … Do you think young people today have revolutionary energy? Ger, Dublin Not at all, I have to say. I think as long as people have smartphones in their hands, they will be too narcotised to rebel. There’s a kind of dropout energy in a lot of young people, which is as completely understandable as it is completely sad. I really feel for them. What is your favourite meal? Douglas, Germany Honestly, my next one. At home, I make a huge amount of schnitzel in all kinds of ways. And multiple types of apple pie. Very pleased (and culinarily jealous) to be giving this answer to someone based in Germany. Celebrity culture and AI promise a world where some people are valued and others deemed worthless. What human qualities do you most value? Sean, Swinford, County Mayo Compassion, tolerance, wisdom, kindness, bravery, strength of character. And GSOH. Across your articles and podcasts, I note you consume a huge amount of news and media. How on earth do you find the time? And do you have to take comprehensive notes in case you need to make connections between people or events at a later date? Simon, Windsor, Berkshire I love the idea of notes, but, no – I have never taken any! Maybe I need to get Stacey Solomon to do an episode of Sort Your Life Out in my memory palace. The truth is my brain just works quite associatively, so something in politics will always remind me of something in sport or music, and it often ends up feeling more illuminating to me that way. I’m intrigued by your somewhat startling animus towards Andy Burnham. What is driving this? Ricardo, Carshalton, south London Listen, I’ve been hurt before. Meet you back here in two years? How posh are you? Rob, New Zealand I guess I can hold my own. What’s the worst thing about working with Richard Osman on The Rest Is Entertainment? Katie, Dublin He’s funnier than me. Also, he only pretends to support Fulham. That second one might not be true – I just wanted to say something in a public forum that would incense him but where he wouldn’t be present to reply. (Try writing to the letters page, Richard – see how you get on.) Are you still on X? If so, why? Caroline, Switzerland Yes, I am. I don’t use it much at all as I find social media a massive time‑suck. I hear Bluesky is truly ghastly, but have never visited. What’s your favourite Brooklyn Beckham career? Martin, Weston-super-Mare, Somerset 2042 chairman of the Federal Reserve. You often draw equivalence between Labour and the Tories: “They’re all as bad as each other.” Do you ever worry that you’re contributing to an anti‑political climate that is one of the factors rendering Britain ungovernable? Shaun, Punta del Este, Uruguay I hope I’ve never used that phrase, Shaun. However, when any side falls short of the standards we should expect in public life, it massively undermines trust in all politicians. That’s happened a lot since the turn of the millennium. But I don’t think Britain is ungovernable, and I fundamentally believe that politics is still the best way we have of making people’s lives better. Will art save us? Steven, London Unclear. Still, what a way to go. What usually drags you out of bed in the morning? Peter, Perth Insomnia’s pretty helpful. But I’ve usually got lots to do and I love a new day. Does anyone care if Prince Harry is in or out? Are the people ahead of the papers on this one? Paul, London I definitely think stories about him and Meghan do a lot of traffic, which is why he gets written about so much. I think a lot of people claim they’re not at all interested and yet still read huge amounts about him. I’m like this about The Rock’s multiple business ventures. Could not care less about them; have read 23 articles this week about them. What makes you feel hopeful and optimistic? Pauline, Bristol Love, human ingenuity and listening to pop music. What’s your favourite word in the English language? Rick, Manchester Cocktailhour. • What a Time to Be Alive! Scenes from a Strange Age by Marina Hyde will be published by Guardian Faber at £20 on 24 September. To support the Guardian, order your copy for £15 at guardianbookshop.com. title: ‘There is light at the end of this tunnel. But the tunnel is filled with sewage’: Marina Hyde on finding hope in political chaos
summary: The Guardian columnist reflects on how she stays upbeat in a chaotic age of ejector-seat prime ministers, Mars-bound baddies and at least one celebrity ski-massacre trial …
text: Let me kick off by letting a little daylight in on magic. If you’ve got a book out in September, you’re probably sending the publisher the final version of the introduction four months earlier. So I guess the moment I truly knew that Keir Starmer was finished was the moment, in the first days of May, when I typed the words “we’ve had three prime ministers since my last book”. At that point it became an absolute cast-iron cosmic inevitability that we would have had yet another prime minister by the time the book was out. Nailed on. It’s the equivalent of lighting a cigarette so the bus turns up immediately. So, four prime ministers in four years … Good times, possibly, for someone whose job involves writing about prime ministers. But not good times for Britain, or indeed for the seemingly endless series of outgoing premiers. Being British prime minister has become the biggest ejector-seat job since the noughties, when the US would announce they’d killed “the al-Qaida No 3” about twice a month. And yet, on a personal level, sometimes I think the weirdest thing about our weird times is that I actually remain a long-term optimist. But I’ll explain that strange little secret later. Because, first up, it must be said that many, many people went too early on the optimism. In the couple of years leading up to the 2024 general election, I did a lot of audience events, and I got to notice that the same question would crop up again and again. And that question, as we inched towards the overwhelming likelihood of a Labour government, was: “What on earth will you find to write about when this is all over?” Well, now. Short answer: this. All this. The long answer – which I gave as tactfully and sensitively as I could at the time, given the political horror show everyone had been living through for the past few years – was to say that while it was a lovely thought that “this” would be “over” with the dispatch of the Conservatives, I regretfully didn’t think it would be. I didn’t think the fundamentals of Britain’s decline were remotely easy to deal with, and I didn’t think the Labour leadership were any good, or had any realistic idea of how to get growth, or were so infinitely morally superior to the Tories that it would be like living in some kind of serene yesteryear utopia, where you went back to only having to check the news every week or so. And when you did, the news was still mostly as you left it. No one had kidnapped a president, attempted to annex a country, or done ketamine in the White House. Equally, I didn’t want to be a complete Debbie Downer, so I’d try to end the answer on an up note, saying stuff like, “But, you know, maybe it’ll all turn out great!” If you’re watching the events of the past few years on catchup – or simply using this article to get you up to speed – then I apologise for dropping a spoiler in here. But, hand on heart, it all did not turn out great. If it’s possible to get buried by your own landslide, Starmer achieved it. Within months of “the grownups” being in charge, quite a few people already wanted the toddlers to be given the reins again. And a whole lot more wanted flashy Uncle Nigel to have his turn instead. I find it hard not to have at least some sympathy with many of these reactions in the abstract. After years of dysfunction and desperation, people are right to think they deserve better, even if you disagree with how they think that better will come about. It’s when they stop even expecting anything better at all that a country feels most lost. Still, what a cast of characters has adorned public life in recent years. I’ve always found it helpful to think of the people I write about as characters in a drama/comedy/extreme horror movie. Maybe it puts things at one remove and makes it easier to find the jokes. In fact, my favourite emails are always from Guardian readers in far-flung corners of the globe who write and say things like, “I have zero idea who any of these people are, but I enjoy the soap opera.” Even so, at no point during the last few years did I have an absolutely clear handle on who many of the lasting leading lights of this show would be. Some public figures who I thought would stick around ended up lasting the equivalent of a three-episode arc. Farewell, Rupert Murdoch’s dental nurse turned prison chaplain fiancee – we knew you too little. (Please remember, this was the year in which Murdoch – then 92 – got engaged twice.) I knew Liz Truss had deteriorated beyond safety standards – lettuce rejoice! – but her failure to reckon with her reckoning meant she kept popping back up, along with some of Britain’s other, worse exes. Boris Johnson, say, who protested his innocence from the maximum-security international lecture circuit, at least until Nigel Farage hit on the tactical masterstroke of naming an immigration wave after him. Even former president Donald Trump seemed like an ex after he was found to have broken a few laws – until he broke every law of politics and became current president Donald Trump once again. Others were unexpectedly promoted from the chorus line and ended up becoming stars. Take Lauren Sánchez. You could be forgiven for thinking that Amazon founder Jeff Bezos placed a personal ad in Billionaire magazine – “Top 3 Croesus seeks force of nature” – and the rest was history. But just a few short years ago, Lauren was actually still just a “journalist and helicopter pilot” – not Mrs Bezos, nor the recipient of multiple philanthropy awards. Not, in fact, an astronaut. Or take Mark Zuckerberg. At his regular summonses to Washington, the Meta boss once used to apologise for things and dressed like the reluctant teenage best man at his mother’s third wedding. He now thinks all previous apologies were a mistake and dresses like an Armenian who owns an adult webcam business. Or take ChatGPT, which a few years back would itself have sounded like the name of a premium-rate adult sexline, but is now responsible for everything from your work presentation to an unspecified percentage of global policy drafting, to informing you why it is that guy won’t message you back. Strange to think that just four years ago Farage was enjoying one of his 37 retirements from public life. Then in June 2024, he unresigned again, and this time it was serious. His party, which has had more previous aliases than a rogue double-glazing salesman, was now called Reform. Nigel rapidly gained a whole new friendship group – and, in typical Farage style, lost some of them pretty fast, too. Sad to see him go no-speaks with a trillionaire we came to know as the US president’s “first buddy”. But, thanks to Elon Musk, we got to see a president turning the White House lawn into an electric-car dealership. (“Wow! Everything’s computer!”) Love him or hate him, let’s just agree Mars would be a great place to keep Elon. In fact, if there’s space in the space compound, I’d love him to take Fifa president Gianni Infantino, whose baddie glow-up has been as swift as it was inevitable in his endlessly rancid organisation. Upbeat moments? In terms of landmark events in legal history, we were gifted the no-stakes hilarity of the Gwyneth Paltrow ski-massacre trial. We got the tireless heroes of the Post Office scandal. We entered the jam‑pushing years of Duchess Meghan, Montecito’s most down-to-earth homemaker. That said, some things don’t change. It was yet another difficult few years for “difficult” men, with female TV stars and beloved female authors still lagging vanishingly far behind in the sexual misconduct stakes. Come on, gals – harassing, grooming or assaulting much younger juniors is an absolutely essential part of the artistic/retail mogul process! Meanwhile, Gregg Wallace, hemmed in for lucrative decades by a BBC that simply failed to recognise his behaviour was some kind of disability, finally released himself back into the wild. And we had Jeffrey Epstein, a guy who bizarrely turned out to be one of the most consequential figures in transatlantic public life, capable of wreaking the highest-level havoc from beyond his grave. Some got away with posthumous exposure; Russell Brand simply rebirthed himself as a messiah figure in a Thames baptism performed by Bear Grylls. And all the many, many hangers-on and enablers who stood discreetly by for these men simply melted back into the world, presumably waiting for the next situation vacant. As for the whole tenor of the period we have just lived through – in fact, are still living through – it’s hard not to look back on it and feel that chaos and disorder is now the norm. In fact, it’s hard not to look out of the window on any day and not feel it’s now the state in which we live. Let’s face it, the arc of history hasn’t been having a normal one for a while. Or, to put it another way, we seem to be living through a period of political and social entropy, having moved from a state of something that felt more like order towards increasing instability and an agonising loss of institutional effectiveness. Nothing brings it home like the US president using his private social media platform to share an AI-generated video of a swimming-trunked him and Benjamin Netanyahu sipping cocktails on sun-loungers in a lavishly redeveloped “Gaza riviera”. No, wait – nothing brings it home like the US national security adviser accidentally adding a journalist to a Real Housewives-style group chat that also included the defence secretary and the vice-president, in which live and operational details of a US forces mission were shared alongside punching fist emojis and metaphorical drink tosses at the Europeans. But I do want to end this on an up note, because – strange as it might seem, in the circumstances – I am an optimist. No, but really. Always have been. I do have faith that humans can get ourselves out of a lot of the holes we’re in, even if we fall into some others in the process. We’ll fix a lot of the problems that right now feel intractable. And, sure, we’ll create some more seemingly intractable problems along the way. That’s inevitable. But I just cannot help feeling that humans are amazing and ingenious and hardwired to make it. To quote The Big Lebowski: “I guess that’s the way the whole darned human comedy keeps perpetuating itself, down through the generations, westward the wagons, across the sands of time.” Strikes and gutters, ups and downs. Yep, I truly do believe there is light at the end of this tunnel. Unfortunately, the tunnel is filled with sewage – but the glimmer is there. Can I let one other chink of daylight in? Like a lot of deadlines, in my experience, that final, final book introduction deadline that I mentioned up the top of this article turned out to not actually be final. And so it is that I contrived to do a genuine last‑minute rewrite to keep pace with the sheer warp‑speed churn of leaders charged with rescuing the UK from the mess it’s in. But I swear to God, if anything happens to Andy Burnham between you reading this and the book being published in a couple of weeks, I will not be responsible for my actions. OK, OK. I will be responsible for my actions – but you’re going to need to give me a pass on being responsible for the error. Because, if we’ve learned anything over the past four years – and I’m not especially convinced we have – it’s that life moves pretty fast. • What a Time to Be Alive! title: All eyes on Saxony-Anhalt – what will AfD do if it wins German state poll?
summary: Sunday’s election could bring in Germany’s first far-right state government since the Nazi era
text: Germany is embarking on a crucial election period this month, with three key state polls that could markedly change the political terrain and make life decidedly harder for the federal government under the chancellor, Friedrich Merz. All eyes are on Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, where about 1.7 million people are eligible to vote, followed by Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin on 20 September. In all three contests, the far-right, anti-immigrant Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) is expected to make strong gains. What is the AfD and why is the Saxony-Anhalt vote so significant? Founded in 2013 as an anti-euro force but later morphing into an anti-immigrant party, the AfD has harnessed and amplified the frustrations of voters aggrieved and vexed by economic stagnation, rising immigration and cultural shifts. Latest polls have put it at around 40-42% in the state, placing its ambition to achieve its first absolute majority at state level within reach. Securing power in the state would mark a first for the far-right since the second world war. This matters for the whole country. State governments in Germany are represented in the upper house of parliament, the Bundesrat, so have broad powers over education, culture and ‌domestic security. For the chancellor, the leader of the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), an AfD takeover in the state could be the biggest disaster yet of a term already marked by seemingly relentless setbacks. The AfD’s leadership see their potential to gain power at state level as a natural springboard to electoral success at the next federal election in 2029. Currently the party is the main opposition in the Bundestag. The populists’ main obstacle is the stubborn resistance of other parties to collude with them, referred to as the Brandmauer, or firewall. However, this approach would be null and void if the AfD wins an absolute majority. What has the party said it plans to do if it gets into power in Saxony-Anhalt? On migration and identity, it has vowed to start deporting “irregular migrants” from “the first minute” and to foster patriotism by replacing the state’s current promotional slogan, “Think Modern”, with “Think German”. Cultural offerings deemed anti-German would be subject to a clampdown and funding to public broadcasters it views as “leftwing propaganda lackeys” would be drastically cut. In the education sector, German flags would replace rainbow flags in schools, students would sing the national anthem, and the children of asylum seekers would be educated in separate classes. Home schooling – long banned as a reaction to the Nazi era – would be allowed again, and the history curriculum would be changed to move away from what the AfD sees as an excessive focus on the Nazi era. Russian teaching would be expanded and programmes focused on combating rightwing extremism would be axed. On the environment, the party wants to ban windfarms. On family, it wants to boost the German birthrate by introducing “welcome money” for couples who have children, reducing childcare costs, and offering free school meals. On security, it wants to push for widespread changes to the domestic intelligence agency, the BfV, which has classified the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt branch as rightwing extremist. It also wants to introduce “citizens’ watch” groups to assist the police in attempts to clamp down on leftwing extremism. Critics of the last proposal have compared the idea to the auxiliary police structures set up by the Nazis, which led to the creation of a police state. Who is the face of the party in Saxony-Anhalt? Ulrich Siegmund, the party’s photogenic 36-year-old poster boy, has a considerable TikTok following and has been received like a pop star by supporters wherever he goes in the state, often travelling on a moped from East Germany’s pre-unification era. A former air freshener salesman with a degree in business psychology, he embodies a charm and wit that his party colleagues have often lacked. When Der Spiegel magazine recently ran a front page story calling him Germany’s most dangerous man, he gleefully signed the magazine at rallies. What stands between the AfD and an absolute majority? While a win for the AfD is now seen as a given, its prospects of winning an outright parliamentary majority are far from certain and, this being German election law, rather complicated. A lot depends on whether smaller parties reach the 5% minimum needed to make it into parliament. If they fail, the AfD would need less than 50% to form a government. The CDU and other mainstream parties, like the Social Democrats and the Greens, have voiced their intention to form a coalition if they gain enough votes among them. The CDU has repeatedly refused to coalesce with the AfD, and has also refused to work with the far-left Die Linke. However, it may well need Die Linke’s support to form a minority government. Die Linke would probably offer that, but mainly because it will not want to go down in history as the party that let the AfD come to power.

title: Feeling Bayeux tapestry Fomo? Check out these ancient artefacts instead
summary: From iron age knitwear to stone circles, the UK has a wealth of alternatives if you missed out on British Museum tickets
text: Perhaps you got tickets for the British Museum’s “stupefying” Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which opens to the public on Thursday – and bully for you if so. Very likely, though, you didn’t. While tens of thousands of tickets were snapped up in minutes when they first went on sale in July, most of those who joined the frenzied online queue were left with an empty basket and a millennium-sized dose of Fomo. More tickets for slots in early 2027 will be released next month, though demand is certain to far outstrip supply again. So as narrative embroidery madness seizes Britain in the coming months – with dinner party chitchat and Instagram reels consumed by discussions of medieval couching stitch and the identity of the mysterious Aelfgyva – how will the have-nots cope? Luckily (and also thanks to centuries of conquest, piety and colonialism), Britain is home to a ridiculous wealth of ancient artefacts that are just there, all the time – no online queues or anything! Here are some less celebrated treasures to check out while everyone else is elbowing through the crowds in Bloomsbury. Iron age knitwear If it’s old textiles you’re after, this one’s a cracker. The Orkney hood, found in a peat bog on the Scottish islands in 1867, was made and worn between AD250 and 615 from three separate pieces carefully stitched together, possibly by the child who wore it. Now housed in the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh. The world’s oldest wooden church Down an unassuming lane between Chelmsford and Harlow in Essex is an equally unshowy wonder – what is thought to be the world’s oldest surviving wooden church. Greensted church has been much added to since its oak trunk walls were built around 1053, but a millennium later they are still there holding up the roof. The church, wonderfully, is thought to have housed the body of St Edmund on his way to be buried at what would become Bury St Edmunds. It still holds weekly services. Countless other medieval church marvels Where to begin? The parish churches of Britain have been described as the nation’s greatest art collection, a vast and ubiquitous repository of jaw-dropping wonders that are almost always free and accessible. There are far, far too many to mention, but the ornate 15th-century rood screen at Llananno in Powys, Anglo-Saxon carved beast heads at St Mary’s Deerhurst in Gloucestershire and spectacular angel roofs in Swaffham, Norfolk, and March, Cambridgeshire, will do for starters. Stone circles that aren’t Stonehenge For those who prefer to avoid the coach parties and the A303, the UK has plenty of other Neolithic sites to wonder at. There are, in fact, at least 1,000 stone circles in Britain and Northern Ireland, from the village-swallowing Avebury and spectacularly sited Castlerigg to lesser-known beauties like the Hurlers in Cornwall, made up of three stone circles, or Beaghmore, a modest and lovely monument complex in the hills of County Tyrone that has seven. Carved crosses The greatest marvel of the 4.4-metre-high, implausibly slender Gosforth cross is perhaps that it’s standing at all, 1,100 years after it was raised in a small Cumbrian churchyard. But its carvings are pretty marvellous too. Made by Vikings that had converted to Christianity, its designs show deities from the Nordic myths alongside the crucified Christ, the sacred Norse tree of Yggdrasil winding stylised roots around the shaft of the Christian cross. The nearby Anglo-Saxon cross at Irton is smaller but older (early ninth century); many other examples are scattered across western Britain and Ireland. The world’s oldest woven garment More ancient textiles, and here’s one to really blow the millennium-old Bayeux tapestry out of the water. The Tarkhan dress, a linen garment excavated from an Egyptian cemetery in 1913, has been radiocarbon dated to the fourth millennium BC, making it more than 5,000 years old, or at least 500 years older than the Great Pyramid of Khufu. It is housed just seven minutes’ walk from the British Museum, at University College London’s Petrie Museum. • This article was amended on 6 September 2026. The Tarkhan dress dates back to the fourth millennium BC, not the fourth century BC.

title: Country diary: The wild, riotous sounds of otters in battle | Cal Flyn
summary: Isle of Lismore, Argyll: They skim over the surface like stones, making such a hullabaloo you could hear them a mile away
text: I hear them before I see them: a wailing, or something more like ululation. High-pitched, repeated vocalisations that are neither man nor cat, but somewhere in between. I throw open the cabin door, unsure what to look for, and for a moment see nothing new: only the rocky strand and the sweep of dark wrack high above the shoreline. The strange, warbling sound comes again. Ai-ai-ai-ai. Not quite screaming, not quite howling, not quite trilling, but all of those things at once. A flash of movement in the water, perhaps 50 metres out. A small, dark body leaps from the surf, followed smartly by another. My eyes struggle to understand what I’m looking at. Tiny figures catch a millisecond of clear air, then slice back through the surface, like dolphins or porpoises. But the silhouette is all wrong. And there, again – two small heads pop up, turn to one another, and seem to wrestle. Ai-ai-ai-ai. Are they playing? Fighting? Their forms are slick and dark. When one launches again from the water, I see it clearly: four limbs, and a long tail – two otters, locked in battle. Over a fish perhaps, or one of the crabs we were watching earlier from the rowing boat as we drifted on the breeze, hands trailing through saline, watching the tiny creatures on the seabed below like tourists from a cable car. They tussle and twist. Then one breaks free and makes a dash for the shoreline. The other shrieks and follows, both now skimming over the surface like stones. What drama! You would hear them a mile away. The otters disappear behind a boulder, and for a moment all is silent but for the wash of the waves. It has gone 8pm. The sun is lowering in the sky, ready for bed. The wind ruffles the heads of the trees on the island in the bay. A pair of little egrets pick their way through the shallows, pause to examine their surroundings, then move on, feet lifted high and deliberate. Then the voices come again. Ai-ai-ai-ai. The soap opera continues unseen. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: ‘Every girl now wants to be a boxer’: excitement in Katie Taylor’s home town for her valedictory bout
summary: Irish boxer lauded for her tenacity and inspiration before her last fight in front of 80,000 people at Croke Park
text: When Katie Taylor steps into the ring on Saturday night to defend her titles and once again enthral Ireland, there will be a bittersweet tinge. After a singular career that pioneered women’s boxing, the super-lightweight champion and Olympic gold medallist is bowing out. She is 40 and it is to be her final bout. “The end of an era, isn’t it?” said Trevor McMahon, her brother-in-law and founder of a gym where she trains. “It’ll be an amazing night but it’ll also be a little bit sad. Everything she did, it might not ever be achieved again.” There is consolation in the manner of her farewell. Taylor will fight in front of an 80,000-strong roaring, pulsing crowd at Dublin’s Croke Park, the citadel of Irish sport, in a valedictory like no other. Before tickets went on sale in June, some worried that a boxing match might not fill such a vast stadium. The event sold out in 17 minutes. Westlife and other musical acts have joined the bill, adding to the sense of extravaganza. The national broadcaster, RTÉ, will broadcast proceedings free to air, so every home and pub can tune in for Taylor’s showdown with Flora Pili, an unbeaten French champion. David Finnegan, 55, who was selling Taylor hats, flags and posters from a stall in her home town of Bray, County Wicklow, this week, said: “Business is tipping away. This is her farewell, everyone wants to be part of it.” Catherine Hill, 45, had a precious ticket and wanted a Taylor T-shirt for the occasion. “It’s going to be amazing for Katie, the whole country and all women,” she said. “Every young girl now wants to be a boxer or an athlete. It wasn’t like that before.” Another customer, Denise, 71, bought flags for a pub in Kerry where she planned to watch the bout. “What I love about Katie is that she’s not full of herself. She’s down to earth and still meets up with her friends here. She’s so good with the children.” Even those with no interest in boxing have been swept up in excitement for an athlete who is adored for blazing a trail in female sports with talent, grit and humility. Encouraged and trained by her father, Pete, Taylor began sparring as a young girl at a gym so rudimentary it was nicknamed the Tin Can. Women and girls were banned from the ring in Ireland and the UK, so she disguised herself as a boy and signed up to bouts as “K Taylor”. Father and daughter helped to persuade Irish authorities to lift the ban in 2001, when she was 15, and were instrumental in having women’s boxing added to the Olympic Games. Taylor won gold at London 2012 and went on to headline Madison Square Garden and win an epic trilogy with Amanda Serrano. McMahon, whose Liberty Boxing gym hosts Taylor during her return visits to Bray, said: “The talent was always there but it was more the dedication. She knew from the get-go what she was going to do. When she comes down to train in the club, the place is packed.” The last time Croke Park hosted a boxing match was in 1972, when Muhammad Ali fought Alvin Lewis. McMahon said Taylor’s farewell promised to be even more special. Pili, 29, has won all 12 of her professional fights and holds the IBO world super-lightweight title. She will be no pushover but McMahon said Taylor was determined to add another belt to her titles and go out on a high. “No matter how tough the fight is, Katie always seems to rise to the occasion. If she’s beaten, you’d have to carry her out of there in a box.” Laney O’Connell, 28, who lives on the estate where Taylor grew up, said she had inspired girls to be fit and active. “When you meet her, she’s completely normal. I don’t think she realises just how big she is,” she said. “And it’s great to see the country represented by a woman instead of a man, especially not McGregor,” she added, referencing the mixed martial artist Conor McGregor. Anne-Marie McHugh, 58, speaking below a supermarket’s Taylor mural, hoped that Bray’s most famous daughter will enjoy a restful post-boxing life. “It’s time for her to relax,” she said. “She’s earned it.”

title: ‘Then who or what did we cremate?’ Daughter’s horror at finding bones in British wildfire victims’ car
summary: Danielle Gillam-Kirton claims police botched investigation into her parents’ deaths in Spain and is demanding answers
text: When Danielle Gillam-Kirton’s parents, Pete and Fran Gillam, were killed in July’s Spanish wildfires, she felt her nightmare could get no worse. The much-loved couple had built their home in Bédar in Almería after retirement, becoming part of a tight-knit community. Fran, a former headteacher, loved to organise quiz nights to raise money for the local school and the couple enjoyed playing padel at a nearby sports club. Spanish police told Gillam-Kirton that the vehicle in which her parents died had been “inspected meticulously” and no possessions had been found. But Gillam-Kirton, an assistant headteacher from Nottinghamshire, was sure her parents must have been wearing their wedding rings when they died. She was invited to search the vehicle herself, which was parked in a police compound in Mojácar. “You won’t find anything,” she was told. She describes crying out in shock when she looked through the door of the burnt-out car. On the front seats was what appeared to be a human hip bone. “I honestly can’t describe what that felt like. I remember staring at what was in my hand, and the slow realisation of what I thought I was looking at hit me. I shouted out in shock,” she says. She and her partner searched the car and found more bones, which appeared to be the remains of the couple. They also found her parents’ mobile phones, sets of keys, jewellery, money and other personal effects. The Gillams were among 14 people killed in the fires, including Belgian, French, American and Spanish nationals. Some of the bereaved families are now searching for answers and claim the Bédar authorities have botched the investigation into their deaths. There has already been a funeral for the Gillams. “It makes you wonder: who or what did we cremate?” Gillam-Kirton says. She is demanding answers from the Spanish government and asking the UK Foreign Office to hold the authorities to account. The bones she found have been sent for DNA testing after weeks of delay from the Bédar local authority. Forensic scientists who have looked at pictures of the bones have told Gillam-Kirton they appear to be human. “The whole sequence is incredibly difficult to understand. We were told there was nothing left, and yet when we were finally able to look ourselves, we found significant personal belongings and what appeared to be human remains,” she says. “We were initially told it was probably animal remains.” She says she had to push the Spanish authorities to send them off for DNA testing. “The bones were big. I can’t see how a large animal like a cow would have climbed into the passenger seat of the vehicle during a fire.” Gillam-Kirton says she helped another family who were told their loved ones died while attempting to escape the fires on foot and that their remains had been cleared by a forensic team. She arranged for a search party – including a police officer and one of the victim’s relatives – to travel to the hillside on which they died. There they found what appeared to be human bones lying in plain view along with various personal belongings. “These were people who were caught in the same horrific fire as my mum and dad,” she says. “They lost their lives in terrifying circumstances and they deserved dignity and respect, in the way they were treated at the time and afterwards. And for us and the other families, those personal belongings aren’t just objects. They’re the last physical things connecting us to the people we have lost.” Gillam-Kirton has previously criticised the Spanish authorities for failing to alert her parents to the danger of the fire in good time. Though the fire alert came at 4.30pm, the evacuation order did not come for another three hours and was delivered by a lone police officer, who was “frantically driving from house to house”. Thirteen residents from the Gillams’ village died. Gillam-Kirton says she wants the UK government to “keep pressing the Spanish authorities for proper answers”. She adds: “Eight British people died in this fire, including my mum and dad, so I think it is really important that the UK government continues to take an interest in what happened. After all, we are talking about the treatment of British nationals – the deceased and the living.” She and the other families are asking the Spanish authorities for “a proper, thorough and transparent investigation … and I mean the whole thing, not just what caused the fire, but what happened during the emergency response, what warnings were given, when they were given, who received them, what evacuation arrangements were in place and what happened to the victims afterwards”. Initially, the Spanish authorities blamed the victims for not understanding or following the evacuation instructions. However, it later emerged that no such instructions were given. “I think that’s one of the things we’ve found hardest,” Gillam-Kirton says of the police response. “At the beginning, there seemed to be a lot of emphasis on the idea that the victims had ignored instructions or hadn’t evacuated when they were told to. And that was incredibly painful for us. And now, months later, we’re still asking basic questions.” She adds: “That, along with what appears to us to have been a lack of proper search-and-preserve procedures at the scene, has left us feeling that there has been a real lack of empathy towards the victims and their families.” The families hope that if there is a proper investigation into the deaths of their relatives and the behaviour of the authorities afterwards, others will not have to go through the unbearable situation they have had to face. “Wildfires are becoming more frequent and more severe, and communities are going to face these situations again,” Gillam-Kirton says. “There will be another fire somewhere, and there will be other people who need to be evacuated. “If you don’t properly investigate something, you can’t learn from it. We don’t want Mum and Dad to simply become two names in a list of people who died in a wildfire. We want to understand what happened to them, and if something went wrong, we want the lessons to be learned.” The Foreign Office said that any investigations were the responsibility of the Spanish authorities. A spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British couple who died in Spain, and our thoughts are with those affected by the devastating wildfires.” The Bédar local government has been contacted for comment.

title: Judge refuses to block Pentagon from firing Stars and Stripes journalists
summary: Ruling allows defense department to proceed for now in exerting greater editorial control over military news outlet
text: A federal judge has declined to stop the Pentagon from firing journalists who say they were illegally punished for speaking out about the need for the Stars and Stripes publication to maintain its editorial independence. The ruling by US district judge Trevor McFadden allows the Pentagon to proceed for now in exerting greater editorial control over the historically independent military news outlet. The journalists are unlikely to prove that the Pentagon violated their first amendment free speech rights, according to McFadden, a Donald Trump appointee. He said Stars and Stripes’ editorial independence “is not at stake here”. “Plaintiffs argue that their termination will chill the protected expression of themselves and others at Stripes,” McFadden wrote. “Plaintiffs have failed to demonstrate a chill here.” Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin and Middle East reporter Lara Korte sued last Thursday in Washington DC, to challenge their firings by the Pentagon, which partially funds the news outlet. The lawsuit says that Pentagon officials directed Lederer to fire Slavin and Korte after the publication of an 11 August article detailing deteriorating conditions and mental health crises aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln. Lederer declined to do so and later announced his retirement, saying the Pentagon had installed a new deputy publisher without his knowledge. McFadden, however, concluded that Slavin and Korte were legally dismissed for giving interviews to CBS News as part of their official duties as public employees and not as private citizens. “They are being fired for giving pre-approved interviews on their paper’s behalf in which they largely toed the company line,” the judge wrote. “Whatever else such a scheme may violate, it does not clearly offend the first amendment.” The defense department and defense secretary Pete Hegseth are among the lawsuit’s named defendants. McFadden’s ruling deals a blow to the journalists, whose lawsuit argues that they should be reinstated to their jobs. An attorney for the journalists called the ruling “disappointing”, according to CNN. At least two other lawsuits accused the Pentagon of interfering with Stars and Stripes’ editorial integrity and independence. Pulitzer-winning reporters Susan Dardarian and William Church, who serve as advisory board members to the publication, sued the Pentagon in June, accusing the military of illegal censorship. The publication’s former ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, sued the Pentagon the same month, saying she was fired in retaliation for an opinion column, in violation of her first amendment rights.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy calls air truce as Kushner and Witkoff head for Kyiv via Moscow
summary: Direct hit on SBU headquarters in Kyiv targeted intelligence chief; airline suspends Moscow flights after Zelenskyy warning. What we know on day 1,655
text: Two ⁠US peace negotiators ⁠will visit Ukraine ⁠on Sunday after visiting ⁠Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on ⁠Friday. Ukraine’s president said Kyiv ‌would ‌guarantee the safety ‌of Russian airspace during the visit of Steve Witkoff ‌and Jared Kushner to Moscow, after which they are expected to travel on to Kyiv. He called on Russia to also halt ⁠its air attacks on Ukraine during the negotiators’ visit. Donald Trump, the US president, said: “We ‌have an idea for peace … I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two ‌great negotiators.” The New York Times reported that Washington has asked both sides for a ceasefire during the envoys’ visit. Kushner is Trump’s son-in-law and Witkoff deals in real estate. A Russian strike killed four people in Kamianske, a city in the Dnipropetrovsk oblast of south-eastern Ukraine, the head of the regional military authority said on Saturday morning. Five more were wounded, including a 30-year-old woman who was placed in intensive care. The headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency took a direct hit from a Russian drone on Friday, Amy Hawkins reports from Kyiv. Zelenskyy said he had instructed the SBU to deliver an “appropriate, tangible response” to the strike, while the foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described it as a “major escalation”. Zelenskyy said: “The drone was aimed directly at the office of the head of the security service in that building.” At least nine people were injured in Friday’s strike, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. Air ⁠Tanzania said it was ⁠suspending ⁠flights from Dar es Salaam ⁠to Moscow from Friday, becoming ⁠the first airline ‌to do ‌so after ‌Zelenskyy warned this week that the skies over ‌Russia were unsafe because of Ukraine’s retaliatory drone attacks. The airline said on Facebook that it took ⁠the step after “a routine risk assessment of the operating environment ‌along the route”. Vladimir Putin on Thursday falsely claimed that Ukraine was threatening to attack civilian aircraft. Moscow has protested to the UN’s aviation agency after Ukraine asked it to have member countries keep their airlines out of Russian airspace. “Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such – not a single civilian aircraft,” Zelenskyy said during the week. “There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account.” A “massive” overnight Russian attack on the Odesa region killed one person and injured at least five others, including a child, regional head Oleh Kiper said on Friday. The attacks damaged multiple residential buildings, including two multistorey blocks. Strikes elsewhere in Ukraine killed two police officers in Dnipro, officials said, while a drone attack in Kyiv wounded three people after hitting a residential building. In Russia, a large-scale Ukrainian drone strike hit the Black Sea resort city of Sochi and the nearby district of Sirius, regional officials said on Friday. They said the attack sparked a blaze at an oil depot. Russian media outlets reported two oil depots were hit, with one fire in Sochi and another in Sirius. Finnish authorities said they were investigating how a Russian-made drone ended up on the shore in the Pellinge archipelago east of Helsinki. Finland’s border guard said it appeared to be a Geoscan 701 drone, manufactured by a Russian company. “The device model in question is used by both state and civilian operators, and it is not possible at this stage to determine its intended use or identify the country or entity operating it.” A World Health Organization warehouse storing humanitarian medical supplies was struck during an air attack on the Kyiv region, continuing what the WHO said was a pattern of such attacks across Ukraine. In 2026, at least 20 attacks have affected depots storing humanitarian goods including healthcare supplies, said a WHO spokesperson in Geneva. A vice-president in the far-right party of French presidential contender Marine Le Pen has sparked a furore by saying France would “turn off the tap” to Ukraine if National Rally (RN) came to power. Louis Aliot claimed the RN “condemned the Russian aggression” but said the war had “weakened Europe”. One of Le Pen’s leading rivals in the elections, centre-right politician Edouard Philippe, who served as Macron’s first prime minister, retorted that “turning off the tap to Ukraine is serving Russia”. “Weakening Ukraine, as Marine Le Pen wishes, is threatening the security of Europe and France. I will do everything to prevent it.” Le Pen herself entered the fray, claiming that her party was pushing for a “diplomatic resolution of this abominable war”. The head of Memorial, Russia’s Nobel peace prize-winning rights group, has told AFP she fears a fresh crackdown after September’s legislative elections, with more people arrested and sent to fight in Ukraine. Elena Zhemkova also vowed to keep up the fight for human rights in Russia, despite her group being declared illegal and herself forced into exile. “Unfortunately, I think that now everything is getting worse, but not so fast,” the 65-year-old said. “But after the elections, there will be a very sharp deterioration.”

title: US judge extends block on Trump order to restrict mail-in voting
summary: Indira Talwani’s ruling presents major setback for president as first states begin to send out mail ballots for midterms
text: A federal judge on Friday again blocked Donald Trump’s executive order to impose sweeping restrictions on mail-in voting, the latest in a legal back-and-forth playing out less than two months before election day. US district court judge Indira Talwani initially placed a temporary order blocking the president’s mandate and has now extended that prohibition with a stronger preliminary injunction. The ruling comes hours after North Carolina became the first state to start sending out mail-in ballots for the 3 November midterm elections. Talwani referred to the tight timeline in her ruling. “Plaintiff States are required under state law to mail millions of ballots to voters on a prescribed timeframe. As detailed below, they are unable to pivot this late in the election cycle, nearly guaranteeing significant disenfranchisement for eligible voters,” the judge wrote in her ruling. Trump signed an executive order in March that would create a nationwide list of verified eligible voters, compelling the US Postal Service (USPS) to work with states to establish lists of mail-in voters before elections. The result would mean a limited ballot delivery only to voters on those lists. The Trump administration had already appealed against her temporary block to the supreme court, and it appeared the justices were likely to have a final say on the matter. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment, but the administration quickly appealed Friday’s ruling. The USPS has said in recent court filings that the technology needed to administer the order isn’t even available. Earlier this week, a USPS whistleblower came forward and warned of “potentially catastrophic problems” if the agency were to try to carry out the order. After Trump signed the order, a coalition of 24 state attorneys general sued the USPS to challenge the rule. They also filed a motion for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction as litigation was ongoing. Oral argument on the coalition’s request for a preliminary injunction was held on Thursday. “We’ve now secured longer-term relief that will keep the USPS changes blocked while our case moves forward,” said Rob Bonta, the attorney general of California, who co-led the state coalition. “We will continue to take all steps to stop the Trump Administration from trampling on voting rights and restricting mail voting.” The order allows states to voluntarily use the new system. To date, not a single state has announced that it will do so. A coalition of voter service and civic groups, plaintiffs represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) in the lawsuit, issued a statement: “Today’s ruling makes it crystal clear: The US Postal Service must deliver all election mail. USPS has no authority in the Constitution or federal law over how states administer mail voting. And the President cannot order the Postal Service to create a disruptive new bureaucracy that will throw the election into chaos and disenfranchise untold numbers of voters.” Trump has long sought to limit mail voting, even though he himself often uses that method to cast his own ballot. He has falsely blamed mail balloting for his 2020 election loss, spreading baseless claims of fraud, but has so far been unable to change the longstanding voting procedure. An initial executive order Trump issued last year to change election rules, including a requirement for people to show documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote, was halted by federal judges. They ruled that the constitution gives states and, in some cases, Congress the power to set voting procedures, not the president. After Trump issued his mail voting executive order in March, Democrats and voting rights groups filed several lawsuits. Two ended up before Talwani, who placed an initial hold on the order in June, prohibiting its implementation until after November. But the supreme court late last month overturned that order. Its conservative majority pointedly did not say Trump’s move was legal but found the lawsuits were filed prematurely before the US Postal Service issued its rule on how it would implement the order. The rule came out just before the supreme court released its ruling, and the plaintiffs refiled their suits.

title: Trump order directs officials to consider stripping protections for gray wolves
summary: Interior department given three months to decide whether wolves can be removed from endangered species list
text: Donald Trump signed an executive order on Friday directing the interior department to consider de-listing gray wolves from the Endangered Species Act and to contemplate whether the agency could make it easier to authorize killing them. The order gives interior secretary Doug Burgum three months to determine whether gray wolves and Mexican gray wolves have recovered enough for the federal government to de-list them. But the US Fish and Wildlife Service, a division of the interior department, has already attempted to de-list the gray wolf – a decision that is currently tied up in litigation. A 2022 federal court order has left wolves protected by the ESA across most of their range in the lower 48 states. The major exception is in the northern Rocky Mountain states of Montana, Idaho and Wyoming, where states manage wolves. In Minnesota, wolves are classified as “threatened” rather than “endangered”. The USFWS has not attempted to de-list the Mexican gray wolf, a rare sub-species that was reintroduced to New Mexico and Arizona in 1998. The current recovery plan for Mexican gray wolves requires a population average of more than 320 animals for four years in a row before federal authorities consider de-listing. Arizona and New Mexico counted a total of 319 animals at the end of 2025, triggering the first year in which officials can start counting to make the case for de-listing. But Mexican gray wolves also face dire threats from lack of genetic diversity, according to Michael Robinson, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. Premature de-listing, he said, would likely invite challenge from environmental groups. “We’re going to be fighting every step of the way, with information, with science,” Robinson said. “That should be the core of the decision-making process.” Trump’s order also directs federal authorities to urge states to remove protections for gray wolves and loosen local restrictions on wolf killing. The order drew sharp criticism from environmental groups. “Once again, we see this administration attempting to override the checks and balances provided by bedrock environmental laws like the Endangered Species Act in order to create industry carveouts and distract from other bad policies that are proving unpopular,” said Leia Barnett, New Mexico conservation lead for WildEarth Guardians. “Directing federal agencies to pressure states into rolling back their own wildlife protections isn’t just bad policy, it’s an attempt to bypass the very framework Congress built to keep species recovery decisions insulated from political whims.” The federal government systematically trapped and killed wolves in the US through the late 19th and early 20th centuries, pushing them to the brink of extirpation from the contiguous states, largely to protect livestock from predation. Ranchers still largely view the animals as a nuisance that threatens their already slim profit margins. Trump’s order was part of a broader series of measures aimed at protecting ranchers and American beef production. Trump appeared to suggest his order would make it easier to shoot wolves, despite the fact that most of them remain protected. “You can shoot them as of today?” Trump asked at the signing ceremony, referring to Mexican gray wolves while talking with an Arizona rancher. The comment drew laughter. US agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins interjected to say that interior secretary Burgum “has to do a little magic, but yes”. Gray wolves are protected under the Endangered Species Act across most of their range in the lower 48, making it a federal crime to kill one in most cases, regardless of Trump’s order. But Trump raised the issue again at the signing ceremony. A rancher told the president that people in his home state of Washington struggle with wolves, noting that in one case a pack of wolves caused a young girl to climb a tree to safety. “You’re allowed to go and take care of it,” Trump told the rancher. “If you say so, sir,” he replied. “We have no choice,” Trump said. “I’ve been hearing about it for a long time.”
