title: Rescue of Nepal hydropower workers ‘triumph for humans and humanity’, tunnelling expert says
summary: Arnold Dix, an Australian engineer and geologist who worked at Ground Zero after 9/11, says finding two workers alive in Trishuli 3A ‘gives us hope’
text: There is renewed hope amid the devastation wreaked by the flash flooding disaster on the Nepal-Tibet border as the world witnesses “one of the great rescues of the 21st century”. Nine days after the deadly floods, two workers were pulled out alive from a flooded hydropower tunnel in Nepal. Sanjay Shah and Kabir Maharajan were rescued from the Trishuli 3A hydropower project on Friday, more than a week after a glacial collapse created a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept away buildings, roads and bridges along the border between Nepal and China. Hundreds more employees who worked in various hydropower projects along the banks of Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers remain missing, but the Australian engineer and geologist Arnold Dix, who was invited by Nepali authorities to advise on the Trishuli 3A operation, says Friday’s successful rescue will help lift spirits. “We’ve found two people alive, so that gives us hope,” Dix says. “After more than a week, everyone’s exhausted, but this spurs us on to try even harder and it now also gives us focus for how we might approach other rescues in other locations. “We now have proof that people can survive this long.” Dix has previously assisted at other disaster sites such as the 2023 Silkyara tunnel operation, where all 41 workers were rescued after a tunnel collapsed in India, and the tunnels of Ground Zero after 9/11. But with almost 30 hydropower projects reported damaged, the Nepal floods are unlike any other disaster he has worked on. “Normally, I deal with a single disaster – this is 27 concurrently,” he says. On his specific rescue operation, workers had already had trouble identifying the location of Trishuli 3A. They then had to work out which tunnel would give access to the power station before the digging could begin. But as the process began, rocks the size of vehicles blocked rescuers, forcing them to use explosives. This isn’t the preferred method, as it can pose risks to those on the other side, Dix says. When they reached the tunnel, rescuers found it was full of water, forcing them to dig an emergency trench to try to drain it. They worried the workers inside could have already drowned, but on Friday morning about 50 metres in, they reported hearing a faint voice. The team called out, “Don’t panic, we are rescuing you.” From inside the tunnel a voice replied: “OK.” Watching the video of the men pulled from the tunnel alive reminds Dix of why he does this. “We do it because we’re decent human beings and that’s what human beings do: help one another,” he says. “This is a real triumph for humans and humanity.” Another 40 workers are believed to be trapped inside Trishuli 3A and rescuers face significant risks. If there is water in the tunnel ahead of the team and they break rock, they could drown, and as they are now below flood-plain level, water could also inundate rescuers from behind. “Yes, we have the reward of having rescued two people now, but we have to be so careful,” Dix says. “The team’s lives are at risk right now and if they can’t get out in time they will drown. “Like, this is not a drill, we are witnessing one of the great rescues of the 21st century.” The rescue team was on Friday tunnelling to what is known as the “Goldilocks zone” at the top of the 11-storey Trishuli 3A power station, where they are hoping to find more survivors. More than 270 people have already been rescued from various hydropower projects. At least 1,294 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to the country’s disaster management agency. Thirty-eight Australian government officials, disaster response specialists and humanitarian workers are now on the ground in Nepal assisting in search-and-rescue and relief efforts. The latest cohort to arrive – a 15-person Australian Disaster Assistance Response Team providing specialist drone services – landed in Kathmandu late on Friday night. A further seven disaster victim identification specialists from the federal police will leave Australia on Saturday. As at 4 September, the Nepali government has reported 1,294 confirmed deaths, while 5,053 people remain missing, including 583 foreign nationals. As at 5 September, the Chinese government reported 31 confirmed deaths and 531 missing people, with 261 of those being foreign citizens. Additional reporting by Ben Doherty

title: Death on the road to Rafah: the night the IDF targeted World Central Kitchen aid workers
summary: The Israeli army had helped plan the delivery of food aid on 1 April 2024, but things went wrong from the beginning and ended in seven deaths
text: On the evening of 1 April 2024, a team of aid workers from World Central Kitchen (WCK) stood on Gaza’s Mediterranean shore overseeing the unloading of a barge full of desperately needed food on a makeshift jetty made of sand and rubble. The Gaza war had been raging for six months and Israel’s closure of land crossings had left the whole territory facing the threat of famine. WCK and local Palestinian contractors had constructed the jetty out of everything they could lay their hands on, including debris from the bombed house of one of the contractors, so that the pallets of humanitarian assistance could be delivered by boat from Cyprus. A consignment of 200 tonnes of rice, flour and other proteins had arrived two weeks earlier, the first sea shipment to dock in Gaza since 2007. This was the second shipment and it was even bigger, with enough food to prepare more than 1m meals, as well as a Ramadan gift of dates from the United Arab Emirates. The choreography of the delivery had been coordinated over several days with the Israeli army, and an officer was on the jetty to observe the proceedings. In the midst of a devastating bombing campaign after the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023, this humanitarian effort was supposed to be carried out under internationally agreed military protection. The shipment had been unloaded by 8.30pm but despite the lengthy planning, there was a delay in receiving final Israeli security clearance for the eight hired trucks and two WCK escort vehicles to leave the jetty. By the time the green light came from local Israeli commanders and the convoy began to move south, night had fallen. There was no initial overhead surveillance but two drones joined somewhere along the route to the first stop, a WCK welcome centre 6 miles to the south. Those drones were assigned to the Israel Defense Forces’ (IDF) Nahal brigade, which had not been fully briefed on the aid convoy’s itinerary. A special adviser assigned by the Australian government to assess the case (in the interests of justice for the Australian victim Lalzawmi Frankcom), found that “specific details about the pre-coordinated WCK aid mission had not been passed down from higher levels of Southern Command to the brigade and UAV [unmanned aerial vehicle] operator”. Local guards At the WCK welcome centre, a few local men hired as guards were waiting, at least one of them armed. At a time of widespread hunger, many food convoys had been mobbed by desperate crowds as well as organised gangs, some of whom may have had been linked to Hamas, though Hamas never had the grip on food deliveries alleged by the Israeli authorities. Using local security for aid deliveries was not unknown in Gaza, but it was directly against WCK policy to use armed escorts. The WCK says it is unclear why the local team on that night agreed to accept armed guards. The official Israeli version of events suggests it was “due to the convoy’s delayed departure, during night-time hours,” and noted it “was not coordinated with IDF authorities”. The official Israeli version does not say how many armed men were waiting for the convoy (unofficial versions vary between two and four), but drone footage reportedly showed one of them climb on top of the cabin of one of the trucks and fire a shot in the air shortly afterwards, for reasons that remain unknown. The Nahal brigade officers and the drone operators assigned to them concluded it was a Hamas hijack, based in part on the false assumption that such hijackings were commonplace. “The troops also identified vehicles surrounding the trucks in a manner that, in their assessment and based on accumulated operational experience, corresponded to a scenario in which the Hamas terrorist organisation had taken control of the convoy,” the official account says. The Israeli military prosecutor’s version of events, published last month to justify his decision not to pursue criminal proceedings, does not mention the breakdown in communication between the army’s coordination and liaison administration, which handles humanitarian needs in the territory, and the Nahal brigade controlling that sector of the Gaza Strip. Furthermore, the prosecutor’s version says efforts by IDF personnel to contact WCK were unsuccessful. But according to WCK sources and the Australian report on events, contact was established that night with WCK headquarters in the US, which in turn got in touch with an employee in Gaza. According to the Australian report, the WCK worker on the ground told headquarters staff the guards only had “fake guns”. It remains unclear what the basis for that claim was, but the WCK assured the IDF that it had not lost contact with the convoy and it had not been hijacked. Arrival at destination It is unclear whether this exchange with WCK was relayed to the Nahal brigade before the strikes. But even if it was not, the fact that the convoy of eight food trucks continued on its journey and arrived at its intended destination, the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, should have been ample proof that the aid had not been seized by Hamas. The military prosecutor’s summary acknowledges that the “convoy arrived at the designated warehouse and unloaded the aid” but does not address the seemingly straightforward conclusion that it had therefore not been diverted. The IDF has yet to release audio recordings of military communications that night. After the trucks entered the warehouse, the WCK workers and the local guards stayed outside by their own vehicles for about 10 minutes. That short period, observed by operators of Israeli drones, appears to have helped seal the aid workers’ fate. As far as the Nahal brigade’s chief of staff, reserve Col Nochi Mendel, was concerned, they were “mingling” with Hamas. Under the very loose procedures of “incrimination” that delegate much to the discretion of field commanders like Mendel, the WCK workers became unwitting targets as they celebrated the completion of a successful delivery of aid, because they were in the proximity to armed men. “There was incrimination. The incrimination was according to the rules,” Mendel said. “There were armed men there with certainty. With certainty, they [the aid workers] had mingled with armed Hamas men.” Other IDF officers have confirmed to the Guardian that such a process of guilt by association is used widely to determine targets, though different field commanders use different standards in making decisions. The Israel military prosecutor, in making his assessment on criminal responsibility, did not address the practice of incrimination in targeting. Parting of ways After the brief pause outside the WCK warehouse in Deir al-Balah, the guards and the WCK workers went in separate directions. “The WCK vehicles departed together west towards the coast. Concurrently, the vehicle containing the locally contracted security personnel, including the previously identified gunmen, drove north,” the Australian report says. It also makes clear that the IDF was aware of this parting of the two groups. “One UAV tracked the locally contracted security vehicle heading north for approximately three minutes until it arrived at another warehouse where up to four gunmen were identified exiting the vehicle and entering the building,” the report says. “A decision was made to discontinue targeting them due to the time available before they entered the northern warehouse.” The military prosecutor’s version makes no mention of this drone or the fact that the suspected gunmen were seen driving off in a different direction and entering a separate building. It claims instead that “several individuals mistakenly … identified as armed persons” were observed getting into WCK vehicles. That is at odds with the Australian report and the accounts of Israeli officers familiar with the investigation. They said a bag was spotted by a drone operator being put in a WCK car, and that the operator mistook it for a gun, though sources briefed on the drone video said that later analysis showed no sign of a suspicious bag. Whether or not it was a gun was irrelevant as far as Mendel was concerned. He saw his task as carrying out the government policy of crushing Hamas governance in Gaza, which included stopping its seizure of aid deliveries. “If a Hamas operative takes over a truck and after that he sells it and that’s how he recruits more people, then what does it matter if he’s armed or not?” Mendel said. *** In its economical, dry prose, the Australian report describes what happened next as the WCK workers left the warehouse at about 11pm. “The WCK vehicles proceeded west to the coast. Due to the time delays encountered, rather than return to the WCK welcome centre as planned, a decision was made to return directly to the accommodation in Rafah,” the report says. “After turning south on to the coast road, the three WCK vehicles were struck in relatively quick succession, each strike being approximately two minutes apart. There were two survivors from the strike on the first (up-armoured) vehicle who quickly moved to the second vehicle, then two survivors from the second (up-armoured) vehicle who moved to the third vehicle. There were no survivors from the third (soft-skinned) vehicle. Over the four-minute period 23:09 – 23:13, the seven WCK workers were killed – likely one in the first vehicle, two in the second and four in the last.” The seven victims of the IDF drone strikes were from the UK, Australia, Poland, Palestine and the US. The Britons John Chapman, James Kirby and James Henderson were working as security consultants. Saifeddin Issam Ayad Abutaha, a Palestinian driver and translator, was the youngest killed, at 25. Frankcom, Damian Soból, a Pole, and Jacob Flickinger, a US-Canadian dual citizen, were humanitarian workers for WCK. The military prosecutor claimed that in turning south towards Rafah, the WCK workers were “deviating from the route that the organisation had coordinated in advance with the IDF”, giving weight to the Nahal brigade’s mistaken impression that “Hamas operatives had taken control of the convoy”. Mendel also mentioned this “deviation” as a mitigating factor. However, the Australian report found that the fact that the WCK workers had changed their route only became known after they were killed, and “as such it did not play a factor” in the decision to open fire. The official Israeli version of events says Mendel and his brigade fire support commander ignored an order on the night of the airstrike from a superior officer to cease any attacks on humanitarian convoys, but Mendel has said the order is a fabrication. “It never happened, never existed,” Mendel said. “No operational directive reached the brigade to cease the strikes … We checked it a thousand times.” In explaining his own decision-making, Mendel stressed he was carrying out Israeli government policy by stopping Hamas taking control of food deliveries. He had been lauded by his superiors for ordering strikes on several earlier alleged Hamas attempts to hijack aid. In his mind, the events on the night of 1 April 2024 fitted the same pattern. “I didn’t plan to kill the aid workers,” Mendel said, but added: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.” Justifying this conclusion, he said: “They were mixed together with Hamas operatives …near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on.” In a written statement, WCK said: “It is extraordinary to learn now that some in the IDF considered our humanitarian work to be enemy activity based on the flimsiest evidence, or no evidence at all. “This undefined, unjustified and unlawful view is a mortal threat to all humanitarians. The IDF’s shifting excuses and explanations for these unlawful airstrikes are precisely why we continue to demand an independent investigation with the full release of the IDF’s evidence.”

title: Ex-safety manager given 19 months’ prison over five-year-old’s hyperbaric chamber fire death
summary: Jeffrey Mosteller pleaded no contest to charges relating to burning death of Thomas Cooper in Michigan
text: A former safety manager has been sentenced to one year and seven months in prison in connection with the death of a five-year-old Michigan boy who was killed in a fiery January 2025 explosion inside a hyperbaric oxygen chamber. Jeffrey Mosteller, 66, received that sentence after pleading no contest to involuntary manslaughter in Oakland county circuit court in Michigan on Monday. He worked as the safety manager at the Oxford Center, an alternative healthcare facility that treats children with a range of health conditions – including autism, ADHD and autoimmune diseases – using hyperbaric oxygen therapy. Mosteller faced up to 15 years in prison before being handed his 19-month sentence. Five-year-old Thomas Cooper, of Royal Oak, Michigan, was undergoing treatment for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and sleep apnea at the Oxford Center in the Detroit suburb of Troy when a fire erupted inside the hyperbaric chamber. That triggered an explosion which killed Cooper. According to an expert who viewed video of the case, the child had squirmed enough to pull the sheet off a mattress inside the chamber, causing a spark of static electricity. That spark became a flash fire that incinerated him within seconds because of the oxygen-rich environment surrounding him. Cooper’s mother was badly burned on her arms and chest while desperately trying to open the tank. Mosteller is one of four former Oxford Center employees charged in connection with Thomas’s death. The other three were still awaiting trial at the time of his sentence. The Oxford Center founder and chief executive, Tamela Peterson, 58, was charged with second-degree murder. Facility manager Gary Marken, 65, was charged with second-degree murder and involuntary manslaughter. And Aleta Moffitt, 60, who was operating the chamber when it exploded, was charged with involuntary manslaughter and intentionally placing false medical information on a medical records chart. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cleared hyperbaric chambers to be marketed as safe and effective for 13 disorders, including severe burns, decompression sickness and non-healing wounds. The therapy works by delivering pure oxygen to a person’s body inside a pressurized chamber. Despite its FDA approval in certain cases, hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) has been a growing source of controversy as the safety of these chambers have been called into question. Many allies of Trump administration health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr have endorsed HBOT, but many others have expressed skepticism towards the treatment’s increasing push into the healthcare mainstream. Cooper’s parents filed a $100m wrongful death lawsuit against the clinic and the chamber’s manufacturer over their son’s death.

title: Democrats demand DHS documents in investigation into Rohingya refugee’s death
summary: Lawmakers condemn agency for ‘obstructing the pursuit of justice’ over death of nearly blind Nurul Amin Shah Alam
text: Democratic lawmakers are demanding that the Department of Homeland Security turn over records and fully cooperate with an investigation into the death of Nurul Amin Shah Alam, a nearly blind Rohingya refugee who died after US border agents left him outside a closed coffee shop on a freezing night in Buffalo earlier this year. At a press conference in Buffalo on Friday, standing just a few feet away from where Shah was found dead, Tim Kennedy of New York was joined by Bennie Thompson of Mississippi, the ranking Democrat on the House homeland security committee, Lou Correa of California and Nellie Pou of New Jersey in calling on DHS to cooperate with the Erie county district attorney’s investigation. Kennedy said: “The Erie county medical examiner has ruled his death a homicide, yet DHS still won’t hand over a single meaningful record. Not to my office, not to attorney general [Letitia] James and not to the Erie county district attorney. Simply put, they are obstructing the pursuit of justice by local law enforcement.” Kennedy added: “Mr Shah Alam’s family deserves to see justice served by our legal system. I won’t stop demanding it until DHS complies.” Shah Alam, 56, was a Rohingya refugee who had lost much of his sight and spoke little English. On 19 February, after his release from the Erie county holding center, he was taken into the custody of US border patrol agents while his family waited outside the jail expecting to bring him home. Hours later, agents left Shah Alam outside a closed Tim Hortons coffee shop. His family and attorneys were not told where he had been taken or where agents had left him. Five days later, Shah Alam was found dead roughly four miles away. In April, the Erie county medical examiner ruled his death a homicide, determining that he died from complications of a perforated duodenal ulcer precipitated by hypothermia and dehydration. The district attorney’s office is continuing to investigate the circumstances surrounding his death. Kennedy has also sought legislative changes in response to the case. In June, he introduced the DHS Release Transparency Act, which would require immigration authorities to notify a detainee’s designated family member, attorney or other contact before the person’s release and provide information about where the individual is being released. In March, New York attorney general Letitia James opened a formal investigation into Shah’s death. But in August, James closed the criminal investigation, citing the refusal of US Customs and Border Protection to cooperate. According to a letter obtained by Investigative Post, James had requested that CBP identify the agents who “retrieved and released Mr Shah Alam” and produce “all records related to the detainer, transport, custody, dispatch communications, GPS/vehicle data, body-worn camera footage, and incident reports.” CBP declined to share any information, according to Investigative Post. The New York attorney general’s office then referred the investigation to the Erie county district attorney. On 2 September, Kennedy and Thompson sent a formal letter to DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin, who had said during his confirmation hearing in March that the department was investigating Shah’s death. In the letter to Mullin, the lawmakers demanded that “DHS fully comply with the Erie county DA’s investigation”. The lawmakers wrote that six months after Shah’s death, they had not received “a single meaningful or substantive response” from DHS, despite multiple oversight letters to the department. Speaking at the press conference, Thompson added: “If DHS has nothing to hide, then they need to turn over the records and cooperate fully with the Erie County law enforcement. It is that simple.”

title: Six-week-old child in Pennsylvania died from measles, coroner says
summary: Officials decline to confirm whether death was one of two announced last week as Lancaster county outbreak grows
text: A six-week-old child in Pennsylvania died from measles, the Lancaster county coroner has determined, following two measles-related deaths in the county last week. The determination comes as Lancaster county faces a growing measles outbreak. Stephen Diamantoni, the county coroner, confirmed the death to multiple news outlets and said that the infant had Amish lethal microcephaly. Children with the condition typically live to only five to six months, and it can make children more vulnerable to respiratory infections. State health officials have not confirmed whether the six-week-old was one of the two deaths announced last week, according to the New York Times. The first death, on 14 August, involved an infant whose mother had measles and transmitted it to the child. In that case, the coroner told WGAL that a ruptured spleen, not measles, was the cause of death. Measles, however, was listed on the newborn’s death certificate, the outlet reported. The Atlantic reported that the parents believe their baby died from measles. Pennsylvania has counted nearly 400 measles cases across 28 counties, nearly half of which are in southern Lancaster county. Most of the cases reported to state health authorities are in adults between 18 and 49. Official tallies are typically an undercount of actual cases. At a news conference last week, the Pennsylvania governor, Josh Shapiro, and the state’s secretary of health, Debra Bogen, said two Lancaster county residents had died in cases described as “measles-associated”. They did not provide further details, citing privacy laws and respect for the deceased and their families. The recent deaths have fueled a dispute between Shapiro, a Democrat, and the US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr. Officials strongly suggested that the two deaths were caused by measles when they announced them, but the distinction of “measles-associated” led some on the right to dispute whether measles was actually the cause. Shapiro had criticized Kennedy, a longtime vaccine skeptic, over his history of misinformation surrounding vaccines. The governor said that Kennedy’s rhetoric has not helped contain the measles epidemic, which has pushed US cases to the highest number in over three decades. Kennedy responded by suggesting Shapiro’s side had fabricated the deaths in an effort to blame the health secretary. He also accused Democrats of using tactics similar to those employed during the pandemic to counter critics and encourage vaccination. “The performance was a replay of the Democrats’ Covid playbook: fear-mongering, misinformation, finger-pointing, and the weaponization of infectious disease fears for political gain,” Kennedy wrote on social media. As of Monday, top US health officials and government agencies were not including the two recent measles-associated deaths in their official counts. Kennedy also gave an incorrect number of measles deaths during a recent interview with Fox News. Debra Houry, a former CDC chief medical officer, and Demetre Daskalakis, a former director of the CDC’s National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases, criticized, in a piece for Stat News, the way health and administration officials have turned deadly diseases into political talking points to be debated. “Chicken noodle soup and vitamin A are not substitutes for vaccination, as the secretary of health claimed in 2022 while standing in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, the epicenter of the current outbreak,” the pair wrote. “The best way to protect children is neither complicated nor new: provide clear information and make it easier for families to get vaccinated.”

title: Trump to take gifted Qatar jet to Ireland despite questions about its security
summary: President was moved to a separate aircraft during a July trip after officials learned of a possible Iranian threat, leaving questions about the plane’s defenses unanswered
text: Donald Trump intends to use the Boeing jet gifted by Qatar for his trip to Ireland next week, marking the first time the aircraft will leave the US since concerns were raised over whether it can adequately protect the president from attack. The decision, a senior administration official told the Washington Post, comes weeks after the president suggested the plane would be grounded for about a month while it underwent unspecified security upgrades. Asked to explain further, a senior administration official speaking on background told the Guardian: “We don’t comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force One. We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure and reliable capability for the president of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture.” The jet was converted for presidential use earlier in Trump’s term after the two custom-built Boeing aircraft intended to eventually serve as Air Force One were delayed for years. Those planes, still not ready, are designed from scratch with elaborate missile-defense systems built in, which the $400m “palace in the sky” has never been confirmed to match. Doubts about the plane’s defenses entered the collective psyche again after Trump’s last trip abroad on it, to a Nato summit in Turkey in July. It later emerged that Trump had in fact been spirited away via a catering truck on to a separate, older aircraft after officials learned of a possible Iranian threat in Ankara, leaving the plane he had boarded to fly on as a decoy. Aboard the original, possibly targeted flight were the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio; the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent; several senior aides; and the traveling press pool – the latter, who were definitely not told about the threat, were asked to keep their window shades closed. The episode has now been dramatized in a new Netflix mini-documentary, and has drawn widespread accusations and furor that Trump had been willing to treat his own officials and journalists as expendable for his own safety. In the meantime, whatever security upgrades the jet has actually received since being grounded remain a mystery even now. “It is the greatest presidential plane ever built,” the senior administration official concluded.

title: Lindsay Clancy: five key moments from ‘America’s saddest murder trial’
summary: Massachusetts mother accused of fatally strangling her children faces possibility of retrial after judge declares mistrial
text: The trial of Lindsay Clancy that gripped headlines in recent weeks, drawing renewed attention to the state of maternal mental healthcare in the US and postpartum psychosis, has ended with a mistrial. This now leaves Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of fatally strangling her three children in January 2023 who pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, open to the possibility of a retrial with a different jury. As the public now waits for what will happen next, here are five key takeaways from what has been called “America’s saddest murder trial”. Patrick Clancy: Lindsay Clancy ‘described thoughts of hurting the kids’ Lindsay Clancy’s ex-husband, 36-year-old Patrick Clancy, took the stand as a key figure in the case, testifying about his wife’s worsening mental health in the months leading up to the killings of five-year old Cora, three-year old Dawson and eight-month old Callan. Patrick Clancy described Lindsay as a “very dedicated” mother who struggled with her mental health and “just had a really hard time being separated from them”. Approximately two months before the killings, Lindsay “described thoughts of hurting the kids or them having some sort of ailment”, Patrick Clancy testified. He said his then wife told him that she did not have a specific plan to hurt the children and did not think she needed to be separated from them. “It was very confusing because a minute later, she was making them lunch or playing with them or getting ready for bed or whatever it was,” Patrick Clancy said, adding that Lindsay was not displaying “any intention” of hurting the kids. He also testified that Lindsay began expressing suicidal thoughts in December 2022, saying: “She started to say that she was suicidal.” After killing her children, Lindsay allegedly attempted to take her own life by jumping from her home’s second-floor window which left her paralyzed from the waist down. Lindsay Clancy’s chaplain: “She said to me … ‘I’m so glad my children are safe’” after killings Sheila Cavanaugh, a chaplain at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston, Massachusetts, who met with Lindsay Clancy numerous times after the killings of her children, also testified in court. “Her emotional state was very neutral, a flat affect, but I remember vividly the first thing she said to me,” Cavanaugh testified, recalling her conversation with Lindsay at the hospital where she was still “covered” in tubes and wearing a neck brace. “We had been praying together, and so when I went in on Tuesday the 31 [of January], she said to me as I held her hand to comfort her: ‘I am so glad my children are safe,’” Cavanaugh said. Cavanaugh further testified that Lindsay Clancy said she had heard a male voice several times, which “according to Lindsay, told her that if she did not follow the command, neither she nor her children would be safe”. “She alluded to the fact that it was a male voice and it was persistent,” Cavanaugh said. During cross-examination, when asked why her notes did not mention the voice, Cavanaugh explained that she was “not there to evaluate the patient” but instead to “bear witness to their suffering”. Testimonies from Lindsay Clancy’s mother, sister and former mother-in-law Lindsay Clancy’s mother and sister also testified about the deterioration of her mental state in the months leading up to the killings of her three children, describing increasing paranoia, insomnia and suicidal thoughts. Paula Musgrove, Lindsay Clancy’s mother, testified that her daughter had become increasingly paranoid in the fall of 2022. Musgrove said Lindsay Clancy was afraid to sleep alone and believed the medications she was taking “were destroying her mind”. In December 2022, Musgrove testified she was in the kitchen with Lindsay Clancy and Patrick Clancy when “she told us she had thoughts of harming the children.” A text message from Lindsay Clancy to her mother shown in court also detailed her worsening condition. It read: “Mom, will you please come up and stay with me for a bit? I’m really sick. Something is wrong … I had horrible insomnia all night, and I just don’t know how I am going to get through the day … It’s just really scary, and I don’t want to be alone.” Lindsay Clancy’s sister, Allison Ozga, similarly testified about her sister’s declining mental state. During Thanksgiving 2022, Ozga said Lindsay Clancy’s “mood did not look good”. By December, Ozga testified that her sister “very much decompensated”. “I’m in a really tough spot,” Ozga recalled her sister saying, adding that toward the end of December 2022, Lindsay Clancy told her she “had suicidal ideation every day for a month.” Meanwhile, Lindsay Clancy’s former mother-in-law, Susan Clancy, testified that Lindsay Clancy was “begging for help” as her mental health struggles worsened. “Lindsay was struggling, we were all concerned,” Susan Clancy said. She also confirmed that her son went skiing after dropping Lindsay Clancy off at Women & Infants Hospital of Rhode Island for treatment in December 2022. Lindsay Clancy supporters rally outside courthouse Over 300 supporters, mostly women, rallied outside the courthouse in Plymouth, Massachusetts, in support of Lindsay Clancy as the trial shed light on women’s struggles with mental health. Many of the supporters wore pink with the words: “Believe”, “She Needed Help” and “Peace For Lindsay”. Speaking to the Associated Press during the rally, April Vincent, a 52-year-old paralegal from Providence, Rhode Island, said: “Women are being dismissed, neglected and ignored when we speak up … We’re scared because nobody takes us seriously.” Jeanne Zaborski, a 72-year-old retired nurse from Rockland, Massachusetts, told the outlet from the outside of the courthouse: “It’s very sad … I am a mother. I am a grandmother. I have a sister who had problems after birth and it’s just very sad. I hope Lindsay gets the care she needs and deserves and other women will come together like we did today.” Civil medical malpractice lawsuits remain under way Lindsay Clancy and her ex-husband, Patrick Clancy, have filed several civil lawsuits against doctors and hospitals involved in Lindsay Clancy’s care. Lindsay Clancy alleges negligence and medical malpractice, while Patrick Clancy alleges wrongful death. Lindsay Clancy’s lawsuit alleges that the defendants “each failed to properly diagnose Lindsay’s bipolar disorder with postpartum onset and instead subjected her to a disorganized, uncoordinated course of polypharmacy that exacerbated her condition and precipitated a severe psychotic break.” Patrick Clancy’s lawsuit similarly alleges that “the bevy of diverse and powerful medications they misprescribed coupled with their abject failure to appropriately monitor Lindsay resulted in Lindsay’s mental health deteriorating to the point of suicidal ideation and requiring in-patient care”. “Ultimately, defendants’ negligent treatment of Lindsay, including their complete failure to recognize and address the radical erosion of her mental health, resulted in tragedy, namely, allegations that Lindsay took the lives of her children,” his lawsuit adds.

title: Judge declares mistrial in Lindsay Clancy case after jury deadlocked again
summary: Defense lawyer had asked for time to request emergency stay after jury was split 11 to one
text: The judge in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children, has declared a mistrial after the jury could not reach a unanimous verdict and remained deadlocked after a week of deliberations. Jurors in Plymouth state court spent more than 38 hours in deliberations over the charges against the 36-year-old woman, which came on the heels of a weeks-long trial that directed national attention to maternal mental health issues that can occur postpartum. The 12-person jury was made up of nine women and three men and, according to the notes given to the court, was split 11 to one. After the jury returned without a verdict for the third time, Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial but was interrupted by a last-minute request from Clancy’s lead defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, who requested one hour to petition for an emergency stay to seek relief from a superior court judge. That emergency filing with the Massachusetts supreme judicial court asked a single justice to order Sullivan to further question the dissenting juror, arguing the juror was “biased” and, per jury notes, unwilling to follow the court’s instructions on reasonable doubt. “Intervention is necessary in this case to avoid an avoidable mistrial of a case that is so time and labor intensive and that has captured so much public attention,” the filing reads, which also claimed that the court had “abdicated its responsibility to ensure the integrity of the jury”. The filing also asked that the juror be barred from further deliberations if Sullivan determined that they could not follow the instructions issued by the court. “A mistrial at this point is entirely avoidable, but only if the court does its job,” the filing says. Additionally, the filing claimed the court “reflects a bias against those who suffer from debilitating mental illness”, arguing that mental illness is a “protected category” under the fifth and 14th amendments of the US constitution. The filing was discussed with the Massachusetts supreme court justice Dalila Argaez Wendlandt during a Zoom hearing that was open to the public for viewing. Prosecutor Jennifer Sprague summarized what happened with the jury and their repeated notes indicating a deadlock before defense attorney Dana Goldblatt argued that the supreme judicial court had the discretion to order the trial court to make the inquiry of the juror. Wendlandt then said she would take the matter under advisement. The petition was subsequently denied. Clancy, a former neonatal and delivery nurse, had been accused of strangling her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, in the family’s Duxbury home in January 2023. Prosecutors argued in opening statements that Clancy had “coldly and efficiently executed” her children, doing so with “no hesitation, with deliberate premeditation and extreme atrocity and cruelty” after she “drew her husband out of the house, their father, so that she had the opportunity and the time to carry out these murders”. But Clancy’s defense team argued she was “suffering from psychosis” when she killed her children and allegedly attempted suicide by jumping from an upper window in her home, which left her partly paralyzed. Reddington told jurors that Clancy suffered from postpartum depression after giving birth to her third child, Callan, and been prescribed a variety of medications. “This is a young woman who, with her husband, tried very hard to get the help she needed,” he said. Clancy has not denied that she killed her children, but her not-guilty plea was predicated on a lack of criminal responsibility because, as her defense team said, she was suffering from postpartum psychosis, which included auditory hallucinations that commanded her to harm her children, and undiagnosed bipolar disorder. Under Massachusetts law, the defendant must have “retained the substantial capacity to appreciate the wrongfulness or criminality of their conduct and to conform their conduct to the requirements of the law” in order to be found guilty. Throughout the trial, jurors heard from Clancy’s former husband Patrick Clancy, her mother and aunt, and an array of psychologists and treating physicians. The court heard that Clancy had been prescribed 13 different medications for anxiety and sleep, which the defense said may have exacerbated her symptoms of depression. Clancy had checked herself into a psychiatric clinic in the weeks before the killings. Later, on 24 January 2023, she sent her then husband out for food and to collect pharmacy medications. In that time, police say, she strangled their children with exercise bands. Her ability to orchestrate a window of time to carry out the killings, prosecutors argued, was evidence of premeditation. Before resting his case last week, Reddington called forensic psychiatrist Dr Phillip Resnick to testify that Clancy had “severe depression” and a history of anxiety, which increased after the birth of her children to the point that she “felt she couldn’t function”. “At the time of the crime on Jan 24, 2023, Ms Clancy was frankly psychotic,” Resnick said. “She was clearly psychotic on that day.” After the declaration of the mistrial, prosecutors have the option of trying Clancy again. The court has set a status conference for 9am ET on 29 September. Clancy’s criminal trial will be followed by a civil claim brought by both Lindsay and Patrick Clancy against her medical and mental healthcare providers. The former couple claim the providers committed medical malpractice by failing to properly diagnose, treat and monitor her severe postpartum psychiatric condition. After formally declaring the mistrial, the judge thanked the jury for their time and consideration. “Each one of you knew how long the case was going to go. You knew how difficult the case was going to be to listen to facts-wise, but still, you braced for that duty,” Sullivan said before dismissing them. He also indicated that should there be a re-trial, he would want it to happen “sometime in the fall”. Plymouth county district attorney Tim Cruz told reporters that Clancy’s trial had been “an emotional trial for everybody”. “This was and has always been about getting justice for those three little babies,” Cruz said. “We’re here at this courthouse today because those children are not. Our priority has always been to fight for Cora, for Dawson and for Callan.” Cruz also praised assistant district attorneys Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham, whom he said “are both mothers themselves – and went home to their families after each long day in court”. Reddington addressed reporters outside the courthouse, too, saying that Cruz “knows he was crushed”. “I’m representing a woman who is a fantastic, wonderful individual,” Reddington said. “This woman is so brave, so awesome. She sat there through seven weeks of the trial, where nobody had anything bad to say about her except the two prosecutors.” Reddington also thanked the jury, “minus one” – referring to the holdout juror whom he said he “hope[s] they can sleep at night”. In response to how Clancy’s parents are doing after the mistrial, Reddington said: “Not good.” “They know that they were robbed by one [juror] for whatever [their] agenda was,” Reddington remarked. “And I got a funny feeling that [the jury] would have gone on for another week if they had to. So I hope that [juror] can sleep well at night.” “If we didn’t have that one individual, we would’ve had a verdict and we would be out of here,” he continued. He added that Clancy is “like a daughter to me”. It was not immediately known what outcome the 11 decided jurors had voted for. Reddington had earlier said that, judging from a jury note, one juror “clearly and unequivocally” would not apply the concept of reasonable doubt “to the evidence to return a not guilty verdict”. Reddington also said that if Clancy is retried, he will “request” that the jury be sequestered. After Friday’s mistrial declaration, Patrick Clancy’s lawyer, David Meier, issued a statement saying his client was “grateful to the court and to the jurors for their hard work, their commitment and their perseverance”. “The loss of Patrick’s children is something from which he will never recover and from which there will never be closure,” said the statement, obtained by a CBS Boston reporter. “The prospect of reliving this tragedy through another trial is extraordinarily painful – for Patrick, for his family and for all us.” Donald Trump also weighed in on the trial, telling reporters at the White House that the case was a “horrible tragedy” and a “terrible situation”. “I assume there’s going to be another trial,” the president said. “She did a horrible, horrible thing. Can’t be worse. “There’ll be a price. It’s going to be a mental institution or jail or something ... It’s too bad.” • In the US, the national maternal mental health hotline is 1-833-852-6262. In the UK, the Pandas foundation offers support via Whatsapp on 07903 508334. In Australia, the national maternal and perinatal mental health hotline is 1300 726 306

title: Lindsay Clancy judge declares mistrial – what happens next?
summary: The case essentially goes back to the same status as before the trial began, and prosecutors have to decide whether to try again
text: A Massachusetts jury was unable to come to a unanimous decision in the trial of Lindsay Clancy, a mother accused of murdering her three children, and a mistrial has been declared by Judge William Sullivan. The 12-person jury was made up of nine women and three men and, according to the notes given to the court, was split 11 to one. Clancy doesn’t deny strangling her children at their home near Boston, but says she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and that led to her actions. After the killings, her husband found her injured in the yard, where she landed after jumping from a second-story window. She was left paralyzed from the waist down. Prosecutors argued she knew what she was doing in a deliberate act of murder. So what happens now? Mistrial A mistrial means the case essentially goes back to the same status as before the trial began, with the 36-year-old former nurse charged with murder and held at a psychiatric hospital awaiting a resolution of the criminal case. Will prosecutors try again? Prosecutors have to decide whether to try again with a new jury for the case. If they do attempt a second trial, the jury selection process would begin again and a new trial would be scheduled. However, the exact type of charges could potentially be different. Plea deal? Prosecutors could also offer a plea deal to Clancy, said Brad Bailey, a Boston defense attorney and legal expert. “Any time the threat of a retrial with murder one hanging over the client is re-interjected, defense lawyers will, at the very least, explore whether or not there’s any interest in a resolution,” Bailey told the Associated Press. Give up? The district attorney’s office could also decide to not retry the case out of a sense that another mistrial is likely in the complex and emotional case. “Sometimes they decide not to, because of the sense that there may be the same result each time they try it, and because of the expenditures involved in trying the case to begin with, particularly when you have expert witnesses,” Bailey said. “Those are going to be expensive cases.” What will the defense do? Clancy’s defense team will almost certainly push to drop the charges against their client. Bailey expected her defense attorney to aggressively lobby against another trial if a mistrial is declared, making a case to the district attorney’s office along the lines of: “‘Why are you doing this to this poor woman? She’s still clearly obviously suffering. She’s been punished with her paralysis and, worse than that, the loss of her three children.’” The court has set a status conference for 9am ET on 29 September. • In the US, the national maternal mental health hotline is 1-833-852-6262. In the UK, the Pandas foundation offers support via WhatsApp on 07903 508334. In Australia, the national maternal and perinatal mental health hotline is 1300 726 306. title: ‘‘Never Forget’ is not a slogan’: Mamdani designates 9/11 as a Day of Remembrance and Service
summary: The New York City mayor will sign two executive orders honoring those impacted by the attacks, as he faces campaign to exclude him from the 25th anniversary commemoration
text: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani is set to designate September 11 as a Day of Remembrance and Service ahead of the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks. Mamdani’s office announced on Friday morning that the mayor will sign two executive orders honoring victims, first responders, survivors, city workers and families affected by the attacks. The orders will also strengthen the city’s ability to protect New Yorkers and maintain essential services during emergencies. The first executive order is expected to designate time on September 11 for a moment of silence honoring those killed in the attacks, as well as those who have suffered health consequences in the years since. It will also encourage city agencies to hold memorial ceremonies, educational programming and other remembrance activities. The designation would mark the first city-level action of its kind by a New York City mayor, Mamdani’s office said. The second executive order will overhaul the city’s emergency continuity plans for the first time since 2007. It will also create a new interagency team to coordinate the city’s response and continuity planning. In a statement on Friday, Mamdani said: “I am honored to establish the City’s first Day of Remembrance and Service on September 11th to remember those we lost on that horrific day and the first responders, families and city workers whose lives were irrevocably changed in the aftermath. Through this executive order, we are calling on New Yorkers to honor their memory through service and deep reflection. “We must also recognize that remembrance carries a responsibility to strengthen our city, protect New Yorkers and ensure that government is prepared to deliver for people no matter the circumstances. ‘Never Forget’ is not a slogan. It is a commitment that we must carry forward through action. And that is precisely what these two executive orders demonstrate,” he added. The city’s fire department commissioner Lillian Bonsignore echoed similar sentiments, saying: “Service was the legacy of those who answered the call on September 11, 2001, and those who have died since. The greatest tribute we can pay them is to continue serving one another with compassion, courage and a shared commitment to building a stronger New York.” Mamdani’s announcement comes amid a wave of attacks, some Islamophobic, targeting the 34-year-old democratic socialist, who is the city’s first Muslim mayor. A recent petition with more than 98,000 signatures, including from family members who lost relatives in the attacks, calls for Mamdani to be excluded from September 11 commemorative events marking the 25th anniversary. Among other claims, the petition accuses the mayor of supporting individuals whose public statements or records are viewed as “dismissive of American institutions or insufficiently critical of extremist ideologies”. Former New York governor George Pataki, a Republican, has also said Mamdani should skip the 9/11 memorial. But other families and local lawmakers have pushed back. Elizabeth Miller, whose father was killed in the attacks, told CBS earlier this month: “The focus should be on where are we in this world, 25 years later?” “Mayor Mamdani has assured 9/11 families that he wants to be there to honor our loved ones, and I think he should be allowed to do that,” added Miller, the project director of September 11th Families for Peaceful Tomorrows, a remembrance organization. In a separate statement, the organization said: “We strongly condemn the anti-American accusations and Islamophobic sentiment underlying the effort seeking to prevent him from being at Ground Zero. “For decades, we have firmly maintained that Ground Zero is sacred space and should never be used as a platform for political speech or partisan politics. Ground Zero remains a burial ground.” Meanwhile, city council speaker Julie Menin called the push to exclude Mamdani “absolutely inappropriate”, adding: “I think mayor [Mike] Bloomberg made a terrific decision in making sure that there were not political speeches because, again, it shouldn’t be politicized … So, those that are trying to politicize this, what is happening on the 25th anniversary, I think that that is unfortunate.” Responding to a question about how he felt about the petition a few weeks ago, Mamdani told reporters: “I will proudly honor the families, the survivors, the first responders, forever impacted by that horrific terror attack, by standing alongside them at this year’s 9/11 commemoration, reaffirming that we will never forget the solemn day felt by all of us who call this city home, and frankly, by all of us who call this country home.” Even before taking office, Mamdani faced Islamophobic attacks on the campaign trail, including from his political opponents, former governor Andrew Cuomo, House Republicans who have called for his deportation, as well as Donald Trump.
