title: Farage seeks to shore up damaged leadership as scandal engulfs Reform conference
summary: Splits emerge within party after resignation of officials reported to police for apparent plot to evade donations law
text: Nigel Farage sought to shore up his damaged leadership on Friday as he attempted to distance himself from two of his most senior officials reported to the police for apparently plotting to evade the law on foreign donations. As the scandal engulfed Reform UK’s party conference in Birmingham, Farage was forced to suspend close aides Dan Jukes and head of policy James Orr after an undercover investigation by reporters from a group called Verbatim. He later acknowledged Jukes and Orr had made “human error” and were “not authorised” to act in the way they did when trying to orchestrate donations to benefit the party from a fake US businessman, who was not permitted to give money. The Met police are now assessing the evidence after a complaint that Farage, Orr and Jukes may have broken political funding laws, with sources suggesting a full investigation is highly likely to be launched. They all deny wrongdoing. One possibility would be for the police to extend an existing Met investigation into whether Reform took donations channelled through an intermediary from potentially impermissible sources, which the party and donors deny. Orr is an associate professor of divinity at the University of Cambridge who had been working for Reform, reporting directly to Farage, since February. In relation to the undercover footage of Orr, a spokesperson for the university said Cambridge was “looking into these matters”. Jukes is Farage’s closest aide, and has been at his side for more than a decade working on communications and strategy. Farage had been introduced by Jukes to the would-be donor from the US promising to give £500,000 despite not being eligible, who was really an undercover reporter. The Reform leader then appeared to endorse the scheme for the impermissible US donor to give money through his son, a UK intermediary, by saying “thank you, both” and “all above board”. After dismissing the sting as a “hoax”, Reform began an organised campaign to limit the damage to Farage personally before his main conference speech, after a summer of scandals over his finances, including an undeclared gift of £5m. Addressing the allegations, the Reform leader responded by reading out a legal statement in which he dismissed the allegations as “a little local difficulty” and described the reports as “an exercise in entrapment”. Farage claimed Orr and Jukes had merely been “contractors” who engaged in “loose pub talk, including a couple of boasts that simply were not true”. One party figure, Nadine Dorries, claimed Jukes had merely booked transport and carried bags, despite being a senior adviser integral to Reform’s operations and success for many years. When it was put to Farage that he had thanked the bogus donors and understood what was going on, he said: “It was the middle of the byelection. I was told I had to go and meet these people. I didn’t have to, but I did. I was told they had a global family trust headquartered in London. I asked the question: is this all above board?” The Reform leader also insisted that the party’s internal processes would have stopped any impermissible donors and said neither Jukes nor Orr should have been carrying out fundraising. He said a suggestion by Jukes in the footage that other foreign donations had been channelled through UK intermediaries was not true and the donors did not exist. The pair were caught out after being filmed by undercover reporters from the group Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, and broadcast by Channel 4 News on the eve of Reform’s party conference. In the footage, Orr and Jukes appeared to help orchestrate an impermissible donation of £30,000 from the fake US donor, which was used to pay for polling that would benefit Reform and made front pages of national newspapers. The money from an American company was transferred to the polling company JL Partners after being organised at the behest of Reform to boost its policies and political narrative. It was not declared to the Electoral Commission. Jukes went on to discuss whether the US businessman could give £500,000 through a UK intermediary, who was an undercover reporter, and introduced the would-be donors to Farage at a lunch in Clacton over oysters and champagne. Jukes issued a statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals using selective editing who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.” Orr said: “I have agreed to step down from my current role at Reform UK pending the outcome of the party’s internal investigation into the conduct of the program, with which I will cooperate fully.” The Lib Dems have asked the standards commissioner to investigate Farage’s conduct. The row comprehensively overshadowed the first full day of the party’s conference with every Reform politician repeatedly questioned over the scandal. It also exposed splits at the top of the party, with Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, strongly distancing himself from Jukes and Orr. He told reporters “anyone who supports Reform is disappointed”, and added of the investigation: “It’s just not something I am personally involved in.” He also launched a personal video about his backstory, leading to speculation he could attempt to run for the leadership as a rival to Robert Jenrick or Richard Tice if Farage were to be forced out over his financial scandals. However, some Reform insiders are convinced Farage will part company with Yusuf before long, partly over his ambition and combative style on social media, including one post on X that saw him accused of racism towards a Somalia-born Labour councillor. Farage is understood to have used a rude term about Yusuf recently in relation to his troublemaking on social media. One senior Reform figure said they believed Yusuf would have to go as a precondition for some sort of reconciliation with Rupert Lowe, whose party, Restore Britain, has eaten into the party’s voters on the hard right. Farage has recently condemned Lowe as vindictive, but some of their friends believe a rapprochement could be possible if Yusuf were no longer in the party. Reform had wanted the main event to be Farage announcing a deal with the hard-right French National Rally president, Jordan Bardella, to return small boats crossing the Channel if both parties achieve power. However, a press conference was dominated by questions about the foreign donations scandal. Farage’s main speech was later delayed by security concerns after climate protesters disrupted Tice’s stage appearance. More activists later repeatedly interrupted his address. While waiting to go on stage, the Reform leader danced and sung with the crowd. He began his speech by calling for Andy Burnham to hold a general election and accusing Labour of planning to put up taxes. The speech was light on policy but Farage at one point hinted he could look at the way judges are appointed in future – suggesting the party could look at a system of political appointments as is the case in the US.

title: US immigration judges told to slash time given to people awaiting visas or green cards before being deported
summary: Exclusive: Mandatory training for judges also urged them to threaten attorneys who accept too many cases
text: Immigration judges across the United States have been instructed to deny some of the most vulnerable people appearing in court the time needed for their visas or green cards to arrive – putting them at imminent risk of being thrown out of the country as the Trump administration continues to intensify its mass deportation campaign, the Guardian has learned. Among the immigrants affected are abused and abandoned children and survivors of violent crime, according to the US government’s own training materials, which were shared exclusively with the Guardian. Judges also appeared to be discouraged, under a hardline interpretation of existing policy guidance and laws, from giving people more than 10 days to find an attorney before proceeding with a case, a deadline that made critics balk. “I thought, who has time to find an attorney in 10 days?” one source familiar with the training told the Guardian this week, under the condition of anonymity to protect against feared retribution from the Trump administration. The source added: “There is no room to be kind; there is only urgency to make them leave [the US], one way or the other.” According to the source, hundreds of immigration judges attended a mandatory presentation in recent days about “continuances” – a legal tool which has historically been used to give immigrants more time to find lawyers, build their cases or wait for approval of their applications for documents at another federal immigration agency. The virtual training session was led by a veteran immigration judge, Keith Hunsucker of the board of immigration appeals, the immigration courts’ appellate branch. He denied over 80% of asylum cases for much of the time that he was on the bench in immigration court before moving on to other roles. The visual presentation was called “Motions to Continue: Efficiently Advancing Cases to Completion”, according to images of the slides used that were shared with the Guardian. The training’s thrust was to tightly restrict continuances in favor of faster adjudications, even when granting more time would allow people to receive legal protections to remain in the US, such as a visa or green card they have qualified for or had approved and are simply awaiting. A deportation slams shut some of those pathways and yet is a much more likely outcome when continuances are denied and rulings are made abruptly. The logic presented in Judge Hunsucker’s training was to cut out inefficiencies and avoidable delays, amid a backlog of roughly 3.2m pending immigration court cases nationally. “Where a party lacks diligence and ‘sleeps on their rights,’ a continuance is unwarranted,” the presentation slides read. But the development raises concerns that the crackdown will instead harm immigrants with legitimate cases. The executive office for immigration review (EOIR), which houses the immigration courts, is not part of the independent judicial branch of the federal government. It sits within the Department of Justice, where the US attorney general can make precedential decisions and otherwise exercise control. In response to the Guardian’s request for comment, an unnamed justice department spokesperson said in a statement, in part: “Reducing the immigration court backlog remains one of the highest priorities for this administration. The Justice Department is restoring integrity to our immigration system by hearing cases fairly, expeditiously, and uniformly, in accordance with the law.” An unnamed EOIR spokesperson similarly replied that the agency “prioritizes the timely completion of all cases and immigration judges are obligated to adhere to current immigration law, regulations, precedent decisions, and EOIR policies to ensure cases do not languish [and] are handled in a timely and lawful manner. Unnecessary delay hurts both aliens with meritorious claims and the American public who wish to see aliens with non-meritorious claims removed as quickly as possible.” Amid the Trump administration’s anti-immigration agenda, accelerated adjudications and extraordinarily large mass hearings have become fixtures of the immigration court system, with continuances fewer and farther between, and often for shorter lengths of time when granted, even for children. The presentation slides shared with the Guardian appear to formalize that trend across immigration courts, cautioning judges that “some continuances are sought solely for the purpose of delay” and “persons illegally present in the United States who wish to remain have a substantial incentive to prolong litigation so they may avoid deportation as long as possible”. “Continuance requests solely for dilatory purposes should not be countenanced by Immigration Judges,” one slide read, even though it has long been incumbent upon judges to discern between due process and unnecessary delays. For instance, many documents are held up because of processing backlogs and tight quotas at US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), which comes under the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Such long waits are beyond the control of the applicant or the justice department. In particular, the training suggests that an approved visa petition should not delay deportation proceedings if the visa itself is not yet available because of annual quotas but would be issued to the qualified recipient at a later, albeit unspecified, date. And it explicitly targets the special immigrant juvenile (SIJ) classification for abused, abandoned or neglected youth, as well as U non-immigrant status for survivors of especially egregious crimes. The prospect of routine denials of continuances so someone can find a lawyer to represent them is also a harsh turn for immigrants pleading their cases. From 2019 to 2024, only about a quarter of people with attorneys were ordered removed from the US, compared with over 60% who were unrepresented, according to the American Immigration Council. But with demand exceeding supply, only about a fifth of immigrants were represented when they were ordered deported in June. Yet the presentation warns that despite the desperate demand, immigration attorneys risk punitive measures for accepting what are deemed too many cases. “Where a practitioner takes on more cases than he or she can responsibly and professionally handle,” the slides read, “it may be appropriate for an Immigration Judge to consider referral to EOIR disciplinary counsel for further action and possible sanction for a violation.”

title: ‘I can’t be bought,’ Nige tells Reform’s faithful – however different it may look | John Crace
summary: Just as the party leader had hoped to change the narrative, along came Channel 4 News to spoil his conference fun
text: Why, oh why, oh why? You could almost feel Nigel Farage’s frustration. Why was it always him? Surely it was about time someone gave him a break. There he was trying to earn some money from a Thai crypto billionaire and a gold bullion dealer, and yet still Reform kept getting linked to dodgy cash. It was almost as if a pattern was emerging. First there was the £5m gift, then the Posh George donations via Dicky Tice, and now Channel 4 News had done a sting on him and two of his most trusted aides in which it looked as if they were happy to break the law on political donations. Life can be so damned unfair at times. Always kicking you when you are down. The headlines from Reform’s party conference in Birmingham were meant to be all about Nige declaring a national emergency the moment he got in to No 10. Instead he was dealing with a rather more pressing crisis. Every time he tries to persuade the country he’s running a serious party and that it isn’t a one-man band, something seems to happen to make it look like a dodgy, third-rate clown show. Operation Failed Clean-up was initially left in the hands of Richard Tice and Lee Anderson. Imagine how bad it has to be for these two to be left in charge. Dicky is one of the least plausible politicians you can hope to find, so he didn’t even appreciate the irony of claiming it was all an establishment plot run by leftwing eco activists. As for Lee, he was adamant that the two Reform members involved – James Orr, a Cambridge associate professor and supposed brains behind the party, and Dan Jukes, Nige’s trusted right-hand gofer for more than a decade – had been out of line and suspended from the party. More than that, they weren’t coming back. More than that he couldn’t say as an investigation had been started. So who was leading the investigation, he was asked. “I don’t know because the investigation hasn’t started,” Lee replied. Sometimes he runs Dicky a close second. Others were equally as confused. Danny Kruger was in a more forgiving mood and thought there might be some way back for Orr and Jukes once the Reform investigation had exonerated them. Nadine Dorries speculated that maybe they hadn’t known they would be breaking the law. Though the undercover footage rather indicated they had known exactly what they were doing. That accepting money from foreign donors was not an alien concept. Nige was just baffled. Fed up. Couldn’t believe how this had happened. Orr and Jukes were just contractors. Freelance labourers who had been brought in to paint the kitchen and had overstayed their welcome. He didn’t even know them, had barely met them. Even though both had been the closest of mates with him. Nige is never slow to throw comrades under the bus. It’s the narcissist’s first line of defence. Self-protection at all costs. At a lunchtime press conference, he had more to say. First he announced he had a spontaneous statement to make that sounded as if it had been carefully worded by his lawyers. It’s probably been an expensive day for Nige. It was a hoax. No laws had been broken. No money had been taken. Except Reform had allegedly taken £35,000 to pay for the opinion poll, and the film suggested they would have been more than happy to take the £500,000 if it had been genuine. Details, details. It was all a misunderstanding. James and Dan had just misspoken. And he couldn’t believe he had been caught on film having a “man of the people” champagne and oysters lunch with them and the undercover journalists in Clacton. Because he had only ever been in Clacton once in his life. What were the odds? “It was just some jack-the-laddery,” he said. “Pub talk.” Quite right. Which one of us hasn’t spent a long time chatting about crimes we were going to do and their exact modus operandi every time we have a couple of drinks? Still, at least some things about the Reform conference were business as usual. The queues. Who would have guessed that 8,000 people might turn up at once when you had already sold 8,000 tickets? This came as a surprise to the organisers. And to the member who had turned up dressed as Richard I. Where better to find support for a crusade against Muslims than at the Reform conference. First we take Birmingham, then we take Baghdad. With the conference already running an hour late before it had even started, it was left to Jeremy Kyle to fill in. He interviewed one punter who told him that all woke people should be hung. This was a little extreme even for Jezza. And there are plenty of people he would like to hang. Finally, though, we were up and running. First a tribute to Ann Widdecombe, then Anderson being given licence to try out his standup routine. Suella Braverman was a proper man, he insisted. Don’t call us, Lee. We’ll call you. Then came Zia, the self-appointed shadow home secretary who is too unpopular in his own party to be allowed to stand for election. All he really wanted to talk about was small boat crossings. The audience whooped regardless. The guest speaker was Jordan Bardella, the president of the far-right National Rally party in France. Not the sharpest pencil. He started by congratulating Nige on his brilliant win against the establishment bin in Clacton. It’s possible he doesn’t understand English humour. He then praised the Brits for standing up to Hitler in the war. A bit rich from a man whose party was founded by Nazi collaborators. The session closed with a handshake for Nige as they signed a new version of the entente cordiale. Much of the afternoon was a write-off. Matt Goodwin, Sarah Pochin, Dicky. I mean, who really cares? They are all lightweights. That just left Nige to round things off. Eventually, after yet another unscheduled delay and some 80s wedding filler songs. Cue some tacky smoke and pyrotechnic effects and the appearance of the Messiah. “I can’t be bought,” he declared on the video above him. Except it rather looks as if he can. The rest of the speech – with a few interruptions from protesters – was standard Nige. He would change the world in 100 days and sack any ministers who failed. There’s going to be a lot of ministerial vacancies. There was the invention of a reality where he was the Divine. It was all just lazy. Boring. Just one reference to the ongoing crisis. “The party has done nothing wrong,” he said. Mmm. With respect, that’s not something he gets to judge.

title: Cambridge University examines conduct of academic suspended by Reform UK
summary: James Orr, an associate professor, was shown in Channel 4 News footage apparently trying to sidestep electoral law
text: Cambridge University has said it is examining the conduct of James Orr, its associate professor and a top Reform UK aide, after he was filmed appearing to try to circumvent electoral laws on foreign political donations. Orr, the suspended head of policy for Reform, is one of two senior officials to step aside after claims that he orchestrated a plot to have polling paid for by a foreign firm – something that is impermissible under British electoral law. The academic was filmed by a group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, seemingly attempting to sidestep election laws. In a statement shared with the Guardian, a spokesperson for the University of Cambridge said: “The university is looking into these matters.” Orr is an associate professor of religion at Cambridge’s divinity faculty and teaches students at the university. Little known outside UK and US political circles, Orr has been a highly influential intellectual force within Reform. He was labelled the party’s “philosopher king” by the news organisation Politico. A key attraction for senior figures in Reform when appointing Orr was his high-level US political contacts within the Maga movement. JD Vance, the US vice-president, has called him his “intellectual mentor” and his “British Sherpa”. Footage broadcast by Channel 4 News on Thursday night showed an undercover reporter posing as a UK-based supporter in conversation with Orr. Orr discussed commissioning polling that was secretly organised by Reform, but suggested it be paid for by a US company belonging to the fake supporter’s supposed father. In a separate clip, Orr can be heard saying of the poll funding arrangement that Nigel Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it is the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. Reform UK initially described the Channel 4 News and Verbatim investigation as a “hoax”. On Thursday evening, Orr posted a video on his X account in which he said: “There is absolutely no way this could amount to a benefit or donation in kind at all.” He dismissed Verbatim as “politically motivated actors trying to discredit a political opponent through dubious legal means”. Still, on Friday morning he and Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Farage who has also denied wrongdoing, stood down pending an internal party investigation into the claims raised by the broadcast. Farage, who was also featured in the investigation meeting with the fake supporters, distanced himself from Orr and Jukes on Friday. The party leader told reporters: “The two individuals involved are not even part of our fundraising team, so they should have gone through the appropriate channels. Checks would have been made and they would never, ever have got to sit down at a table with me.” The Guardian has approached Orr for comment.

title: Cambridge University asks former chief crown prosecutor to open Arday review
summary: Nazir Afzal to focus in review’s first stage on support given to professor in immediate period before his death
text: The University of Cambridge has asked Nazir Afzal, a former chief crown prosecutor for north-west England, to lead the first part of its review into the death of the scholar Jason Arday. Arday died at his home in south London on 14 August, nine days after his resignation as a Cambridge professor amid swirling allegations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career. Prof Deborah Prentice, Cambridge’s vice-chancellor, said the time since Arday’s death had been “a period of profound sadness and reflection” for the university, and she sought to defend her institution from criticism. “We worked very hard to support Professor Arday during an appalling period of external criticism and focus but given the devastating outcome, we are all asking ourselves whether we could have and should have done more. This review will answer that question,” Prentice said. “We are committed to ensuring that any recommendations arising from the review are addressed and adopted with clear accountability for delivering necessary changes.” Arday was named professor of sociology of education at Cambridge in 2023, with the university highlighting his appointment as the university’s youngest ever black professor at the age of 37. Arday denied accusations of plagiarism levelled against him but on 5 August the university said it would hold an investigation into his academic qualifications. Arday resigned hours after the investigation was announced. Prentice said the review would be in two parts, with the first, led by Afzal, to focus on the support given to Arday in the immediate period before his death. Afzal said: “I am honoured to have been asked to lead part one of this important independent review. At its heart is a person, a family and a community who have been profoundly affected by Professor Arday’s death. It is important that we approach this work with both rigour and humanity. “My responsibility will be to listen carefully, examine the evidence thoroughly and understand what support, interventions and protections were available to Professor Arday in the period before his death. We must be willing to ask difficult questions, including whether more could and should have been done. This work will be conducted independently and with urgency.” Afzal, a University of Birmingham graduate, is the chancellor of the University of Manchester, having been head of the CPS in the north-west of England during which he prosecuted child exploitation rings in Rochdale. In 2022 he led an independent review into London fire brigade that exposed a culture of misogyny, racism and bullying. Prentice said: “I am very grateful to Nazir for agreeing to lead this part of the review. He is a highly respected legal professional who will ask challenging questions about the support that was offered to Professor Arday during his time at Cambridge.” The university said the review’s second stage would consider “the wider context of Professor Arday’s time at the university”, including the recruitment of senior academic staff, the university’s response to allegations of research misconduct, and the support it gave to academics “subject to extraordinary public and media scrutiny”. Cambridge said it would appoint an independent external chair for the second part and an expert panel “including individuals with lived experience” to advise the review. It said part one of the review was expected to report within three months, and the second part within six months of establishing the expert panel. Earlier this week, Jacqui Smith, the minister responsible for higher education, told parliament that she was “more than just keeping an eye” on Cambridge’s response to Arday’s death. Smith said England’s higher education regulator, the Office for Students, had the powers to investigate further if necessary.

title: Trump’s ex-labor secretary drank on job and created ‘toxic’ work environment, report alleges
summary: Labor department report alleges Lori Chavez-DeRemer also made a staffer attend a strip club while on a personal trip
text: Donald Trump’s former secretary of labor, Lori Chavez-DeRemer, drank during working hours, kept alcohol on federal property and made a staffer attend a strip club while on a personal trip, according to a new report by the Department of Labor’s office of inspector general . Chavez-DeRemer was appointed by Trump to serve as labor secretary in January 2025 and resigned in April 2026 amid the misconduct allegations. The 38-page report contains striking allegations that Chavez-DeRemer “engaged in an inappropriate relationship” with a bodyguard, accepted gifts without properly reporting them under ethics rules and directed employees to perform personal tasks for her, including going to her home to organize her bedroom closet during work hours. The report also said she contributed to a “toxic, intimidating and humiliating” work environment. Thirty-eight witnesses provided testimony for the report, which stemmed from an anonymous complaint filed with the office, prompting an investigation that began in January 2026. Collectively, they alleged that Chavez-DeRemer created a “hostile work environment” during her relatively brief tenure as labor secretary. Chavez-DeRemer’s attorney, Nick Oberheiden, said in an emailed statement in response to the report: “Secretary Chavez-DeRemer is not surprised about the report: the report is untimely, moot, built around undisclosed individuals, and concludes what Ms Chavez-DeRemer always knew, namely that she did not break any laws.” The US Department of Labor said in a statement on the report and its findings: “The department respects the integrity of the inspector general’s investigation and refers you to their office on all matters related to the report.” The report accused Chavez-DeRemer, who previously served as a member of Congress, of using agency funds for personal travel, citing interviews with witnesses who identified “at least thirteen trips to destinations where Chavez-DeRemer visited family or her other personal residences and five trips to Las Vegas, Nevada”. Chavez-DeRemer’s lodging exceeded allowed reimbursement rates, including three nights at a “luxury hotel and spa” in Palm Beach, Florida, it stated. The report also alleged Chavez-DeRemer and her aides “regularly drank alcohol in Chavez-DeRemer’s study during official duty hours” and employees who abstained were ridiculed for doing so. During personal travel to Oregon last year, Chavez-DeRemer “requested an off-the-record stop at an establishment that was determined upon entry to feature partially nude dancers”, the report alleged. “Chavez-DeRemer then took additional money from her purse and asked the agent to drop the bills one by one onto the partially nude woman,” it stated. “The agent again hesitated and sought intervention from ASAIC 1, who told him to follow Chavez-DeRemer’s instructions. The agent complied against his wishes.” The report also alleged Chavez-DeRemer’s staffers contributed to a hostile work environment, which included holding “beatdowns” where her aides “berated employees for perceived performance deficiencies”. Two of her top aides, Department of Labor chief of staff Jihun Han and deputy chief of staff Rebecca Wright, left the agency in March 2026 amid the investigation into their misconduct. The report alleged Wright “reportedly evaluated applicants in part by appearance and weight, including Wright relocating an employee’s desk because she did not want a ‘fat person’ visible in the front office and making derogatory comments regarding another employee’s appearance and hygiene”. Witnesses in the report also accused Wright’s aides of openly investigating employees to try to find out who had provided information to the media and had advised the firing of three employees they suspected of doing so. “Witnesses further stated that Wright advised an employee not to cut her hair above her shoulders to avoid ‘turning into a lesbian’,” it stated. “During a conversation with an employee and Chavez-DeRemer, Wright discouraged this employee from using the [Department of Labor] daycare center based on the race of the daycare staff differing from that of the employee’s children. Chavez-DeRemer did not address Wright’s comments or acknowledge that they were inappropriate.”

title: In the picture and missing out | Letters
summary: A camera can interfere with fully experiencing the moment, writes Greg Lewis, while Alan Payling recalls the privacy of the photo booth
text: Phoebe Greenwood is right (Sunsets, disasters, dinners: we now record them all with our phones. But what is that doing to our souls?, 29 August). Having been a photojournalist, I find that the camera can interfere with fully experiencing the moment. Many years ago, my wife discovered previously unknown relatives in Denmark. When we visited, they took us to a cemetery where one of her ancestors was buried. She stood there quietly for a few minutes and began to cry. I started photographing and suddenly realised that I had shifted into work mode, both physically and mentally. I put the camera down and gave her a hug. After deciding that I wasn’t going to take photos when not working, we were on a whale-watching trip. I was the only one who saw the whale. Everyone else was looking at their mobile phones. Greg Lewis Clovis, California, US • In the absence of a personal camera, in the late 1960s, the commonly used alternative for young lovers to record their undying devotion to each other was the photo booth. Apparently they were used by some to provide passport photos, but I recall that on Friday and Saturday evenings in Birmingham city centre, they were an essential part of a good night out. Not only would you get four photos to share; the curtain also provided a few moments of privacy, although only from the waist upwards! Alan Payling Torquay, Devon • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: UN votes to adopt new world map that shows Africa’s true scale
summary: Togo-sponsored resolution called to phase out traditional map that depicts continent as similar size to Greenland
text: The United Nations has voted to adopt a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favour of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size. In a session at its headquarters in New York, the UN general assembly officially retired the 16th-century Mercator projection in favour of one based on the more accurate 2018 Equal Earth design. At the session, 164 countries voted in favour of the resolution. Only the US voted no, with its representative saying the resolution was “superfluous”. There were six abstentions. UN resolutions are non-enforceable, so countries and institutions will not be mandated to use only the new projection or forbidden from using the old one. However, the outcome is expected to result in an update of classroom curriculums and everyday technology given the wide usage of the Mercator projection in education, technology and governance. Togo, which spearheaded a campaign for the resolution on behalf of the African Union, said the resolution “recognises and affirms that disproportionate cartographic representations, particularly those resulting from the Mercator projection, have had lasting cognitive, educational, cultural, geopolitical and socioeconomic effects, contributing to a drastic reduction in the perceived size of Africa and other regions of the world in the global collective imagination”. Speaking before the resolution passed, Robert Dussey, Togo’s foreign affairs minister, said: “This discussion is not a political discussion [but] a scientific discussion, because there is scientific proof so we all have to accept the reality.” The Mercator layout was introduced by the Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569 to help sailors navigate the seas. Almost five centuries later, it remains the global standard. Because of its projection style, however, regions near the equator appear significantly smaller than they are, whereas high-latitude areas look much larger. For example, the map shows Africa as being similar in size to Greenland, but the continent is 14 times larger than the Danish territory. “You could fit the United States, China, India, Japan, Mexico and much of Europe into Africa and still have land to spare,” says a petition on Change.org for the #CorrectTheMap campaign, which has more than 11,000 signatures. The African Union endorsed the campaign in August 2025 and then asked Togo to spearhead its adoption. On Friday, before the vote, France’s foreign minister spoke in support of the resolution. “[We] will abandon the Mercator projection in favour of map representations tailored to specific uses, more faithful to actual surface areas and in line with the recommendations of cartographers and scientists,” Jean-Noël Barrot said during a speech at the Sorbonne University in Paris, in a move seen as part of France’s push to increase goodwill among its former colonies. France will now use the Eckert IV projection, which is close to the Equal Earth projection recommended in the resolution. Historians and geographers have said for years that the Mercator projection is rooted in western stereotypes. Activists have echoed this, with some coining the term “cartographic colonialism”. Some argue that the map has subtly shaped international power dynamics by minimising the physical presence of the global south and visually inflating northern hemisphere nations while shrinking equatorial regions. This is said to have reinforced systemic biases in international trade, development priorities and educational frameworks. One of the Mercator projection’s most prominent critics was Arno Peters, a German historian, who launched the Peters world map based on the Gall–Peters projection in 1973. It has often been used as an alternative to the Mercator map. Togo’s #CorrectTheMap campaign promoted the use of the 2018 Equal Earth design, which was developed by an international team of cartographers. Supporters say it will help to reverse perceptions of Africa and decolonise global curriculums. Some analysts agree. JJ Enoch, a London-based senior associate at JS Held, a geopolitical risk advisory firm, said the Mercator projection visually diminished Africa’s true scale. He linked the campaign to a quest by African nations for “greater influence in global institutions and greater control over how the continent is represented”. He said: “Adopting an equal-area map … would provide a more accurate basis for education and public understanding, while signalling that Africa’s demographic, economic and geopolitical importance should no longer be viewed through inherited and distorted conventions.” Togo’s government is planning an event in Lomé, the Togolese capital, with Unesco, the African Union and tech brands such as Google Maps during the first quarter of next year to map out the implementation of the resolution. Speaking before the vote, Dussey said: “To those who say why now, I say: why not? When we look at the world map … it is time for us to change the narrative.” He added: “It’s time for us in Africa to take responsibility to change what we can change ourselves.”

title: ‘There’s no plan’: as instability in global bond markets rises, what are the knock-on effects?
summary: From mortgages to inflation, concerns about the public finances of major economies have wide-reaching consequences
text: When Donald Trump was asked recently about the threat of rising interest rates on US government debt, he told baffled reporters: “The ultimate intervention is our military. And if we have to use that, we will.” Perhaps not surprisingly, his bellicose words did not soothe fractious bond markets, and his resumption of the bombing campaign against Iran only made matters worse. The past fortnight has seen a wave of instability sweeping through government bond markets in major economies – with knock-on effects for millions of borrowers. The interest rate, or yield, on 10-year US government borrowing hit 4.8% on Friday, up from 4.64% 10 days ago. At one point midweek, the 30-year yield touched its highest level since 2008. Neil Shearing, the chief economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, said one impetus for the current wobble had been markets taking a fresh look at the state of US public finances. “There’s been a recalibration,” he said. Total US government debt has surged past $40tn (£29.5tn), and annual deficits are forecast to be an eye-watering 6% of GDP for the foreseeable future. Such figures were long deemed barely to matter given the status of US government bonds, or treasuries, as the ultimate safe-haven investment. But as the events that led up to the 2008 financial crisis revealed, things don’t matter in the markets until they do. “I think we are starting to see a more realistic reassessment of the fiscal pressure in the US,” Shearing said. “What marks the US out is that there’s not really an acknowledgment of the fact that there might be a problem. There’s no plan.” Russell Jones, a veteran bond market analyst at Llewellyn Consulting, said: “The thing about economics is that often markets delay the judgment and, you know, you can’t really time when they suddenly decide that that’s enough.” The US treasury secretary Scott Bessent’s recent fumbled attempts to intervene in financial markets – to help Tokyo prop up the yen and then to calm bond yields – have only added to the sense that policymakers are panicking. Layered on top of these concerns is a more immediate worry about inflation taking off again as a result of renewed hostilities in the Middle East. Oil prices have risen back above $90 a barrel since the US and Iran resumed tit-for-tat attacks. That has increased expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates – another factor that puts upward pressure on yields. Every pronouncement by policymakers is being closely scrutinised for clues, including a key speech by the new Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, last Friday that was read by markets as signalling a willingness to act. The European Central Bank is expected to lead the charge with a rate rise next week, but markets are telegraphing higher borrowing costs across major economies. That includes the UK, where investors are now pencilling in three quarter-point rate rises over the next 12 months, and Japan, where the decades-long period of deflation and rock-bottom rates is finally coming to an end. A dramatic expansion of borrowing by AI “hyperscalers” in the US, to help fund the massive planned expansion of datacentres, has offered investors an alternative home for their cash – and raised questions about the market’s ability to absorb so much debt simultaneously. Recent calculations by the investment group Vanguard put the value of debt issued by five major tech companies at $135bn (£100bn) this year, up from an average of $35bn between 2020 and 2024. There is potentially an even more fundamental explanation for an upward shift in borrowing costs, too – based on the growing prevalence of inflationary shocks not just as a result of geopolitical chaos but because of the climate emergency. Some economists, including the Bank of England policymaker Swati Dhingra, have argued these increasingly regular shocks, as a result of extreme weather events and resulting economic upheaval, could lead to structurally higher interest rates. Whatever the causes of rising bond yields, the impact is already rippling out worldwide. Public borrowing has increased dramatically in recent years as policymakers have stepped in to cushion consumers against Covid shutdowns, wrestled with sharply higher energy prices since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and stepped up defence spending. That means small changes in global interest rates can have an outsized impact on government budgets. In the UK, where £1 in every £12 of public spending already goes on debt interest, Andy Burnham, the prime minister, was pressed this week by the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch, about the rising cost of government borrowing. Higher yields on gilts, as UK government bonds are known, will feed through into predictions of higher interest rate costs for the Treasury ahead of the new chancellor John Healey’s autumn budget. David Aikman, the director of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, urged the government to take the opportunity to implement spending cuts and/or tax increases to help insulate the UK from higher borrowing costs. “There will be a lot of talk about the fiscal rules. I think that’s slightly missing the point,” he said. “The big point here is we’ve just got a lot of debt, whether you’re missing the rules or not. And it means we’re really vulnerable.” On the other side of the world, Australian policymakers have been wrestling with similar challenges. Bond yields have breached 15-year highs just days after the country passed A$1tn in government debt. The timing of the two milestones comes at a difficult time for a Labor government that is under pressure to rein in historically high levels of spending. Falling house prices in a property-obsessed nation are adding to a mood of discontent. Bets have firmed that the Reserve Bank of Australia could deliver another interest rate hike later this month to tame stubbornly high inflation. Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, has been at pains to highlight Australia’s relatively strong budget position internationally. Australia’s debt is equivalent to about half the size of the economy, which pales against other advanced nations. Similarly, the commonwealth is running deficits, but of less than 1% of GDP. Chris Richardson, an independent budget expert, said Australia’s government indebtedness wasn’t “bad by world standards”. “But it’s still a lot of debt. And the higher cost of money means the difficult choices that were there already are that much harder.” For developing countries, these issues are all the more urgent. The International Monetary Fund warned earlier this year that these economies had become more exposed to the risk of higher interest rates, because of the growing importance of lending from short-term investors such as hedge funds, which tend to be more flighty during periods of market volatility. Matthew Martin, of the advocacy group Development Finance International, said: “A lot of these countries are very near the edge, and if they have to go back to the markets and refinance another bond at 1% or 2% higher than it was before, that will mean even less money to spend on climate action, health and education.” If higher yields are sustained, the effects will be felt far beyond the world’s treasuries, muddying the maths for corporate investments and putting upward pressure on mortgage rates, which in the UK have already started to rise. Aikman argued corporate balance sheets worldwide looked less shaky than before the global financial crisis. “We’re not in the place we were in the run-up to 2008,” he said. But he pointed to “pockets” of concern, including the huge scale of debt-fuelled private equity projects that could prove vulnerable in a world of higher rates. By the end of the week, the sell-off sweeping global bond markets appeared to have eased, for now. But it left yields at levels significantly higher than three months ago – and delivered a painful reminder to policymakers, including Burnham, that in globalised financial markets their plans can be buffeted by forces far beyond their control.

title: Nicola Close obituary
summary: Other lives: Public health leader who transformed her professional organisation and played a key role during the Covid-19 pandemic
text: My friend Nicola Close, who has died aged 75 of cancer, was a public health leader who made a major contribution to the field as chief executive of the Association of Directors of Public Health (ADPH). Starting as its sole employee in 2007, she built an influential organisation currently employing 19 people. This became especially evident during the Covid-19 pandemic, when directors of public health, whose role includes providing local leadership and implementing national guidance, were thrust into the spotlight. To support members to work more effectively, and strengthen communication between central government and local communities, Nicola helped break down barriers to data sharing, and secure regular meetings between directors of public health and UK chief medical officers. In 2025 she was made MBE for services to public health. Born in Poole, Dorset, to June (nee Orson) and Douglas Close, a firefighter, Nicola attended Monmouth school for girls before studying mathematics at Somerville College, Oxford. There she met and married a fellow student, John Gilbert, in 1972. Divorced in 1982, she married Roger Flatman two years later. During the 1980s Nicola gained an MA in philosophy (logic) from Birmingham University. She then worked as a maths and computing teacher at Westbourne high school in Ipswich, while also gaining a computer programming qualification and working as a computer analyst. In 1985 she moved to Cambridgeshire, as a consultant educational research analyst, and an adult education tutor. In 1994 she was appointed regional health authority clinical audit coordinator for East Anglia. I first met Nicola during this time, when I was completing specialist training in public health. Evidence-based medicine was becoming increasingly important to health policy, and public health had a lead role in promoting these initiatives. Nicola was well set to apply her mathematical, computer and teaching skills to public health practice, and in 1997 she became education and development officer with the Anglia Clinical Effectiveness Team at the Institute of Public Health in Cambridge. In 2001, she became director of Alpha (Access to Learning for the Public Health Agenda), providing public health and clinical governance education across the NHS, local authorities and voluntary sector. Nicola, who was also a council member of the UK Public Health Association, recognised that wider social, economic and environmental factors determine health and wellbeing and, alongside her professional and family life in Littleport, Cambridgeshire, became a governor of Soham village college in 2004, two years after the terrible murders of two girls by the school caretaker. She went on to serve as chair of governors from 2007 to 2009. In 2006, during my final year as president of ADPH, I approached Nicola to help organise our annual conference. Her marriage to Roger ended in divorce in 2010. She is survived by four children, George and Heather from her first marriage, and Luke and David from her second, seven grandchildren and a brother, Douglas.

title: Investigations launched into polling firm at centre of Reform UK allegations
summary: British Polling Council and Market Research Society announce inquiries into JL Partners, which has been accused of breaking transparency rules
text: A polling firm at the centre of allegations that Reform UK breached electoral law is being investigated by two industry bodies. JL Partners, which is run by former Conservative aides, has been accused of breaking transparency rules by failing to declare that three separate polls had been commissioned by the party. The company is a member of the British Polling Council and the Market Research Society, who say the identity of a client commissioning a poll should be disclosed when the results enter the public domain. Both organisations confirmed on Friday that they had launched inquiries into JL Partners. The reviews have come after Channel 4 News broadcast footage gathered by undercover reporters during a year-long investigation into Reform’s finances on Thursday night. Investigative journalists from Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a Reform donor and his American father, who paid for more than £30,000 of polling from JL Partners that generated positive headlines for the party. Nigel Farage, the party leader, was filmed saying the polling was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”. In the footage, Farage appeared to welcome the suggestion of a larger donation to the party. He was told the UK-based son could be registered as the official donor, despite the money originating from his father. Farage said: “Both of you, thank you.” In the UK, only those registered on the electoral roll are permitted to donate to political parties, meaning the polls and the proposed larger donation could both be classed as illegal. On Friday, as its annual conference got under way in Birmingham, Reform said it had suspended two senior officials who were filmed as part of the Channel 4 News investigation. James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a senior adviser to Farage, were both recorded apparently plotting to bypass electoral laws. The first poll, conducted in January, related to the Labour government’s aborted plans to cancel some local elections, which Reform strongly opposed. The poll indicated Labour would face heavy defeats if these went ahead. The second, published in April, suggested that two-thirds of voters wanted the then prime minister, Keir Starmer, to resign. The third, released in June, appeared to show that support for Reform among trade union members was drawing level with Labour. JL Partners’ co-founder James Johnson was covertly filmed discussing the Reform polling, telling one of the reporters that his company had done “a little bit of informal rule-bending” in relation to one survey. He admitted that it “should have disclosed who the client was” when publishing the data. The results of the polling appeared on the front pages of the Times and the Daily Telegraph. Both newspapers said they had not been aware that the polling had been commissioned by Reform. The British Polling Council said on Friday that “all data and research findings made on the basis of social or political polls conducted in the United Kingdom … must include reference to the client commissioning the survey”. It added that it was clear its rules had been breached in relation to the polls paid for by Reform. “According to the programme, this may have been deliberate,” a spokesperson added. “We are seeking further information from the BPC member concerned and expect them to make information available after further consideration.” The Market Research Society said: “MRS is aware of the Channel 4 reporting involving an MRS Company Partner. The matter is being referred to the Market Research Standards Board (MRSB) for review in line with its established complaint procedures.” JL Partners told Channel 4 News: “Despite there being no concern about the accuracy of our work, the report did reveal weaknesses in our procedures. For that reason JL Partners is reviewing those procedures in order to eliminate possible grey areas and ambiguities and strengthen our safeguards for the future.” The company did not respond to follow-up queries from the Guardian.

title: Russia strikes Ukraine intelligence HQ in ‘major escalation’
summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says he has told SBU to deliver ‘appropriate, tangible response’ to Kyiv strike
text: The head office of Ukraine’s SBU intelligence agency has been hit in a Russian drone attack, sending plumes of black smoke rising into the air in the heart of Kyiv. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said he had instructed the SBU to deliver an “appropriate, tangible response” to the strike, while the foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described it as a “major escalation”. The streets around the SBU headquarters were cordoned off shortly after Friday’s attack, with armed officers patrolling the area. Numerous ambulances and emergency services vehicles were stationed around the site, which is close to St Sophia Cathedral, a Unesco world heritage site. “Unfortunately, a Russian drone hit the central building of the SBU on Volodymyrska Street in Kyiv, opposite the St Sophia Cathedral,” Zelenskyy said in a post on Telegram. “The drone was aimed directly at the office of the Head of the Security Service in that building.” Kyiv has been under a barrage of daily drone and missile attacks from Russia for over a week. Zelenskyy on Friday called for Russia to halt its attacks during a visit of US negotiators, Steve Witkoff ‌and Jared Kushner, to the city on Sunday and said Ukraine would guarantee the safety of Russian airspace while they were in Moscow. Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors which can shoot down incoming threats. Many of the recent Russian strikes have been by new-model jet-powered drones which can reach speeds of 250mph, making them hard to intercept. It is rare for government buildings in central Kyiv to be reached by Russian strikes, especially in broad daylight. The explosion from the hit on the SBU building could be heard from several blocks away. The incident is likely to intensify the escalating attacks that Moscow and Kyiv have been launching at each other in recent weeks in efforts to destroy each other’s resilience and morale. It will also raise questions about Kyiv’s ability to defend its key infrastructure against Russia. Sybiha said the attack was “a major escalation that demands resolute responses” and called on international partners to “unequivocally condemn these actions and step up pressure on the Putin regime”. At least nine people were injured in Friday’s strike, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko. Stanislav Zavertailo, the co-owner of the nearby Zavertailo cafe, said one of his customers was injured in the strike, which sent shockwaves through his premises, shattering all the windows. “It’s a normal cafe,” he said. The customer was “eating one of our famous poppy seed rolls” when the attack occurred, he added. Staff and customers rushed into an underground shelter after the strike, fearing a double-tap attack, a tactic which Russia has employed, in which a second drone is sent in soon after the first, hitting emergency service workers. An hour later, there had been no second strike, but Zavertailo said he did not feel at ease. “We are all waiting for another attack,” he said. The SBU is responsible for coordinating complex operations against Russia, including last year’s Operation Spiderweb which destroyed aircraft worth billions of pounds inside Russia. Friday’s hit was “awful” said a Zavertailo cafe employee who had recently emerged from the underground shelter. As “a person who lives in Ukraine for all this time, it’s just hard”. The strike came two days before Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were expected to visit Kyiv for the first time. US-led diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s four-and-a-half-year invasion have stalled in recent months as the US has shifted its focus towards the war with Iran. Additional reporting by Illia Dyadik

title: New York City police fatally shoot man who climbed up Brooklyn Bridge cables
summary: Officers clipped to bridge had tried to talk man, who was holding a knife, into coming down safely, officials say
text: New York City police shot and killed a man on Friday morning after he climbed on to the cables of the Brooklyn Bridge and approached officers with a knife extended, New York police department officials said. At a news conference on Friday, NYPD officials said that a 911 call came in at around 3.28am on Friday morning, reporting that a man was walking on the beams of the Brooklyn Bridge. Officers with the NYPD’s emergency service unit (ESU) responded to the scene, and saw a man “walking on the bridge cables”, Gerald Dowling, the commanding officer of ESU, told reporters. “Members of ESU climbed on to those cables and attempted to establish a verbal dialogue with the male and safely remove him from the bridge,” Dowling said. Dowling noted that the officers spent almost an hour speaking with the man, explaining that they were there to help, and tried to convince him to get down from the bridge safely. During the interaction, the officers observed that the man was holding a knife, he said. The man told the officers: “I want to die, I want you to kill me. I have a bomb. You are not going to make me do something bad to the cops.” Throughout the interaction, Dowling said, the officers continued trying to convince him to get down safely, while also issuing “multiple verbal commands for him to drop the knife”. After about an hour, hundreds of feet above the East River, the man “began to quickly descend the cable of the bridge towards the officers”, Dowling said, adding that at the time, the officers were still clipped to the bridge and positioned below the man on the same cable. Dowling said that when ESU officers are “conducting high-angle rescue”, they wear safety gear, including a harness, which is “physically clipped into the bridge” for their safety and noted that “being secured to the bridge drastically impacts the speed of their movement”. “The officers began to move backwards away from the male, but they were not able to move as quickly as the subject who was approaching them,” Dowling said. “When the male got within approximately 3ft from the closest member of ESU, he raised his arm with the knife extended outward towards the officer.” At that point, Dowling said, an ESU officer “who was on the roadbed of the bridge discharged his weapon one time, striking the male”. Dowling said that the officers then brought the male down from the cable and began rendering aid. The man was transported to a local hospital where he was pronounced deceased. A knife and a flashlight were recovered from the scene. Officials said that the entire incident was captured on police-worn body cameras. On social media, the police shared a photo of what they said was the knife recovered from the scene. The police have not yet released details regarding the identity of the man. “This incident is being investigated by the force investigation division,” Dowling said. “Members of ESU are specially trained for these types of high-risk and incredibly dangerous situations. They receive extensive instruction on de-escalation and how to engage with individuals compassionately.” The New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, issued a statement on Friday morning that NYPD emergency service unit officers “worked to de-escalate the situation for approximately an hour and urged the man not to jump”. Mamdani echoed Dowling, noting the man was holding a knife and threatening the officers, “coming within close proximity to a number” of them. “One responding officer discharged his weapon and struck the man,” Mamdani said, adding that the man was pronounced dead at a nearby hospital. “As is standard when an NYPD officer discharges a firearm, the department will conduct an internal investigation, and body-worn camera footage will be released,” he said. The shooting came several days after police shot and killed a woman in Times Square after she attacked two people with knives, killing a 32-year-old woman.

title: Germany urges EU to cut Russians’ holiday visas after sabotage attacks
summary: Belarusian said to have had tourist visa issued by Italy is investigated over alleged attempt to attack Leipzig airport
text: Germany is urging its European partners to introduce tighter limitations on Russian citizens entering the EU on tourist visas, after recent sabotage attacks which Berlin has blamed on Moscow. German authorities are investigating a Belarusian national, who also holds a Russian passport, over the alleged attempt to attack Leipzig airport using drones and explosives. The man is alleged to have entered the Schengen area on a tourist visa issued by the Italian embassy in Minsk, the capital of Belarus. Security sources said he did not appear to have ever travelled through Italy. Germany’s foreign ministry has complained that too many visas were being issued to Russians. “The number of visas issued for Russian nationals for holidays in the European Union is too high,” a spokesperson said. Sources close to the government say the sheer number of visas being issued to Russians goes against the spirit of sanctions related to the Ukraine war, and make it impossible to know who is entering the EU and for what purpose. Figures show that Italy issued more Schengen visas than any other country in the bloc in 2025; between them, Italy, France and Spain received three-quarters of all visa applications from Russians, according to Euractiv. Italy issued more visas to Belarusians than any other EU country last year, and the number has risen sharply since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. According to European Commission statistics analysed by the Italian news website Linkiesta, Italy issued just 2,968 visas to Belarusian citizens in 2021, compared with 50,709 last year. A similar trend can be seen with Russia. Italian visas issued to Russian citizens rose from 63,894 in 2021 to more than 165,000 in 2025, almost tripling despite the war. Germany’s government this week announced measures to hit back at the Kremlin, after it said Russian intelligence was likely to have been behind the alleged Leipzig plot. These included closing the Russian consulate in Bonn, summoning the Russian ambassador to the foreign ministry, and tightening the monitoring of Russia’s shadow fleet of illegal vessels carrying oil in the Baltic Sea. The EU also announced a 22nd package of sanctions, and said it was expanding its list of Russians who would not be allowed to enter the EU. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, has ordered checks on the visa issued to the Belarusian suspect in the Leipzig case. “There is a process for granting visas, because certain requirements have to be met,” Tajani said. “If people meet those requirements and there is no alert concerning them individually, the visa is granted. If that is what happened, we will try to understand why that visa was issued.” Estonia, Finland, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland and the Czech Republic have all but stopped issuing visas to Russian citizens, adopting national restrictions that go beyond EU measures. But several other member states have continued granting large numbers of visas, in some cases increasing them. “Countries closer to Russia geographically, or with sizeable Russian minorities, are shutting their borders altogether or sharply reducing the number of visas they issue, including to students,” said Eleonora Tafuro Ambrosetti, a senior research fellow and co-head of the Russia, Caucasus and Central Asia Centre at the Italian Institute for International Political Studies (ISPI). Roderich Kiesewetter, a leading foreign and security policy expert for the governing CDU in the Bundestag, called on the EU to immediately suspend its tourist visa programme for Russians, calling it “untenable” from both a security and moral perspective. Kiesewetter said the security risk posed was “enormous”. The ability for Russians to move freely within the EU with a visa was being “exploited for espionage and sabotage”, he said. He urged the EU to restrict giving visas to Russians “to the absolute minimum”. “This excessive issuance of tourist visas to Russians contradicts the European strategy of isolating Russia,” he said. “It creates a false impression of normalisation for wealthy Russians, precisely those who benefit from the Kremlin’s reign of terror.” He said it was not right that Russia “wages daily a brutal war of aggression and annihilation against Ukraine while Russians continue to holiday without a care in the EU”. Some anti-war Russian activists in Europe have argued that tightening visa controls for all Russian citizens may do little to curb Moscow’s sabotage campaign. They point to a shift in tactics by Russian intelligence services, which increasingly rely not on professional operatives sent across Europe but on people recruited remotely, often through Telegram channels and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out individual tasks. This allows the Russian intelligence officers directing the operations to remain safely at home. In several recent cases prosecuted in Germany and Lithuania, the alleged recruits were Ukrainian or Baltic citizens rather than Russians.

title: Israelis shoot dead two Palestinian teenagers after settlers encircle village
summary: Troops escort settlers into al-Mughayyir and raze village outside Hebron as ethnic cleansing of West Bank continues
text: Israelis have shot dead two teenagers in a Palestinian village encircled by settlers, and Israeli troops have razed an entire village outside Hebron, in the latest attacks in a surge of Israeli terror and ethnic cleansing across the occupied West Bank. The shootings targeted Khalil Abu Alia, 16, who was about to start 11th grade at the al-Mughayyir boys school, and 19-year-old Omar al-Nassan, who graduated from the same institution with top marks this summer. The teenagers were killed soon after sunset, when a group of settlers entered the village under police and military escort to steal dozens of sheep from a Palestinian home, village residents and Israeli activists said. Snipers took up position on rooftops and one shot Abu Alia in the neck, his English teacher, Waheed Abu Naim, said in a phone interview. The boy was on the doorstep of his home when he was targeted. Al-Nassan was shot twice, the second time in the back, residents and activists said. Both teenagers died before they made it to hospital. A spokesperson for the Israeli military said Israeli police, army and settlers had entered the village to take sheep claimed by settlers from a Palestinian home. The spokesperson provided no evidence of ownership, theft or investigation into stolen goods. When Palestinians resisted seizure of the sheep by throwing stones and cinder blocks, the troops shot them, the spokesperson said. “The forces responded by firing at key instigators in order to remove the threat. Hits were identified.” Abu Alia was killed by a soldier. It was not clear whether Al-Nassan was shot by a soldier or a settler. Video shared with the Guardian shows dozens of settlers approaching the village and appearing to liaise with Israeli troops. The Guardian could not independently verify the date the footage was filmed. Israeli soldiers and militants had already killed three other students from their school’s 470-strong student body this year. The other victims were a 17-year-old player from the Palestinian youth football team shot in June, a 14-year-old gunned down at the school gate in April, and another 14-year-old killed outside the village mosque in January. “We don’t know how long these crimes are going to continue,” said Abu Naim, who had taught all five boys, and said many more of his students had been injured by Israeli attacks. His brother was also killed by settlers in April. “This week we are making extra security preparations for the new semester, which starts in three days,” he said. They have built a higher wall around the school, topped by a fence, and strengthened gates to the compound. They are also making teaching contingency plans, because the village has been under tightening siege for the past two weeks. Since late 2023, Israeli barricades blocked all but one road into the village, and at least eight settler outposts surround it in all directions. In late August, soldiers and settlers began closing the one remaining lifeline out of al-Mughayyir for hours at a time, setting up a temporary checkpoint near the school in the morning and evening. At least eight families had fled in the past week because they were unable to commute to work, renting flats in other places, Abu Naim said. The school has 26 teachers but only nine live in the village, and they fear the other two-thirds may not be allowed to reach their classrooms on Monday. In the south Hebron hills, Israeli forces spent the day razing the homes of 12 Palestinian families who lived in the community of Khirbet al-Taban. All 70 residents are now homeless, including 28 children. Israeli troops demolished all buildings and destroyed water cisterns, storage, livestock pens and caves, the Israeli-Palestinian rights group B’Tselem said in a statement. It was the 66th Palestinian community wiped off the map since October 2023, with 18 others partly displaced, the group said. Nearly 5,000 people have been forced from their homes, almost half of them children. “Israel is continuing to erase Palestinian communities at an accelerating pace as part of the ethnic cleansing it is carrying out in the West Bank,” said Yuli Novak, the executive director of B’Tselem. “The world continues to stand by as Palestinians and their lives are left completely exposed to Israeli violence.” A spokesperson for Cogat, the Israeli military agency that manages civilian affairs in occupied Palestine, said troops were carrying out “enforcement activity” against illegal construction in a military training zone. In 1981 Israel designated the Masafer Yatta area, including Khirbet al-Taban, as Firing Zone 918. It has been working since to push out the roughly 1,200 Palestinian residents who remain. They have been fighting expulsion in Israeli courts for decades, slowing but not stopping demolitions. As Palestinian communities have been wiped out, illegal Israeli settlements have expanded, with 11 outposts inside the firing zone, housing some of the most notoriously violent Israeli settlers. None have been targeted for removal.

title: Reform UK exposé comes just as Farage was hoping to change the narrative
summary: With senior party figures appearing split and leader’s favourability rating dropping, questions about donations are causing yet more headaches
text: Midway through an event at Reform’s annual conference on Friday there was question for the audience: who was worried about a Channel 4 News exposé of potential wrongdoing by party officials over donations? Almost no hands went up. The faithful might be sanguine. But make no mistake, Nigel Farage faces yet another problem. Careful plans have been again upset. After months of answering – or primarily dodging – questions about his own finances, Farage had planned to use Reform UK’s biggest conference yet to make a blitz of policy announcements. These are still happening, not least among them the revelation that a Farage-led government would declare a “national emergency” on the first day it won power, so as to get to grips with the grave problems he says the UK must tackle. But he and other senior party figures are being forced to field endless questions about whether the senior aides Dan Jukes and James Orr really were open to illegal donations from overseas, and if they were not, why Farage’s right-hand man and his policy head have been suspended. Dealing with unexpected crises is a core task for party leaders. But after so much focus on Farage’s undeclared £5m gift, and free of the chore of a self-imposed byelection to return to parliament, he was hoping to make news in other ways. Day one of the aftermath has exposed another problem: party figures do not appear unified about how to deal with it. In early media interviews on Friday, Lee Anderson, the Reform chair, said there was no way back for Jukes and Orr: “They’re gone.” But since then, a series of other figures have said they are merely suspended pending an investigation, indicating a route back. As the day progressed, the rhetoric toughened. Reform had been the victim of a “sting” and “entrapment”, Sarah Pochin, one of the party’s MPs, told a fringe event. Much of this is just reaction in real time. But if there is a split between Anderson and others in the party, that means another headache for the Reform leader, who also has to deal with the combustible Zia Yusuf, the party’s home affairs spokesperson, whom Farage is known to have described in private with a derogatory expletive. Most of all, however, the looming problems lie outside the necessarily insular world of Birmingham’s NEC and its thousands of Reform delegates. In a variation of the famous Ernest Hemingway description of becoming bankrupt – “gradually, then suddenly” – one of the more important rules of politics is that voters pay limited attention to claims of sleaze or ineptitude, until they do. As Boris Johnson and his Conservative successors found to their cost, party reputations are built up very slowly but can erode at some speed. Reform is not yet at this point. But the metrics are far from reassuring, not least Farage’s net favourability rating with YouGov, which has fallen to minus 44. According to another pollster, Ipsos, even before the new revelations, just 20% of Britons thought Farage was “an honest person”. In another study, by More in Common, concerns around sleaze were named as the biggest barrier for people voting for Reform. All this must be put in context. Farage achieved something unprecedented in taking a new party and topping more than 150 successive polls. No leader could keep that going for ever, especially with a charismatic new prime minister in No 10. But time is not necessarily on his side. Even though a general election is not needed before mid-2029, Reform is working on the assumption Andy Burnham will seek his own mandate next year. It is in this landscape that the loss of two very core party figures is so damaging, all the more so if they end up under formal police investigation, let alone in court. Farage sought on Friday to distance himself from Jukes and Orr, calling them “contractors”. This is very obvious nonsense, given Jukes has been at his side for a decade and Orr was trusted with devising the party’s policy. A shadow has been cast over the two of them, with the potential to darken much further if police or the elections watchdog take action. And that shadow could yet fall on Farage himself.
