title: Texas man sentenced to 20 years in prison over death of teen in 1980s
summary: James Elmore Jr sentenced in death of Laura Miller, whose body was found in 1986 in notorious ‘Texas Killing Fields’
text: A man found guilty in the death of teenager Laura Miller, whose body was recovered in 1986 in the notorious so-called “Texas Killing Fields”, was given a 20-year prison sentence on Thursday. James Elmore Jr received that punishment from a Galveston county jury that a day earlier had convicted him of manslaughter in connection with Laura Miller’s death, which inspired her father, Tim Miller, to launch Texas EquuSearch, a non-profit organization specializing in searching for missing people. Elmore, 61, was determined to have helped administer a cocaine dose that killed Laura, who went missing in 1984 – and whose corpse was located two years later in League City, Texas, on land along Interstate 45 south-east of Houston. That stretch constitutes the infamous Texas Killing Fields, where the bodies of more than 30 girls and young women have been discovered, as chronicled in a Netflix documentary along with various books and movies. Investigators suspect multiple people are responsible for those deaths, most of which are unsolved. But Laura’s death proved to be an exception after Elmore called Tim Miller in 2022. Elmore told him that he was there when Laura died, prompting both men to meet repeatedly afterward. Tim Miller, 79, even produced a video showing him and Elmore visiting locales involved in Laura’s death. And jurors saw that video after authorities charged Elmore in Laura’s case with manslaughter in late March, setting the stage for a trial leading to his conviction on Wednesday and sentencing on Thursday. Jurors concluded that Elmore prepared a vial of cocaine that his longtime friend, Clyde Hedrick, gave to Laura. Investigators surmised that Hedrick was responsible for the deaths of Laura and three other women left in the Texas Killing Fields between 1984 and 1991: Audrey Cook, Heidi Fye-Villareal and Donna Prudhomme. But Hedrick died by suicide in March at age 72 shortly before Texas prosecutors sought to obtain an indictment charging him and Elmore. Furthermore, Hedrick had been convicted of manslaughter in 2014 in the death of Ellen Beason, who went missing in 1984 and whose body was found a year later. He had been released on parole in 2022. At Elmore’s trial, his attorney, Bill Agnew, maintained that his client “didn’t have anything to do with this”. But Elmore was “the one guy standing” after Hedrick’s suicide, Agnew contended. The jury, meanwhile, heard from Tim Miller as he addressed Elmore while testifying the trial. “You handed [the cocaine vial] to Clyde Hedrick,” Tim remarked, pointing at Elmore and crying. “You handed it.” Charges of evidence tampering and possession of child abuse imagery remained pending against Elmore as of Thursday. He was tentatively scheduled to be tried on those counts in October. Elmore’s sentence in Laura’s death came about four years after an Oklahoma death row inmate, William Reece, pleaded guilty to the murders of two girls and one woman whose bodies were in the Texas Killing Fields: Laura Smither, 12; Jessica Cain, 17; and Kelli Cox, 20. Reece received sentences of life imprisonment for each of those murders. During Elmore’s court proceedings, Tim Miller alluded to his tireless efforts to learn precisely what had happened to Laura – and his dissatisfaction with what he considered to be an inadequate law enforcement investigation into her disappearance. He dedicated himself to becoming an expert in finding missing people or their remains – and he started Texas EquuSearch in 2000. The group’s name nods to the fact that its volunteers occasionally conduct searches on horseback, though they also mount all-terrain vehicles, boats or backhoes. A 2022 Houston Chronicle article reported that the organization worked on about 100 new missing persons cases annually. According to its website, Texas EquuSearch had found about 580 people alive and another 560 or so deceased. “I begged – I pleaded – for somebody to do something,” Miller said to the jury at Elmore’s trial about the years-long uncertainty surrounding Laura’s whereabouts and the exact circumstances of her death. “I knew something happened to Laura – I just knew it. I just didn’t know what it was.” He had previously told the Guardian that his mission to find missing people would not end with the conclusion of Laura’s case. “We got a lot more girls to find,” Miller said, “and a lot more families to help.” The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Milky Way at the dining table: Bath art show celebrates 18th-century brother and sister astronomers
summary: Exhibition opens in former home of William Herschel, who discovered Uranus, and his comet-spotting sibling Caroline
text: From the garden of their Georgian townhouse in Bath in the late 18th century, a brother and sister made a series of extraordinary astronomical discoveries. A new art show in the house where the siblings – William and Caroline Herschel – worked and lived highlights their pioneering spirit and their domestic arrangements. The Irish artist Grace Weir, who created the exhibition in what is now the Herschel Museum of Astronomy, said she was deeply interested in the science that went on at the house, including the discovery of the planet Uranus, and fascinated that it took place in such a cosy environment. “It is a home,” Weir said. “Science does not take place in a vacuum. They would have had conversations about their discoveries across the dining table.” One of her artworks, On the Construction of Heavens, was inspired by William Herschel’s drawing of the Milky Way in 1785. Weir has had a copy of the drawing embroidered on to an antique linen tablecloth, which is laid over the family dining table. “William and Caroline must have spoken about the shape of the Milky Way right here,” Weir said. “That would have been an unusual thing to talk about back then.” In the basement workshop, where William Herschel built his own telescopes, Weir has installed an LED digital counter that records the distance of Uranus from the Earth as it changes. A key element of the show is to make sure Caroline Herschel gets her share of the credit for the pair’s advances in science. William Herschel was a self-taught amateur astronomer who came to Bath from Germany in 1777. His sister followed, initially as a housekeeper. She quickly became his assistant, recording his findings, helping him with calculations, keeping his telescopes in order but then made discoveries of her own, finding eight comets and becoming the first woman in England to be paid as an astronomer. One of the most striking pieces Weir has created is a tribute to Caroline Herschel’s comet-spotting abilities. Called An Imperfect Account, it features a piece of meteorite and a piece of obsidian in the shape of one of Caroline’s worry beads. Weir said: “William had to persuade her mother to let her come to Bath. He recognised her intelligence and once she got here, they were incredibly collaborative. They drove each other along, they understood each other.” The pieces created by Weir are scattered around the house, meaning the visitor has to look for them. Weir said people were losing the art of observing closely. “The Herschels were masters of long looking, something we are losing by scrolling,” she said. Amy Frost, a senior curator at Bath Preservation Trust, said it was the first time in the museum’s history that contemporary site-specific artworks had been integrated. “It’s really exciting for us – it feels like a thread being created through time,” she said. The exhibition, called The As-Yet Unseen (a quote by William Herschel predicting the discovery of the planet Neptune), runs from 5 September until 3 January 2027. A second exhibition studying the work in photography of William’s son, John Herschel, also runs until January. For full details, see here.

title: North Carolina becomes first state to send out mail-in ballots for US midterms
summary: State decides to proceed hours after Trump administration asks supreme court to let it carry out proposed crackdown
text: North Carolina became the first state to start sending out mail-in ballots for November’s US midterm elections on Friday, as Donald Trump’s administration fights to impose sweeping restrictions on the practice before millions of Americans cast their votes. The state’s decision to proceed – hours after Trump’s officials asked the supreme court to let the administration press ahead with its proposed crackdown – comes amid deep uncertainty over whether new federal rules governing mail ballots will be allowed to take effect, and whether the US Postal Service can implement the changes in time. North Carolina is first out of the gate because its state statute requires county boards to begin sending absentee ballots 60 days before a general election – one of the earliest start dates in the country. Other states set their own timelines, ranging from a few weeks before election day to, in a handful of cases, similarly early starts, meaning most will follow in the coming days and weeks. The Trump administration asked the supreme court on Thursday to let it revive a rule barring the postal service from delivering ballots in states that don’t share voter data with the federal government, and requiring ballot envelopes to be screened against new standards before delivery. D John Sauer, the US solicitor general, told the justices that a lower court’s freeze on the plan was causing “serious irreparable harm” to the government, states and voters. It is the second time in weeks the administration has turned to the court over the plan, part of an executive order Trump signed in March directing agencies to compile citizen lists for use in screening mail ballots. A federal judge in Massachusetts, Indira Talwani, blocked the plan in June, ruling that it encroached on states’ constitutional authority over elections. The supreme court’s conservative majority sided with Trump in August but called the challenge premature, leaving the door open for further litigation once the plan was finalized. Talwani froze key parts of it again on 27 August. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, who oversees emergency applications from the region, has not granted the administration’s request for an immediate stay. Instead, she has given challengers until Tuesday to respond, a timeline that leaves little room for the postal service to act before ballots need to be in voters’ hands nationwide. Underscoring how tight the window has become with barely two months left before polls open, a postal service official told the Massachusetts court this week that the agency was still refining its screening system and expected to make it available to states on a voluntary basis “sometime next week”.

title: What is the latest finance scandal facing Reform UK?
summary: The potential breaches of the law exposed in an undercover film, what police say, and the party’s likely defence
text: Nigel Farage is facing yet another finance scandal following an undercover investigation into how Reform UK is funded. The potential wrongdoing – denied by the party – appears serious enough to have been immediately referred to the police by Labour and the Liberal Democrats. Here are the main legal issues for Reform and what any investigation will have to consider. What are the key allegations against Reform? There are at a number of separate possible strands for the authorities to investigate: 1. That Reform’s Dan Jukes and James Orr orchestrated payments totalling £32,500 for political polling from a donor who aides believed to be based in the US and therefore was not permitted to give money (but who was actually an undercover reporter). The payments should also probably have been declared to the Electoral Commission as a benefit in kind. 2. That Nigel Farage knew about the scheme, and congratulated the fake donors, saying “Boom – it worked”. 3. That a senior aide suggested a proposed £500,000 donation from the impermissible US businessman could be made via a UK intermediary. 4. The same aide suggested that similar arrangements may previously have been used to channel money from foreign sources to Reform through declared UK donors who were family members. 5. That Nigel Farage tacitly condoned the proposed £500,000 arrangement, saying “thank you both” when it was explained. What are the potential breaches of the law? The actions of the Reform aides, the party’s registered treasurer and possibly Farage himself could fall foul of section 61 of the Political Parties, Elections and Referendums Act 2000, which covers offences concerning arrangements intended to evade the restrictions on political donations. Labour believes section 61(1) applies where a person knowingly enters into, or does an act in furtherance of, an arrangement that facilitates or is likely to facilitate a donation to a registered party from a person other than a permissible donor. The commissioning of £30,000 of polling could apply to this, as well as the attempt to solicit the larger £500,000 donation. Reform may argue it did not commission the polling funded by the US donor – or that Farage did not know of Reform’s involvement – but the footage makes that difficult. The law states that a donation to a registered party includes any money spent in paying expenses incurred directly or indirectly to the party. In relation to the proposed £500,000, it could also breach clauses that prohibit disguising the true source of a proposed political donation through an intermediary – although it is a grey area whether the impermissible donor or the party are ultimately liable for this. What have the police said? For now, the Met police have said they will assess the matter and any further evidence. No announcement of an investigation was expected on Friday, but sources suggested a full inquiry was a highly likely outcome. Police are already investigating donations to Reform made by Fiona Cottrell, the mother of Nigel Farage’s aide George Cottrell. The pair have been interviewed under criminal caution by Scotland Yard detectives. In a previous letter to the Guardian, lawyers for George Cottrell said “his mother’s donations have been entirely her own decision, and are a matter for her”. They added that suggestions he “has donated impermissibly to Reform UK are unfounded”. Scotland Yard is also looking at two donations of £250,000 made to the party by Britain Means Business, a party fundraising vehicle controlled by Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, in the weeks before the 2024 general election. The Guardian previously revealed that Fiona Cottrell made a £1m transfer to Britain Means Business shortly before the donations were made. About half of the funds were then passed to the party. Could there be more to investigate? In a conversation with the undercover reporter posing as the UK-based son of the proposed US donor, Jukes is recorded saying: “But, you know, serious point, [redacted] donates to us, and he donates through his son, the, the [redacted] they donate through their …” The undercover reporter replies, “Through their kids yeah”, to which Jukes responds: “The [redacted], [redacted], one of the two. [Redacted]. [Redacted]. The [redacted] are Reform donors. It’s the father and it’s the son, so, so that’s one of the ways in which we do it.” There is the potential for these names to emerge in the course of reporting over the next few days, which may widen the scope of any police investigation. What about the Electoral Commission? The watchdog was described in one video as “useless” by Orr, the party’s head of policy, as he debated how donations for polling could be made by the impermissible foreign donor. It has said the matter is now for the police, but it will surely launch its own investigation into potential failures to make declarations after that is complete – which could lead to fines. The commission may also renew its case for tougher laws and powers on the sources of donor funding. What is likely to be Reform’s defence? Reform has suspended the two aides involved, Jukes and Orr, which appears to be the start of a process to distance Farage from the affair. It is also arguing that it did not formally commission the poll and therefore it was not a benefit in kind. Footage from Jukes and Orr suggests otherwise. On the £500,000 donation, the party will argue that it never took place and would have been caught by its due diligence processes if it had got that far.

title: Deadly escalation in Black Sea attacks prompts fears of even higher food prices
summary: Russian and Ukrainian strikes in July killed more crew than in whole war to that month, preventing grain exports
text: A summer of hostilities in the Black Sea proved deadly for seafarers, as Russia and Ukraine attacked each other’s ships and port infrastructure, preventing vital grain exports and prompting concerns that the conflict will push global food prices even higher. More crew were killed in the Black Sea in July than during the entirety of the war before that month as the conflict has intensified, making the body of water the most dangerous in the world for commercial shipping. This is despite the conflict between the US and Iran, with vessels still being targeted in the strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Gulf of Aden. As many as 23 people died in July as a result of attacks on 35 ships in the Black Sea, according to estimates from the Turkish seafarers’ union Türkiye Denizciler Sendikası. Attacks on vessels continued into August and escalation in the Ukraine war has prompted the head of the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization, to condemn the “deterioration of maritime security around the globe”. Russia first launched waves of attacks on port infrastructure and vessels anchored in Ukrainian Black Sea ports in the months after its invasion in 2022, preventing Kyiv from exporting grain. In July, Russia again struck Ukraine’s main grain export hubs of Odesa and Chornomorsk. However, the recent escalation in the Black Sea and neighbouring Sea of Azov – connected by the Kerch strait – has also resulted from Ukrainian retaliatory attacks. Drones have hit Russian vessels, including tankers Kyiv says belong to a shadow fleet of hundreds of ships used by Russia to evade sanctions on its oil exports. Ukraine has targeted ships and port buildings at the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, vital for oil and grain exports. In a grim illustration of the danger to vessels and their crew, an abandoned Russian-flagged cargo ship – with a burned-out command deck – recently ran aground on Turkey’s Black Sea coast as startled holidaymakers looked on. The Omskiy-107’s crew abandoned ship after it was hit by a Ukrainian drone near Novorossiysk, leaving the unmanned vessel to drift hundreds of miles and end up close to the Bosphorus, the narrow strait straddled by Istanbul that is one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. Shipping in the region is under increased threat, according to analysts at the maritime risk intelligence firm Vanguard. “Merchant vessels are now more likely to be affected because of the ports they visit, their trading activity and the cargoes they carry. Attacks have also extended beyond ports and their immediate approaches, increasing the risk to vessels across a wider area of the Black Sea,” they said. The precarious maritime situation has already significantly reduced Russian and Ukrainian grain exports, raising concerns the disruption will worsen the impact of other food price shocks and hurt countries reliant on imported wheat, barley and maize. Russia is the world’s largest grain exporter, with its produce mostly going to the Middle East and north Africa, particularly Turkey and Egypt, while Ukraine is the fifth-largest. In July, Russia suspended shipping in the Sea of Azov after a wave of Ukrainian drone attacks, before deciding to redirect some grain exports to alternative routes such as via the Caspian and Baltic seas and the Pacific. However, more than 70% of Russia’s seaborne grain exports are shipped from Black Sea ports, and a further 20% from the Sea of Azov, according to analysis from Oxford Economics. “I have seen estimates that Russian grain exports were down to 40% of normal export capacity in August,” said Tatiana Orlova, the lead emerging markets economist at Oxford Economics. Ukraine, which had a bumper and early grain harvest this year, has also found itself unable to export large volumes through its Black Sea ports. Kyiv exported only a third – about 1.4m tonnes – of the grain it could have exported, using sea, rail, river and road, according to recent comments from Ukraine’s food minister. Global wheat prices have been trading higher in recent weeks, but remain below levels at the beginning of the Ukraine war in 2022. However, analysts say the latest disruption to seaborne grain exports is likely to push prices higher and exacerbate other food supply shocks, including the Iran war and lower European grain yields after extreme summer heat and the rapidly developing El Niño weather system. Global food prices are forecast by Oxford Economics to rise by nearly 12% this year and a further 4.8% in 2027. Unlike in 2022, when many big food importing countries were caught napping by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, “a lot of countries have grain stocks, which should help, so there is better preparedness for this kind of shock”, said Orlova. “But it is pretty clear the food price is going to be affected.”

title: Woman, 45, killed in Florence in seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August
summary: Lorena Isceri was thrown off a motorway bridge, allegedly by ex-boyfriend Federico Vella
text: A 45-year-old woman abducted and thrown off a motorway bridge near Florence has become the seventh alleged femicide in Italy since mid-August. Lorena Isceri was abducted on Thursday afternoon, allegedly by her ex-boyfriend, Federico Vella, in the Rifredi area of Florence, before being forced into the boot of his car and driven towards a bridge on the A1 motorway. Isceri, who worked in the veterinary sector, still had her phone and managed to call an emergency helpline, telling operators she had been abducted. Vella, 38, stopped the car, snatched the phone and allegedly threw her off the bridge, before jumping off himself. After Isceri’s call to the helpline, police traced her phone signal but arrived too late to prevent her murder. Officers are establishing whether Isceri was killed before she was thrown off the bridge. Isceri’s mother told SkyTg24 that she had last heard from her daughter on Thursday morning, and said she sounded fine. When asked about the relationship with Vella, she said Isceri had spoken to her about it and was “very afraid”. Italian interior ministry data had indicated a downward trend in femicides during the first six months of 2026. Figures compiled by the feminist alliance Non Una di Meno showed that as of 8 August, 40 women had been killed so far this year. But numbers have risen since 15 August, Italy’s Ferragosto national holiday, with seven women, including Isceri, killed by a current or former partner. Giorgia Meloni’s ruling coalition, which on Friday celebrated becoming the longest-serving government in the history of the Italian republic, had pledged to crack down on gender-based violence after the strong public reaction to the killing of Giulia Cecchettin, a 22-year-old biomedical engineering student, by her former boyfriend, in November 2023. Two years later, the government approved a law that for the first time introduced a legal definition of femicide in criminal law, punishing it with life in prison, while increasing sentences for crimes including stalking, sexual violence and the sharing of intimate images without consent. However, a campaign to educate schoolboys about healthy relationships was thwarted after the government made it conditional on parental approval. Luisa Rizzitelli, the Italy coordinator of One Billion Rising, which campaigns to end violence against women, said: “Perhaps Meloni is right to celebrate her government’s longevity, because there is precious little to celebrate in terms of concrete results. “The approach to the tragic issue of male violence against women has been based on security policies while completely lacking strategic, structural programmes for training and prevention. The stubborn refusal to implement sex and relationship education in schools is a major factor fuelling the epidemic of femicides in Italy.” In the UK, Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123 and the domestic abuse helpline is 0808 2000 247. In the US, the suicide prevention lifeline is 988 and the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the crisis support service Lifeline is on 13 11 14 and the national family violence counselling service is on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines can be found via www.befrienders.org • This article was amended on 5 September 2026 to correct the spelling of Giulia Cecchettin’s surname.

title: Colombia president provokes disgust by posing with bodies of ‘terrorists’
summary: Abelardo De La Espriella posts video of himself with rows of body bags as performative populism continues to sweep Americas
text: Colombia’s hardline president, Abelardo De La Espriella, has provoked outrage after posting a video on social media in which he strides through rows of white body bags that he says contained the corpses of 23 “neutralised” guerrillas. De La Espriella took power last month vowing “all-out war” against illegal armed groups and he published the footage on Thursday in an apparent attempt to show he was fulfilling that pledge. “I promised to confront terrorism without hesitation and I’m keeping that promise,” the far-right politician wrote above the video. “I did not come to play nice with murderers, extortionists and child recruiters. I came to defeat them … Long live Christ the king!” Celebrating the military operation in the Colombian Amazon during which the 23 alleged terrorists were killed, De La Espriella declared: “We are utterly determined to destroy you, who are a cancer.” The body bag footage, set to a stirring Hollywood-style score, was condemned by human rights activists and the president’s political opponents. Iván Cepeda, the leftwing candidate beaten by De La Espriella in June’s election, wrote on X: “He strolls among the bags with the corpses. He nearly treads on them with contempt. He calls himself a Christian but in reality he’s an unscrupulous being lacking the slightest sense of humanity.” The leftwing lawmaker Daniel Monroy accused the president of “necropolitics”. He wrote: “This is one of the most bizarre things we’ve seen. Strolling among the dead, while invoking the name of God, just to justify an unnecessary spectacle.” De La Espriella’s predecessor Gustavo Petro tweeted: “This is called turning death into a trophy – something only soulless people can do … The soulless find it easy to kill for the sake of killing.” De La Espriella hit back at his critics, posting: “Forgiving terrorists is God’s business. Sending them to meet him – if that’s where they’re headed – is the president’s job.” De La Espriella’s post captured the bellicose and performative political zeitgeist sweeping the Americas, where a growing number of rightwing populists are seeking to woo voters with promises of ferocious, TikTokable crackdowns on crime. The genre has been pioneered by El Salvador’s authoritarian president, Nayib Bukele, with slick videos of his notorious mega-prison, and Donald Trump, who has repeatedly published footage showing alleged drug boats being blitzed in the Caribbean and Pacific. Ahead of Brazil’s October elections, several candidates are promising lethal attacks on the drug traffickers who control Rio de Janeiro’s favelas. “We’re going to stain the ground red with the blood of these lowlifes,” one candidate, Renan Santos, said recently, promising “a bloodbath” if he won power. Flávio Bolsonaro, the main challenger to the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has vowed to wage war on “narco-terrorists”, although he and close allies have themselves been accused of having ties to organised crime. “Criminals will be taken out of circulation, either standing up or lying down,” Bolsonaro has said. In Rio, Felipe Curi, a former police chief running for congress, has posted AI-generated videos depicting him shooting armed men in the favelas. Campaign propaganda features his image superimposed on pictures of the corpses of some of the 122 people killed during the city’s deadliest ever police raids. “I arrest crooks,” Curi boasts in one video, “and I neutralise them if they react.”

title: Populism poses serious challenge to independent central banks, Bailey says
summary: Bank of England governor says central bankers must explain decisions or risk being seen as ‘unrepresentative elite’
text: The governor of the Bank of England has said the rise of populist politicians presents a serious challenge to independent central banks. As Nigel Farage’s Reform UK gathered for its annual conference in Birmingham, Andrew Bailey said central bankers must be prepared to explain their decisions to the public or risk being attacked as an “unrepresentative elite”. Bailey was speaking at a conference at the London School of Economics. In an address peppered with historical references, from Alexander Hamilton to Thomas Hobbes, he said central banks must not take their “legitimacy for granted”. Bailey said populist parties’ pitch for power “often rests on the claim that a particular political movement alone represents the authentic will of the people. Any institution seen to get in the way becomes an unrepresentative elite standing between the people and their will, and thus an obstacle to popular sovereignty.” He added: “This is a serious challenge. We have developed systems of government (in the broadest sense of this term) in which legitimacy rests in the plurality of society, not in the preferences of any single group within it.” Populist parties, especially of the right, have been riding high on both sides of the Atlantic in recent years. Attacking traditional institutions – including central banks – often forms part of their platform. Farage has previously suggested he would like to replace Bailey if Reform comes to power. In the US, Donald Trump repeatedly launched tirades against the former Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell over the central bank’s failure to cut interest rates. Bailey was among the international central bankers who signed a joint statement defending Powell against Trump’s criticism and stressing the importance of independence. The Bank of England was made independent by the Labour government in 1997, handing decisions on interest rates from the chancellor to a nine-member monetary policy committee (MPC) chaired by the governor. After the 2008 global financial crisis, which led to a significant proportion of the UK banking sector being nationalised at taxpayer expense, the Bank of England was given additional responsibilities for financial stability. Bailey said on Friday that insulating the Bank from politics had made it better able to fulfil its role of maintaining “the monetary and financial conditions that make sustained prosperity possible”. He said: “Institutions that exercise significant authority should expect scrutiny. Such scrutiny is a sign of democratic health. But we should also recognise what is at stake.” The MPC is split over how to respond to rising inflation as a result of the Iran war. Bailey has stressed that in a weak jobs market, he does not yet see signs of the “second-round effects” that can embed inflation throughout the economy as workers bid up their wages to keep pace. The MPC voted to keep interest rates on hold at 3.75% at its last meeting in July. But three members voted for a rate rise, including the Bank’s hawkish chief economist, Huw Pill, who used a speech on Thursday to reiterate that in the face of rising inflation, Threadneedle Street should act “clearly, promptly and decisively”. At its next policy meeting on 17 September, the Bank is also expected to announce whether it will press ahead with its controversial policy of quantitative tightening. The Bank has been progressively selling off the bonds it acquired though the emergency policy of quantitative easing – creating money to help stave off recession. Critics, from Reform to leftwing thinktanks, have argued that these sales tend to drive up the yield, or interest rate, on government bonds, which move in the opposite direction to prices. That makes it more expensive for the government to borrow, a pressing issue at a time of febrile bond markets. Bailey will appear before MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee next week to explain his thinking.

title: For Gloria Steinem, fashion was about much more than aesthetics
summary: In an era when feminists were stereotyped as unattractive, the pioneering writer’s style created a Trojan horse
text: When people wanted to dismiss Gloria Steinem, they spoke about how she looked. Talking about the pioneering activist and journalist who turned feminism into a major civil rights movement, it might seem reductive to focus on her glasses. But after Steinem – whose death at 92 was announced on Thursday – wore them on the cover of Newsweek in 1971 next to the cover-line The New Woman, the lightly tinted aviators – often worn over her hair – became an accidental form of self-branding that made her instantly recognisable. They were as indelibly linked to her legacy as Ruth Bader Ginsburg’s jabots or even Anna Wintour’s sunglasses. They also became one of her greatest weapons. Never mind that she had to wear them. Coming from a nearsighted family, she bought the oversized men’s wire Ray-Ban Bausch & Lomb aviators in the late ’60s because she found standard women’s frames too small. “People were always pinching me on the cheek and so I felt I had a very fat face,” she told Teen Vogue in 2011. “Those things were undercurrent somewhere, you know, causing me to wear my hair down and wear big glasses.” She was also an anxious public speaker, and liked to hide behind them. In the end, along with the centre-parted hair, the bell-bottoms, ribbed polo necks and low-slung concho belts, her look would become a sort of aesthetic armour which charmed and disarmed her critics. It was never about fashion. To Steinem, getting dressed and indeed controlling one’s image were simply part of a woman’s right to choose; clothing as agency. Today’s politicians strategically use clothes to shape public opinion, but Steinem’s style was less about optics and more about creating a Trojan horse. Because once she had our attention, whether at a rally or on TV, she could quickly pivot to delivering uncompromising messages on reproductive rights or systemic sexism. During the height of the women’s lib movement, her bohemian-tinged wardrobe reflected the fashion of its era. But it also felt relatable. She was the poster girl for politicised youth: Love Story prep meets downtown thrift store. This was particularly pertinent given how relentlessly the mainstream media stereotyped feminists as unattractive. Steinem understood the media landscape better than many, and used her personal image to challenge the patriarchal assumption that smart women should blend into the background – or even that feminists looked like bra-burning radicals. Yet Steinem’s look was scrutinised like that of no other woman in politics, often by other women. Even at the height of her career, the Washington Post columnist Maxine Cheshire described Steinem as “the miniskirted pinup girl of the intelligentsia”. In the early days of Ms magazine, which she founded in 1971, she indeed wore miniskirts, but became more famous for her tight high-waisted jeans, which she described as “anti-fashion” but were largely about practicality. At the women’s conventions, they were putting the tables out, printing flyers. She wore what she wore because it was easier to do her job. Her influence on fashion might be more cultural than actual – her blond-streaked hair has even been adopted by gen Z – but she certainly wielded influence over the industry. Unsurprisingly, she turned up on various fashion mood boards, including those of the designers Roland Mouret and Michael Kors. In turn, Steinem occasionally also wore Kors pieces. Her fringed jackets and boho-inflected blouses wouldn’t look out of place on a Celine or Chloe catwalk today. Steinem herself had some interest in trends, but was largely influenced by Audrey Hepburn, Wonder Woman and women she met around the world. As she once said: “Fashion in the past meant conforming and losing oneself; fashion in the present means being unique and finding oneself.” As she got older, the hair got shorter and the clothes grew more sober. In the spirit of Steve Jobs, she leaned towards an all-black get-up, something she “inherited” from other New Yorkers, she said earlier this year. “You didn’t have to worry about what matched what.” But she always played with accessories, zhushing up her bodysuits with waist-grazing necklaces, though her real weapon were the belts, worn partly because you didn’t have to change your clothes, and partly because they had “a resonance from the past before patriarchy came along”, as she told Lena Dunham in 2015. It was also a great way to offset the activism pins, little signifiers which she integrated directly into her wardrobe, though her greatest “statement” look was probably the “I had an abortion” T-shirt she wore aged 70 (Steinem had an illegal abortion aged 22). Earlier this year, Steinem opened up her New York brownstone to auction off 40 personal belongings to raise money for her foundation. Pieces included enamel and silver-tone belts, block-printed jackets and various fringed jackets with activist pins still attached. But the clue was always in the sell – “Own a piece of history”, it read. And as someone who ultimately proved that a woman didn’t have to disguise her femininity to be taken seriously as an intellectual and political force, what a history that was.

title: Reform officials ‘plotted to break law on foreign donations’ in undercover film
summary: Investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News shows man posing as ‘impermissible donor’ paying for polling that helped Reform
text: Nigel Farage is facing fresh criticism on the eve of the Reform UK party conference after some of his team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News. A group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party. The polling was not attributed to Reform, and was reported in the Telegraph and the Times without those newspapers knowing that it was commissioned by the party and paid for by the US donor. The benefit in kind was also not reported to the Electoral Commission. In footage of another meeting, a senior adviser to Farage, Dan Jukes, appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son. When the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thank you both.” The investigation will reopen intense scrutiny of Reform’s approach to donations and its finances, which are already the subject of a standards inquiry and police investigation. Reform said it had been “the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate-change activists posing as would-be party donors” and the party denied any wrongdoing. In Channel 4 News’ investigation, broadcast on Thursday night, footage shows that the fake UK-based supporter also had conversations with Reform UK’s head of policy, James Orr, who talked about commissioning polling that would be paid for by the US-based father. In the film, Orr can be heard saying of the arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untowards about it at all”. Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”, adding: “It worked. Boom.” Jukes, a close aide to Farage, was also filmed meeting the fake donor, and at a Reform UK reception where in one conversation he appeared to introduce the undercover operative as “key donor for off-the-book project”. In footage of a meeting with the fake US donor, he is heard describing the polling as “clandestine” and “hugely important”. The polling, conducted by JL Partners, made headlines before the local elections in May. The foreign source of funding and its links to Reform were not publicly disclosed, and the Telegraph said it had now suspended the articles about the polling, while the Times said it was not aware of the relationship with Reform. After Channel 4 News’ broadcast, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said the “scandal goes right to the top of Reform UK”. She added: “Nigel Farage needs to urgently prove today that his top team haven’t broken the law and secretly plotted to undermine our democracy.” Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, called on the police and the Electoral Commission to investigate. A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK has a robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission. The hoaxers are ‘Verbatim Investigations’; a new company, incorporated in July 2026 in an attempt to mask their true identity: the Centre for Climate Reporting.” The party claimed the group’s methods had previously been “rebuked by members of the United States Congress” for “videos [that] appear to be substantially edited, creating an incomplete record of the conversation”. The investigation is likely to create a serious problem for Farage as he attempts to turn the page on Reform’s summer of funding scandals, with his party conference speech scheduled for Friday. In the speech, he will boast of record donations compared with the other parties, including £4m from a crypto billionaire pardoned by Donald Trump in the last quarter. The Reform UK leader will tell the annual Birmingham gathering that the party is “much stronger than we were last year”, saying that it has the highest number of members and has brought in the most donations. Farage will also seek to look to the future by claiming he would declare a “national emergency” in order to pass legislation day and night if made prime minister, insisting he believes Reform UK will win the next election. The party outperformed Labour and the Conservatives with donations of more than £5m in the second quarter of this year, new figures from the Electoral Commission show. However, it remains reliant on a handful of mega-donors who have been based abroad and could be caught by the government’s new £100,000 annual cap on overseas funders which requires donors to have been a UK resident for 12 months. The biggest donation in the last few months was the £4m from Ben Delo, a crypto entrepreneur who has been based in Hong Kong in recent years but in April said he was moving back to the UK. Delo, who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money-laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business, before being pardoned by Trump, has previously given Reform £4m. Party sources said it was “very confident” that none of Delo’s latest £4m would need to be returned due to the cap when the legislation is passed. The government has said donors would have to have been on the UK electoral register for at least 12 months and meet a residency test showing that they are “genuinely resident at a UK address”. Any gifts over the £100,000 cap from an overseas-based donor would have to be handed back once the new legislation is passed if deemed to be impermissible under the new law. Reform’s confidence in the donation would suggest Delo has been on the UK domestic electoral register and believes he could meet the residency test when the donations were made in April and May. Delo did not respond to a request for comment. Christopher Harborne, the Thailand-based billionaire who has given the party £15m and £5m to Farage personally, did not give any cash after the cap was introduced in March. The £5m gift to Farage from before the last election is under investigation by the standards commissioner, and Reform has slid in the polls since the amount was first revealed by the Guardian.

title: Florida woman who fatally shot man to not face charges due to ‘stand your ground’ law
summary: Melissa Payne shot and killed 62-year-old Bart Diguglielmo, who was unarmed, in June in dispute over a parking space
text: A Florida woman who shot and killed a 62-year-old army veteran in a dispute over a space at a Walmart parking lot will not face charges because of the state’s stand your ground law, prosecutors said. Melissa Payne opened fire in June on Bart Diguglielmo, who was unarmed, during the incident in North Lauderdale. Security cameras and cellphone video of passersby captured the argument and Payne firing a single shot. On Thursday, prosecutors for the Broward county state attorney’s office ruled that Payne was protected by the 2005 law, which insulates from criminal charges any person who uses deadly force when they fear an imminent threat to their life, or the likelihood of serious bodily harm. Although Diguglielmo had no weapon, he was seen on the video circling Payne and her vehicle, and moving towards her several times, leading prosecutors to conclude she acted in self-defense. An amendment passed by the Florida legislature in 2017 to the original stand your ground law requires the state to prove “by clear and convincing evidence” that a person’s use of force was not justified. Assistant state attorney Stephen Zaccor said in a “close-out memo” for the case on Thursday that his office was unable to clear that bar. “The video does not demonstrate that [Payne] was in the right, rather it demonstrates that the State of Florida cannot overcome her claim that she was in reasonable fear of great bodily harm by clear and convincing evidence,” the memo said. “Florida is a Stand Your Ground State. [Payne] did not have to wait to be attacked before resorting to deadly force. She did not have to retreat as long as her fear was reasonable and no evidence has been presented to disprove that.” Videos of the incident, which were widely scrutinized after the 30 June encounter, show Diguglielmo “aggressively approach” Payne, according to the memo. The incident followed an argument between the two over who reached a parking space first. In audio recorded on a police officer’s body cam, Payne said Diguglielmo refused to back off or walk away, and she shot him once in the abdomen. “He’s made several threats about doing something to my vehicle,” Payne said, reported by NBC6 South Florida. “You’re following me, I circled around the cars, I told him several times to back up. You walked up on me several times and it went from there.” Payne was arrested and placed in handcuffs, and later released. Melissa Rodriguez, attorney for Diguglielmo’s daughter, Amanda, told NBC that the family was “disappointed” Payne would not face charges. “All of the references are damage to the vehicle, damage to property, and while I understand this was a heated situation and a lot might have been said, damage to property does not constitute a reasonable ground for deadly force,” she said.

title: Man jumps out of first-floor window to escape kidnappers in Lincoln
summary: Five jailed after targeting victim and subjecting him to ordeal linked to past relationship breakdown
text: Dramatic footage shows a kidnapped man jumping from a first-floor window into a tree before running into the street and, by chance, coming across a police car. Lincolnshire police said the ordeal of the unnamed man had been “horrifying” and the presence of a marked police vehicle “may have saved his life”. DC Liam Henderson said the CCTV footage captured a desperate moment in which the victim “quite literally risked everything to get away from those holding him captive”. Lincoln crown court heard that the victim had been targeted and subjected to a terrifying ordeal linked to a past relationship breakdown. On 4 July 2025, he was lured to an address in Market Rasen where it soon became clear he would be unable to leave. Inside the address were Brad’Lee Ranyard, Nathan Gladwell, Jackson Nicholson, Craig Ranyard and Danielle Thompson. For hours the victim endured violence and intimidation, police said. He was “repeatedly assaulted, threatened, humiliated and tormented” by his captors, who filmed the abuse on their mobile phones and laughed. The next day the man was forced into the back of a Isuzu pickup truck and driven along back roads to a property in Lincoln. He arrived at 7.30am and was again held against his will. At 11.23am the man seized his opportunity. He can be seen diving from the window into the tree, before getting to the ground and running into the street. Footage from a police car, which had turned into the street, shows the man running towards it saying: “Let me in, let me in”. Police said the officer immediately recognised the man’s distress, realised he was fleeing a dangerous situation and took him to safety. Henderson, who led the investigation, said: “This was a sustained and deeply distressing ordeal in which a man was subjected to violence, threats and humiliation at the hands of people who appeared to find amusement in his suffering. “The victim showed remarkable courage in seizing the opportunity to escape.” Henderson said it was sheer chance that a police car had entered the street. “That moment changed the course of events and allowed officers to get him to safety when he needed help most,” he said. “We often hear concerns that victims may feel alone or that help will not arrive when it is needed. This case is a powerful reminder that when someone reaches out for help, we will do everything we can to protect them and bring those responsible to justice.” Police said the victim had given permission for the footage, which also shows the arrests, to be shared. A judge at Lincoln crown court gave nine-year jail terms to Brad’Lee Ranyard, 20, and Nicholson, 25, for kidnap and false imprisonment. Craig Ranyard, 42, was jailed for five years and three months after being convicted of false imprisonment. Thompson, 38, was jailed for four years and nine months after being convicted of false imprisonment. Gladwell, 36, was jailed for three years and seven months after being convicted of false imprisonment.

title: Two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet floods
summary: Officials say pair were rescued from Trishuli 3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal after being trapped at depth of 170 metres
text: Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods buried the projects in deep mud and left them trapped. The workers were rescued during an operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel, a hydropower project in one of the areas worst affected by last week’s floods, according to the army spokesperson Brig Gen Raja Ram Basnet. Sanjay Shah, a foreman, was the first to be rescued and was taken to the army barracks in Trishuli. Another person, identified as Kabir Maharjan, a project supervisor, was also pulled from the tunnel. They were recovered from a depth of 170 metres (558ft) inside the tunnel, Basnet said. A senior police official confirmed that a body had also been found during the rescue operation, which has yet to be identified. By Friday afternoon, police confirmed they had halted the search as they had found no more signs of life. Nepal’s army released images of Shah being pulled from the small dark entrance of a tunnel. He emerged covered in mud but conscious and was carried from the site on a rescuer’s shoulder. Speaking to army officials after he was rescued, Shah’s first question was: “What day is it?” Shah said he had been in the tunnel’s control room at the time of the flood, alongside about 40 to 45 others. “Since I was in the control room, my responsibility was to save everyone’s lives,” he said. “After such an accident, I couldn’t just run away by myself. I had to save everyone.” He said that after realising there had been a major accident, he raced through the tunnel telling people to run and save themselves. “In doing so, I lost time. In the end, I couldn’t get out myself,” he said. To keep himself calm in the darkness of the tunnel, Shah said he spent his time chanting mantras. He said that while trapped, he had heard the voices of three or four others. “We were communicating by shouting to each other from nearby. There could also be people inside the powerhouse. Some of them may not have been able to escape,” he said. Officials said the two men had been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Shah was said to be stable but Maharjan was in a critical condition and had been transferred to intensive care. Hirashova Maharjan, Kabir’s wife, said he had been in shock at first and was not talking, but had since said “a few words”. She said he had an injury to his leg and was extremely jaundiced. “He did not even recognise me initially. He only said: ‘Where am I? What happened to me?’ He did not say anything else,” she said. “He is better now. He said he wanted some water, so I gave him water. Then I asked him if he recognised me, and he said yes. He nodded his head.” “We had almost lost hope,” she said, adding that when she saw the photos of him being pulled from the tunnel, “I was so happy that I cried.” Most of the hydropower projects along the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet. At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 remain missing, according to Nepal’s disaster management agency. Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on the hydropower tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week in air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued across several projects. Large boulders and flood waters had deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels. Speaking over the phone from the rescue site, Amrit Thapa, deputy superintendent of the armed police force, who is part of the seven-person search and rescue team, said they had managed to crawl the length of the tunnel looking for survivors. They were accompanied by a team from the Nepal army. “The team crawled through areas for about 10 to 15 metres and reached the main section,” said Thapa. “When we went to the final point, we found a body on the remaining upper level.” Thapa said that “except for two sections, the entire tunnel was filled with debris. After checking everything, we did not hear any further voices. We also searched the entire powerhouse area, but so far, nothing else has been found.” Army and specialist teams have been working round the clock to try to clear debris from the tunnel entrance. At least 550 workers are missing from the hydropower project along the Trishuli River, according to the Independent Power Producers’ Association of Nepal. In total, local authorities estimate about 900 workers are missing from 12 hydropower projects high up in the Himalayas, with about 500 believed to be trapped in tunnels. Rescue efforts have also focused on Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, where Nepali authorities said they were confident that 46 workers trapped in an underground chamber in the plant were still alive.

title: US added 162,000 jobs in August, with unemployment rate holding steady
summary: Number of new jobs being added has been fluctuating, with private companies adding 38,000 jobs in August
text: The US economy added 162,000 jobs in August, an uptick after a sluggish summer for the labor market. The unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%, still down from its most recent peak of 4.5% last November, according to new data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Despite the relative stability of the unemployment rate, the number of new jobs added to the economy has been fluctuating, going from 214,000 in March down to a 21,000 gain in July and then back up in August. Figures for job growth in June and July were both revised up. After revisions, job growth in June was 31,000 jobs, up from an initial 20,000, and July was revised up by 44,000 jobs, from an initially reported loss of 23,000 to a gain of 21,000. Economists had predicted gains would be at least 50,000 new jobs. Earlier in the week, the payroll firm ADP reported private companies added 38,000 jobs in August, lower than initial expectations and the lowest month for new jobs since January. Meanwhile, outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported that layoffs have been going down and are 41% lower than cuts that were announced by this time last year. Economists have pointed out that the labor market appears to be stalled in a “slow hire, slow fire” state, with neither growth nor contractions in jobs. A separate BLS report from earlier this week showed job openings and layoffs had changed little in July. The number of people quitting their jobs also remained flat, suggesting workers are feeling less confident about their ability to find another job. For many Americans feeling frustrated about the economy, a lackluster job market feels especially painful when paired with rising prices. US inflation has increased significantly since the start of the war with Iran, with the annual inflation rate going from 2.4% in February to 3.4% in July. In May, price increases reached 4.2%, the highest rate since 2023. In recent weeks, persistent inflation has started to have a domino effect in the US economy after a sell-off in the US bond market. Yields for US Treasury bonds have been going up since the start of the Iran war, suggesting that investors are concerned about the long-term health of the economy. Higher yields could push up the price of loans, including mortgages, car loans and the interest rate on student debt, making things even more costly for Americans. Economists are expecting at least one interest rate hike from the US Federal Reserve before the end of the year. Higher interest rates could help lower inflation, but at the risk of destabilizing the labor market. Last week, Kevin Warsh, the Fed chair, gave his debut speech at the Fed’s symposium in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, where he said the Fed was still committed to getting inflation down to its 2% target rate, but held off on making any firm suggestions on the central bank’s next move. “We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” he said. “Otherwise, we have work to do.” Donald Trump on Friday celebrated the new job figures and threatened to “stop trading with countries with which we have a deficit” if the Fed doesn’t lower interest rates. “A STRONG COUNTRY MEANS A LOWER INTEREST RATE –IT’S A BETTER CREDIT… Very simple!” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “We should have the LOWEST RATE of any country in the World, like ‘the old days’.”

title: Seeds of hope: how a local farming project is offering a lifeline to Gaza
summary: Family-run Al-Qarara Seed Bank is helping to counter acute food insecurity after being destroyed in the war
text: Salama Ayesh Muhanna still remembers the first seeds he planted on his family’s land in al-Qarara, Gaza. At just 17, Muhanna had proudly sprouted cucumbers. “I was very happy because I saw the results,” Muhanna says. “We were farmers at heart.” Now 71, he is an agronomist, a community leader and the founder of the Al-Qarara Seed Bank. The original project, founded in 2017, was situated near the eastern border of Gaza in al-Qarara, an area now completely flattened and inaccessible. Back then, Muhanna had a large home, olive trees, land of his own, and a successful seed bank operation with dedicated storage and equipment. Everything was destroyed early in Israel’s brutal military campaign, but after being displaced to Deir al-Balah in 2024, Muhanna and his daughter Hanadi, 38, are now hard at work, regrowing seed collections at Gaza’s only seed bank. Outside the tent where they currently live in a displacement camp, summer temperatures climb to almost 35C. Another tent houses their small but growing collection of open-pollinated, non-GMO seeds, including local wheat and vegetables such as okra and spinach. Each day, Muhanna rises early to check on the project, a 200-metre-wide plot of land where the family lives, collects seeds, and experiments with new crops. He inspects the seeds to assess their quality, waters crops and checks on seedlings. As the manager of the seed bank, Hanadi deals with local farmers and oversees the growing seed collection – all while studying agriculture and food sovereignty online via a programme partly tied to Coventry University and the Gaza Urban Agriculture Forum. Muhanna jokes that his hard-working daughter will be “managing her father” by next year. The project has two main aims. One is to collect and preserve the seeds of local plants that may thrive better in this landscape. “The war forced farmers to resort to local seeds,” says Hanadi, because of the ongoing blockades on seed imports, rocketing food prices and growing hunger across Gaza. Yet it appears that this focus on local seed varieties – “baladi” seeds – may prove more effective. That, Muhanna says, is because “local seeds are resistant to drought, fungi, and pests”. “During the war, they’ve been our lifeline,” he adds. The project’s other aim is to create a node for seed distribution for farmers who need to save every possible penny. The seeds, once collected, are distributed among Palestinian farmers and families in Deir al-Balah who then return the same amount after harvest. Approximately 200 farmers have so far benefited thanks to Muhanna and Hanadi’s seeds, with support from the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC). Beyond multiplying seed collections, it is helping Palestinian farmers reclaim agricultural agency and self-reliance – providing for families despite devastating restrictions on resources including vital humanitarian aid. The seeds are deeply connected to memories of the Palestinian land Muhanna has always called home – and could, he hopes, be key to future food sovereignty in Gaza. “The pumpkin plant reminds me of my father and mother,” he says. “It grew on the vineyard where we lived when I was little.” The needs have never been more urgent. At least 1.2 million people in Gaza now face acute food insecurity amid an escalating humanitarian crisis, according to a new report by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC). Despite growing alarm among humanitarian organisations, Israel continues to block access to agricultural land and the import of seeds and organic fertiliser. Meanwhile, dwindling water supplies, degraded soil and deadly remnants of explosives make farming a treacherous practice. “Walking in the streets is unsafe, and walking on the land is unsafe,” Muhanna says, adding that the psychological impact affects their work. “The war destroyed my hope.” Despite immense challenges, the family know their seeds are helping the community while preserving indigenous species against agricultural monopolies, and safeguarding Palestine’s agricultural heritage. As Muhanna puts it, seeds are “my identity, my patriotism, my nationality”. Pat Griffiths, ICRC’ spokesperson in Jerusalem, said: “This is about agency. It’s about dignity. It’s about being less dependent on what is or is not allowed to enter Gaza. As the occupying power, Israel has an obligation to make sure that Palestinians in Gaza have access to the food, goods and items that they need to live.” There is still a long way to go in returning the seed bank to its former size. Muhanna says that before the war, they had about 42 types of local seeds. “Now we have about 28.” There is also another looming challenge that could affect the seed bank’s future. “Climate change is what controls us,” Muhanna says, as he sips his tea and shelters inside from the sun. “When the weather is hot, the seeds spoil.” Sometimes he has to plant almost a month later than normal, delaying harvests in a race against time to gather resilient seeds for the future. Still they keep going, experimenting in their fields to see which local seeds produce the best yields. And with almost 2.5 tonnes of seeds collected so far – better than last year – there are signs that the efforts are working. With each seed, there is hope in Gaza that sovereignty over food security can soon take root. “Any country in the world that doesn’t have sovereignty over food security isn’t a country,” Muhanna says. “If we establish sovereignty over food security, then we’ll be a real country.”
