title: Tennessee is about to execute its first woman since 1819. Her case raises troubling questions | Austin Sarat
summary: Christa Pike’s planned execution is emblematic of America’s broken death penalty system
text: On 30 September, the state of Tennessee plans to put Christa Pike to death. She would be the third person brought to the death chamber in the Volunteer state this year, one of which was stopped after it was botched. She would join 17 others who have been put to death there since 1960. None of them were women. In fact in all of US history, only 578 women have been executed, a little more than 3% of our country’s total. The last one was Amber McLaughlin, killed in Missouri in 2024. If Pike is killed, it would be Tennessee’s first execution of a woman since 1819. So, on the face of it, the fate that awaits Pike is unusual. But on second glance, it displays many of the hallmarks of America’s broken death penalty system. Like many who end up on death row, Pike had an unspeakably difficult childhood. She was raped and abused and, when not being subject to such horrors, was abandoned and neglected by her parents. So it was not surprising when Pike turned to violence, and with two others committed a murder when she was still a teenager. As the psychologist and trauma expert Bethany Brand explains: “At 18 years old, her immature, traumatized brain made her exceptionally vulnerable to impulses and extremely poor decisions … Unmedicated and untreated, she was not able to put the ‘brakes on’ her bipolar- and trauma-triggered emotions.” When it came to her trial, Pike’s lawyer failed to present mitigating evidence that was readily available to him and to uncover any new mitigating circumstances. As the professor Deborah Denno explains: “Specifically, counsel chose not to present defendant’s social history evidence … claiming that the … materials in particular contained double-edged information,” namely information that might have hurt as well as helped her. And now as she awaits her execution, she has legitimate concerns that, given her distinctive medical and emotional problems, when the state tries to kill her, she will face a torturous and cruel death. But so far, courts have chosen to look the other way. If they continue to do so, Pike will take her place among America’s relatively exclusive club of female execution victims. It is such a club because while women commit about one in eight homicides in the United States, they tend to commit murders that fall below the threshold of crimes that prosecutors, judges and jurors consider to be the worst of the worst. As the professor Elizabeth Rappaport argues: “Two thirds of women who kill, kill family members and lovers … [and] [t]hese crimes almost never result in death sentences, regardless of the sex of the killer.” Pike was obviously not one of those killers. And her victim was murdered in a gruesome manner. A local television station in Knoxville, Tennessee, says prosecutors claim Pike “tortured and killed” her victim because Pike thought she was trying to steal Pike’s boyfriend. This crime is reminiscent in its brutality to the one committed by Karla Faye Tucker in Texas in 1983. She and her co-defendant killed their victims with a pickaxe. Tucker became something of a celebrity after having a sincere and profound religious conversion on death row. Texas Public Radio reports that her case “attracted national attention by many of America’s top televangelists, including Pat Robertson. He appealed to the Texas Governor George W. Bush … to commute Tucker’s sentence,” something that Bush refused to do. Tucker was put to death in 1998, making her the first woman executed in Texas since 1863. Fast forward to January 2021, when the federal government under Donald Trump executed Lisa Montgomery. Here, again the crime for which she was convicted was particularly gruesome. In 2004, Montgomery crossed state lines “ostensibly to purchase a puppy from Bobbie Jo Stinnett, a 23-year-old dog breeder who was eight months pregnant. Instead, Montgomery strangled her, cut her fetus from her womb and tried to pass the surviving baby off as her own.” Like Christa Pike, Montgomery “had brain damage and severe mental illness that was exacerbated by a lifetime of abuse, including child sex trafficking, gang rape and physical abuse largely at the hands of family members”. She was killed by lethal injection, making her just the fourth woman ever executed by the federal government. It put a woman to death for the first time in 1865, when it hanged Mary Surratt for her role in the assassination of Abraham Lincoln. At the time, according to the National Museum of Women’s History, “most people, including the military judges who issued the guilty verdict, could not believe the United States government was going to execute a woman.” There is a bit of that sentiment reflected in the news coverage of Pike’s case. Even as this society seeks to achieve gender equality, there is still something unsettling at the prospect of putting a woman to death. In Pike’s case, what should truly be unsettling is not her gender, but rather the prospect of putting to death someone whose crime was as much the product of society’s failure as it was of her criminal intent. For women as well as men, capital punishment offers no solution to the problems that give rise to the most serious crimes. Austin Sarat, associate dean of the faculty and William Nelson Cromwell professor of jurisprudence and political science at Amherst College, is the author of Gruesome Spectacles: Botched Executions and America’s Death Penalty

title: Weather tracker: Hurricanes in the Pacific, but none yet this season in the Atlantic
summary: The current record for the latest Atlantic hurricane formation could be broken this year
text: There are currently two category 4 hurricanes and one category 1 hurricane in the Pacific at the same time. Meanwhile, the Atlantic has been devoid of hurricanes so far this season, making it only the eighth year in the satellite era (about 1960 to present) to go into September without a hurricane. Forecast activity remains quiet for the next seven days at least. This means there is a chance the current record for the latest Atlantic hurricane formation – 11 September in 2002 and in 2013 – will be broken. Category 1 Hurricane Marie, category 3 Hurricane Karina, and category 4 Hurricane Lowell are spinning around in the Pacific. The National Hurricane Centre says there is too much uncertainty around Lowell to determine potential impacts on Hawaii, whereas Marie and Karina are not currently expected to have any impacts and should stay in open waters. On average, there are only eight Pacific hurricanes a year according to the NHC, so to have three at the same time is very unusual. This isn’t the first time this has happened, though. Back in 2015, there were also three hurricanes in the Pacific simultaneously. All three were category 4 strength. Meanwhile, Tropical Storm Edouard made landfall in Louisiana at 11.25 UTC (12.25 BST) on 1 September, bringing strong gusts, heavy rain and flooding. These impacts were mostly felt in south-west Louisiana and south-east Texas, the highest wind gust being 69mph at the Beaumont/Port Arthur airport. The resulting disruption included power outages and school closures. Flash flooding continues to be a risk across east-central Texas this week. Other parts of Texas have been under an extreme heat warning this week. The heat index value – a measure of how hot it “feels” to the body when humidity is combined with air temperature – has reached up to 46C (114.8F) for the southern tip of the state. The National Weather Service has highlighted heat-related illnesses as the main potential effect. Parts of Europe have just come to the end of their warmest summer on record. Countries such as the UK, France and Belgium have broken their mean temperature records by large margins. France exceeded its previous record by 0.8C, previously set in 2003; while the UK exceeded its previous record by 0.4C, set in 2025. Not all data has been released yet, but it is almost certain that more countries will follow.

title: Digested week: Tom Tugendhat is a serious politician. What’s he doing in a Reform-lite Tory frontbench? | John Crace
summary: Want to see how small the gene pool of Tory talent is? I give you Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor. Also this week: Starmer’s Fomo, and telly wars
text: Monday It’s the end of summer and Kemi Badenoch chose to mark the occasion with a reshuffle of her shadow cabinet. Her aim is apparently to get the Tories match fit in case Andy Burnham calls an early general election, but the vibes are much more rearranging the deckchairs on a sinking ship. After all, when the gene pool of talent is that small, there’s not much you can do. James Cleverly got the ball rolling by announcing he was planning to be the Conservative candidate for London mayor in two years’ time. He may have his work cut out. London is a liberal, multicultural city and unlikely to be won over by a party giving up on net zero and the European convention on human rights. Cleverly’s replacement as shadow housing secretary is Katie Lam, who was only elected two years ago but has been desperate to attract attention by consistently saying the most offensive thing she can think of. This may not end well. Priti Patel’s departure as foreign secretary was no great surprise as she has always been a liability, but Kemi’s decision to appoint Tom Tugendhat in her place did raise eyebrows. Tom has always been from the One Nation side of the party and Kemi didn’t seem to realise that when he said: “If I had known Kemi was this good I wouldn’t have stood against her,” he had merely been joking. He is at least a serious politician in the way Priti never was, but you also can’t help wondering if he is really signed up to Kemi’s Reform-lite Tory agenda. Still, Tom has never been one to shy away from going to war with anyone, so he and Kemi will have something in common. That just leaves the change of shadow chancellor. It goes without saying that Mel Stride had always been endearingly hopeless, but the choice of Andrew Griffith to take over is bewildering. The Tories always like to play up Griffith’s career in business, but what the rest of the country will be focusing on is that he was the co-author and defender of Liz Truss’s disastrous mini-budget. So maybe his economic judgment is not that sound after all. It should also be remembered that Griffith was Boris Johnson’s “net zero business champion” in 2020; something he and Kemi are also hoping to forget. Maybe the key to understanding Griffith is that he is just a career opportunist who doesn’t really believe in anything. In which case he may fit in just fine. Tuesday One politician who won’t be hurrying back to Westminster for the start of the new parliamentary session is Keir Starmer. He has just announced he is standing down as an MP. The only recent former prime minister to remain a backbencher and regularly turn up to debates in the Commons was Theresa May and she cut a somewhat sad figure. Her attendance was impressive but she never appeared to have any friends. Just sitting by herself, lost in her own thoughts. What Keir is thinking now is anyone’s guess. We don’t all get the summer we were hoping for – I certainly didn’t – but Starmer’s must have been borderline surreal. It must be so hard for a prime minister to learn to switch off. One day you’re the centre of attention with constant demands on your time, the next you’re a virtual ghost. A person of little importance. Most former prime ministers have a tormented shadow to them, even years after they have left Downing Street. As if they still can’t believe that the voters or their own MPs have rejected them. Keir will have been expecting to have spent the last six weeks on constant alert. Dealing with world events and travelling the country to convince everyone he was actually working. A prime minister needs to be visible, or their enemies assume they are skiving. Instead, his phone will have gone quiet with no one making any demands on his time. The fear of missing out must have been intense. He might have wished Burnham well in public but in private he wouldn’t have been too sad if Andy was struggling just a little bit. Just about all we did hear about Keir during the break was that he had donated a copy of Tom Baldwin’s biography of himself to the No 10 library. Which felt, somehow a little desperate. Somewhat tragic. Why not break with tradition and leave a work of fiction? Rebecca; or The Age of Innocence. Something that just oozes class. But instead, like many prime ministers, he couldn’t resist giving a rose-tinted version of his deeds that will never be read by anyone. It will survive to collect dust. Which only goes to show that with many politicians, it really is all about them. Wednesday Most of us go through life collecting bits and pieces. What others might call clutter. Items that shape the identities of our homes. Starting with the basics. Tables, chairs, beds, chest of drawers, kitchenware, that sort of thing. Then books, televisions and sound systems. But what happens to all this when we die? How much will remain? In my mother’s case, the answer was almost nothing. My mum died last year at the age of 101, her last seven years spent in a care home as her Alzheimer’s prevented her from living on her own. So the house she and my father – he died in 1999 – had bought for their retirement years earlier had to be sold to pay for her care. My sisters and I spent several weekends going through the contents prior to the sale, trying to work out what to keep and what to do with the rest. Almost everything went to a house-clearance firm. We had no use for the beds or the furniture because we all had our own already and didn’t have the space for any more. It was all rather melancholic. There were several items my mum had inherited from her parents that she had always said were quite valuable. We got an expert in who told us they were all cheap reproductions. My grandmother had been ripped off. All we kept were a couple of pictures, some personal effects and a few small items to furnish her new room at the care home. When she died, we had 10 days to clear out her room and almost all of this went too. Her clothes, her chair and a few books that she had never read because of her dementia. The only things that really remained of value to us were her photograph albums. These were her memories. The last surviving physical links not just between us and her, but between her and our father, between her and her parents and grandparents. Many of these photos I had never seen while she had been alive. In generations to come, not even these will remain when people die. Everyone’s photos will be on their phone or laptop. My mum never held with either. We gave her a mobile about 20 years ago but she always refused to use it so there was no point ringing it. So more than a century of a life well lived reduced to almost nothing. Just a few precious keepsakes that mean everything but are of little financial value. And when my sisters and I die, our mum will die again. Dust to dust. Thursday The naming wars have been hotting up. First Donald Trump declared he was renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. Then, during one of his regular hissy fits with the Canadians, he changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America by presidential decree. You can sense a theme emerging. And earlier this week he was openly fantasising of calling the strait of Hormuz the strait of Trump. Just imagine having so much narcissism and so little imagination. Not so long ago, the Donald came close to calling Greenland America, so there’s no way of really knowing where this one is going to end. Why not call the Atlantic Trump Ocean and the Pacific America Ocean? It’s odds on that he will demand that part of the moon will be named after him when Nasa lands astronauts back on the lunar surface in a few years’ time. Weirdly, many Americans think this behaviour is quite normal. In a spectacular display of presidential brown-nosing, Google even marks the changes on its maps for a US audience. Google Lake Ontario in the UK and you get Lake Ontario (Lake America). You’d have thought a better response would be to just ignore the president and wait till he went away. Canada has tried being rational. It explained the lake had been called Ontario since the 17th century, long before the USA and Canada existed in their current forms, and was an Iroquoian word meaning “beautiful lake”. All this was far too complicated for The Donald. So now the Canadians have upped their game by putting up giant Lake Ontario signs by the lake, only for Trump to post a video of himself kicking over the sign and replacing it with Lake America. It’s like dealing with a five-year-old. So maybe we’d all be better off treating him like one. At least we’d all have more fun. The Canadians could start by renaming the US half of Lake Superior as Lake Inferior. Mark Carney could sign that off in a day and then Google would be obliged to make the changes on its maps. Maybe. But we could all join in. Burnham could rename the US the United States of Greater England. Pretend independence had always been a big mistake. The perfect 250th anniversary present. Friday This time of year always makes me feel depressed. The days getting shorter, the weather colder. Most years, this can be offset a little by the start of the Premier League football season. This autumn, not so much. Despite having spent more than a third of a billion pounds on new players, Spurs are at the bottom of the table. Played two, lost two. Goals scored, nil. At least you have to admire the consistency. Yet again we have a manager who is calling for patience, that it will come right in the end. Maybe it will, but it doesn’t feel like it at the moment. Still, on the plus side, we have the new autumn TV schedules with the broadcasters having waited until we had all stopped enjoying ourselves outdoors before giving us something half decent to watch. The current onscreen battle in our house is between the BBC and ITV. Vigil versus Trigger Point. Suranne Jones v Vicky McClure. Two dramas on to their third and fourth series respectively that are dominated by badass women tasked with saving the world. We are a lot further into Trigger Point than we are into Vigil, but that’s only because ITV has put the whole series up on its streaming site. And I am loving both in a particularly mindless kind of way. As much for the nonsense as the drama. The entire plot of Vigil depends on the security services turning to the same two Scottish policewomen, who just happen to be in a relationship and have seamless childcare, every time the country is on the verge of war. We are currently both in Scotland and Svalbard, where everyone seems to have a secret to hide. Trigger Point is even wilder. Two bombs go off in central London and no one seems to bat an eye, as all attention is on the one that Vicky has defused. Almost all bombs seem to be neutralised by cutting the red wire. If someone else tries to defuse a bomb then they will almost certainly get blown up. Meanwhile there is a member of the security services who couldn’t be overacting to look suspicious any harder if she tried and no one seems to notice. Thank God for Vicky, or we’d all be screwed. Digested week in pictures

title: ICE bans hugging inside California’s largest detention center. Families are fighting back
summary: In the California City facility, ‘contact visits’ are strictly forbidden – but detained residents aren’t staying quiet. Are officials listening?
text: Teresa Reyes drove 300 miles to be with her son on his 32nd birthday in May, but she couldn’t give him a gift, share a meal with him or give him a hug. She couldn’t even touch him. Her son, Guillermo, a tattoo artist from San Jose, is locked up in the California City immigration detention center, California’s largest Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility, and the only way he can see his mother is behind a thick pane of glass. The detention center, housing roughly 1,600 people in a desert region north of Los Angeles, has denied contact visits to all people held inside since the Trump administration opened the site one year ago. That means no one inside the facility, which is run by the private prison firm CoreCivic, can sit with or embrace family members who travel to the remote site for visits. Instead, families are left talking through phones while their relatives sit in an adjacent room, separated by glass barriers. “I want to hold my son, I want to touch him, I want to assure him everything is going to be OK, but I can’t,” said Reyes, 63, speaking in Spanish. “When I see him, I have to hold back tears. I have to pretend to be strong, because I don’t want him to think I am suffering.” The total denial of contact visits is an extreme restriction for any prison or detention site where people are locked up long-term, particularly a facility holding people accused of immigration violations. Prisons across the US housing people convicted of serious criminal offenses typically operate visitation rooms where families can sit at tables, only temporarily barring contact visits when there are safety concerns. The harsh policy, advocates say, is part of the Trump administration’s strategy of placing more and more people in crowded facilities while their cases drag on, subjecting them to prison-like conditions and restricting their connections to the outside – all of which can increase pressure to accept deportations. In California City, detained residents aren’t staying quiet, instead working with advocates to launch a public campaign, pleading with their warden to let them hug their relatives. Is he listening? Six months of ‘isolation’ Allen Tayson, 37, spoke over the loud clangs and shouts behind him. The father of two from Gilroy, a California city south of San Jose, was appearing on a video call from inside the California City facility, his face going in and out of focus, with the ICE messaging app blurring the background behind him. “We feel isolated in here,” he said. “Everything is meant to break you down and discourage you and make you give up hope. If I was able to hug and hold my wife and kids, it would be like a brief getaway that would take me away from this setting. I’d cherish every second.” Tayson, a repair shop worker, hasn’t been able to hold his family since February when he was detained by ICE at his green card interview at a United States Citizenship and Immigration Services office. Tayson is from the Philippines and came to the US as a child. He and his wife, Samantha Sanchez, a US citizen, have known each other since they were teenagers and married in 2016. They have a 14-year-old son and five-year-old daughter – and Sanchez is now seven months pregnant. Tayson has missed nearly her entire pregnancy. “I’m so used to taking care of my family, and I feel so helpless every single day that I’m here and my family has to figure out a way to get by without me,” said Tayson. When Tayson arrived at California City and learned contact visits were banned for all, he and his wife made a choice: she would not travel 300 miles to visit if they couldn’t have contact. They knew first-hand how painful that process could be. When their son was around three years old, Tayson had a stint in a jail for firearm felony charges that were later dismissed. That facility only allowed visits behind glass, and at the end of one visit, his son reached out to hug his father and collided with the glass. Tayson is haunted by his son’s look of disbelief and vowed that would never happen again. So the family talks on video calls, which cost 21 cents a minute, or $6.30 for half an hour, a cost that adds up as Sanchez works to provide for her two kids – all while navigating a high-risk pregnancy. “I have this baby growing inside me, and he hasn’t even touched my belly,” Sanchez said. She wants to see her husband in the flesh so she has some reassurances that he is physically OK. She is trying to manage her stress and depression, worried her declining mental health will lead to pregnancy complications: “It would just be a bit of relief on my nervous system to hug him.” Their five-year-old daughter asks daily when her father is coming home, Sanchez said. She often catches her daughter praying alone. “She says, ‘I’m just talking to God, so he can help dad.’” A nationwide problem The lack of access to visitation is a growing human rights crisis across the US, advocates say. Of the 10 ICE detention centers with the largest populations, four entirely bar contact visits – California City, the Stewart detention center in Georgia, the south Texas processing center in Pearsall and the Montgomery processing center in Conroe, Texas, according to ICE’s websites. Michelle Brané, a former immigration detention ombudsman for the Department of Homeland Security, said before 2016, it was common for ICE facilities to offer contact visits. But in Trump’s first term, more detention centers began only offering visits behind glass – and it has been a persistent problem since. Some detention centers, including Otay Mesa in San Diego, have at times had particularly restrictive set-ups, with families arriving at the facilities to discover the visit involves them video conferencing with their loved one in another room, often with a poor connection, said Brané. Brané, now executive director of advocacy group Together and Free, said detention officials have often claimed there wasn’t enough space in the facilities to accommodate contact visits. That explanation rings hollow for the current administration, which has allotted record funds for detention, she said. “When you have as much money as this administration, there’s no excuse for inhumane conditions.” After auditing California City in the spring, the California department of justice said the prohibition on contact visits appeared to violate a CoreCivic policy that the company provided to the state, which stipulated that there should be opportunities for physical contact and those visits should only be restricted for “security risks”. A photo of the visitation area published by the state justice department showed there was space for contact visits. The room has picnic tables, which families used years prior when the facility was a state prison. But now, ICE detainees aren’t allowed to sit at those tables or enter that part of the room. Instead, the photo showed, there is a row of windows at the edge of the room where the detained immigrants can speak through phones – the only available option for visits. The Rev Deborah Lee, executive director of the Interfaith Movement for Human Integrity, a group supporting detainees, said some visitors have struggled to hear through the phones that families and detainees have to use to talk to one another. Because only one person can speak through the phone at a time, group conversations weren’t possible. “It’s just a denial of people’s humanity,” Lee said. During a visit in July, Lee’s group ran into the California City warden, Christopher Chestnut, the reverend recalled. When she asked him why no one could have a regular visit, he told her that facilities with contact visits had higher overdose rates, without providing further explanation, according to Lee. ICE did not respond to requests for comment. Ryan Gustin, a CoreCivic spokesperson, defended California City’s policies, saying in an email: “Facility leadership, in conjunction with our government partners, has determined that non-contact visitation is the most appropriate approach given security considerations. As with correctional and detention facilities across the country, preventing the introduction of contraband is a significant safety and security concern.” Gustin added that CoreCivic “recognizes the importance of maintaining family and community connections for individuals in our care” and that under “applicable detention standards”, individual facilities have the authority to set visitation policies based on “factors including facility design, operational requirements, staffing considerations and security protocols”. ICE and CoreCivic did not respond to interview requests for the warden. ‘Mom can have a voice’ In the face of long-term detention without contact visits, California City residents began organizing. In April, Gustavo Guevara, who had been detained at the facility since it opened in August 2025, helped organize a letter within his dorm demanding officials offer regular visits. He said the idea spread to other dorms, with residents writing their own demand letters. Some residents had come from other ICE facilities where contact visits were allowed, so were bewildered and angry to lose that access. People were especially anxious about never getting to say goodbye to relatives if they lost their cases. “Not only are you immediately deprived of that human interaction, but what is hanging over your head is the possibility of being sent to another country, not knowing if you’ll ever hold your loved ones again,” he said. Guevara and others worked with the California Collaborative for Immigrant Justice (CCIJ), an Oakland-based non-profit that advocates for detained people, and a coalition of activists delivered the letters to the warden and helped launch a “Hugs Beyond Bars” campaign. Some residents had advocates film them on video calls pleading for contact visits, which were published on social media. Allen Tayson also recorded himself reading his own demand letter, which the coalition released on Instagram. “Across all the dorms, people could unite behind this,” said Val Suarez, CCIJ community and legal organizer. “They saw this big family room that used to be a visitation room which proves there really is no reason for them to not have access to this.” It felt achievable. It was personal for Guevara, who had a close friend visit him regularly at California City behind glass. That was until June when he was deported to Mexico. Guevara never got to hug him and doesn’t know if he’ll see him again, he said, but he’ll continue advocating for contact visits for those he left behind. Last month, Samantha Sanchez also joined CCIJ for a visit to US senator Alex Padilla’s office in San Francisco urging Congress to pressure CoreCivic to provide visitation. “I wanted my kids to see that mom can have a voice – that I’m doing this for dad and other families,” Sanchez said. The senator’s office seemed sympathetic to their pleas, advocates said. But so far, CoreCivic and the California City warden have not responded to their demands. During Teresa Reyes’s visit with her son in May on his birthday, she noticed there were vending machines for visitors and hoped to buy a snack for her son, but learned that was not possible. When advocates accompanying her asked if the staff could make an exception and give her one brief hug, the officers said no, she recalled. She hasn’t been back to California City since May – and will only return if she can hug her son.

title: JD Vance accused of ‘gaslighting’ after saying he is ‘skeptical’ US struck Iranian wedding  | First Thing
summary: Vice-president’s claim US-Iran conflict is not war draws ridicule from Democrat Ro Khanna. Plus, iconic feminist Gloria Steinem dies at 92
text: Good morning. The US vice-president, JD Vance, has responded to claims that an American strike was responsible for killing four people, including a child, at a wedding celebration in southern Iran by saying that “sometimes things happen”. The deaths were reported by the Iranian Red Crescent, which operates independently of Tehran and is treated by most international monitors as a credible source on casualty figures. In a further comment, described by the congressman Ro Khanna, a Democrat from California, as “gaslighting”, the vice-president said the conflict between the US and Iran, which has stretched into a seventh month and caused the deaths of 18 US service members, was not presently “a war”. Iranian authorities have put the overall death toll from US and Israeli strikes in the thousands, figures outside observers, including US-based monitoring groups, have broadly corroborated. What did Vance say? At a White House press briefing he said: “I will say that the Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far, so I’m extremely skeptical of this. What I can say with 100% confidence is that, unlike the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the US never targets civilians in combat. We never will do that. We never have done that, and unfortunately, obviously, sometimes things happen”. Donald Trump has repeatedly threatened to blow up Iran’s civilian infrastructure. What is happening with US military leadership? Trump on Thursday named Adam Telle as the acting army secretary after the departure of Daniel Driscoll amid widespread reports of tensions with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth. Telle is currently the assistant secretary of the army for civil works. Far-right Israeli minister outlines plan to remove all Palestinians from Gaza Israel’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has outlined a plan for the illegal forced expulsion of all Palestinians from Gaza, with the intention of sending them abroad. The forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva conventions, but as a tightly fought election approaches in Israel, political figures have competed over the harshness of their visions for the strip. Ben-Gvir’s comments follow those of the defence minister, Israel Katz, who said Israel was seeking the Trump administration’s approval to displace Palestinians from Gaza, which he said was still under discussion after being “frozen” by the US president. Katz said Israel would facilitate the emigration “by any means”, implying a policy of coercion. What has the House decided about university boycotts of Israel? The House has passed a Republican-backed bill that would penalize universities that participate in boycotts of Israel. “This legislation is about a simple principle: our colleges and universities should not discriminate against Israel,” said Tim Walberg, the Republican chair of the House education committee. Thirty three Democrats broke with the rest of their party to vote in favor. It now goes to the Senate for consideration. Two workers pulled alive from tunnel nine days after Nepal-Tibet flood Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after being trapped by deadly flash floods that buried the project in deep mud. The workers were rescued during a continuing operation at the Trishuli 3A tunnel in one of the areas worst affected by last week’s deadly Nepal floods. Officials said the men had been flown to a hospital in Kathmandu. Nepal’s communication minister, Bikram Timilsina, said officials still hoped more workers would be rescued. At least 1,287 people were killed in the floods and more than 5,000 are missing, Nepal’s disaster management agency said. Missouri supreme court throws out new congressional maps backed by Trump The Missouri supreme court has unanimously blocked new congressional districts backed by Trump from being used in the November election, and ordered a statewide vote on whether to uphold or reject the new map. The decision on Thursday marks a rare setback for Republicans in a national redistricting battle. Missouri’s new districts were used in the August primaries. The state supreme court said they cannot be used in the November general election – or ever again – unless voters first uphold the new districts, after citizens submitted petition signatures seeking a referendum. In other news … The UN general assembly will vote today on a resolution for the world to formally phase out the traditional Mercator map of the globe in favor of one that more accurately displays Africa’s size. The deadlocked jury in the Lindsay Clancy trial went home without a verdict Thursday after a dramatic sixth day of deliberations. The billionaire financier Leon Black failed to appear for a US House deposition about his Epstein ties, instead launching a lawsuit against the committee. Excavation work on Trump’s towering, gilded Washington arch is to begin in the next two weeks, despite the plan facing a lawsuit. Fox News Media has abruptly ousted Maria Bartiromo, one of its most well-known hosts and anchors, without explanation. Stat of the day: Thieves steal more than 70,000 pints’ worth of Guinness from depot in England Two trucks were driven into an industrial estate in Runcorn, north-west England, on Monday. They were attached to trailers that were already holding about 800 barrels – or $155,000 worth – of the famous Irish drink, and made off with them. Culture Pick: Turning Point – Generation 9/11 The US will soon cross the point at which half its population were born after 11 September 2001 or were too young to remember the attack. David Smith looks at a new Netflix documentary about those events and their global impact, as memory begins to give way to history. Don’t miss this: Gloria Steinem, groundbreaking feminist, dies aged 92 Hillary Clinton was among those remembering Gloria Steinem yesterday, hailing the American feminist icon who died at 92 at home in New York City as “one of the architects of the entire structure of women’s equality”. We have a gallery of Steinem’s life in pictures, a review of the activist’s forthcoming memoir, which now stands as a posthumous testament to her remarkable life, and a selection of her wit and wisdom in her greatest quotes. In a column, Moira Donegan says Steinem personified America’s feminist movement, and we would also like to hear your tributes and memories. … or this: Art Garfunkel on a rich, restless life A beautiful interview with Art Garfunkel, one of the purest voices in the rock/pop canon. And yes, his relationship with Paul Simon does get a mention or two. Climate check: Strongest El Niño on record forecast Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology is the latest body to issue a warning over El Niño, saying it has already broken records, with Pacific Ocean temperature change exceeding 3.6F in six months. Last Thing: I didn’t know I was pregnant until I gave birth Aubrie Morris recounts what must one of the strangest surprises anyone can have – unexpectedly delivering a baby you did not know you were carrying. title: Reform UK suspends two senior officials after undercover report on donations
summary: Revelations are further blow to Nigel Farage before conference speech, with Labour reporting party to police
text: Reform UK has suspended two senior officials after they were filmed in an undercover investigation appearing to plot to get around electoral laws on foreign donations. In a blow to Nigel Farage hours before his conference speech, the party said it had launched an investigation into the actions of James Orr, the party’s head of policy, and Dan Jukes, a senior aide to Farage, after the broadcast by Channel 4 News. Jukes and Orr were filmed by a group of investigative journalists called Verbatim, founded by the Centre for Climate Reporting, helping to orchestrate a plot apparently to bypass election laws. The journalists posed as a potential Reform supporter and his wealthy American father, an impermissible donor, who paid for £30,000 of polling commissioned by Reform and which benefited the party when it was published in national newspapers. If found to have been a donation in kind and made from abroad, it would have been impermissible as it was a foreign source and was not registered with the Electoral Commission. Farage was subsequently caught on camera in a meeting with the fake US donor in Clacton where he appears to be celebrating the success of the poll, saying it was “amazing” and provided “bang for buck”. He said: “It worked. Boom.” The Liberal Democrats and Labour have reported the actions of Reform to the police to investigate whether there has been a breach of electoral law. The Electoral Commission, the watchdog that oversees the rules around party donations, said it had been in touch with the Metropolitan police and was “considering all relevant information”. On Friday morning, Farage said the party had done nothing wrong and no rules were broken, saying on LBC that polls were funded by foreign sources all the time. However, a Reform spokesperson said the officials would be suspended pending an investigation, saying: “Reform UK has launched an investigation following the broadcast of a Channel 4 News programme. Both individuals involved have stepped down from their respective positions pending the outcome of the investigation. “The party believes it is important that the investigation is allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice. No further comment will be made while the investigation is ongoing.” An Electoral Commission spokesperson said: “We are considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are in touch with the Met police.” They said any potential attempt to evade controls on donations was for the police to consider. They also said they were not responsible for approving Reform UK’s or any other party’s donor vetting process, after Farage’s party said it had a “robust vetting process for prospective donors approved by the Electoral Commission”. Reform initially described the investigation as a “hoax” and dismissed those behind it as activists, in a series of counterattacks against the outfit behind the undercover filming. But by Friday morning, it had taken action, as the statement announced the investigation into Orr and Jukes, in what appeared to be an attempt to distance Farage from their actions. However, there appeared to be some controversy over how to deal with Orr and Jukes. Lee Anderson, the party’s chair, said they were not coming back, telling Sky News: “I think it’s only right and proper that we’re fair, open and transparent and get this investigation launched today. And the two people concerned in the video, they’ve gone. “There’s no chance of them coming back. They’ve stepped aside. We’re a serious party, you know, and sometimes in politics, you have to make tough decisions, harsh decisions. I think this probably was an easier decision, being given the option to stand down. They have gone.” But Richard Tice, the deputy leader, later did not rule out them returning to their roles after the inquiry. He also told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme the party had a legal opinion from a KC saying no rules had been broken and he believed Channel 4 News had broken rules with entrapment. Asked by the Guardian at a fringe event at the Reform conference whether the pair had, as set out by Anderson, gone for good or might return the future, Danny Kruger, the MP who leads Reform’s preparations for government, indicated it was the latter. He said: “My understanding is that they have been suspended pending an investigation.” The footage is likely to continue to raise awkward questions for Farage, on the day of his conference speech, about whether there are other instances of Reform aides having attempted to circumvent electoral law. It is likely to reopen intense scrutiny of Reform’s approach to donations and its finances, which are already the subject of a standards inquiry and police investigation. In footage of another meeting, Jukes appeared to suggest to the fake UK-based supporter that his US-based father could make a substantial donation by channelling it through the son. When the possible structure was explained to Farage, footage of a meeting between him and the fake donors shows him saying: “Thank you both.” At another point, Orr appeared to suggest that the fake UK-based donor and his US father might secure a meeting with Farage if he could promise a five- or six-figure sum – a meeting that later took place in Clacton over oysters and champagne. In a different clip, Orr can be heard saying of the poll funding arrangement that Farage “doesn’t know, won’t know” and it was the kind of thing he would “rather not know”. At one point the footage shows him saying it was “totally legit” and with “nothing untowards about it at all”. Jukes, a close aide to Farage, was also filmed meeting the fake donor, and at a Reform UK reception where in one conversation he appeared to introduce the undercover operative as a “key donor for off-the-book project”. In footage of a meeting with the fake US donor, he is heard describing the polling as “clandestine” and “hugely important”. The polling, conducted by JL Partners, made headlines before the local elections in May. The foreign source of funding and its links to Reform were not publicly disclosed. The Telegraph said it had suspended the articles about the polling, while the Times said it was not aware of the relationship with Reform. After Channel 4 News’s broadcast, Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said the “scandal goes right to the top of Reform UK”. She added: “Nigel Farage needs to urgently prove today that his top team haven’t broken the law and secretly plotted to undermine our democracy.” Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, called on the police and the Electoral Commission to investigate.

title: Iranian town mourns after deadly strike on wedding
summary: Mourning turns to anger as residents of Kuhestak say Baloch communities are being placed in path of conflict
text: People in Kuhestak, a predominantly Baloch city in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, are mourning after a strike on a wedding killed at least four people, including a child, and injured more than 60, according to local authorities. The blast hit at around 9.30pm on 1 September, turning a night of celebration into one of devastation for the small coastal community, which is on the strait of Hormuz. In the aftermath, videos shared on social media by friends and relatives of the wedding couple showed rubble, flower garlands and decorations scattered among debris and bloodied shoes. Asked about the strike on Thursday, the US vice-president, JD Vance, said the US would never target civilians in combat but that “sometimes things happen”, adding that he was sceptical of Iran’s reports. He did not acknowledge that the killings had been confirmed by an internationally recognised humanitarian body. According to Iranian state media and people interviewed by the Guardian, the house belonged to Ali Mallahi, a local fisher who was celebrating his daughter’s wedding. In a video published by state media, Mallahi stood amid the rubble of what had been his home and said he was saddened by the attack but thanked God that the casualties weren’t higher. Residents said the celebrations had only just begun. Friends and family were waiting for the bride and groom, and many guests had yet to arrive for the henna ceremony. Witnesses who spoke to the Guardian said the attack had left residents angry and in deep mourning. Ahmad*, a local barber who witnessed the aftermath, said the entire neighbourhood had been devastated by what happened. “I don’t really have words. Ours is a small town and we all know each other and are brothers. We are all mourning. I visited the house and the media won’t report it, but it wasn’t just one house. Many houses around the site have been damaged and neighbours were directly hit by sharp objects when the explosions happened”. “We are not carrying coffins on our shoulders, we are carrying the dark future that awaits us all in the south,” Ahmad added. Moein Arjomand, director of the Balochistan Human Rights Documentation Network, said local responders were facing growing obstacles investigating the explosion. “Our team has been facing a lot of difficulties due to the internet [shutdown] and witnesses and relatives telling us they were banned from speaking to any foreign rights groups and foreign media,” he said. “I tried arranging interviews for international media with the relatives, but they are worried about the consequences and I couldn’t arrange them.” Despite the internet restrictions and apparent warnings against speaking out, locals and relatives of the couple have continued sharing videos documenting the aftermath on social media. In one video, Yaqoob Mallahi, a relative of the bride, shared footage of his seven-year-old son, Sepehr, lying in a hospital bed with his head bandaged. Arjomand said at least six victims remained in serious condition in the intensive care unit of a hospital in Minab, about 18 miles (30km) away. “Bandar-e-Kuhestak is a small town and the local clinic is not equipped to handle casualties like this, so the injured were taken to the hospital in Minab,” Arjomand said. A video posted by local activists showed the family of Amir Mohammad Karimi, the four-year-old victim, mourning over his body as he was buried on Thursday. A 16-year-old boy, Mohammad Mallahi, was also killed by shrapnel while riding his motorbike nearby. Videos of his funeral, attended by dozens of local people, were shared online. “We have another funeral on Friday, this time a young woman, and we will all be there,” Ahmad said. “I can only pray to Allah that no more of our blood is shed and our injured come back home from the hospital.” Ahmad was referring to Asiyeh Molainejad, 22, another relative of the bride who was declared dead on Thursday. Beyond the immediate grief, the attack deepened a sense among some Baloch residents and activists that civilian deaths in their communities receive comparatively little attention. Farzin Kadkhodaei, a human rights activist from Balochistan, said the circumstances of the deaths had made the loss particularly painful. “The human cost is devastating. These were Baloch civilians gathered for a wedding, and losing their lives in the middle of what should have been a joyful occasion is heartbreaking,” he said. “Their families are now left with unimaginable grief, while the injured have to live with the physical and emotional consequences.” Chakar Baloch, 35, a fisher, said the attack reinforced a feeling among local people that civilians living along the Makran coast were being placed in the path of conflicts over which they had little control. “My overall view is that we are the victims. We are the people who live along the Makran coast and for years we’ve gone out to sea, struggled to earn our bread, and just wanted to stay alive,” he said. When asked if local people were demanding answers about the strike, a Baloch resident of Sirik said western media did not understand their plight. “Who do you want me to demand answers from?” she said. “From the US that has attacked us in this war? Or the regime which has brought this war to our doorsteps? Tell me from whom I can demand and I will answer your questions.”

title: Six people refused to get off ICE deportation plane – now they’re held in limbo in Equatorial Guinea
summary: Believed to be first US deportations to fourth country, six face ‘horrific conditions’ in Equatorial Guinea, say lawyers
text: In late August, around 20 people were put on a flight in the US, shackled at the wrists, waist and ankles, and sent to Liberia as part of one of the largest third-country deportation arrangements of Donald Trump’s second term. Although more than 23,000 people have been sent to 26 countries other than their own since last year, that day saw something that had not happened before: six people refused to get off the plane – and were instead taken to another country. Four Cubans, one Brazilian and one Cameroonian refused to disembark in the Liberian capital Monrovia on 20 August; some of them were allegedly assaulted by ICE agents, who returned them to the plane and promised they would be taken back to the US. A few hours later, however, they were dropped off in another African country: Equatorial Guinea, one of the world’s most repressive and corrupt regimes, where armed men took them to a former luxury hotel turned detention centre in the capital, Malabo, where they have been held ever since. Meredyth Yoon, the litigation director at Asian Americans Advancing Justice-Atlanta, said: “It’s the first time I’ve heard of people being deported to a third country, refusing to disembark, and then being hastily deported on the same flight to a fourth country.” The lawyer, who is in close contact with the group, said they were put on the flight without agreeing to, or even knowing they were being sent to Liberia, let alone Equatorial Guinea. She said they are now being held in “horrific conditions of confinement”, unable to leave the hotel or even contact their families, watched by armed guards, with restricted access to food and no access to basic hygiene items or medical care. Yoon said: “Their families are terrified, deeply concerned about their safety. They haven’t done anything wrong, and they’re being held against their will without knowing what will happen to them.” Although deportation by the US to a fourth country appears to be unprecedented, nearly 60 other people, mostly Africans from other countries, have been deported directly to Equatorial Guinea since November. The country remains far behind Mexico, the main destination for third-country deportees, which has received more than 19,000 people, but Equatorial Guinea has received more than any other country in Africa so far. The agreement with Liberia provides for the transfer of up to 1,200 people. The flights to Equatorial Guinea are part of a deal secured by vice-president Teodoro Nguema Obiang Mangue, known as Teodorín, the son of the dictator Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, the world’s longest-ruling head of state, who has been in power for nearly half a century. Teodorín, who has faced criminal proceedings in other countries over money laundering and corruption, had been barred from entering the US. In France, he was tried in absentia and convicted of money laundering, embezzlement of public funds and corruption in 2017, with the conviction upheld by an appeals court in 2020. Investigations by the US Senate and the Department of Justice (DoJ) concluded he used bribery and extortion to fund a wild spending spree in Equatorial Guinea, and he eventually reached a settlement to avoid trial. However, the US state department granted him a one-month waiver so he could attend the UN general assembly in New York last year. He then travelled to Washington and secured the third-country deportation deal, under which the US would pay his government $7.5m (£5.5m). Tutu Alicante, founder and executive director of the Washington-based NGO EG Justice, said: “For Teodorín, as someone who is about to replace his father as president, having the US on his side is much more important than the money.” Alicante has also been closely following the situation of about 30 deportees currently being held at the Bamy hotel, owned by Mbasogo’s family and which sits inside an isolated, walled compound heavily patrolled by armed soldiers. “The conditions they’re being held in are inhumane,” said Alicante. “We’re talking about individuals who have not committed a crime in the US, and they’re locked up 24/7 in small rooms, and many have been deprived of food and water for considerably long periods.” The Guardian exchanged text messages with one of the Cubans who arrived in late August, who said they were “very saddened” and “desperately hoping to draw attention to what is happening to us, in the hope that someone with the power to help will take pity on us”. He soon stopped responding, however, because guards had confiscated all the phones to prevent the deportees from speaking to media outlets. Among them is a man with a large ventral hernia who, after resisting landing in Liberia, was allegedly thrown down the aircraft steps by ICE agents. Last week, he told the Spanish newspaper El País he urgently needed reconstructive abdominal surgery but, when he was taken to a hospital in Malabo, was allegedly denied treatment because he had no documents. “They cannot legally obtain a status there because Equatorial Guinea doesn’t have a legal framework for asylum, so they’re in this limbo,” said Alicante. The deportees face two options: indefinite detention at the hotel or being sent back to their countries of origin, as has already happened to almost half of those who have arrived since November. However, according to the monitoring project, Third Country Deportation Watch, many of these individuals had previously been granted withholding of removal by US immigration judges who found that they faced a real risk of persecution, torture or death in their home countries. Immigration lawyers have said the Trump administration is using third-country deportations as a legal loophole to indirectly force asylum seekers back to their home countries. A spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security said: “All of these illegal aliens were deported to a safe third country. We are applying the law as written. “If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them, period. The Trump administration is utilising all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised.” The governments of Equatorial Guinea and Liberia did not respond to requests for comment. Last May, UN human rights experts urged Equatorial Guinea to stop sending US deportees back to their home countries, but, as the Guardian has learned, the practice has continued, with at least four Ethiopians sent back to Ethiopia last Wednesday. “This is happening in Equatorial Guinea, in Eswatini, Sudan, Ghana, Liberia; in so many places where they are sending mostly innocent people who have not committed a crime in the US. This is unconscionable,” said Alicante.

title: Private equity faces existential crisis in US as unsold companies pile up
summary: Private equity firms and the companies they own employ over 13 million, from startups to rural hospitals and large retailers, but experts’ concerns of collapse are growing
text: Retail stalwarts Saks and Eddie Bauer filed for bankruptcy. Kmart and JoAnn Fabrics are gone for good, a trail of layoffs and disappointed customers in their wake. Hospital giant Steward Health Care collapsed, costing thousands of jobs and leaving several communities without a local hospital. These once-trusted US companies have one thing in common: they were owned by private equity investors, who load companies with debt when they buy them and squeeze out profits as they restructure. The business model is now facing an existential crisis that may have profound ramifications across the US. Once fringe financial players, private equity investors have bought up vast swathes of US, UK, European and Australian industry, from local dentists to shopping mall anchors and fast-food chains and even the video games company EA. In the US, these firms and the companies they own, employ more than 13 million people in everything from quirky startups like Dave’s Hot Chicken, Two Men and a Truck and School of Rock (all owned by Roark Capital) to the US’s largest pet retailer PetSmart (BC Partners) and classics Birkenstock (purchased by L Catterton in 2021) and Pyrex (owned by Centre Lane Partners). Private equity investors also bought thousands of healthcare facilities in the US in recent years, including non-profit hospice care, rural hospitals and small-town dentists’ offices. But this wave of buyouts is running smack into a wall of persistently high interest rates, rising buyout prices and pressure over moribund returns. Private equity funds are sitting on a “record number of unsold companies, many of which they’ve been unable to sell … or at least unable to sell at the prices that they’re looking for”, said Jim Baker, the executive director of the Private Equity Stakeholder Project, an industry watchdog. The US’s over 13,500 unsold companies in private equity portfolios include 2,563 consumer products and services companies, PitchBook data shows, and 1,536 healthcare companies. Hundreds of these have been sitting in PE portfolios for years longer than funds historically like to keep their investments. A growing concern is that “eventually, the companies that have accumulated this much debt are going to collapse”, said Audrey Stienon, Industrial Policy Program Manager at Open Markets, an anti-monopoly thinktank that is examining private equity’s role in the greater economy. And often, what private equity buys up “are really, really important businesses”, Stienon said, providing jobs or vital services to local communities. “When they go down, either you need to bail them out, or you need to find someone to save them, or else you’re just stuck with fewer options for consumers down the line.” Executives in the industry argue their deep pockets will help businesses weather any upcoming crisis. “Private equity-backed businesses face the same higher interest rates and economic pressures as other companies, but they also have committed investment partners that can provide additional capital and keep investing through difficult periods,” Will Dunham, the president and CEO of American Investment Council, an industry trade group, said in a statement. “Ultimately, private equity only succeeds when the businesses it invests in succeed over the long term,” he said. High rates, more competition Think of private equity deals like buying a home, explains Brad Lipton, director of corporate power and financial regulation at the Roosevelt Institute. Investors buy the company with a hefty loan, like a mortgage, but plan to sell in a matter of years. But unlike with a mortgage, the company is on the hook for making payments, not the buyer, and the buyer almost always plans to sell in a few years. “Interest rates being unexpectedly high may have complicated exit strategies,” Lipton said. Private equity firms promise investors higher returns than the stock market, in exchange for holding on to their money for a longer time period, generally 10 years, a business model that’s been the same for decades. “What has changed is that the price of buying a target company has gone through the roof,” as the number of private equity funds increased, explains Rosemary Batt, a Cornell University management and labor professor who studies the industry’s impacts on workers and companies. Healthcare companies that once sold at 11 times EBITDA, a measure of enterprise value, are now priced at 18 times or more, for example. That makes exiting the investment for a profit even more difficult on investors – and on customers and employees. The higher prices for buyouts are “putting even more pressure on PE firms to squeeze the juice out of their portfolio companies”, Batt said, at a time when there’s almost no regulation governing how they do that. “They can engage in financial engineering or just slash and burn on the operating side,” Batt said. “And it takes years for anyone to really see it.” As they hold the company, these investors generally channel free cashflow to “creditors and equityholders, often constraining capital expenditures, worker training, and safety investments”, the University of Chicago’s Business Law Review warns. Tightening macroeconomic conditions can result in forced restructurings “that are costly and value‑destroying for the going concern”. One vulnerable area is rural hospitals and other health provider chains which could face cashflow issues, making debt payments even more difficult, as the Trump administration’s cuts to the Affordable Care Act tax credits and Medicaid bite, warns Pablo Willis, spokesman for the Americans for Tax Fairness, which is advocating for changes to how private equity managers compensation and the firms overall are taxed. “There’s bound to be a very negative effect,” he said. A lack of financial transparency means it is hard to predict where or when, though. Companies owned by private equity generally don’t disclose their debt levels or other financials unless they go public or issue bonds themselves. “By design, the industry takes place in the shadows,” Lipton said, so “everything has to begin with the thought that we don’t have a lot of clarity.” More bankruptcies ahead In a hint of the turmoil to come, private equity-backed companies have accounted for the lion’s share of big corporate bankruptcies in 2025 and the first half of 2026, research from the Private Equity Stakeholder Project shows. The biggest determinant of whether or not a company will go bankrupt is leverage – the amount of borrowed money explains Edith Hotchkiss, a finance professor at Boston College. Private equity-backed companies are no more likely to default than other similarly leveraged firms, but their business models mean they have more debt. They carry debt of about 50% of their enterprise value, recent studies show. US consumers have felt private equity’s impact through the deteriorating quality of some fast-food outlets and disappearing stores as brands under PE ownership go broke. Other industries have been hit too. More than 60% of big manufacturing bankruptcies in the US last year were private equity-backed, Baker said, as were an outsized number of healthcare bankruptcies. Still, the number of PE-backed companies entering bankruptcy declined in 2025 from the year before, even as overall bankruptcies climbed, S&P found, as more companies pursued out-of-court settlements. The entire process is disruptive by nature. “By definition there is not enough money to go around to pay” a company’s debts, Roosevelt’s Lipton said. “Someone is going to lose out and all too often that can be workers” who are owed pensions. “It is a cause of concern for workers and consumers left holding the bag,” said Lipton. New rules ahead Private equity operates without the rules and regulatory oversight of publicly traded companies. The industry has long argued that because it caters to sophisticated, high-net worth investors, it doesn’t need the same scrutiny. But tens of thousands of layoffs, high bankruptcy rates, and the soaring wealth of dozens of private equity billionaires has created bipartisan momentum for more oversight, even before the current interest rate crisis. And Donald Trump’s push to allow everyday Americans to invest in the sector through their retirement plans has raised new concerns. Congress’s June housing bill curbs private equity investments in single-family homes. November’s midterm elections, which are widely expected to deliver one or both houses of Congress to Democrats, could see a sea change for the industry in Washington, while several states are pursuing their own regulation. “For private equity, the question increasingly is not whether Congress will investigate private equity firms and their practices, but rather where the scrutiny will turn to next,” corporate law firm Holland and Knight warned this month. Multiple bills are circulating on Capitol Hill that would regulate how private equity is taxed, how it can invest in certain industries and how fund managers and investors can take profits. States’ bills would limit private equity in healthcare, scrutinize deals more closely and put caps on debt. The “Let Kids Play” Act seeks to ban private equity from youth community sports, now a “$40bn industry dominated by private equity, with the singular goal of extracting as much profit as possible from families”, it contends. The Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren, one of the industry’s most vocal critics in Washington, is leading a healthcare bill that seeks criminal penalties for “executives who loot health care entities like nursing homes and hospitals if that looting results in a patient’s death” and clawbacks of PE compensation. Whether US consumers see some relief could depend on what state they live in, or what other issues Congress takes up in the fall. “Even Democrats will be very hard pressed to do much,” if they have any clout in Congress, Batt predicts, because they have so much on their plate. “The best opportunities right now are for local and state level initiatives,” she said.

title: Volkswagen to cut further 50,000 jobs as it ends row with union over revival plan
summary: Under-pressure carmaker will shed 15% of workforce and halve its product line in sector’s biggest ever restructure
text: The car company Volkswagen has approved controversial plans to shed 100,000 jobs in a battle for survival as it faces fierce competition from Chinese rivals. After the latest round of talks this week, the company announced a further 50,000 job cuts and agreed a staggered end to current production at four German plants: Emden, Zwickau, Hanover and the Audi site in Neckarsulm between 2031 to 2034. There are no specific plans beyond that. The agreement came as a surprise after a meeting of shareholders, unions, and state representatives on the supervisory board in what was seen as a considerable test for the German carmaker’s chief executive, Oliver Blume. He had gone as far as to arrange an emergency meeting if the package was rejected in preparation for a potential showdown with unions. “This is a strong signal for the future,” said Blume, who now has a mandate for what the company previously called the “most strategically profound transformation programme” in the history of the VW group. He was booed last month by staff during a tour of the company’s headquarters in Wolfsburg, northern Germany, as part of a dialogue about the need to address the company’s financial challenges. IG Metall, the company’s biggest staff union and representative on the supervisory board, said concessions had been made on both sides to avert “a dangerous escalation of the conflict”. Chief among these was a stay of execution for four plants threatened with closure in exchange for an agreement on staff reductions. The deal includes a sweeping cost-cutting plan to cut a further 50,000 positions by 2030, bringing the total job losses in the pipeline to 100,000. “Concrete solutions must now be developed for all locations … we expect the board to now do its homework based on the compromise reached and deliver results promptly,” said Christiane Benner, the first chair of IG Metall, and Daniela Cavallo , the chair of the General and Group Works Councils of VW. Blume said the company would be investing “a three-figure billion sum” in the next few years “to make our iconic brands even more attractive, stronger and more competitive”. The supervisory board acknowledged that there was over capacity in Europe to produce 500,000 vehicles for which there was no market. Plans to turn a plant in Osnabrück into a defence factory were abandoned this year after objections from Qatari investors. The number of car models VW group produces, which includes the Bentley and Audi brands, will be slashed by half. “It is essential to systematically align workforce levels with economic realities,” VW said. The total of 100,000 cuts will be the largest restructuring ever carried out in the global automotive industry and amounts to about 15% of the carmaker’s employees. Volkswagen employs more than 650,000 people across all its brands, which also includes Skoda, Seat, Porsche, Cupra and Lamborghini. Analysts at Deutsche Bank said the approval of the restructuring plan was a “fundamental breakthrough” and proved wrong investors who believed the carmaker to be “unfixable”. “The unanimous approval is, in our view, a fundamental breakthrough and a much-better-than feared outcome,” the analysts said in a note to investors on Friday. “To be clear [the] agreement does not solve Volkswagen’s challenges overnight. Execution remains key. The market debate was never about whether Volkswagen had challenges. It was about whether those challenges could realistically be addressed within Volkswagen’s complex governance structure. [The] agreement does not end that debate, but it provides the strongest evidence yet that the answer may be yes.” VW has faced increasing pressure from Chinese competition in Europe, decreasing sales in China and hefty US tariffs. Even before that, it was struggling for years with falling profits and overproduction in Europe. Analysts at Citi called the deal a “brave and rational plan”, adding that it was a “realistic decision for all concerned”. “Given VW’s German plant competitiveness and lack of global revenue opportunities, VW simply had no other choice,” the analysts said. “Given VW’s supervisory board structure, this illustrates also the responsibility the workers council has taken for ensuring the long-term survivability of the VW core business in Europe.” Shares in VW rose 8% in early trading on Friday. The tough market in China has also hit other carmakers. BMW, for example, cut its profit guidance for this year because of the disruption caused by the Iran war and the company’s struggles in the Chinese market.
