title: British army told to halt non-essential training exercises to save money
summary: Collective training exercises for UK-based units to be suspended for most of this year amid budget pressures
text: The British army has been ordered to halt non-essential training exercises in an effort to save money. Troops preparing to be deployed or on deployments, those who are on standby or in a quick-reaction role will continue to train as normal. But collective training exercises for UK-based units are being suspended for most of this year amid budget pressures. Cancelled exercises include those involving tanks and Apache helicopters, according to reports in the Times and BBC. The army did not deny the cuts and said a training regime informed by lessons from the Ukraine conflict – such as on drone warfare and modernisation – was being prioritised. An army spokesperson said: “Our training continues and we are prioritising activity that contributes most directly to readiness, deployability and operational effectiveness. We are also investing £2bn to transform training for the British army over the next 15 years.” Andy Burnham is under pressure to increase defence spending to 3% of national income by 2030, rising to 3.5% by 2035. At prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, Burnham was urged by the chair of the Commons defence select committee, the Labour MP Tan Singh Dhesi, to “urgently commit to charting a pathway to reaching 3% of GDP spend on defence by 2030 which, as his chancellor rightly noted, is critical to keeping our country safe”. Dhesi told the prime minister that “vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough”, when it came to funding the UK’s armed forces Plans set out in the defence investment plan (Dip) include defence spending rising to 2.7% of GDP by 2027-28, but there are no firm details on how further increases will be achieved beyond that date. The Treasury has consistently said the government will set out plans for reaching 3% and 3.5% at the spending review, due to take place next year. The chancellor, John Healey, resigned from Keir Starmer’s government as defence secretary in June, in protest against what he argued was the then prime minister’s failure to adequately fund defence. But in his new post in No 11 Downing Street, Healey has made clear he will wait until next year’s spending review before presenting a plan to meet Labour’s pledge of devoting 3.5% of GDP to defence by 2035. Healey will present his first budget on 28 October and needs to find approximately £1.4bn a year over the next three years to pay for Starmer’s defence investment plan – which Healey in his last job derided as inadequate.

title: Moveable feast: myna birds on Sydney train looking for food not ‘joyride’ in viral video
summary: Mynas are ‘incredibly good learners’ and likely hopped on the inner-city train to scrounge, expert says
text: A viral video of common myna birds appearing to calmly ride a Sydney train in place of winged flight has shocked social media users. But not experts, who say it makes perfect sense that avian life has adapted to routinely navigate public transport. Bird life is ubiquitous in Australia’s urban landscapes. They appear in our shopping centres, our workplaces, our homes. To witness a feathered friend on a train isn’t exceptional. But ABC producer Jackie Dent was surprised to hear, when encountering a pair of myna birds on Sydney’s inner-city North Shore line last month, that they were apparently regular commuters. The duo were casually perched atop a seat together, well behaved and unmoving. Dent hopped on at Roseville station and observed the birds “very relaxed and at home”. “I got off at Chatswood to change trains and spoke to a lovely train guard to raise the alert that two birds were stuck on the train,” she wrote on social media alongside a video of the duo. To her surprise, the guard responded that they “always” caught the train, jumping on and off between Lindfield and Artarmon – supposedly to scrounge for food. Her post quickly went viral and the comment section blew up, with others sharing stories of birds they’d witnessed exhibiting the same behaviour. “I’d always watch them when I caught the train to Lindfield in my uni days! They know exactly where they are going,” one user wrote of myna birds. Sean Dooley, a senior advisor at BirdLife Australia, said it was “unusual” for birds to fly on to trains but not “unexpected”. “The common myna is a highly intelligent bird,” he said. “It does seem very likely that it is the same birds riding the same train … to take advantage of food resources along the line.” Common mynas are monogamous and territorial, so the duo are likely a couple. But Dooley said the habit could also spread to other mynas, as they share behaviour. “They’ve learned to exploit all sorts of food resources from us, and they’re particularly good at feeding on the waste that we have, whether it’s in bins or stuff that’s strewn around,” he said. “Clearly they’ve worked out that there’s a veritable smorgasbord along the Northern line.” Andrea Griffin, an associate professor in wildlife conservation at the University of Newcastle, said the video “doesn’t surprise me at all” as mynas are “incredibly accustomed” to living around humans, dating back to ancient Egypt. They’re also “incredibly good learners” – mynas can mimic speech if kept by humans, have good memories and know how to navigate home from large distances. “I would say it’s the same birds [getting on and off the train],” she said. “I suspect that a few birds have learned to do this. Mynas are quite loyal to their foraging areas so those birds would predictably be on that platform every day around the same time.” As to what prompted them to make the leap on to an approaching train, Griffin echoed Dooley’s suspicion that it was food-driven. “They’re not trying to go somewhere,” she said. “They’re not going out for a joyride. “All you need, basically, is to have a bird where the door opens and there’s some food at the entry and they hop on. And then they learn, ‘oh, this is quite a good foraging ground. I might do this’.”

title: Save the Children aid for 1.5 million in need wiped out by Iran war oil shock
summary: Charity says extra delivery costs equivalent to 47 health clinics in Afghanistan operating for six months
text: The charity Save the Children has said the oil price shock unleashed by Donald Trump’s war on Iran is forcing it to “spend more to reach fewer children”. The NGO analysed the increased costs of transport, fuel, food and medical supplies as a result of the Middle East conflict. It calculated that the extra burden of delivering aid had already been $13m (£10m), which could instead have allowed it to reach an additional 1.5 million children. Willem Zuidema, Save the Children’s global supply chain director, said: “The conflict in the Middle East is not only putting children at risk in the region but also globally, because every spike in fuel prices drives up the cost of every truck, every shipment, every box of supplies we deliver around the world. We are being forced to spend more to reach fewer children.” Developing countries have tended to be hit hardest by the oil shock, which the International Energy Agency has called the largest disruption to supplies in history. Many governments have introduced restrictions on energy use. Save the Children operates in about 110 countries, with a particular focus on safeguarding children’s rights. Its health and nutrition programmes reached more than 30 million children last year, including in hard-to-reach countries such as Afghanistan. The charity said the additional costs of delivering aid were equivalent to 47 health clinics in Afghanistan operating for six months, or five 30-bed hospitals in Somalia operating for a year. Before the conflict, the oil price was expected to be about $60 a barrel during 2026. After the US administration went to war with Iran, prompting Tehran to choke supplies though the strait of Hormuz, it surged above $100 a barrel. Prices declined after the US-Iran ceasefire in the summer but have jumped back above $90 in recent days as hostilities have resumed. Recent US rhetoric about increasing economic sanctions on Iran has raised fears the conflict could continue indefinitely. With the strait of Hormuz also an important conduit for fertiliser, the crisis has increased the prices of other commodities including food. Zuidema said Save the Children had been working to source alternative supplies and transport routes in an attempt to keep costs under control. “Despite the extreme challenges and rising costs, our teams are working around the clock to find alternative and cost-effective ways to deliver essential supplies and ensure we reach children where it is needed the most,” he said. The higher price of providing aid is coinciding with declining global aid budgets. The Trump administration has gutted USAID, the country’s development agency, and the UK is among the other countries reducing spending. The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, which gathers authoritative data, found that global aid spending plunged by 23% in real terms last year. Save the Children has previously criticised the UK government’s deep cuts to the overseas aid budget, with Moazzam Malik, its director, calling them a “tragedy”. Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, who oversees aid spending, has been urged by charities and some Labour backbenchers to set out a path to fulfilling Gordon Brown’s promise to spend 0.7% of national income on aid. Save the Children was set up in 1919 by two sisters, Eglantyne Jebb and Dorothy Buxton, who were horrified by the impact of a post-first world war export blockade on children in Berlin and Vienna.

title: UK has not done enough to prepare for shocks to food supplies, says watchdog
summary: National Audit Office urges government to act as climate crisis, disease and cyberattacks pose growing risks
text: The climate crisis, disease and cyber-attacks pose growing risks to the UK’s food supplies and the government needs to act to make the system more resilient, according to the public spending watchdog. The National Audit Office (NAO) is urging the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) to work more closely with households, communities and businesses to ensure the flow of crucial food into the country can withstand supply shocks that are becoming increasingly common and severe. Its latest report found Defra – the department responsible for security of food supply – had taken some steps to better prepare for future shocks, but said it had not done enough in recent years to get citizens and industry to plan for possible emergencies. Britain relies on overseas imports for more than a third of its food, most of it entering through four ports – Dover, Felixstowe, Southampton and London Gateway – making supplies particularly vulnerable to potential disruption. The NAO’s report comes after months of warnings about the resilience of the UK’s food supply chain from experts who have told households to build up a stockpile of long-life items they could rely on in an emergency. Britons are less prepared for potential future catastrophic events than citizens of several other European countries, according to government research. The supply chain has already come under pressure during the Covid-19 pandemic and after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, although businesses including the nation’s largest supermarkets managed to keep goods flowing, in most cases without the need for significant government assistance. However, Defra is less confident about the private sector’s ability to withstand future shocks, such as extreme weather events, without greater government intervention. Food industry businesses praised Defra’s engagement with them during the pandemic, but told the NAO it had communicated with them less frequently since. The report said the companies had limited input into the government’s plans for reacting to supply disruption, which could mean officials created proposals that would not work in practice. Gareth Davies, the NAO’s head, said: “Recent disruptions have shown the resilience of the UK’s food supply chain, but risks are increasing in likelihood and severity. “Defra should learn from approaches taken in other countries, and strengthen preparedness for emergencies by testing plans with local government and industry.” The government has designated food as one of 13 critical national infrastructure sectors it considers essential for the proper functioning of the country. However, food industry representatives have said that does not go far enough and have called on ministers to add the UK’s cold stores and food transport hubs to the critical list, which would ensure their power supplies would be maintained in the event of widespread outages. The NAO report comes just a few months after the trade body for cold storage and logistics, the Cold Chain Federation, accused the government of “complacency” over national food storage and urged ministers to make potential disruption to the UK’s food system an “immediate national priority”. The last national exercise testing Defra’s preparedness for catastrophic events that would severely disrupt the availability of food took place in 2023, but did not include most supply chain businesses, the NAO found. In addition, local resilience forums indicated they lacked clarity from Defra on what would be expected from them in the event of disruption.

title: What we know about the link between Nepal’s flash floods and our climate crisis
summary: In this week’s newsletter: The full scale of the disaster is still emerging, but as rescue efforts continue, scientists warn that a warming Himalayas could mean more deadly hazards
text: At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu. Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing. As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event. Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.” More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines. In focus What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the ⁠area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event. “It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”. As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating. While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising. “Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.” With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk. Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally. Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts. “Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska. To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous. As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.” • To read the complete version of this newsletter – subscribe to receive Down to Earth in your inbox every Thursday.

title: Revealed: how companies ‘secretly’ use billions of litres of public water in drought-hit England
summary: Exclusive: As millions of people face hosepipe bans, many companies are not required to report, let alone cut, use of public supply
text: Less than 1% of businesses in England use more water than the daily needs of 10 million people, as millions of households face hosepipe bans and three-quarters of the country is in drought. Businesses across England use 2.6bn litres a day from the public water supply, which includes potable and non-potable water provided by water companies. In total, businesses account for about 30% of public supply use, with two-thirds of their consumption in water-stressed areas, according to Mosl, the organisation that operates England’s business water market. Tracking industrial water use appears difficult. Regulators say they are frustrated by a lack of data and “commercial secrecy”, and the water sector says it is prevented from planning effectively for growth industries. The biggest users of the public water supply include oil refineries, chemical plants and paper mills, and some face no requirement to cut their consumption. Mosl’s map of business water supply points, ranked by volume used, showed the site of ExxonMobil’s Esso refinery at Fawley, Southampton, as the largest user of public water supply. However, the site includes a number of other operators that also use the water, including waste, gas, chemicals and energy companies. Mosl cited the refinery’s water use in written evidence to a House of Lords committee as an example of “the high volume of water wastage in industry that is not disincentivised by government or the regulatory framework”. Mosl did not name the refinery but described its location, which was also visible on its map of supply points. ExxonMobil disputed Mosl’s figures, saying its water use was commercially confidential. Mosl said it planned to ask the committee to redact parts of its evidence. During reporting, Mosl also removed a report and its supply point map from its website. The refinery said the “vast majority” of the water it used came from the Solent strait for cooling, while “industrial water” was used for processes that could not easily be reduced without shutting down operating units. Potable water accounted for less than 1% of total consumption, it said. Apart from refineries, other major users of the public water supply include paper mills and companies in the chemicals and soft drinks industries. But the overall picture of business water use is incomplete. One in 10 businesses are not metered, meaning their use is not measured or reported. Of those that are metered, only 11% have smart meters. Despite Mosl collecting data on water taken from the public supply, it is not free to share all of it, even with government departments, according to Mosl’s chief executive, Sarah McMath. McMath told the House of Lords committee that when the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) or the Environment Agency requested data, Mosl had to negotiate a bespoke agreement to share it. Mosl was working with the water regulator, Ofwat, to change this, she said, so that data would be shared when it would benefit “the environment or society”. A lack of data is already affecting national water planning. Gaps in local authority growth plans, combined with what the Environment Agency and Ofwat describe as “commercial secrecy, especially in the energy sector”, mean plans are often based on assumptions. The Environment Agency and Ofwat are calling for mandatory reporting of current and projected water use across all sectors to improve water security. A spokesperson for Mosl said: “Our data highlights both the opportunities and regulatory barriers to incentivising businesses to use less water. Rather than focusing on individual users – many of whom are actively seeking to reduce their water demand – we should focus on creating the right conditions to invest in water efficiency and increase water reuse where it is safe and practical.” Water resources planning assumes business water consumption will fall by 9% by 2038 and 15% by 2050. But the trade body Water UK argues the assumption is unrealistic as demand grows from new homes, as datacentres, hydrogen production and other developments. It wants water companies to be able to plan for projected demand rather than government reduction targets. Companies are not required to report all their water use, and for some, the more water they use, the cheaper each unit becomes. One operator told Mosl that a single UK datacentre uses 219m litres a year. It also has a tankered-water supply on standby if its mains connection fails, as well as its own borehole as a backup. Businesses can also take water directly from rivers, lakes, aquifers and the sea via abstraction . This is regulated separately by the Environment Agency. Some abstraction is invisible. Anyone can take up to 20,000 litres a day from a stream, borehole or spring without a licence or reporting it. The gap covers an estimated 850,000 people and organisations across England, mostly on farms and in rural areas. Richard Benwell, the chief executive of the NGO coalition Wildlife and Countryside Link, said: “It’s surely an injustice that petrochemical and fossil fuel companies most responsible for the climate crisis are also draining … water supplies and drawing more water from our parched environment. The water campaigner Feargal Sharkey said: “Yet again, regulatory ineptitude is allowed to triumph over the needs of people and the environment. While water supplies run dry, corporate bank accounts are flooded with the proceeds of corporate greed.” Defra said the government was taking “decisive action to secure water supplies”, including planning to build nine reservoirs and investing in infrastructure. A Water UK spokesperson said: “Supplies are increasingly at risk because England’s official forecasts for how much water the country needs rely on flawed assumptions. The water needed by fast-growing datacentres is explicitly excluded from the forecasts. “At the same time, lower water bills have been prioritised over building a resilient system, meaning in some places water companies only have 2% of water spare to deal with increased demand.” The Environment Agency said abstraction licences had strict conditions and were reviewed regularly, and that it was working towards the 9% reduction in business water use from the public supply. Meanwhile, England’s water companies are losing about 2.2bn litres of water a day through leaking pipes.

title: Friday briefing: ​What does the acquittal in the Caruana Galizia case mean for the safety of journalists?
summary: In today’s newsletter: Nearly nine years after Daphne Caruana Galizia was killed, the not‑guilty verdict for Yorgen Fenech ​has come to symbolise the struggle against the increased attempts to silence reporters
text: Good morning. Malta is reeling today from the shock acquittal of one of the country’s wealthiest and best-connected men for involvement in the murder of the anti-corruption journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. As the EU’s smallest member state once again faces intense international scrutiny over its response to the 2017 killing, opposition MPs are demanding the parliament be recalled for an immediate debate on a verdict that Caruana Galizia’s eldest son Matthew has denounced as “justice denied”. Caruana Galizia’s death brought angry crowds on to the streets; triggered a political crisis that resulted in the then prime minister, Joseph Muscat, being driven from office, and galvanised a cross-European reporting team to continue her investigations. One of those reporters is Juliette Garside, the Guardian’s European financial affairs editor. I spoke to her from Malta’s capital Valletta, where she’s digesting the aftermath of the country’s most consequential murder trial in recent times. But first, the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Nigel Farage is facing fresh criticism on the eve of the Reform UK party conference after some of his team were filmed appearing to plot to avoid electoral laws on foreign donations in an undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News. Nepal-Tibet | Two people have been pulled out alive from a hydropower tunnel in Nepal nine days after deadly flash floods left them trapped. UK news | Homeowners in the UK are braced for a jump in mortgage rates, driven by higher inflation and interest rate increase expectations amid turmoil in the global bond markets. US-Israel war on Iran | The US vice-president, JD Vance, said “sometimes things happen” when asked on Thursday whether an American strike was responsible for killing four people, including a child, at a wedding celebration in southern Iran this week. Climate crisis | British people have been urged to have enough food and water on hand to survive a few days without power or water, as the UN said the El Niño climate phenomenon was “supersizing before our eyes”, exacerbating extreme weather events worldwide. In depth: ‘This signals you can kill journalists with impunity’ Nearly nine years after Caruana Galizia’s death in a car bombing in October 2017, Yorgen Fenech, the head of one of Malta’s most successful business families, was found not guilty of both counts with which he had been charged: complicity in voluntary homicide, and association with the intention of committing a crime. Always a possibility, the complete acquittal – delivered by the jury at 7.30pm on Wednesday evening – was unexpected, after the longest-running murder trial in Maltese history which had gripped the small country over 55 days. As family members broke down in tears, Fenech exited the court house to chants of “mafia”. Following him into the balmy evening came Caruana Galizia’s sister, Corinne Vella, who told reporters: “This signals you can kill journalists with impunity.” Demonstrators later assembled outside the parliament building to demand action. Although five other men were convicted of carrying out the assassination and procuring the bomb used to kill the one of Malta’s most prominent journalists, Fenech’s acquittal leaves many unanswered questions. Fenech had been accused by prosecutors of paying €150,000 (£129,000) via a middleman to have her killed – so if he wasn’t the mastermind, who was? Caruana Galizia’s immediate family are bitterly disappointed, says Juliette. “She hadn’t investigated [the other men who were convicted]; they had no power or political influence. The only prosecution that really mattered to the family was this one.” The verdict was also a huge shock for the political establishment: “You got the sense they wanted a guilty verdict as a strong demonstration within the EU that Malta was able to hold people accountable”. For campaigners who regard the case as a landmark action in the fight to protect press freedom in Europe there is considerable dismay – Reporters Without Borders said it was “beyond outraged”. *** The Daphne Project Juliette talks to me as she’s packing up her hotel room and I can hear the sound of the suitcase zips. Whatever you might assume from Lois Lane, in my experience journalism is often about the mundane logistics. “This is a story of many twists and turns, but at base it is a story about press freedom, and one woman who pursued corruption at its highest levels,” she tells me. Juliette first became aware of Caruana Galizia’s work a year before she died, when she made contact with her eldest son Matthew, who was working with his mother on a tranche of leaked documents from the Panama Papers that suggested Labour figures set up offshore companies soon after entering government. She remembers the day Caruana Galizia was killed: a contact sent her a photograph of the mangled car wreckage, and Juliette ran over to the foreign desk to press the editor to give the assassination the coverage it deserved. “She was killed because she was an incredibly effective investigate journalist. She set her sights on the most powerful people in the country. She was interested in where crime and politics collided.” The Guardian later contacted Caruana Galizia’s family to follow up on what could be done – and the Daphne Project was born, a loose collective of journalists, from Reuters, the Times of Malta, Le Monde and Süddeutsche Zeitung, who agreed to work together to complete her investigations. Juliette met the family again in a safe house near London in November 2017, where they were having a break from the spotlight in Malta and also taking security advice. Before her murder, Caruana Galizia endured a campaign of intimidation including the killing of her pet dogs and fires set in her home – her remaining family were now targets. These attacks had intensified as she began to dig into a leak about a flagship power station project. “Matthew told us about the leak she’d been investigating, detailing the bizarre way the power station deal was structured. That’s what we focused on.” But the Daphne Project also asked questions about the police investigation into her death. “The administration that she attacked hadn’t bargained on much interest in her death outside Malta,” Juliette says. “But when the family took their campaign to the European parliament and the Daphne Project gave it an international news platform, that really forced the Maltese police to go higher than the hit men.” *** What next for Malta? While acknowledging that it is important to respect the verdict of the jury, Juliette says there’s a sense among the Maltese media that this is a chilling verdict: what happens the next time a journalist writes about corruption? The editorial headline in the Times of Malta yesterday was bleak: “We’ve turned the clock back to 2017”. It is likely that the prosecution will appeal, and details of the close relationship between big business, police chiefs and regulators exposed in the trial may feed into a number of other pending corruption cases both of which are unlikely to have got this far without the diligent reporting that followed her assassination. “What would really be unusual is if people got convicted,” Juliette adds. But, just like that Times of Malta headline, Juliette worries that the country has returned to business as usual. Malta has a small economy that runs on patronage; the political class is tribal and split between two parties, Labour and Nationalist. “There’s not much means to get neutral, independent information.” “After her death, it initially felt like the beginning of a stronger civil society, but the momentum behind change has slowed”. *** What next for Europe? A public inquiry into Caruana Galizia’s killing concluded in 2021 with a recommendation to introduce Europe-wide laws to protect journalists from strategic lawsuits against public participation, known as Slapps, which are increasingly used to silence whistleblowers, victims of sexual assault and those who report on them. Caruana Galizia was facing 47 lawsuits when she died. Although this was voted through by the European parliament, no member state has yet implemented it. Yesterday, European parliament president Roberta Metsola vowed to continue fighting for justice for Caruana Galizia in a Facebook post addressed directly to the assassinated journalist. “When they assassinated you, in broad daylight, outside your family home, we promised that we would not let them sweep it under the carpet … That promise holds today,” she wrote. “Hopefully this will be an impetus for EU member states to put this law on to their statute books”, says Juliette. There’s more to be done. An unsuccessful car bomb attack on an Italian investigative reporter, Sigfrido Rannucci, which appeared to be timed to coincide with the eighth anniversary of Caruana Galizia assassination, has intensified European Commission concerns about the silencing of government critics. Meanwhile, at a UK level, two private members’ bills designed to crack down on these potentially financially devastating lawsuits were introduced just before summer recess and are expected to attract cross-party support. The Guardian is now part of the UK Anti-Slapp Coalition, a group backed by charities including Amnesty International and Index on Censorship, and Juliette has written at length about how the courts have been weaponised in particular against victims of sexual violence. “The fact that the public know what a Slapp is at all – and that there’s now a coordinated push to protect whistleblowers, journalists and victims of sexual assault from being sued by those who wish to silence them – is all because of what happened to Daphne. That is her legacy.” What else we’ve been enjoying The life of Gloria Steinem, the groundbreaking feminist campaigner who died on Wednesday, is poignantly remembered by Moira Donegan, who asks what the movement will be without her. Jacqui Housden, newsletters team Michael Sheen spoke about his forthcoming play on Welsh rebel leader Owain Glyndŵr and how this important part of his country’s history was never taught to him at school. Katy Vans, newsletters team Laura Snapes’s takedown of the cosy treatment of Josh Homme, another male rock star who has attacked women, was much needed. Poppy For those like me who have watched the satirical film Mountainhead, this article that delves into why Peter Thiel has moved to Argentina is fascinatingly worrying. Katy I liked our tribute to Chicken Shop date, which is coming to an end after 12 years. Poppy Sport Tennis | Naomi Osaka recovered from a mid-match slump to beat Katerina Siniakova 6-2, 5-7, 6-1 and reach the third round of the US Open. Women’s Cricket | England sealed victory in their one-day international series against Ireland with a straightforward six-wicket win at Derby on Thursday, after seamer Issy Wong took a career-best five for 33. Boxing | Irish fight legend Katie Taylor can cap a special career by retiring as the undisputed super-lightweight champion with victory against Flora Pili on Saturday. Something for the weekend Our critics’ roundup of the best things to watch, read, play and listen to right now TV La Mesías (Mubi) | ★★★★★ A Spanish show centred on an estranged brother and sister, who discover their siblings have become a viral pop band, La Mesías is nothing if not singular in its vision. As well as being incredibly long (some episodes clock in at close to an hour and 20 minutes), it is – and I mean this lovingly – truly bizarre. There are about 10 plotlines too many, and some of the episodes drag, but as a work of art, this series is a triumph – a nightmare-inducing thriller with ambition. Hannah J Davies Film Late Fame | ★★★★☆ There’s a marvellous tenderness and generosity to this elegant tale of autumnal regret; an intimate movie acted with effortless grace by Willem Dafoe. In fact, this is yet another of his almost numberless performances of intelligence and self-possession. Screenwriter Samy Burch has adapted a novella by Arthur Schnitzler, which has been directed by critic turned film-maker Kent Jones. Their movie finds a new variation on the theme of life’s lost opportunities for love, lust and success, and how, as mortality’s shadow closes in, one might be tempted to risk everything for a last chance at worldly triumph. Peter Bradshaw Music Adéla: Prima | ★★★☆☆ There’s something striking about a pop star, voice larded with Auto-Tune, opening a song with the line “I can’t really sing”. That said, it’s very much on brand for Adéla Jergová, who has chosen to differentiate herself by spiking her songs about hedonism and messy sexual encounters with a kind of meta commentary on what it is to be a female pop star. Prima definitely feels like a debut album and there are moments where it sinks into boilerplate pop, but failing to be a perfectly turned finished product on arrival is hardly a crime: rather, it suggests an artist who has room to grow and develop. On the basis of what’s here – which is frequently sharp, funny and daring – watching Adéla do just that should be fascinating. Alexis Petridis Books The Bridge by Colm Tóibín Twenty years ago, Tóibín published A Long Winter, a steadily desolating novella set in the high villages of the Catalan Pyrenees in which a woman walks out of her house and her life, starts along the mountain road and disappears in the snow. Now, in The Bridge, a single year has passed and we follow Miquel, the woman’s son, as he ekes out an existence with his hurtful, unyielding father. It’s a memorable short work in which the author’s unsentimental prose is flawlessly matched to the austere worlds of people enduring, in their different ways, lives stripped back to the bone. Alexandra Harris The front pages “Britons warned to get ready for biggest El Niño in a millennium”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while Metro says “Hot as El”. The Times writes “Army halts training exercises to save money”, the Telegraph has “Argentina threat to Falklands oil fields”, and the Express says “Kemi: We must act now before it’s too late”. The i Paper leads with “Putin growing more reckless as his inner circle shrinks, warn UK security insiders”. The FT’s top headline is “Europe faces winter with lowest ever gas reserves as Gulf-led shortages bite”, the Mail has “Met chief stunned by release of serial criminals”, and the Mirror says “Reform: Back Britain … with our Chinese tat”. Today in Focus: The Latest ‘Godzilla-level’ El Niño could cause hottest year on record The UN has warned that the El Niño climate phenomenon is ‘supersizing before our eyes’. The event is forecast to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will almost certainly shatter temperature records. After a summer of record-breaking heatwaves and extreme weather due to global heating, El Niño means 2027 is almost certain to be the hottest year ever recorded. Lucy Hough speaks to environment correspondent Damien Gayle – watch on YouTube. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Photographer Temi Adegbayibi started out shooting his church’s worship band and small gigs as a hobby. Now, at 26, his portfolio includes Jorja Smith, Basement Jaxx and Ezra Collective – and his work has been exhibited at the Royal Albert Hall, where he has also become an in-house photographer. His intimate, energetic images celebrate movement and Black joy, while documenting a generation of British musicians. “Maybe someday someone can look at an image and think: ‘That’s what jazz gigs were like back then,’” he says. “That’s the hope.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

title: Air pollution from ships may be more harmful than road traffic emissions, port study finds
summary: Scientists say ultrafine particles in cruise ship emissions associated with reduced ability to resist common viruses
text: More than 2.5 million cruise passengers travelled through Southampton in 2025. It is also the UK’s leading vehicle and deep-sea trading port. You can see the ships and port machinery from miles around. All of this is downwind of a city of 260,000 people. A team of 32 researchers began investigating air pollution from the docks in 2018. Their research has revealed that the types of air pollution that come from ships may be more harmful than those from road traffic. With help from the port staff, the team spent more than two years sampling air pollution in the port. Each source had different characteristics. Downwind of the cruise terminal, the air pollution had a clear signature with tiny ultrafine particles, smaller than the wavelength of light, containing metals including vanadium, nickel, cobalt and molybdenum. The researchers also looked at how the ultrafine particles collected near the cruise terminal affected lung cells, including tests on cells donated by people in Southampton. Prof Matthew Loxham, the project leader from the University of Southampton, said: “The ultrafine particles in these ships’ emissions were more able to drive cells to release a range of chemical communication signals associated with inflammation and reduce their ability to prevent the replication of viruses.” Further tests suggested that this cell inflammation and reduced ability to resist common viruses was due to vanadium particles. There was a clear relationship between ultrafine vanadium downwind of the cruise terminal and the number of cruise ships in port. Loxham said: “When crude oil is refined, naturally occurring vanadium tends to be concentrated into the heavy fuel as petrol and kerosene are removed. When heavy fuel oil, which is used by many ships, is combusted, a portion of the metal vaporises and ends up in the exhaust.” Dr Nat Easton, one of the researchers, said: “I was surprised how much more vanadium and nickel was in the cruise ship-associated particles than the container ship-associated particles. At times, all five cruise terminals have a ship in port, and a cruise ship can house over 5,000 passengers. Each of these can have their engines running for heating, hot water, lighting and cooking in a way that cargo ships do not need to.” A spokesperson for Associated British Ports (APB) said: “The port of Southampton is a leader in introducing measures to improve air quality, being the first port in the UK to introduce large-scale shore power connections so vessels can shut off their engines at berth.” About 15% of cruise ships now use shore power. APB voiced concerns about aspects of the methodologies in the study and the strength of inference in some of the findings that have been presented to the media. There are no measurements to assess the spread of ultrafine particles or vanadium from the port. Easton said: “These harmful effects were linked to both chemical composition and ultrafine particles. Neither [are] routinely monitored.” A new EU directive will require ultrafine particle measurements, including around pollution hotspots such as ports and airports, but this does not apply in the UK.

title: Europe calls out Russia’s ‘hybrid war’ in public. But how can it make Putin pay?
summary: Governments are now quicker to point the finger at Moscow, but critics say their inaction invites more sabotage
text: Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign across Europe appears to be gathering pace again, confronting governments with a problem they have struggled to solve since the start of the war in Ukraine: how to impose a meaningful cost on Moscow for attacks that remain deliberately below the threshold of conventional war. Over the past month alone, an explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport, Poland has faced suspected acts of sabotage, and a string of unexplained explosions and fires have hit defence facilities supplying Ukraine across Europe. The attacks, aimed at sowing chaos and undermining support for Ukraine, vary widely in their ambition and sophistication, but share a common feature: they are often difficult to trace conclusively back to Moscow. That ambiguity is built into the way the operations are organised. Russian intelligence services have shifted away from relying primarily on professional operatives dispatched across Europe. Instead, suspected saboteurs are increasingly recruited remotely, including through Telegram channels, and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out individual tasks – allowing the Russian intelligence officers directing them to remain safely at home. The pattern was evident in Denmark this week, where authorities warned that Moscow was recruiting Danish citizens to carry out sabotage against defence companies with ties to Ukraine. But the growing scale of the attacks, and the speed with which European governments are now prepared to point the finger at Moscow, suggest the mood may be changing. When an incendiary parcel burst into flames at DHL’s Leipzig hub in July 2024, it took about nine months before German investigators reported a concrete link to the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency. This time, Berlin moved far faster. Within days of the second incident at Leipzig airport, German officials publicly blamed Moscow – a sign both of growing confidence in identifying Russian operations and diminishing patience with what officials see as an increasingly brazen campaign of sabotage. Yet while Berlin has become quicker to point the finger at Moscow, its punishment for now has followed a more cautious path. Germany’s response to the failed Leipzig drone attack appeared calibrated to keep tensions in check, underscoring the harder question of what Europe can actually do beyond sanctions and diplomatic expulsions without risking a direct military confrontation. Berlin announced the closure of a Russian cultural centre and a Russian consulate, prompting Moscow to shut down the already gutted Goethe-Institut – a measured retaliation rather than a real escalation. Europe’s room for retaliation is also constrained by the powers given to its intelligence agencies. Unlike the CIA, many European services are primarily tasked with collecting intelligence and have far less latitude to conduct covert operations abroad. That leaves governments with relatively few tools between diplomatic and economic punishment on one end of the spectrum and overt military action on the other. To counter the shortcoming, several EU states, including the Netherlands, have recently put forward bills that would greatly expand the surveillance powers of the country’s intelligence agencies One area where Europe can point to more tangible action is its growing willingness to detain vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet. On Wednesday, Norwegian authorities seized a Russian vessel in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at Ukraine’s request. But critics argue that such measures are still not enough to deter Moscow. “Every time we do nothing, we invite Putin to continue,” said one EU lawmaker, speaking on condition of anonymity. That argument has been made most forcefully by Poland and the Baltic states, which have consistently pushed their western European allies to take a harder line against Moscow. “Hybrid war is not just a nuisance on the internet,” the Polish foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said on Thursday. “Hybrid war means assassination squads, it means arsonists, it means blowing up moving trains, like in Poland, it means breaches of airspace with drones and cruise missiles.” “We need to convince Putin that such actions are not for free,” he added. At the same time, Sikorski also appeared to acknowledge, somewhat jokingly, the limits of Europe’s existing toolkit. Recalling Poland’s response to previous suspected Russian operations, he said: “Every time Russia committed arson or tried to blow up a moving train … I closed one Russian consulate, but I ran out of consulates to close.” Jakub Krupa contributed reporting

title: Country diary: It’s 10am at the Melplash Show and the cider contest is well under way | Sara Hudston
summary: Bridport, Dorset: Away from the sheep, pigs and Martin Clunes’s horse, I find a bounty of local ciders – and concern about this year’s apple harvest
text: It’s Melplash Show day and all of Bridport is here. Crowds jostle for a look at the pigs, cattle and sheep. The actor Martin Clunes, who lives locally, leads one of his heavy horses into the ring, a big strawberry roan gelding with a mane plaited with ribbons. Everyone ignores the celebrity: they are far more interested in the finer points of his horse. In the handicrafts and local produce tent, lines of glass cider bottles glow palest amber and urinous gold. The two judges, the cider-maker Ross Mangles of North Down Orchard, and the cider writer James Crowden, began tasting at 8.30am. Fortified with a block of blue-veined cheddar cheese, a packet of cream crackers and a glass of water, they have sampled all 36 entries by 10am. When I join them for the results, the winning bottles are at least a quarter empty, and Ross and James are feeling upbeat. The competition is for traditional non-fizzy cider and divided into three classes – dry, medium and sweet – with a trophy for the best in show. Ross explains that they look for clearness, balance and roundness of flavour, and offers me a taste of the overall champion. It is a sweet cider and beguilingly smooth, but I prefer the winner of the medium category, which has more tannin. Made just outside Bridport by a non-commercial producer, it is a classic, traditional farmhouse style, fermented from a mix of old apple varieties whose names are a roll call of autumn: Dabinett, Breakwell’s seedling, sweet Alford and crimson king. Next year’s entries may not be so numerous because the summer drought and prolonged high temperatures mean the apple crop is around 80% down. “We were expecting a bad year as last year was very good – apple yields alternate between good and poor years – but this has been much worse than we thought,” says Ross. He still has juice supplies left from last year’s pressings, but other producers are struggling. Small-scale cider-making has undergone a revival in Dorset, in recent times with villagers forming clubs dedicated to the art of the apple. New orchards have been planted and ancient varieties rediscovered. Drinkers are hoping for a bumper crop next year to fill the depleted barrels. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: ‘This could just be the beginning’: minorities fear first far-right win in German state election
summary: As polls point to victory in Saxony-Anhalt for AfD party promising deportations, people face agonising choice: stay or go
text: As the Bible study session wrapped up, leaving worshippers to mingle over cake and coffee, Fatemeh, 44, fought back tears as the conversation turned to Sunday’s state election in Saxony-Anhalt. “I worry about it every day,” she said. “I can’t stop thinking about my son and what might happen to us.” Three years ago she fled Iran with her son after he was stopped by police during a protest over the death in police custody of Mahsa Amini. They ended up in Saxony-Anhalt, where, as they await a final decision on their asylum claim, she has watched him blossom into a gifted athlete and develop a knack for repairing vehicles. Fatemeh worries about what might happen after the elections. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian Looming over their lives, however, are the politics of Saxony-Anhalt. Polls have suggested that the election on Sunday could yield Germany’s first-ever state government led by the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), shattering a postwar taboo and leaving Fatemeh and her son’s fate in the hands of a party that has promised to launch deportations “from day one”. That possibility has left her racked with worry. “They might send us back to Iran,” she said. “As a converted Christian, that could mean the death penalty for me.” It was a glimpse of the stakes at play in the election. Polls suggest the state’s AfD, whose antisemitic, anti-Islam and anti-migrant discourse has contributed to authorities classifying the party as “firmly rightwing extremist”, is poised to win the most votes. The square in the centre of Magdeburg where the Christmas market attack took place on 20 December 2024. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian A strong showing in the election could allow it to govern Saxony-Anhalt, turning the eastern state into Germany’s first testing ground for the AfD’s long-running hostility towards migrants, including refugees, Muslims and the LGBTQ+ community. “We’ve never seen emotions run so high over an election,” said Undra Dreßler of Lamsa, an umbrella group for migrant organisations in the state. Calls were coming in daily, she said, as people wrestled with whether the time had come to pack up their lives and start over again somewhere else. “People are really worried and scared,” said Dreßler. “For those with migrant backgrounds, it feels like this vote is about their right to exist and their security.” The pages-long manifesto for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt promises a “complete, 180-degree” overhaul of the approach to migration, from educating refugee children separately to redirecting funds earmarked for integration to a unit focused on remigration, and calling on federal officials to stop recognising Ukrainians as war refugees. In June, Dreßler’s organisation appealed to Germany’s 15 other states, calling on them to prepare to take in refugees from Saxony-Anhalt after the election. “It’s a precautionary measure,” she said. “The social climate here is already extremely heated. We don’t know what will happen after the elections.” Left: A billboard in Magdeburg shows the AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund and the slogan ‘everything is possible’. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian. Right: Siegmund addresses delegates at the federal congress of Generation Germany, the party’s youth organisation. Photograph: Jens Schluter/AFP/Getty Tensions have run high in Saxony-Anhalt since late 2024 when a Saudi man drove his car into a crowded Christmas market in Magdeburg, killing six people and injuring hundreds more. Authorities described the attacker as an anti-Islam activist who was sympathetic to the far right. Even so, rightwing voices seized on the moment to scapegoat migrants and minorities for the ills of a state long ravaged by deindustrialisation and depopulation. In the aftermath of the attack, reports of racist attacks soared as migrants and people of colour told of being spat on, threatened and, in some cases, physically attacked. “By mid-2025, we had received as many reports of racist insults and attacks as we did in all of 2024,” said Dreßler. “As forces on the right become stronger, everyday racism and discrimination have become part of everyday life.” On the streets of Magdeburg, many shared their own brushes with overt racism. “When you’re on the street, some people harass you verbally,” said Kirti, 27, a student from India. “They show you the middle finger.” An AfD billboard reads ‘All for our children’. The party has promised to educate refugee children in the state separately. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian Kirti moved to Magdeburg just over a year ago to study for a master’s degree, becoming part of a cohort of foreign students for whom reports of racism were all too familiar. “I heard of one incident where a student was travelling on a train and people were throwing stones at the door, but the door was closed,” he said. “So people are more concerned about going out. They go out with fear, rather than feeling safe.” A recent survey suggested that as many as 80% of people with a migration background in Saxony-Anhalt are considering leaving, said Ketevan Asatiani-Hermann, who leads the board of the Advisory Council for Integration and Migration in Magdeburg. As questions swirl over what the AfD could realistically do if the party garners enough votes to govern alone, a chorus of voices has begun to warn of the fallout. Saxony-Anhalt is a rapidly depopulating state where the average age of 48.2 ranks as the highest in Germany. “So the fear is that we lose people because of what happens on 6 September,” said Asatiani-Hermann. “And Saxony-Anhalt is dependent on migrants, so it’s absolutely necessary that they stay here.” Ketevan Asatiani-Hermann says Saxony-Anhalt is dependent on migrants and it is ‘absolutely necessary’ they stay. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian Foreign nationals account for about 9% of the state’s population – compared with approximately 15% nationwide – with many playing a critical role in sectors such as hospitality and care for elderly people. In May, the state medical association said that more than one in four doctors working in Saxony-Anhalt’s hospitals, or 27.1%, do not hold a German passport. “In many regions of the state – especially in rural areas – comprehensive healthcare coverage would no longer be possible without foreign colleagues,” it said, citing the possibility of longer waiting times or facility closures if some of these doctors were to leave. “Migrants make up a huge part of healthcare. If you were to take them out, the whole system would collapse,” said Hamid, 41, a paramedic originally from Iran. “So it’s like if you have a bus and you take off all the tyres. You cannot move.” Hamid, a paramedic originally from Iran, says without migrants in Magdeburg, the ‘whole system would collapse’. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian At Magdeburg’s synagogue – whose light-filled foyer includes a mural showing one of the few remaining photographs of the original synagogue that was destroyed in a 1938 pogrom – people listed their concerns about an AfD majority, from whether it would affect the funding they receive, to what the party’s plans for a “remigration offensive” would mean for the Ukrainian refugees who had joined their congregation after Russia’s full-scale invasion. The far-right party has also promised to make changes to the school curriculum, in what one party member described as “more Bismarck, less Hitler”. The underlying assumption was that the focus on the rise of National Socialism and the Holocaust – as opposed to the unification of Germany by Otto von Bismarck – had shifted the guilt over what had happened to the current generation, said Igor Mendel Itkin, the synagogue’s rabbi. “They think: ‘If we get rid of this, we will feel free.’ But I think it will be the other way around,” he said. “You cannot get rid of this ghost; you can pacify it, but you cannot get rid of it. If people don’t learn about it, then something like this could happen again, maybe not with the Jewish people, but maybe with the Muslims.” He pointed to Saxony-Anhalt’s AfD manifesto, which makes no mention of the Jewish community but includes promises to “exhaust all legal means to restrict the influence” of Islam, even as it notes that Muslims account for just 2-3% of the 2 million people in the state. Rabbi Igor Mendel Itkin with Maria Schubert at the Magdeburg synagogue say an AfD win is ‘unimaginable’. Photograph: Christian Jungeblodt/The Guardian An AfD win would put Jewish people in a complicated position, said Maria Schubert from the Synagogue Community of Magdeburg. “If they win, we don’t know how we will act with them. For me, it’s unimaginable,” she said. She worried that it could also be a dilemma faced by others if Sunday’s election turned out to be a bellwether of shifting political forces rather than an outlier. “I see it as a threat, in that this could just be the beginning. In other German states, many are looking at Saxony-Anhalt to kick things off,” she said. “I mean, at the beginning, nobody took Hitler seriously.” The AfD was approached for comment. With contribution from Niclas Boenki

title: Pedicures and a pair of socks: sailors from USS Abraham Lincoln go wild in party resort of Pattaya
summary: Despite the fame of its red light district, many sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln opt for the ‘simple stuff’ like socks, decent food and some pampering
text: On Thursday morning in Pattaya’s Colour Nail salon there isn’t a spare burgundy lounger to be seen as sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln – male and female alike – settle in for pedicures to take the edge off a gruelling deployment. More sailors are waiting outside for their turn and Arisa Suekkanya, a worker at the salon, says she is “excited” the US military chose Thailand as their first port of call after a record uninterrupted 286 days at sea. The aircraft carrier has been plagued by reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health onboard, including attempted suicides, making headlines around the world and provoking criticism of Donald Trump’s war against Iran. The ship’s captain admitted to a lack of fresh fruit and vegetables but said reports about the living conditions were largely exaggerated. Some of the thousands of crew gave their view while on leave. Adam*, who is on his first deployment, says the living situation is like “being stuck in your bedroom with all your family” but that building relationships with fellow crew and “finding your people” made the difficulties worthwhile. The Guardian has chosen to change the names of the sailors spoken to because they were told not to speak to the media about conditions onboard. For him, the food was the hardest thing to swallow. “I almost choked on this many times,” he says, as he describes eating “uncooked beef” and sliced up, uncooked potato. According to Adam, the decline in living standards was down to the battle conditions imposed during Operation Epic Fury rather than the unprecedented length of deployment. Another crew member, Marco* agrees, saying there was a necessary deterioration during this “battle rhythm” period when it would have put them at risk to restock. Trent* admits the hardest part of the deployment was “pushing through, keeping the mentality” despite the hardships. Dane* says “a load came off my shoulders” when he stepped on dry land again after his first deployment. He acknowledged it was “tough but we had a job to do.” He said that on the previous evening, “I ate to my heart’s content. Me and Thai food might be best friends after this.” Another serviceman, who did not give his name, hinted at the toll the long deployment had taken: “Some people adapt to it, but not everyone.” Boom time for the big brands Pattaya is a city well known for its red light district and colourful nightlife, but for many, the desires were more prosaic. Tim* was in the Vans store in the mall on Thursday. “It’s the simple stuff like new socks” he was after, holding the pair he was about to purchase. Another sailor, David*, has bought his wife a Hello Kitty soft toy from H&M. He says it was his fourth deployment, and agrees this would have been quite long for sailors on their first. At least for Adam, the past few months have made him all the more grateful for his first night ashore, as he orders two burgers at Burger King and makes plans to order a tailored suit and explore Thailand’s east coast. Many local businesses have put up signs welcoming the American visitors, offering incentives like tailors Tito Fashion advertising “specially for US Navy ready in 24 hours”, while Thai restaurant Imm-Oon Na offered 10% off for anyone presenting a valid military ID. But the draw of the familiar American brands also proved irresistible. In the mall, the likes of Nike, Victoria’s Secret and Starbucks all reported a spike in sales. The town is hoping the Lincoln’s crew will provide an economic boost. The war in the Middle East has created a downturn in tourism in Thailand, and the rainy season has slowed things, too. Pattaya’s mayor, Poramet Ngampichet, says if each American spends US$100-$150 per day the visit could generate about $100m Thai baht ($3m). However, not all businesses can take full advantage of the 5,000 sailors, who have not been able to spend money for nearly 10 months. Emma Moontee, who runs a gift stall at a night market, says she has only sold one fridge magnet souvenir to a sailor, but hoped there would be more. The crew has also been advised not to go to the beer bars along Soi 6 after sunset, one of the most infamous areas of the town’s red light district where bar girls line the street – and can occasionally be seen physically pulling in male tourists. However, the main strip – known as Walking Street – is not off limits. Dense with clubs and go go bars featuring pole-dancing girls, the night’s revels are largely kept private from the outside’s street view and passersby. Wittaya Phoobantad, who works at Poker Bar on the beachfront, about a 10-minute walk from Soi 6, says: “You can see [sailors] walking around but because Soi 6 is banned most of them don’t come in, just go direct to Walking Street.” On Walking Street a massive neon sign has been built at its entrance saying: “Pattaya City is pleased to welcome USS Abraham Lincoln carrier and its personnel.” Venues like the Sapphire Club offer 10% off to US service members. Pattana Prasomsup, who works at M’s Mojito, says the 10 crew who visited the bar on Wednesday night provided a “good boost” but noted they appeared quite cautious about interacting with bar girls. Pattaya is familiar with the US military, who experts agree was the dominant influence in creating the sex tourism industry – and the modern city that developed around it. The once quiet fishing village was drastically transformed in the space of 15 years after becoming an official R&R destination for US soldiers during the Vietnam war, causing a boom in hotels, massage parlours and bars, where heavy drinking and paying for female companionship became the norm. Most of the workers in the sex tourism industry are not local but have themselves migrated to Pattaya, commonly from Isan – Thailand’s poorest and least economically developed region in the north-east – as well as neighbouring Laos and Myanmar or further afield. Back in the mall, Puangbubpha Duangsri, who works at American Eagle, says in the off season they’d usually make 70,000 Thai baht in a day, but on Wednesday they made over 200,000 baht after the sailors arrived. By lunchtime on Thursday, they had already made over 100,000 baht. “Can they stay an extra week?” she says. * Names have been changed

title: EV sales outpace petrol cars for first time as Australians dodge soaring fuel costs
summary: New record for Australia as more than 27,000 EVs sold in August, driven by the rising cost of fuel and new government policy
text: Electric vehicle sales in Australia exceeded petrol cars for the first time last month as a transformation driven by high fuel prices and government policy encouraging clean car uptake accelerated. More than 27,000 EVs were sold in August, a new record for a single month and representing 24.9% of new cars sold. The climate-friendly technology surpassed both petrol vehicles (nearly 26,000 sold) and diesel cars (23,600). If plug-in hybrids were added, the proportion of new cars with a plug jumped to 36% of sales. The rise in EVs has been helped by two factors – the war in Iran pushing up oil prices and making running a petrol car significantly more expensive, and the introduction last year of a federal vehicle efficiency standard that required auto companies to cut average tailpipe emissions year-on-year. The latter has triggered a big increase in the number of models of low and zero-emission cars available at a range of prices. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Australia had previously trailed most OECD countries in EV take-up, and the technology has been the focus of political scare campaigns, including former prime minister Scott Morrison claiming in 2019 that introducing a vehicle efficiency standard would “end the weekend”. They made up less than 2% of sales just four years ago and about 8% last year. The climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, said EV sales surpassing petrol cars was a “landmark moment”. “Australians have seen through the scare campaigns and are voting with their wallets for cars that are cheaper to run, cleaner and reduce their exposure to international petrol price shocks,” he said. Toyota was Australians’ most popular car brand in August, followed by Chinese EV manufacturer BYD and trillionaire Elon Musk’s Tesla. Five of the top 10 brands were Chinese: BYD, GWM, MG, Geely and Cheery. The Tesla Model Y was the most popular new model, with more than 6,400 sold. The Electric Vehicle Council said there had been a “structural shift in the way Australians choose their cars”, with both economic and environmental benefits driving the change. The council’s chief executive, Julie Delvecchio, said there were now nearly 200 EV models on offer. “The priority now is to make the benefits of going electric accessible to more Australians, including people in regional communities, apartment residents and the 30% of Australians who rent their home,” she said. The Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries CEO, Tony Weber, said consumer choice and competition were rapidly reshaping the new-vehicle market and infrastructure settings needed to keep pace. “Accessible and dependable charging will remain critical to consumer confidence, particularly on highways, in rural and regional areas and for motorists without access to charging at home,” he said.

title: ‘Everyone seems to have forgotten’: In Tibet, flood-hit families search for the missing and grapple with China’s silence
summary: Relatives try to piece together information found online and from Nepal as Tibet advocates groups say information is suppressed in China
text: Fan Hong last heard from her husband on the morning of the Nepal-Tibet disaster. More than a week later, the 31-year-old is desperately searching for information about Lin Bo, who was working on a Chinese highway project in Nepal. Struggling to get information from authorities, Fan turned to social media for help. “My husband works on a project in Nepal, about 5 kilometres from the Gyirong border crossing. I want to know what the situation is, but I haven’t been able to reach him,” the 31-year-old from China’s Sichuan province wrote on Rednote. Her post has gained more than 18,000 likes and nearly 4,600 comments. She is one of many in China with missing loved ones trying to piece together information they are finding online, as Tibetan advocate groups say information is being suppressed on that side of the border. Lin began working on repairing the Syaphrubesi-Rasuwagadhi Highway – which links Nepal to Tibet, China, through the Gyirong border crossing – in 2024. He had been living on site and working on a 16km stretch of the road. Fan says that rescue missions into the construction site have stalled. She says relatives of survivors are asking the Chinese authorities for permission to send up their own drones or helicopters to look for the missing. “I feel more disheartened with each passing day. Feel colder and colder inside,” she told the Guardian. “I don’t even have any tears left.” It is just over a week since the collapse of a glacier triggered devastating floods along the Nepal-Tibet border, destroying entire villages and killing more than 1,200 people. On Wednesday, 4,216 remained missing, according to Nepal officials. Chinese authorities say 541 remain unaccounted for on the Tibetan side, including 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries. The relatively low official death toll from the Chinese authorities has also raised some concern among Tibetan advocacy groups, given the scale of the destruction seen in video footage. “All we can do is imagine – and that should terrify us,” said Tenzin Choekyi from Tibet Watch. As of Thursday, China had officially reported 21 people killed. While in China, the official narrative heavily focuses on rescue efforts, online posts across Chinese social media show an emotional outpouring of grief and mourning. On Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, photographs of missing border inspection officers are shared under the hashtag “Salute to heroes guarding the nation’s gateway”. In China, families with missing loved ones say they are relying on information from Nepal, as well as foreign embassies and social media. Tibetan advocate groups say information on the Tibetan side of the border remains heavily restricted. On 30 August, Tibetan police reported that 10 people had been punished for spreading what authorities called “false information” about the scale of the disaster online. “This crackdown is obstructing not just public reporting of the disaster and relief efforts but the basic work of establishing whether communities are alive and receiving the support that they need,” said Tencho Gyatso, president of the US-based Tibetan advocacy group the International Campaign for Tibet (ICT) “Sources are now afraid to speak to outside groups including ICT. One source told ICT it was “extremely unsafe” to speak. Another asked us not to make further contact given the potential ramifications,” she said. Fan says she is mainly relying on information from Nepal. “Everyone seems to have forgotten about the workers on the Syaphrubesi–Rasuwagadhi Highway project … All the news coverage is about the hydropower station [in Nepal]. Families of foreign tourists who went missing in Tibet are also desperately searching for information, British nationals Sridhar Avvari, 43, his wife, Deepti, 41, and their 14-year-old son Abhinav went missing near the immigration area at Gyirong on 26 August, close to the Nepal-Tibet border. The family lives in India and relatives believe they went over to the Tibetan side. In a call to the family days earlier, Deepti Avvari told them that there would be no signal but would talk when she returned to an area with network activity. After the flash flood, calls to Deepti’s phone stopped connecting. “There was no signal, so we can’t talk … After coming down, I will call you again,” Deepti told Priyanka Rapaka, her sister in law. They are desperately waiting for updates. “We didn’t get any information from China … We are checking online only who are rescued and … how many are dead,” Rapaka said. Chinese authorities say they are now able to reach the main disaster zone by road. According to state media they are describing the region as an active search and rescue operation and are searching for hundreds of missing people. Naresh Goyal is anxiously waiting for news about his sister, Neetu Goyal Tiwari, a 51-year-old missing British national who flew from India to Kathmandu on 14 August to join an Isha Foundation pilgrimage. “The last message received is that they have reached Gyirong immigration office. “They said they are going to check out.” He says he found his sister’s name on a list of missing people circulating on social media, but said he is unsure where the list originated. Getting information out of the Chinese authorities has been difficult. “Whenever we ask the China government, they are telling us that they will update us through the embassy of the UK,” he says. “It is very painful here Now we have spent at least seven days and every minute we are waiting,” Goyal says.
