title: OpenAI hails ‘new era of artificial general intelligence’ with Astra model release
summary: Astra’s arrival comes days after Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, described AGI as an ‘irrelevant marketing term’
text: The president of OpenAI, Greg Brockman, has claimed the world has entered a new era of artificial general intelligence after the release of his company’s latest model, Astra, which it described as the “world’s most intelligent and aligned model”. Brockman made the claim on Thursday as the San Francisco company released the model only weeks after a serious AI safety incident involving other models under its development caused international concern and a pause in Astra’s training. Artificial general intelligence – or AGI – is a fuzzy threshold that has long been talked about as a target for the AI industry. It has been defined as an AI system’s ability to learn, reason and apply knowledge across a wide range of tasks and domains at a human level or higher. OpenAI has defined it as “autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work”. Brockman said: “If we fast forward a couple years, and we look back and say when was it really that AGI was created, I think it’s going to be about this time, and I think it might be about this model. “I think that we’re at a point now where these models are solving unsolved 100-year-old math problems, but you can also use them in order to accelerate the economy [and] in order to benefit you and your personal life … I think it’s not unreasonable to feel that we are now in the AGI era.” OpenAI said Astra was a “major advance for scientific discovery, mathematics and health”, could fill out tax returns, build computer-game scenes, draw architectural visualisations, order food and do a job search in 2 minutes 51 seconds that would take a human five hours. Days earlier Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive, was asked how he was feeling about AGI. He told the Sources podcast: “At best it’s a very poorly defined term. I was going to say it’s like an irrelevant marketing term.” Last month OpenAI was forced to shut down parts of the model’s training in response to what Altman called a “legitimate AI safety accident and alignment failure” that “shouldn’t have happened”. Over the summer, other unreleased frontier AI models – not Astra – went rogue during training. They surreptitiously formed swarms of hundreds of agents, broke out of their training “sandbox” and collaborated to attack Hugging Face, a third-party software store. The incident – believed to be the first autonomous cyber-attack – stunned even seasoned AI safety experts. Astra has what OpenAI calls a “critical” level of cybersecurity capability. That means it may hack into software in a way that, according to the company’s own classification, “could lead to catastrophe from unilateral actors, hacking military or industrial systems, or OpenAI infrastructure”. But OpenAI said it was carefully aligned to “refuse to comply with advanced cybersecurity tasks” such as finding unknown flaws which create openings for malicious hackers. The company will only allow “less restrictive access to an initial set of trusted cybersecurity defenders” who could use its prowess to strengthen rather than attack cyber defences. On one hacking test it achieved a perfect score of 100%, compared with 5.5% on Open AI’s previous cutting-edge cyber-capable model, GPT-5.6 Sol. On another it scored 42% compared with 30%, using fewer resources. But OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said: “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder.” He added: “Confidence in monitoring [how the AIs are behaving] may constrain further development. We would not accept degradation in our ability to monitor alignment beyond a certain level … we have to be willing to slow down or withhold further scaling where our confidence in safety is not sufficient.” The launch continues a torrent of new AI models from the leading US companies, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX, as well as their Chinese rivals. The race to release ever-more advanced AIs comes as OpenAI pushes towards a stock market listing that it hopes will value it at more than $850bn (£625bn). Anthropic is also targeting an IPO which could value it as high as $2tn. Meanwhile, more than 1,000 employees at frontier AI companies, including senior figures at OpenAI and Anthropic, recently signed a joint letter this summer that warned the companies were “under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration”. They called on the US government to “support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.”

title: Far-right Israeli minister outlines plan for removal of all Palestinians from Gaza
summary: Itamar Ben-Gvir claims proposal for illegal forced displacement of 2 million people is ‘realistic’ and ‘concrete’
text: Israel’s far-right national security minister has set out a plan for the illegal forced expulsion of all Palestinians from the Gaza Strip, with the intention of sending them abroad. Speaking in the run-up to close-fought Israeli elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir said the plan aimed to remove 250,000 Palestinians from Gaza in the first year, followed by the rest of its population of roughly 2 million over the next six years. “It’s realistic,” Ben-Gvir said, claiming there were countries that were “ready” to take in Palestinians from Gaza, without naming which ones. While the forced displacement of civilians in occupied territory is considered a war crime under the Geneva conventions, Israeli political figures have competed over the harshness of their visions for Gaza, rebuffing efforts by the US president, Donald Trump, to advance a half-baked and largely moribund ceasefire deal that has been marked by continuing Israeli attacks. Ben-Gvir said the far-right Jewish Power party would demand “a ministry in charge of emigration” during the formation of the next government, adding that his plan was “the result of a year and a half of work and … is concrete”. The proposal is contained in a 20-page document with the euphemistic title of “National Work Plan for Voluntary Emigration from the Gaza Strip”. Despite the use of the word “voluntary”, the plan will be seen as coercive by the international community because of the dire conditions imposed on Gaza’s population by Israel and because of Ben-Gvir’s explicit intention: to remove Gaza’s Palestinian population. Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza. Ben-Gvir’s comments follow hard on the heels of comments by Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, who said Israel was seeking the approval of the Trump administration to displace Palestinians from Gaza, which he claimed was still under discussion after being “frozen” by Trump. Katz, at a conference hosted by the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth, said Israel would facilitate the emigration “by any means”, implying a policy of coercion. Trump himself provoked international outrage at the beginning of his second term with a suggestion that all 2 million Palestinians leave Gaza and that the US redevelop the territory, a proposal he later walked back. With elections in Israel in October, Ben-Gvir has made a series of inflammatory interventions aimed at his far-right base, including sharing footage from a site where Palestinians convicted of deadly attacks by Israeli military courts – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – are to be executed. In another video, he revelled in the mistreatment of Palestinian prisoners in Israeli custody. Polling suggests that Jewish Power, the party led by Ben-Gvir – who has convictions for incitement to racism and support for a terrorist organisation, and who has been put under sanctions by various countries – would gain about seven seats. The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for his part staged a visit to a military outpost in Gaza on Wednesday to insist that Israel would not withdraw from the areas of Gaza that it occupies. “We are not withdrawing. We are staying on this line. We control 60% of the strip. And there is still more to come, because we are eliminating the terrorists who threaten us – we do this day in and day out,” he said. According to Israel’s deputy chief of general staff, Maj Gen Tamir Yadai, the country now controls 65% of Gaza. This is far beyond the 53% agreed under the ceasefire brokered last year by Trump. As well as pushing for the expulsion of Gaza’s population, Ben-Gvir has called for the deportation of two MPs and others “who are disloyal to the state of Israel” – including Jews – saying he would promote such a policy if he is included in the next government.

title: Hundreds gather to urge Scottish government to pause datacentre boom
summary: Opposition mounts as at least 20 projects proposed, including one in Fife billed as second largest in world
text: Kat Jones may be the closest thing Scotland has to Erin Brockovich in 2026. Standing in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat outside Holyrood, the 52-year-old is revving up the crowd of protesters around her. “Who is here from Lammermuir? Ayrshire? What about Aberdeen?” she calls to the crowd. On Thursday, hundreds travelled to Edinburgh to call for an immediate moratorium on Scotland’s datacentre boom, which includes one project in Auchtertool, Fife, that has been billed as the second largest in the world. Jones, the director of the NGO Action to Protect Rural Scotland, is spearheading a campaign demanding a pause while the Scottish government produces analysis on the environmental impact of the centres, and clear planning guidance on the definition of a “green” datacentre. She is a whirr of action: greeting, encouraging, emailing and introducing. Thursday’s protest was the biggest yet. In John Swinney’s programme for government on Tuesday, Scotland’s equivalent to the king’s speech, the first minister said he would take a strategic approach to datacentres with “expectations around environmental sustainability, resource use, community benefit”, but stopped short of agreeing to a moratorium. For the campaigners, this is not enough. From Dunbar to Greenock, there is fierce anger at the speed and scale of the projects in the planning pipeline. At least 20 are proposed so far, with more rumoured. Some are planned in the countryside not far from small villages, others next to care homes and residential housing. Kathleen White, who is campaigning against a proposed £2bn datacentre in Lammermuir hills in the Scottish borders, said the project did not make any sense in her area. “We are from a small village of about a hundred people. The project is planned about a mile up the road,” she said. “There’s a reservoir and an angling spot. It’s an upland area with dark skies. The datacentre buildings would cover eight hectares [20 acres] of mostly concrete in a greenfield area. It is going to be a monstrosity.” The rising public anger about the datacentre buildout that underpins the global AI boom is a growing threat to the UK’s strategy. Keir Starmer’s government leaned heavily on AI as a means to turbocharge a limp economy while he was prime minister. Crucial to this were “AI growth zones”, which were areas where Britain planned to build massive AI datacentres in the hope that jobs and growth would follow. The Guardian’s investigations have called into question the numbers and reasoning behind this strategy. The UK’s grid is strained, and proposed datacentres are meeting stiff resistance in London and elsewhere in the south of England. This spring, British officials pushed would-be AI datacentre developers to look north – suggesting Scotland, with its renewable energy and abundant water resources, is better-equipped to support the country’s efforts to keep up in the AI race. One of the UK’s five AI growth zones will be in Lanarkshire, a rural area outside Glasgow. Mounting public anger – and a potential moratorium – could jeopardise this pivot. But Jones rejects any suggestion that the moratorium campaign is standing in the way of progress. “People who are campaigning locally on issues that matter to them a lot get accused of being nimbys. But this is a campaign that has national and international consequences. Datacentres are some of the biggest buildings on the planet, they use so much energy. “Local campaigners are the most motivated to oppose them because they are a direct existential threat to the places they love, right near their homes, near hospitals, near schools.” The opposition to large-scale datacentres has also been backed by the Scottish Greens and by Reform UK. Reform has raised concerns about the number of projects, while the Scottish Greens have backed the moratorium – echoing the campaigners’ demands for a national framework. Ross Greer, co-leader of the Scottish Greens, who was outside Holyrood with protesters, said: “If we want to have the internet, we need datacentres and Scotland already has plenty of them. “But those proposed would require more energy than all of Scotland needs at its peak at the moment. That is clearly not possible.” The Scottish government has said that all planning authorities must notify ministers of new datacentre applications exceeding 50MW within a week to help monitor their impact on infrastructure, but underscored that the centres are important for economic growth. The public finance minister for Scotland, Hannah Mary Goodlad, said: “We must balance the economic and employment interests in developing datacentres with national energy, climate and community wealth building ambitions, which are vital to our future prosperity, as well as the potential impact on local communities. “I am clear that voices of communities that will be affected will be central to any considerations on datacentres.” But Jones and the campaign want more. She fears that Scotland could be overwhelmed without a formal national strategy. “We are not saying everything needs to stop for ever. But it’s moving so fast. We need a pause.” • This article was amended on 7 September 2026 to remove a quote from Ross Greer that had understated the power that would be needed by the proposed datacentres.

title: Thieves steal more than 70,000 pints’ worth of Guinness from depot in Cheshire
summary: Police say two lorries were driven into industrial estate in Runcorn and attached to trailers holding about 800 barrels
text: The famous tagline “Guinness is good for you” applies only when the drink is bought and paid for, police have said, after thieves made off with more than 70,000 pints’ worth in Cheshire. Officers said they believed two lorries were driven into a depot in Runcorn on Monday and attached to waiting trailers holding a combined total of about 800 barrels before being driven away. Cheshire police said they hoped for a full recovery of the stolen barrels, and had appealed for witnesses who may have seen a lorry entering the Aston Lane area at about 7.45pm. The first lorry was said to have connected to the HGV trailer before leaving the depot at about 7.55pm in the direction of the Mersey Gateway bridge. The second lorry arrived at the same site at 9.12pm and connected to another trailer before leaving at 9.30pm in the direction of Rainhill and Watkinson Way, police said. DS McClatchy said: “It is famously said that ‘Guinness is good for you’, but that is only the case when it has been bought and paid for. “It is with this in mind that we have wasted no time in launching inquires to identify those responsible for the theft of £115,000 worth of Guinness and the two trailers that housed the barrels. We will settle for nothing less than the full recovery of all the items stolen.” When including the value of the trailers, the total value of the items stolen is estimated at about £205,000. McClatchey asked anyone with information to speak to officers. “We would also ask any motorists who were driving in the area at the time of either of the incidents to please review any dashcam footage to see if you have captured anything that could aid our investigation.” The stolen barrels, containing about 70,400 pints of Guinness, had been intended for delivery to pubs. Diageo, which owns the brand, has a packaging warehouse on the Whitehouse industrial estate on Aston Lane. Police believe both HGVs were driven by men. The first driver was described as white with a short dark beard, and wearing a beanie hat. The second was believed to have been wearing a cap. The trailers were described as white tri-axle curtain-side trailers with branding for the logistics company GXO on the curtains and rear doors. The trucks have the unique ID numbers DL736 and DL542 on the top left corner of their rear doors.

title: Sabotage, leaks and political ties: the story of the Daphne Caruana Galizia murder trial
summary: Maltese businessman cleared of involvement in journalist’s death, but trial revealed challenges faced by those leading search for killers
text: The conclusion of the longest-running murder trial in Maltese history has left a country in turmoil, and a grieving family still searching for answers. At 7.30pm on Wednesday, gasps and cheers echoed around hall 22 of the courts of justice in Valletta, as a jury pronounced a businessman accused of ordering the murder of the investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia not guilty. Yorgen Fenech, 44, had been facing a life sentence if convicted. Now, after nearly seven years in and out of custody, he is free to return to a gilded life as the heir to one of Malta’s biggest fortunes. In her reporting, Caruana Galizia had taken aim at many powerful figures, including Fenech and the politicians he was close to. Her revelations, and the fallout from her violent death in a car bombing in October 2017, had ultimately led to the resignation of the prime minister, Joseph Muscat, and several members of his government. Within weeks, three hitmen accused of planting the bomb were arrested. Two were sentenced to life in prison after pleading guilty to murder, while the third was given a reduced 15-year sentence in exchange for evidence against his accomplices. After Wednesday’s decision, the long search for whoever was responsible for hiring them must begin again. The opposition leader, Alex Borg, has demanded the recall of parliament from its summer recess, and called for the government to act to strengthen press protection and anti-corruption measures. “We believe journalism is the backbone of a democracy,” he told the Guardian, describing the failure to find the culprits as a black mark against the Labour government. The party has been in power since 2013. Caruana Galizia’s family described the verdict as “justice denied”. The attorney general is considering whether to appeal for a retrial. The chances of success may be slim: both charges brought against Fenech were dismissed by an 8-1 majority. It had taken nine years, a relentless family campaign and a determined judge to bring Fenech before a jury. In the end, they took him at his word. During his evidence, he was adamant: “I never ordered Daphne Caruana Galizia’s murder, or anyone else’s. I had no role in her murder.” While the identity of the mastermind remains a mystery, what the trial did reveal was the full extent of the challenges faced by those leading the search for Daphne’s killers. Witness after witness spoke of attempts to block and sabotage the murder investigation. As detectives worked to identify all of those involved, from the bomb makers to the hitmen to their ultimate client, they heard evidence that the most sensitive details were being leaked. Most disturbingly of all, the jury was told much of the information was coming from the prime minister’s right-hand man. “Don’t worry about me, nobody can touch me,” Fenech was heard saying in secret recordings that formed a cornerstone of the case against him, and played to the jury. The man who had made those recordings was a taxi driver, Melvin Theuma, who testified to acting as the middleman between Fenech and the bombers. He was the key prosecution witness, having secured a pardon two years after the murder in return for giving evidence. In July 2020, he was taken to hospital in a critical condition. Overcome with remorse, he had attempted suicide while staying at a safe house, and it took intensive support to get him back in the stand. What follows is the story of the search for those responsible, based on pre-trial hearings, the trial itself, and related court cases. Consumed by an investigation that would kill her In the last summer of her life, Caruana Galizia was deeply isolated. As a younger woman, she had not only been brilliant, but strikingly beautiful, with big statement earrings and shining black hair. She had co-founded a national newspaper, was a lifestyle magazine publisher, and had become one of Malta’s most-read columnists, all while raising three sons. In later life, it was the investigative work that consumed her. Her blog Running Commentary was among the most-read news sites in Malta, but its popularity, and her often scathing satires of public figures, made her a target. She had as many detractors as fans, and on social media she was vilified as a “witch”. There were arson attacks, and the family dogs were killed. “I was worried about her,” her middle son, Andrew, told the trial. “The atmosphere around her was horrible. People would stare at her in Valletta. She wouldn’t leave the house.” Caruana Galizia knew she was at risk and had already started varying her routine. For added security, she drove a rental car. It was in that car that she died on 16 October 2017, aged 53, metres from her house. A bomb placed under the driver’s seat ripped through the vehicle, scattering burning remains across the road and into a field. Barricaded inside their home, sheltering from the media storm, Daphne’s sons and her widow, Peter, wondered who they could trust. They felt sure her work would hold clues, but also that they could not hand sensitive source material to the police. Her eldest son, Matthew, a software engineer who had been part of the reporting team that won a Pulitzer prize for the Panama Papers, a giant leak of offshore company data, suggested contacting journalists outside Malta. “I didn’t have the resources to do the investigation on my own,” he told the jury at Fenech’s trial. He reached out to the Guardian, which joined Reuters, the non-profit Forbidden Stories and others to form the Daphne Project. Before her death, Caruana Galizia had published a series of stories that plunged the Maltese government into scandal. She had found evidence in the Panama Papers that the energy minister, Konrad Mizzi, and the prime minister’s chief of staff, a businessman turned political fixer called Keith Schembri, had set up offshore companies held via anonymous trusts. Posts she published, read out during the trial, suggested she thought they were planning to use these to receive kickbacks. Those allegations are now the subject of a criminal case, in which Fenech, Schembri, Mizzi and others are pleading not guilty to corruption, trading in influence and criminal association. At the time she died, Caruana Galizia was receiving a leak of information about a large government contract – a concession to build a €500m gas power plant that would supply electricity for the national grid. The leak came from the servers of the company building the plant, Electrogas. One of its shareholders was Fenech, and the email traffic suggested he was a driving force, handling communications with the government, and the refinancing of a crucial bank loan. The jury heard how, in her blog, Caruana Galizia had described the venture as a “magic new corruption power station”. The prosecution had claimed, in its closing submissions, that Fenech’s motive for ordering her murder was to prevent any further revelations. The Electrogas data was shared with the Daphne Project. As reporters combed the files, following the money trails, Keith Arnaud, a homicide detective, searched for the killers. At first he made rapid progress, thanks to the FBI. The agency’s cellphone analysis team had been in Europe when the bomb went off, and they diverted to Malta, landing there within hours. The hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio, and their accomplice Vincent Muscat, had used burner phones but they had been careless, often carrying them alongside their usual mobiles. The FBI made the link, tracing a text message sent by George to detonate the bomb. In December 2017, the trio were arrested. In April 2018, Vincent Muscat told police he was ready to turn on his accomplices, in exchange for a shorter sentence. While the hitmen had never known the identity of their ultimate client, Muscat had the name of the middleman: Melvin Theuma. The mosquito and the lion For Theuma, a fatherless teenager, the Malta Racing Club was a home from home. He started as a groom, tending to the ponies that pull small carts around the bare-earth track. Before long he was working as a scout for a bookmaker. The old betting shop still stands across the street from the Fenech family stables. Theuma and Fenech became friends, but it was not a relationship of equals. As the taxi driver said in court: “I was hanging out with a lion, and I’m a mosquito.” Police said in court they had identified Fenech as a suspect by September 2018. But it would take until February 2019 for a warrant to be authorised to intercept his calls. The person signing the warrants was the prime minister, Joseph Muscat. From the beginning, Muscat had been receiving updates about the investigation directly from Arnaud and his colleagues. That decision was controversial because, along with his ministers, he had been one of the main subjects of Caruana Galizia’s reporting. Muscat has indicated it was customary for the prime minister to sign warrants in cases of national importance. He has previously said he fulfilled his duties “without fear, prejudice or favour”. In a statement on Thursday, he said that from the beginning, and while he was still in office, “no one was protected from or immune to justice”. Schembri was allowed to attend the police briefings and told the trial he was kept informed throughout. The two men were close – Schembri had started out as Muscat’s campaign manager – but Schembri had another good friend: Fenech. They had played football together as children, and when Fenech, a few years younger, stepped up to run his family business, Schembri had mentored him. They would often holiday together and gather for family events. Schembri is accused of repeatedly leaking sensitive details about the homicide investigation to Fenech. He denies the allegations, and is being prosecuted over the matter in a separate criminal case. During his trial, Fenech sought to paint Schembri as the ultimate mastermind, describing himself as a go-between, passing messages to Theuma. Fenech’s lawyers depicted the taxi driver as a blackmailer and a liar, and accused the police of framing Fenech because they had failed to properly follow other leads. They said the searches at Schembri’s home and his office had been bungled. His phone, active 28 minutes before the raid, was never found. “All roads lead to Keith and all bridges leading to Keith were burnt,” Fenech’s lawyer said. “And so a bridge had to be built to Yorgen Fenech.” Schembri denies any involvement in the murder. In their evidence, police said he was never a murder suspect. Under questioning, Fenech admitted paying €400,000, via Theuma, to the hitmen to cover their legal bills. He said this was to keep Theuma calm, and that the cab driver had “drained” him of money. He also admitted giving Theuma money before the murder, but said he warned that it should not go ahead, telling the taxi driver to “stop it here”. He admitted passing information about the police investigation from Schembri to Theuma, starting soon after the assassination. “Keith Schembri was continuously informed and in a way you can say real time,” Fenech told a court in 2019, in a constitutional case regarding his right to a fair trial. “The information was passed to me by Keith Schembri but it came from Mr Arnaud, and he used to tell me that it came from Mr Arnaud.” Recordings, messages and testimony from Fenech himself indicate that in the first months after the murder he had passed on to Theuma the identity of who had made the bomb and the date on which the police were planning to arrest the hitmen. When the police raided their shed by the docks, they had already thrown their mobile phones into the water, and one of them had written his wife’s number on his wrist. In April 2018, Fenech also shared that Vincent Muscat was offering to become a witness for the prosecution. The news sent Theuma into a spin and he started to record his exchanges with Fenech, using a spare phone switched to airplane mode so it would not ring. It was around this time that Arnaud’s investigation seemed to lose momentum. Eventually, details of what had been uncovered began to leak. By May 2019, reporters had Theuma’s name. Europol, which had been supporting Arnaud and his team, threatened over the summer of 2019 to withdraw unless arrests were made. The family were also losing patience. “We had known what was being alleged about Melvin Theuma for months,” Matthew Caruana Galizia has said. “And it reached a point where I just wanted to go into the street and spraypaint his name on a wall. I wanted the world to know that he was the middleman, to just push the police into action.” While the walls around the prime minister and his friends looked strong from the outside, when the police finally went for Theuma, Joseph Muscat’s administration crumbled. Theuma had been warned of his planned arrest date but police swooped two days early, on 14 November 2019. Fenech had urged him in messages beforehand to dispose of the evidence. The jury saw one message in which he said: “Be 100% sure everywhere is clean.” But Theuma held on to his recordings. On 19 November, the prime minister signed a memorandum guaranteeing Theuma immunity from prosecution in exchange for testimony. Within hours, Fenech was making preparations to flee, messages seen by the jury suggest. “Go while you’re still in time,” his uncle texted. He planned to sail to Sicily, and then head for France. However, the police had been tipped off. His yacht was intercepted a mile off the coast, and he was arrested. The interrogation tapes, played at his trial, showed he offered to implicate Schembri in return for a pardon. As Fenech talked, heads rolled. Schembri was arrested in relation to the suspected leaks, and resigned. The economy minister, a frequent subject of Caruana Galizia’s blog, suspended himself and Mizzi, by now reassigned from energy to tourism minister, quit, citing “political, extraordinary and general circumstances in the country”. Public outrage brought hundreds on to the streets, filling the grand plaza outside the prime minister’s office, chanting: “Mafia, mafia.” Fenech’s pardon request was rejected and on 30 November, he was charged. Two days later, Joseph Muscat resigned. Defiant to the end, he insisted: “This case cannot define everything that our country is.” The saga is once again drawing attention from outside Malta. Shami Chakrabarti, the British Labour peer, has been appointed rapporteur of a Council of Europe investigation into the Maltese government’s response to the murder. Caruana Galizia’s family members intend to give evidence at the first hearing next week. “The failure to ensure individual accountability for the murder risks perpetuating a culture of impunity,” Chakrabarti said on Thursday. “A culture where … those who try to shine a light in the darkness pay the ultimate price.”

title: Pro-Palestine activists who were sentenced as terrorists launch appeal
summary: Barrister representing four who smashed drones at Israeli arms factory says ruling of ‘terrorist connection’ led to heftier sentences
text: Palestine Action activists who were the first defendants convicted of property damage whose offending was deemed to have a “terrorist connection” have launched an appeal of “fundamental constitutional importance” against the judge’s finding. Charlotte Head, 30, Leona Kamio, 31, Fatema Rajwani, 22, and Samuel Corner, 24, received lengthy sentences in June for smashing up drones and other equipment at Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems’ factory in Filton, Bristol, in 2024. Mr Justice Johnson’s decision to sentence them as terrorists after a jury found them guilty of non-terrorism offences – they were committed before Palestine Action was banned – has been criticised by civil liberties groups, including Liberty and Amnesty International. Simon Natas, of ITN solicitors, who is representing the four prisoners, said serious property damage, which can constitute terrorism, was not clearly defined and could catch a wide range of offending, making the appeal of “fundamental constitutional importance”. He said: “The only way you can determine what ‘serious’ means is by going back to what was said during the Terrorism Act [passing through parliament]. Jack Straw was the home secretary at the time. And when he presented the act to parliament he said that terrorism was, or involved, the use of serious violence. “So … it had to be designed to create a climate of extreme fear and undermine the foundations of government. So, really, what we say is the government set the bar for what terrorism is very, very high.” He said the bar had not been reached in this case and that there had been no intention to influence the government or to intimidate the public, or a section of the public, as required for a terrorism finding, “because the intention here was simply to damage weapons to prevent them being sent to Israel … and used by the Israeli military”. While Corner was also convicted of grievous bodily harm without intent for striking Sgt Kate Evans with a sledgehammer, no terrorist connection was applied to this offence. A press conference on Thursday was told that Johnson’s ruling on a terrorist connection meant that the four received heftier sentences. They will also serve at least two-thirds of their tariff in prison, much longer than the norm, and must rescind their political views to obtain parole. Additionally, they will also be subject to 15 years of terrorist notification requirements on release, which includes informing police of any new devices, relationships, bank accounts or addresses. Kamio’s mother, Emma, said that 40 quadcopter “killer drones” had been destroyed during the offending, and that the activists had been trying to save Palestinian children’s lives. She warned that “the floodgates” would open, with more terrorist connection findings in similar cases if the appeal were unsuccessful. In a statement from prison, Head said: “Our case has been politically manipulated to justify the proscription of Palestine Action.” A statement supporting the appeal by the leading human rights lawyer Michael Mansfield KC said the integrity and fairness of jury trial had been undermined. “In effect, the judge can recategorise and upgrade an offence post-conviction,” he said. A single judge will decide whether to grant the prisoners leave to appeal.

title: Rich people more likely to steal children’s sweets, finds Ig Nobel prize-winning study
summary: We round up the winners at awards for achievements that ‘first make people laugh and then make them think’
text: It’s that time of year again: a select group of scientists have been summoned to a ceremony to receive coveted prizes, be showered in paper planes, and leave with a 10tn dollar bill, albeit in the form of a phased-out note from Zimbabwe. It is, of course, the annual Ig Nobel awards. Not to be confused with the more prestigious and career-changing Nobel prizes that will be announced in Scandinavia next month, the satirical Ig Nobels are awarded for achievements that “first make people laugh and then make them think”. On Thursday, real Nobel laureates were on stage to hand out the awards and winners were giving “24/7” lectures: describing their work in 24 seconds and then in seven words. Here are the 2026 winners. Economics: evil rich people Are rich people really worse behaved than the rest of us? Through a series of experiments, psychologists amassed evidence that the upper classes are indeed more prone to behaving badly, from being oblivious to other road users, lying at work and taking treats meant for children. “I’ve followed the Ig Nobels since my early college days. I didn’t think I’d ever win one,” said Dr Paul Piff, a social psychologist at the University of California, Irvine. Piff and his colleagues found that upper-class drivers were more likely to cut other cars off at junctions and ignore pedestrians at crossings. Wealthier people also appeared more willing to lie at work. In one experiment, volunteers were left alone with a jar of sweets ostensibly meant for children. When the researchers returned, upper-class people had snaffled nearly twice as many candies as lower-class people. “The general pattern seems to be that with wealth and rising power, you become less engaged with the needs of others and less burdened by the needs of social relationships,” Piff said. “Taking candy from children might be the least of our worries but it’s emblematic of the tendency to prioritise one’s own needs over those of others.” Biomechanics: the definition of kissing Researchers at Oxford University ensured the UK could hold its head high after winning the biomechanics prize. “The whole team is thrilled,” said Dr Matilda Brindle. She and her colleagues investigated the evolution of kissing and needed a scientific definition of the act. They settled on “non-agonistic interactions involving directed, infraspecific oral-oral contact with some movement of the lips/mouthparts and no food transfer”. Brindle, who is writing a book on non-reproductive sexual behaviour, has also studied the evolution of masturbation, making her a strong contender to become the Marie Curie of Ig Nobels by winning more than once. “We’re so focused on penises, what they do and why they are important, but all these other sexual behaviours are important,” she said. Physics: The splashless urinal A team of students led by Kavee Thurairajah at the University of Waterloo in Canada worked out that urinal splash is almost entirely eradicated if the stream strikes the urinal at less than 30 degrees. They went on to design a urinal whose shape ensures minimal splash regardless of the user’s aim. “I am very proud,” said Dr Zhao Pan, who runs the lab. Peace: The power of mutual enemies It is natural to want friends that are kind to us, but our friends interact with others in the world in ways that can affect our lives. Dr Jaimie Krems at the University of California, Los Angeles, showed there’s plenty of room for attack dogs in our friendship groups, as long as they target those we dislike. “Sometimes we want our friends to be more vicious and indifferent when they interact with our enemies,” she said. “I’ve felt, in many instances, incredibly loved when people have carried my hate for me and been willing to have my back.” Biology: The science of stepping on snakes Researchers in Brazil donned safety boots to explore what made venomous snakes bite in defence by softly stepping on different parts of their bodies. Pressure on the head triggered most bites, they had found, but the study had been retracted by the Scientific Reports journal as the team did not have ethical approval to step on the creatures. Ig notable mentions The chemistry prize went to an international team that found cockroach milk contains three times as much energy as cows’ milk, while the olfaction prize went to scientists who discovered babies smell wonderful to their parents, but teenagers do not. Other researchers landed prizes for turning mosquito proboscises into 3D printing nozzles, clarifying the aerodynamics of nose blowing, and burying underpants to monitor soil quality.

title: Nvidia to buy developer platform Hugging Face in $12.9bn deal
summary: Semi-conductor giant bets that support for open AI models could offset potential slowdown in demand for chips
text: Nvidia will buy the popular developer platform Hugging Face for nearly $13bn, betting that support for ⁠open AI models could offset a potential slowdown in demand for the semiconductor giant’s chips. Shares ⁠in Nvidia were ⁠slightly lower after the $12.93bn (£9.57bn) deal – which ranks among its biggest ever – was announced for the database of AI models on Thursday. Hugging Face, based in New York and backed by the likes of Intel, Advanced Micro Devices and Amazon, was founded in 2016 by the French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf. Nvidia is already a major open AI player in the US with ⁠its widely used Nemotron model and vocal support for the technology. Acquiring Hugging Face will give it direct access to a platform developers use to ⁠collaborate and test and share tools, potentially providing insight and data that could help it narrow the technology gap with top American and ‌Chinese labs. “Nvidia gains visibility into customer’s preferences and the AI models they use,” said Naveen Chhabra, principal analyst at Forrester. “They can see which models are trending, what datasets customers are downloading, and the architectures that are gaining traction weeks before they hit mainstream tech news.” Demand for open-weight models ‌has surged from businesses balking at the steep bill of deploying generative AI. Chinese companies ‌such as DeepSeek, Moonshot and Z.ai have emerged as crucial players with models that can match the best from the US in tasks including generating computer code at a lower cost. There are fears that some US firms could become reliant on Beijing’s models even as both countries race to dominate a technology they see as crucial to their future. The Trump administration has scrambled to respond to the wave of open models from China, weighing whether to restrict their use while also worrying about stifling American businesses that have taken to using them. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, was a signatory of an open letter earlier this year from major tech firms that advocated for open models and warned against government regulation that would stifle their use. Huang pledged that Nvidia would keep Hugging Face open after acquiring it. “Hugging ‌Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem,” said Huang, adding that his company’s chips would not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face. Under the deal, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors, while offering an equity-based retention program of up to $1bn for employees who join Nvidia. For Nvidia, building up its open source business may help it cushion a demand slowdown from customers such as ⁠Meta, OpenAI and Microsoft, which are developing their own AI chips to cut reliance on its costly and supply-constrained processors. Several Chinese chip-making firms have also made recent advancements that could further disrupt the balance of power within big tech, though they face strict international export controls. It has been a volatile year in the market for chipmakers, with a chip stock selloff in July wiping $1tn from the market caps of leading firms. Nvidia shares bounced back in August, though, with a strong revenue forecast leading to the second-biggest one-day gain in market history – adding $442bn to the company’s market value. Hugging Face has also been in the news recently after a hack by rogue AI agents that escaped OpenAI’s testing ‌environment. Beyond hosting AI models, it offers datasets, software libraries and cloud services used to build and deploy AI applications.

title: Grinding up fish to feed to fish is ‘absurd’: fears over UN aquaculture plan
summary: Huge rollout of fish farms could harm ecosystems and threaten vulnerable communities’ food sources, say experts
text: Nearly half of the world’s wild fish catch will be ground into animal feed for farmed fish if plans to expand aquaculture go ahead, a report has found. The UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) is aiming to increase aquaculture – where fish are farmed rather than caught in the wild – production by 75% by 2040, according to its sustainable development goal roadmap. Separately, the FAO’s “blue transformation” agenda aims to meet growing global demand for seafood, improve food security and eradicate world hunger by 2030. But an analysis by Changing Markets Foundation found the plans would potentially pull tens of millions of tonnes of fish from the oceans each year to feed species such as salmon and shrimp. Aquaculture adds to the intense pressure on overexploited fisheries because food is removed from marine ecosystems and the coastal communities that rely on them. Aquaculture supplies more than half of the aquatic animals consumed worldwide, according to the report. Carnivorous farmed species are commonly fed fishmeal and fish oil made by grinding down smaller wild fish such as anchovies and sardines. “These fish are naturally carnivorous species, so that is what they would eat in the wild,” said Tara Ganesh, a senior campaigner at Changing Markets Foundation. “You can’t suddenly raise a salmon overnight that is vegetarian.” Although producers had reduced the amount of wild fish used for each kilogram of farmed fish, she said this did not mean the industry’s total consumption was falling. Modelling produced with the University of British Columbia found that, if industry trends continued, up to 34.6m tonnes of wild fish could be caught and fed to farmed species annually by 2040. The FAO has not specified which species or farming systems should deliver the 75% increase in aquaculture. Changing Markets Foundation modelled several possible routes to the target and found that, under a scenario weighted towards feed-intensive species such as salmon and shrimp, demand for wild fish could rise to 41.4m tonnes – equivalent to 46% of the global wild-fish catch in 2020. Muhammed Oyinlola, an aquatic ecologist at the University of British Columbia, said: “Our modelling shows that the outcome is not inevitable. A more diversified option favours growth in lower-input species, while ambiguity leaves the door open to growth that threatens communities, fisheries and the climate.” The scale of the impact would depend heavily on which species and production systems were expanded, the research said. But neither the FAO’s roadmap nor its guidelines for sustainable aquaculture specify how its growth target should be met. The report also says safeguards addressing the nutritional and food security effects of aquaculture trade and consumption were removed from successive drafts of the guidelines without explanation. The FAO acknowledged that growth concentrated in feed-intensive species could increase pressure on wild fish, but said its target did not assume this and rejected claims that food-security safeguards had been removed from its guidelines. A spokesperson said: “Historical evidence also indicates that growth in aquaculture production does not translate mechanically into proportional growth in the use of wild fish for feed.” They said the quantity of wild fish used for reduction to fishmeal and fish oil has declined significantly from its historical peak - from 30m tonnes in 1994 to 18m tonnes in 2024 – despite the fact that fed aquaculture production has expanded from 10m tonnes to 74m tonnes over the same period. Changing Markets Foundation examined a December 2023 workshop in Ghana organised by the FAO in collaboration with the Global Roundtable on Marine Ingredients, an industry coalition. “Small-scale fisheries representatives instead called for sardinella to be reserved for direct human consumption and for fishmeal factory expansion to be halted,” it said. West African participants later said the official account of the workshop did not reflect what they regarded as broad opposition among African groups to turning edible wild fish into fishmeal. In a report presented to the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva in June, Elisa Morgera, the UN special rapporteur on climate change, said using nutritionally valuable fish to produce fishmeal and fish oil raised “serious human rights concerns” because it could reduce people’s access to food. Changing Markets Foundation said the consequences were already visible in Senegal, a west African centre for fishmeal and fish oil production, where factories compete with local communities for the same fish. Ganesh said: “A large share of those fish come from much poorer communities where that fish is an essential source of nutrition, but also really essential for the livelihoods of coastal communities and artisanal fishers.” Women who process, smoke and sell fish also risk losing an important source of income. Annual fish consumption per person in Senegal fell by more than 10kg between 1999 and 2019, according to the report. A 2021 Changing Markets Foundation investigation estimated that enough fish to feed 33 million people across west Africa was instead being turned into animal and aquaculture feed each year. The foundation said the FAO’s target could be met while keeping demand for whole wild fish well below 2020 levels by reducing fishmeal and fish oil use and directing more growth towards species requiring fewer marine ingredients. Changing Markets Foundation is urging the FAO to introduce safeguards that prioritise edible wild fish for human consumption and direct aquaculture growth towards species requiring little or no fishmeal or fish oil. “There is an urgent need for safeguards in the FAO’s policy to explicitly preserve wild fish for human consumption,” Ganesh said. She said the modelling exposed “the absurdity of production systems that essentially rely on other fish to make fish”, adding: “It’s a net loss of fish – a net loss of nutrition.” • This article was amended on 11 and 17 September 2026. An earlier version said that the Food and Agriculture Organization’s aim to increase aquaculture production by 75% by 2040 was part of its “blue transformation” agenda; in fact, that is a separate FAO programme with its own targets. And further detail from the FAO was added regarding the quantity of wild fish used for reduction to fishmeal and fish oil.

title: Climate injustices have been laid bare in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster | Letters
summary: Letters: Prof Lyla Mehta says the glacial floods and loss of life are a stark reminder that climate disruption is global and highly unequal. Plus letters from Lynda McDonald and Jan Bengtsson
text: The recent glacial collapse and catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet are not isolated tragedies (Report, 28 August). They reflect accelerating climate disruption that disproportionately affects the countries and people that are least responsible for global emissions. As climate change intensifies, glaciers around the world, including in the Himalayas, are melting at unprecedented rates, destabilising ecosystems and causing glacial collapse and ice-and-rock landslides, destroying settlements, villages and livelihoods in minutes. No one died when a Swiss glacier collapsed last year, owing to early-warning systems that were in place. But a lack of early-warning systems means that the disaster in Nepal and Tibet has led to hundreds of deaths and thousands missing. Events like these are not “natural disasters”. They are due to global warming and climate injustices, and also flawed development policies, including rampant property developments on vulnerable floodplains. They call for better disaster preparedness and investment in early-warning systems. Most importantly, they require global action. The UK has long positioned itself as a leader in international development and climate action. Yet recent UK commitments have fallen far short of what is required – including the decision to raid the diminished aid budget to switch international climate finance grants to loans, to fund a bus-fare cap. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, recently spoke compellingly about the need to put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations. These words must now translate into action. The UK must step up its development commitments and funding for climate adaptation, and loss and damage, to support those living on the frontlines of climate change. The recent glacial floods remind us that climate disruption is global, and highly unequal. The UK must act urgently. Anything less is a failure of responsibility. Prof Lyla Mehta Institute of Development Studies • Sunil Acharya is correct when he states: “The countries that benefited most from fossil fuel-driven growth have a responsibility to cut emissions rapidly” (Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis, 28 August). This was the founding principle of the global “contraction and convergence” framework, tabled by India, China and the African Group of Nations in Kyoto at Cop3 in 1997. Had we enacted this, we would now be on a safe, and equitable, 30-year contraction path, avoiding the worst of the climate crisis and ensuring our survival. Instead, we remain adrift, with no viable solution or plan. Is it really too late to adopt this framework? Lynda McDonald Portaferry, County Down • The key question is: who should pay for this disaster? Yes, the rich world should pay, but the bills should be sent to all the fossil-fuel companies that have known this risk for at least half a century and have ignored it. If they refuse to pay, all of us in countries that have profited from the fossil-driven benefits of “progress” should, through our governments, pay a progressive tax on all things based on fossil fuels, to cover the past, present and future costs of climate change. Jan Bengtsson Uppsala, Sweden • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: How 20mph on our roads benefits everyone | Letters
summary: Letters: The advantages of 20mph speed limits are celebrated by Rod King, while John Hopkin says drivers who speed won’t be deterred unless tougher action is taken against them
text: Thanks to Christian Wolmar for his insightful article on a 20mph limit and how it would be a good thing for Birmingham (Dear culture-war motorists, look to the future. We’ll all be driving at 20mph soon, 28 August). He is right to identify that the world has changed from when the car was king and we planned our city mobility almost exclusively around automobiles. At 20’s Plenty for Us we have seen our movement developing from being classed as radical in the 2000s, to progressive in the 2010s and the new normal in the 2020s. As 20mph limits have been adopted by progressive authorities, we have seen the significant benefits extend beyond pedestrians and cyclists to those who drive. There is clear evidence that when implemented on a wide scale, as in Wales, the average motorist benefits. Journeys for drivers took less than a minute more on average, and journey times were more reliable; car, van and taxi occupant casualties on urban and village roads were reduced by 29.6% in the first year; and insurance costs were reduced by £45 for the average driver owing to 20% fewer damage claims. These are real gains for the average motorist, who also benefits from 20mph being the foundation for people to choose to walk or cycle instead of being in another car in front of them. Of course, when they are not in their car, the same people benefit, and their community becomes a safer and less stressful place. Some drivers will always object to community needs being placed above their own judgment. But the world has changed, and soon a 20mph speed limit will be the urban and village norm, making all of our places better places to be. Rod King Founder and chair, 20’s Plenty for Us CIC • Good luck to Birmingham city council with their plan for a blanket 20mph speed limit. However, many speed cameras were turned off a decade ago to make austerity savings. As a result, current speed limits are widely (and sometimes enthusiastically) ignored with apparent impunity – particularly, it seems, the existing 20mph limits on residential roads. If there’s a war on motorists here, it is one that motorists are now winning: if existing limits are not enforced, it seems unlikely that simply extending the zone will result in a change in behaviour. John Hopkin Moseley, Birmingham • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Donald Trump’s shallow renaming of the Great Lakes | Letters
summary: Letters: Readers respond to the Trump administration’s decision to change Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’
text: I think too much is being made of this (Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order, 2 August). It is common for geographical features straddling borders to receive different names in different jurisdictions. Consider, for example, Lac Léman and the Bodensee, La Manche and Les Îles Malouines. Wales has only recently reclaimed Yr Wyddfa and Bannau Brycheiniog, and for a reminder and dramatisation of how renaming played out in Ireland, look no further than Brian Friel’s Translations. Perhaps we can look forward to Lake Cleveland (previously Erie) and Lake Trump (previously Superior)? Owen Stewart Gatley, Greater Manchester • Donald Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario to Lake America (Report, 27 August) could be an ominous precedent for this country if Reform UK or Restore Britain come to power. In his dystopian vision of the future, the novelist Islwyn Ffowc Elis foresaw Wales being renamed Western England by the government in 2033. David Pope Royal Wootton Bassett, Wiltshire • Most Americans will have learned the mnemonic HOMES for the Great Lakes (Huron, Ontario, Michigan, Erie, Superior). With Donald Trump’s renaming, what will this be replaced by? SHAME, perhaps? James Lindesay Leicester • A new name for America (Letters, 30 August)? Trumpton, with its cast of characters including Musk, Musk, Altman and Thiel, Bezos, Zucky and Huang. Rob Horne Coventry • How about South Canada? Or, alternatively, North Mexico? Andy Cook Honley, West Yorkshire • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Abundant common fossils don’t need to be protected | Letter
summary: Letters: Museums have countless examples of the common fossils from these Lower Jurassic rocks, says the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre’s Phil Davidson
text: The vast majority of the fossils revealed on this rapidly eroding part of the Jurassic Coast hold very little scientific importance and are not in need of protection or recording (Letters, 28 August). Museums around the world have countless examples of the common fossils from these Lower Jurassic rocks, thanks to the efforts of fossil collectors, who since the pioneering palaeontologist Mary Anning (1799–1847) have saved fossils from the same process that reveals them, the action of the sea. The majority of these scientifically important fossils are saved from destruction after the winter storms, not during the peak tourist season in the summer. Allowing tourists to collect and take home their discoveries helps them foster a sense of curiosity and encourages an interest in the natural world, which is especially important for future generations. As in any busy tourist destination, there will always be ill-informed tourists. Some visitors have not worked out which rocks to crack open successfully yet, but the next rough sea or storm will wash new fossils out of the mudslides, and if they are not collected they will be damaged and destroyed by the sea. Here at the Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre, our educational charity welcomes in excess of 100,000 visitors a year. It is free for all to enter and learn more about the past, present and future of our amazing coast through our award-winning displays of recent fossil finds. We also maintain the west Dorset and Undercliffs Fossil Recording Schemes and have records of over 600 fossils of scientific importance that have been discovered here, many by members of the public. We work with academics, researchers, landowners and the public to deliver ethical collecting guidelines (fossil codes), which are management tools on this part of the world heritage site. Phil Davidson Palaeontologist, Charmouth Heritage Coast Centre • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Reform’s media presenter worked for Chinese state propaganda channel
summary: Party podcast and social media host Ray Addison fronted films about province where China is accused of genocide
text: Reform UK’s top media presenter has worked for a Chinese state propaganda channel within the past year, the Guardian can reveal. Ray Addison, who presents the political party’s in-house podcast and social media campaigns, fronted films about Xinjiang province – where the Chinese government is accused of committing genocide – for state media in September 2025. In the videos, entitled Raymond’s Xinjiang Stories, some of which praise Chinese infrastructure, Addison described himself as a CGTN correspondent. The series was made after Addison left GB News in 2024, where he had worked as a news presenter and reporter. Xinjiang province has attracted international attention because of alleged human rights abuses against the region’s Muslim Uyghur population by the Chinese state, including claims of forced labour, sterilisation, re-education and mass surveillance. Addison’s work for China contrasts with the hard line Reform has taken on Chinese issues ranging from industrial relations to suspected Chinese state espionage within Westminster. In a social media video posted by GB News in January, Nigel Farage said of the UK’s relationship with China: “I’m very, very nervous about the extent to which China has effectively spied on us, stolen many of our industrial secrets. I’m worried about the extent to which they’ve infiltrated, using money, British universities. We must be cautious about the relationship.” The videos presented by Addison for CGTN are publicly available on YouTube and carry a warning stating that “CGTN is funded in whole or in part by the Chinese government”. CGTN lost its licence to broadcast in the UK in 2021 after the regulator Ofcom determined it was ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. US goverments under both the previous Trump and Biden administrations have formally described China’s actions against the Uyghurs and other ethnic groups in the province as genocide. The UK government has not made a formal declaration but has noted concerns about alleged human rights abuses in the region. In 2021, British MPs voted to declare that China is committing genocide against the Uyghur people in Xinjiang. Suella Braverman, now a Reform MP, has also made public statements to this effect. On 14 January 2025, before she defected from the Conservative party to Reform, she posted on X: “China is committing genocide in Xinjiang, funding Putin’s war of aggression in Europe and has committed acts of cyber-terrorism against the British people.” Addison is paid by Reform to produce content about the party and creates social media videos as well as presenting its The Reform UK Podcast. In recent days he has fronted the party’s social media promotion of its conference, which is being held in Birmingham. The party has sought to capitalise on Farage’s fanbase by advertising its podcast on the basis of exclusive interviews with the party leader and other senior party figures. Several countries have banned or limited imports of Chinese cotton from Xinjiang because of allegations that the regime uses Uyghur slave labour to process the material. In one video posted on YouTube in September 2025, which appears to be filmed in Xinjiang, Addison describes the “gorgeous [cotton] fields all around me” and in solely favourable terms describes how technology is being used to boost cotton yields. He adds: “Xinjiang’s cotton story is no longer just about scale, it’s about transformation.” Reform’s deputy leader, Richard Tice, has said the party was concerned about a range of behaviour by the Chinese Communist party, including its threat to Taiwan. “We are very anxious about multiple areas of what China is doing, and I think we need to be much stricter on it,” he told a podcast last year. Tice went on to say that the last Conservative government had been “too permissive” of China and called for the west to make it clear to China it would “come down like a ton of bricks” both militarily and economically. Iain Duncan Smith, one of a number of British MPs and peers targeted by Chinese sanctions, criticised Reform’s engagement of Addison. “There is a question of what due diligence will have been carried out. Everything in China is controlled by the state and if you have someone who has been employed by state media then that means they will have been employed by the state,” he said. Reform was aware of Addison’s work for a Chinese government-controlled media outlet before he was appointed. A spokesperson did not answer specific questions about its vetting process. A Reform spokesperson said: “Reform UK stands by its critical comments regarding China. Ray has worked for a number of British media outlets such as GB News. He has had a successful career in journalism all over the world. Ray Addison has never tried to hide where he has worked, it’s all over the internet and easily found with a Google search.”

title: Nobel laureate Machado: ‘Illegitimate’ Venezuela regime has no right to strike US oil deal
summary: Opposition leader says interim government lacking democratic mandate to negotiate on natural resources
text: The Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado has questioned Donald Trump’s oil deal with Venezuela’s interim government, saying the country’s natural resources do not belong to “an illegitimate regime”. In her first public comments since Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Venezuela last Friday, Machado walked a diplomatic tightrope between challenging the agreement and trying not to rile the White House. In a video posted on social media, the Nobel peace prize winner said: “Of course the United States is the principal partner Venezuela needs to fully develop its strategic potential. This is what the majority of Venezuelans believe … and it is something I’ve spent my whole life defending.” However, Machado said, the current occupants of the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas were “enemies of the US”, saying they did not have the right or the democratic mandate to negotiate Venezuela’s natural resources. “The wealth of our subsoil does not belong to an illegitimate regime – it belongs to the Venezuelan people,” she said, adding that supporters felt “sadness and anger” at being excluded from the decision-making process. Venezuela has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves with an estimated 303bn barrels, of which more than 65bn barrels are involved in the agreement. Trump’s deal was struck with the un-elected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, who took power in January after her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces. Many observers expected Trump to replace Maduro with Machado, a conservative democracy activist who later gave the US president her Nobel prize award. But instead Trump backed Rodríguez, threatening: “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price – probably bigger than Maduro”, and sidelined Machado. The White House claims the oil deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia. Speaking outside the Miraflores palace on Wednesday, the US energy secretary, Chris Wright, said the aim was “to massively grow production and economic opportunities in Venezuela”, adding: “President Trump has a clear mission in Venezuela. The mission is to bring peace, freedom, opportunity, and prosperity to everyone in Venezuela.” But there has been widespread condemnation of what critics call a predatory and colonial-style land grab. Machado’s supporters fear the deal makes Washington far less inclined to push for fresh presidential elections. Machado’s movement is widely believed to have beaten Maduro by a landslide in the last such vote, in 2024, but he refused to accept the result and clung to power until his dramatic rendition on 3 January this year. On Wednesday, Trump and Rodríguez brushed off questions about when an election might be held. “You had a very powerful, very nasty dictatorship in Venezuela – and they’re just not going to be ready for it yet,” Trump told reporters, before adding vaguely: “But soon.” Rodríguez said: “There will be an electoral process, but when Venezuela is ready. “I don’t set dates,” she added.

title: US House passes bill penalizing universities that participate in boycott of Israel
summary: GOP-backed bill mandates institutions receiving federal funds not impose restrictions on programs related to Israel
text: The US House of Representatives on Thursday passed a Republican-backed bill that would penalize universities that participate in boycotts of Israel, or attempt to prevent students from taking part in exchange programs with the country. The Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act passed by a 237-169 vote, with 33 Democrats breaking with the rest of their party to vote in favor, and only two Republicans opposed. It now goes to the Senate for consideration. The measure would require that colleges and universities who participate in federal student aid programs not participate in boycotts of Israel and also mandates that institutions receiving federal funding for international study and foreign language programs certify annually that they do not impose restrictions on their students participating in programs in Israel, or on students from Israel participating in programs on their campuses. House Republican leaders had brought the measure to the floor as they attempt to exploit divisions among Democrats over hot-button issues ahead of the midterm elections, in which voters will decide control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s term. “This legislation is about a simple principle: our colleges and universities should not discriminate against Israel, Israeli institutions or Israeli students, and federal taxpayer dollars should never support institutions that engage in such discrimination,” said Tim Walberg, the Republican chair of the House education committee. After the 7 October attack and Israel’s invasion of Gaza, student and faculty groups at some universities intensified calls for administrators to participate in the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against the country, but were largely unsuccessful. Bobby Scott, the top Democrat on the education committee, criticized the bill as unnecessary and potentially in conflict with first amendment protections of protest. “No college or university has embraced the BDS movement anyway. So, we should combat antisemitism wherever it occurs, but we should not do so by punishing protected speech or conflating a student’s view with university policies,” he said. Democrats who voted for the bill typically face tough re-election contests in November, or are supporters of Israel. Josh Gottheimer, a New Jersey congressman who co-sponsored the legislation with Republican Virginia Foxx, described the proposal as “narrow and tailored” and necessary to combat antisemitism. “No student, no professor should be shut out of research, study abroad opportunities, or academic partnerships or feel unwelcome in the classroom because of where they are from or what religion they practice. Yet that’s exactly what the boycott-divest-sanction movement seeks to do – targeting one country and one religion: Israel and Judaism,” he said. The question of support for Israel has divided House Democrats in recent months. In July, more than 100 House Democrats supported a bill cutting off some military aid to the US ally amid accusations its military’s actions in Gaza constituted a genocide.
