title: Gloria Steinem obituary
summary: Unflinching campaigner for women’s and civil rights who galvanised a generation of activists
text: Gloria Steinem, who has died aged 92, was a writer, community organiser, political campaigner and a charismatic feminist activist who called herself “an entrepreneur of social change”. She spent much of her life on the road, often accompanied by equally committed fellow campaigners. Steinem loathed public speaking, but during two years travelling in India in her 20s, she moved from village to village, with “a sari, a cup and a comb” in a group countering religious intolerance. She said she learned then, as Gandhi taught, that a message was all the more powerful delivered “eye to eye”. Steinem, unlike some of her contemporaries, never recanted or modified her many causes, which included civil rights, violence against women, and the struggle for equality. She continued to argue that every economics course ought to start not with production but with reproduction, and an understanding of the patriarchal instinct to restrict a woman’s right to contraception and abortion. She was one of Donald Trump’s most outspoken critics throughout his rise to power. She labelled him “harasser in chief”, a man whose rhetoric and conduct ran counter to the values she had dedicated her life to advocating. Like many of her generation, Steinem came to feminism at the end of the 1960s. In the early days of the women’s movement, as separatists, socialists, radicals and essentialists deifying the feminine made their arguments, Steinem initially described herself as a humanist. She had had a “vagabond childhood”, living in poverty for several years as the sole carer of her mentally ill and sometimes violent mother, Ruth. Her mother’s indifferent treatment by the male medical profession, Steinem wrote later, fuelled her sense of injustice and put her on the side of the underdog. Steinem lived with the fear that she too might experience mental illness, ending up like her mother “wandering the streets in a night dress”. In 1963, when Betty Friedan published The Feminine Mystique – describing the frustration of affluent, well-educated, middle-class white women trapped in domesticity – Steinem was “a girl reporter” living in New York, working on The Beach Book, a compendium of extracts from literature about beaches and tips on what to do in the sun. A rising media star who was later described, to her annoyance, as “the world’s most beautiful byline”, she had already begun to make connections: she asked the economist JK Galbraith to write the foreword, and he agreed. For another journalistic assignment that year, she spent three weeks undercover as a Playboy bunny for Show magazine, detailing the poor conditions and humiliations of wearing satin rabbit ears and a fluffy tail. The resulting article, A Bunny’s Tale, made her name. Steinem became a highly paid writer for magazines including McCall’s and Glamour, and interviewed, among others, Gore Vidal, James Baldwin and Paul Newman, as well as taking on “girl writer” tasks such as analysing textured stockings for the New York Times. Concurrently she was politically active, campaigning and fundraising for, among other causes, the anti-Vietnam war movement, the Democrat George McGovern’s campaign for the presidency, and Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta’s battle for fair wages for migrant farm workers. As Steinem later wrote, she was “working on one thing and caring about another”. In 1968, the millionaire Clay Felker launched New York magazine, and hired Steinem to write a political column, The City Politic. A year later, she attended a “speak out”, organised by the radical feminist group the Redstockings, at which women spoke about their illegal abortions. As Steinem later put it, she felt “a big click”. Women were not to blame, but a sexist and misogynistic system that forced them to have dangerous terminations. The humanist had become a feminist. “Once the light began to dawn I couldn’t understand why I hadn’t figured out any of this before,” she said. Later that year, in New York magazine, she wrote the landmark article After Black Power, Women’s Liberation. Steinem was born in Toledo, Ohio, a second daughter for Ruth (nee Nuneviller) and Leo Steinem. Leo owned a summer resort in Clark Lake, Michigan, where swing bands would play. In the winter, the family took to the road in a trailer. Leo bought and sold antiques and used the children to charm away the debt collectors. In My Life on the Road (2015), Steinem said it was the equal relationship she had had with her father – for all his irresponsibility towards his family – that provided the foundation for the strong friendships and love affairs she later had with men including the film director Mike Nichols and the jazz musician Paul Desmond. Gloria’s mother had been a reporter on the Toledo Blade, sometimes writing under the name Duncan Mackenzie. When her first daughter, Susanne, was six, and a few years before Gloria’s birth, Ruth had a nervous breakdown and never worked again. She spent time in a series of psychiatric hospitals, and became addicted to a sedative called chloral hydrate. When Gloria was 10 her parents separated, her sister went to college, and she was left alone with her mother, occasionally receiving $50 from her nomadic father. In Ruth’s Song (Because She Could Not Sing It), one of the essays in her 1983 collection Outrageous Acts and Everyday Rebellions, Steinem described the woman who had “lived too little”, but who had encouraged her daughters to get an education and learn the meaning of choice. Steinem laid no blame. “I knew my mother loved me, but she couldn’t take care of me.” Steinem majored in government at Smith College, Massachusetts, and in 1956, a year after Sylvia Plath, she graduated with distinction. In a stopover in Britain on the way to India and an academic scholarship, she had an illegal abortion aged 22. On her return to the US in the 1960s, she began to build a reputation as a journalist. In 1962, the year Helen Gurley Brown published Sex and the Single Girl, encouraging women to become financially independent and not wait for a wedding ring to take lovers, Steinem wrote an article for Esquire titled The Moral Disarmament of Betty Coed. Still not identifying with women’s liberation, she wrote perceptively: “The problem is that many girls … who depend on the roles of wife and mother for their total identity are being pressured into affairs they can’t handle and jobs they pretend to like.” By 1970, at Vassar College, New York, at the first of what were to be many commencement speeches given to graduating students, she showed an acute understanding of the depth of conditioning: “Our first problem is not to learn … but to unlearn,” she said, and “woman means submission, black means inferior … preconceptions embedded so deeply in our thinking we may not know they are there.” The women’s movement advocated no leaders, so some fellow activists were incensed when the media appointed Steinem as chief spokesperson. Her streaked blond hair, aviator glasses, wit, soft-voiced calm and miniskirts appealed. In 1975, the Redstockings claimed that Steinem had been “meteorically installed” as the leader of the movement by the CIA. Steinem had briefly co-founded a CIA-financed organisation, Independent Research Service, in the late 50s when, she said, the CIA was among the good guys. Unlike contemporaries such as Germaine Greer, Shulamith Firestone and Kate Millett, Steinem never wrote a seminal work, but she was a powerful polemicist, funny and had a way with words that her critics found too pat. “The human race is like a bird with two wings,” she said, in one of thousands of lectures. “If one wing is broken, the bird can’t fly.” Steinem fretted all her life that the media opted for trivialisation when it came to reporting what she saw as one of the greatest social changes in history, the rise of second-wave feminism, which led to changes, as the New York Times put it, from the boardroom to the courtroom to the bedroom. (The first wave was in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.) In 1971, Steinem helped to found the National Women’s Political Caucus, which encouraged women to run for political office. In the same year, Esquire published The Awesome Power of Gloria Steinem, largely an analysis of her impact on men. In a comment that was emblematic of the casual sexism of the time, the talkshow host David Susskind said: “What Gloria needs is a man.” In 1971, Steinem co-founded Ms, the first magazine owned and run by women. Critics predicted it would sell fewer than 20,000 copies. The first issue, published that December as part of New York magazine, sold 300,000 copies, sold out in eight days and attracted tens of thousands of subscriptions. Steinem said she would stay for two years, but in fact did not leave until the magazine was sold to Fairfax in 1987 – later she was part of the Liberty Media group that took it back into independent ownership. Ms had numerous internal battles about how radical it should be and funding was a constant struggle, since advertisers wary of articles such as If Men Could Menstruate shunned it. Later it went ad-free. When Steinem turned 50, in 1984, a birthday gala was held at the Waldorf Astoria in New York. Dinner was $250 a head – it was yet another fundraiser for her causes – and among Steinem’s friends in attendance were Jackie Kennedy Onassis and Betty Ford. Two years later Steinem was diagnosed with breast cancer. She subsequently suggested she had “burned out”. She went into therapy to discover why she had spent a lifetime as, she said, “Ms Fix-it”, avoiding confrontation, resistant to introspection, constantly on the move, battling a fear of overeating. Her next book was Revolution from Within: A Book of Self-Esteem (1992), for which she received a $700,000 advance. Critics worried that the book’s references to Steinem’s inner child meant the personal had become more important than the political; that psychobabble had taken over from protest. But her activism, apparently reinforced by meditation and visualisation, continued robustly. She went on supporting the Ms Foundation for Women and in 2005 co-founded the Women’s Media Center, to improve women’s representation in the media. As she said: “If you can’t see it, you can’t be it.” As Steinem’s official biographer, Carolyn G Heilbrun, said in The Education of a Woman (1995), Steinem was a woman of contradictions: the feminist photographed in a bubble bath; the loner who was always in the spotlight; the compassionate listener who seemed accessible to no one; the person who hated to offend – but who still offended many, including full-time housewives, anti-abortionists and Friedan. Friedan accused Steinem of attracting what she called “the lavender menace”, lesbians, to the cause. She said Steinem was from the “bra-burning, anti-men, ‘politics of orgasm’” school of feminism. In turn, Steinem lightly mocked the plight of rich, white, middle-class women suffering from “the problem that has no name”. It might be painful, Steinem said, but you didn’t die of it. Ironically, several decades later, during the 2008 race for the Democratic presidential candidacy, Steinem controversially gave her support not to the black outsider Barack Obama, but to Hillary Clinton, the ultimate example of the white, privileged woman. In 1998 in a newspaper column, she also defended Bill Clinton against sexual allegations, to the confusion of many of her supporters. In 2000, Steinem married David Bale, an entrepreneur and animal-rights activist. She said they married because he was South African and needed a visa. Later she wrote: “He … loved me out of old ruts and patterns and choices.” He died in 2003. Steinem’s sister, Susanne, died in 2007. In 2013, Obama presented Steinem with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, one of many awards she received during her life. A year later, Rutgers University established a chair in her name to fund teaching and research into equal representation in the media. Until her death, she continued to travel, lecture and organise with a family of female friends. She gave the New York home that was her sanctuary to Gloria’s Foundation as a place for women to meet, speak out and organise. The latest of her books, An Unexpected Life, is due to be published later this month. In an interview with the New York Times in 2022, she was asked her view on women’s progress towards equality. “I feel proud,” she said. “And I feel mad as hell we are still dealing with the same old issues.” • Gloria Marie Steinem, feminist, writer and civil rights campaigner, born 25 March 1934; died 2 September 2026

title: EU’s ability to defend against invasion remains in doubt, finds official report
summary: Fragmented infrastructure and reliance on US continue to hinder ‘defence readiness’, says European court of auditors
text: The EU’s ability to respond to a foreign invasion by 2030 remains in doubt due to a continuing reliance on the US and fragmented national defence systems, according to a report from its official auditor. The European court of auditors (ECA) said the EU was much better prepared than before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine of 2022, but achieving its goal of defence readiness by the end of the decade would be difficult. “Achieving defence preparedness in the EU by 2030 remains challenging,” said Marek Opioła, an ECA member who led the review of the EU’s defence policy published on Thursday. “There are still major difficulties such as fragmented national systems or industrial bottlenecks. We also still rely on the United States.” Speaking to the Guardian, he stressed the EU could “still make major progress” if it sharply increased defence spending and rapidly expanded ammunition production. Between 2020 and 2025, EU member states increased defence spending by 79%, a response to the Russian threat and a belated effort to meet Nato spending targets. In November 2024, the EU met its pledge of providing 1 million rounds of ammunition to Ukraine – eight months behind schedule. The EU set the goal of defence readiness by 2030 last year, after intelligence services warned that Russia could be ready to wage a large-scale war in Europe around that time. The bloc’s financial watchdog said major difficulties had to be overcome to reach this target, defined by a senior auditor as “having strategic autonomy” and “the ability to independently sustain high-intensity warfare”. The senior auditor said the EU was better prepared than 2019 when a similar review was conducted, but warned that fragmented national defence industries and “insufficient cooperation” between EU governments contributed to a risk of duplication in spending or persistent gaps in military capabilities. Emblematic of the dysfunction – although not mentioned in the report – is France and Germany’s decision to abandon a €100bn project to build a joint fighter jet, because the lead companies were unable to resolve disputes over leadership and control. The report highlighted a possible tension between short-term battlefield needs and a “Buy European” policy that aims to reduce dependencies on foreign suppliers. Between February 2022 and June 2023, 78% of EU governments’ defence acquisitions were sourced outside the bloc, with the US alone representing 63%, according to one study cited by the ECA. The senior auditor said purchases from the US went up after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine “which was understandable because the EU needed to find capabilities that were available quickly”. The official added that “early signs of improvement in that situation” were visible, although the auditors did not have complete data to draw conclusions. The EU has set requirements that common defence spending should benefit domestic defence industries or those of closely-associated countries, such as Ukraine and Norway. But some flexibilities have been allowed where Europe is unable to produce critical supplies in time. After a brutal summer of deadly Russian missile and drone attacks, this week Ukraine asked for an exemption from Buy European procurement rules to acquire US-made Patriot interceptors using the EU’s €90bn support loan. The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said on Wednesday that Ukraine had requested funding “worth several billion euros” for air defences, including Patriot air-defence systems. A commission spokesperson said Ukraine’s request for Patriot interceptor missiles “would require a derogation” from rules requiring majority European content in military purchases under the loan. “The final say is with the member states and of course our hope would be that this would soon be granted,” the spokesperson said. The senior auditor said sometimes “it may make sense” to buy outside “when you have a short-term urgent need”. The person added: “Even if you buy something that you don’t have in-house, you [should] always have a plan how to develop that critical capacity in the long-term within the European Union.”

title: Kemi the Valkyrie spoils for a fight and has the Russians in her sights | John Crace
summary: Tory leader scents Labour weakness on defence spending and declares it’s 2030 or bust
text: There’s something about Kemi Badenoch making a keynote speech – everything she does comes billed as keynote these days – about defence that makes most normal people a little nervous. Because when Kemi talks about defence, what’s really on her mind is war. Starting one, if possible. Kemi is never happier than when picking a fight. With herself, if no one else is around. You get the feeling that, left on a desert island she would be dreaming of Apocalypse Now. Flying low over the Mekong delta in a helicopter gunship, the Ride of the Valkyries playing through her earphones while she yelled: “I love the smell of napalm in the morning.” Still, you can’t blame an opposition leader for opportunism. It’s the crumbs they live off. And the Tories reckon they have identified a Labour weakness. John Healey resigned as defence secretary a few months back over Keir Starmer’s reluctance to come up with a plan of spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030. Now that Andy Burnham has appointed him chancellor, Healey seems suddenly rather reluctant to make the commitment he was asking of Rachel Reeves. Much happier to be pushed back to the longer-term goal of 3.5% by 2035, with the heavy lifting being done sometime, maybe never, after the next election. There are some decisions politicians choose to defer indefinitely. It’s possible Healey will surprise us all and announce he is resigning again in protest at his own refusal to meet the 2030 target. But as of today he’s still very much in No 11 and, after some confusion at Wednesday’s prime minister’s questions, the government position is the 2035 deadline. So Kemi and a few members of her shadow cabinet decamped to the slightly surreal setting of Scotland House London – the inside looks like a greenhouse and is about as sweaty – to tell the country it was 2030 or bust. If we delayed any longer, we would all be dead. If the Russians didn’t kill us, she would. The future of the world depended on her. Andrew Griffith, Kemi’s new shadow chancellor, made the introductions. You’d have imagined he might be a little embarrassed about his part in writing the Liz Truss mini-budget and his vociferous support for it thereafter, but he isn’t a man much given to self-reflection. Rather, it’s as though he imagines he is doing us all a favour by sharing his brilliance. He started by paying tribute to his predecessor. Poor Mel Stride. Loyal but expendable. Kemi has just revealed her full shadow ministerial team and The Melster is about the only Tory MP not included in Kemi’s new shadow ministerial team. Then came Kemi. Wake up, peeps, she said. We were as good as at war already. Cyber-attacks. Russian drones on Leipzig airport. A Russian attack on a Nato country nailed on for the next few years. She marvelled at Poland for its 300,000-strong army. That was the kind of country she wanted to lead. She forgot to mention that if she had been prime minister we would probably have been at war earlier this year. She had been all for joining Donald Trump’s war on Iran. It could have been us who killed some women and children at a wedding party this week. What an opportunity missed. It was all very black and white. If we spent 3% we would all definitely be safe. The Russians and other hostile countries would immediately back off. But a penny less and they would attack for sure. They could spot weakness. So Kemi was preparing for war. She would not shy away from sending men and women to possibly pointless deaths. There would be many more corners of foreign fields that would be forever England. Just as arbitrary was how this was all to be paid for. It’s almost become axiomatic in rightwing circles that the extra money for defence should be found by cutting the welfare bill. In other words, it’s the poorest and most vulnerable people who will be funding the military. This drew applause from the large audience. All of whom looked as though they were quite comfortably off and would therefore be spared the pain of making any sacrifices themselves. Which is exactly how they like it. That’s what makes them proud to be British. When it came to the details of where the savings were to be made, Kemi came over all vague. Mumble, mumble. Moving on. Though most of us could have sworn that some of the cuts had already been announced last year and that she was effectively trying to spend the same money twice. But Kemi was adamant that Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, had been all over the details and that nothing had been left to chance. Which wasn’t quite as reassuring as Kemi had hoped. There was also a commitment to save the money from a Chagos deal that had yet to be agreed and hadn’t even been spent. If I filled in my tax return with such creativity, HMRC would have some questions. But it’s the leader of the opposition and none of this may ever happen so none of this really matters. Kemi ended with a sneer at cheaper bus fares – why can’t people take taxis – and a whole list of taxes she would either abolish or cut. Weirdly, she didn’t think to end the pension triple lock, which most economists think is the only sane thing to do. The audience wouldn’t have been so keen on that. All this was said with an effortless confidence. Even when she was talking nonsense and contradicting herself. I guess you could call that Kemi’s USP. Her answers to questions about why anyone should bother to listen – when it had been the Tories who had hollowed out the defence budget over the past 14 years – varied from the peace dividend, to everyone had done it, to it had been nothing to do with her and the Conservatives were starting again from scratch. Ground zero does a lot of heavy lifting for Kemi these days. On one thing she was clear. Are we going to war? asked a reporter from the Express. Hell, yeah, said Kemi. Just watch me. She wouldn’t rest until every child could sleep safe in their bed while missiles were raining down across Britain. It was just a shame that for some kids, those beds might no longer be their own. Kicked out of their homes and forced into insecure accommodation the councils can’t afford. Still, I guess they can get used to a cardboard box. That will teach them to adopt welfare as a lifestyle.

title: Manchester synagogue attack: ministers seek to block MI5 files from inquest
summary: Government lawyers tell coroner disclosing intelligence would pose serious risk to national security
text: Ministers are seeking to block intelligence material from being heard at an inquest into the death of two men killed in the 2025 Manchester synagogue attack. Lawyers for Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, told a coroner on Thursday that disclosing the MI5 files would pose a serious risk to national security. Melvin Cravitz, 66, died as a result of multiple knife wounds inflicted by the attacker, Jihad al-Shamie. Adrian Daulby, 53, was killed by a single police gunshot wound as he held the building’s doors shut against the terrorist. A senior coroner is due to examine the deaths of the two men at the Heaton Park Hebrew synagogue on 2 October last year during Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. The full inquest will focus on al-Shamie’s background, as well as what the state knew about him before the attack. It will also examine security at the synagogue, the role of the state in assessing the risks to the Jewish community in Greater Manchester, and the response to the attack. Mahmood told the Commons on 13 October that al-Shamie was “never referred to the Prevent programme, nor was he known to counter-terrorism policing or the security services”. At a pre-inquest review on Thursday, barristers for the families of Cravitz and Daulby said they were concerned that the emergence of MI5 material “may contradict” that statement. Anna Morris KC, representing Daulby’s family, said there had been a “demonstrable lack of candour” by the security services in other proceedings, including the inquiry into the Manchester Arena attack. She said Daulby’s family were “concerned that this application [by the Home Office] and the information behind it may contradict statements made public by security services and counter-terrorism police that the suspect was not known to counter-terrorism police”. The deaths of Daulby and Cravitz are being examined by Alexia Durran, the chief coroner of England and Wales, at Manchester coroner’s court. Edward Pleeth, counsel to the inquest, told the hearing the government was seeking to withhold “potentially relevant security sensitive material held by MI5” and “potentially relevant security sensitive material held by counter-terrorism police”. Pleeth said this unspecified material was judged by the government to “cause serious harm to national security” if it was disclosed publicly. He said the inquest legal team was satisfied that the information was so sensitive it could not be aired even in a redacted form. There was “no adequate alternative to complete non-disclosure”, Pleeth said, describing the concerns about its disclosure as “well-evidenced”. Durran is now considering whether to ask the government to convert the inquest into a statutory public inquiry to allow the MI5 material to be heard in private. Unlike public inquiries, coroner’s inquests cannot legally consider evidence given in secret hearings. Neil Sheldon KC, representing the Home Office, described the MI5 material as a “discrete body of information” that had been “identified as relevant and has the potential to impact the inquest”. The application to block the information from being heard publicly was not an “extreme approach” but was “cogent, compelling and supported by detailed analysis”, he told the court. Victoria Ailes, representing Cravitz’s family, said his family had “questions in this entire area” and were concerned that this new material came after “statements by the secretary of state to the House of Commons [that al-Shamie] was not known to counter-terrorism police or the security services”. Al-Shamie, a Syrian-born UK citizen, launched the attack while wearing what seemed to be a suicide vest. Before police arrived, the 35-year-old called 999 and pledged allegiance to Islamic State. Last month, a man who conducted hostile reconnaissance at a military base alongside al-Shamie was jailed for life with a minimum term of 16 years, after admitting preparing acts of terror. Mohammad Asim Bashir, 31, and al-Shamie travelled by car to the UK Defence Academy in Shrivenham, Swindon, in August last year, two months before the synagogue attack. Bashir was identified when counter-terrorism officers searched al-Shamie’s mobile devices after the Heaton Park attack. However, Greater Manchester police said last month that officers had seized his phones months earlier in 2025 after unrelated arrests, but that they were not examined until after the attack. Another man, Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim, was charged on 21 August with failing to disclose information in relation to the synagogue attack. Hakim, 49, pleaded not guilty at Westminster magistrates court. He is due to attend a hearing at the Old Bailey on 25 September.

title: Aid operations in aftermath of deadly Nepal floods hampered by conditions | First Thing
summary: Guardian reporters in Nepal have witnessed first-hand the scenes of destruction and grief after the flash floods
text: Good morning. Thousands remain missing and the delivery of aid has been hampered by treacherous conditions in communities almost wiped out of existence by the flash flooding in Nepal and Tibet. A week after the disaster, survivors who fled up mountainsides are still being collected by army helicopters and evacuated. The mountain village of Syabru Besi was among those destroyed, with even the road to the village gone. According to local government officials, at least 500 people there are missing, a quarter of the population. Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Gaurav Pokharel have been in the Betrawati and Rasuwa districts with the photographer Ahmer Khan. In this video, Ellis-Petersen explains what she has seen alongside haunting footage of the debris. They have spoken to multiple survivors in a region now full of human suffering. Israel Katz said there was “no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration”. Child sexual abuse survivor alleges Elon Musk’s AI chatbot used photos of her to generate new illegal images A survivor of child sexual abuse has sued Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company, alleging that its Grok chatbot used pictures of her abuse to generate new illegal pornographic images that depict her. But here, because you can associate it with the series, we know that it is an identifiable victim who is still alive and was a real child in the photo.” Neither xAI or SpaceX, which acquired the company in February, returned requests for comment regarding the lawsuit. The Trump administration is supporting OpenAI in ⁠a lawsuit against the New York Times, arguing in favor of the use of copyrighted writing to train AI. In a brief filed to the court, the Trump administration said: “The US has a strong interest in continuing to develop a robust and competitive artificial intelligence industry.” JD Vance says he’s doing ‘God’s work – and if that leads to the end times, OK’ JD Vance has said he was “doing as much of God’s work as possible” and that he was OK “if that leads to the end times”, which he says “are coming”. The US vice-president made the comments during a podcast interview with Bryce Crawford, a 22-year-old evangelical host. Vance said: “I think there are things about the world that make me feel, like, not shocked if the antichrist was walking among us.” He pointed to AI, using the example of an acquaintance who uses AI as a marriage counselor, which he described as “kind of satanic”. Vance, who published a spiritual memoir earlier this summer about his conversion to Catholicism, said: “I think you got to just kinda try and have an attitude of: the end times may be coming, in fact they are coming, it’s just a question of whether they’re coming thousands of years down the road, or a few months down the road.” In other news … Cassandra Wilson, a Grammy-winning jazz singer, has died aged 70. Labelled the US’s best singer by Time magazine in 2001, Wilson was best known for her genre-bending voice. Google has defeated the US justice department’s attempt to force it to sell some of its ad technology in a win for the firm against US antitrust enforcers’ attempts to break up big tech. The clothing company Patagonia has joined a lawsuit challenging Donald Trump’s decision to reduce the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments in Utah. title: BoM forecasts strongest El Niño on record as research points to ‘alarming’ climate change influence
summary: Bureau of Meteorology suggests El Niño has already broken records, with Pacific Ocean temperature change exceeding 2C in six months
text: The growing El Niño weather phenomenon to Australia’s east is already breaking heat records, with forecasts showing it may easily surpass previous events, according to Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology. Separate research suggests climate change has greatly shortened the odds of the event hitting record extremes. On Thursday, the UN’s weather agency said the event in the Pacific was continuing to strengthen and would probably persist until early 2027, warning it had the “potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world”. The UN secretary general, António Guterres, said: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.” In an update this week, the Bureau of Meteorology said the El Niño was now forecast to peak in late spring or summer and “reach levels above the warmest observed since reliable records began in 1950”. El Niño events tend to mean hotter and drier conditions for Australia’s south and east in winter and spring, and can increase the risk of heatwaves, drought and bushfires. El Niño strength is assessed by analysing sea surface temperatures in a region of the equatorial Pacific known as Niño 3.4. The bureau has said the strength of an El Niño does not necessarily mean stronger effects for the continent. However, bureau analysis of the unfolding event suggested this El Niño had already broken records. “We have been looking at the rate of warming observed in the last two months and it has been faster than any other event. Not only is it strong, but it has escalated rapidly,” said Felicity Gamble, a senior climatologist at the BoM. Gamble said the relative sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region for the month of August were likely to be between 2.2C and 2.3C above average – higher than any previous August since 1950 (the year after which records are considered to be more reliable). Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletter She said forecasts were suggesting relative sea surface temperatures in that region could peak over 3C above average, compared with the highest previous figure of 2.6C observed in January 1983. Gamble said the relative sea surface temperatures in the Niño 3.4 region had warmed by more than 2C between February and July. She said: “No other period in the historical record exceeds that. This is the first event where we have had that change exceed 2C in the space of six months. “We could be seeing a record in terms of the strength, and also the rate of warming and the duration.” Climate experts have said El Niño will likely combine with climate change to push global temperatures to record highs next year. Gamble said in the Pacific region El Niño was already contributing to droughts in Papua New Guinea, with food and water shortages and major wildfires in Indonesia. This winter was Australia’s third-warmest on record and the hottest on record for New South Wales, Tasmania and Victoria. Scientists at the University of Melbourne have released preliminary research into the influence of climate change on the predicted peak of El Niño. By analysing historical records and comparing climate models with and without the influence of greenhouse gas emissions, the scientists found climate change had made “an event of this magnitude” six times more likely. The study has been submitted to a journal for peer review, but the authors said they had used a methodology common to many other published studies. Dr Andrew King, one of the co-authors of the research, said: “This points to the fact that there is likely a climate change role here in the chance of having these extreme El Niño conditions. It seems likely there is a human fingerprint emerging in this event. “We are seeing something that does not appear to have happened before and that is alarming.” The bureau’s long-range forecast for September to November points to an increased chance of below average rainfall for the south and east, but above average for most of the continent’s western half. Temperatures are also likely to be above average south of the tropics.

title: US commerce secretary erroneously said no Americans have died in Iran war, Trump claims
summary: President said Howard Lutnick had Venezuela operation on his mind when he was discussing Iran war on CNBC
text: Donald Trump has claimed his commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, erroneously stated that no Americans had been killed in the war with Iran because he was thinking about a previous US operation, in Venezuela. The claim, at odds with the Pentagon’s count of 18 US service members dead in the US-Israel war on Iran, sparked a swift backlash as Trump struggles to end the conflict after six months. In a post on his Truth Social platform on Thursday, the US president wrote: “Sec. Lutnick had Venezuela on his mind when he said nobody was killed. 18 people were killed in Iran!” The rebuke came a day after Lutnick appeared on CNBC’s Squawk Box and framed the Trump administration’s approach to Iran as primarily economic. Describing the strategy as an “economic choke-out”, he erroneously told the network there had not been American deaths in the conflict, adding that he was optimistic bond markets would respond well to the approach. Lutnick this morning acknowledged the mistake, posting on X that he had misspoken and also claiming he had been thinking of the US operation in Venezuela, where US forces captured Nicolás Maduro in January with minimal US casualties. The Pentagon said seven US troops were injured and none were killed in that operation, while Venezuelan officials put their overall death toll at 47, and Cuba said 32 of its military and police personnel were killed. Trump’s post landed as Iranian authorities detailed heavy casualties from the latest US strikes. Iran’s health ministry said Tuesday night’s strikes killed 18 people and wounded 108, while the country’s Red Crescent identified that four people were killed and 67 wounded when a US strike hit a wedding ceremony near the coast of the strait of Hormuz, which also killed a child. Reuters said it was able to verify the location of the damaged building using satellite imagery. A US Central Command spokesperson, Capt Tim Hawkins, said the US military does not target civilians and that the reports, which originated with Iranian state media, were being reviewed. The strikes were part of a broader operation that Central Command said hit Iranian air defense systems, radar installations, maritime assets, mine-laying equipment and communications sites near the strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway through which a large share of the world’s oil passes. The Pentagon’s capacity to independently verify such claims has been sharply reduced. Its Civilian Protection Center of Excellence has been cut from 40 staff to nine since the start of last year, according to the Pentagon’s own inspector general, while the department has also stopped developing a database meant to track civilian harm from US operations. The episode has exposed a wider tension in how the White House is presenting the conflict. Officials have sought to characterize the campaign (estimated to have cost at least $37.5bn as of July) against Iran in economic terms even as it continues to produce US military deaths, mounting Iranian civilian casualties and rising oil prices. Polling from UMass-Amherst in late August found that 54% of Americans disapprove of the war initiated by the US and Israel, and one in six Trump voters would go back and change their vote in 2024. The current round of fighting began after the US struck rocket launchers on Larak Island that officials said were being prepared to mine the strait, prompting Iranian missile and drone attacks on US and allied positions in Jordan, Bahrain, Kuwait and Iraq. Jordanian authorities said 13 ballistic missiles were fired at the country, of which 10 were intercepted. Trump described Iran’s retaliation as a “love tap”, but warned that further strikes remained an option. “It was a very heavy attack last night, and we’re prepared to do another one anytime we want,” he said earlier this week.

title: Yen soars as Bank of Japan tipped to raise interest rates
summary: Jump lifts currency to highest level against dollar in a month, while global markets remain jittery
text: The Japanese yen has soared by more than 2% against the dollar amid speculation the Bank of Japan is set to raise interest rates. The latest jump on Thursday lifted the yen to its highest level against the dollar in a month, at 155.57, and followed a 0.9% move the previous day. Global markets remain jittery after this week’s dramatic government bond sell-off – caused by fears of a fresh inflation increase as a result of higher oil prices. Investors have been reassessing their expectations for the future path of interest rates, in Japan and across other major economies. Remarks by a Bank of Japan policymaker, Hajime Takata, suggesting it needs to move more “nimbly”, appeared to have heightened the prospects of a decisive move. The chief executive of the financial adviser deVere, Nigel Green, said the scale of the yen appreciation over such a short time period underlined the febrile state of markets. “Markets this jumpy don’t need a shock to move hard, a rumour is enough,” he said. Citi said in a note to clients that Takata’s remarks were the “strongest messaging we’ve heard from the board and reintroduces the idea of an expedited rate hike trajectory”. The Bank of Japan has been incrementally raising rates for the past two years, after the economy finally shrugged off decades of deflation, or falling prices – but its main policy rate was left unchanged at 1% in July. Markets now believe there is a 77% chance of a rate rise at the BoJ’s next meeting, which starts on 17 September. Commenting on the latest market moves, Japan’s vice-finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, said he was “neither satisfied nor reassured”, and policymakers “remain on a state of heightened alert”. The global bond market sell-off – pushing up the yield, or interest rate, on government borrowing – intensified earlier this week after the US Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, used a speech last Friday to indicate that he was determined to bring inflation back to target. Warsh had previously baffled some investors by withdrawing the Fed’s approach of signalling future rate moves, known as “forward guidance” – but in Friday’s speech at the central bankers’ conference in Jackson Hole, he said that if inflation did not move towards the 2% target the Fed would have “more to do”. The dollar weakened on Thursday after the Fed governor Christopher Waller indicated he was leaning towards keeping interest rates steady at this month’s meeting of Fed rate-setters. “I’m going to paraphrase John Lennon here: ‘give disinflation a chance’. We can wait one meeting,” Waller told Reuters. The dollar dropped further against the yen after his comments, and was also weaker against the pound and the euro. The bond sell-off appeared to have eased on Thursday, with yields on 10-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hovering at about 5.1% in morning trading – having touched the highest level since 2008, close to 5.3%, earlier this week.

title: Rise of far-right leader Roberto Vannacci challenges Meloni as she celebrates Italian milestone
summary: Futuro Nazionale party’s speedy poll rise poses questions whether PM will return to her roots before election
text: Giorgia Meloni’s government has become the longest-running in Italy since the second world war – a milestone the prime minister is determined not to let pass unnoticed. In the port area of Bari, the capital of the southern Italian region of Puglia, where Meloni hosted the G7 in 2024 and where she spends her summer holiday, preparations are well under way for a festival-style showcase of her rightwing administration. On Friday, there will be food trucks, water stations and traditional Puglian light shows as part of celebrations to entertain an expected crowd of 10,000 people bussed in from across Italy. Militants from the youth wing of Meloni’s far-right Brothers of Italy party have fanned the city’s squares and beaches for days, handing out flyers promoting the celebrations while wearing T-shirts featuring the official slogan: Il Governo più stabile, l’Italia più forte (the most stable government, the strongest Italy). Meloni, who just a few weeks ago was booed at the opening ceremony of the Mediterranean Games in Taranto, farther south in Puglia, will address the audience in the evening, surrounded by her coalition allies – Matteo Salvini, the leader of the far-right League, and the conservative Forza Italia’s Antonio Tajani. “This moment will be written in the history books,” said Michele Picaro, a Brothers of Italy MEP and former Bari councillor. “We are the longest government in the history of the Italian Republic and this must be celebrated.” Beneath the triumph, however, the outlook for Meloni is less settled. True, she has enjoyed a political stability that eluded her predecessors. Brothers of Italy is still the country’s biggest party. But in recent months, the political landscape has shifted with the emergence of a challenger – not from the left or the centre, but from someone who is even further to the right than Meloni. Since its launch in February, Roberto Vannacci, a former army general, has seen his far-right party, Futuro Nazionale, rise to about 8% in the polls, surpassing his former compatriots in the League months ago and this week eclipsing Forza Italia, too. Vannacci first entered the public eye in 2023 after self-publishing a book filled with racism, homophobia, Islamophobia and antisemitism. The subsequent backlash cost him his army job, but propelled him to the top of the bestsellers list. Helped along by ample coverage in the Italian press, he capitalised on the notoriety and in 2024 was elected as an MEP for the League, later leaving Salvini’s party to set up his own. “I read his book because I always think you need to know the enemy,” said Giulia Pastorella, an MP and vice-president of the small centrist party Azione (Action). “And I thought, this is exactly the kind of thing you might hear people talking about in the bar. Here’s a military man, who is really a mirror of the worst impulses of people. The scary thing is, I think he’s genuine and not a PR construct.” Vannacci’s policies, such as they are, are extreme. Futuro Nazionale’s recently published manifesto says that “abortion is not a right” and calls for gay people to be banned from TV between 6am and 11pm so children aren’t exposed to what it describes as “homosexualist” content. It also proposes introducing military education in high schools and a “remigration” plan to remove irregular immigrants and foreign nationals who commit crimes. On foreign policy, Vannacci has campaigned to stop weapons and financial aid to Ukraine, saying if he could choose between Vladimir Putin or the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he would choose Putin. In July, he organised a “Futuristic Triathlon” in the northern seaside town of Sanremo, billed as an event to “temper the mind and body” in an echo of the fascist aesthetics and themes of the Mussolini era. Far from being a treated as a pariah, however, Vannacci’s party has proved moderately successful, luring defectors from the three main ruling coalition parties. It is also actively courting disillusioned voters from the Five Star Movement, a key ally in a broad but perennially fractious leftwing coalition led by the Democratic party. For the government, he represents a dilemma. Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy has neofascist roots, has governed more moderately than many had expected, cultivating a pragmatic and, crucially, pro-Ukraine image abroad while still deploying hardline rhetoric on choice occasions for domestic audiences. That positioning, however, has left a vacuum on the far right that Vannacci has exploited. The question now is: how will Meloni respond? Until now her ruling coalition had mostly coasted along, propped up by a strong parliamentary majority. Her government is largely regarded to have been fiscally prudent, but has steered clear of major structural reforms. Instead, it has heavily focused on security and continues to vigorously expand legislation on law and order. “This government has wasted the huge occasion that stability gave them,” said Lia Quartapelle, an MP with the Democratic party. “None of the core issues have been addressed – we have stagnant productivity and growth, salaries that have lagged behind for many years and an education system that is not up to the pace.” Pastorella said a focus on foreign policy had also contributed to Vannacci’s success. “Meloni hasn’t really done much at home but has been very present abroad,” she added. “The Italian electorate is tired of talking about foreign policy and would rather discuss national politics – this is precisely what Vannacci has understood.” Picaro batted away questions about recent polls. “This is a government that is more used to working than looking at percentages,” he said, citing lower unemployment, reduced irregular immigration, cutting taxes for the self-employed and an initiative in the south to boost entrepreneurial investment. Pastorella said that, far from being strong and stable, Meloni had struggled to keep her coalition united while dealing with various scandals, including ones that led to a tourism and a culture minister being forced to resign. With the possibility of an election as early as April, time is now of the essence for the prime minister. In recent weeks she has pivoted back to hardline rhetoric, most notably in her reaction to the influx of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta. She is also trying to push through a highly contentious electoral law that would give a majority bonus to any alliance winning more than 42% of the vote, which critics say is aimed at increasing her group’s chance of victory. If Vannacci continues to strengthen, Meloni might be tempted to accommodate him before the vote, a move that would risk repelling moderate supporters. Or she could clinch a post-election pact to maintain power, resulting in what many both inside and outside Italy would see as a frightening shift to the extreme right. As government supporters head to Bari, Alessandro Cattaneo, an MP with Forza Italia, thinks it won’t come to that. “We in Forza Italia believe that Vannacci is too far removed from our political culture,” he said. “It would not be possible to govern with him … the coalition needs to continue to work seriously for the remainder of this administration and explain better to people what we have done. The best antidote to the extreme right is to show our seriousness.”

title: Iran targets US bases as Israel warns sanctions could drive Tehran to ‘desperate steps’
summary: Air bases used by US in UAE and Kuwait hit as Israeli defence chief says Iran’s regime fears collapse due to economic pressures
text: Iran has continued to demonstrate an ability to target bases in the Gulf used by the US despite six months of war and a new sanctions regime described by the Trump administration as an “economic D-day”. As Iran’s military targeted US bases in the United Arab Emirates and Kuwait, despite threats of further strikes by the US president, Israel’s defence chief warned that economic pressures from the sanctions could lead Tehran to escalate to more “extreme measures”. “This morning, the army hit the satellite communication systems, equipment depots and fighter aircraft hangars of the terrorist US army at the Ahmad al-Jaber air base in Kuwait with missiles and drones,” the Iranian military said on Thursday in a statement carried by state television. The “location of forces and radar systems of the child-killing US army at the Al Minhad air base in the UAE were also attacked by missiles and drones of the army”, it added. In a post on X, Kuwait’s ministry of defence said its air defences had intercepted missile and drone attacks during a “blatant Iranian aggression”. The Kuwaiti statement came after the US allies Bahrain and Jordan said their air defence systems intercepted several Iranian air attacks on Wednesday. Fighting between the US and Iran has increased this week after the US hit Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz on Sunday, claiming that Iran was planning to use them to shoot mines into the waterway. The latest flare-up in the conflict comes amid little evidence that the Trump administration is succeeding in advancing its nebulous war aims either on the battlefield or via mediation, despite the US president’s repeated claims to have opened the strait of Hormuz to oil traffic. Instead, traffic through the key maritime passageway remains far below prewar levels, with oil prices remaining stubbornly elevated ahead of US midterm elections. Oil prices jumped again on Thursday after the Iranian strikes. Among the weapons Iran has used this week is its Kheibar Shekan medium-range ballistic missile system. The cheap and accurate missile can be launched within minutes and has become a staple of Iranian strikes. The rocket’s solid fuel motor means it does not require lengthy fuelling. It can be deployed very quickly to avoid detection and can be armed with a powered and steerable final stage to help beat anti-missile systems. Despite claims by the Trump administration that Tehran is running out of rockets, Iran continues to fire missiles that are considerably cheaper to produce than the US interceptors used to shoot them down. Iran has claimed as recently as the end of August that it maintained both missiles stockpiles and the ability to manufacture them. “Initially, some believed that Iran had only a limited number of missiles and that its stockpiles would eventually be depleted as the war continued,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesperson Brig Gen Hossein Mohebbi said. “However, that assumption proved incorrect, as Iran’s missile capability has remained sustained and its missile production has continued.” Mohebbi’s characterisation of Iranian missile stockpiles could not be verified. The continued strikes came as Israel’s defence minister, Israel Katz, said that while the new US economic sanctions appeared to be effective, the increased pressure could lead Tehran into extreme measures. “We see signs indicating that the heavy economic pressure they are under, and the fear of an uprising and the collapse of the regime, may push them to desperate steps,” Katz said at a ceremony for defence ministry employees. The hawkish minister reiterated the threats against the Islamic Republic that he has made in recent months. “An Iranian attack on Israel will free Israel from any existing constraint,” he said. “We will strike all of Iran’s national military and civilian infrastructure – including energy infrastructure – and push Iran deep back into the stone age.”

title: Leon Black fails to appear for US House deposition about Epstein ties
summary: Billionaire financier, who previously walked out of a deposition, instead launches lawsuit against the committee
text: The billionaire financier Leon Black did not appear on Thursday in front of the House oversight committee for a scheduled deposition about his ties to Jeffrey Epstein, and has instead launched a lawsuit against the committee arguing that it does not have the authority to compel him to turn over non-disclosure agreements. Black was a top Epstein client over several years, and the committee is investigating the men’s relationship as well as the existence of any NDAs to which Black is a party. Black’s name has come up repeatedly in the Epstein files. He has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing and has said that he regrets dealing with Epstein. Black’s lawyers said in a statement on Thursday morning announcing the lawsuit: “The Committee is on a fishing expedition that oversteps its authority and completely ignores its responsibility. This is no longer about finding the truth about Epstein. It is about trying to destroy Mr Black. We were left with no choice but to file this lawsuit in response to an abuse of Congressional power.” The lawsuit, filed in the US district court for the District of Columbia, seeks to stop the committee from enforcing its subpoenas. In the statement, they added: “We want to reiterate that Mr Black had no awareness of the criminal activities that led to Epstein’s arrest in 2019. “Mr Black never abused a woman,” they said. “He never was with an underage woman. He never engaged in sex trafficking. He never paid Epstein for access to women. He was never blackmailed by Epstein.” In a statement on Thursday, Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the oversight committee, called for Black to be held in contempt after his refusal to appear. “By refusing to testify today, Leon Black is now defying two congressional subpoenas,” said Garcia. “His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable,” Garcia added. “We must hold him in contempt immediately.” The new development on Thursday, comes as Black first appeared before the committee in June for a transcribed interview, but the testimony ended abruptly after members from both parties said that Black refused to answer questions about NDAs. That day, James Comer, the Republican who chairs the committee, issued two subpoenas to Black, one demanding he produce “all non-disclosure agreements to which he is a party”, and another to appear before the committee again. In August, in a letter to Black’s attorney, Comer threatened to hold Black in contempt if he refused to comply with the committee’s subpoenas or refused to appear for his deposition, which had been scheduled for 3 September. On Thursday morning, Comer criticized Black in a statement, though stopped short of signalling a contempt vote. “It’s a shame Leon Black is hiding behind litigation rather than provide answers to the American people,” Comer said. “Our deposition is moving forward this morning for the record and there will be an empty chair for Mr Black. I will speak with our members about next steps.” Earlier this week, ahead of Black’s scheduled deposition, over a dozen survivors of Epstein’s abuse urged Black to comply with congressional subpoenas. “Black’s use of NDAs underscores why Congress must scrutinize the agreements in his possession and determine whether they shed light on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and others in Epstein’s orbit” the survivors wrote. “If Black continues to withhold responsive records or refuses to comply with the committee’s demands, Congress should use every tool available to enforce its subpoenas,” they added. Black’s lawsuit alleges that the two subpoenas issued to him are “invalid to the extent they exceed” the committee’s “delegated authority in seeking private information that bears no legitimate connection to OGR’s legislative purpose”. “Additionally, the subpoenas would also expose women who value their privacy, who have no known or public connection to Epstein, who bargained for confidentiality and have refused to release it, and who have no ability to protect themselves and their privacy before the Committee,” the suit says.

title: Shootout in Kyiv between Ukrainian spy services ‘disgraceful’, says Zelenskyy
summary: Domestic security service says clash with military intelligence directorate ‘definitely shouldn’t have happened’
text: Several people have been injured in a shootout in central Kyiv between two branches of Ukraine’s security services, in an incident Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “disgraceful”. The shootout, which took place on Wednesday morning in a downtown area of the capital, was between officers from the domestic security service, the SBU, and the military intelligence directorate, the HUR. The SBU said in a statement on Thursday that the shootout “definitely shouldn’t have happened” and that it was assisting state investigators. The clash appears to have been sparked by the SBU’s recent arrest of a Russian man fighting for Ukraine under the supervision of the HUR. Local media reported that while the SBU was searching an apartment linked to the investigation, HUR officers arrived and shots were fired; three HUR officers were injured. The SBU said that, together with the HUR, it had foiled a Russian-backed terrorist plot targeting a Russian opposition leader who had recently arrived in Ukraine. In a separate statement, the SBU said its officers had come under armed attack while conducting an investigation and they had used their weapons in response. On Thursday, the SBU released a video of the Russian national fighting for Ukraine who had been arrested last month. In the video, the man says he was contacted by a person from Russia acting for Moscow’s intelligence agency who wanted to recruit him to assassinate Ukrainian defence personnel and other individuals. The man’s lawyer told local media that the video had been recorded under pressure and was being released to “whitewash” the shootout. The man has since been released from SBU custody. Hours after the shootout, Zelenskyy fired the SBU’s head of the department for the protection of state secrets, Oleh Khramov. “Shooting here in Ukraine is permitted only at Russian occupiers, in defence of Ukraine. Our state will never regard any other shootout as acceptable,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post. The incident comes at a delicate moment for Zelenskyy. He has recently faced down calls from a sacked defence minister to hold wartime elections. The demand, from Mykhailo Fedorov – whose dismissal triggered a wave of protests – was the biggest challenge to Zelenskyy’s authority from inside Ukraine since the start of the Russian invasion. Zelenskyy also recently sacked a presidential deputy chief of staff amid reports she was being investigated in connection to an alleged money-laundering scheme. The president said the shooting on Wednesday needed to be investigated by both the SBU and the HUR. Ukraine’s main investigative agency has also opened an investigation. In a separate incident, a 71-year-old man was shot outside a medical clinic on Thursday morning in Kyiv and remains in a “serious condition”, according to the the Kyiv city prosecutor’s office. An investigation has been launched into an attempted murder. The shootings come as Kyiv withstands an intense period of Russian bombardment. Air raid alerts have been active for extended periods in the daytime as well as overnight in the capital. Across the country, at least five people were killed in strikes on Wednesday night. Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors capable ⁠of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles. Ukraine has also increased its use of long-range drones to target deep into Russian territory. This week Zelenskyy said that Russian airspace was becoming unsafe for commercial airlines because of the growing number of drone attacks. On Thursday, Russian media reported that the military officer who ordered a missile strike on the Okhmatdyt children’s hospital in Kyiv in July 2024 had been shot. Maj Gen Nikolai Varpakhovich was reportedly shot twice by an assailant riding a motorbike and wearing a helmet. The officer remains in a critical condition.

title: John Lewis to launch YouTube chatshow to improve AI search results
summary: Department store chain’s Gift List ‘vodcast’ will be hosted by TV presenter Angela Scanlon
text: John Lewis is launching an online chatshow and social media studio to help make itself and its products more visible to chatbots and more prominent in AI search results. The department store chain’s Gift List “vodcast” hosted by the TV presenter Angela Scanlon will air on YouTube with clips disseminated via other social media channels and comes after the success of its sister chain Waitrose’s Dish podcast. The premise is guests discussing good and bad presents they have given and received, with the broadcaster Louis Theroux appearing on the first show. There will be six episodes running up to Christmas, with more planned if the series takes off. Shoppers are increasingly influenced by the likes of ChatGPT and Gemini to find and recommend products and also by information on social media such as Instagram and TikTok. The AI large language models tend to prioritise third-party advice and live content when formulating their responses, which is forcing retailers to change their marketing plans. The department store’s outgoing boss, Peter Ruis, said that a year ago just 0.3% of its customers were searching for products via AI large language models such as ChatGPT, but that had already risen to 2.5%, and usage was growing exponentially with all ages using the technology. Being able to rapidly respond to trends and interests with clips of influencers or experts filmed for social media – such as the opening of the British Museum’s Bayeux tapestry exhibition, which is expected to spur an interest in cross stitching, or the launch of the Harry Potter TV series before Christmas – has become just as important as the group’s festive TV ad or its ‘never knowingly undersold’ price pledge. Ruis, who departs John Lewis this weekend after almost three years as managing director, said John Lewis had to move with the times as it faced an economy which was “a bit swirly”. He said the chancellor’s budget announcements next month would come at a “critical period” for retailers and he wanted to see more help on business rates. Ruis said strong trading this week and a string of recent innovations, including modernised cafes and sports departments as well as the social media push and a recent “toy boom”, made him optimistic about the run-up to Christmas. Details of John Lewis’s half-year figures will be released next week. Ruis said it had been a “summer of winners and losers” but indicated there was now “decent momentum” as shoppers still had money to spend. The chain rang up record sales of garden furniture, fans and air conditioning over the summer but Ruis said it was not yet clear if the “Burnham bounce” over the summer would last. “People are not going to splurge when you have got inflation swirling,” he said. “It’s not an easy economy. It’s not easy for customers and inflation is kicking in and the fuel pump is costing people a lot of money.” Ruis last month announced his abrupt departure, saying he was going to “pursue new projects”. He gave no further clue on his future plans on Thursday but said there was “no misalignment” on strategy with John Lewis’s relatively new chair, Jason Tarry. “We are getting things done at pace,” Ruis said, adding there was “never a good time” to leave but it was “far better to leave a winning team at the top of its game and all that excitement with events next year to unveil, rather than finishing bottom of the league and running out of the door”. Ruis insisted his departure did not indicate that he had lost hope in the future of John Lewis, saying it was not a traditional department store reliant on fashion and beauty like Harvey Nichols, which was bought out of administration by Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group last month. He said John Lewis sold a third of all UK prams and pushchairs, garden furniture and the latest technology and “this is not stuff Harvey Nichols can sell”.

title: Teenager in Wales given detention sentence for stabbing teacher in head
summary: Judge voices concern about possible copycat incidents after boy, 16, found guilty over attack at school in Pembrokeshire
text: A judge has expressed concern over possible copycat attacks on school staff as he sentenced a teenager who stabbed a teacher in the head to four and a half years in youth detention. Judge Thomas KC said it was the second such attack in south-west Wales in two years and that the authorities might have to consider what security measures were in place to protect teachers. The boy, who was 15 at the time of the attack, approached the history teacher Vicki Williams when she was alone in a classroom at Milford Haven comprehensive school in Pembrokeshire, and asked her to check his work. He shut the door of the classroom, pulled out a kitchen knife with a 20cm (8in) blade and attacked Williams. She managed to grab the knife from him and he fled. Williams sustained a wound to her scalp, scratches on her back and minor cuts to her hands. Christopher Rees KC, prosecuting, told Swansea crown court the attack in February had been “carefully planned” and that the boy had waited until the teacher was alone. The boy, who is now 16 and cannot be named, was found guilty by a jury of wounding Williams with intent. Williams told the court she thought she was going to die and expressed anger that her young daughter could have been left without a mother. In victim personal statements she said she had been unable to return to teaching and was suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. She said she always kept the doors of her home locked, had installed security cameras there and had not been able to be left alone in the weeks after the attack. Williams said she felt guilty she had not been able to return to work and help her students and colleagues. She said she was nervous around young men and scared to go to the area where her attacker lived. “I don’t think I could be the same teacher I was before,” she said. If someone asked her for help, she feared she would “freak out”. Thomas said the boy had not said why he attacked Williams but that it might have been that she had upset him in some way. The judge also said he was part of a group of boys “winding each other up to do stupid things to teachers”. Thomas added: “You are much bigger and stronger than she is and you knew that.” He told the boy: “You could have killed her.” In April 2024 a schoolgirl attempted to murder two teachers and a pupil by stabbing them with a blade at a school in Carmarthenshire, south-west Wales. She was detained for 15 years. Thomas said: “I have concerns there may have been here or will in the future be a copycat element,” and that the authorities needed to be aware of this when considering security measures. He told the boy: “I want anyone who is ever thinking in the future of doing the same to know what will happen to them if they do. They will spend a lot of their teenage years and perhaps beyond unable to go out with their friends, go and do what they want, go on holidays, have fun, be with their parents, follow their hobbies, and do what the rest of their friends are doing.”

title: Spain’s PM says no evidence ‘whatsoever’ Morocco behind Ceuta border breach
summary: Pedro Sánchez continues to defend Rabat after police report claiming border forces helped 70,000 cross border
text: Spain has seen no evidence “whatsoever” that Morocco planned or facilitated a mass border breach into its north African territory of Ceuta, the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has told parliament. The address on Thursday followed the emergence of a police report, commissioned by a judge and widely quoted in the media, claiming Moroccan border forces had actively aided about 70,000 people to cross the border in late July. “I ‌can assure you ‌that no institution – not the diplomatic service, nor the European Commission, ‌nor any international body – has provided the Spanish government with any solid evidence that Morocco planned or carried out the incident. None whatsoever,” Sánchez told parliament. Speaking the morning after about 50,000 people marched in Madrid to protest his handling of the Ceuta crisis, the socialist prime minister also denied the government had received any warning of the mass breach, saying no reports to authorities had anticipated “the scale or probability of what eventually happened”. Sánchez has repeatedly defended Morocco during the crisis, highlighting Rabat’s cooperation in returning most of the migrants in the days after the surge. But he said on Thursday that Spain had summoned Morocco’s ambassador on 21 August because of “unacceptable statements” made by two ministers over Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish north African territory. Last month, Morocco’s justice minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi, publicly reiterated Rabat’s sovereignty claims over the cities. Sánchez said he had “for now” ruled out Moroccan government involvement but conceded that Moroccan forces had allowed crossings to occur during a key 10-hour period on 30 July. Many of those who crossed said in interviews they had been actively encouraged to do so. Moroccan officials have denied enabling the crossing. Alberto Núñez Feijóo, the leader of the conservative People’s party, called on Sánchez to resign for his “incompetence and complicity”. In response to Sánchez summoning the Moroccan ambassador to discuss the crisis, Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, said: “Morocco doesn’t need an ambassador in Spain – you are its ambassador.” As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter Ceuta at the end of July. The influx unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration. On Thursday, Sánchez appealed for European solidarity over the crisis. He did not single out any countries by name but, in a pointed passage apparently aimed at Italy and Denmark, the two countries that had led public criticism of Spain, said the principle of solidarity should apply to Ceuta as much as it applies to Greenland and Lampedusa. Although 90% of the people had returned to Morocco within 24 hours, several thousand, including at least 500 minors, are thought to remain, either living on the street or in makeshift shelters. Amid calls from Vox to return them to Morocco, Sánchez reminded parliament that under Spanish, European and international law, migrants had a right to be treated as individuals. “You can’t just grab someone by the arm and drag them across the frontier as though they were a sack of dirt,” he told MPs. In reference to the hundreds of destitute minors, Aina Vidal of the leftwing group Sumar, said: “They’re children, not invaders, not soldiers. They didn’t come carrying bombs, they arrived wearing water wings, in tears.” It seems likely the government will invest in facilities in Ceuta to accommodate the remaining migrants rather than risk the political backlash both in Spain and across Europe were they to bring them to the mainland. There is also evidence that, faced with hunger as well as hostility from many local people, some migrants have already begun going back to Morocco. However, as Sánchez told parliament, the per capita income of Ceuta is eight times that of Morocco and “even if we build a wall 100 metres high there will still be people prepared to throw themselves into the sea to get across”. “We will not stop working until Ceuta emerges from this difficult situation: stronger, more prosperous, and more integrated with the rest of Spain and the EU,” he added. Additional reporting by Jakub Krupa

title: Invasive tropical mosquito found breeding in east London
summary: Climate crisis could increase incursions of Aedes aegypti, which can transmit Zika virus and dengue, experts say
text: A mosquito capable of transmitting tropical diseases has been found breeding in homes in east London, with experts warning that the rapidly warming climate will lead to greater “incursions of invasive mosquitoes”. This is the first time the species has been identified breeding in the UK and the fourth time it has been detected. Aedes aegypti, which are normally found in tropical and subtropical regions, can transmit dengue, chikungunya and Zika virus in countries where these infections are circulating. While these diseases are rarely deadly, they can cause complications, with Zika linked to serious problems during and after pregnancy. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said the risk to the public was low, with no evidence that the mosquitoes in east London have have caused human infections. The initial finding was reported through UKHSA’s mosquito watch surveillance scheme. The agency said the species could have come into the UK in vehicles, baggage and imported plants and, if the insects found a suitable climate, they could survive. It said that despite evidence of breeding, the species was not established in the UK and could not survive for long in the typical UK climate, which was too cold. However, the agency warned that in a warming climate, “we will continue to see incursions of invasive mosquitoes, and increased reports of them being able to survive in the UK”. David Smith, the advocacy and social change manager at the charity Buglife, said the rapidly warming climate was creating conditions that were more favourable for exotic and potentially invasive species to establish in the UK. A study earlier this year found that chikungunya, an excruciating tropical disease, can now be transmitted in most of Europe because of higher temperatures caused by the climate crisis. The analysis was the first to assess the effect of temperature on the incubation time of the virus in the Asian tiger mosquito. Smith said: “Recent reports of non-native invertebrates, including mosquito species, highlight the urgent need for the government to strengthen biosecurity, improve surveillance and address pathways such as the movement of potted plants and soils, through which numerous invertebrates can hitchhike undetected.” The UKHSA said control measures had been implemented to destroy the larvae, and the area would continue to be monitored closely to identify and eradicate any further mosquitoes and larvae. It advised residents to remove standing water from gardens and outdoor spaces, including from buckets, containers, paddling pools and plant pots, to reduce opportunities for all species of mosquitoes to breed.
