title: Kemi Badenoch condemns Reform UK’s ‘authoritarian’ press bans
summary: Tory leader says Nigel Farage’s party would seek to abuse state power, as she also defends her housing benefit plans
text: Reform UK’s decision to ban some journalists from its conference shows that Nigel Farage would use state power to target opponents and be authoritarian in government, Kemi Badenoch has said. Answering questions after a speech on defence in London, the Conservative leader was asked about Reform’s decision to refuse accreditation to a series of journalists for its conference this week. One of the journalists was Anna Isaac, the Guardian’s City editor, who broke the story that Farage had accepted an undeclared £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne. Farage’s attacks on the media were “very personal” at times, Badenoch said, also citing the targeting of journalists by Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesperson. She continued: “I think you could … [see] what kind of government they would be – authoritarian and using state power actually to pursue opponents is what they’ve effectively been threatening. “We believe in free speech. We believe in a free press. And yes, of course, that might be painful for us as politicians, but public scrutiny is part of the gig. If Nigel Farage can’t handle difficult questions about his dodgy £5m then he shouldn’t be a politician.” Reform refused to say why it had banned Isaac. In other questions at the event, Badenoch defended her party’s new policy of cutting housing benefit as a way to finance increased defence spending, but declined to say if any savings might be cancelled out by other costs, for example by people being made homeless. In an announcement overnight, the Conservatives said they would make defence spending hit 3% of GDP by 2029-30 through £10bn of savings, primarily from social security. A significant chunk of this would be made by cutting local housing allowances, which sets out how much housing benefit people receive in their local area for private tenancies. This has been frozen anyway since 2024, and already does not fully cover the majority of rents. Asked whether the assumed savings factored in likely knock-on costs, for example people losing their homes and having to seek emergency accommodation from councils, Badenoch slightly evaded the question. “It all needs to be coordinated,” she said. “What we are doing on defence is very closely linked to welfare. My shadow welfare secretary, Helen Whately, is looking at all of the impacts across the board, because we know that every change does create a new situation.” Badenoch stressed what she said was the urgent need for increased defence spending given the threat from Russia, saying that other European countries like Poland and Germany were moving more quickly. She said: “Like Keir Starmer, Andy Burnham is kicking defence spending into the long grass. I cannot tell you how urgent this is.” Burnham’s government has pledged to meet a Nato commitment of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035, but has delayed giving a timing for reaching 3% of GDP. As Starmer’s defence secretary, John Healey insisted this should be reached by 2030, but has dropped the target as Burnham’s chancellor. Separately, Badenoch rejected concerns that her policy to bar non-UK nationals from social housing could see a repeat of the Windrush scandal, where checks on immigration status saw people who had lived their lives in the UK denied access to services. She said: “I don’t think that this is anything like what happened with Windrush, where there were people who had citizenship but couldn’t prove it. And there are lessons that have been learned around the administration of those schemes.”

title: ‘We need a touch of humanity’: Swedish opposition pledges to help Britons facing deportation
summary: Exclusive: Centre party says it will change law to end plight of those hit by post-Brexit policy if it gains power in upcoming election
text: A leading Swedish opposition party has promised an urgent reprieve for British nationals facing deportation from the country over Brexit administrative issues. Niels Paarup-Petersen, the migration spokesperson for the Centre party, said it would introduce laws to end the suffering of people such as the 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas if, as polls project, it forms a new centre-left coalition after the general election in 10 days’ time. Thomas has been told to leave by next Wednesday after 21 years in Sweden. Paarup-Petersen said if his party got into power it would reopen the application process so British citizens threatened with deportation could reapply to stay in Sweden. He said: “We have seen many appalling cases, people who are in a vulnerable state who have every right to be here but are being denied that right because of a minor administrative problem. There has been no leeway whatsoever. “People are paying the price, but Sweden doesn’t win either. We need a slight touch of humanity here.” His declaration comes after a British man was detained in Stockholm by police on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation, the latest in a string of cases involving British citizens in the past month. The man’s wife pleaded with Andy Burnham to intervene, but so far no British politician, or official at the European Commission, has commented on the controversy which the Left party has said was “damaging” relations with the UK at the time of a potential reset with the EU. Al Pinkerton, the Europe spokesperson for the UK’s Liberal Democrat party, also called on Burnham to intervene: “This is the human cost of Brexit: British citizens who built their lives in Europe decades ago now facing detention and deportation. “The extraordinarily high refusal rate in Sweden should set alarm bells ringing in Downing Street. Andy Burnham must urgently raise these cases with the Swedish government and demand that the protections promised to British citizens under the withdrawal agreement are being honoured.” Paarup-Petersen’s intervention comes amid growing controversy over what he says is the “appalling” approach of Sweden’s current right-wing government towards British citizens caught out by Brexit. He said Sweden’s hardline approach to immigration seemed to have infected the approach taken to its obligations under the EU-UK withdrawal agreement, which was a legally binding treaty designed to give lifelong rights to EU citizens in the UK before Brexit and British nationals living in the EU before the end of the transition period in 2021. “Unfortunately I am not surprised because there is no middle ground here on migration. It is just hard rules and there is little consideration of the way people live in reality,” he said. “I was surprised to hear about the number of British people living here who did not know about the application deadline and that is a big issue.” Paarup-Petersen said the European Commission should be able to help but “this is a problem that we can solve in Sweden” quickly with the help of the British embassy. “We have an election in a week and I hope we can change things quickly because this is very much a Swedish problem as it looks like other countries in the EU do not have the same problem.” Sweden goes to the polls next Sunday with recent polling showing four centre-left parties including the Centre party and the Social Democrats on track to unseat the government’s centre-right coalition. Two weeks ago the centre left held a 10 percentage point lead for the 13 September ballot, according to an opinion poll by the public broadcaster SVT. Paarup-Petersen’s promise comes after weeks of revelations about British citizens who had made Sweden their home long before Brexit who had received removal orders or had already been deported. They include Thomas, a former nurse who has told how she is “sick” with worry at the prospect of leaving her home and proximity to her son, grandchildren and her husband’s grave. Others include 34-year-old John Sellers, who was deported in January even though he had lived in Sweden since he was 10 years old, and George Mason, 74, who needs round-the-clock care for dementia and who has lived in Sweden for 25 years. Paarup-Petersen said the wider immigration system in Sweden was “messed up”, with one case of a 95-year-old wheelchair-bound Iraqi woman who was told she would be deported after 20 years in the country.

title: Australian science prize awarded to researcher studying memory accuracy of domestic violence survivors
summary: Helen Paterson’s work on advancing how police and courts understand memory is recognised in prestigious Eureka prizes
text: Memory is an imperfect thing: research shows that recollections of single events – a purse being snatched, say – differ from those about repeated or ongoing events, such as incidents of domestic and family violence. “What our research shows is that compared to a single-event witness, a repeated-event witness tends to report more gist-like details, the overall details of what typically would happen, and the things that remain constant between the episodes,” said Helen Paterson, an associate professor in forensic psychology at the University of Sydney. “Sometimes they confuse one episode with another.” Paterson’s work has important implications for victim-survivors of domestic and family violence and how their testimony is received. “If they’re saying this in trial, it’s defence 101 to say … they’ve made this inconsistency, therefore their whole memory is unreliable,” she said. “But we do know what they do report tends to be highly accurate in that it did happen to them. It’s just they might mix up the episode in which it happened.” Paterson’s work has also found that repeated-event witnesses are perceived to be “less honest, less cognitively competent, and less overall credible than the single-event witnesses – which is pretty concerning that the more repeatedly you are victimised, the less credible you appear to others”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email In recognition of her work in advancing how police and courts understand victim-survivor testimony in such cases, Paterson was awarded a prestigious Eureka prize on Thursday night. Established in 1990, the Australian Museum Eureka prizes recognise the work of Australian scientists and science communicators. Paterson was recognised for excellence in forensic science – one of 19 categories – at an event at Sydney town hall. She hopes the award will help elevate the voices of victim-survivors. “Often we don’t give them the support and encouragement, and we don’t believe them and see them as credible as we should.” Also among the winners was Assoc Prof Jane Tiller of Monash University, recognised for driving national legislative change that bans life insurers from discriminating against people due to genetic test results. Passed into law in April, the ban will come into effect on 8 October. The legal change will enable scientists to use genomics more effectively to prevent conditions such as cancer and heart disease, Tiller said. “The biggest reason that people don’t want this testing is because of fear of insurance discrimination,” she said. The legal change was a “critical barrier that we needed to remove”. “We want to … start finding young people who we know have very high risks of diseases that we can prevent, and give them the screening, the surveillance, the health tools available to them to prevent or treat those diseases early.” Prof Georgina Long, who alongside the late Prof Richard Scolyer was named Australian of the Year in 2024, won the Eureka prize for scientific research, for her pioneering melanoma work. Four other Australians of the Year have previously received Eureka prizes: Prof Tim Flannery, Prof Ian Frazer, Prof Michelle Simmons, and the late Prof Alan Mackay-Sim. Also among Thursday night’s winners were Australia’s marine heatwaves forecasting tool, developed by the CSIRO and Bureau of Meteorology; the Women’s Microbiome Innovation Group, a Melbourne-based research collaboration that discovered that bacterial vaginosis is sexually transmitted between partners; and Prof Yansong Shen of the University of New South Wales, who developed a scalable low-cost process to recover valuable metals and silicon from used solar panels. The Australian Museum director and chief executive, Kim McKay, said: “This year’s winners are tackling some of our greatest challenges: protecting our environment, advancing healthcare, informing public policy and inspiring the next generation of scientists. “World-changing discoveries do not happen overnight. They are built on years of dedication, collaboration and sustained investment.” • In Australia, domestic and family violence counselling is available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org.

title: Crypto billionaire pardoned by Trump gives Reform UK another £4m
summary: Party confident money from Ben Delo will not be caught in new overseas donor cap
text: Reform UK has been given a further £4m from the British crypto billionaire Ben Delo, with the party saying it is confident the businessman – who was formerly based in Hong Kong – will not be caught by the new overseas donor cap. Delo, who was convicted in the US in 2022 for failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls in his cryptocurrency business, before being pardoned by Donald Trump, has previously given Reform £4m. His £8m in gifts shows the rise of Reform’s mega-donors and makes him the party’s second biggest contributor after the Thailand based crypto investor Christopher Harborne, who has given £15m to the party since the last election, as well as £5m to Farage personally before May 2024. According to new donation figures from the Electoral Commission, Harborne did not give any money in the second quarter of the year and neither did the billionaire Sasan Ghandehari, who recently pledged to give millions. Harborne and Ghandehari could potentially be caught by the donor cap applied since March this year, which states donors must be on the UK domestic electoral register for at least 12 months to avoid being subject to a £100,000-a-year annual cap. Delo had been expected to come under the cap after writing in the Telegraph that he had made his first donation since the start of the year, before the government’s cap on donations to political parties by British citizens living abroad. However, a Reform source said the party was confident it would not have to return any of Delo’s latest £4m, raising the prospect that he may have been on the UK domestic electoral register for longer than previously thought. Andy Burnham’s government is considering whether to bring an annual cap on donations from UK donors as well as overseas ones, after launching a new taskforce and promising to “tackle the issue of UK based mega-donors”. However, it stopped short of bringing in a cap in the new elections bill this week amid worries among trade unions about their ability to donate. The latest donor figures show £17m being given to the parties in the second quarter of the year, compared with £11m the previous year, as the parties start preparing for the possibility of an earlier election under Burnham. Labour received £650,000 from the Autoglass founder, Gary Lubner, and the supermarket tycoon Lord Sainsbury, while the entrepreneur Ali Mosawi donated £550,000. The Conservative party lagged behind Reform and Labour, getting £265,000 from Flowidea, a firm owned by the banker Henry Angest. Restore Britain received its largest ever donation: £250,000 from Cade Hill Investments, owned by the tech entrepreneur Simon Galbraith. Delo, who was pardoned by Trump last year, is said to be in the process of moving back to the UK. In his Telegraph article in April, he explained his motivation for turning to Reform, saying England was his home and that “the biggest obstacle to national recovery is the entrenched self-deception of our elites”. “Their regime of nonsense now poses such a grave threat to the UK that, for the first time in my life, I’ve become politically active,” he wrote. “Since the start of this year, I have donated £4m to help Nigel Farage to build Reform UK into a genuine alternative party of government. It is already leading in the polls by virtue of recognising and articulating the full scale of the problems our country faces. For the first time, I feel that serious people are looking honestly at what it might take to fix Britain.” He said that as a person on the autism spectrum, he did not like it that “the official culture of government now forces everyone to be chronically dishonest”, citing expression of views on transgender people. Delo was convicted in the US in 2022 after pleading guilty to violating the Bank Secrecy Act by failing to implement adequate anti-money laundering controls at BitMEX, the trillion-dollar cryptocurrency exchange he co-founded. In his Telegraph article, he wrote: “I helped build one of the world’s first major crypto trading platforms, fell foul of US regulators, accepted a plea bargain and a civil fine for a regulatory failing that isn’t even a crime in the UK, but then ended up being pardoned by Donald Trump, the US president, anyway.” Delo, an Oxford graduate who describes himself as a champion of free speech, supports more than 50 organisations across the political spectrum and public life, as well as non-affiliated groups and individuals. A Guardian investigation into Delo’s political base in Westminster found he had given support in kind to Rupert Lowe, an anti-migration MP challenging Nigel Farage from the right, while also connecting with more mainstream figures including the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, and the former cabinet minister Michael Gove. Delo’s lawyers previously told the Guardian that he provided space for those with diverse views to express them, and financial support to a broad range of organisations, many of which had conflicting views. This did not mean he endorsed the opinions of each, they said.

title: Apocalypse prep or pure pragmatism: what is behind Peter Thiel’s move to Argentina?
summary: Relocation coincides with proposed laws that opponents say would entrench power of US tech billionaires in country
text: Dozens of protesters converged on Peter Thiel’s mansion in Buenos Aires this week after a congressional session raised questions about the billionaire’s presence in the country. In white masks, they held signs saying “Peter Thief” and “No to the Peter Thiel law” in front of the wrought-iron gates of the $12m (£8.9m) residence, which Thiel bought in April as he moved his family to Argentina. There is broad unease at the tech magnate’s presence in the country. His move has been characterised as part of a plan to hedge against world war three: Argentina, agriculturally rich and deep in the southern hemisphere, might just be the ideal place for a tech billionaire to wait out the apocalypse. But recent developments in the country suggest Thiel could have more pragmatic considerations. Last week, Argentina’s chamber of deputies held a six-hour debate on a set of sweeping regulatory changes put forward by Javier Milei’s rightwing government shortly after Thiel moved to Buenos Aires. They invited Thiel, Milei and an official linked to Argentina’s intelligence services to answer questions. “None of them answered, and none of them came to the meeting,” said Juan Marino, a member of the chamber of deputies and the leader of the Piquetero party. Marino said the new laws amounted to a “technofascist legislative package” aimed at entrenching the power of US tech billionaires in the country. Thiel has not publicly advocated for them, but Marino and others have said that their timing was suggestive. The meeting in the chamber of deputies came after Argentinian deputies from several parties made public requests to the government for information about Thiel, his meetings and his businesses. None have been answered. One of the laws, the “super RIGI”, would put in place an investment regime offering foreign companies a minimal tax rate and a 30-year guarantee against regulatory change. It specifically names AI datacentres among investments it hopes to attract. Another, which failed, aimed to eliminate most of the restrictions around foreigners buying land in Argentina. A final decree would require some civilian government departments to share vast amounts of personal data on Argentinian citizens with the state intelligence services. There is no evidence that Thiel has advocated for these laws directly. But in the months after he moved to Buenos Aires, he held closed-door meetings with Milei and key presidential advisers. It is uncommon for a foreign investor to have this degree of access. In the regulatory package, Marino and others see the footprint of Thiel’s larger techno-libertarian interests. The decree that gives vast amounts of Argentinians’ personal data to state intelligence services comes as Argentinian deputies have asked increasingly pointed questions about whether Palantir, the company Thiel co-founded, has undisclosed contracts with the state, which have gone unanswered. The land law, said Marino, could have paved the way for semi-autonomous “startup cities” – such as the controversial Próspera development in Honduras – that Thiel has advocated as a way for libertarians to carve out zones outside state control. “Argentina is kind of a laboratory,” said Cecilia Nicolini, who represents Argentina at the Mercosur regional parliament. US tech billionaires, she said, “are using Argentina as a laboratory, because they have a person in power, Milei, who is even more crazy than they are”. Over the summer Milei wrote an article in the Financial Times advocating the creation of “non-human corporations” – “entities operated by AI agents or robots”. It parallels a vision put forward by OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, who predicted in 2024 that the world could soon be run by AI-owned companies. It also raises dark, thorny questions about the legal liabilities of those entities. Nicolini said: “It’s not just that [Thiel] chose Argentina in terms of, it’s a secure place to live in a world that is facing a number of wars, etcetera. “But really, behind it, I think there is a clear plan. And it is related to reforms that Milei is trying to pass, with some success in some cases, and in others, backlash.” Thiel was approached for comment.

title: Dozens of trapped hydropower tunnel workers in Nepal could still be alive, official says
summary: About 46 people believed to be trapped in ‘room-like’ structure inside hydro plant tunnel on Nepal-Tibet border
text: Nepal authorities have said they are “confident” that dozens of workers in Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant are still alive, more than a week after deadly flash floods left them trapped in an underground chamber. Authorities said that at least 639 workers were still missing from hydropower plants built along Nepal’s Bhote Koshi and Triushuli rivers. Most of the projects were destroyed when a surge of water, debris and mud came coursing down the river valley last week, triggered by ‌the collapse of a melting glacier on the border between Nepal and China-controlled Tibet. The deadly flash floods reached up to 100mph (160km/h), according to scientists, and travelled more than 60 miles down the river valley, wiping away whole villages, bridges, and hydropower dams. At least 1,252 people have been confirmed dead from the floods. More than 4,200 remain missing. According to a preliminary estimate by the UN Development Programme, the disaster created at least 2.2m tonnes of debris, including parts of buildings, rocks and sediment. Large boulders and flood waters deluged the hydropower tunnels, blocking off the entrances, and some were buried deep in mud. Rescue efforts have increasingly centred on these tunnels, where authorities believe workers may ⁠have survived for more than a week due to air pockets. So far, more than 270 people have been rescued from the hydropower projects. Speaking on Wednesday, officials said they believed 46 people were still alive in an underground room in Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, and efforts were ongoing to locate them using excavators and other heavy equipment. “We are very confident that they must be alive after one week because … they have food and water over there in the building,” Amhsu Kiran Shahi, a board member of the Nepal ⁠electricity authority, told Reuters. Durga Gurung, 60, said his brother Jhappad Bhujel was among those trapped in a hydropower tunnel. “Right now, we are just relying on God,” he told the Guardian. “We have not been given any information about whether the people inside are alive or not. “Neither the army nor the people from the electricity authority are telling us anything. So many days have passed that we have reached a point where it feels like all we can do is hope for a miracle.” “Our relatives are sitting inside a dark tunnel,” he added. “How long can they possibly survive?” Major rescue operations were under way or planned at four hydropower projects. Two sites – the Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project and the Upper Trishuli 3A facility – where about 90 people are missing, offered the strongest prospect of finding survivors because of the presence of air inside the tunnels, Shahi said. The Rasuwagadhi hydroelectric project is located in Rasuwa district, about three miles away from the border with Tibet, which was one of the areas of Nepal hardest hit by the floods, and remains almost inaccessible except by helicopter. “This is the only project where it’s possible to walk through ‌the tunnel,” Shahi said. “The army tried doing that three days ago, but they didn’t find the room. We are going in again.” At the Upper Trishuli 3A facility, another project hit by the floods, it took rescue workers almost six days to find the tunnels ⁠because of the thick mud. The authorities believe about 30 to 40 people may still be alive in the tunnel. “We are expecting [survivors] in there because we are told there is a dry space inside. We are trying to break into the tunnel now,” said the Nepali army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet on Wednesday. The army said the search and rescue operation would go on for as long as there was hope for survivors, but that efforts would also continue to recover the dead bodies. “We are using every technology available in Nepal ‌right now, and we are taking help from the Indians, Chinese, Koreans. We have experts from Australia too,” added Basnet. Families of those still trapped in the projects have returned to the Nepal electricity office for the past eight days, in the hope for information. Laxmi Adhikari’s brother Jeevanlal Adhikari had gone to the Trishuli 3A Hydropower Project to test the machines, when the floods hit. She accused the authorities of withholding information from the families, and of not acting fast enough to save their relatives. “We have been running from one ministry to another and from disaster management authority to another government office, trying to find my brother,” she said. “We keep going from place to place, but the rescue operation has not been accelerated.” She said the lack of answers made the wait even more painful: “When the water came rushing in, where did he go? Did he manage to get to safety? They haven’t even given us definite information about whether our people are alive or not.” Nepal has invested more than $9bn (£6.7bn) in building hydropower dams across the mountains, huge sums given the country’s small economy. According to preliminary surveys, the floods debilitated or destroyed 11 hydropower plants and knocked out about 10% of Nepal’s total electricity-generation capacity. According to the authorities, more than 20,000 houses will have to be rebuilt in the aftermath of the flood. Nepal has put the cost of recovery at more than $5bn (£3.7bn).

title: Care workers and others fleeing UK modern slavery win visa reprieve
summary: Home Office concedes skilled workers abused by sponsors can change employer and complete visa term
text: Care workers, chefs and others in danger of losing their migration status under post-Brexit rules if they leave an exploitative employer will be helped by new visa changes, the Home Office says. Officials said if an employee was found to be a victim of modern slavery they would be allowed to work for any employer for the remainder of their visa. The migration status of people on skilled worker visas was tied to a sponsoring employer, under a scheme introduced to fill post-Brexit labour shortages by Boris Johnson’s Conservative government in 2021. It meant workers on that route, who have no recourse to public funds, risked having to leave the UK if they lost their job and could not quickly find a new sponsoring employer. Campaigners have been warning the rule was being exploited by rogue employers, who use workers’ precarious status in the UK to underpay them, force them to put in long hours, or to force them into zero-hour conditions. From Thursday, the restriction tying an individual’s immigration status to a specific sponsor will be lifted if they receive a positive “conclusive grounds” decision formally recognising them as a victim of modern slavery through the national referral mechanism – the UK’s framework for identifying and supporting victims of modern slavery and human trafficking. The Salvation Army’s deputy director of anti-trafficking and modern slavery, Maj Heather Grinsted, said: “Allowing survivors to work for another sponsor for the remainder of their visa is a crucial way to help them rebuild their lives safely and with dignity.” However, Dr Dora-Olivia Vicol, CEO of the Work Rights Centre, cautioned that while the changes “could be a gamechanger”, the impact depended “on how accessible the modern slavery framework is”. She added: “For almost three years we have warned the Home Office that the sponsorship system instituted after Brexit is a recipe for labour exploitation, and have urged officials to free people’s visas from their employers’ control.” Last week the Guardian reported that the number of employers being stripped of their licence to sponsor workers for abuses had hit record levels. More than 6,600 sponsors have been stripped of licences since Labour came to power. Of these, more than 4,400 were in the year to June 2026, a 140% rise on the year before. Modern slavery can include abusive working and living conditions, withheld wages, deception, intimidation, threats, violence, controlled movement, or confiscated passports. Ministers say the rule change will help care workers, chefs, hospitality staff and others who came to the UK in good faith, but faced abuse. Where evidence of criminality is identified, sponsors will be referred to the police. The minister for migration and citizenship, Jo White, said: “No victim of modern slavery should be trapped with an exploitative employer because of their immigration status. These changes will give victims the freedom to leave abusive workplaces and rebuild their lives. “While we support them, we are also cracking down on those responsible. Rogue sponsors who exploit workers will face the full force of the law.” The government says it is also making it easier, through the immigration white paper, for sponsored workers to change employer, strengthening protections against exploitation. A lack of safeguards had led unions and some councils to introduce their own provisions, with Unison working with care workers and councils to produce a migrant care workers charter. Last year 111,000 skilled worker visas were granted, 76% fewer than at the peak in the year ending December 2023. The fall came after new overseas applications for care worker visas were stopped after July 2025.

title: Sadiq Khan cleared of car tax conviction caused by ‘scam’
summary: Magistrates in Hereford withdraw case against London mayor over untaxed Nissan Micra that is not his
text: A car tax conviction against the mayor of London has been withdrawn after it transpired that he was targeted by a “scam” that led to him being fined for failing to tax a car that was not his. Sadiq Khan was found guilty last month under what has been described as a system of “conveyor-belt justice”, in which magistrates decide on hundreds of cases a day, sometimes spending less than a minute on each. City Hall officials say the 24-year-old Nissan Micra did not belong to Khan or Transport for London. The case was formally reopened at a magistrates court hearing at Hereford justice centre on Thursday and withdrawn by a panel of magistrates after a request from the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA). Neither the mayor nor a representative from the DVLA were present at the court for the one-minute hearing. A legal adviser told the panel of magistrates that they may be aware of the case since it was “widely publicised” on Wednesday, adding: “The DVLA have requested that the original matter, if you consider it to be reopened, be marked withdrawn.” Chair of the bench, Mrs Digings JP, said: “We accept the reopening of the case as requested. Further to the request from the DVLA, we are going to mark the matter as withdrawn.” The mayor has been the focus of protests in the past by motorists angry at the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone in London. Some said they planned to register cars in Khan’s name to make him liable for the £12.50 daily charge. After the conviction emerged on Wednesday, a spokesperson for Khan said the mayor had been the target of “a scam, which is a crime”. “It’s not the first time the mayor has been the victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle. Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware,” they added. Khan had been convicted in his absence by a magistrate – who was sitting in a private hearing of the single justice procedure – and was ordered to pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs and to settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra.

title: Working-class ER nurse seeks to flip battleground Wisconsin House seat
summary: Mitchell Berman is among Democrats the party hopes can flip a Republican-leaning district in November’s midterms
text: Democrats are targeting vulnerable seats this midterm election with working-class candidates they hope will resonate with voters exhausted by the economy. Some candidates are new to politics, and many have backgrounds as union members and leaders, which the party hopes will give them an edge over Republican incumbents as people have grown weary of Washington and the higher cost of living. One of these new candidates is Mitchell Berman, an emergency room nurse who Democrats hope will flip a Wisconsin House seat by emphasizing his experience as a worker. “Being a nurse working in the emergency room, we don’t have the luxury of standing around and not delivering for our patients. We have to make sure that we are addressing concerns in the immediate, making sure that when our patients come in, they leave the emergency department in better condition than they arrive,” Berman said. “That is not happening for folks here in our district.” Berman is running in a swing district that polling shows is leaning Republican for the House race. It’s the same district that former House speaker Paul Ryan represented from 1999 until he left office in 2019, when he was replaced by Bryan Steil, a corporate attorney and former Ryan aide. Berman is trying to convince voters that Steil has been out of touch with voters who are seeing costs rise because of White House policies. The campaign is paralleling Steil with Berman, who has worked in healthcare for more than 20 years. “Coming from a working-class background, understanding what folks are going through [and] having walked a mile in my neighbor’s shoes gives me the ability to look at legislation from the perspective of having some empathy and understanding for what people are dealing with,” Berman said. He recalled when Scott Walker, the state’s former Republican governor, passed Act 10 in Wisconsin, which stripped collective bargaining rights from most public sector workers in the state, and the negative impact it had on workers. Berman specifically cites his membership in unions as helping him understand how workers have to fight for fair pay and benefits. “Just seeing the benefits packages, seeing the work-life balance that was afforded to us because of that union was just incredible,” Berman said, adding that workers getting a seat at the table is “the only way they’re going to be able to have a voice when it comes to making sure they get treated fairly”. In Wisconsin and throughout the midwest, the decline of manufacturing has also hit the region hard as offshoring and trade policies have decimated the industry. Manufacturing jobs in the state declined from 560,000 in 2001 to 460,000 in 2025, with healthcare jobs surpassing manufacturing in the state for the first time. From January 2025 to January 2026, the state lost 9,500 manufacturing jobs. Tariffs have led to the loss of 3,910 jobs in Wisconsin, and they are also costing households in the state an additional $1,095 a year, according to a July 2026 report by the Midwest Economic Policy Institute and the University of Illinois Project for Middle Class Renewal. Trump has continued to push widespread tariffs, with claims they would bring US factories “roaring back”. Berman noted that his opponent has defended tariffs, despite the higher costs they bring to voters. While he is not against targeted tariffs, the current tariffs have created “an atmosphere and an economy that makes it difficult for manufacturing jobs to survive”. “Right now people in the district feel betrayed by Bryan Steil because he had made promises to bring costs down, but things have only gotten worse here for people, and I think that’s because of policy positions he’s championed, allowed and abdicated to Donald Trump,” Berman said. “People are starting to recognize that a lot of the woes that they are feeling, when it comes to looking at their bank account at the end of the month, are because of poor decisions made by my opponent.” Steil’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment. • This article was amended on 16 October 2026. Paul Ryan represented Wisconsin from 1999 to 2019, not 2015 to 2019 as an earlier version said.

title: Colorado’s Republican governor nominee linked to controversial anti-sex-trafficking ministry
summary: Marx’s All Things Possible Florida model uses private funds for cop pay and surveillance tools without public oversight
text: The All Things Possible ministry (ATP) is an unusual, and critics say potentially dangerous, operation. It has in the last year funded surveillance equipment and salaries for out-of-state law enforcement agencies, hired a range of private security and intelligence contractors, and is connected to a network of other self-appointed sex-trafficking rescue groups whose leading figures have attracted significant controversy. And its founder is the man who wants to be Colorado’s next governor. Victor Marx, the Republican gubernatorial nominee and until his campaign commenced last October was chair and president of ATP. Since then, his ministry and his political organization have overlapped. The man running Marx’s campaign, former US army intelligence operative Harry “Buddy” Jericho, has also been central to ATP’s effort to operationally merge its raid-and-rescue ministry with law enforcement agencies in Florida. The ministry’s website says it exists to set sex-trafficked women and children free “Spiritually, Emotionally, & Physically” – work it says since 2003 has taken it to some of “the most menacing places on earth” including Afghanistan, Cambodia, Iraq, Nigeria and the West Bank. According to Marx’s 2024 memoir, rescue missions have often involved assembling paramilitary teams in foreign countries. Since 2021, the ministry has increasingly run a domestic model, first with “Skull Games” events that “Special Forces (SF) intelligence operators or those equally qualified work alone or in teams” to crowdsource intelligence on alleged victims and offenders to pass on to police, and now by directly funding out-of-state law enforcement agencies. According to tax and electoral filings, Jericho has earned hundreds of thousands of dollars as Marx’s campaign manager, as a paid director of ATP, as the director of the initiative funneling money and volunteer manpower to police, and as chief executive of an intelligence company the charity paid more than $100,000 in a single year. As governor, Marx would have authority over Colorado’s large state police force. In Florida, his charity is already running a controversial model of how policing can be paid for: private donations from anonymous benefactors fund officer salaries and surveillance equipment outside any procurement process or public vote. Elizabeth Joh, a law professor at the University of California, Davis, who has written on private influence over policing for two decades, said she had never encountered such an arrangement. “To whom are these dedicated sworn officers accountable?” she asked. Even where a donor sets no formal conditions, she said, “the nature of the funding implies that straying from the donor’s expectations would threaten current and future funding.” What she wanted to know was what measures the Florida agencies had put in place “to assure that private wishes don’t influence public choices”. The Guardian contacted Marx and Jericho for comment. Only Jericho responded. ATP’s chief executive, Chaz Yandall, answered separately on the ministry’s behalf. A subsequent email attributed to “The All Things Possible Team” said: “We wanted to clarify that All Things Possible Ministries is a completely separate organization from the Victor Marx 2026 campaign.” Victor, son of Karl Marx narrowly won the 9 July Republican gubernatorial primary in Colorado despite a campaign that saw him telling unverified stories about being forced to commit murder at seven years old by an abusive stepfather, his refusal to say how many people he may have killed as an adult, his claim to have called in US airstrikes as a civilian, and his boasts of performing exorcisms over the phone. Marx was known as Vaughn Victor Kennedy when he served as a US marine in the 1980s, according to posted images of service records he produced under questioning earlier in his campaign. On a website dedicated to rebutting “public claims” about his earlier life, the candidate says he changed his previous last name (shared with the allegedly murder-inducing stepfather) “after reconciling with his birth-father, Karl Marx”, who on Marx’s earlier account had spent time as a “practicing warlock”. Victor Marx set out ATP’s overseas missions in The Dangerous Gentleman, his self-published 2024 memoir. He recounts assembling “a paramilitary security team” of “experienced former CIA guys, Marines, Navy Seals, and Delta guys” and leading it into Iraq and Syria during the war against Islamic State. According to Marx, his teams bought “military-grade vehicles, ammunition, guns” and kept “an armory of weapons” at a base of operations. On the Iraq-Syria border, a member of his security detail asked permission to shoot a man who was watching them, and on his own account, Marx replied: “Do it.” The whole operation, he wrote, was paid for by “Americans who gave money to support this sort of craziness”, and twice he states that the ministry never took US government money. He has repeatedly given his anti-trafficking work a supernatural cast, telling a TPUSA-affiliated podcast in 2023, “I hunt pedophiles, but I also hunt demons.” Taskforce In 2025, however, a slide deck published to ATP’s website announced that the ministry would pivot from overseas rescue missions to close partnerships with domestic law enforcement agencies, with initial plans for ministry members to act as sworn officers. It would also pursue sponsorship deals “funded by ATP’s high net worth donors” which would procure surveillance equipment and software for local, state and federal agencies. The new initiative was to be called the Protecting Children’s Innocence taskforce (PCI-TF). The deck, whose metadata indicates it was created on 5 March 2025, says that following internal discussions “ATP redirected overseas efforts to support U.S. law enforcement in improving arrest rates,” beginning with “a thinktank with experts, including legislative allies … to strategize U.S. child sexual abuse efforts”. But the scope went well beyond a thinktank. “Task Force members are sworn by law enforcement agencies, working side-by-side with their teams,” the deck says. Members would support “warrant creation, suspect tracking, and case documentation to streamline the path to prosecution”. An organization chart names Jericho as director. That model was not built, according to Jericho. He said that “some early organizational documents contemplated models under which personnel might obtain appropriate status through a cooperating law-enforcement agency,” that it was “an early concept while the organization was being developed”, and that the taskforce “ultimately pivoted away from that model”. Yandall said no one acts as a sworn officer, auxiliary officer or special deputy on the taskforce’s behalf. But memorandums of understanding signed with the Leon and Wakulla county sheriff’s offices (WCSO), obtained by the Guardian, show the ministry retained a say in how the operations it funds are staffed. Both require the sheriff’s office to “designate an Assigned Person, following her/his approval by the PCI-TF GEB” – a government executive board on which each participating agency holds a single vote and which meets quarterly. The Wakulla agreement goes further, providing that the officer is “to be selected collaboratively by PCI-TF and Wakulla County Sheriff’s Office” and will “be evaluated at regular intervals based on performance standards that are both established and maintained by the GEB in collaboration with PCI-TF”. Both agreements also ask the agencies to report back. Under a heading on performance evaluations, they list search warrants served, arrests and indictments, devices examined, media files reviewed and confirmed as child sexual abuse material, “number of convictions and sentencings associated with reported cases” and “total years of incarceration sentenced during the reporting period”. The same section states that the reporting “is not intended to direct, govern, or interfere with the agency’s independent operations”. The 2025 proposal deck envisaged that PCI-TF would support “warrant creation, suspect tracking, and case documentation to streamline the path to prosecution”. The ministry would provide “funding for essential operational needs, including surveillance equipment, data analysis software, and training programs”, by “leveraging the generosity of high-net-worth donors to supplement agency budgets and expand their investigative capacity”. PCI-TF’s current public description of its mission on its website is less detailed: among other things, the taskforce says: “We see the protection of innocent children as a gospel calling.” Asked whether the taskforce is a separate legal entity from the ministry, Yandall said: “PCI-TF is not a separate nonprofit and does not have a separate EIN.” The Guardian could not find a separate entity of that name registered anywhere in the US, and the URL victormarx.com/pci redirects to atpministries.org/pci. Agreements signed with Florida sheriffs say otherwise. The Wakulla memorandum opens by naming the parties as “the Protecting Children’s Innocence Task Force (PCI-TF), a 501(c)(3) nonprofit” and the sheriff’s office. A clause headed Authority adds that the taskforce “operates in accordance with all applicable federal and state laws and under its nonprofit charter”. Identical wording appears in the agreement signed by the Leon county sheriff, Walt McNeil, on 17 September 2025. All Things Possible is not named as a party to either. At least one of the sheriff’s offices contacted by the Guardian is still operating under the assumption that PCI-TF is an independent organization. Geneva Stokely, a WCSO spokesperson, wrote: “The MOU identifies the Protecting Children’s Innocence Task Force as the entity providing funding to the Wakulla County Sheriff’s Office. The MOU identifies PCI-TF as a 501(c)(3) nonprofit but does not identify the sources of PCI-TF’s funding. WCSO does not have information identifying the sources of PCI-TF’s funding.” The Gainesville police department chief, Nelson Moya, wrote: “I am not aware of who funds the ministry or PCI.” What ATP bought the police The public debut came on 6 November 2025 at Cascades Park in Tallahassee, where the ministry launched the operation alongside five agencies including the sheriff’s offices of Leon, Wakulla and Jefferson counties, the Tallahassee police department and federal Homeland Security Investigations. Locally it was named the Big Bend Protecting Children’s Innocence taskforce, and it was reported that “the project is being sponsored by All Things Possible Ministries”. A Leon county sheriff’s office budget amendment attached to the county commission’s agenda for 27 January 2026 records $210,000 arriving at the department. The agreement itself sets out what the money buys: salary and benefits for an internet crimes against children detective at $114,689.90 a year, training for seven detectives and supervisors, a $35,000 vehicle, an Intel Talion forensic workstation at $23,712, and a dedicated internet line at $1,200 a month. Spending on licenses for GrayKey and Cellebrite, two commercial tools used to extract data from locked phones, is listed as “To Be Determined”. In neighboring Wakulla county, the ministry funds an entire detective post. The agreement commits it to salary and benefits “not to exceed $132,050.36 a year”, and itemises the rest: a $30,000 Equinox, a Dell desktop at $3,509.11, a vest at $1,500, a Class A uniform with duty gear at $820, a filing cabinet, a desk, a desk chair and the detective’s firearms, a handgun at $481 and a rifle at $1,737. Colonel Chuck Whaley, of the sheriff’s office, reportedly said the arrangement came at no cost to taxpayers On both agreements, the taskforce’s point of contact is Jericho, at an address on the Marx campaign’s domain. Asked why, he wrote: “I maintain several professional email accounts and receive correspondence across them. I do not recall why I used the campaign-domain address in that particular instance, and I will not invent an explanation years after the fact. The use of that email address did not mean the campaign was involved in the underlying ATP matter.” Both agreements run three years and both require the sheriff’s office to “make a reasonable effort to obtain the required funding pursuant to the three-year schedule outlined above, particularly as PCI-TF funding phases out”. Leon’s schedule funds the post at 100% in each of the three years, to 14 September 2028. At the end of it, the counties are apparently expected to carry a detective, a vehicle and a forensic suite that were created outside normal county budgetary processes. When asked about this aspect of the arrangement, Stokely, the WCSO spokesperson, said that this was not a commitment in the MOU, which she wrote “does not establish what will occur with the position following the conclusion or discontinuation of PCI-TF funding”. Beyond Big Bend The Big Bend agencies were not the only recipients. Reportedly on 18 September 2025, seven weeks before the Tallahassee launch, the Gainesville police department announced its own partnership with the taskforce, 150 miles away in Alachua county. Chief Moya said the taskforce gave it a server valued at $223,733.14 and that because it arrived as a donation, “it did not go through the city procurement process.” The ministry also paid for three Gainesville officers to attend one of its Guardian Retreats. Yandall said ATP had now run five, “assisting and training nearly 100 law-enforcement officers” in “mental, physical, and spiritual health protocols”. Asked for a total figure for what it has given each agency, he said only that the expenditure was “documented through ATP’s financial records”. Sheriff’s deputies were working under the ministry’s banner before the public launch. In early October 2025, four weeks before the Tallahassee announcement, detectives in the criminal investigations division at the Wakulla county sheriff’s office “who are assigned to the Protecting Children’s Innocence Task Force (PCI-TF)” completed the arrest of nine registered sexual offenders and one sexual predator in an operation called Not-a-Fan, according to a statement issued under the sheriff’s office’s own byline. Eight of the 10, it said, were arrested “by authority of arrest warrants obtained by PCI-TF Detectives”. Both the ministry and Jericho reject that description. Yandall said PCI-TF “does not prepare, apply for, or obtain arrest warrants”, and that warrants, arrests and other enforcement decisions rest with the agencies and the courts. Jericho said taskforce personnel had not participated in preparing or obtaining warrants in live criminal cases, applied to judges for them, or served them. The Florida department of law enforcement’s own account of the same operation, published on 14 October 2025, lists the same 10 defendants and the same charges but does not mention the taskforce. It names FDLE, the sheriff’s office, Homeland Security Investigations and the state attorney’s office, says only that “arrest warrants were obtained”, and dates the arrests to 7 and 8 October. Since then, the taskforce has been named as a participating agency in a series of north Florida operations that have produced dozens of arrests, several of them alongside federal agencies. Operation Safe Harvest in March, which produced 20 arrests, was credited in media reports to the Tallahassee police department, the Leon county sheriff’s office, FDLE, the FBI, Homeland Security Investigations, the US Marshals Service – and the ministry’s programme. The Guardian contacted all the involved agencies for comment. In their response, Homeland Security Intelligence wrote that the taskforce was no longer active, and that: “Any financial contributions or equipment provided by the non-governmental organization in the form of a grant to support task force operations are managed exclusively between those organizations and the respective state or local law enforcement agencies. HSI is not a party to those arrangements, and its participation remains strictly focused on the federal law enforcement mission.” None of the Florida money has yet appeared in an ATP tax return. The payments fall in the 2025 financial year, and that return is not due until 15 November 2026, 12 days after the election. Buddy Jericho Harry William “Buddy” Jericho, 49, a resident of Dunedin, Florida, has been a constant companion of Marx’s in his spiritually inflected pursuit of sex traffickers. There is little publicly available information on his early life. On LinkedIn, he claims separate stints in the US army and the Defense Intelligence Agency. A biography circulated in 2023 describes him as a “former intelligence officer, whose service record includes 14 combat deployments alongside special operations forces while serving in the US Army and as a DoD Civilian”, spanning conflicts “including those in Bosnia, Iraq, and Afghanistan”. An army spokesperson, Heather J Hagan, confirmed in an email that Jericho was an enlisted intelligence analyst in the regular army from May 1996 to January 2005, with several deployments to south-west Asia – in federal government parlance the Persian Gulf region including Iraq – between February 1997 and October 2004, and that he left as a staff sergeant. Enlisted soldiers are not officers. Hagan listed no combat or valor decorations, and no deployment to Bosnia. Jericho said the army account was “generally accurate” and that confusion arose from biographies combining his army service with a later civilian career at the Defense Intelligence Agency, where he says he worked from about 2005 to the end of 2011 in an operations officer role. “The word ‘officer’ in that context refers to my civilian intelligence position,” he said. “I was not claiming that I had been a commissioned military intelligence officer.” Most of the deployments, he said, came in the DIA period and so would not appear in an army record. He said his combat-zone deployments were to Iraq and Afghanistan. The Guardian has contacted the DIA to confirm his tenure. Marx’s book devotes extended passages to a close friend, “Buddy”, who is never given a surname. “Buddy is on my board of directors,” he writes, “and he is considered perhaps the best interrogator of terrorists our country has had in recent decades”. He adds that “Buddy has performed more than three thousand interrogations for United States military and civilian law enforcement agencies.” Jericho said the figure covers “interrogations, debriefings, screenings, interviews” across his whole career and is “a conservative career estimate rather than pretend I can produce an exact count decades later”. He said he was never a law enforcement officer and never exercised law enforcement authority. Jericho has been on the board of ATP since 2020 and a paid member since 2023, according to tax filings. Since last October, he has been Marx’s paid campaign manager, according to Colorado electoral filings and a post on his own LinkedIn profile. ATP also paid Indago technologies, a private intelligence firm, where Jericho is CEO, more than $100,000 as a contractor in 2024, according to its tax filings. Asked whether he was drawing three paychecks in two Marx organizations and one contractor to Marx, Jericho said the roles were “not all held simultaneously in the manner your question suggests”. ATP payments listed in tax filings, he said, were not for his board seat, which was unpaid, but a fee as a 1099 contractor for running the taskforce. Of the payments to Indago, he said the money went to the company rather than to him, that he did not recommend it, participate in the decision, vote on it or approve the payments, and that ATP’s leadership knew he was its founder, chief executive and shareholder. He could not recall what conflict disclosure paperwork the ministry used and would not speculate about a document he had not reviewed. He also said he had “completely turned over responsibility for PCITF to someone else” several months before taking on substantial responsibilities with the campaign. He signed the Wakulla agreement as the taskforce’s “Director & Board member” on 17 September 2025, and is the named contact on the Leon agreement that commenced on 15 September. Since joining, he has become the campaign’s dominant public voice, defending its repeated campaign finance filing slip-ups, explaining a claimed endorsement from former Republican governor Bill Owens that Owens had not in fact given, and writing to primary debate organisers to set unusual conditions for Marx’s appearances. Skull Games The Florida operation was not the ministry’s first attempt to put volunteers alongside police. Skull Games – weekend events at which volunteers were handed police cold cases and told to identify traffickers and their victims – began as an ATP project, run in partnership with Echo Analytics, a company Jericho founded. A presentation obtained by the Guardian, produced by a company founded by Jericho in October 2022, where he was still serving as CEO at that time, describes volunteers as “Special Forces intelligence operators or those equally qualified” who crowdsource open-source material into “lead packets on trafficked victims, missing kids, and persons of interest”, and who may “proactively search escort-ads”. When the Intercept examined the operation in July 2023, it reported the use of sock-puppet accounts and commercial surveillance tools including face recognition, and events powered by the Israeli surveillance firm Cobwebs Technologies, banned by Facebook in 2021 in a crackdown on “surveillance for hire”. Running it was Jeff Tiegs, then ATP’s chief operating officer, who was compensated $116,000 a year, according to its tax filings. The US army confirmed to the Guardian that Tiegs served as an infantryman from April 1987 to April 1995 and as a special forces officer from May 1997 to October 2015, deploying six times to Iraq and once to Afghanistan, and left as a lieutenant colonel with a Silver Star. The two organisations formally separated in 2023. Tiegs left ATP that May, Skull Games received its own tax-exempt status in July, and at the end of that month Tiegs said the two were “separate and distinct” and that Marx had no role at Skull Games. But ATP’s return for the same calendar year records a $70,000 grant to Skull Games, described as support for outreach to at-risk people – almost a fifth of everything the new charity raised that year. Both organisations’ tax returns for 2023 list him as a board member – ATP’s under the name Buddy Jericho, Skull Games’ under Harry Jericho. Money has also moved between the ministry’s orbit and other rescue groups. Our Rescue, founded by the former federal agent Tim Ballard and the subject of the 2023 film Sound of Freedom, gave Skull Games $15,000 in 2025. Ballard resigned in September 2023 amid sexual harassment allegations, weeks before five Utah women accused him of sexual assault; he denies wrongdoing, and Salt Lake City prosecutors declined to charge him in November 2025. The organisation is now run by Derek Benner, a former executive associate director of Homeland Security Investigations – the same federal agency that partners Marx’s taskforce in Florida. The accountability gap Seth Stoughton, a law professor at the University of South Carolina and a former police officer, said multi-agency taskforces are routine, and that a taskforce is not a legal entity in its own right. “The task force itself does not employ anyone or own assets, and it cannot get sued,” he said, since members remain employees of their home agency. Private money does make its way into policing, he added, pointing to Mothers Against Drunk Driving, which has funded specialised drink-driving enforcement units. “What makes this one weird,” he said, “is that the entity behind that designation, and at least some of the funding, isn’t another governmental agency.” Asked what a defence lawyer would do on learning that a privately funded body had been involved in the investigation that produced their client’s arrest, Stoughton wrote: “A good defense lawyer is going to run this one to the ground.”

title: Women are giving their partners the ‘Illiterate Boyfriend’ test: ‘Do your best to pronounce these words’
summary: People online are distressed at men butchering words such as ‘hyperbole’ and ‘hors d’oeuvres’ – highlighting a gender reversal in ‘intelligence gaps’
text: There are common non-negotiables we look for in a prospective partner. They should be kind, caring and thoughtful. Having a shared interest helps. So does remembering important dates and anniversaries. But how much does it matter if they know how to pronounce the word “gnocchi”? Turns out that’s a potential dealbreaker, at least according to a (rather judgy) cohort on TikTok. See: the “Illiterate Boyfriend” trend, which is testing some couples on the app. Users have compiled a list of what are essentially SAT words for women to ask their male partners to read. Many of these men – this is an overwhelmingly heterosexual activity – fail to finish the list unscathed. They trip over entries such as “hyperbole”, “cynicism”, “diaphragmatic” and the oft-butchered French term, “hors d’oeuvres”. “I want you to do your best to pronounce these words,” one woman asks her boyfriend in a clip viewed more than 8.8m times. He gamely nails his first attempt, reading off the herb “thyme”. But he’s less successful with “epitome”, “challah” and “fuchsia”. (“Foo-chia?” he guesses). “Conscientious” and “faux pas” also prove tricky. He ends up with a score of five out of 17, or 29% – very much a failing grade. The couple laughed through the exercise, but viewers were not as charmed by an adult man struggling through what they considered basic vocabulary. “The fact that his vote matters just as much as mine is really pissing me off,” one woman wrote in the comments section. “I’m gonna be honest girl, this is worth breaking up with him over,” read another comment. Two of the words the man correctly identified were “colonel” and “regime”, which, to one user, was evidence of a red flag: “he’s obviously a Republican”. (Maybe he just has an interest in military history, a time-honored hobby of boyfriends everywhere.) Regardless of political affiliation, it seemed fair game to dunk on Mr Foo-chia. One final quip from a viewer: “He’d be so upset if he could read these comments.” The test made its way around TikTok, with more young couples joining in, to similarly bleak results. Even those men who did well got caught up in the pop-misandry circus. One man zipped through the list, ending with a perfect score and a self-satisfied grin. It was not the flex he might have hoped for. “This is the barest fckn minimumest [sic] of bare minimums,” one woman commented. “The men are being praised for literacy we’re in hell,” wrote another. Distress over so-called “intelligence gaps” brings to mind a phenomenon that reverses decades of dating precedent: women are now more likely to marry less-educated men than men are to marry less-educated women. This is not necessarily by women’s choice; it is the new dating pool. According to a 2024 Pew Research report, in 1995, young men and women were equally likely to hold a bachelor’s degree. Now, 47% of women ages 25 to 34 have one, compared with 37% of their male counterparts. “We do have in our mating market an oversupply of educated women and an undersupply of formally educated men – I’m talking academically, not necessarily in their skill set, emotional or social intelligence,” said Dr Wendy Walsh, a clinical psychologist and expert at DatingNews.com. Dr Jess Carbino is a former sociologist for Tinder and Bumble who studies dating apps. When she polls people on what they look for in a partner, “intelligence” is rarely in the top three desired traits. “They say things like humor, kindness, attractiveness, typically,” she said. “Maybe people on the coasts – New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco – might say intelligence. But by and large, that’s not one of the top things being measured.” And there are so many different ways to consider intelligence, spelling being a way to formally test fourth-graders, not romantic partners. One thing people do want is an equal. “It’s not necessarily that someone needs a specific degree or to know every word in the dictionary,” said Robin Hamilton, a couples therapist. “It’s more: are you able to communicate with me, are you able to meet me halfway with the subjects that I’m talking about?” One of those subjects might be reading, an indicator of vocabulary range. Men’s rates of book reading have slipped over the past decade; nearly half of all women read just one novel or short story in 2022, but only one in four men did. According to data from Tinder, mentions of books in bios on the dating app jumped 40% this year among women, but only 23% among men. Women believe they see this disparity playing out on TikTok, even if it is through an ultimately meaningless list. It is elitist – and naive – to draw any real conclusions about what makes a good partner based on a reading test. This “Illiterate Boyfriend” list contains words that may be more indicator of class than intelligence, conflating education with one trait women have prioritized for hundreds of years, mostly due to necessity: having money. But the trend also reflects a wider disillusionment among straight women, who are significantly less likely to want to date than men are, partly because they say it’s hard to find someone who checks all their boxes. “He looks at the word ‘queue’ and pronounces it ‘qwi-wee’?” one woman said in a video responding to the test. “And you still have sex with him?” “It’s rage bait for women who are frustrated and angry with the mating marketplace that is slanted unfairly” against women, Walsh said, adding: “It’s OK to date a guy who can’t say epitome or niçoise. I have a PhD, but I need spellcheck for hors d’oeuvres.”

title: Off-grid UK-Australian couple describe ‘anguish’ at removal of children by Italian court
summary: After judge allows partial access rights, Catherine Birmingham and Nathan Trevallion say the enforced separation ‘broke each of our hearts’
text: A couple have told of their heartache, trauma and stress after fighting for two years for their right to parent their children as they choose in the glare of the world’s attention. The three children of a Melbourne woman, Catherine Birmingham, and her British partner, Nathan Trevallion, were removed from their “dilapidated” off-grid home in Italy last year. It sparked global conversations about state intervention and alternative lifestyles. They were raising the children on a property in the woods in the Abruzzo region, where they grew their own food and homeschooled the children. In September 2024, the family was hospitalised after eating poisonous mushrooms they had picked, which brought them to the attention of authorities. In November 2025, the juvenile court ordered the removal of Utopia Rose, nine, and six-year-old twins Galorian and Bluebell to a residential care facility, citing a lack of hygiene, social interaction, toilet facilities and schooling. Birmingham stayed with them until March, when she was ordered to leave under a new court ruling. On Wednesday, an Italian court approved a staged process that would allow a “gradual reunification process”, and could eventually allow the children to leave the facility. “The ruling partially revises previous court decisions and sets out a ‌gradual reunification process, ‌allowing the children to return home for daytime visits immediately and, from October, for weekend ‌overnight stays with their family,” their lawyer, Simone Pillon, said. In a statement released on Thursday, the couple said the “long-awaited decision, which our entire family awaited with anguish, arrived with a harshness that broke each of our hearts”. They asked whether forcing school attendance was “fair, legal, and respectful” of their parental rights and the rights of their children, saying they chose Italy for reasons including its homeschooling rights and support for family bonds. The parents have said that doctors say the children’s health is at “serious risk” and “the only way to reduce this risk is to return them home immediately”. “We are deeply concerned for their health,” the parents wrote. “How will they be well if they are forced to travel back and forth from their home to the foster home, then to school, and then back to the foster home again, all while still being kept apart from their parents? “How will they fare in the evening when, after an afternoon spent at home with their friends and pets, they must return to the foster home?” Even Italy’s hard-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, has weighed in. She expressed “alarm” over the children being taken into care, while the deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, compared the case to a kidnapping. But the judiciary’s union said the court’s decision was based on factors including the children’s safety, sanitary conditions and education. After the latest decision, social services will monitor the process and make an assessment before any permanent reunion can happen. The couple wrote that the authorities wanted to impose a standard. “And those who don’t follow it lose their children,” they wrote. “We are deeply saddened by this. “We have continued to collaborate and engage with everyone, even under extreme trauma, stress, exasperation and concern for our children knowing their daily suffering but we will always demand respect for our parental rights and, above all, for our children’s rights, especially their right to health – mental, physical and emotional.” The couple plan to appeal for a complete and faster reunification.

title: ‘We continue to suffer’: victims of apartheid-era Sharpeville massacre demand compensation
summary: Claim relating to 1960 attack on hundreds of protesters part of wave of litigation over apartheid crimes in South Africa
text: The day dawned brightly on 21 March 1960, as residents of the South African township of Sharpeville gathered to protest against pass laws, which forced “Black, Indian and Coloured” South Africans to carry documents at all times specifying where they were allowed to be. Abraham Mofokeng joined the march, one of dozens organised nationwide by the Pan Africanist Congress (PAC), a breakaway group from the African National Congress (ANC). “The weather was very nice, the sun was out. You could not have suspected that the day would go so horribly,” said Mofokeng, who was then a 20-year-old factory worker. Mofokeng, now 86, was among the thousands gathered peacefully outside the police station in Sharpeville, which is about 40 miles south of Johannesburg in a heavily industrialised region known as the Vaal Triangle. The crowd was singing, he said, when officers opened fire without warning. At least 91 people were killed and 238 injured, in what became known as the Sharpeville massacre. As Mofokeng fled, a bullet grazed the inside of his right foot, ripping his shoe off. A woman fell to the ground before him; he jumped over her and kept running. Only later, when he noticed blood running down his legs, did he realise he had been shot in the back, where a bullet remains lodged in his spine. Mofokeng is among three claimants suing the South African government, in a case filed on Thursday, for compensation for the massacre. If the case is successful, dozens more could file claims. The case is part of a wave of litigation demanding justice for apartheid-era crimes, amid widespread disillusionment with ANC-led governments that have failed to rectify South Africa’s huge racial inequality and poverty since the end of apartheid over three decades ago. In January 2025, 25 survivors and relatives of victims of apartheid state violence sued South Africa’s government for failing to prosecute cases referred to it by the post-apartheid Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC). That May, the president, Cyril Ramaphosa, announced a judicial inquiry into potential political interference, which is still ongoing. Spokespeople for South Africa’s justice department did not respond to a request for comment on the Sharpeville compensation case. In the immediate aftermath of the Sharpeville massacre, police claimed protesters had been throwing rocks at them. “I don’t know how many we shot,” said Col J Pienaar, the local police commander, according to a story published by the Guardian the following day. “It all started when hordes of natives surrounded the police station. My car was struck with a stone. If they do these things they must learn their lesson the hard way.” In July 1961, in response to victims filing compensation claims, the white minority regime passed a law indemnifying the government and anyone acting under its authority for any actions taken “in good faith for the prevention or suppression of internal disorder, the maintenance or restoration of good order, public safety or essential services, or the preservation of life or property”. The law, which was made effective retrospectively from the date of the massacre, is still in force today. The claimants’ legal team is arguing that the law is unconstitutional. The claimants are hoping to get compensation of about 500,000 rand (£23,000), said Daniel Leader, a partner with the UK law firm Leigh Day, which is advising the South African legal team, led by Lawyers For Human Rights, an NGO. Mafokeng was awarded 30,000 rand as a one-off payment, after the TRC concluded in 2003. The TRC had recommended annual reparations payments of about 20,000 rand for six years. “We continued to suffer,” said Mofokeng, who still lives in Sharpeville. “Especially now … I am struggling and my health is not up to standard.” The other two test claimants were children when their fathers were killed in the massacre. Paulina Mathinye was five when her father, Samson, was shot. “Every time he came back from work, I would be so happy to see him that I would run to him, and then he would pick me up,” she said. Mathinye did not initially understand what had happened that day in 1960. “I kept on asking my mum: ‘Mummy, why are you crying?’” Mathinye’s mother struggled to raise her five children on a domestic worker’s wages and Mathinye, who had wanted to train as a teacher but could not afford the bursary, had to leave education at 17 to find work. Mathinye, who is now 71, said she hoped for compensation that would make up for some of what she lost when her father died. “Some of my friends are teachers, some of them are nurses, and I’m staying in the same house that my father did,” she said. Sharpeville’s problems did not begin with the massacre in 1960, but with the dispossession of Black South Africans from productive land, their forced removals to townships and their exclusion from the economy, said Vincent Thamae, a PAC member who supports the massacre victims and their families. “When people talk about compensation now,” he said, “compensation is a concept to them that includes all the land that they lost, the economy that they were taken out of and even how they have been treated in the new democracy.”

title: Housebuilder Crest Nicholson warns of annual loss in ‘subdued’ property market
summary: Firm will complete fewer homes than expected in year to 31 October – between 1,350 and 1,400
text: The British housebuilder Crest Nicholson has warned of a surprise loss this year as it bemoaned difficult trading in a “subdued” property market. In an unscheduled trading update, the company said it would complete fewer homes than expected in the year to 31 October – between 1,350 and 1,400, down from its previous estimate of 1,400 to 1,500. Conditions in the property market have been “more subdued” than expected during the summer, which is typically quieter as many people go on holiday. Crest said its sales rate had slowed over the past six weeks compared with the first half of the year as “affordability constraints and competitive pricing” dragged down demand. The company now expects to slide into the red, with an operating loss of about £10m, reversing an earlier forecast of a profit of between £5m and £10m. It is the third profit warning since April. The Crest share price plunged more than 10% on Thursday morning. Building material prices remain about 3% to 4% higher on average. Crest has closed one divisional office and cut 50 jobs in recent months. It reported a pre-tax loss of £35.2m for the six months to the end of April. However, it is reducing its borrowings faster than expected, and expects net debt of £70 to £90m at the end of October, down from the £100m to £120m flagged previously. The Surrey-based company has been trying to renegotiate its banking covenants with lenders for some time to ensure it has enough funding in the future. It described the talks as constructive but anticipated “some slippage in the current timetable”, indicating the negotiations were taking longer than expected.
