title: Wife of British man at risk of deportation from Sweden calls on Burnham to intervene
summary: Case is latest in string of post-Brexit deportations from country, which has been criticised for high refusal rate for British people to remain
text: The wife of a British man detained by police in Stockholm on Tuesday ahead of a threatened deportation has pleaded with Andy Burnham to get involved in the Brexit catastrophe unfolding for many British citizens in Sweden. Charles, who does not want to be fully identified, and his Swedish wife, Lily, were summoned to the police station at 10am on Tuesday, where he was told he would be held at a detention centre and deported within the next two weeks. Lily, who is a lawyer, was told to go home and get his passport despite her protests that there was a court process under way appealing the deportation order. “I feel shame,” said Lily, who asked that their family’s surname not be published. “To me, Britain represents freedom for human beings, and then to see this British man in detention just because he wants to be with his wife and live in his house, this is not right. “What kind of country are we living in? Is this civilisation? They don’t care about human rights. This is a European country, but it looks like Sweden is like somewhere like Afghanistan,” she said. Lily met her husband in the UK after starting a law degree in London in 2010. She now works for the local authority in Stockholm and returned to Sweden in 2015, with her soon-to-be husband joining her in 2017, three years before Brexit. A former business consultant, now retired, Charles made an application to remain in the country before the deadline for applications after Brexit. His application was rejected two years later in 2022 and the family have been fighting deportation ever since with “six or seven” appeals, said Lily. “The Migration Agency has hunted us for five years.” During the summer the couple received a text asking them to show up at their local police station on 1 September. “They told us they needed to talk and we should show up at 10am. They didn’t say anything about deportation or to bring passports. “When we arrived they told us that they needed to talk to Charles privately, and after three hours they told me they were taking him to the detention centre and that they would deport him. “I told them that they can’t do this because his case is in court and they have to wait for the outcome, but they told me they were going ahead,” said Lily. She has pleaded with Andy Burnham, the UK prime minister, to intervene. “Why can’t Andy Burnham talk to the Swedish government? How many British families have to suffer in Sweden before Andy Burnham gets involved? How many families have to leave their homes, be forced into selling their houses? “This is not humanity. This is not right. They should threaten the trade agreement,” she added. Charles’s case comes amid growing controversy over Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement, which is supposed to have protected EU citizens in the UK and British citizens settled in the bloc before Brexit. Among those threatened with removal in the past month are 78-year-old British widow Joyce Thomas, who has been in the country for 21 years, and George Mason, a 74-year-old man in dementia care who has been in the country for 24 years. A 34-year-old man revealed this week he was deported from Sweden in January despite having been in the country since he was 10 and being married to a Swedish woman in Gothenburg. Two years ago another British woman, Kathleen Poole, was threatened with deportation because she had not provided financial statements to the Migration Agency while in full-time dementia care. The Swedish migration minister defended the country’s implementation of the withdrawal agreement, saying the Migration Agency was following the rules and had granted a number of residency permits for Britons who had “reasonable grounds” for late applications. However, concerns have been raised formally by the UK government through the EU-UK specialised committee, the official platform to raise issues over the working out of the Brexit deal, over the high number of late applications for post Brexit residency being rejected. Sweden, along with 12 other EU member states, opted for a constitutive system requiring citizens to formally apply to extend their residency rights post Brexit. Others, like Spain, opted for a declaratory system requiring Britons to simply register their presence initially. Lily says she and her husband phoned the authorities and used the correct form for residency and have been fighting ever since. The latest statistics from the 2024 European Commission annual report show that 14,233 applications for post Brexit residency have been decided in Sweden. According to analysis by the UK government, 27.5% (3,918) of applications have been refused, “a refusal rate three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3 and 4%”. Sources added that this “constitutes 12% of all refusals across the EU member states, even though UK nationals in Sweden makes up only 1.55% of the total population of WA beneficiaries in EU member states”. Denmark faced a similar controversy two years ago, but legislation was introduced to give British nationals a second chance to make the residency application.

title: More than 800 students and teachers in Indonesia suffer food poisoning after eating government free meals
summary: Hundreds of students fall ill in three seperate incidents in Java and Sumatra this week as criticism of president’s flagship program grows
text: More than 800 Indonesian students and teachers have fallen ill in separate incidents of food poisoning linked to President Prabowo Subianto’s free-meals program this week, with dozens hospitalised after they with struck with nausea, vomiting and stomach aches. The president’s flagship free-meals program was launched last year to tackle malnutrition, with meals distributed to more than 62 million students and pregnant women across the country. But the multi-billion policy has been plagued by controversy, including recurrent cases of food poisonings, alleged corruption, leadership changes, and complaints it is a major lag on the budget. This week 566 students fell ill after eating the government’s free meals in Sidoarjo, East Java, with 88 of them hospitalised. In Nganjuk, also in East Java, 49 students fell ill on Wednesday after eating a free meal of fried rice, chicken and tofu. Another 237 students and teachers in Agam, West Sumatra, also fell ill after their meals on Wednesday, according to local media reports. Eggs were suspected to be the cause. The regional government in Agam has reportedly suspended distributing the meals, pending an evaluation. The kitchen linked to the Sidoarjo case was also suspended on Wednesday. In the past year many Indonesians have complained about the program, writing on social media about maggots in tempeh, shards of glass in rice, and food trays washed in dirty water. Overall, 37,600 people are believed to have suffered food poisoning linked to the free meals as of 8 Aug., according to Network for Education Watch, a non-governmental watchdog. Charles Honoris, a lawmaker and member of the sole political party outside the governing coalition, described the situation as a “failure of the system”. The National Nutrition Agency has blamed previous cases of food poisoning on improper food storage and late delivery of cooked meals. Prabowo has also played down the scale of the problem, saying that of more than a billion meals served, poisoning cases represented just “0.0017% – quite a proud achievement”. He also said the policy had improved school attendance and achievement. In July, a survey by pollster Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting showed only a third of people were satisfied with the scheme, with the reported cases of poisoning cited as a major reason. Despite the mounting criticism, Prabowo told parliament last month the program would be continued, and promised that improvements would be made. “We start with the most fundamental aspect: nutrition. Our children must not study while hungry. No child can learn effectively if they are hungry,” he said. “We cannot accept a situation where one in four Indonesian children suffers from stunting,” he continued, “We cannot accept that.”

title: Thursday briefing: What life is like in a West Bank village under siege from Israeli settlers
summary: In today’s newsletter: After a summer of increasing violence and settlement expansion in the West Bank, a Palestinian-American details his experience returning to his besieged village
text: Good morning. In the coming days, Andy Burnham’s new government is expected to announce a ban on trade with Israeli settlements on the West Bank. It’s a move long anticipated by campaigners, and after a summer of escalating violence across the West Bank and the expansion of Israeli settlements that are illegal under international law, the UN was warned last month that the area is “at breaking point”. But this is not just a story about high level diplomacy and global trade. It is a story about people’s homes and gardens – people who simply want to walk around them in peace. One of those people is Loui Abu Ridi, and this morning marks the 26th day that his house in the northern West Bank village of Qusra has been besieged by settlers. First, the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | In his first prime ministers questions, Andy Burnham blames the Conservatives’ legacy for leaving the UK vulnerable to market turmoil. US news | JD Vance has said he is “doing as much of God’s work as possible” and that he is OK “if that leads to the end times”, which he says “are coming”. Tech | The UK government does not know what the country’s datacentres are being used for, despite fears over the growing environmental cost of the AI boom, a freedom of information request has found. Nepal-Tibet | There is a high chance that dozens ⁠of workers may be found alive after a week trapped in an underground chamber at Nepal’s Rasuwagadhi hydropower plant, a ⁠Nepal electricity authority official has said. Defence | A former defence minister has admitted misleading parliament over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans. In depth: ‘We live hour by hour’ Over the past two years, Loui Abu Ridi and his family have worked hard in their garden, which overlooks the village of Qusra, planting cherry, fig and olive trees, installing solar lights and a path to walk through the saplings. But in recent months, harassment by local settlers has intensified: they smashed windows, ripped out cabling and attacked his brother with rocks. They brought their sheep into Ridi’s yard – the sheep ate the saplings. Then, at the start of August, a group of settlers erected a tent outside his house and encircled two others, trapping the residents and blocking access to food and medical supplies. “When my brother called the police, they sent the military,” Abu Ridi explains, “but instead of helping him, they took selfies with the settlers”. “Now, we live hour by hour,” he tells me. The jeopardy is constant: just before we speak, a group of armed militants was circling his property in an ATV. His 83-year-old mother has run out of medicine, but any supplies must be negotiated via the village mayor and take days to arrive. His neighbour’s children should have gone back to school this week after the summer break. “Those kids, they cannot live their childhood. They cannot even go out in their yard to play.” I don’t speak Arabic, but Ridi speaks fluent English – he’s Palestinian-American, and grew up in Qusra, but left to study in the States, and he now runs a chain of gas stations in Ohio. With the assistance of the US embassy, he returned to the West Bank from midwest America soon after the siege commenced in August to be with his mother, brother and sister. “I was escorted into my house and since then, I have not left.” *** What is the West Bank, and who lives there? It’s nearly 20 years since I last visited the West Bank, and I can still remember the scream of a Palestinian mother as a bulldozer splintered the walls of her two-storey house, smashing bright, woven rugs and framed family photographs into dust and debris. The destruction of Palestinian homes and the expulsion of communities has been continuing for decades on this area of land on the west bank of the river Jordan. Since the Six Day War in 1967, the area, including Gaza, has been under Israeli occupation. The first Israeli settlements were established on the West Bank soon afterwards, backed by politicians across party lines, and have been formally recognised as violating international law ever since, although Israel has long disputed this interpretation. In 2024, the International Court of Justice declared that Israel’s continued occupation of Palestinians land unlawful. The 1995 Oslo peace deal created three administrative areas in the West Bank intended to constitute a future Palestinian state, a prospect consistently undermined by successive Israeli governments and their supporters in the settler movement. That encompasses both hardline right factions who claim historical and religious rights to the West Bank as the ancestral land of the Jewish people and other groups, and politicians on the left, who claim Israel needs to occupy Palestinian land as a security measure. While population counts vary, B’Tselem, the Israeli Information Centre for Human Rights in the Occupied Territories, estimates there are around 700,000 Israelis living illegally in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and more than 3.5 million Palestinians who call it home. *** How has the violence escalated? Since the Hamas atrocities of 7 October, when 1,200 predominantly Jewish people were killed and 251 taken hostage, settler expansion and accompanying violence on the West Bank has sharply escalated. According to UN figures, between 7 October 2023 and 21 June 2026, 1,105 Palestinians – at least 242 of them children – were killed in the West Bank. What is happening is ethnic cleansing. B’Tselem keeps a detailed chronology of violence, demolitions and displacement, estimating just under 5,000 people have been expelled since 2023, and over 60 communities have been wiped off the map. They are clear that this is the continuation of a systemic campaign rather than sporadic acts of violence by a handful of rogue extremists. The Israeli state has given settlers guns and uniforms, as part of locally established reserve units, and other equipment they use to terrorise Palestinians, including all-terrain vehicles. The aim is to push Palestinians into disconnected enclaves while establishing infrastructure for settlers to use, B-Tselem said, and supported by much of the Israeli government, including the far-right finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, a settler himself. Indeed, Orit Strook, Israel’s settlement minister, drew heavy criticism from opposition politicians and families of 7 October victims, when she described the period of rapid expansion of Israeli settler control in the West Bank after the attacks as “a time of miracles”. In the past month alone, B’Tselem identified further escalation, with hundreds of settlers targeting larger Palestinians villages, attacking families, setting fire to houses and cars, and taking over farmland. Examples of Israeli aggression towards foreign visitors have gained more international attention: British activist Finn Joughin was abducted by armed settlers, then deported from Israel, and NBC News correspondent Matt Bradley required medical treatment after his crew was attacked by masked settlers. But, as Abu Ridi describes, settlers are largely acting with impunity. B’Tselem believe they are using the window before Israeli government elections in the autumn to “change the reality” on the West Bank. The Israeli government is moving ahead with the E1 project, a plan to build thousands of homes on occupied land between East Jerusalem and the Ma’ale Adumim settlement on the West Bank, which many international critics argue would cut the West Bank in two and make the creation of a future Palestinian state even harder, if not impossible. *** Will the sanctions make a difference? On Tuesday, foreign secretary Ed Miliband told MPs: “This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution. We will act, and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks.” And, the new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has previously made it known he wishes to take a more “robust” position on Israel than his predecessor Keir Starmer. However, this has not been welcomed by all quarters of his party, with Labour Friends of Israel warning that a ban on trade with settlements could become a de facto boycott of Israel due to the difficulty of separating out settlement goods from those made within the internationally recognised borders of the country. That in turn would cause significant harm to the UK’s Jewish community, the group say. But, a recent Amnesty briefing argues that the government can use the same enforcement framework already in place for trade sanctions following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, which distinguishes between goods originating in occupied Ukrainian territory and those originating in Russia. And within Israel, security chiefs have demanded the government take action to “eradicate Jewish terrorism” on the West Bank. With Israel more isolated internationally than ever, Abu Ridi has tried to use his dual citizenship to draw attention to what is happening across the West Bank. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – usually no ally to the Palestinian cause – recently described the actions of the settlers besieging Abu Ridi’s home as those of “terrorists”. “I am a Palestinian-American. But I’m not the only one living this life. There are hundreds and thousands of Palestinians in the West Bank, being threatened and beaten by Israeli extremists, and forced out of their houses.” At the end of our call, we speak a little more about his garden. Since the beginning of the siege three weeks ago, the settlers have stopped encouraging their sheep on to his property. “I was just talking with my brother about this,” he says. “We’ve started seeing green leaves, so there’s hope for those trees, if the settlers stay away from my yard.” What else we’ve been enjoying We’ve previously covered how big money is distorting politics on First Edition, so it’s very disappointing that Burnham has backtracked on a £500,000 cap. George Monbiot’s column on this is essential reading. Hettie This NYT report on the runway success of Delhi’s sprawling metro system neatly unpicks how it was built from scratch in one of the world’s most densely populated cities (£). Michael Freelancers are being hired to clean up “AI slop”, neatening and retouching content created by machines. It’s soulless work, Aaron Mok finds in this grimly fascinating piece. Hettie I’ve enjoyed so many of Simon Hattenstone’s recent interviews, and his tete-a-tete with Mr T is no exception. Michael When Stephen Buranyi first told me he was investigating the secretive world of restaurant influencers, I couldn’t wait to read what he found. His long read is well worth your time. Hettie Sport Tennis | Katie Boulter was outclassed 6-1, 6-0 in the second round of the US Open in New York, continuing the British No 1’s poor form. Cricket | Brydon Carse has been left out of England’s squad for the final Test of the summer, against Pakistan at Edgbaston next week, with police still investigating allegations of an assault connected with the late-night incident at a Derby bar last month. Football | Manchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign Enzo Fernández from Chelsea. The front pages “PM tries to calm bond markets as sell-off threatens first budget”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the FT says “Burnham seeks to shield steel and farming from ‘Made in Europe’ push”. The Times’ headline is “‘Vibes’ won’t defend UK, Burnham told by Labour”, the Telegraph writes “Tories will cut benefits to hit 3pc on defence”, and the Mail leads with “Kemi: I’ll slash benefits bill to boost defence”. The i Paper’s front page says “Britain’s royals face Russian cyber threat in ‘grey war’”. The Sun splashes “One in the eye for Andy”, the Mirror has “A right whinger”, and the Express says “Voters would punish you if triple lock goes”. Lastly, Metro has “Sad pathetic creeps.co.uk”. Today in Focus: The Latest Iran retaliates after US strikes reportedly kill wedding guests Iran has accused the US of a ‘war crime’ after a missile blast killed at least four people, including a young child, and injured 68 at a wedding at a private house in southern Iran. A month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran appears to have collapsed again, after US strikes on Saturday on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including the Gulf States. Lucy Hough speaks to Middle East correspondent Will Christou. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad For many people of colour, finding a reliable place to take care of your hair can be a battle. New York thinks it has an answer to that problem. As of this month, a new law means every hairdresser studying cosmetology will be specifically trained to work with all hair types. In time, this will make many salons more accommodating to more hair types. “No New Yorker should ever walk into a salon and be turned away or receive substandard care because of their hair texture,” New York state assembly member and bill sponsor Michaelle Solages said. “Now, with the adoption of this legislation, they won’t have to.” Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Quick crossword Cryptic crossword Wordiply

title: From ‘psyops’ to ‘hysterical hysteria’: how GB News and Talk TV lost their cool in the heatwaves
summary: Thousands of heat-related deaths in record-breaking temperatures appeared to only intensify hosts’ climate denials
text: As the first heatwave of the record-breaking summer arrived on 23 May, GB News host Cristo Foufas was not happy: “I am sick to death of the naysayers saying firstly that we’re all going to die and that we have to put out heat alerts, because, you know, just drink some water and drink a bit less rosé in the sunshine.” “We used to call it Darwinism,” replied co-host Renée Hoenderkamp. She is a medical doctor. The arrival of the intense heatwave in late June – the most extreme recorded in Europe – didn’t change the tone. “People die each year from vending machines falling on them, and coconuts hitting their heads. People die, unfortunately, that’s a reality of life, and things get hot,” said Will Kingston, a presenter and contributor on GB News, a free-to-air television news channel. “It doesn’t mean you have to go about changing your life in ways big and small to accommodate for it.” Over on TalkTV, a British streaming news channel, there was also little empathy as the country sweltered in deadly heat. “I’m very sorry if someone dies because of the heat, but I don’t think that’s a reason for us never to be allowed to take a flight again, or stop being allowed to eat meat,” said the presenter Julia Hartley-Brewer on 24 June, citing policies no one is putting in place. Her guest, the conservative commentator Benedict Spence, agreed: “One way or another, something’s going to get you.” As that heatwave reached its peak, the TalkTV host Kevin O’Sullivan was getting hot under the collar about the “asinine snowflakery” of climate concern: “Our hysterical hysteria over climate change because we’ve had a few nice days … It’s a nice day. Now we call it … a death risk.” Then the numbers came in. The May and June heatwaves had killed about 2,700 people prematurely in England and Wales, according to an analysis based on the relationship established between heat and mortality in previous data, published on 13 July. Cue a meltdown from O’Sullivan: “No such thing happened. They’ve sort of qualified it – and said 2,700 people might have died – and this has been apparently gamed by computer programmes and God knows what.” The report was “just disgraceful climate change scaremongering” and “absolute poppycock”, he said. On GB News, the presenter Kingston was also deeply unimpressed: “If there is one thing that Covid taught us, it is that modelling is effectively guesswork from clever-sounding people with an ideological agenda.” These hot takes did not age well. On 30 July, the UK Health Security Agency announced that 2,877 people had died because of the May and June heatwaves, using data on actual recorded deaths. Many heat-related deaths are among elderly people and those who are already unwell, factors that apparently made their premature demise less important for some contributors, such as Ross Clark, who had told TalkTV on 25 June that they were “perhaps on the point of dying anyway”. Presenters and guests on both channels frequently pointed to the higher level of deaths from cold in winter. None were asked why any reduction in winter deaths due to global heating would mean the rising number of heat deaths in summer was acceptable. And it’s not even true any more: the most recent figures from the Office of National Statistics show 2,805 heat-related deaths in England and Wales in 2025 compared with 2,244 cold-related deaths. Instead, one TalkTV presenter, André Walker, decided that one man in particular had blood on his hands: “I believe by the end of his career, Ed Miliband will have killed 100,000 people because of his crazy green energy policies that freeze people in the winter and cook them in the summer.” He offered no evidence for this attack on every climate-denier’s bogeyman, the former energy secretary. You might think it would be hard to deny the basic reality of climate change as the temperatures soared outside. You’d be wrong. There was straightforward denial on GB News with, for example, the presenter Nana Akua calling the climate crisis a “scam” as the hottest May ever recorded ended; Hoenderkamp blaming the sun (an ancient climate myth); and the fashion designer and regular contributor Jeff Banks saying, wrongly, that: “The facts are that carbon dioxide in the atmosphere has been declining for the last 150 million years.” Over on TalkTV, Hartley-Brewer blithely told viewers in late June: “We’ve always had freak weather.” Not like this we haven’t, according to hundreds of scientific studies. Let’s take a short break, for a fact check. The world’s climate scientists, in reports signed off by 192 national governments, have been clear for more than a decade that 100% of global heating since 1950 has been caused by human emissions and activities. Every heatwave is being made more intense and more likely as a result of fossil fuel burning, and rising global heat kills one person a minute around the world, according to a major recent report in the Lancet. Back to the channels, where the heat the country was enduring, if not its cause, was undeniable. Cue the presenters turning their fire on the weather forecasts. “The weather maps, they used to go orange and red. They’ve now lowered the threshold so it’s bright red. It’s obviously … a psyops operation,” said the TalkTV host Ash Gould. Who was behind this conspiracy was not revealed. Another TalkTV host, Alex Armstrong, was also frothing about maps: “They’ve literally coloured the country black – because it’s like a nuclear holocaust level. They’ve gone nuts, these climate fanatics.” He did not explain what maps he meant, and they were not shown to viewers of the programme. One issue that got the TV stations hot under the collar was air conditioning, which, ironically enough, was barely needed in the UK until the climate crisis drove up temperatures. Foufas said on GB News: “Here in the UK, remember we’ve all been told to rip out our air conditioning because it’s not conducive to net zero.” This blanket statement appears to be based on a single planning dispute in Camden. “It’s actually still illegal in new-build homes to fit air con,” chimed in Hartley-Brewer on TalkTV. It’s not illegal, for either new or existing homes. And the unrelenting attacks on net zero, a policy now at the heart of the right’s culture war, carried on. “The biggest psychosis of our age is climate alarmism and net zero,” the contributor Paul Cox told TalkTV. “Net zero being a product of the monetisation of climate alarmism.” The presenter Alex Phillips did not challenge him. Instead, she insulted Miliband as “a meme and a congested ukulele player”. A few more examples: net zero is a “deranged religion”, a “crazy ideology”, a “fallacy [that] doesn’t exist”, “lunacy” and “madness”, meaning “we all have to eat insects rather than beef and lamb”. Just to be clear, net zero is the principle, dictated by the laws of basic physics, that until we stop adding greenhouse gases to the atmosphere, it will continue to get ever hotter. But even if net zero was admitted as necessary, excuses for inaction abound on the channels. For example: the UK emits only 1% of global emissions, making action pointless. What about all the other countries that only emit a small percentage? Another favourite: the supposed cost of net zero, often backed by figures conjured up by analyses which ignore the costs of maintaining the status quo or climate damage. Net zero will have “smashed the economy to bits”, according to Cox on TalkTV. “It’s going to be less expensive to deal with the consequences,” said the GB News presenter Jacob Rees-Mogg. Despite being a former energy and net zero secretary, he is also wrong: a multitude of serious assessments over decades have shown reaching net zero is cheaper than not doing so, including work by the government’s own official independent advisers. For those on GB News and TalkTV, the answer to high energy bills is drill, baby, drill! TalkTV’s Jeremy Kyle quotes Donald Trump: “We have, in his words, liquid gold under the North Sea.” In fact, according to the UK Energy Research Centre, the idea that more North Sea oil and gas could cut energy bills for UK consumers or improve energy security is a “delusion”. Perhaps the conspiratorial mindset that sometimes leaks out on the channels can explain all this cognitive dissonance in the face of record heat, thousands of deaths and all the hard evidence? Commentators on the channels call net zero “a road to communism” and “socialist-style, communist-style control”. Apparently, it is easier for some to deny reality than accept that some big problems require a collective response. The GB News presenter Bev Turner is particularly enraged when her kids are sent home from overheated schools: “When the weather gets warm and the government says it’s too hot to go out, stay at home – we are priming them for climate lockdowns, that is all this is.” There’s a lot of talk on these billionaire-owned, heavy-loss-making TV channels about deranged ideologues. But reviewing the summer meltdown on GB News and TalkTV, I think I found them – right there in the studios. title: London’s first self-driving taxis for hire hit the streets
summary: Wayve robotaxis added to Uber app and will have human in front ready to take over if needed – but only 15 cars licensed
text: Londoners are now able to hire self-driving taxis for the first time, after rides in Wayve’s autonomous vehicles were added to the Uber app on Thursday. The chances of landing a robotaxi on request immediately are slim, with only 15 vehicles so far licensed. That contrasts with the more than 100,000 private hire vehicles in the capital – roughly the same number of Uber customers who have registered to take autonomous rides. The cars will still come with a licensed human driver sitting in the front seat, ready to take over the controls should the need arise. Transport for London last month licensed Uber and the UK tech company Wayve’s modified Ford Mustang cars as private hire vehicles, whose conditions still require a safety driver supervising. Regulatory approval for vehicles in fully autonomous operations without a safety driver needs to be granted under a separate government process and agency, the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency, and is now seen as unlikely this year. Nonetheless, Thursday’s launch marks a significant milestone and has allowed Uber to steal a march in the race by tech companies to bring driverless taxis into London, seen as a crucial market for a wider European rollout. Google-owned Waymo and the Chinese company Baidu are testing their robotaxis in the UK capital. Alex Kendall, the chief executive and co-founder of Wayve, said he was proud to introduce the company’s AI Driver technology to the public for the first time in London, “our home city and one of the most complex driving environments in the world”. Kendall said the technology was “still maturing” but robotaxi services without a safety driver would come, although he declined to predict exactly when: “I don’t want to put a timeline on it, but we’re pushing as fast as we can.” He said Wayve would be moving to “scalable manufacturer-produced vehicles” – new Nissan Leaf robotaxis with its technology – and needs to “validate the safety metrics on that platform”, as well as secure regulatory approval. “We’re working on all three in parallel. As soon as they come together, we’ll launch [fully] driverless services,” Kendall said. Wayve’s self-driving technology is based on an AI learning model rather than the mapping used by rivals such as Waymo. On a brief autonomous test drive with the Guardian in Westminster this week, all passed smoothly, with Kendall notably pleased by the car deciding to pull away again and re-park after stopping in front of gates that other cars were attempting to pass through. “That was quite human-like – really cool,” he said. “We’ve done a lot work to make sure the car can park in appropriate spots that are socially acceptable.” The cars will be hailed and unlocked through the Uber app. The driver will introduce themselves with an appropriately robotic script, explaining that they will no longer speak during the ride but can be requested to take over control of the vehicle if the customer prefers. While they will be the first self-driving cabs for hire in London, fully driverless services are in operation in many cities worldwide, primarily in the US and China, as well as the United Arab Emirates. Uber partnered in launching Europe’s first commercial robotaxi service earlier this summer in Zagreb, Croatia, with a human driver onboard as in London. Sarfraz Maredia, the head of autonomous mobility at Uber, said the London launch was “a major milestone in scaling safe, accessible AV technology in a city with some of the world’s most complex roads”. He said: “The benefit for consumers should be, over time, that it’s both safer and cheaper. Today, nobody’s able to operate AVs cheaper than a traditional human-driven ride, so that’s going to take a while to prove.” Maredia said Uber had heard concerns from drivers but said he believed they would not be put out of work: “One of the most common ones we hear from our drivers is: ‘Hey, I drive in this city and it’s very complex, and I don’t think this product is going to be able to compete with me anytime soon.’” He added: “We always want Uber to be a platform where both human drivers and AVs can operate, and because the market and our business are still growing here we think that’s going to be true for a long time.” Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, said: “This is a major milestone for the future of transport in London, as British innovation brings this technology on to our roads and gives passengers more choice. “Today’s announcement further cements Wayve’s status as a technology trailblazer here in the UK, and highlights how British innovation is helping drive investment and growth in transport.” David McMullen, a senior organiser at the GMB union, said: “With hundreds of thousands of people employed to drive every day, we need to be really careful with the rollout of driverless cars unless we are prepared to see unprecedented levels of social and economic disruption.”

title: The place that never freezes: the Arctic habitat where global heating threatens more ice, not less
summary: The race to study the North Water between Canada and Greenland before it changes has led to a bold plan for an Inuit-run protected area
text: Electric-blue meltwater sprays up under Terry Noah’s snowmobile as he races across sea ice extending out from Canada’s northernmost public community: Grise Fiord in Nunavut, a hamlet of 144 people closer to Murmansk in Russia than the Canadian city of Toronto. The bay’s cliffs loom higher and higher like stone icebergs as he approaches his destination across the bay. Noah pulls his sled carefully over a seal’s breathing hole, about the circumference of a basketball. Using a custom-made winch, he lowers a submersible instrument into the sea below the ice. Noah will bring the data it collects back to his shipping container-based mobile lab and beam the data to the south, where his collaborator, research scientist Andrew Hamilton at the University of Alberta, can review it. As the climate emergency thins the ice, jumbles up the seasons and forces millennia-old Inuit cultures to adapt, Noah is part of a scientific effort that extends far beyond Grise Fiord. He says: “This science work, it’s the first step to preparing.” The data Noah is collecting will help Hamilton and Noah understand changes taking place in Jones Sound, which empties into Baffin Bay to the east. There, in the bay’s northern reaches, one of the Arctic’s most important ecosystems is in the midst of a political and environmental upheaval – and Noah, Hamilton and a coalition of scientists have plans to better understand the changing waters before they’re beyond recognition. It is an area of 85,000 sq km (33,000 sq miles), bigger than Austria, that goes by at least three names: 19th-century whalers called it the North Water; Kalaallit (Inuit of Greenland) call it Pikialasorsuaq, or “the great upwelling”; and to the Inuit of Nunavut, it is Sarvarjuaq, “the place that never freezes”. A stretch of year-round open water (known as a polynya) this far north is a boon to life of all kinds, from the algae that bloom in the summer and feed an entire web of other creatures to the whales that need access to the air in the depths of winter. Polar bears are drawn in by the whales, seals and walruses that migrate there; seabirds, too, have flown and paddled their way there by the millions, over millennia. All of that activity is why the polynya is the focus of a unique proposal to become an internationally protected area jointly managed by Greenland and Canada. A 2017 report by the Pikialasorsuaq commission recommended the two countries create an Inuit-managed protected area. Canada followed up in March this year by designating the Sarvarjuaq marine protected area on its half of the zone, stretching 1,000km from just south of the open Arctic Ocean to northern Baffin Island. But Greenland has fallen behind on its promises for protection. Sara Olsvig, a former member of the Greenlandic parliament and chair of the Inuit Circumpolar Council until earlier this year, says it is not wise to move too quickly when the fundamental cultural rights of Inuit could be at stake. “Some of the very good initiatives within conservation and nature preservation, and so forth, have unfortunately also resulted in violations of the rights of Indigenous peoples,” she says. As negotiations slow, the physical process of change continues unabated, and the efforts to understand the polynya are accelerating. The polynya’s size and shape ebb and flow with the seasons – depending, in part, on an “ice arch” that forms across its northern tip in Nares Strait. The arch, a strong crescent-shaped bridge of ice, jams the strait, preventing sea ice from being blown south from the Arctic Ocean. The lack of ice keeps the polynya open to the sunlight and the air, allowing algae to grow, the seabirds to dive and the whales to blow. Nearly 20 years ago, the Nares Strait ice arch failed to take shape for the first time. Now it often does not form – and in those years, the polynya itself has a harder time staying open through the spring. Instead, the sea ice drifts down to cover the water’s surface. It is an unusual and perverse effect of warming: more ice, not less, could ultimately become the problem here. “I would say that at some point, when the ice bridge disappears, you’re probably going to have a drastic reduction in productivity – a collapse of the polynya,” says David Harning, a climate scientist at the University of Colorado, Boulder. Finding out what is happening beneath the surface has become critical as the planet warms, and the Inuit experience that change first-hand. Researchers met in Nuuk in the autumn of 2025 and had initial conversations about developing what Hamilton calls an “observatory” to monitor the polynya from all sides. That would require the involvement of a lot more people like Noah on both sides of Baffin Bay, but many Inuit do not have passports, and bringing them together physically is proving to be a problem. “Being able to connect the knowledge of these communities between Canada and Greenland is super important in order to really understand how that environment is changing, because they’re the ones that are there every day of the year, all year long,” says Hamilton. “The scientific aspect is important because it’s very difficult to understand how the ocean temperature is changing 300 metres below the surface unless you have particular instruments that you can deploy to measure those changes. But there are many other observations that I think are super critical to understand holistically what’s happening there.” A few minutes after dropping his submersible to take measurements, Noah is packing it up for the return trip. Today’s journey was just off the coast of Grise Fiord, but others take him further afield, sometimes with his 13-year-old daughter, Madison, but often alone, hopping from station to station like a hunter checking his traps. But Noah’s circle is widening. Wearing smart glasses that beam images to social media via portable satellite internet, he is a globally connected Inuk, part of a generation that grew up sharing hunting stories on Facebook. Now, they are sharing data, too, recreating the knowledge transfer that helped Grise Fiord survive those hard early years. It is data that can help Inuit – and the rest of the world – understand their vast and rapidly changing home. Noah has already been in talks with Hamilton about becoming a trainer for other communities, building a network across the High Arctic from Pond Inlet to Resolute to Arctic Bay, to monitor their home waters. The hunting and the science are all part of the same reconnection to the land. “I get to take my friends out here,” says Noah. “And while we’re hunting, we’re collecting data.” • A version of this article was originally published in Canada’s National Observer and has been republished by Seascape as part of the Guardian’s ClimateDesk partnership. title: Australia’s new environmental protection agency approves coal project, angering climate groups
summary: Queensland open-cut Saraji mine will be able to keep digging until 2055 as Anthony Albanese denies tensions with Pacific leaders over fossil fuels
text: Australia’s new national agency for environmental protection has approved its first coal project, allowing a Queensland open-cut mine to keep digging until 2055 while clearing threatened woodland and koala habitat. The confirmation of the extension of the Saraji mine, which digs and exports coal for steel making, comes after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, denied this week there was tension over Australia’s fossil fuel exports during talks with Pacific leaders. The National Environmental Protection Agency confirmed to Guardian Australia it had approved the BHP Mitsubishi Alliance (BMA) mine extension to dig a further 55m tonnes of coal between now and 2055. The approval is the agency’s first green light for a coal project since it began operations on 1 July after being created during reforms to national environment laws last year. An agency spokesperson said the approval came with “strict conditions to protect threatened species and water resources” and would limit clearing of habitat for threatened koalas, ornamental snakes and squatter pigeons. In its application, BMA said it would likely have to clear 9.7 hectares of endangered koala habitat, 14.2 hectares of vulnerable ornamental snake habitat, 39 hectares of habitat of the vulnerable squatter pigeon and 3.1 hectares of threatened Brigalow woodland. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The agency’s approval said the company must not clear more than 132.5 hectares of ornamental snake habitat, 162 ha of squatter pigeon habitat and 11.5 ha of koala habitat. At this week’s Pacific Islands Forum, Albanese said the meeting’s “entry fee for credibility” was “taking climate change seriously”. When asked about fossil fuel expansions, Albanese denied leaders of Pacific nations who fear for their country’s future because of rising sea levels had raised objections. “No, they don’t do that,” he said. “Australia is highly regarded when it comes to climate change, and the talking down of Australia does not happen from outside Australia. I’ll make that point. “The Pacific leaders have respect for the position that we’ve taken, and they also understand with the transition, because they’re dealing with it as well, that the transition can’t happen overnight, that it requires strategies and policies to be put in place.” Ben McLeod, a senior adviser at the Climate Council, said burning coal overseas to make steel would release about 120m tonnes of CO2 into the atmosphere over the life of the mine. Australia’s current annual emissions are 455m tonnes. “This leaves us incredulous,” said McLeod. “The prime minister said the entry fee for the forum was taking climate change seriously, but then we get this approval of 55 million tonnes of coal. It is hard to see how those two things are compatible.” He said the approval by the new agency illustrated the government’s reforms to environment laws had not been strong enough in dealing with climate pollution. He said the climate “does not care” if the emissions from burning coal were to generate electricity or make steel, and pointed to International Energy Agency advice that to meet net zero emissions by 2050 there was no requirement for more coalmines. Greenpeace Australia Pacific said the Saraji approval was the 37th fossil fuel project approved by the Albanese government, and was a “double talk” and an “affront” to Pacific leaders and communities. Dr Simon Bradshaw of Greenpeace Australia Pacific said: “It is deeply insincere for prime minister Albanese to meet Pacific leaders here in Palau to discuss security, the energy crisis, and regional threats, while his government fast-tracks the biggest security threat to the Pacific, the climate crisis. “We are witnessing dangerous climate change driven by the production, export and burning of fossil fuels, wreaking havoc across the world. Continuing down the path of fossil fuels and approving new coal is an act of recklessness at a pivotal moment in the world’s energy transition and response to the climate crisis.” Dr Coral Rowston, director of the group Environmental Advocacy Central Queensland, said the mine’s extension would put more pressure on threatened species and on water quality in the Fitzroy River catchment during flooding. A government spokesperson said the National EPA was Australia’s first independent environment regulator and was a “cornerstone” of environmental law reforms. “The Albanese government remains committed to action on climate change and our net zero targets. That’s why we reformed the safeguard mechanism in our first term, to ensure the country’s biggest emitters begin the work to reduce their emissions. This site is subject to the safeguard mechanism.” The mechanism does not account for emissions generated from burning Australian fossil fuels overseas. The statement said the government was reviewing the mechanism, which was “on course to deliver its proportionate contribution to Australia’s legislated 2030 emissions reduction target”.

title: Ukraine war briefing: ‘Shameful’ – Zelenskyy furious after shootout between Kyiv’s spy services
summary: Only shoot at Russian occupiers, president says, after three officers wounded in clash; Patriots could take years to make, says Rubio. What we know on day 1,653
text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy blasted Ukraine’s SBU and GUR after a shootout in Kyiv between the two intelligence and security services reportedly left three officers injured. The SBU is Ukraine’s internal security service, like MI5 or the FBI. The GUR, or HUR, is its armed forces counterpart and also carries out military activities and special operations. Reports said the gunfight stemmed from the SBU taking into custody a leader of an anti-Kremlin Russian unit that fights for Ukraine under the watch of the GUR. Ukraine’s president called the situation “absolutely shameful” as he called in prosecutors and investigators, as well as firing a senior SBU officer. “Here in Ukraine, shooting is only permissible at Russian occupiers in defence of Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said. “Our state will not perceive any other shootout as something that anyone is allowed to do.” Russian drones hit central Kyiv on Wednesday in a seventh ⁠day of intense strikes on the capital. Explosions were heard again in the early hours of Thursday morning. On Wednesday, 11 people were wounded, and residential and ⁠university buildings damaged. Russia also struck power facilities in the southern Odesa region with missiles and drones, authorities said, knocking out power to more than 350,000 homes. Two people were killed and eight wounded in strikes on the south-eastern city of Dnipro, the regional governor said, where food warehouses and educational buildings were damaged. Norway has seized ⁠a Russian cruise ship over unpaid compensation for the illegal annexation of Crimea. In April ⁠2023 a tribunal in The Hague ordered Russia to pay Naftogaz $4.22bn to compensate for its Crimean assets that were seized when Moscow’s forces invaded. Naftogaz is a Ukrainian state oil and gas firm. Russia has refused to pay the compensation. Naftogaz said the seizure was ordered by the ‌Nord-Troms and Senja district court on 31 August. It said the vessel, the Professor Molchanov, was owned by Russia and used for commercial expedition cruises, including to the Norwegian archipelago Svalbard. Ukraine has urged the UN’s aviation agency, the ICAO, and its member countries ⁠to ban their airlines from Russian airspace, a day after Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned it was “becoming completely unsafe” because of Ukrainian drones. Ukraine wrote to agency seeking “the full prohibition by ICAO member states of civil aircraft operations within the airspace of the Russian Federation”. In response to Ukraine’s warning, the ICAO called on its members to ensure the safety of civilian aircraft. “Long-range weapons systems, unmanned aircraft systems [UAS], global navigation satellite system radio frequency interference, and advanced air defence systems are among the military technologies jeopardising civilian aviation.” It could take Ukraine several years to start building Patriot air defence interceptors and doing so is not an immediate solution for Kyiv, Marco Rubio has said. “I mean, these are highly sophisticated weaponry,” the US secretary of state told Fox News. The US was negotiating with Ukraine over licensed production of Patriot missiles, Rubio said. “That may come to fruition, but it really won’t solve the short-term challenge that they’re pointing to,” he said, adding that “the whole world is asking for more air interceptors” but US needs came first. “It’s become the number one defence need on the planet, not just for Ukraine, but on the planet,” including in the Middle East because of the US-Israeli war against Iran. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s air raid alerting system would be revised into two tiers – red for missiles, yellow for drones – allowing for more “predictability and a better understanding of how to react”. He added that curfew ⁠hours would be reduced and more above-ground transport options offered to compensate for metro closures. The measures were a response to “Russia’s changing tactics” and “its use of drones to wear down civilian life in our cities and disrupt normal economic activity across our country”, Zelenskyy said. Belgium has continued to block EU attempts to use €200bn in frozen Russian assets for Ukraine’s benefit. Opposition from Belgium has forced EU members to instead give Ukraine a €90bn loan off their own backs – but as that fund runs down, four countries have pushed to reopen the debate on the Russian assets. Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, said the Belgian government’s position remained “unchanged … Using these assets through a process akin to confiscation carries significant risk.” The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said after ministerial talks in Ireland that fresh funds for Ukraine should ultimately come from Russia. “That is why some of the member states were proposing to go back to the discussion of the frozen assets. And we will continue that discussion.” Britain’s sanctions enforcer, the OFSI, has fined Citibank £4.7m (US$6.35m) for failings and errors that led to banned Russians getting access to funds. Most of it happened between February and November 2022, the OFSI said. The CBNA London branch processed 970 payments totalling £19.7m – some for state-owned shipping company PJSC ‌Sovcomflot, as well as Alfa-Bank, PJSC Gazprombank and Credit Bank of Moscow. The agency did not consider there to have been any intent by CBNA London to breach sanctions, and the bank voluntarily disclosed most of the breaches. A Citi spokesperson said it ‌welcomed the conclusion of the ‌case and took sanctions compliance seriously.

title: China’s falling emissions amid Iran war spark hope of decarbonisation watershed
summary: Oil consumption plummets and EV sales soar as analysts say demand may not fully return even if crude price falls
text: China’s carbon dioxide emissions fell by 1% after the outbreak of the US-Israeli war on Iran, thanks to a sharp reduction in oil consumption and a steady rise in the use of electric vehicles and public transport, analysis shows. The report reveals the role of clean energy in cushioning the price shocks caused by the strait of Hormuz crisis to the world’s biggest oil importer. It also reinforces hopes that China, which is the world’s biggest greenhouse gas emitter, may be nearing a turning point in decarbonising its economy. China was able to increase overall transportation use, despite cutting oil imports by 32%, according to second-quarter energy data reported by the country’s National Bureau of Statistics and analysed for Carbon Brief by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. The reduction – equivalent to about a million barrels a day – from the world’s biggest petro-customer helped to stabilise global oil prices, which nevertheless surged by about 60% in the weeks and months after the first US airstrikes in late February. How that was achieved has been the subject of considerable speculation. The analysis indicates that about two-thirds of the fall in imports came from running down, rather than building up, strategic oil stockpiles. The remaining third was largely covered by a reduction in demand. The country’s use of oil fell by 9% overall and by 16% for transport. While large numbers of petrol and diesel vehicles stayed off the roads, there was a surge in journeys by electric cars, buses, trains and trucks. This electrifying trend had begun long before the strait of Hormuz crisis. China is by far the world’s biggest manufacturer, user and exporter of batteries, e-vehicles, wind turbines and solar panels. The disruption of oil supplies from the Gulf has strengthened the economic and strategic imperative of reducing petro-dependence. In the first half of 2026, China’s shift towards electric vehicles displaced the equivalent of the UK’s entire oil consumption over a six-month period. Analysts predict much of this demand will not return even if global oil prices fall. “In a qualitative sense, there’s no question that the transport sector decarbonisation has been accelerated,” said Lauri Myllyvirta, the lead analyst at the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. “It’s a validation of the energy security strategy that China has in place … It’s very clear that electrification is the winning strategy to insure against these kinds of shocks.” Myllyvirta noted this was the first time China’s overall emissions had fallen due to a reduction in oil use rather than in coal consumption. In fact, coal generation rose during the quarter due to shifting economic incentives and delays in adapting the country’s grid, which caused considerable wastage of wind and solar power. Despite this, observers believe the longer-term trend in China is away from fossil fuels. Dr Muyi Yang, a senior analyst at Ember, which will next week publish a separate overview of China’s energy trends, said a fossil fuel peak was coming into view at the provincial and sectoral level. “The Iran crisis reinforces the case. The way China has been able to absorb its impact strengthens the confidence to go deeper and further. “The risk of oil-import dependence increasingly comes from the geopolitical domain. This is a risk no country can effectively manage. So the more effective strategy is to reduce that exposure altogether. And China’s experience is demonstrating that this works.”

title: Suspect and two victims dead at apartment shooting in downtown Minneapolis
summary: The city’s police department and mayor warn the public to stay away from the Loring Park neighborhood nearby
text: Two people were killed and the suspect was dead after a shooting at an apartment building in downtown Minneapolis on Wednesday afternoon, officials said. One shooting victim died at the scene. A second died after arriving at Hennepin county medical center, a hospital spokesperson said. Gunfire erupted on the upper floor of a high-rise apartment building, according to city officials. Video posted to social media showed police aiming rifles upward at an apartment tower near the Minneapolis convention center. After receiving several 911 calls, officers entered the building at about 4.39pm. They followed the sound of shots and encountered a “haze”, which limited their sight, officials said. Two officers were wounded by the gunfire, with one sustaining a non-life-threatening injury to the leg and a second undergoing surgery. Authorities have not publicly identified the suspect. Julius Bailey was sitting outside his apartment building when he heard gunshots and saw a man he recognized as a resident of the building holding a pistol. Bailey said he heard a woman screaming and immediately started running away. He said he counted eight shots. Bailey said he recognized the man holding the gun because he was someone who was known for showing off his weapon. Bailey said he had tried to avoid the man since moving into the building in June. “I could tell he was trouble,” he said. Chris Miller, who also lives in the apartment building, said he heard a rapid succession of gunshots and quickly ran outside for safety. He said he believed he knew who carried out the shooting and that he encountered someone in the hallway with a handgun earlier this week and reported that person to management. The Minneapolis police department and mayor Jacob Frey warned the public to stay away from the densely populated Loring Park neighborhood nearby. “Grateful to law enforcement actively working to ensure the safety of our neighbors in Downtown Minneapolis this afternoon,” Minnesota governor Tim Walz said in a statement. “Minnesota is praying for our first responders.” The FBI has extended its resources to aid law enforcement on the ground, director Kash Patel wrote in an X post. The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Epstein survivors urge billionaire Leon Black to cooperate with House panel
summary: Black called on to comply with subpoenas and appear as required to clarify connections to convicted sex offender
text: More than a dozen survivors of Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse have called on the billionaire Leon Black to appear before the House oversight committee in order to clarify his connections to the late disgraced financier and convicted sex offender. In a letter released on Wednesday, the survivors urged Black to comply with congressional subpoenas ahead of Thursday’s deposition before the House oversight committee. “We are survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell’s abuse and exploitation, and we are calling on Leon Black to appear as required before the House oversight committee on Thursday,” the statement said. “We are also calling on Black to fully comply with the committee’s subpoenas, including its demand that he produce all responsive nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in his possession.” Black, the New York private equity investor, paid Epstein tens of millions of dollars in fees during work he has described as tax and estate-planning services. He has already faced accusations of purposely delaying and disrupting the panel’s inquiry. The letter further stated that “Black’s use of NDAs underscores why Congress must scrutinize the agreements in his possession and determine whether they shed light on his relationship with Jeffrey Epstein and others in Epstein’s orbit”. “If Black continues to withhold responsive records or refuses to comply with the committee’s demands, Congress should use every tool available to enforce its subpoenas.” Last week, the Republican chairman of the House oversight committee, James Comer, threatened to hold Black in contempt if he fails to fully cooperate with the panel’s investigation into Epstein. Black had not yet confirmed his appearance before the committee as of Tuesday, a person familiar with the matter had told the Guardian. In a previous statement before the oversight committee in June, Black denied knowledge of Epstein’s crimes, writing: “I did not know about this nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019.” However, Black acknowledged that he was aware that Epstein had pleaded guilty in 2008 “to state charges relating to prostitution involving a minor”. In a speech from the House floor this week, Thomas Massie, the Kentucky Republican who recently lost his primary to a challenger backed by Donald Trump, read aloud the names of several friends and associates of Epstein, including Black. Massie called on the Department of Justice to investigate the group of men and women whom the representative referred to as “perpetrators” of Epstein’s crimes. Massie also emphasized that despite the fact it has been nearly a year since Trump signed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, millions of the Epstein files remain unreleased.

title: Nuclear bomb test veterans were victims of one of ‘greatest scandals in Britain’, says ex-defence minister
summary: Exclusive: Tobias Ellwood says he gave MPs inaccurate information in 2018 provided by his department, the MoD
text: A former defence minister has admitted misleading parliament over the existence of crucial medical records relating to nuclear bomb test veterans. Tobias Ellwood has said he unwittingly gave MPs incorrect information in 2018 when he told them he had been unable to locate information on veterans’ blood tests after being given incorrect information by officials at the Ministry of Defence (MoD). Veterans have been fighting for years to see the records as many look to prove that years of serious illnesses such as cancer were linked to their experiences testing nuclear weapons. Ellwood’s admission will increase pressure on the MoD to explain whether its officials have helped prevent those veterans get justice. In a piece for the Guardian, Ellwood says: “In December 2018, as defence minister, I inadvertently misled parliament. “Asked whether blood samples had been taken from service personnel for radiological monitoring during the nuclear bomb tests, I relayed the line provided to me by the Ministry of Defence: it was ‘unable to locate any information’ suggesting blood samples had been taken for radiological monitoring at the tests. “I now know the reality was very different – these samples were taken across the armed services branches. But those veterans seeking compensation for serious illnesses developed after radiation exposure have been unable to access them.” He added: “This is among the greatest scandals in Britain, and it must be addressed.” An MoD spokesperson said: “This government commissioned and completed an extensive records discovery exercise, examining tens of thousands of documents to address long-standing questions from veterans about blood and urine testing policies during the nuclear testing programme. “The findings have now been published in full, following regular engagement between ministers, nuclear test veterans and community groups throughout the process.” Between 1952 and 1967, about 22,000 British military personnel took part in 45 large-scale nuclear weapons tests in Australia and the South Pacific. Some pilots flew through mushroom clouds, some troops crawled through fallout and many witnessed the first test wearing little more than short-sleeved shirts and shorts. Large numbers later suffered blood disorders and cancers, which they believed were caused by exposure to radioactive fallout. Most were denied pensions because of their ill health. Unlike other nuclear-armed countries such as France, the US and the Soviet Union, the UK has never compensated those involved in testing atomic bombs. The case has been compared with the infected blood scandal, which saw more than 30,000 people contract HIV and Hepatitis C in the the 1970s and early 1990s after being given contaminated blood and blood products. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has previously said he was misled by officials when he claimed as health secretary in 2009 that there was no evidence that people were knowingly given contaminated blood. His claims echo those being made today by Ellwood. Burnham has also been a vocal supporter of the nuclear test veterans in recent years. As Greater Manchester mayor in 2022, Burnham said: “If the state was conducting medical tests upon servicemen and not informing them when they found serious irregularity, that is at least misconduct in public office, and more serious, perhaps gross negligence manslaughter, in respect of people who died as a result. “Crimes have been committed.” The prime minister is now coming under pressure to begin an inquiry and allocate government money for compensation to the victims. One of the major problems with securing compensation so far has been the lack of medical evidence linking veterans’ health problems to their experiences helping with nuclear tests. The government long maintained that it did not hold any such medical records – a claim that was proved incorrect in 2022 when the journalist Susie Boniface revealed the existence of a database of 28,000 documents known as Merlin. That database had been put together in response to a 2007 lawsuit by 1,000 British test veterans and their families, but the information was classified. Ellwood says he did not find out about the existence of this database until 2022, when details began to emerge in the press. He writes in his piece: “If this information existed within the MoD, why had ministers not been given the full picture?”

title: Andy Burnham targets migrant crisis ahead of Macron’s visit to No 10
summary: PM will aim to centre talks with French president on key foreign policy issues such as Iran, smuggling gangs and EU relations
text: Andy Burnham will begin the process of courting European leaders when he welcomes Emmanuel Macron as the first foreign head of state to visit him in Downing Street. The prime minister will meet the French president at No 10 on Thursday as he looks to make inroads on a number of foreign policy objectives, including curbing irregular migration and sealing a new deal with the EU. The meeting marks one of Burnham’s first forays into foreign policy, having previously promised to remain mostly focused on domestic issues, and comes weeks before a crunch EU summit that could shape much of his future economic strategy. Burnham said in a statement on Wednesday: “The progress we have seen this summer [in bringing down the number of small boat crossings] shows what can be achieved when the UK and France work together. “But I am clear that we cannot be complacent. Smuggling gangs are constantly adapting their tactics, and the UK and France need to respond quickly and stay one step ahead of the criminals facilitating the dangerous crossings. “The small boats crisis is a shared European challenge, and no country can solve it alone. Working with France and our international partners, we will restore order and control to our borders and prevent smugglers exploiting vulnerable migrants.” While Burnham has talked almost exclusively about domestic issues such as the cost of living since becoming prime minister, he is quickly finding himself having to deal with international crises as well. Last month he met the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to help celebrate the country’s independence day, when he announced he would declassify sensitive military information to allow Ukraine to build more cruise missiles. On Thursday he will discuss migration, EU relations, Ukraine and the war in Iran with Macron. The two leaders will announce additional resources for French police to help stop small boats being launched from the country’s north coast and larger “mega-dinghies” departing from the west. Downing Street said on Wednesday that the number of French officers dealing with small boat crossings in northern France would soon rise to nearly 1,050 officers – up by roughly a quarter in four months. The teams will include a specialist 75-person team to seize equipment and arrest smugglers on land. A separate intelligence unit will be expanded from 18 to 30, while another 45 officers will be deployed to the west coast. Irregular migration has fallen down the political agenda in recent weeks thanks to a drop in the number of small boat crossings. This week, Burnham said the drop in numbers to a seven-year low was a result of efforts by his predecessor Keir Starmer to tackle smuggling gangs – though experts say external factors such as an improvement in Syria’s security situation have also played a role. The prime minister will also use the meeting to press Macron to support his efforts to renegotiate Britain’s treaty with the EU. Brussels postponed a planned summit from July to allow the new prime minister time to review tentative agreements made by Starmer, with a new one expected in early November. European countries have been pushing hard for Britain to agree a new youth mobility scheme and to allow their students to pay home fees at British universities – both concessions that Starmer was ready to make, according to recent reports. However, Burnham may take a tougher line on the number of young people he is willing to admit as part of the scheme, having promised to pass all government policies through a “Makerfield test” to measure them against the views of his constituents. In return, Britain wants new agreements to ease trade in electricity and agricultural products, which officials hope will give a timely boost to the UK economy. The prime minister told the Guardian last year he wanted the UK to rejoin the EU, but has since said this would not be something he would actively pursue as prime minister.

title: Apple Maps renames Lake Ontario as ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order
summary: Tech company submits to controversial Trump order to rename body of water amid US trade spat with Canada
text: Apple has renamed Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for US users of its Maps app, after an executive order from Donald Trump to change the name of the Great Lake amid his trade spat with Canada. The Apple Maps app now displays the controversial new name for the lake, which sits between New York state and the Canadian province of Ontario, for users in the US. Apple users outside the country will still see the Lake Ontario name. Apple had been reportedly mulling whether to submit to Trump’s new order after receiving a personal request from the president for the tech company to change the lake’s name. Trump welcomed the news, declaring in a Truth Social post that the adoption of “Lake America” by Google Maps and Apple Maps meant the name change was “complete, ratified, and binding”. However, the US cannot compel Canada – or any other country – to also change the name. The US president officially unveiled the name swap last week. He did not mention his escalating trade feud with the US’s northern neighbors in the order, but the timing suggested a retaliatory move after Canadian officials denounced Trump’s new sweeping tariffs and promised to instate tariffs of their own. Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, rejected the attempt to rename the body of water, saying in a post on social media that the lake’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US Declaration of Independence. Late last month, trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed, with the US subsequently imposing a 50% tariff on several Canadian imports. Trump additionally threatened another round of 50% duties on Canadian steel, trucks, cars and auto parts to take effect in the new year. Carney retaliated with 25-50% tariffs on hundreds of US goods. Rather than mention any of this, Trump instead said in the order that the purpose of the renaming is to honor “the policy of my Administration to recognize the extraordinary contributions of the American people and the rich heritage of our history by naming great natural landmarks for our shared achievements”. Earlier this week, Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, said in an interview with Fox Business that “the president has reached out to Apple directly” and predicted with confidence that US users would “be seeing that change coming up soon”. Apple’s competitor, Google, already made the change over the weekend, with Google Maps now showing the Lake America branding. Google cited Trump’s order and its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS). In a blogpost issued on Saturday, Google said US users would see the Lake America name while users in Canada will see Lake Ontario, and “those outside of the US and Canada will see both names.” The digital name change is unsurprising considering Google Maps was an early adopter of the Gulf of America moniker and still currently displays the title, despite the renaming hardly being a success outside US government lingo. On Tuesday, it was reported that MapQuest, the pioneering online mapping app, reached the No 1 spot on Apple’s App Store after openly rejecting Trump’s request to rename the lake. The app simply posted a screenshot of Lake Ontario on social media last Thursday along with the caption: “We’re not changing it.” The act of defiance was enough to catapult the app into becoming the most in-demand navigation tool in the US.
