title: Sadiq Khan fined over untaxed car falsely registered in his name
summary: London mayor’s office says he is ‘victim of a scam’ after conviction under fast-track system where magistrates can decide outcomes in seconds
text: Sadiq Khan’s office has revealed he was the victim of a scam that led to him being fined for failing to tax a car that did not belong to him. The London mayor was found guilty last month under a system of “conveyor-belt justice”, in which magistrates decide on hundreds of cases a day, sometimes spending less than a minute on each. City Hall officials say the 24-year-old Nissan Micra did not belong to Khan or Transport for London. The mayor has been the focus of protests by motorists angry at the expansion of the ultra-low emission zone in London. Some said they planned to register cars in Khan’s name to make him liable for the £12.50 daily charge. The prosecution was undertaken by the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency, which accused Khan of being the keeper of the vehicle when it was spotted as being untaxed on 24 January. In a move that paves the way for the conviction to be erased after a court hearing on Thursday, the DVLA said on Wednesday evening that the case had been withdrawn after a review and it was investigating the circumstances. “This is a scam, which is a crime,” said a spokesperson for Khan. “It’s not the first time the mayor has been the victim of a scam involving people falsely stating that Sadiq is the owner of a vehicle. Such behaviour is illegal, and the DVLA are aware.” A magistrate, sitting in a private hearing of the single justice procedure in Herefordshire, convicted Khan in his absence and ordered that he pay a £220 fine, £85 in costs and settle the £35.84 bill for unpaid tax on the Micra. The Press Association alerted the DVLA to the criminal conviction on Tuesday and its officials confirmed they were reviewing the case and investigating the circumstances of the prosecution. Court documents show that DVLA letters addressed to the mayor about the unpaid tax bill were sent to a Gordon Ramsay restaurant in east London instead of the nearby TfL offices. The mayor faces the possibility of having to appear in court to try to overturn the conviction. The single justice procedure was introduced in 2015 as a cheaper method of dealing with low-level criminal cases, allowing magistrates to sit alone and in private. The system, which is under government review, was criticised in 2024 when about 59,000 train-fare evasion convictions were overturned for being unlawful. It also emerged that children had been wrongly convicted in the secretive courts. More scrutiny has come over repeated incidents of sick and incapacitated pensioners being convicted for not paying their household bills. In Khan’s case, court records show he was prosecuted by the DVLA after the annual tax on the Micra, which was first registered in 2002, ran out last September.

title: Leipzig airport attack fallout exposes Germany’s deepening divide over Russia
summary: The government’s tougher stance towards the Kremlin is drawing attacks from both the far right and far left
text: Even before the German government laid the blame this week on Russia for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport, the topic of German ties to Moscow was high on the political agenda. But the timing of the unsurprising yet explosive Leipzig announcement – days before a key regional vote – has exposed the extent to which German politics is polarised on the issue. Leading the polls nationally and in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, which votes this weekend, is the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD). The party has repeatedly called for a closer bond with the Kremlin, and crucially, for its cheap oil and gas to flow to Germany once again, despite Moscow’s unrelenting onslaught on Ukraine. Germany is already on tenterhooks. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, had warned that Berlin faced a growing threat of hybrid warfare, and on Wednesday morning, the day after the Leipzig announcement, police were investigating a second sabotage assault on the electricity grid within just 24 hours. An explosion at Augsburg railway station in the early hours of Wednesday morning also initially looked like it might fall into the same category, illustrating the extent to which the country remains nervous and on high ‌alert for attacks on its vital infrastructure. Investigations into all these incidents and others from the near past, many of which are said to be linked, are ongoing, even as authorities warned against drawing premature conclusions. Moscow has denied involvement, and accused Berlin of trying to divert attention from its own domestic problems, including the rise of the far right, and the state’s failure to protect its own infrastructure. The resulting uncertainty, chaos and angst appear to be nothing less than grist to the mill of the AfD. Its foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, accused the government of sorting acts of sabotage “according to political expediency”. While it had “escalated the situation against Russia within days”, he said, the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukrainian operatives are suspected of being responsible for sabotaging a key route for Russian gas to Germany, had so far remained without consequence. (Two Ukrainian nationals named by Germany as suspects have been arrested over the attack, with one last year extradited from Italy and the other currently in Croatia.) “This is not a consistent security policy, but rather a double standard in foreign policy,” Frohnmaier claimed, adding he was convinced the government would use the Leipzig incident “as justification for even more support for Ukraine and an even deeper involvement of Germany in this war”. The AfD, which has called for talks with Moscow, ending sanctions against Russia, and slashing support for Ukraine, has urged the government to lay bare its proof of Russia’s involvement, saying so far the evidence is lacking. Wary of escalating a conflict with Moscow, the government of Friedrich Merz waited days before making its painstakingly worded declaration. In a more frank admission than the German government has ever made, foreign minister Johann Wadephul stated: “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.” The details released on Wednesday of two Russian suspects identified as having been involved in the Leipzig incident are unlikely to assuage the AfD’s complaints or, it would seem, the far-left party Die Linke. Its leading MP, Dietmar Bartsch, said on Wednesday that the suspicions of Russian involvement did not justify the government’s decision to shut down the Russian consulate in Bonn as well as a sprawling Russian cultural centre in Berlin and would not make Germany safer. On the contrary, they increased the risk of a “major war” drawing closer, he said. With the AfD on around 42% in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt and possibly poised to form the first far-right-led administration since the second world war, Merz’s Christlich Demokratische Union (CDU), on around 22%, is under intense pressure. Within Merz’s own party, there have been growing calls for him to toughen his stance against Moscow and pure frustration that it has taken so long. For years, members of his Christian Democrats and his current coalition partner, the Social Democrats, along with generations of diplomats, have remained caught up in, and seduced by, the long-standing romantic notion that Russia could be tamed by trade and energy pipelines, according to the CDU’s Roderich Kiesewetter. The former soldier and the party’s respected foreign policy expert told broadcaster InfoRadio that Germany “must give up its caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil, as well as this romantic notion of Russia as a great cultural nation. Russia cares not a damn about this caution, but rather sees it as an invitation to keep escalating.” He criticised Merz’s recent public reference to Russia as a great cultural nation, “because great cultural nations do not subject their neighbouring states to war, violence and child abductions”. He said it was time for Merz to name the current Russian regime for what it was. Konstantin von Notz, foreign policy expert for the Greens, praised the government’s “significantly clear language” over Moscow’s behaviour, even as he described it as “long overdue”. The extent to which voters in Saxony-Anhalt fear how a further deterioration of relations with Moscow could affect them may yet be felt at the ballot box.

title: Reform UK bans three journalists from its conference after critical reporting
summary: Guardian City editor Anna Isaac among those who had credentials to cover event declined
text: Reform UK has banned at least three journalists from its annual conference who have reported critically on the party and Nigel Farage. The Guardian’s City editor, Anna Isaac, the investigative reporter Peter Geoghegan and the broadcaster and biographer Michael Crick were told this week that their credentials to cover the event, which begins on Thursday, had been declined. The party has billed its conference, which will take place at the National Exhibition Centre in Birmingham, as “the most talked about event of 2026”. Reform figures are hoping to use it as a reset after a difficult summer consumed by questions about an undeclared £5m gift Farage received shortly before he was elected in 2024. A Reform spokesperson said Geoghegan and Crick were refused accreditation because the party viewed them as minor figures. They declined to comment on why Isaac was not given accreditation. After the Guardian contacted Reform for comment, all three received emails saying their conference passes had been reinstated. However, when contacted again by the Guardian, a Reform spokesperson said this had been an administrative error and that they were still not accredited for the conference. They then received further emails confirming their exclusion. Isaac broke the story that Farage had accepted an undeclared £5m gift from Christopher Harborne. Her reporting also revealed that a host of transactions involving Reform UK’s most senior figures and donations to the party caused bankers to report potential money-laundering concerns to the National Crime Agency. The story has caused issues for Farage all summer and he has drastically reduced his time in front of the press. He also resigned as an MP over the furore, prompting a byelection which the other main parties boycotted, leaving Count Binface as his main opponent. Farage won, and was sworn back into parliament on Monday. Geoghegan runs the Democracy for Sale newsletter on Substack and has written for the Guardian and the New York Times. He received the news he had been banned from the conference shortly after publishing a piece revealing negative comments the pro-Reform journalist Isabel Oakeshott allegedly made about Harborne. Oakeshott declined to comment about the allegations when the Guardian contacted her. Geoghegan said: “Reform clearly wants press coverage but it doesn’t want the scrutiny and accountability that comes with it. Farage and co like to present themselves as the anti-establishment insurgents, but banning independent journalists like me from party conference isn’t anti-establishment. It’s the establishment playbook.” Crick said: “I can understand why the Reform high command might not want me talking to ordinary party members.” He published an unflattering biography of Farage in 2022, including details of a letter a teacher once sent to the head of Dulwich college when Farage was proposed as a prefect, complaining about his “publicly professed racist and neo-fascist views”. Crick has also said he believes Farage “panders to racists”. He told the Telegraph this summer that Farage’s fatal flaw was that he was thin-skinned and purged people he disagreed with. On the party’s apparent reinstatements and then U-turn, Crick said: “What cock-up merchants!” A party spokesperson said: “Reform UK accepted 950 of about 1,000 media applications from a variety of outlets, including the entire Guardian lobby team. “Mr Crick works for a university and Mr Geoghegan is a Substack blogger. Neither qualify for a media pass.” The Reform spokesperson refused to give a reason for Isaac’s ban but said: “Anna will still be able to watch the conference proceedings on our livestream if she wishes.” Laura Davison, NUJ general secretary, said: “Reports that Reform UK has chosen to ban journalists who have scrutinised the party from attending its conference are frustrating and concerning. A functioning democracy depends on a free press that can ask political parties difficult questions and hold those seeking power to account.” Pointing to what she called “a wider pattern of intimidation and obstruction of journalists,” and noting that the Conservatives and Labour blocked or removed journalists from their conferences last year, Davison said: “We urge the government and all political parties to demonstrate their commitment to media freedom and uphold the public’s right to be informed. Reform UK should rethink its position and allow journalists full access to the conference.” A Guardian spokesperson said: “Holding public figures to account is the role of a free press and an essential part of the democratic process. Our journalists should be able to ask questions in the public interest and not be deterred from doing their job.”

title: Andy Burnham must face down unions over donation cap | Letters
summary: Letters: It is no use promising to reform politics and return power to the people without addressing the power of the big beasts, writes Paul Sawbridge. Plus letters from Marcus Hallside and Martin Knott
text: So much for a new way of doing politics. Even before parliament had convened under his premiership, Andy Burnham had already stumbled at the first hurdle (Burnham drops support for political funding cap aimed at curbing mega-donors, 26 August). Despite widespread support for hard caps to political donations, and despite years of affirming support for such measures, a whisper of opposition from the union lobby has produced a screeching U-turn. It is no use promising to return power to the people via devolution, employee ownership and so on, and then refusing to address the power of the big beasts of the politics of yesteryear. Come on, Andy! If you are to make any impact on reversing the appalling effects of Thatcherite neoliberalism, you are going to need to show more bottle than this. You should immediately support Stella Creasy’s amendment – and throw in a commitment to a national commission on electoral reform. Paul Sawbridge Ealing, London • The GMB union’s opposition to a cap on political donations raises a question that goes beyond the immediate dispute: when does legitimate defence of an organisation’s interests become defence of a political system that gives that organisation disproportionate influence? Trade unions have a legitimate role in politics. But political finance should ultimately be governed by the democratic interests of citizens, not those of organisations. The same principle must apply to wealthy individuals and corporations. There is a troubling historical precedent. In the 2010 Labour leadership election, the GMB was one of the unions that backed Ed Miliband against his brother, David. David led decisively among Labour MPs and party members, but Ed won overwhelmingly in the union section and ultimately became leader by just 50.65% to 49.35%. The unions did not single-handedly determine that result, but their mobilisation was crucial. It is therefore reasonable to ask whether the GMB has reflected on the consequences of using its organisational power to influence Labour’s political direction. Ed Miliband’s leadership was followed by Labour’s defeat in 2015, the return of Conservative government and years of austerity. His defeat also formed part of the political sequence that culminated in the Brexit referendum. To say the unions “caused” these outcomes would be simplistic. But to pretend that their intervention had no consequences would be equally misleading. The GMB argues that a cap on donations could damage Labour’s ability to raise funds from affiliated organisations. That is institutional self-interest. But it should not be confused with the national interest. Britain needs political finance rules that reduce the influence of money and organised interests, whoever they are. Marcus Hallside Radlett, Hertfordshire • I am in favour of both empowering unions and capping donations. The objectives of union donors are widely different to those of the mega-rich donors. While the latter seek self-enrichment, the unions’ only aim is to enable a society where workers’ rights are upheld and a fair wage is earned, and to increase employment rates. This fits perfectly with the aims of the Labour party: to support everyday working people and provide for those who cannot work. So I say: cap at around £1m to enable unions to donate and to curb the excessive influence of the mega-rich. Martin Knott Edinburgh • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: The $1 Trump coin: legal tender, depending on what you mean by legal
summary: Various laws and 250 years of tradition prevent the likeness of living people from appearing on currency. Donald Trump and Scott Bessent don’t want you to worry about that
text: Two hallmarks of Donald Trump’s second-term: the president’s enthusiasm for putting his name and face on things, and his cavalier approach to established law. Today the president is once again combining both those interests, as the government releases a $1 coin bearing his image, an item of currency that scholars say should be illegal, but which is happening anyway. How many times have you heard that in the last 18 months? The US has had a long tradition of not putting living people on US currencybeginning in the late 1700s when the US Mint, which manufactures and distributes currency, wanted to put an image of George Washington on US money. Washington declined, saying it would be too much like a monarchy putting its rulers on money. In 1866, Congress passed an amendment barring the “portrait or likeness” of living people from appearing on currency. That doesn’t appear to have bothered Trump. His scowling face dominates the new $1 coin, which is legal tender, and looks gold but is actually made from zinc, manganese, nickel and copper. It costs $61 to buy 25 one-dollar coins – you do the math – and about 9m of the coins are being made. They will, according to the US Mint, “honor 250 years of great American heritage”. That all sounds great, if you’re into that sort of thing, but what about the law?. Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary, has argued that during the 150th celebration of America’s “birthday”, the face of then president Calvin Coolidge appeared on a coin, so during the 250th, the Trump coin is fine. The main problem seems to be that there’s a hodge-podge of laws which govern what can and cannot go on a coin. The 1866 ban on featuring living people arose from an impressively creative act of vanity. An incoming five-cent note was supposed to feature an image of the deceased explorer William Clark, but a treasury official called Spencer M Clark took advantage of the pair sharing a last name to instead print his own face on the note. The problem was that members of Congress a) noticed and b) were unamused. They passed an amendment which ruled that US money can only feature dead individuals – but it only applied to paper money. “For me, I would consider it illegal,” Gabriel Mathy, an associate professor of economics at American University who has studied American currency, said of the Trump coin. “But the United States has all these laws, which really are norms because they’re not really enforceable.” The coin hasn’t been produced without a fight. In May, a group of Democratic members of Congress wrote to the treasury department in May, urging them to desist with the coin, pointing to a 2005 law which further restricted which presidents could appear on coins. And in March, James Rickher, a retired attorney in Portland, filed a request to block the coin, arguing it was illegal, but in June a federal judge denied that motion, writing that Rickher had “failed to present evidence that clearly shows he will personally suffer concrete harm from issuance of the challenged coin”, Fox 12 reported. The judge noted, however, that his ruling did not determine whether the coin is illegal or legal. And so today, Americans will be able to honor 250 years of great American heritage by buying a questionably legal one-dollar coin for roughly $2.44. If you’d like to know who came up with such a brilliant plan, just look at the coin.

title: Uber to cut 3,300 corporate jobs in management overhaul
summary: Company says it is slashing 10% of its workforce to make operations ‘simpler and faster’
text: Uber plans to cut its global workforce by about 10% as part of a major restructuring, slashing about 3,300 corporate jobs. The boss of the US-based ride-hailing app, Dara Khosrowshahi, told staff Wednesday that the changes would create a “simpler and faster” business by cutting layers of management and merging teams. Uber also plans to ask more employees to work in the office. Uber, which has its headquarters in San Francisco, did not specify how many roles would be affected in each location that it has offices, including in London. The cuts are the largest since 2020 when Uber laid off 6,700 people in response to a major downturn in rides during the Covid pandemic. Staff affected have been notified, but some countries will have their own local process to follow, according to the firm. Khosrowshahi said in his message that Uber had been growing in the past five years and the business was performing well. “But that growth has also brought complexity: more layers, more coordination, more fragmented ownership, and in some cases structures that made sense when businesses were smaller but no longer serve us well at our current scale,” he said. “The changes we’re making today are designed to do two things: make Uber simpler and faster, and create more capacity to invest in our future.” Uber is also asking the majority of its staff to come into an office, meaning less than about 1% of employees will be working remotely. The move will reinforce a hybrid work policy which requires three days a week in the office. Khosrowshahi laid out organisational changes including combining operational and tech teams, and reducing the number of “micro-teams” – where one or two employees report to a single manager – by nearly 50%. The number of employees who sit more than seven layers from the chief executive has also been cut by 20%. “The decisions we’re making today are difficult, but they will help us build an even stronger Uber for the years ahead,” Khosrowshahi said. Uber is preparing to launch self-driving taxis for the first time on UK roads after partnering with the robotaxi business Wayve and being granted approval by Transport for London last month. The company plans to spend $10bn toward developing its autonomous vehicle business, aiming to form a grip on the burgeoning market of self-driving. Uber also recently struck a $14.8bn deal to acquire the German company Delivery Hero as it jockeys for dominance in the global food delivery market. The company’s UberEats service faces intense competition from rival apps such as DoorDash. Uber expanded rapidly after launched in San Francisco in 2010, and is now valued at more than $150bn.

title: After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepal’s worst-hit districts
summary: Thousands remain missing and aid is hampered by treacherous conditions in communities almost wiped out of existence
text: Searching for the body of his wife in the mud, Dil Bahadur Shrestha lamented that he did not even have a shovel left. For now, he has been using his hands to try to find her as he picks through the ruins of his house. On Wednesday morning last week, Jamuna Shrestha, his wife of 50 years, had been at home in Betrawati on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli River, feeding her beloved chickens and goats. As deadly flash floods coursed down the river valley, Jamuna was last seen going back into her house, trying to usher her chickens to safety, while others fled uphill. Now that house stands like a muddy carcass, everything inside it destroyed or washed away by the violent force of the water and debris that killed more than 1,200 people in Nepal and Tibet. Dil Bahadur Shrestha, 70, had been tending to his rice fields and feeding his cows on the opposite bank when he felt the ground tremble and saw a black wave, hundreds of metres high, coming down the valley. He ran to safety in the forest, but not before watching two bridges get swept away behind him. “When it hit, everything was destroyed within two minutes,” he said. Dil Bahadur Shrestha, who is searching for his wife of 50 years, Jamuna. He knows in his heart that his wife is gone, but like thousands caught up in the disaster, her body has yet to be found and she is counted among the missing. More than 5,000 people are reported missing in Nepal and a further 546 in the Tibet region of China. Rescue workers have still not reached Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s home, so he returned to try to retrieve her body himself. “Maybe she thought the flood wouldn’t reach inside the house,” he said, wiping away tears. The couple had already rebuilt their home once after an earthquake in 2015 that killed about 9,000 people. As he spoke, his frail body collapsed to the barren, muddy ground where his neighbour’s house once stood. “Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone,” he said. “I cannot forget her. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.” A Rasuwa district sign in the flood debris in Betrawati. The scale of the tragedy in Betrawati is unfathomable. It was 8.37am when a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and Tibet crashed into the valley below, setting off deadly flash floods down Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers. By 8.50am, with only a few minutes’ warning, the settlement of Betrawati was engulfed. This once-thriving market town was submerged in mud so thick that only the top two floors of a six-storey building are visible. Most houses were washed away entirely or flipped on their sides by the sheer force of the floods. School buses lie overturned. A grocery shop was swept 200 metres from its original location and lies in ruins. The river itself has diverted to a new path that cuts through where the highway once was. An overturned school bus hit by the flood water. Fragments of the lives of the thousands who lived here lie scattered in the debris: kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses. At least 250 people are missing, Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s brother and sister-in-law among them. As Dil Bahadur Shrestha surveyed the ruins of his life, search and rescue teams stood on the opposite bank, looking for the dead. By the end of the day, they had pulled 24 bodies from a single house. A helicopter thundered overhead, white body bags swinging underneath. “I feel there could still be hundreds of bodies here,” said Dil Bahadur Shrestha. “So many people were swept away all at once, carried off by the raging water.” His voice broke: “Now I’m alone. I am completely alone.” Santamaya Lawat tries to retrieve some of her belongings. A few metres away, Santamaya Lawat, 57, stood shaking a thick cake of dirt from the few clothes and blankets she had been able to retrieve from her brother’s home, now only partly standing, with a gaping hole in the side. Her own house, built just 10 months ago with her life’s savings, was still so filled with mud she had not yet been able to get inside. Five members of her family are gone. Santamaya Lawat has lost five members of her family as well as her home and her brother’s home next door. “My heart broke when I came back,” she said. “This was supposed to be the house I lived in for the rest of my life, but everything is gone. It was like heaven here and now it has been turned into hell.” *** Further up the river, in the district of Rasuwa, on the border with Tibet, the scale of destruction only gets worse. Many of the villages here were swept away entirely and are only accessibly by army helicopter. Some are still so cut-off and the ground conditions so precarious that the fate of hundreds of people remains unknown. On Tuesday, police search and rescue teams confirmed they had finally been able to begin ground operations in the border village of Timure, recovering 90 bodies so far. A week after the disaster, survivors who fled up mountainsides were still being collected by army helicopters and evacuated to the army base in Dhunche, Rasuwa district’s administrative headquarters. The mountain village of Syabru Besi was among those wiped clean away, with even the road to the village gone. According to local government officials, at least 500 people there are missing, a quarter of the population. The village resembles nothing more than a muddy riverbed, just one building left standing. Chhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing. “There were 15 or 16 of us from the village who made it safely to the forest,” said Dorje. “We stayed there for two days before the army came in a helicopter. We had nothing to eat. We survived by drinking water from the forest.” He stood tightly holding the hand of his nine-year-old granddaughter, Ritu Tamang, who wore a big pink rucksack as they waited at Dhunche army base for a ride down to Kathmandu. Rescue helicopters thundered in and out every few minutes. She said quietly that there was “nothing left where our house used to be. I used to go to school and was in Grade 1. Now the school is gone. There are no teachers either.” Chhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing. Chhiring Doreje’s granddaughter Ritu Tamang – waiting to be taken to Kathmandu. With the highways washed away, the only road from Kathmandu to Rasuwa is a perilous unpaved track of mud and stones, weaving through tiny mountain villages. The journey often takes more than 12 hours. The treacherous conditions have made it difficult for aid to reach the worst-hit areas and hindered the rescue and relief operations. Many aid trucks are now stuck in Dhunche, unable to drive further north. At a small relief camp on the road between Betrawati and Dhunche set up by Nepal’s Dhulikhel hospital, people collected medicine and food supplies. Doctors said dozens of the children here had lost their parents in the floods. More than 200 children from the local Nilakantha school, most aged between five and 11, are also missing, believed to have been washed away as they walked to morning classes. Prakash Nepal, a teacher. Prakash Nepal, a teacher, said the school had received a warning just 10 minutes before the flood waters hit, when the school bus was already picking up students. “Luckily, we immediately contacted the bus driver and the vehicle stopped midway so the students were able to survive,” he said. “The surge of water did reach the vehicle, but thankfully it did not cause much damage.” However, many of the local families had been displaced by the 2015 earthquake and still lived in informal settlements along the riverbank. Most of those children had been walking to school when the flood struck. Prakash Nepal’s eyes welled with tears: “We could not save the students who were still on the road.” Amid the tragedy, there were also small stories of hope. Sitting on the porch of their village home in Lachyang, Ram Krishna Neupane, 69, and his wife, Muiya Neupane, 66, said their only son had been working as a vet in Syabru Besi when the village was hit. For two days afterwards they heard nothing and feared he was dead. Then they received a phone call. “He called up from a hospital in Kathmandu; he had been rescued by the army,” said Ram Krishna Neupane. “He could not speak, he was crying so much and we were crying.” It was, added his wife, “a miracle”.

title: Democratic party infighting engulfs center-right over House rules vote
summary: While leaders focused on Hasan Piker, two of the party’s more conservative members salvaged a GOP measure that was poised to fail
text: House Democratic leaders have spent the past few weeks waging a bitter campaign against their own left flank over a leftwing streamer. On Tuesday, it was the party’s center-right who blindsided them. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, announced late on Tuesday that he had asked the Democratic caucus’s committee on caucus rules to consider punishing the retiring Jared Golden of Maine and Blue Dog Coalition leader Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington after the pair sided with Republicans on a procedural vote that had appeared doomed. “The decision by two of our colleagues to blindside the entire House Democratic caucus and join with the Republican majority to pass a procedural rule on the brink of failing represents a significant breach of trust,” Jeffries said in a joint statement issued with the Democratic whip, Katherine Clark, and the caucus chair, Pete Aguilar. “It necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the committee on caucus rules to take this up in short order.” The rebellion lands at an awkward moment for Jeffries. For much of the past few weeks, he and other senior Democrats have trained their fire on the party’s left, repeatedly condemning Hasan Piker, a leftwing streamer, over remarks about antisemitism and the 11 September attacks that he says were taken out of context. That campaign has drawn accusations from progressives that leadership is picking an unwinnable fight with a Twitch personality while ignoring bigger political threats. On Tuesday, the bigger threat to comity turned out to come from the party’s center-right instead. The vote in question was a routine procedural measure known as a “rule”, which the House majority must pass before it can bring legislation to the floor. Five Republican hardliners had planned to vote it down, in a dispute unrelated to its substance, which would have handed the speaker, Mike Johnson, an embarrassing defeat and potentially disrupted the House’s legislative calendar for the rest of the month. Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez supplied the votes that let the rule pass, 210 to 208. Under House rules, a tied vote is treated as a defeat, meaning their support was decisive. It is highly unusual for members of the minority party to back the majority’s procedural rules, which typically pass on party-line votes and are treated by leadership as a basic marker of caucus discipline. Neither Golden nor Gluesenkamp Perez gave Democratic leaders advance notice, according to House Democratic leadership. Clark told reporters shortly after the vote that the move “came as a surprise”. Jeffries later told reporters that the two Democrats “blindsided the entire caucus and created a significant breach of trust”. The rule cleared the way for a package of Republican-favored bills to reach the floor, including a GOP resolution condemning socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America, a measure Republicans are expected to use against Democrats in midterm campaign messaging. That resolution also included a poison pill in the form of a statement of support for Donald Trump’s restrictive voting legislation, Save Act. The stunt was designed to force House Democrats to choose between voting against the resolution in what Republicans would portray as tacit support for socialism, or vote in favor of it and lend a (non-binding) blessing to legislation that experts say could stop millions of Americans from voting. The rule also advanced a bipartisan bill, co-authored by Golden, to shield Maine’s lobster industry from federal whale-protection regulations the fishing industry says could put smaller operators out of business. Golden said that bill was his reason for breaking ranks. “I voted for the rule for one simple reason: it paved the way for a vote on my bill to protect Maine lobstermen from costly, burdensome new regulations that would put them out of business,” he said in a statement. Gluesenkamp Perez, who leads the conservative Democratic Blue Dog Coalition, cited similar concerns for working waterfront communities in her south-west Washington district, jabbing on social media that “what the DC bubble doesn’t get is that working waterfronts require working people”. Golden, who is retiring at the end of this Congress, has also indicated he had lined up other Democratic votes for the rule beforehand, suggesting the move was deliberate rather than a last-minute miscalculation. The episode has exposed deeper strains inside a Democratic caucus that has struggled to project unity since its losses in the 2024 elections. Asked whether the two lawmakers would face consequences, Jeffries told reporters on Tuesday that the matter was “under discussion”. By the evening, he, Clark and Aguilar had escalated that to a formal referral. Axios has reported that stripping Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez of committee assignments was among the options being discussed by frustrated members as a way to “make an example” of the pair, though no decision has been made and it remains unclear what disciplinary powers the committee on caucus rules can actually exercise. Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, both first elected in swing or Republican-leaning districts, have each broken with their party before, including on past government funding bills and an earlier version of a Republican voter-fraud measure. Golden co-chaired the centrist Blue Dog Coalition until Gluesenkamp Perez succeeded him in the role. Johnson, for his part, told reporters after the vote that critics who had predicted his majority would fail to pass the rule “were wrong”. “The rule has passed,” Johnson said. “Many of you thought that would not happen today, but we passed a rule to continue business this week. Republicans are here to work.”

title: Burnham’s first PMQs showed a leader who wants to please – but knows how to push back
summary: Despite a long absence from parliament, Burnham showed he could hold his own and, despite some nerves, even enjoy himself
text: The coming months will show whether Andy Burnham fits Kemi Badenoch’s charge of a leader too obsessed with being liked to make hard choices. One thing, however, does seem clear from his first outing at prime minister’s questions: he likes saying yes. The very first question came from a political opponent – Ann Davies of Plaid Cymru – but Burnham replied as if she was a valued constituent, saying he understood her worries about the prison early release scheme and hoped she could be reassured. By the session’s close, Burnham had responded patiently to MPs from virtually all benches of the Commons, even Reform UK, and committed to a series of in-person meetings, some for himself, others for colleagues. Bonhomie is a necessarily limited political resource, even for new prime ministers who have promised to, as Burnham put it, focus on “problem solving rather than point scoring”. And thus it was that by Badenoch’s third question, Burnham was blaming the economic legacy of previous Conservative governments. By the fourth, he was bringing up Liz Truss’s mini-budget, a near-weekly feature of Keir Starmer’s PMQs repertoire. In fairness, the latter was something of a political open goal given Badenoch’s decision to, in a weekend reshuffle of her shadow cabinet, give the top Treasury post to Andrew Griffith, who worked closely on and then stoutly defended Truss’s 2022 fiscal debacle. What did these 45 minutes of studied empathy, mixed in with a few above-the-knee tackles, tell us? As is generally the case with the PMQs, not much in the way of definitive lessons, but it gave several interesting pointers. PMQs is a hard skill to learn, even for someone like Burnham who spent more than a decade in frontbench posts during his last period in parliament, and he is unlikely to sound as tentative again. Equally, facing a brand new opponent, Badenoch was obliged to test out a few areas of attack, seeing which might stick. The bulk of these were based on a pre-existing Badenoch narrative that Burnham is perfectly nice, but a people-pleaser, a “spendthrift prime minister who wants to say yes to everyone”, as she put it on Wednesday. Burnham did push back at times, insisting his early-weeks giveaways were fully costed and stressing the importance of fiscal discipline. But more often he simply ignored the attacks, setting out a pledge – dismissed by Badenoch as mere “vibes” – to restore the nation’s “sense of positivity, a sense of possibility”. When it comes to assessing PMQs performances, there are two linked caveats, the first of which is that this is primarily a terrain for the pros and the geeks. Few beyond MPs, the media and political fans notice the weekly spectacle beyond a 20-second clip that might crop up in their social media feed. The follow-on is that even doing well at PMQs brings limited benefits, beyond cheering up the faithful. Badenoch was regularly praised for making life uncomfortable for Starmer, but her party is still polling below the level of its disastrous 2024 election defeat. A phenomenon that has echoes of William Hague, a Tory leader who loved the Commons but was not loved by voters. Nonetheless, Burnham and his MPs will do well to study Badenoch’s PMQs attacks. Vibes will only get him so far, and with the fiscal clouds darkening, he will need to not only disappoint some people, but do so obviously. For Badenoch, her first PMQs against Burnham will have told her nothing new, just reinforced some lessons which are not wholly comfortable. To begin with, despite his long absence from parliament, Burnham showed he could hold his own, both at PMQs and at Tuesday’s marathon debut, where he answered 125 questions over three hours. Badenoch should also be mindful of the universal political rule first set out by the pollster and focus group expert Luke Tryl: all things being equal, voters prefer politicians who look as if they actually enjoy the job over those who make it feel like a chore. Yes, he was nervous, at times hesitant. But Burnham clearly relished being at the despatch box, the centre of attention and scrutiny, something Starmer managed rarely, if ever. These are different times.

title: Andy Burnham faces an impossible job. At least he’s got a secret weapon – Kemi Badenoch
summary: Labour is up against a Tory party with a leader who can’t stop getting lost in her own sense of brilliance. And then there’s Andrew Griffith
text: Call it the gentlest of all reality checks. A quantum realignment in expectations. The faintest reminder to both Andy Burnham and Labour backbenchers that international bond markets are impervious to Manchester charm and positivity. Despite a summer of feelgood announcements from the government, there is no escaping the fact that the country is still up shit creek. It’s going to be a tough ride ahead. Nothing will come pain-free. Still, a new prime minister has to learn to take the wins – however small – as they come along. In the wider scheme of things, a good prime minister’s questions means next to nothing: it’s nothing more than politics as performance. Yet it can set the tone and buy a prime minister some goodwill from MPs and the media. Plus, it’s a weekly event so you may as well be good at it. Burnham can be very pleased with his first outing, even if it didn’t go totally as billed. We had been promised a more consensual politics. An end to point scoring. That lasted all of five minutes. After that, it was business as usual. Partly because that’s the way PMQs has always been set up, but mainly because Andy just couldn’t help himself. It would have taken a will of iron to resist. Not least because Kemi Badenoch made it so easy for him. Not for the first time, Labour’s secret weapon is the Tory leader. She just can’t help herself from speaking without thinking, getting lost in her own sense of brilliance and failing to spot the traps she is setting for herself. Still, at least no one can call Kemi boring. Though it is quite hard to see why so many Tories seem to drink her Kool-Aid. You could tell that Burnham was very nervous at the start. Understandably so. Twitchy. Not totally in command. PMQs is always an ordeal and never more so for a leader on whom so many Labour hopes have been pinned. Some of them Burnham has even pinned on himself. “It’s good to be back at the dispatch box,” he began, before listing some of the Labour government’s achievements. Like the number of small boat crossings being at their lowest for years. The Tories barely looked up. It was almost as if they had never been that bothered about illegal immigration, and they certainly weren’t about to give Labour any credit. Opposition parties hate it when something goes well. There’s nothing that suits them better than a country in crisis. They never seem to realise that one day they might be called upon to sort it out. Kemi’s opening gambit was flirtatious. Going out of her way to congratulate Andy on his stamina. Burnham merely nodded. A lot of people had said that to him. Then Kemi decided she had had enough sweet-talk. That was Burnham’s problem. Always promising the earth. Never daring to say no to anyone. Too desperate to be loved to be a good leader. So could he mention anything he had ever cut? First the smile, then the reply. “Tax,” Burnham said. This was effectively game over for PMQs. Kemi had imagined a Keir Starmer-like evasion. A prime minister caught out. She had never dreamed of this. Andy spelled it out. He had removed VAT on electricity bills. He had cut business rates for pubs and hospitality venues. He didn’t choose to point out these cuts had been paid for by cutting a budget for digital ID that had never existed. Best to keep it simple. Next Kemi turned to the bond markets. She seemed to think they had it in for Labour. Burnham kept it pleasant and polite. It was like this. The international bond markets didn’t have a special grudge against him. This wasn’t personal. They hadn’t been waiting for Tuesday’s statement, itching to put interest rates up. This was a global problem. Other countries were also facing rising borrowing costs. And if Kemi really wanted to know where the blame lay, she could take a look at her own party’s 14 years of stagnant growth. It was the Tories who had trashed the economy. He was merely trying to pick up the pieces. He could also have blamed the Iran war and the spike in oil prices. A war for which Kemi had been initially enthusiastic. Her judgment is seldom the best. Now Kemi sounded almost hurt. As if a promise had been broken. Burnham had said there would be no more point scoring, and here he was openly point scoring. I know, I know, said Andy unapologetically. He just couldn’t help himself. It was just too tempting. It made him feel good about himself to hear the laughs and support of his own backbenchers. PMQs wasn’t all about him. It was a team sport. So while he was about it, Burnham had plenty more points to score. Kemi has yet to realise just how vulnerable she has made herself by appointing Andrew Griffith as shadow chancellor. The man who co-authored Liz Truss’s mini-budget and was one of its most outspoken defenders. For Labour this is an open goal and they are going to be kicking the ball into the net as often as possible. Kemi may be a woman who doesn’t believe in history. Who thinks each day is a surprising new beginning. But the country is still a long way from forgiving the Tory party for the lasting damage caused by 49 days of Tory chaos. So the self-harm is going to continue for a while. After failing to rule out further tax rises and spending commitments, Burnham went back to his happy place. Good vibes, hope and positivity. All of which are enough to make this a comfortable first PMQs. But he will be more than aware that this is a half-hour bubble and that life will only get tougher outside it. Though Andy appears to be a sucker for work. He spent the rest of the session offering meetings to virtually every MP. Soon his whole life will be one long meeting. Or a meeting to find out why a meeting was not necessary. Meetings to rule out further meetings. Still, I am sure he will enjoy his meeting with Samantha Niblett, whose stated mission has been to have a summer of sex. And to tell as many people as possible about it. Not everything went Burnham’s way. A disgruntled Tan Dhesi, the Labour chair of the defence select committee, was extremely grumpy about the 3% promise. Or possibly not being asked to be a minister. Still, Andy looked happy enough when the speaker called time. The first PMQs was over and he was 1-0 up. Not that anyone was keeping the score. Much.

title: Russian airspace becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, Zelenskyy says
summary: Ukraine president says aviation industry needs to take account of growing number of Ukrainian drones in Russia
text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has declared that Russia’s airspace is becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, as Vladimir Putin promised to increase strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities in the run-up to winter. The Ukrainian president said there was no intention to directly threaten civilian flights, but the growing number of attack drones being flown into Russia by Ukraine would have to be “taken into account” by the aviation industry. “We want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” Zelenskyy said in a statement. Ukraine’s foreign secretary, Andrii Sybiha, said Kyiv had notified the International Civil Aviation Organization that “Russian airspace is not safe for civilian aviation” because of increased military activity. A rapid escalation of Ukrainian military capability in the past few months has allowed Ukraine’s forces to strike at targets around Moscow, St Petersburg and other locations deep inside Russia. Reliable figures for the number of drone flights are hard to obtain but Ukraine is already capable of launching a few hundred a day, and military sources say the country is chasing a target of 1,000 drones in an effort to hurt Russia’s economy. Justin Bronk, an aviation analyst at the Royal United Services Institute thinktank, said he believed Ukraine could force “periodic closures of Russian airports on a semi-regular basis” by relying on an element of surprise. It could do so by flying small waves of drones at short notice, though trying to close an airport permanently would be difficult, he said, because a sustained attack would become predictable and easier for air-defence systems to halt. Ukraine’s commercial airspace has been closed since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022 because Russia has been able to strike targets throughout the country, making airports unsafe for civilians. This year, Ukraine began bombing oil refineries and warehouses near Moscow and St Petersburg, as well as hitting military and industrial sites at ranges in excess of 2,000km (1,250 miles) from its border. Concerns linger about the safety of civilian aviation in the war zone. A Malaysian Airlines plane flying over eastern Ukraine in July 2014 was shot down by Russian separatists operating a surface-to-air missile launcher. All 298 people onboard were killed. Putin described Zelenskyy’s remarks as “state terrorism”, saying: “Negotiations are not conducted with terrorists.” Giving one of his most detailed updates on the war, the Russian leader told a news conference that Moscow was preparing to increase its bombing of Ukrainian energy facilities this winter, aiming to knock out heating and electricity supplies. “The Russian armed forces have been ordered to prepare and carry out mass strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. They are striking us, and they will get a response,” Putin told reporters after a two-day summit in Kyrgyzstan. “I’m not saying we’ll collapse the economy there, but it’s a serious challenge for them.” Asked whether Russia would strike British military facilities in the UK that produced weapons for Ukraine, Putin sidestepped the question, saying: “That’s a military secret.” Russia earlier accused the UK of “escalation” and threatened “consequences” after reports that British-made drones were used by Ukraine in long-range strikes deep inside its territory. Putin sought to stress that Russian forces retained the initiative on the battlefield in Ukraine, despite Moscow’s slowing progress. He appeared to push back against western intelligence reports suggesting he was being given an overly optimistic picture of the war, saying he relied on numerous sources of information that together provided him with an “objective assessment” of the battlefield. Russia’s sluggish advance on the battlefield has fuelled speculation that the Kremlin could resort to another round of mobilisation, the first since Putin called up about 300,000 reservists in September 2022. Zelenskyy and western officials have said Moscow could be preparing such a move, though its diplomats do not consider it a certainty. Putin dismissed the prospect as “nonsense”. Also on Wednesday, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said a drone attack on Leipzig airport marked a new escalation by Russia, and that it fitted a broader pattern of “repeated incursions in our airspace, drones that paralyse our airports, interference with our critical infrastructure”. The German government said on Tuesday that Russia was responsible for a drone laden with explosives which was discovered at Leipzig airport last month near a Ukrainian plane used to transport weapons. Von der Leyen said: “Europeans are faced with the hard truth that this is the new normal. We have to step up, and that means being ready to respond to Russia’s recklessness faster and better.” The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, told reporters Russia had grown “increasingly reckless” and there had been an increase “in malign activities targeting our territory directly”. The EU is drawing up further sanctions against Russia targeting about 1,600 companies and individuals. Poland’s foreign minister, Radek Sikorski, said the bloc should pass these sanctions in response to the Leipzig attack and others. “Hybrid war is not just nuisance on the internet,” he said, speaking on the sidelines of a meeting with his European counterparts. “Hybrid war means assassination squads, it means arsonists, it means blowing up moving trains, like in Poland, it means breaches of airspace with drones and cruise missiles. We need to convince Putin that such actions are not for free.” The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the Leipzig attacks had the “hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism”, adding that Brussels had summoned Russia’s ambassador to the bloc.
