title: Baby stabbed to death in Sheffield was found on top of washing machine, court told
summary: Two men and two women charged with murder after body of newborn girl found with 33 stab wounds
text: A newborn baby girl died from multiple stab wounds before she was found on top of a washing machine in an outhouse in Sheffield, a court has heard. Two men and two women appeared in court on Wednesday charged with the murder of the newborn, named only as Baby S. She was found with 33 wounds from 15 separate stabbings when police were called to a property in the Wincobank area of the city on Sunday. Andrea Skopova, 20, and Peter Horvath Jr, 19, have been charged with the baby’s murder, as have Horvath Jnr’s parents, Peter Horvath Sr, 38, and Nina Horvathova, 37. The four, all from Slovakia, are additionally charged with causing or allowing the death of a child and perverting the course of justice by taking steps to conceal the killing of an infant. Police were called to a property in Holywell Heights on Sunday morning after reports of concern for the safety of an infant. The prosecutor Luke Hopkinson told the court that Baby S was found wrapped in a towel in a blue bag in an outbuilding at an address in Holywell Heights. A 15-year-old girl, who cannot be named for legal reasons due to her age, has been charged with perverting the course of justice. The girl sobbed in the dock as representations were made about whether she should be released on bail. The district judge Tim Spruce decided she should be remanded in youth custody until Thursday, when she will appear at crown court with the other defendants. The four adults were all remanded in custody following the short hearing on Wednesday. Two women, 26 and 37, who were arrested on suspicion of murder remain on bail. DCI Tom Woodward, of South Yorkshire police, said: “This is a significant step in our investigation into the tragic circumstances that resulted in the death of this baby girl. I would like to thank our communities, who I know will have been deeply impacted by this traumatic incident, for supporting us as we work through this intricate investigation. “We would ask the public to avoid speculating and posting information online about this case while the legal process takes it course. Protecting the integrity of the criminal justice process is crucial to us securing justice for this little girl.” Bouquets of flowers had been left by a police cordon near the property in Holywell Heights on Wednesday.

title: Uber drivers launch European class action over ‘soulless’ and ‘scary’ AI algorithm
summary: Landmark lawsuit claims tech company’s pay-setting system has breached privacy laws and pushed down earnings
text: Uber drivers have launched a landmark legal action against the ride-hailing company claiming they live in “constant fear” of a “soulless” algorithm it uses to set pay and allocate jobs. Drivers from the UK, the Netherlands and other countries have joined the compensation claim that could run into billions of dollars. It alleges an AI-powered pay-setting system breaches data protection laws and pushes down their earnings. The claim has been filed at Amsterdam’s district court, where the $150bn (£111bn) San Francisco tech company has its European HQ. It is the first collective legal move of its kind, according to the European Trade Union Confederation. The case centres on an opaque “black box” algorithm fed on information about drivers, which sets a personalised rate for each ride. Drivers fear it pushes down fares to the minimum they are willing to accept. Drivers have told the Guardian the algorithm has offered the same job to different people at different pay rates and offers them less for a return journey after a long trip because it calculates they will not want to come home empty. “It is like someone watching you all the time and knowing about your weakness – the boss is the algorithm,” said Mohammed Shirwa, a 41-year-old Uber driver in Rotterdam. “All the time the algorithm is learning about you and what you are willing to accept. So the prices go low but you are stuck. It knows you need the job.” Kola Oba, who calls the algorithm “soulless”, was taking a break in Tottenham, north London, with another driver when they were offered the same job. The other driver was offered £27 and Oba was offered £23. The pair suspected it was because Oba, 48, had taken several cheap jobs and the AI assumed he would accept a lower price. Uber has previously said such discrepancies were down to other features of its system including GPS, surge pricing, promotions and testing. “It’s scary – they have all my information and they are using it against my own wellbeing,” Oba said. “It defines how much I earn, how long I have to work, my time with my family, my resting time.” AI models take an increasing role in assigning work to humans by using their rapidly increasing power to learn about a business’s needs and staff behaviour and then acting as a “synthetic manager”. The Dutch data protection authority fined ⁠Uber €825m (£708m) last month for deactivating driver ⁠accounts through automated systems without adequate notice. Uber said it would appeal. The company is also planning to roll out driverless cars in European cities from London to Zagreb, initially with human supervisions. The legal case is being led by the Worker Info Exchange, a campaign group whose founder, James Farrar, secured a UK supreme court ruling that Uber drivers should have worker rights. Relating to about 241,000 drivers across the EU and the UK, the claim alleges that Uber has unlawfully used automated decision-making, including profiling, in dynamically setting pay and allocating work. The lawsuit, which also claims the company unlawfully used driver data to train its AI models, is seeking damages for affected drivers and an injunction to halt the conduct which it claims breaches GDPR data regulations. The drivers claim Uber has operated dynamic pay-setting in the UK since 2023, pushing down their annual incomes by about £5,000. The system was introduced in the Netherlands this year. Uber’s chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi, said in 2023: “I think that what we can do better is targeting of different trips to different drivers based on their preferences or based on behavioural patterns that they’re showing us.” Uber said it did not adjust the price offered for a trip based on an individual driver’s behaviour and that a history of accepting or rejecting trips was not used to personalise pay offers. Instead, it said, dynamic pricing allowed it to increase pay on less attractive trips, boosting a driver’s earning potential. “While we haven’t seen the claim yet, we categorically reject the allegations,” an Uber spokesperson said. “The Uber app uses real-time information about the trip such as journey, duration and destination to calculate fares. “Drivers see their earnings and where a trip is going before they decide whether to accept it. The vast majority of total fares continue to go where they belong: into drivers’ pockets, and the percentage that Uber keeps from fares has remained relatively flat.” A 2025 study by academics at the University of Oxford, which Uber said relied on incomplete and selective data, found there had been substantial cuts in driver earnings after the “dynamic” algorithm was introduced. Farrar said: “It’s bad enough that Uber’s dynamic pay algorithms have squeezed driver pay for years now but the intrusive and underhanded way in which Uber uses its technology to monitor and influence drivers’ behaviour is an affront to their dignity as workers and as human beings.” Anton Ekker, a Dutch lawyer leading the case, said: “A computer algorithm should not independently make decisions that strip individuals of their livelihood. Like so many other online platforms, it should be held accountable for the large-scale exploitation of vulnerabilities of European citizens.”

title: Farage compares standards inquiry to investigations faced by fellow ‘outsider’ Trump
summary: Reform UK leader dismisses criticism of his failure to register £5m gift as a sign of a ‘complainants’ society’
text: Nigel Farage has compared his situation to that of Donald Trump being pursued by investigators for years, saying both of them are “outsiders” up against “the system”, as he admitted having become tetchy and aggrieved this summer. The Reform UK leader has been under huge scrutiny over his finances after failing to declare a £5m gift from the Thailand-based donor Christopher Harborne and further financial support from a friend, the convicted fraudster George Cottrell, before the last election. Harborne’s gift is the subject of an inquiry by parliament’s standards commissioner, which resumed last month after Farage won a byelection in Clacton. Farage maintains the gifts were accepted in a personal and non-political capacity. Speaking in a BBC interview ahead of Reform UK’s conference this week, he was dismissive of the investigation into him, suggesting any sanction imposed by the standards commissioner was unlikely to be fair. He claimed there was a “wilful attempt, and it’s gone on now for months, to say that everything to do with Reform, that every individual involved with Reform is somehow a crook” – which he dismissed as “the establishment in a very coordinated way fighting back”. The Reform leader also suggested the investigations into him, which he characterised as “attacks”, were similar to those against Trump. During and after leaving office the first time, Trump railed against the various criminal cases against him, later accusing the Joe Biden administration of trying to destroy him. He recently failed to overturn 34 felony convictions against him for falsifying business records. Drawing a comparison with the investigations into Trump, Farage said: “Very similar things happened to Trump in America. They went after him for year after year after year … You know, going back two years, we expected there to be these sort of attacks. “I can see the similarities because again, he was an outsider, he wasn’t part of the system. So look, we’ve had to weather this for the last few months. I’ve little doubt that the attacks won’t stop, but I am utterly confident … in terms of the growth, the professionalisation of this organisation, our compliance checks, all of those things, I think we’re in a strong place.” Farage suggested he was likely to be interviewed by the standards commissioner soon, as he dismissed the criticism of him for failing to register the £5m gift as a sign of a “complainants’ society”. The Reform UK leader was pressed during the interview on whether his tone had been out of character this summer, after some inside the party questioned if he had sounded like too much of a victim. Asked about whether he could have taken a sunnier and more optimistic tone instead of an aggrieved one, Farage claimed his family had been targeted with threats to their security and “another huge bout of debanking”. “Have I been pretty ratty over that and upset over that? I will accept. Hands up. I might not have quite been my normal self over the last few months, but you know when it’s your own family, it’s close to home,” he said. “I’ve been around for ever in this game. I’m big enough and ugly enough to take the rough and tumble in the game. I’ve generally, you know, gone through politics with a smile, whatever’s happened. But some of those personal things over the last few months have weighed very heavily.” During the interview, Farage appeared to reject any suggestion of a reconciliation with Restore Britain, which is run by the former Reform MP Rupert Lowe and is posing a threat to the party’s vote on the hard right. The Reform leader accused Lowe of having a “very vindictive motivation” and helping the Conservatives, as well as claiming Restore echoed the language of the 1930s. “The problem is some people around [Lowe] are saying things that we’ve not heard in this country since the 1930s, if we are being really honest about it ... I think the vote for that is very, very small. I believe, and time will tell, but I believe that the next general election will be a binary choice between the Labour prime minister and Reform. And in that instance, you know, people will use their vote sensibly.” There had been speculation earlier this summer that Farage could step away from Reform amid scrutiny of his finances and jostling for position among those senior politicians who could succeed him. Reform UK has slipped in some recent polls having led for more than a year, falling behind Labour and even the Conservatives. Farage told the BBC he would still be leader of the party at the next election. “It’s my responsibility,” he said. “I will be there. To carry the can whichever way it goes.”

title: New York City to ban student AI use in public schools until high school
summary: Teachers and parents have warned against AI use in schools over concerns of ‘cognitive surrender’
text: New York City will ban students’ use of artificial intelligence in public schools through eighth grade, typically age 13 or 14. The prohibition is scheduled to be announced on Wednesday and will go into effect next week. The change is part of a sweeping overhaul of the use of technology in the US’s largest school district, which enrolls roughly 900,000 students a year. In another policy shift, classrooms will keep students off laptops or tablets through the third grade, age nine or 10. The city’s public school technology policies are closely watched by the rest of the United States. Teachers and parents have warned against the use of AI instructional software in schools over concerns about harming children’s mental health and cognitive development, in particular an abdication of reasoning to software, a phenomenon researchers have dubbed “cognitive surrender”, as well as environmental damage. AI use will only be allowed in high school, which begins in the ninth grade in the US school system. Even then, it will be limited to specific uses, such as learning about the technology itself. AI “companion chatbots” offering psychological support will also be banned. The rules allow teachers to use AI for tasks including preparing lessons or writing messages, but they are forbidden from asking AI to grade assignments. The city’s education department recommends limiting screen time to 45 minutes in class for middle schoolers – sixth through eighth grade – and 30 minutes for elementary school students. But the question remains of how to monitor AI use, since it often takes place outside the school environment. The new rules follow an initial framework published in March, which used a traffic light system to determine which tasks AI would be used for. In 2023, the school system forbade students’ use of ChatGPT, though the ban was reversed less than a year later. The 2026 framework, which allowed students to use AI for research, exploration and creative projects, sparked fury among many parents and teachers who considered it too lenient. In response, the city’s schools chancellor, Kamar Samuels, said that leaders had “missed the mark” in their communications, adding his office would carefully review parents’ feedback for incorporation into future rules. The city had long planned to follow the March framework with a more comprehensive “guidebook” to take feedback into account, the education department has said. The department will set up a taskforce made up of teachers, elected officials, experts and union representatives. The taskforce is to produce a report in April, intended to serve as the basis for New York’s AI-in-schools policy.

title: Iran accuses US of ‘war crime’ after missile blast kills four people at wedding
summary: Blast also injures 68 guests at the wedding in southern Iran, prompting fears of escalation in hostilities
text: Iran has accused the US of a war crime after a missile blast killed at least four people and injured 68 who were attending a wedding at a private home in a coastal city of southern Iran, as the fresh exchange of strikes prompted fears of a wider renewal of hostilities. Iranian media said that the wedding ceremony was being held in a home in the city of Kuhestak, Hormozgan province, late on Tuesday when a US missile struck, with shrapnel and debris from the strike killing and injuring people. Among the dead was a four-year-old child, Amir-Ali Karimi, and a 16-year-old, Mohammad Mollahi. “It’s a terrible thing. I’m extremely worried and upset about what happened – really upset,” Ali Mollahi, the father of the bride, told Mehr News. A video of the aftermath shows colourful wedding streamers and decorations strewn across the ground, and shoes abandoned in the rush to escape the attack. “You wicked people have attacked people’s homes and turned their wedding ceremony into a funeral,” said a man filming the aftermath of the strike, shared by Fars news agency. The deputy of the provincial government, Ahmad Nafisi, said first responders had headed immediately to the scene and transferred the wounded to the hospitals. Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson called the US attack a “war crime” and said Iran “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”. The chief Iranian negotiator, Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, said the attack had killed families with children, and called the US the “great Satan”. “If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan and kills like Satan, it’s Satan. Shields a junior Satan that does the same? It’s THE Great Satan,” Ghalibaf said in a post on X. The US attacks followed strikes on Sunday, ending a month-long uneasy truce between the US and Iran, and appeared to signal a resumption of another cycle of escalation. US Central Command (Centcom) said the overnight strikes focused on Iranian military targets, including air defence sites, radars and maritime assets. Iran responded by launching drones and missiles on US bases across the Middle East, including in Bahrain, Kuwait and the UAE. Iran’s military spokesperson, Lt Col Ebrahim Zolfaghari, vowed “heavier, broader, and more crushing and devastating” retaliation. Videos of the aftermath of the strike show a caved-in roof, blown-out windows and ground riddled with debris, as well as walls pockmarked with what appeared to be holes from shrapnel. Footage from a nearby hospital showed women in wedding attire watching as injured children were being treated. “When we arrived there, an explosion occurred. It was very intense. Bricks, stones and cement hit me in the face and head, and many others were injured,” a child who was injured at the wedding told the state-affiliated Fars news agency. A woman with her hands decorated in henna for the nuptials posted a video on Instagram after the attack, saying “my hands and feet are still shaking”. A spokesperson for Centcom, Tim Hawkins, said the US was aware of reports of civilian casualties, but the “US military never targets civilians, unlike the [Iranian Revolutionary Guards Corps]”. In February, a strike on an elementary school killed at least 156 people, including more than 120 schoolchildren. Independent investigations concluded that the US likely carried out the strike with the assistance of AI, though the US government said the incident remained under investigation. Pictures of shrapnel collected at the site of Tuesday’s attack were published on Iranian state media, and appeared to show the internal components of US munitions. Trevor Ball, an independent weapons analyst, identified some of the remnants as belonging to the Standoff Land Attack Missile-Expanded Response (Slam-Er) missile, which is made by the US weapons company Boeing. The Slam-Er is a 1,500-pound, GPS-guided missile touted by Boeing to be “extremely accurate”. It was unclear if the home where the wedding was being held was struck directly, or if a missile hit close to the home and debris from the strike hit the home and its occupants. CCTV footage captured at least six strikes in the area within a minute. A separate strike appeared to hit a communications tower about 150 metres away from the home. Authorities said that several “telecommunications and internet towers and sites were also seriously damaged in the latest strikes”. The US has been targeting communications and radar infrastructure along Iran’s coast to try to stop its blockade on the strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint which prior to the US-Iran war was a transit point for at least 20% of the world’s oil supply. Iran has virtually closed the strait since the start of the Iran war, frustrating the US president, Donald Trump, who is facing a midterm election with expensive gas prices and knock-on inflation across the board. In recent weeks, the US has focused on trying to degrade Iran’s capacity to strike ships transiting the strait to reopen the waterway for traffic.

title: Australia’s economy limps along, but the RBA should take a closer look before raising interest rates again | Greg Jericho
summary: The story of the economy at the moment is one of give and take – and what’s good for investment is ‘bad’ for trade
text: When the Bureau of Statistics released the GDP figures on Wednesday, the June quarter 0.4% growth figure immediately drew headlines of a rate rise to come, but there is little within the GDP figures that suggests an economy needing slowing. Before the release, the average expectation from banking economists and those throwing a dart at a board was that the economy in June would grow by 0.3%. In the end it grew 0.4% and brought out the suggestions that the growth was “above expectations” and thus in some way hot and in need of cooling off by another interest rate rise. The market immediately priced in a rate rise by November. Please. The difference between 0.3% and 0.4% is essentially a rounding error. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email And think on this – the Bureau of Statistics revised the growth for the June quarter last year by more than that difference. Wednesday’s GDP figures suddenly showed the economy didn’t grow as strong in June 2025 than previously thought, but that it grew better in the September 2025 quarter than was first estimated: If the graph does not display click here As it is, 0.4% growth is pretty crap. Sorry, but it is. Over the past 30 years, more than two-thirds of the time the economy has grown faster than that. Given the March quarter had just 0.3% growth, it means in the past six months the economy grew just 0.7% – essentially at half-speed. If the graph does not display click here So forgive me if I am not jumping on board the “we need to raise rates to slow down this super hot economy” train. The news of the economy at the moment is one of give and take. The biggest driver of the economy in March was investment in machinery and equipment (mostly stuff to go in datacentres); in the June quarter, because not as much of that equipment was bought, it was the biggest drag on the economy: If the graph does not display click here Except pretty much all of that datacentre equipment is imported – so what’s good for investment is “bad” for trade. When a company buys equipment from overseas, it increases GDP under business investment. But because imports reduce “net trade” (essentially exports minus imports), it in effect is cancelled out by the rise in imports. This leads to some pretty docile brains (many of whom occupy the White House offices) thinking that imports are bad for the economy, and reducing them will make GDP go up. That is false, not just because the maths doesn’t work like that, but if that imported equipment creates employment, leads to higher wage growth and better living standards, then that is a very good thing. This is important when we look at the current “boom” in investment of machinery and equipment. Over the past three years, such investment has gone up 14%. But if we remove the imports of machinery and equipment, then such investment has actually fallen 8%: If the graph does not display click here Will those datacentres generate employment? I guess through some construction. But given those workers would already have had plenty of work to do building houses and apartments, the overall impact is pretty limited. And no one is going to be building a cafe near a datacentre to capture all the business it will bring in. Much of the “business” of datacentres will occur in other countries, and much of the profits will go there as well. It does, however, make it look like there is a lot of investment going on – and that has made the Reserve Bank worried that things need to cool down. A similar issue applies to household spending. Usually more “discretionary” spending is good. People buy goods and services they don’t “need” when they are feeling secure and happy. In the June quarter, overall household spending grew 0.4%, but discretionary spending jumped 1.4%. This would suggest that people are spending like it’s going out of style. But half of the discretionary spending was on new motor vehicles, and primarily electric ones. In the June quarter Australians bought 10% more vehicles than they had in the March quarter: If the graph does not display click here As the ABS notes, “there were record sales of electric and hybrid vehicles as more households looked to lower ongoing operating vehicle costs”. And why did that happen? Because the Iran war and rising petrol prices suddenly made people think buying an EV or hybrid was not a discretionary choice, but a very essential purchase. If you take out the purchases of vehicles, the ABS notes “the remaining discretionary categories saw subdued growth, where rising cost of living pressures aligned with restrained spending”. The rising costs that most affected households were the increased mortgages. Australian households spent 10.4% more repaying mortgages in the June quarter, which wiped out a third of the increase in household income. Overall inflation in the economy rose by just 3.1% – up a bit, and driven as it has been recently by profits growth rather than wages: If the graph does not display click here So, the economy limps along – amazing, really, given the three rate rises and higher petrol prices. And while investors might believe the RBA will see this limp growth as a reason to raise rates, I would hope they look at the reality rather than the expectations. • Greg Jericho is a Guardian columnist and chief economist at the Australia Institute

title: Temperature check: alarm as prediction markets lean into weather and climate bets
summary: Climate experts warn that US Kalshi and Polymarket users are ‘gamifying disasters’ as they bet on events like heatwaves and daily temperatures
text: Online prediction markets, saturated by money staked on sport, crypto and politics, have now set their sights on a promising new area of growth: betting on the future livability of the planet itself. The rise of gamified predictions on the unfolding climate crisis, and shorter-term weather forecasts, has been underscored by a new deal that allows Kalshi, a leading online financial exchange, to access data from the Weather Company, owner of the Weather Channel, to verify weather-related betting outcomes. The weather is “one of the fastest-growing and most crucial categories” at Kalshi, the company said, with monetized predictions made by people, and bots, on weather and climate events growing 500% in the past year into a $1.1bn market. “The long-term vision is to financialize everything and create a tradable asset out of any difference in opinion,” Tarek Mansour, co-founder of Kalshi, said of the company’s broader objectives last year. Startlingly, Kalshi even claims that this gauge of public opinion can not only act as a financial hedge for businesses exposed to extreme weather, but also help shape the weather forecasts themselves. Kalshi’s betting markets will appear on the Weather Channel’s app, which is used by more than 330 million people worldwide. “Given the severity of the climate crisis, it’s crucial for policymakers and the general public to have well-calibrated forecasting data about future climate impacts,” said a Kalshi spokesperson, citing a company study on how accurate its markets’ predictions are. Asked whether this meant Kalshi saw its weather markets as part of delivering well-calibrated forecasting data, the spokesperson said this was the case. “Weather is the ultimate equalizer – it fundamentally affects everyone and everything,” the spokesperson said. People visiting Kalshi or Polymarket, its main rival, can bet on weather predictions such as how hot it will be in certain places on a given day, as well as longer-term bets – from how many climate-fueled disasters the US will have, to whether the world will avoid catastrophic global heating, to how severe the die-off of corals in Hawaii will be. You can even wager how far Lake Mead, the US’s largest reservoir and a crucial water source for the American west, will drop below its already record-low levels. Last year, amid ruinous wildfires in Los Angeles, there were $1.2m in bets laid on Polymarket on the extent of the fires, with one user posting that “volume so high in this market it cause another fire”. While Polymarket’s international platform still hosts wildfire bets, US consumers are barred from accessing them. Kalshi meanwhile has never offered wildfire markets, citing “perverse incentives”. Distinctions can be hard to draw, though – the websites will allow betting on, for example, the severity of heatwaves in Phoenix, Arizona, even though up to 500 deaths in Maricopa county, which includes Phoenix, are being investigated as possibly heat-related. Excessive heat is the biggest killer among extreme weather events in the US. For scientists and people affected by climate-related disasters, though, it has been troubling to see the painful consequences of an overheating world turned into an online money-making market. When the Eaton fire swept through Los Angeles county last year, killing at least 19 people and razing thousands of buildings, the home of Kaitlyn Trudeau’s grandfather was among those destroyed. While he was unhurt, Trudeau, a climate scientist at the non-profit Climate Central, said it “left a bad taste in my mouth imagining people making money off it. People were posting ‘that was fun, until next time!’ I’d be lying if I said it didn’t hurt a bit. “The dehumanization of these events really concerns me. I worry about the gamification of this because it distances us from the impacts of climate change, it affects our empathy,” said Trudeau, who added that she questioned Kalshi’s blurring of distinction of weather and climate and how such bets are adjudicated. “I find it depressing because it’s distracting us from what we should be focusing on,” she said. “I’m not against prediction markets in general but we need to be clear about the downsides. They aren’t going to reduce the risks of climate change or solve climate change.” Kalshi’s claims around weather forecasting are “confusing”, Trudeau added. “I’d be curious to know which resolved markets are related to future climate impacts and what sources they used to calibrate them,” she said. “Since calibration is measured by comparing many predictions against many realized outcomes, how can a market be calibrated on impacts that, by definition, haven’t happened yet?” Placing bets on the weather or the broader climate is harmful “because of all of the perverse incentives this can create, especially among bad actors with malicious intentions”, said Michael Mann, a climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania who said he worried about the bets fueling conspiracy theories about weather manipulation. Other critics contend that the public’s understanding of actual weather data could be obscured or even altered by big-money betting. Kalshi, Polymarket and the Weather Company all dismissed concerns of potential improper practices, pointing to company policies and federal regulation deterring insider trading and conflict of interest. “We view weather data through the lens of decision intelligence and risk management – not gamification,” said a Weather Company spokesperson about the deal with Kalshi. “This partnership elevates weather data into a highly reliable tool, allowing both individuals and mission-critical enterprises to better quantify and manage real-world weather outcomes.” Polymarket, meanwhile, said it saw itself in grander terms than a mere betting website for people facing the perils of a hurricane, wildfire or heatwave made far fiercer by the burning of fossil fuels. “When tragedy unfolds, people turn to the news for commentary and they come to Polymarket for information,” said a company spokesperson. “While we are not blind to the risks, removing these markets does not prevent a tragedy but makes the most accurate information less accessible to the people who need it most.” While they are booming in popularity, however, the wagering platforms are under increasing scrutiny from federal lawmakers and several states. Last week, a federal appeals court ruled that states can regulate prediction markets like gambling, after a case brought by Nevada, which had attempted to shut down Kalshi. This mounting legal and regulatory pressure means that sites that allow wagers on everything from the value of gold to the words mentioned in a Donald Trump speech may find the climate crisis a less politically fraught arena to focus on, even though the topic still only attracts a small fraction of the bets laid online, experts point out. “They have to convince the courts they aren’t a gambling platform for sports and crypto,” said Jamie Pietruska, an economic historian at Rutgers University. “The weather and climate are seemingly innocuous in comparison. There is a longstanding belief that the weather can’t be controlled so it’s perfect to bet on and different to other categories, such as geopolitics.” Much like how CNN already includes prediction market outcomes in its political coverage, the Weather Channel could soon feature Kalshi odds amid its own forecasts, Pietruska said, further warping public trust in the National Weather Service, the bedrock federal forecasting agency that has faced deep cuts under the Trump administration. “Who is the wisdom of the crowds in that situation? There are casual betters, dumb money and weather trading bots,” said Pietruska. “Is that going to produce a forecast better than a meteorologist? Is that just vibes weather?” What will this all do to the public’s appetite to address global heating? One 2023 study found that participating in a climate prediction market elevated concerns about the climate crisis and even altered the viewpoint of those who denied established climate science. “The only thing that seems to work in changing minds of climate deniers [is] to let them put their money where their mouth is,” said Moran Cerf, a Columbia University researcher who led the study. Still, Cerf said, the negatives of wagering on the climate outweigh the positives. “It’s bad, in one word,” he said. “The prediction markets have taken a turn to the dark side by gamifying disasters. The fact it’s unregulated, unlike the stock market, means it is getting worse, too.” Pietruska shares these misgivings. “I’ve been uncomfortable with this sort of betting for some time. It has serious moral consequences,” she said. “An academic study isn’t the same as the speed and scale of the new casinos that are being set up. “If I go online and see the perception that the world will pass 2C (3.6F) warming by 2050, it creates a sense of a predetermined future, even though this is an aggregation of public opinion. It’s not a truth machine.” Listing climate-related disasters next to the timing of Taylor Swift’s next album or the winner of the next Super Bowl “casualizes and trivializes catastrophe and human suffering”, Pietruska said. “The wisdom of crowds isn’t going to encourage the community building and solidarity we need to address the climate crisis. That is not good, to say the least.”

title: Australians are buying EVs instead of holidaying in Europe – and other things we learned from the national accounts
summary: ABS’s snapshot of Australia’s accounts shows economic growth – albeit low – in the face ‘challenging international circumstances’
text: The Australian Bureau of Statistics released its latest set of national accounts, which give us a snapshot of how the economy is performing in the quarter and what’s happening under the hood. Here are the three things you need to know. The economy is slowing, not collapsing Economic growth eased from 2.5% in the year to the March quarter, to 2.1% in the year to June, the Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showed, while real GDP in the three months to June expanded by 0.4%, a tick higher than in the previous quarter. Growth is softening, but is not disastrously slow, and there’s no sign of the collapse that many feared when the US and Israel began their attacks on Iran at the end of February, triggering a global oil shock. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Jim Chalmers called it a “robust result in challenging international circumstances”. “The Australian economy has obvious strengths, but we can still see in these numbers our three primary challenges: inflation, productivity and global volatility, and we know that each of these puts pressure on people,” the federal treasurer told reporters. Economists predict the economy will continue to slow through 2026, moving towards 1.3-1.5% growth by the end of the year as the Reserve Bank’s interest rate hikes and the high cost of living drag on spending and activity. Stephen Smith, a partner at Deloitte Access Economics, said the “accounts show too little growth and too much inflation”. This winter we didn’t fly north, but we did splurge on EVs Just as the pandemic led to some big swings in behaviours and spending patterns, so has this year’s big shock – the Middle East conflict. The national accounts showed disposable household incomes, after inflation, lifted by a respectable 0.6% in the quarter. That slipped to just 0.3% after adjusting for population growth, but it was at least positive. Belinda Allen, CBA’s head of Australian economics, said this showed households were “largely insulated from the Middle East conflict over the quarter” and there was “only partial pass through of interest rate hikes to date”. What we didn’t do was fly north for the winter. War in the Middle East put the dampers on international travel, not least as high jet fuel costs pushed up the price of air fares. Grace Kim, the Australian Bureau of Statistics’s head of national accounts, said “the number of Australians travelling overseas for the northern hemisphere summer fell for the first time since the Covid-19 pandemic”. So what did we spend our money on? Instead of holidays under the northern sun, we splurged on fuel-efficient and electric vehicles. Record sales of EVs and hybrids bolstered spending in the quarter, the ABS said, accounting for three-quarters of the 0.4% quarterly growth in consumption. Vehicle purchases jumped by 10% in three months as we continued to shift away from gas guzzlers in an attempt to protect ourselves from pain at the pump, both today and in the future, and were helped along by government subsidies. Still, Smith said that absent the spending on fuel-efficient and electric cars, consumption was “far too weak to suggest households are shrugging off cost-of-living challenges”. That said, the household saving rate lifted from 6.4% to 6.5% – pretty much its 20-year average – suggesting households continue to add to their buffers. A bigger population is driving higher growth, not productivity While the economy is expanding, this is entirely due to a higher population – an unfortunate hallmark of Australia’s since the end of the pandemic. Growth in real GDP per person shrank by 0.1% in the three months to June (recalling overall total GDP expanded by 0.5%), and was zero in the previous quarter. Per capita GDP was up by only 0.7% over the year, still below its 2022 peak – and at this rate, won’t get there any time soon. It’s the broadest measure of living standards, and reflects the lived experience of many Australians labouring through a high-cost and low-growth economy. Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said “growth in GDP per capita has clearly slowed compared with the pre-pandemic period”. Our lacklustre productivity performance explains stagnating living standards, and there was no joy in the national accounts by this measure. Real GDP per hour worked – the measure of labour productivity – was flat in the June quarter and 0.2% lower through the year. Kearns pointed out that it’s difficult to raise living standards when productivity growth has averaged just 0.1% since 2018. “Perhaps AI will eventually boost productivity growth and improve the trend in GDP per capita and living standards,” he said. “But that will take time and does not lessen the need for productivity-enhancing reforms and winding back red tape.”

title: Canberra ‘put on notice’ as AI-generated submissions bring false information into parliamentary inquiries
summary: Guardian Australia’s reporting on AI-generated content in inquiries has highlighted its dangers, politicians say
text: The chairs of key federal parliamentary committees have warned that an onslaught of AI-generated material is introducing incorrect or even “hallucinated” information into policymaking, cautioning MPs to be vigilant about the veracity of material. Analysis by Guardian Australia this week found inquiries are being flooded with content created by AI, which is inventing studies and attributing nonexistent research to real academics and authors. In some cases, committee reports have even cited submissions in which the majority of sources appear to be AI-generated hallucinations – which occurs when large language models (LLMs) produce or refer to content that looks real, but doesn’t actually exist. The Liberal senator Paul Scarr said the reporting showed there were clear dangers in an increase in the number of submissions that included hallucinated content. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “The biggest risk is that decision-makers, whether or not they’re in parliament or in business or anywhere else, make decisions based on incorrect information,” he said. “And it increases with the standing of the person or entity that’s making the submission and we all need to be alive to that. “We’ve been put on notice. We really need to check and go the extra mile in terms of checking footnotes and sources and claims which are made in submissions.” Scarr was on a committee in 2023 that received a submission including fake allegations of wrongdoing by KPMG. Guardian Australia reported at the time that the consultancy firm complained to the committee, which one academic took responsibility for. Scarr said that as committees must consider all submissions, “you would hope that it’s evened out somewhat if there are a minority of submissions that have got these errors, but the danger’s there”. Louise Miller-Frost, a Labor MP and chair of the social policy and legal affairs committee, which received a submission with hallucinated references, said committees were becoming more aware of the issue, but that submissions created using AI should not be discarded. She said the findings of the submission with hallucinated content was not different to other evidence given to the inquiry. “I think if they put in something unusual or really salient then you’d have to go down the rabbit hole and go, ‘OK I need to find out more information on that particular submission and then go into the references’ , and then it would be obvious that their references don’t exist,” she said. “I think committees … and committee secretariats are a lot more aware of it now. Some of these committees are dealing with massive quantities of data coming in, which makes it a little bit difficult to check every single reference.” Miller-Frost also noted that AI could be helpful for members of the public who might otherwise have difficulty making submissions. “Some of [the submissions] are from agencies and academics and government departments and they’ve got lots of resources. But we also get, particularly in the social services area, some people who are individuals in the community, and they may not have the time and the capacity and availability to write what they want to write.” The Senate president, Sue Lines, said MPs involved in parliamentary inquiries always tested information presented to them, but said individuals behind submissions were responsible for the veracity of the content. “No doubt committee practices will continue to evolve as the widespread adoption of AI continues, including responding to the likely increase in submissions through the availability of AI tools – which is beneficial in terms of participation but also has an impact on the task of digesting submissions and on resources,” she said. “Committees also set a clear expectation that where an inquiry participant becomes aware that any evidence they have given is misleading they have an obligation to correct it.” Senate advice for inquiry submissions warns that use of AI can present risks to the quality of information and that accuracy is the responsibility of the submitter. Last year the consultancy giant Deloitte issued a partial refund to the federal government after it was revealed that AI tools had included fake references and even a fake court reference in a $440,000 report.

title: ‘How do I not crumble?’ Loved ones of Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet floods fear others are turning away
summary: In Sydney, Akash and his younger brother are just trying to keep going while their parents remain among the more than 4,000 missing people
text: Akash Venkatraman’s parents wished him a happy 22nd birthday before they left for Nepal on a spiritual pilgrimage. Three days later, a glacial collapse sent a torrent of mud, water and debris through the Nepal-Tibet border, bursting the banks of the Trishuli River, and sweeping away homes, bridges and roads. He hasn’t heard from them since. Venkatraman Balakrishnan, 52, and Chitra Venkatraman, 46, are among 38 Australians who have been reported missing after the deadly flash floods and landslides on Wednesday last week. The couple and their family friends – Sreedharan Iyer, 52, Lakshmi Iyer, 50, and their sons Rishab Iyer, 23, and Rudhra Iyer, 20 – had been taking part in a pilgrimage to the sacred site of Mount Kailash. They were staying in riverside accommodation in Syabrubesi with other members of the Himalayan Glacier Adventures tour group the morning the flood came in. In the days since losing contact, Akash has cried – as a psychology student, he knows not to repress his emotions – but he has also tried to keep going. His parents would have wanted him and his 17-year-old brother who is studying for HSC to maintain normalcy, but it is difficult, he says. “What if I graduate and they’re not there? What if I get my first job and they’re not there?” Akash says. “Because everything you do, you do to make them proud.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email ‘That’s my biggest worry’ Akash’s uncle has now travelled to Nepal to search for clues while he and his brother try to help from home. Their family has received an outpouring of support from the community, but as the days pass, Akash worries that Australians’ attention is falling away and that “efforts to find my parents and everyone else with them will also reduce”. “The worst thing that could happen is that they hang on for seven or 10 days and no help comes – that’s my biggest worry,” he says. “Us losing attention could create that situation.” As of Thursday, Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Agency reported 1,204 confirmed deaths and 4,216 missing persons (including 583 foreigners). Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist with identification efforts. Though five Australians previously believed to have gone missing in Nepal have now been confirmed safe, the government still holds “grave concerns” for those still unaccounted for. In Kathmandu, the anxiety is palpable. The wall of missing loved ones at the teaching hospital has quadrupled in size. Other hospitals around the city, like the trauma centre, are also filling up. ‘I can’t’ On Wednesday, Uttam Tamang, 25, was standing outside the National Trauma Centre in Kathmandu, clutching his heart. “We are searching for my brother,” Tamang says. His brother, 25, was an electrician working at a hydro plant in the upper Ruswian region – the army has not been able to get in there yet. Now, Tamang spends his days going from hospital to hospital. “I just,” he touches his chest. “I can’t,” he says. Sita Thapa Magar is standing outside at the teaching hospital – her younger brother, Anil Thapa Magar, is also missing in a hydroplant tunnel in the upper region. And they, like many other families, are also doing the daily rounds of hospitals. She says there has not been enough information from the army about why they haven’t been able to search the tunnels yet. “Every day we are looking for information from the government,” Thapa Magar says through a translator. “But we are not getting much information about the missing. “So we have to come here every day; we give his details. It’s been a week, and still, there is not much information.” ‘Still just a crumb’ As the morgues in Kathmandu fill up, a temporary burial site has been set up on the outskirts of the city. While golfers strode around the course next to the forest on Tuesday, police officials laid 85 people from up the valley to rest. It is one of many temporary burial sites around the country. DNA samples and photographs are being collected so families can later reclaim their loved ones’ remains. In Sydney, Sarada Viswanathan, the partner of Rishab Iyer and a longtime friend of his family, is taking matters into her own hands. The 23-year-old medicine student has set up a search HQ from her Sydney home, where family and friends come together to look for signs of their loved ones. They have been monitoring official Nepali websites and calling embassies and nearby hospitals and camps. Every day, they are tracking down the social media accounts of rescued people to ask whether they recognise any of their family members and have liaised with a Jeep vendor company in Nepal so they can track the cars their relatives were driving. “It’s still just a crumb, and we’re trying to follow that trail, but we need a lot more crumbs and a lot more help to get us there,” Sarada says. Akash and Sarada are calling on the Australian government to increase its military and humanitarian support in Nepal, with their petition receiving more than 12,000 signatures. On Thursday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, announced the government would send a team of specialist drone operators to Nepal and pledged a further $3m in aid, bringing Australia’s total aid package to $11m. The Gyirong Port area, where the Iyer family and Akash’s parents were last believed to have been heading towards, was finally opened on Wednesday. Chinese state media reported the road was open from the Tibetan border and rescue equipment could be brought in. Sarada’s relatives who are in Nepal have been barred from entering the area by the army, so she is hoping Australia’s official on-foot rescue teams will be able to reach Rishab and his loved ones. “I can feel his energy. Even when I’m sitting here, I can feel him next to me, and I can feel that he’s still here, and he’s trying his very best,” Sarada says. “I know that they’re very strong people, they have a very strong will, and I know that they wouldn’t give up. So I’m not going to give up on them either.” Akash could also travel to Nepal to join his uncle in the search effort, but for now he is committed to securing a future for him and his brother. “The next few days is about ensuring that if the worst case happens, how do I not crumble with it?” he says. “Because the worst-case possibility is that I’d have to take care of the family … and take responsibility for our lives.”

title: BP seeks to end years of boardroom turmoil with appointment of new chair
summary: Ian Tyler, already in role on an interim basis, is tasked with shifting strategy to refocus on fossil fuel extraction
text: BP has appointed a new chair after a months-long search triggered by the controversial ousting of Albert Manifold, seeking to draw a line under years of boardroom turmoil at the UK oil and gas company. Ian Tyler, who has served as the interim chair and has sat on the BP board as a non-executive director since April 2025, will assume the role on a permanent basis immediately. His appointment comes after Manifold’s shock removal in late May after only eight months in the role, with BP citing “serious concerns” about his tenure. Amanda Blanc, BP’s senior independent director who led the search for a new chair and also runs the insurer Aviva as chief executive, announced on Wednesday she would stand down at next year’s annual meeting. She was criticised after Manifold’s short tenure as chair, because she had led the process that led to his appointment to replace Helge Lund. When Manifold left, Blanc said he had helped drive BP’s transformation but there had been “governance oversight and conduct issues” which the board deemed unacceptable. Reports claimed senior colleagues had felt belittled by Manifold. He was also accused of aggressive behaviour and acting as if he had been an executive rather than a chair. Manifold responded by accusing the company of firing him without warning and disputed reports about his conduct. Blanc came under fire after praising Manifold for his “relentless focus on performance which is well suited to BP’s needs” when he was appointed chair last July, after what she described as a “rigorous and comprehensive global search”. Tyler is a former chief executive of the construction company Balfour Beatty. He chairs the builders merchants Grafton Group and is a senior independent director of the mining company Anglo American. In the past he chaired Cairn Energy and the housebuilder Vistry Group and served as a non-executive director of the defence contractor BAE Systems. He is tasked with overseeing a shift in BP’s strategy to refocus on fossil fuel extraction and ditch renewable energy investments. The company’s chief executive, Meg O’Neill, urged Andy Burnham last month to make use of the UK’s oil and gas resources even though BP wants to sell its North Sea business. O’Neill took the helm in April, the company’s third chief executive in less than five years. Bernard Looney, who had set a green strategy, resigned three years ago after admitting that he had failed to fully detail relationships with colleagues. He was succeeded by Murray Auchincloss, who was ousted last December. BP came under pressure to improve its performance from the New York hedge fund Elliott Investment Management, which took a stake in the company last year. Blanc said Tyler brought “significant experience providing challenge and support to executive teams, while maintaining strong governance and oversight on behalf of shareholders”. Tyler said: “I will lead the board’s evolution, ensuring we have the depth, experience and capabilities needed to support the company’s strategic priorities and long-term value creation. I am committed to establishing regular and transparent engagement with our shareholders.” He said he had asked Blanc to stay, but she believed that after four years it was an appropriate time for her to leave with a new chair in place. Mark van Baal, the chief executive of the Dutch green activist shareholder group Follow This, said: “Many investors will ask if the new chair is able to fix BP’s broken governance.” He said BP’s last annual meeting in April showed it was “completely out of touch with its shareholders” after protest votes against several resolutions, including an 18% vote against the re-election of Manifold as chair. More than half of the shareholders opposed BP’s plans to scrap its existing climate reporting. “Having been on the board since 2025, Tyler is jointly responsible for BP’s governance problems,” he said. “We’re keen to learn what lessons he takes away from the triple shareholder rebellion in 2026, and how he aims to fix BP’s broken governance.”

title: Tim Cook handed $47m package for new role as executive chair of Apple
summary: Pay and shares deal nearly matches $58m award to John Ternus, his successor as CEO at the $4.7tn tech company
text: Tim Cook has received a $47m (£35m) pay deal as Apple’s executive chair, a remuneration package that nears the level set for his successor as chief executive. Cook, who handed over to John Ternus on Tuesday, will be paid a base salary of $2m and $45m worth of shares. Half of the share award will be based on performance targets being met, while the remaining half will be paid out over four years. Ternus will receive a base salary of $3m and a $55m share award, with the latter more weighted to performance. Cook’s total compensation as chief executive for 2025 exceeded $74m. Cook, who owns more than 3m shares in Apple, has been placed in the multi-billionaire category by Forbes, which estimates his wealth at $3bn. His predecessor, the Apple co-founder Steve Jobs, was paid a symbolic $1 a year but was worth $7bn when he died, including a sizeable shareholding in Disney he acquired after selling the Pixar animation studio to the entertainment conglomerate. Cook took over from Jobs in 2011 having impressed as an operations specialist. The stock has risen 2,200% since he took charge, with Apple now valued at about $4.7tn – compared with about $350bn when he became chief executive. He built the tech company’s sophisticated supply chain and is succeeded by a 51-year-old engineer and longstanding Apple employee, who built products as senior vice-president of hardware engineering. Ternus’s role meant he ran the engineering teams behind Apple’s entire product lineup, including the iPhones that generate most of the company’s revenue. Analysts are not only anticipating new products but also further progress on integrating AI into Apple hardware. Ternus’s first big public moment at Apple will be at its annual iPhone event on 9 September, where a foldable handset is expected to be revealed. New iterations of the Apple Watch and AirPods are also anticipated, although Bloomberg reported last week that AirPods with cameras – another big product rumour – “aren’t launching anytime soon”. Cook’s new mandate includes engaging with policymakers around the world and will involve maintaining the company’s relationship with Donald Trump, as well as overseeing the company’s diplomatic ties with China – a key production hub. In a final memo to employees on Monday, he focused on Apple’s products. “I will miss leading you and being with you for every step, even as I take enormous comfort in handing the helm to someone as brilliant and wonderful and capable as John,” he said. “Few people understand what it takes to build products that change the world the way John does.”

title: Trump ally defends Venezuela oil deal amid ‘gunpoint diplomacy’ criticism
summary: Energy secretary Chris Wright denies US seeks to ‘take’ country’s oil, saying deal is transformation of relations
text: The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, has denied Washington is seeking to commandeer huge quantities of Venezuelan oil, amid growing criticism of Donald Trump’s energy deal with the country’s interim leaders. “Absolutely not,” Wright replied when asked by a CNBC journalist if the US was engaged in a “heavy-handed” attempt to “take” Venezuelan oil in violation of the South American country’s constitution. Wright landed in Venezuela’s capital, Caracas, on Tuesday night, four days after Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history”. “I think we are seeing an absolutely historic transformation of both Venezuela and the relations between Venezuela and the US,” Wright said of the deal, which Trump has claimed will give the US control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil. “This is President Trump’s grand plan to replace conflict with commerce,” Wright said. The White House says the deal will help secure US “energy dominance for the next century” as well as “purging foreign malign influence from our back yard” by excluding China and Russia from oilfields in the country with the world’s largest proven oil reserves. But there has been criticism from across the political spectrum. The Wall Street Journal’s editorial board said Trump’s deal with Venezuela’s unelected interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, “looks less like a normal commercial transaction than it does the famous scene of US businessmen meeting with the Cuban strongman in The Godfather Part II”. “The US government is essentially getting in bed with a foreign dictator and her favored capitalist,” the newspaper complained, in reference to Alejandro Betancourt, the Venezuelan tycoon at the centre of the deal. The economist Francisco Rodríguez told Democracy Now: “It’s clear that this is not a deal that any Venezuelan government would have entered into unless this country had been subject to an invasion, and unless its authorities had been held at gunpoint. So I think we’ve replaced gunboat diplomacy now for gunpoint diplomacy.” Delcy Rodríguez was installed as interim president on 5 January, two days after the president, Nicolás Maduro, was abducted by US special forces during a predawn raid on Caracas. Trump warned Rodríguez, who was Maduro’s vice-president, she would face an even worse fate if she did not toe the US line. Since Maduro’s capture, Rodríguez has made a series of once unthinkable concessions to US officials who their nominally socialist political movement, Chavismo, had spent years denouncing as predatory imperialists bent on stealing Venezuela’s natural resources. On Saturday, Rodríguez claimed the oil deal had “endless” benefits and would help produce more than $209bn in revenues that could be used to improve healthcare and education. “We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” she said during a televised broadcast to the nation. The deal has dealt a body blow to Venezuela’s political opposition, who fear Trump is unlikely to push for a democratic transition or fresh presidential elections given his lucrative arrangement with Rodríguez. “This is a game between the Trump administration and Delcy and her people,” one opposition figure lamented after the deal was unveiled. Speaking at a signing ceremony in the Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas on Wednesday, Rodríguez thanked the Trump administration for its part in what she called a “win-win deal”. She said: “I have faith in the future of Venezuela. What we are doing today represents the future and the hope of the people of Venezuela.”

title: Pete Hegseth criticized for body-shaming Canadian cadets: ‘Literally they’re kids’
summary: US defense secretary faces backlash for attempting to mock Canada’s armed forces amid trade war
text: A social media post by Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, body-shaming female members of a Canadian youth development program remained online on Wednesday despite a furious backlash on both sides of the border. On Monday night, Hegseth posted on X a photograph of two people in uniform with a Canadian flag and the caption “this is real”, an apparent attempt at mocking the country’s armed forces amid the Trump administration’s trade spat with its northern neighbor. However, the photograph was reproduced from an Instagram post by the Vernon Cadet Training Centre in British Columbia, which hosted a summer camp in July for teenagers learning adult skills on the military base. Its subjects are not members of Canada’s frontline military, and the person whose appearance Hegseth was attempting to ridicule is likely a volunteer instructor, critics said. The girl receiving a medal is a teenager no older than 18. The post, widely seen as part of a Trump administration “bullying campaign” over the trade war, was immediately condemned by officials in Canada and in the US. Mark Carney, the Canadian prime minister, called it “beneath the office” of the secretary of defense. Responding on Tuesday to attacks on his country by US government officials, including Donald Trump’s attempt to rename Lake Ontario by executive order, Carney told reporters it was time for Washington to “start being serious” about efforts to de-escalate trade tensions. “When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions,” he said. David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, echoed Carney’s sentiment. “It tells you everything you need to know about the amateur-hour, distracted, bizarre leadership that Americans are being subjected to,” he said. The civilian Army Cadet League of Canada accused Hegseth of online harassment. “Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable,” the group said in a statement. Adam Kinzinger, the former Republican US congressman and a military veteran, was even more outspoken in a post on X. “Literally they’re kids. This is a cadet program and our ass hat of a Secdef is making fun of children,” he wrote. “MAGA [Make America Great Again] males are betas who have to punch down to feel big.” Ruben Gallego, the Democratic Arizona senator and a former marine, called the post “stupid” and “disrespectful”. Danny O’Regan, a Canadian veteran writing on X, also criticized the post. “The Secretary of Defence is body shaming cadet groups,” he said. “This is not a military unit. They are kids looking for adventure, test themselves and align themselves with the values of service. Don’t be a Pete.” The Pentagon, meanwhile, defended Hegseth. On Tuesday, Jacob Bliss, the defense department’s deputy press secretary, said: “The X post speaks for itself.” The incident comes as Hegseth faces increasing pressure on several fronts. The US army chief Dan Driscoll resigned this week, reportedly after months of internal clashes with Hegseth. Democrats have accused the defense secretary of having “hollowed out” the military’s senior ranks. On Wednesday, Iran accused the US of a “war crime” after four people were killed, including a four-year-old child, and dozens injured in a reported missile strike on a wedding at a home in the south of the country. The ongoing Iran war has also left the US with a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors, the Associated Press reported, sparking fears among Nato allies of increasing vulnerability to a potential Russian military attack. Hegseth has previously been critical of body shapes in the US military, telling senior commanders in Virginia last year that “fat troops are tiring to look at”. Ordering military officials to crack down on a lack of physical fitness, he said: “It’s tiring to look out at combat formations, or really any formation, and see fat troops.”

title: In a Big Win, Google Avoids a Breakup of Its Ad Tech Business
summary: In a long-awaited decision, a federal judge said Google must change its ad tech business to address antitrust issues, but did not disclose the measures.

title: What’s really behind Trump’s deference to Putin?
summary: Whether or not US president fits the definition of a Russian asset, his actions align closely with the Kremlin’s interests
text: Could Donald Trump be a Russian asset? The headline on a review in the Guardian of my new book Betrayal has provoked heated international debate. Written by the historian Lawrence Freedman, the piece generated thousands of comments from across Europe and beyond on social media. Many people responded with a single word: “Duh!” Trump’s relationship with Vladimir Putin is the biggest mystery in international politics. In 2017 I wrote a book called Collusion, which set out Moscow’s operation to support and cultivate Trump, going back decades. The US president, of course, denies links with Russia. But in his second term, his behaviour towards Putin has been as weird and perplexing as during his first. For example, at the Alaska summit last year the US president applauded his Russian counterpart, meeting him at Anchorage airport and rolling out a red carpet. Trump seemed uncharacteristically nervous, as he waited for Putin to emerge from his plane. At their joint press conference after talks, he allowed the Russian president to speak first. It was a bizarre act of deference. Why? There are, I think, overlapping reasons for Trump’s submissive behaviour. I explore them in Betrayal, (which is published this week in Denmark by Politikens Forlag, with Italian, Finnish and Ukrainian language editions to follow.) As I mentioned in a Q&A with Guardian readers, one factor is ideological: Trump’s Maga supporters see Russia as an “anti-woke” kindred state. Putin leans into this idea, positioning himself as a defender of conservative values, under threat from a decadent and godless Europe. High-profile Trump supporters have travelled to Moscow. Erstwhile Maga cheerleader and former Fox News host Tucker Carlson even absurdly praised the Russian capital’s well-stocked supermarkets. Another explanation – advanced by Fiona Hill, the former White House adviser – is strongman envy. Trump would like Putin’s freedom of action, when it comes to making money and crushing opponents. It is evident the US president prefers the company of autocrats. By contrast he frequently badmouths European democrats, among them the former British PM Keir Starmer (“no Churchill”), and Giorgia Meloni (“I felt sorry for her”.) A third theory is kompromat, a KGB term to describe potential compromising material. We know from declassified records that the Czechoslovakia secret police began spying on Trump in the 1970s, when he married a woman from behind the iron curtain. He visited Moscow in 1987, on a trip organised by a Soviet state agency, and subsequently made many visits to Russia including in 2013 for the Miss Universe beauty pageant. What exactly happened on these excursions is unclear. But I know from my own experience in Moscow – I was the Guardian’s bureau chief from 2007 to 2011 – that Russia’s intelligence agencies are adept at surveillance operations. Shortly after I arrived, the FSB broke into the apartment I shared with my wife and our two children. They left clues, busting open the window in my son’s bedroom, with a perilous drop to the courtyard below. The British embassy advised us our home was bugged. Possibly, Putin’s ghost-like spies had installed video cameras too, we were told. Over the next four years we experienced on-off harassment from a shadowy and paranoid state. There were mysterious break-ins, veiled threats from foreign ministry officials, and a summons to visit Lefortovo, the FSB’s infamous pre-detention centre and gloomy prison. Undoubtedly, the KGB and FSB will have spied on Trump too, as well as on other high-profile foreign guests. A 2020 report by the US Senate intelligence committee alleged that the FSB has secret cameras inside the Ritz-Carlton hotel, where Trump stayed during his 2013 trip. There will be tapes. They may be innocuous. But Putin knows what they show, and Trump knows that Putin knows. *** Consequences remain the same Does this make Trump an asset? My conclusion is that the terminology doesn’t much matter. As the chess champion Garry Kasparov notes, if Trump were an asset, or an agent of influence, what exactly would he do differently? Since 2025 he has stopped direct US military aid to Kyiv, humiliated Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, and repeated Kremlin lies and disinformation. The US president’s Russia-friendly actions have consequences. I have been visiting Kyiv for nearly two decades, and have spent much of the past five years reporting from Ukraine and the frontline. I was in the capital in February 2022 when Putin tried to seize it. Since then, the conflict has evolved. It is no longer fought with armoured vehicles and tanks, and has become instead a hi-tech aerial battle. Most nights, Russia bombards Kyiv with kamikaze drones and ballistic missiles. Ukraine, meanwhile, carries out its own long-range strikes. It has the world’s most innovative drone and counter-drone industry. But Kyiv badly lacks US-made Patriot interceptors – the only system capable of shooting down fast-moving ballistic missiles. Trump refuses to send Patriots or allow Kyiv to develop its own version under licence. And so civilians die – families, elderly couples, teenagers – entombed under the ruins of pulverised apartment blocks. At night you hear explosions, a moped-like growl from enemy drones, and booms from Ukrainian air defence. Asset or not, Trump is doing little to make this horror stop. Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest, is published in the UK by Guardian Faber. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com.
