title: Mass breeding of game birds without welfare checks may be curtailed in England
summary: Campaigners say pheasants and partridges reared ‘on industrial scale’ do not have same protections as chickens
text: The government is considering a crackdown on pheasant shooting in England as part of a consultation on strict new animal welfare laws that would affect shoot organisers. Ministers are already considering plans for the issuing of licences for those who run game bird shoots. The proposals mean anybody associated with wildlife crime, such as the poisoning or shooting of birds of prey, would be banned from hosting shooting events. Every year, thousands of people descend on the countryside to shoot pheasants and partridges. Millions of the game birds are released in advance of the shoots. Many are brought over from France as chicks and eggs, and reared by gamekeepers until they are ready to be released for shooting in the autumn. Grouse are wild rather than reared or farmed animals. While chickens and other farmed birds have to be looked after to minimum animal welfare standards, these strict legally binding standards do not apply to game birds. Poultry birds, for example, have minimum space standards for their cages and have to be provided with enrichment, such as perches and items to scratch and peck. Chicken and other poultry farms are subject to regular animal welfare inspections, which are not in place for sites rearing pheasants and partridges. Claire Bass, the director of campaigns at Humane World for Animals UK, said: “The shooting industry breeds millions of birds on an industrial scale, and these animals have fallen through the cracks of animal welfare law. Confined in barren wire cages for most of their lives, birds suffer stress-related injuries and feather loss and are exposed to blazing summer heat and other weather extremes.” The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) is consulting on possible changes to this, and is proposing to bring in animal welfare laws to reflect those in place for farmed animals. The licensing scheme could address the issue of the mass release of pheasants and partridges into the countryside, experts have said, because estates would have to abide by environmental standards. Releasing large volumes of non-native birds means they compete with songbirds for food, and pollute the soil and waterways with their dung. Dr Ruth Tingay, a co-director of Wild Justice, said: “Putting an end to the rearing and annual release in to the countryside of an estimated 60 million non-native game birds for shooting should be the government’s focus. If they stop that, then the associated welfare issues would also be sorted. Defra needs to stop tinkering around the edges and deal with this head on.” Critics have said this is a continuation of Labour’s fight with the countryside. Rural areas have, according to polling, abandoned the party after its unpopular inheritance tax for farmers and a new tax on tractors, as well as being accused of botching the farming subsidy scheme. Tim Bonner, the chief executive of the Countryside Alliance, said: “At a time when there are so many issues facing rural communities, it makes no sense for the government to waste time rehashing non-issues: time that could be much better spent legislating to help rural communities. To many in the countryside, this will seem like yet another example of toxic culture war policies. The new government should think long and hard about whether that is the relationship they wish to have with the countryside, or whether they will embark on a more positive and productive course.” The consultation also seeks to gather evidence covering the effect on wildlife and protected habitats, the spread of disease, animal welfare, wildlife crime and the use of natural resources. The Defra minister Sue Hayman said: “Gamebird shooting has been part of rural life for many years, but it is important to understand the effect it can have on wildlife, the environment and the welfare of the birds themselves, whilst supporting our rural communities. We want to hear from all those with relevant knowledge and experience so that any future decisions reflect the best available evidence.” • This article was amended on 8 September 2026 to more clearly specify that the strict legally binding standards that apply to chickens and other farmed birds do not to game birds.

title: Architect of UK’s AI strategy joins Anthropic amid conflict of interest warning
summary: Matt Clifford will stay as chair of government funding body for tech projects alongside his senior role at US firm
text: The architect of the UK government’s AI strategy has joined the US startup Anthropic in a senior role a year after stepping down from his Downing Street post. Matt Clifford, a successful tech investor, was appointed as AI opportunities adviser by Keir Starmer last year but resigned from the unpaid role six months later for personal reasons. His move to the company behind the Claude chatbot has raised concern, with the head of the House of Commons science, innovation and technology committee, Chi Onwurah, saying that his decision to remain as chair of the government-backed Aria funding body represented a “clear conflict of interest”. Clifford will be Anthropic’s managing director, international affairs, and will lead the company’s engagement with governments outside the US including in the UK, Europe, Asia-Pacific and India. Anthropic said Clifford would remain as the chair of Aria, the UK’s Advanced Research and Invention Agency, which funds “moonshot” science and tech projects. He will also maintain his chair role at Entrepreneurs First, the tech venture capital firm he co-founded. He was appointed chair of Aria in 2022. Anthropic said Clifford would step back from any matter involving the company at Aria. But Onwurah said the roles clashed and she called on the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, to intervene. “His intention to remain as chair of Aria, which spends taxpayer money on cutting-edge research, much of it related to or driven by AI, is a clear conflict of interest and I look forward to the AI minister setting out clear boundaries,” Onwurah said. Anthropic said its commercial relationship with Aria was handled by a separate team to Clifford’s and he did not make procurement or programme-level spending decision at Aria anyway. “Matt has no involvement in any decision touching Anthropic, and that arrangement has been agreed with Aria and the Department of Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, which is responsible for appointing Aria’s chair,” the company said. The UK government has been approached for comment. Several senior politicians have taken roles at Silicon Valley firms in recent years. The former deputy prime minister Nick Clegg took a senior post at Meta in 2018. Last year the former prime minister Rishi Sunak took advisory roles at Microsoft and Anthropic, and the ex-chancellor George Osborne joined OpenAI. Commenting on his role at Anthropic, Clifford said the most important decisions about AI would be made by companies and governments together. He said: “Countries everywhere want real agency over how this technology is built and used, and my job is to make Anthropic a genuine partner in that – in Europe, Asia and beyond.” Anthropic is preparing for a stock exchange flotation that could value the business at $2tn (£1.5tn). Tom Brake, the chief executive of Unlock Democracy, a not-for-profit campaign group, said the move showed that “the revolving door is a problem for advisers as much as it is for ministers”. “Taking extensive knowledge obtained within government, about a policy as sensitive as AI, to a private sector company shortly after leaving government gives that company a huge advantage,” said Brake, a Liberal Democrat MP from 1997 to 2019. “Regardless of any safeguards, this weakens the government’s hand when pushing for a precautionary approach towards AI development.” Beeban Kidron, a crossbench peer and prominent critic of the government’s AI policy, said: “We need more independent politics which puts the interests of workers, citizens and society at the forefront of our relationship with the tech sector.” An Anthropic spokesperson said the UK was “one of dozens” of governments Clifford’s team would engage with. “We hire people with expertise and who understand how government works because our work requires it – in every market, not just the UK,” they said. Clifford began his tech career in the private sector. Prior to his government work, he was an established figure on the UK tech scene as a co-founder of Entrepreneurs First, which has helped build tech companies with a combined worth of more than $20bn. Clifford worked with Sunak’s government as his representative to the 2023 AI Safety Summit in the UK, and helped create the organisation that later became the world-leading AI Security Institute. He was appointed as Starmer’s AI adviser after drafting the government’s AI action plan, which supports the creation of AI growth zones to host datacentres and the building of the UK’s own AI models.

title: UK government does not know what datacentres are being used for, FoI request shows
summary: Lack of information raises fears over environmental impact of the AI boom
text: The UK government does not know what the country’s datacentres are being used for despite fears over the growing environmental impact of the AI boom. When asked in a freedom of information (FoI) request who was using the largest sites and what for, the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology said it did “not hold the requested information”. The ministry has since been dissolved. With hundreds of datacentres awaiting planning permission and 315 queueing to connect to the National Grid, there is growing concern over a lack of transparency and justification for these projects given their environmental impact. Ministers announced plans in January to allow qualifying datacentres to opt into the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project scheme. This lets developments bypass local planning committees by securing approval from the government. Campaigners say this “insulates” datacentres from local scrutiny. Zack Polanski, the Green party leader in England and Wales, said: “The government plans to steamroller over local opposition so private companies can build these facilities – yet they can’t even explain what the benefits are and who is benefiting.” Datacentres use a huge amount of resources. The Guardian revealed last month that two planned sites will have higher carbon emissions than ExxonMobil in the UK, with concerns raised over how this will fit within the country’s carbon targets. The government designated datacentres as critical national infrastructure in 2024 and campaigners fear this could mean the water-hungry sites are prioritised over households in times of drought. Water UK, the trade body representing water companies in Britain and Northern Ireland, warned in July that the UK did not have enough water for the datacentre expansion. Polanski said: “What is more ‘critical’ than people’s access to water? What is more ‘critical’ than our need to transition to a low-energy, low-pollution world so we can put the brakes on climate extremes?” While there is consensus that datacentres can provide some essential services, there are concerns that developments with a huge environmental impact and local opposition are being prioritised regardless of their use. Oliver Hayes of Global Action Plan, the environmental charity which submitted the FoI request, said: “It’s highly likely that we’re going to end up seeing datacentres given favourable and preferential treatment when it comes to resources that are actually running chatbots or enabling people to do benign and very wasteful, pointless things. “At the more serious end, these datacentres could be powering chatbots that enable people to nudify teens without their consent and much worse, frankly.” With reports that the Scottish government is inching toward a moratorium on new datacentres, there is growing pressure for the UK government to follow suit. Friends of the Earth is calling for a ban on new sites until environmental safeguards are in place. The campaign group wants the government to publish clear environmental rules for new and existing datacentres, including requirements for 100% additional renewable energy generation for new projects. Anisah Khan, the campaigns manager at Global Action Plan, said: “When individuals across the country are facing hosepipe bans and essential housebuilding is being delayed because datacentres are gobbling up grid connections, what we need is not more chatbots at any cost.” The government did not respond to a request for comment over its failure to say what large datacentres were being used for. A spokesperson said: “A pause on building new datacentres would simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on other countries for the processing of sensitive health and defence data. Put simply: it would be a disaster for jobs and national security.”

title: New York law requires hairdressers to learn how to work with all hair types
summary: New law requires cosmetology classes to give instruction on all hair types from the kinkiest to the straightest
text: As of 1 September, a new law in New York state requires hairdressers studying cosmetology to be trained to work with all hair types. “This is about equal access to service,” assembly member Michaelle Solages, who sponsored the law, said in a statement earlier this year. “No New Yorker should ever walk into a salon and be turned away or receive substandard care because of their hair texture. Now, with the adoption of this legislation, they won’t have to.” The law, signed by Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, requires cosmetology and natural hair styling classes to include instruction on hair types from the kinkiest to the straightest. Additionally, the new training will require students to learn about hair and scalp properties, hair care and styling techniques associated with textured hair. Students will have to demonstrate their proficiency on state licensing exams. The number of hours required to receive a license will not change. Schools have had three years to prepare for and comply with the new law, which was signed in 2023. “By embedding the new instruction into existing programs, these changes will expand skills and service without increasing costs, and will ensure that haircare professionals are prepared to serve all of their clients,” Solages’s statement said. In January, New Jersey signed similar legislation into law, which likewise expanded textured hair education. New Jersey’s legislation requires students to receive training on textured hair, includes curly hair in written and practical testing on the state’s licensing exams and calls for schools to have appropriate training tools.

title: Andy Burnham blames Tory legacy for leaving UK economy vulnerable
summary: In first PMQs clash with Kemi Badenoch, prime minister rejects comparison to Liz Truss’s government
text: Andy Burnham blamed the Conservatives’ legacy for leaving the UK vulnerable to market turmoil, in his first prime ministers’ questions clash with Kemi Badenoch, as the UK’s borrowing costs climbed further. The Conservative leader compared the market pressure on Burnham’s second day to Liz Truss’s mini-Budget. But the prime minister said it was the Tories’ failure to address the UK’s growth and debt which meant the economy was exposed to market shocks. Badenoch challenged Burnham to be honest over whether tax rises were coming in October’s budget. The prime minister said his first move in office had been to “cut tax”, in reference to VAT on energy bills, but stopped short of ruling out any rises. UK government borrowing costs rose again at the start of trading on Wednesday, as 10-year bonds jumped by four basis points – hitting the highest level since June 2008. The turmoil erodes the fiscal headroom available to the chancellor, John Healey, for the autumn budget. The rise has been linked by some economists to Burnham’s doubling down on his commitment to public control of utilities in his statement to the Commons on Tuesday, though most market strategists say it is mainly down to a jump in oil prices. One of Burnham’s close allies, the economist Jim O’Neill, said on Tuesday night that the prime minister’s statement had been “the last thing that investors want to hear on a day where all of this is going on in the background” and said traders were asking: “Who’s going to get real in this country about the challenges of getting our debt down and controlling spending?” Criticising Burnham’s three-hour statement in the Commons the day before, Badenoch on Wednesday said: “He did not say no to a single spending request … And personally, I think it’s delightful that he wants to make everyone happy. But a prime minister needs to be a leader, not a people pleaser.” She said: “[He] did not rule out tax rises. Instead, what he did was lots of point scoring. He says he wants new politics, he says he wants honesty. “The fact is, gilt yields now, the cost of borrowing is far more than it ever was under Liz Truss. That budget failed because spending was announced before the money to pay for it, which is exactly what he is doing right now.” Burnham said his commitments over the summer had been funded and the government would maintain fiscal discipline in the budget. “The turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they [the Tories] left behind. We’ve had the fastest growth in the G7. Borrowing fell to its lowest level in six years. We’re cutting the deficit faster than any other G7 country. That is problem solving rather than point scoring,” he said. Asked again to rule out tax rises, Burnham said: “I’ve already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I’m not going to … write the budget here, that will be the matter for my right honourable friend [the chancellor]. “I took a deliberate decision to set an early date for the budget, so that we reduced the period for prolonged speculation of the kind that she is wanting us to indulge in today.” Burnham, who had said he hoped not to indulge in too much party political attack, criticised Badenoch for her shadow cabinet reshuffle where she sacked the former shadow chancellor Mel Stride and replaced him with Andrew Griffith, a Treasury minister under Truss. He said Truss’s tenure had been “a short-lived government that crushed confidence in the economy and hammered people’s mortgages. [Badenoch] took a decision at the weekend: she removed a shadow chancellor who said that the Truss mini budget was a mistake, and she replaced that shadow chancellor with one that helped to write it.” In an attempt to calm the markets, he said his would be a government “grounded in fiscal responsibility”. “It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents. And that’s the approach that we will take. And that’s the one I would suggest to the party opposite should follow too.” Later in the session, Burnham was pressed by Tan Dhesi, the Labour MP who chairs the Commons defence committee, about whether he could commit to defence spending reaching to 3% of GDP by 2030. Burnham appeared to imply this would happen, saying: “I’ve made that commitment, made it very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time.” However, this appeared to be a mix-up over dates, as Burnham has thus only pledged to reach 3.5% by 2035, a commitment he reiterated in his exchanges with Badenoch.

title: Tumbler Ridge mass shooting victims file 30 new lawsuits against OpenAI
summary: The company says it prioritizes safety, but suits allege its ChatGPT bot induced shooter to carry out attack in Canada
text: OpenAI faces 30 new lawsuits filed on behalf of victims of the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting. The suits, filed on Wednesday, allege the company’s ChatGPT chatbot induced the shooter to carry out the attack in rural Canada in February, in which eight people were killed and dozens more wounded – most of them children. “These were people who really endured just total hell that day,” Jay Edelson, the lead lawyer representing the plaintiffs, said in an interview. “Young kids who watched their teachers die, watched friends die and thought they were going to get shot and killed.” These new lawsuits, filed in federal court for the northern district of California, come after Edelson filed seven initial suits in April – bringing the total number of cases against OpenAI for the Tumbler Ridge shooting to 37. All of the suits allege that the violent intentions of the shooter, identified as 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar, were well-known to the senior leadership of OpenAI, which failed to report her to the authorities. Employees on the company’s safety team had flagged the shooter’s account to executives eight months before the attack, describing her in internal messages as “a credible and specific threat of gun violence against real people”, according to court filings. OpenAI banned her account, but she was able to quickly create a new one, the suits claim. The lawsuits accuse OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, of negligence, aiding and abetting a mass shooting and product liability. Jason Kwon, OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, said in a statement that he thinks about what happened at Tumbler Ridge every day and that the company works hard to create standards for reporting cases to law enforcement. “The professionals working on these teams choose to do this incredibly difficult work because they care so deeply about keeping people safe,” Kwon said. “They come to work every day knowing that they may have to make a decision that they’ll think about for the rest of their lives.” A groundswell of cases have been brought against OpenAI and other tech companies alleging that their chatbots exacerbate mental health crises and provoke violent acts. OpenAI has been sued in seven separate cases that blame ChatGPT for acting as a “suicide coach”. A criminal investigation and civil lawsuit, brought by the attorney general of Florida, accuses OpenAI of concealing safety risks after a mass shooting at Florida State University. The shooting in Tumbler Ridge took place in a secondary school, shortly after Van Rootselaar killed her mother and 11-year-old brother in their family home. The new tranche of lawsuits includes cases from the family of one girl who was shot, along with the principal, teachers and students. The attack was one of the deadliest mass shootings in Canadian history. In the aftermath, questions swirled in the small British Columbia town about how it could have happened. Edelson singled out Chris Lehane, who is OpenAI’s head of global affairs and a former member of Bill Clinton’s administration who specialized in opposition research. He said Lehane was one of the people who received warnings from the company’s safety team but overruled repeated appeals to alert the authorities. That decision was also sanctioned by Altman, the lawsuits allege. “What’s clear is that OpenAI over and over has made decisions to hide how dangerous their platform is because they’re worried about regulation and public pushback,” Edelson said. In response, OpenAI’s Kwon said: “It is absolutely false to say Chris Lehane was involved with our original referral decision … It’s also completely untrue to say that the people at the center of these challenging decisions do not prioritize safety, or that there are ‘political’ or ‘public relations’ factors at play.” When the first seven lawsuits were filed against OpenAI in April, the company published a blogpost about its “commitment to safety”. Altman also sent a letter to the Tumbler Ridge community apologizing for not notifying Canadian police about what OpenAI knew regarding the shooter’s potential threat. “While I know words can never be enough, I believe an apology is necessary to recognize the harm and irreversible loss your community has suffered,” Altman wrote. David Eby, the British Columbia premier, posted the letter to social media with the comment: “The apology is necessary, and yet grossly insufficient for the devastation done to the families of Tumbler Ridge.”

title: Swedish minister defends strict post-Brexit removals of Britons
summary: Minister says Sweden has ‘fulfilled its commitments’ amid criticism of ‘unjust’ deportation decisions such as case of Joyce Thomas
text: The Swedish government has doubled down on its position on removing and deporting British citizens on the grounds they were late to apply for permission to stay after Brexit. The migration minister, Johan Forssell, issued a robust defence of the Swedish migration agency’s implementation of the Brexit withdrawal agreement on Wednesday in response to a question from an MP about the case of Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old British widow who has been ordered to leave the country after 21 years. Forssell said the European Commission, which is legally mandated to ensure EU member states implement the withdrawal agreement correctly, was onboard with Sweden’s approach. “The migration board has followed up on the application of the withdrawal agreement and the assessment is that Sweden has fulfilled its commitments. This assessment is shared by the commission,” he said. There has been growing controversy over removal orders issued to British citizens who did not know that Sweden was one of 13 countries in the EU that required formal applications to stay in the country post-Brexit. In another case, a 34-year-old British man, John Sellers, has been deported despite having lived in Sweden since he was 10. Thomas’s local MP, Häkan Svenneling, of the Left party, told the Guardian: “It seems to me that the Swedish government thinks everything is fine even though British citizens are being deported from Sweden right now. Not acting is also an action in this situation. What Sweden needs is a new government and a new migration minister who stops deporting people with strong connections to Sweden.” In his written answer to Svenneling, Forssell offered British citizens facing deportation a sliver of hope. He said: “The relationship with the UK is very important to Sweden and the government will continue to safeguard the correct implementation of the withdrawal agreement. As part of this, the government is investigating whether further measures can be taken to facilitate the process in the future.” Thomas has been told she must remove herself from Sweden by Tuesday 8 September or face deportation and a potential ban from the Schengen area. She is one of several British citizens who have been faced with removal orders after the migration agency rejected their late applications to stay. The UK Foreign Office has raised Sweden’s approach to late applications for post-Brexit residency a number of times in the specialised committee on citizens’ rights, a structure set up to ensure the withdrawal agreement is implemented properly. David Milstead, who runs the grassroots organisation Brits in Sweden, said the Swedish response was not a surprise. “The government was hardly going to disown the decisions of [the migration agency] or the Swedish courts. The real question is whether Sweden’s approach is consistent with EU law and the [withdrawal agreement],” he said. He pointed out that under the agreement, the UK was obliged to set up a statutory body, the Independent Monitoring Authority (IMA), to independently ensure the Home Office implemented the Brexit deal correctly, while the European Commission performed the correspondent role for EU member states. “The IMA has taken a much more robust approach. It is hard to imagine it not challenging the UK had it operated a policy like Sweden’s, which would have put the rights of around a quarter of a million successful late applicants [in the UK] at risk,” Milstead said. “Sweden’s approach now needs either to be tested before the European court of justice or addressed through measures that remedy the problem. The government’s response leaves open the possibility of change, and that must include fixing unjust deportation decisions.” The European Commission has been approached for comment. According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025 a total of 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. Analysis by the Foreign Office found this was 32.9% of the 7,565 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU member states over this period. Although it is not possible to determine exactly how many were in Sweden prior to the end of the UK-EU transition period, it is likely that the majority will have been. Thomas has been in Sweden for 21 years and says her late husband inquired about the impact of Brexit and was told by the authorities there was nothing they needed to do to remain in the country legally. The couple moved to the country to be close to their son and grandchildren, and Thomas said she had been left feeling sick with worry after receiving the removal order.

title: US woman gets 38 stitches after being bitten by otter in Lake Tahoe
summary: Woman from Reno was swimming near Hidden beach when river otter attacked her, Tahoe’s second incident in a month
text: A swimmer at Lake Tahoe in Nevada was bitten by a river otter and needed to get 38 stitches for her wounds as well as rabies shots, local media have reported. Lynnette Bellin from Reno was swimming near Hidden beach on the Nevada side of the popular tourist attraction on Sunday when she was attacked by the creature. “I just felt something grab me by my leg and pull me under. And it was so powerful. It felt like it was a human,” Bellin told the KCRA3 television news station. “This otter just started coming after me, teeth and claws, and, you know, my only thought was like, I got to get away from this. But it kept following me,” she added. “I tried to swim away from it at one point and it was just attacking my feet.” Eventually, Bellin told the broadcaster, she was able to scramble out of the lakes on to some rocks and make it to a hiking trial. First responders then took her to a hospital for medical assistance. Otter attacks are rare, though wildlife officials always advise people to give the wild animals distance if they see them. This is especially true in late summer when otters may be defending their young. “It’s very rare for us to see something like this,” Kenzie Margiott, a spokesperson for the Nevada department of wildlife, told KCRA3. However, this is the second otter attack at Tahoe in a month. South Tahoe Now reported that earlier in August, a man was attacked by an otter on the California side of the lake near Pope beach. That swimmer also ended up in hospital with eight bite wounds.

title: Taxing the banks: what Europe’s windfall levies brought in as Burnham eyes his next move
summary: Ahead of a crucial budget, four countries’ experiments offer a mixed verdict on how to tax bumper profits
text: The countdown is on. Two months out from Andy Burnham’s inaugural autumn budget, bank executives are wringing their hands over whether the government will target their bumper profits with fresh taxes. The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly considering a windfall tax on both banks and oil companies in the late October Westminster setpiece. The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years, largely off the back of rising interest rates. They are now in the crosshairs of campaigners – including the Trades Union Congress (TUC) and campaign group Positive Money – who say a tax increase could help cover rising household bills as part of Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living. The TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, who has been pushing hard for a new bank tax said: “Britain’s largest banks are making a fortune. Not because they’ve suddenly become more competitive or improved their services to customers, but because high interest rates mean that, right now, they can sit back and watch the money roll in. Inflated mortgages are fuelling record bonus pots. “With energy bills edging towards record highs this winter, the government is going to need to provide more support for households – and taxing banks’ windfall profits is the obvious way to pay for it.” Any move in the UK would echo similar efforts in mainland Europe to make lenders pay more tax to help offset surging living costs and higher defence spending. Here are some of the tools different governments used, as well as the benefits and pitfalls of targeting the profits of some of the world’s largest banks. Spain: taxed and undeterred Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, revealed plans for a windfall tax in 2022 that would raise €3bn from banks over the following two years to help alleviate cost-of-living pressures. It spooked investors, wiping more than €5bn off the value of Spanish-listed bank stocks, but politicians pushed ahead: putting a 4.8% “solidarity tax” on the domestic revenue of banks whose income passed €800m. That included fees and net interest income, – the amount of money banks make from loan charges, minus what they pay on deposits. The €800m threshold and the focus on domestic revenues meant it broadly excluded small local banks and most foreign lenders’ Spanish operations. Big banks and lobby groups filed legal challenges over the tax, while the European Central Bank (ECB) warned that Spain risked disrupting monetary policy, and damaging lenders’ capital positions, which help to cushion the blow of economic shocks. Politicians eventually decided to extend the levy a further three years to 2027, after successfully raising €1.3bn in the first year, and €1.7bn in 2024. Banks now face a sliding tax rate of between 1% and 7%, with the highest rate hitting lenders such as Banco Santander whose annual revenue from interest and fees surpassed €5bn. The extension triggered a fresh spate of legal challenges by banks and lobbyists, and criticism from both the International Monetary Fund and ECB, which warned it could hit bank profits, push up borrowing costs for low-income households, and make Spain’s banks less competitive on the international stage. Lithuania: a defence spending boost Lithuania’s government decided to roll out its own windfall tax on banks in 2023, after forecasts showed lenders were due to rake in €1.3bn in net profits that year. That was three times higher than 2022, following a surge in interest rates sparked by Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The 60% tax, which applied to any net interest income that was 50% higher than the previous four-year average, was used to fund infrastructure projects and boost defence spending amid Russian threats. Politicians agreed to exclude income from any newly agreed loans, to prevent a situation where banks stopped issuing mortgages and business loans to avoid paying tax. The levy helped raise about €250m in 2023 and €247m in 2024, representing 0.3% of the country’s annual GDP, before being extended by an extra year. The European Commission appeared to support the move, saying it helped cut public debt at a time of regional security threats. But the tax is said to have spooked foreign firms, with the central bank having repeatedly tried to lure new lenders “with no significant success”, according to an EU report. The banking sector said it also disadvantaged lenders serving local customers, while letting others such as Revolut, which is registered in the country but serves mostly non-residents, off the hook. Czechia: ‘unrealistic expectations’ Czechia announced its own three-year windfall tax on banks to help cover consumers’ soaring electricity and gas prices in 2022. The temporary measure, lasting from 2023 to 2025, involved a 60% tax on any profits that were more than double (120%) the previous four-year average. Deeply unpopular with businesses, the tax also caused friction within the far-right ODC civic democratic party, which said it was interfering with the free market and contradicted core conservative values. Czech finance minister, Zbyněk Stanjura, talked about scrapping the tax a year earlier than planned, but later admitted the levy had not yet covered state costs linked to the energy crisis. While the finance ministry originally hoped to collect more than 30bn Czech koruna from the country’s six largest banks, it quickly became clear they would fall short of those targets. “It is unclear whether this was due to unrealistic expectations driven by a vision of easy extra revenue and convenient scapegoating of big corporations, or whether the delayed implementation of the tax (from 2022 to 2023) and the behavioural responses by businesses were not duly considered,” the law firm A&O Shearman said in a 2024 report. The country ended up raising just 1bn Czech koruna, months before the tax expired in December 2025, according to figures reported by local broadcaster Ct24. Italy: a tax that fell flat While plans for a windfall tax by prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing government gained international attention, it was one of the least effective levies. Meloni’s team shocked markets in August 2023 after revealing plans for a 40% tax on banks’ net interest margin. The move drew the ire of banking lobby groups and wiped €10bn off shares in financial services companies, forcing politicians to water down the proposal a day later with a cap that halved the estimated tax takings to €2.5bn, from €4.9bn. The rules eventually came into force in October that year, but not before being diluted further. Banks – which are already subject to higher corporation and regional taxes in Italy – were allowed to choose one of two options: pay a tax equivalent to 0.26% of the risky assets on their balance sheets – ensuring those with safer loans paid less – or keeping the money on their balance sheets but putting aside two-and-a-half times that amount into their own reserves to cushion the blow of any economic shock. Unsurprisingly, all banks chose to put the money in reserve, scuppering original hopes that extra funds could help support mortgage holders and cut taxes. However, Italy’s deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, has now revived plans for a new tax three-year levy, that would involve a 5% tax on the profits of Italy’s 10 largest banks. What if the UK followed suit? If current trends continue, the UK’s four largest banks will rake in £60bn in profits for 2026. Windfall taxes have been used on banks in the UK before, notably in the early 1980s when Margaret Thatcher’s then chancellor, Geoffrey Howe, accused high street banks of escaping the recession and in the 1990s by Labour chancellor Gordon Brown to generate extra revenue. Calculations by campaign group Positive Money suggest that the UK could raise up to £10.9bn this year from adopting Czechia’s model; up to £6.95bn by following Spain’s sliding tax scale; and £2.2bn by following in Lithuania’s footsteps. “Plenty of countries have successfully taxed banks’ windfall profits,” the TUC’s Nowak said. “We’re calling for an increase in the bank surcharge to raise billions for the Treasury to cut bills across the country. This is an easy win for government – and the chancellor should ask the banks to pay a fairer share”. The world’s most powerful banker, JP Morgan boss, Jamie Dimon, has repeatedly warned the UK government against increasing taxes on banks. The chief executive of lobby group UK Finance, David Postings, said the banking sector “is a major contributor to the public finances, paying over £43bn in tax last year,” a figure which includes income tax payouts on staff salaries. “Banks based here already pay a corporation tax surcharge and the bank levy, giving them a higher total tax rate than in other major financial centres. Increasing sector‑specific taxes would risk damaging the UK’s international competitiveness and make it harder to attract investment.”

title: Freelancers are getting buried with ‘soulless’ AI slop cleanup: ‘It’s a shame we need to do it’
summary: As more companies turn to AI, they’re hiring freelancers to clean up its mistakes rather than create original work
text: Lisa, a freelance graphic designer based in Spain, noticed a shift in her work after the release of ChatGPT in 2022. She went from receiving slow one-off jobs creating logos and packaging to an onslaught of requests asking her to fix versions that were generated by artificial intelligence – from sharpening fuzzy images for printing to turning flawed designs into usable files. By 2025, Lisa, who asked not to be fully named to avoid solicitations, said 90% of her incoming logo and packaging design requests required cleaning up AI-generated content, work that accounted for 60% to 70% of her annual income. But the grind was exhausting. Clients lowballed her;' some AI-generated designs were so flawed that she had to recreate them from scratch and she worried about being complicit in AI-driven copyright infringement. By the end of the year, she began turning those jobs down. “It was just so soulless,” said Lisa, who now focuses on “human-made designs”. Lisa is part of a growing group of creative freelancers being hired to clean up AI slop, a term used to characterize low-quality, AI-generated output. As businesses use tools like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude to produce marketing copy, illustrations, books and videos, they are hiring creative professionals to humanize AI-generated copy, repair botched images and salvage flawed footage. The work serves as a stopgap in an increasingly challenging job market, supplementing income for those who freelance full-time or on the side. But clients often underestimate the time and skill involved, expecting cleanup to be quick and cheap when it can require as much work as creating something original, freelancers said. And while the high volume of cleanup gigs can be lucrative, freelancers are divided over the trade-off. Some find it tedious and creatively unfulfilling, while others enjoy the challenge. As AI improves, freelancers question how long the demand will last and where they’ll turn once the jobs dry up. For now, demand for AI cleanup work is growing. On Freelancer.com, a contract work platform with more than 88 million users, job listings tagged with phrases such as “correct AI”, “AI hallucination” and “AI error” rose 87% to 10,760 globally between August 2025 and June 2026, according to internal data shared with the Guardian. The jobs were concentrated in graphic design, followed by video editing, proofreading and content writing. Upwork saw AI remediation gigs jump 70% year over year, and Fiverr saw keyword searches for “AI cleanup” services grow more than 20 times between 2023 and 2026, according to data shared with the Guardian. The specter of AI could spell trouble for the creative freelance labor market. Listings for freelance jobs exposed to automation fell 21% in the eight months after ChatGPT launched and image-creation gigs dropped 17% after AI image generators arrived, according to a 2025 study published in the academic journal Management Science. And those losses have continued, according to a 2026 study. Meanwhile, more workers are turning to freelance work as companies cut staff and hire less, intensifying competition. The average project on Freelancer.com drew 54 bids in 2025, up 8% from the year before, according to the site’s annual report. But as companies cut costs, they’re changing the nature of freelance assignments, from requests for creative work to sprucing up AI output. Matt Barrie, CEO of Freelancer.com, said the cleanup work is often commissioned by small companies and entrepreneurs using AI to produce a first pass, only to run into problems they don’t have the expertise to solve. “[AI output] needs a human to turn it into something polished that can actually be used,” he said. The time and money saved on the first draft can be eaten up by the “incredibly time-consuming” work of preparing it for commercial use. The rise of the AI cleanup crews For some freelancers, cleanup is taking up a growing share of their workload and traditional creative projects are becoming harder to find. Todd Van Linda, a full-time freelance illustrator in Florida, began taking AI cleanup gigs in 2023 as his usual work drawing illustrations, video game art and architectural plans became less steady. The work typically involves filtering out visual noise, improving resolution, and hunting for glitches like an extra toe. “Money”, Van Linda said of his motivation. “The jobs were there to be done.” Though some clients expect AI cleanup to cost less than original work, Van Linda won’t lower his rates. When one prospective client offered about $500 to repair 13 to 15 AI-generated illustrations for a children’s book, with the expectation that each should take about 15 minutes, he turned it down. He said projects can take between a few hours of work to days depending on the scope. His rate is $65 an hour and “doesn’t go down from there”, he said. For Kym Dunbar, a freelance writer and editor based in Australia, AI cleanup now accounts for about 60% of her workload, as writing work like blogs and website copy have dwindled. As a result, Dunbar said her monthly earnings from writing original content have fallen to roughly a third of what she made during the pandemic. Dunbar stumbled into cleanup work in 2024, when a client asked her to revise an AI-generated article. She quickly learned to spot recurring problems, from repetitive language and awkward paragraph structures to a lack of emotional nuance. Since then, she has worked on about 40 AI-generated nonfiction books, longform articles and technical papers. “There’s a lot less good projects available for writers and editors these days,” Dunbar said. But “cleanup” can understate how much work is involved. Nathan McConnell, a multimedia editor who freelances on top of his full-time job, started editing AI-generated videos in 2023. His work has ranged from removing reflections from AI real estate videos to fixing robotic voiceovers and malformed 3D models. The requests have increased from two or three projects in 2023 to eight to 10 so far this year, he said. One client brought him roughly 100 AI-generated images of humanoid animals for a tarot deck riddled with extra fingers, two left feet and other mistakes. McConnell spent two to three hours repairing each image in Photoshop, expecting the project to take nearly two weeks to finish. But after making the first 10 cards, he called the project off because of health issues and constant changes requested from his “persnickety” client. Not everything that lands in McConnell’s inbox can be saved, he said. That could look like videos where the physics feel off, like shadows falling the wrong way, or animations that repurpose another creator’s work without permission. “I’ve told a client before that it’s ‘too’ slop,” McConnell said. “There’s no way I can fix this.” While McConnell and Van Linda would rather make original work, not everyone finds fixing AI outputs dispiriting. Dunbar considers it “interesting” and “challenging”, and takes satisfaction in turning a weak draft into polished prose. What troubles her is that people increasingly see AI not as a tool, but as the “be-all and end-all” of the creative process. “I just feel it’s a shame we need to do it,” Dunbar said. Slop cleanup jobs may not last It’s unclear whether cleaning up AI-generated slop will remain a viable source of work. Dunbar isn’t convinced it will. She believes much of the work humanizing AI could dry up within five to 10 years as models improve and allow businesses to generate usable content themselves. McConnell sees it differently, arguing that AI still needs to be “babysat” to catch mistakes an untrained eye might miss, from logos that violate brand guidelines to objects that appear and disappear in videos. “We need people [to fix] problems that AI is creating,” he said. But Van Linda is already creating a different path. After he stopped taking AI cleanup gigs late last year, he has seen more clients, some of whom have been dissatisfied with AI, seeking original, hand-drawn work. “Quite frankly, this kind of thing has gotten extremely distasteful to me,” he said about AI cleanup work. Though Lisa, the freelance graphic designer, updated her profile to say she no longer works with AI-generated images, she still gets requests to edit them. She occasionally takes cleanup gigs for clients who come to her after getting poor results with AI. But some clients “straight up lie” and pass off the images as original creations. “They say ‘I don’t use AI,’ but there’s a “[Google] Gemini logo on the bottom,” she said. But just in case AI makes her job obsolete, she has a plan. Lisa has begun returning to the canvases, watercolors and other physical art she practiced before she pursued a career in graphic design. She predicts that within “another year or two”, AI will be able to do logo and packaging design as well as she can, leaving only “the best of the best” able to make a living. “I don’t know if I’m good enough to survive the digital stuff,” she said.

title: ‘It always comes around’: fans react to conviction in Tupac Shakur’s murder 30 years later
summary: Rapper’s supporters reflect on ‘astonishing’ events leading to Duane Davis being found guilty over 1996 fatal shooting
text: A criminal conviction this week in the murder of Tupac Shakur, the first since the rapper was gunned down in 1996, sent shock waves through his sea of fans who have waited three decades for answers. Duane “Keffe D” Davis, a former California gang leader, was found guilty of murder on Monday for the role he played in orchestrating the fatal shooting of Shakur. The case relied on several confessions from Davis, including his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, in which he described the events of 7 September 1996. Davis said he came up with a plan to retaliate against Shakur after the rapper’s entourage attacked Davis’s nephew in the lobby of the MGM Grand hotel. Some of Shakur’s legions of fans reflected on what the artist meant to them while expressing bittersweet joy about the long-awaited moment. As a teenager, Kelly Wilson, 48, was enamored with hip-hop’s boy wonder. (Shakur was just 25 years old when he died.) “There was a lot of depth to him that I just didn’t hear elsewhere,” the Seattle area resident said on Tuesday. During his life, Shakur faced blowback over lyrics his detractors regarded as glorifying violence or gang culture. But he was also lauded as an inner-city chronicler, whose pen cast unrelenting social critiques of racial inequality, police brutality and other issues of the time. “I’m as white Irish as you get,” Wilson said, but he connected with Shakur’s overarching philosophy, which Wilson described as: “Speak for the people who don’t have a voice.” His children grew up steeped in Shakur’s legacy. One of them, 22-year-old Julian Wilson, drew a parallel to Davis’s trial and one of the first songs in Shakur’s discography that he deeply studied. The music video for Hail Mary, a track he recorded in 1996, begins with a scene where one incarcerated man laments being wrongfully imprisoned. “Revenge has a funny, funny way of settling the score, and when it happens, you will know,” a fellow inmate consoles him. “That’s always stuck with me. Some things may take time, but it will always come around,” Julian Wilson said. “Even then, they still had faith that justice was going to be served no matter how long it took.” The elder Wilson felt mixed emotions about Davis’s guilty verdict. “It’s nice to have the final chapter written for the family and those that need that healing,” he said. At the same time, Wilson called the verdict “long overdue”, adding that others who may have been more culpable have since died. (Authorities have long suspected Davis’s nephew, Orlando Anderson, of being the gunman. Anderson died in 1998.) Casey Rain, a British musician, was a moderator for HitEmUp.com, a forum dedicated to Shakur that was popular in the early aughts. “I don’t mind admitting that there was a time in the years immediately following his passing where I definitely bought into some of those conspiracy theories. A lot of people did because we didn’t have access to the information that we have now,” Rain said, referencing longstanding fan theories about who killed Shakur, or whether Shakur was secretly still alive. “Everything surrounding his murder has kind of existed in this middle ground of historical events and folklore. For somebody to be convicted of doing it, that grounds it and makes it real,” he continued. “This isn’t a sort of hip-hop, folklore, mythology story. This is a 25-year-old man that was murdered.” In the end, Rain was also struck by how the case against Davis relied on his own admissions regarding the deadly night. “It finally got solved because one of the people involved in it just wouldn’t shut up talking about it. It’s a really strange kind of irony. It’s astonishing,” Rain said. Davis is set to be sentenced in October. The 63-year-old is facing at least 40 years in prison. • This article was amended on 2 September 2026. Orlando Anderson died in 1998, not 2004 as an earlier version said.

title: ‘It’s a fever dream right now’: sailors of USS Abraham Lincoln voice joy after arriving in Thailand
summary: Shore leave in Pattaya, known for its red light district, comes after reports of deteriorating living conditions onboard the vessel during record stint
text: At Pattaya’s Hard Rock Cafe and hotel, the city’s mayor and police officials, along with women in traditional Thai dress, waited to greet the sailors who were arriving in civilian clothes, bags slung over their shoulders, off the buses. The USS Abraham Lincoln’s crew of 5,000 had not been on shore for nearly nine months, a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea. Crew appeared to have been told not to speak to the gathered journalists about the reportedly deteriorating living conditions onboard but said they were looking forward to being on dry land, sleeping and going home. One sailor, Breese, who did not want to give his surname, said “it’s a fever dream right now” and he was looking forward to trying Thai food for the first time and meeting new people. Once a quiet fishing village, Pattaya was transformed during the Vietnam war into one of the most infamous red light districts in the world with the arrival of American troops using military bases in Thailand. At its peak, tens of thousands of US military personnel came through each year, said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor specialising in tourism at Bangkok University. “In my opinion, it’s really the founding influence for the town. The US military turned a quiet fishing village into a global destination for an international nightlife and entertainment hub in about 15 years,” he said. Although the American troops left by the mid-70s, the sex industry infrastructure continued to grow, with European tourists taking their place, and more recently waves of Chinese and Russian visitors, Pipatpong said. The Hard Rock hotel is around the corner from the Soi 6 alley, known for its go-go bars, one of the many areas that contribute to Pattaya’s sex tourism industry. Soi 6 and the neighbouring area would be off-limits for crew after sunset, said Pattaya’s mayor, Poramet Ngampichet. However, Walking Street, the town’s other entertainment and red light district, was displaying a massive neon sign at its entrance saying: “Pattaya City is pleased to welcome USS Abraham Lincoln carrier and its personnel.” The sailors were being released in staggered groups, so not everyone was out. Shakeira Fairfax, who had travelled all the way from New Jersey, had to wait one more day to be reunited with her sailor daughter, Jada Fairfax. Fairfax said she was mostly excited. “I just want to pick her up and spin her around. She’s my baby always,” but, she said, “I don’t know who I’m welcoming home.” Jada finished her basic training last October and was shipped out a month later, two months before the US and Israel launched their war on Iran. Jada celebrated her 25th birthday onboard in June. Fairfax said there was an “abrupt” stop to communication when the war broke out, but she had since been able to check in with her intermittently and send care packages. The ship’s captain, Dan Keeler, acknowledged to the media that the carrier “looks like a dirty car in a parking lot”. As for the reports of the conditions onboard, he said: “I don’t know how to say it other than there’s a disconnect between reporting back home and what’s happening on the ship.” Keeler added: “First-time sailors are going to complain about the food, the living conditions, similar to sending kids off to college for the first time. We did get caught up in an election cycle and got thrown around like a football.” Keeler said there was plenty of food on the ship but admitted it became hard to get fresh fruit and vegetables, which stopped being served. “I am looking forward to a fresh salad.” They also had to be careful with supplies of soap and toothpaste to ensure every sailor could receive some, he added. Asked about the reports of attempted suicides onboard the ship, Keeler did not answer, saying there was an open investigation. As for comments from Donald Trump, which included claims that the 270-day deployment was “not nearly long enough”, Keeler told the Guardian: “The president speaks for himself.” Crew from the USS Higgins also arrived at the Hard Rock hotel. When asked about the conditions onboard the two vessels, Ethan Johnson, a cook on the Higgins, said: “We joined the military, it’s not a cruise ship.” Johnson said there was plenty of meat and vegetables onboard the Higgins. As well as being prohibited from entering certain areas, sailors are also being prevented from doing any water sports in the area, owing to the potential danger. They will also not be allowed to visit pharmacies as Thai authorities do not want sailors accessing medicines that do not require a prescription in Thailand but may need a prescription in the US, Poramet said. Kristopher Robinson, a naval attache with the US embassy, said Pattaya was chosen as the destination for rest and relaxation because the “people of Thailand have a history of being wonderful hosts not just to US sailors but people from all around”. Robinson said the crew would take as much opportunity for rest as possible and conduct themselves in accordance with US and local laws. “Sailors here, like all tourists, they’re going to enjoy Pattaya’s great food and wonderful culture,” he said.

title: US-Iran hostilities resume amid concerns at Hegseth’s military leadership | First Thing
summary: Leading Democrat accuses secretary of defense of causing ‘lasting harm’ to US forces
text: Good morning. The US has launched more airstrikes on Iranian targets, prompting counterstrikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan and Iraq. The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before this weekend’s strikes, but recent promises by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly the conflict could spill back into military action. The Iranian Red Crescent said four people, including a child, were killed and more than 50 were injured when shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a home where a wedding celebration was taking place in the city of Kuhestak. The US central command spokesperson Capt Tim Hawkins said: “The US military never targets civilians.” Why are there concerns about US military leadership? A senior Democrat accused Pete Hegseth of having “hollowed out” the army’s senior ranks after its top civilian leader, Daniel Driscoll, resigned. Senator Jack Reed said: “It is far past time for Trump to recognize the lasting harm Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense … cultivating a culture where dissent is punished and competence is secondary to personal allegiance.” How do officials appear to have profited from AI stocks? Emil Michael, a Pentagon official who is overseeing military artificial intelligence policy, reaped profits this year of up to $24m by selling his private investment in Elon Musk’s AI company. He has now sold his holdings in another AI company for between $5m and $25m, according to records seen by the Guardian. Trump homeland security chief says ICE agents could be sent to polling places In another move that threatens to intimidate voters at November’s midterms, the US homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, on Tuesday said that federal immigration and customs enforcement (ICE) officers could be deployed to polling sites across the country. Mullin said: “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. If we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be.” In a separate statement, the department said: “ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.” Federal law prohibits military personnel or other “armed” agents from being “at any place where a general or special election is held”. What has a whistleblower identified as a risk to mail-in ballots? A new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for the midterms was thrown together so hastily, and tested so little, that a single scanning glitch could mean entire batches of ballots are turned away, a whistleblower has told Congress. Tucson police investigate deadly shooting outside gay bar as hate crime Authorities in Tucson, Arizona, are investigating a shooting outside a gay bar that left three people dead as a possible hate crime. Police said: “Initial evidence suggests the suspect confronted the victims in the parking lot. The suspect was in possession of a note with several LGBTQIA+ associated businesses written on it. The department is currently investigating this homicide as a hate crime.” What is the latest legal setback to the Trump administration’s attack on LGBT+ rights? A federal judge has dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit challenging California’s policy of allowing transgender youth to play on sports teams. The justice department had been fighting for a year to force California to ban trans girls from women’s sports, with the president directly singling out one trans track and field athlete in online attacks. US officials defend Venezuela oil deal amid questions over rebuilding plan Trump administration officials have defended a highly contentious deal giving the US control of a significant chunk of Venezuelan oil reserves. Last week, Donald Trump announced a deal that would give the US “majority” control over 65bn barrels – roughly one-fifth – of Venezuela’s oil reserves. US officials said the agreement would create a stable economic platform to restore Venezuelan democracy after nearly three decades of autocratic rule, but the pact has provoked outrage among Venezuela’s opposition, already furious that democracy has yet to return to the country eight months after the removal of Nicolás Maduro by US special forces. In other news … The accused in the killing of Charlie Kirk, Tyler Robinson, must stand trial and is eligible for the death penalty, a judge has ruled. The Democratic contender Abdul El-Sayed has hit back at JD Vance after the vice-president described him as representative of “terrible evil”. The incumbent senator Ed Markey, 80, has won the Massachusetts Democratic primary despite his opponent claiming he was too old to be effective. Tiger Woods is set to change his not guilty plea in the DUI case stemming from a crash in Florida this year. A federal judge dismissed the remaining claims against Lizzo’s production company, declaring the case brought by her former wardrobe stylist could not proceed. Stat of the day: USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thai port after gruelling 270 days at sea The US aircraft carrier at the center of a row over conditions on board after months at sea as part of Trump’s war against Iran has finally arrived at a Thai port. Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on the vessel have made headlines around the world. Well Actually: How do you define good health – and achieve it – in a broken US medical system? Elle Hunt speaks to Dr Lucy McBride, whose new book aims to help people navigate US healthcare – and to tread carefully in the wellness industry. Don’t miss this: As Nepal’s morgues fill, Parkrit hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother Cait Kelly has been in Kathmandu in the aftermath of the devastating floods in Nepal. A week on from the disaster, she reports how authorities are urging relatives of the thousands of missing and dead to provide blood samples. … or this: Modern Family’s Mitch and Cam on their hilarious and groundbreaking love The on-screen love between Mitchell (Jesse Tyler Ferguson) and Cameron (Eric Stonestreet) in Modern Family was a rare example of a gay couple raising a child on TV. Hannah Verdier has spoken to the two actors whose chemistry made them one of the most adored on-screen couples of the era. Climate check: Global heating will hit at least 1.8C, UN warns, and there are ‘no good outcomes’ A report by the UN Environment Programme has confirmed overshooting the 1.5C goal inscribed in the Paris agreement is now “unavoidable”. It said the best hope to limit the impact was to adopt an “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway, but that human health, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies could all be severely damaged, and some losses would be irreversible. Queensland police are investigating after about 5,500 Dorper sheep worth more than $1.2m USD were allegedly stolen from a farm in western Queensland. title: Teamsters union leaders support Republicans despite members endorsing Democrats
summary: Sean O’Brien, president of 1.3 million-strong union, was also first to speak at the Republican national convention in 2024
text: The powerful Teamsters union is backing Republican candidates in the 2026 election cycle even after members have voted to support their Democratic opponents. The 1.3 million-strong union’s president, Sean O’Brien, angered many members and union leaders in 2024 when he became the first union president to speak at the Republican national convention (RNC). The latest moves by the union’s leadership are further stoking tensions within the union. “The Republicans have done nothing but take a gun to our head at every turn. And why we think that we can somehow change their behavior, I don’t understand it. It’s not a logical argument,” said John Palmer, who was elected on O’Brien’s slate in 2021 as an at-large vice-president on the Teamsters executive board, but who broke ranks in criticizing O’Brien’s RNC appearance in 2024. “I live in Texas. I’m a moderate guy, but I know when somebody’s trying to cut my throat.” The national union declined to make an endorsement in the 2024 presidential election for the first time since 1996, claiming a majority of members supported Trump after they supported Biden in 2020, though Teamsters locals and councils representing 1 million members at the union independently endorsed Harris. So far this election cycle, O’Brien has made two personal contributions – both to Republicans. O’Brien donated $1,000 to the Republican US Senate campaign of Scott Brown in New Hampshire on 19 February 2026. Brown appeared on O’Brien’s podcast, Better Bad Ideas, on 25 February. The only Teamsters’ local in New Hampshire, Teamsters Local 633, endorsed Brown’s Democratic rival Chris Pappas for the Senate race in April 2025. Teamsters Local 633 did not respond to multiple requests for comment. O’Brien also made a $1,000 donation in May 2025 to another Republican, Markwayne Mullin, now Trump’s secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. The two have clashed spectacularly in the past. During a US Senate hearing in November 2023, Mullin challenged O’Brien to a fight while reading aloud social media posts made by O’Brien that were critical of Mullin. After Trump’s 2024 election win, Mullin and O’Brien publicly made amends during Lori Chavez Deremer’s confirmation hearings for secretary of labor in February 2025. Teamsters local members and the Teamsters leadership are differing on endorsements in several key races. In April, the Pennsylvania Conference of Teamsters voted by voice to endorse Paige Cognetti, Scranton’s Democratic mayor, in her congressional race in Pennsylvania’s eighth congressional district. “As mayor, Paige has taken on special interests and fought for reform. She turned down a [city-issued] car, eliminated cash payments and cut costs, leading to budget surpluses and a credit rating that went from junk to investment-grade,” Bill Hamilton, president of the Pennsylvania Conference of Teamsters, said at the state union’s annual meeting where they endorsed Cognetti. But the Teamsters’ political action committee (Pac) subsequently endorsed Rob Bresnahan, a Republican congressman, following a $5,000 donation to his campaign in May 2026. Bresnahan appeared on O’Brien’s podcast in January 2026. Following the endorsement, Hamilton released a statement backing Bresnahan. “Rep Bresnahan has always had our backs, particularly when he played a critical role in the successful bipartisan push to pass the Faster Labor Contracts Act in the House of Representatives,” Hamilton said in a statement in June 2026, which did not address his conflicting endorsement of Cognetti. “The Teamsters support candidates who support us regardless of their party affiliation, and for that reason Robert Bresnahan has our unwavering endorsement.” Hamilton did not respond to multiple requests for comment. In August, O’Brien visited the congressional district and added an endorsement of his own for Bresnahan. In June, O’Brien announced the Teamsters were endorsing Chris Swanson for governor of Michigan. He lost easily in the Democratic primary to Jocelyn Benson, who had received endorsements from Teamsters Locals 283, 406, 243, 1038, 247 and 337 in Michigan, the majority of the union’s locals in the state. The Teamsters have also thrown their weight behind Max Miller, Ohio’s beleaguered Republican congressman. Miller has faced resignation calls from his own party over domestic abuse allegations and has argued in court filings that allegations made by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, daughter of the Republican US senator Bernie Moreno, have cost him union support in his re-election bid against ironworker Brian Poindexter. Miller was among 16 congressional Republicans who met with O’Brien at a roundtable discussion in November 2024, as the Teamsters under O’Brien have refrained from criticizing actions by the Trump administration that have been opposed by the majority of the largest labor unions in the US. In July 2026, the Ohio Conference of Teamsters announced its endorsements, which included Miller, citing his vote for the union-backed Faster Labor Contracts Act, though Miller’s lifetime voting score on labor issues is rated at 14% by the AFL-CIO. The Ohio Conference of Teamsters did not respond to multiple requests for comment. O’Brien’s 2024 appearance at the RNC marked a shift from his rhetoric when he ran to lead the union in 2021, when he called Trump “our enemy” and criticized the previous Teamsters leadership for not doing enough to stand up to Trump’s first administration. O’Brien defended the appearance at the RNC as the union has since shifted toward supporting more Republicans, even as the Trump administration has taken several actions undermining labor unions and collective bargaining rights, including an ongoing attempt to eliminate collective bargaining rights for more than 1 million federal workers. O’Brien faced an attempted challenge to his leadership earlier this year, but the slate of candidates failed to receive the 5% of delegates required to make the ballot. O’Brien’s slate was then re-elected, unopposed, to another five-year term. O’Brien and the Teamsters did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
