title: Family pays tribute to New Mexico man killed by bear: ‘He was a strong person’
summary: Relatives of Benjamin Halona remember his career as wildlife firefighter and his zeal for selling tamales
text: Relatives of a New Mexico man who was fatally mauled by a bear inside his home recently say they are choosing to remember his firefighting career and zeal for peddling tamales rather than his rare, brutal manner of death. As Benjamin Halona’s sister, Gloria Halona, and her daughter, Samantha Vandever, put it, that is the least he deserved after the quiet dignity that he showed becoming a widower in February and subsequently grappling with health problems that required him to use a walker and a wheelchair to move around. “He was a really strong person,” Gloria Halona said of her brother in a telephone interview that she and Vandever granted on Monday. “And, even though he didn’t have a lot, he was happy.” The pair did not mind sharing new details about the 20 August bear attack that killed Benjamin Halona, 67, as he recovered from a devastating seizure that had drastically limited his mobility. They said Halona stayed back at his home in the Navajo Nation community of Crystal, New Mexico, while his stepson, Casey, had gone to the post office. Casey was brought into Halona’s life by his wife, Bernadine, who died six months earlier from illness. He heard Halona lock the front door, according to Gloria and Samantha. But, when Casey returned home, they said, the door was ajar, and there was a bear inside turning its nose toward him. Casey instinctively locked himself inside his room; barricaded the door there with a dresser and other heavy items; hid in a crawlspace in his closet; and used a cellphone to dial for emergency help. He also called Gloria and Samantha, who recounted driving over to him and seeing the bear outside the home. Samantha said she was driving and honked the horn at the bear at her mother’s behest. The bear fled, and a police officer shot the animal, they said. The mother and daughter then went inside the home and encountered a “horrific scene” that made it clear the bear they had seen had just killed Benjamin. The fact that Benjamin’s walker was inside his room undisturbed made them wonder if he spent his final moments hearing something at the front door and unlocking it mistakenly believing it was his stepson struggling to get inside. “It was a lot for us,” Samantha said. A Navajo Nation police department spokesperson on Monday declined to discuss Halona’s death, saying the agency had released what it could in a statement on the day of the bear attack. That statement said a bear had killed a man in Crystal, had fled into nearby woods, and was killed by police. It also extended condolences to the man’s family. Regardless, Samantha and Gloria said they had been coping as well as possible by recalling much more pleasant memories of Benjamin. He sold tamales locally that were a community favorite, they said. They said he was also fiercely proud of having served his Native American reservation as a wildland firefighter – and of the nicknames given to him by his friends and loved ones: Ponjo, Mountain Man and Tamale Man. Halona’s fandom of the Grammy-winning country singer Waylon Jennings was also a major aspect of his personality, Gloria said. She spoke about how her brother got to share a personal moment with Jennings months before the latter man’s February 2002 death. Jennings had traveled to Navajo Nation at the time to perform at a fair. Family members managed to arrange a brief meeting, which was photographed and saw Halona and Jennings sing Love of the Common People, which the crooner memorably recorded. “We’re living in the love of the common people, smiles from the heart of a family man,” some of that song’s lyrics say. “Daddy’s gonna buy you a dream to cling to, Mama’s gonna love you just as much as she can.” Jennings complimented Halona by telling him that he sounded better than the country legend Willie Nelson, Gloria said. She added: “That was probably the happiest moment of Benjamin’s life.” Perhaps unsurprisingly, Halona’s fatal bear mauling prompted an intense community reaction. The Navajo people, for one, regard bears as sacred – and here, they had lost both Halona and a spiritual animal. There also had evidently not been a deadly bear mauling in New Mexico since 2001, according to a comprehensive list with information about ursine attacks. That 2001 case, furthermore, had been the first fatal New Mexico bear attack in a century, the Associated Press reported. Nonetheless, eight days before Halona’s death, New Mexico wildlife officials had warned of “an increase in the number of bears involved in human-bear conflict throughout [the state] in 2026”. They asked the public to avoid leaving garbage and fallen or rotten fruit out, which could draw bears into populated areas amid the severe drought conditions that New Mexico was experiencing. Meanwhile, Gloria and Samantha said his survivors – among them two siblings, four children, five stepchildren, 15 grandchildren and one great-grandchild – were finding support in each other. They said they had also drawn a measure of comfort from the strong attendance at community memorials organized in Halona’s honor as well as at his funeral services on 29 August. “He endured a lot in his life – especially during his death,” Vandever remarked of her uncle. “And we’re all heartbroken that this had to happen to him.”

title: ‘Pitiful’: experts condemn initial US aid contribution for Nepal flood victims
summary: Sum of $500,000 has been increased as death toll passes 1,000 but specialists decry Trump dismantling of USAID
text: Aid experts have denounced the US’s “embarrassing” and “pitiful” initial response to the Nepal flood disaster after the US state department announced it was releasing $500,000 in emergency funds to help the relief effort. The modest sum – which has since been increased – allocated in response to the devastation caused by mudslides in the mountainous Asian country was mocked on social media, where users contrasted it with the amount spent on other Trump administration priorities. The death toll from last week’s flash floods has passed 1,000, with 4,400 people still unaccounted, according to officials in Nepal and China. Rescue teams are trying to find workers trapped in hydropower tunnels, which were buried in mud. The US contribution has been upped to $3.6m, which state department officials say will be used to deliver food assistance to feed 10,000 affected households for up to three months, and pay for emergency items such as blankets, mosquito nets and shelter sheets. However, seasoned humanitarian aid specialists suggest even that contribution is inadequate and say the US response has shrunk to a shadow of its previous capacity by the dismantling of USAID, the country’s main foreign assistance organization, after Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year. The organization’s functions were taken over by the state department after USAID was terminated as an independent agency in July 2025 after being dismantled by the unofficial “department of government efficiency”, spearheaded by Elon Musk. The state department says the US continues to support Nepal’s flood early warning system through grants. However, foreign aid specialists highlighted the initial $500,000 sum as symbolic of the inadequacy of current US efforts compared with what would have been offered before USAID was dissolved. The state department has countered by saying it was “was designed to get immediate assistance moving while assessments were under way” and insisted the dismantling of USAID had “not slowed the US response”. Mark Ward, a former head of USAID’s disaster response team, who was nicknamed “Mr Disaster” by President George HW Bush because of his prominent role in relief efforts, called the announcement “embarrassing for the United States and a bit of a slap at Nepal”. Under USAID, Ward said, the amount would have been decided by a disaster assistance response team, which would have been on the ground immediately to assess needs because of the close working relationship the agency had with Nepal, a known natural disaster zone. “They would have done an assessment very quickly with the Nepalese authorities, and then we would have decided on a number,” said Ward. “I’m sure it would have been a lot more than the figure that we’ve seen.” His sentiments were echoed by George Ingram, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and a former staff member of the House of Representatives foreign affairs committee. “I was embarrassed for America,” he said. “It would have been better for them not to announce it. “It’s too early to know what the total magnitude of the US assistance should be, but an initial offering of half a million dollars is pitiful. I do not recall a major disaster like this in which the US initial reaction was such a paltry amount. “They should have said nothing focused on saying we need to figure out what the needs are.” After news of floods broke last week, Karoline Leavitt, the outgoing White House press secretary, said the US embassy in Nepal was “in close contact with local authorities on the ground”. “We’ve offered our help and assistance but of course, the first priority for this president and for Secretary Rubio will always be Americans,” she told Fox News. “We’re focused on rescuing every American that we possibly can.” Ward, who worked on previous disasters in Nepal, said it was the country that the USAID had the closest relationship with because of its susceptibility to earthquakes and other natural catastrophes with humanitarian consequences. “There was no country that we had a better relationship with than Nepal in their disaster management capacity, for the simple reason that nobody has more disasters than Nepal because of its topography,” he said. “We always had disaster experts there on our staff working with these guys, getting them ready for the next disaster, and they’re obviously gone now, with the dismantling of USAID.” Current relief efforts are now being led by Nepal’s neighbors, India and China, said Ward, who argued that the US decision to skimp on foreign aid was a false economy. “Is it really in the interest of the United States to have China and India in the lead?” he said. “The United States is safer when the world is more stable. “If the world is unstable, there are more refugees trying to cross borders, and eventually, maybe ours. Maybe American troops have to deploy. So dealing with natural and man-made disasters before they get out of hand is in the interests of the United States, and it’s dirt cheap compared to the kinds of money you need to respond to a civil war, an insurrection or a refugee crisis.” A state department spokesperson defended the US response as “fast, flexible, and driven by conditions on the ground – not arbitrary funding targets”. “This is a needs-based, adaptive model that allows the United States to get assistance out the door immediately rather than delay action while waiting for a complete picture of a rapidly evolving disaster,” the spokesperson said. “The result is tangible assistance reaching affected Nepalis now. “The United States is continuing to assess the situation and will adjust its response as circumstances warrant.”

title: New constitution in Guinea-Bissau will undermine democracy, opponents say
summary: Referendum result means fewer seats in parliament and new rules on candidates, ahead of December elections
text: Guinea-Bissau voters have approved a new constitution, which critics say will undermine democracy, that significantly expands presidential powers ahead of elections due in December. According to provisional results, 70% of voters approved sweeping changes in the tiny west African state’s first constitutional amendment since revisions that ended the one-party socialist state more than three decades ago. The turnout for Sunday’s referendum was reportedly over 55%, amounting to an estimated 544,060 people. The new constitution will reduce the number of seats in parliament from 102 to 65 and cut electoral constituencies from 29 to 12. New provisions will require presidential candidates to have lived continuously in the country for at least five years before the vote, which is believed to target diaspora-based politicians with significant followings. The referendum’s outcome is expected to pave the way for December’s elections, which many hope will steady the political landscape in Guinea-Bissau, which has been through a series of politically turbulent periods since its declaration of independence from Portugal was globally recognised in 1974. Since then it has had at least 10 coup attempts, half of which have been successful. The most recent came after last November’s disputed presidential elections. Both candidates declared themselves winners, citing electoral malpractice by the other’s camp. The military forcefully intervened, setting up a transitional ruling council headed by Gen Horta Inta-A Na Man, a former military chief of general staff. Na Man said: “What we want after this referendum is to allow whoever wins the elections to see out their mandate without hindrance.” Nelson Moreira, the second vice-president of the transitional council, said the outgoing constitution, which came into effect in 1993, had often been cited as “the cause of instability in Guinea”. The leading opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), which was barred from fielding a presidential candidate in the 2025 election, had asked its supporters to boycott the referendum, which it called a democratic farce. “What will happen on 30 August is the continuation of the coup d’état carried out on 26 November,” its leader, Domingos Simões Pereira, had said.

title: Range Rover launches its first electric vehicle, with starting price of £154,070
summary: Fully electric SUV unveiled after year-long delay and will be built at Jaguar Land Rover’s plant in Solihull
text: Range Rover has launched its first electric vehicle – a year later than planned – offering a greener option for fans of gargantuan British-made SUVs who are also conscious about the climate crisis. Due to be built in Solihull, the home of the marque since 1970, the vehicle comes with an eye-watering price tag, starting at £154,070. However, the delayed launch marks a milestone departure from cars powered by fossil fuels for Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which is owned by India’s Tata Motors but headquartered in Coventry in the UK. It also provides a much-needed moment of positivity for JLR, which reported falling profits earlier this year as it counted the cost of Donald Trump’s tariff wars and supply chain disruption after a crippling cyber-attack last year. JLR said it had given extra training to 10,500 staff working on the project and that the car had undergone testing equivalent to 38 trips around the world, more than any other Range Rover. The company said the luxury vehicle, which can reach 60mph in 4.3 seconds, heralded “a new era of enhanced refinement and capability”. While the model’s electric powertrain will limit its impact on the environment compared with JLR’s petrol and diesel models, SUVs of its size are consistently linked to higher numbers of road deaths in accidents involving pedestrians. However, Range Rover’s bespoke commissioning service does mean that buyers have an “extended choice of near limitless paint colours and finishes, elevated materials, tailored colour combinations and personalisation details including unique embroidery”. Martin Limpert, the managing director of Range Rover, said the vehicle was the end product of a “decade of considered engineering and technological development”. Production at Solihull will be supported by the automaker’s propulsion manufacturing centre, in Wolverhampton, which makes battery packs and electric drive units, as well as traditional internal combustion engines.

title: No eggs, no potatoes but ‘a lot of imagination’: how Spain cooked in war’s hunger years
summary: Book recreates recipes from period following end of Spanish civil war when people faced food shortages
text: Few dishes are simpler to prepare than Spain’s signature dish of tortilla de patatas, which – aside from disputes about onions – requires nothing more than two basic ingredients and a pinch of salt. But where to begin if you have neither eggs nor potatoes? That is the question the chef and food writer Berta Álvarez Acal sets out to answer in Recetas de Guerra (Wartime Recipes), a compilation of recipes covering the years of hunger after the end of the Spanish civil war in 1939. In the case of the tortilla de patatas, the absent eggs and potatoes were substituted by moistened bread and onion to try to simulate the texture of an omelette. “There was a formula using water, bicarbonate of soda and a bit of oil which simulated an egg perfectly and the potatoes are substituted by bread to make a tortilla that really is delicious,” Álvarez said. In the recipe for “fried squid without squid”, deep-fried onion rings masquerade as squid while the “wartime hake” is instead salt cod. As for the “wartime and postwar breakfast”, this consists of “coffee” made from a blend of barley, malt and chicory. “I got the idea for the book when I came across one of my great-aunt’s handwritten recipe books and I noticed that some of the recipes were marked ‘wartime’,” Álvarez said. “That led me to research recipes from other sources such as Ignacio Doménech, who wrote a book during the war about how to substitute ingredients and how to make the most of leftovers.” She added: “Doménech showed us hundreds of examples of how, with a lot of imagination, we could survive those terrible days of starvation.” Some of Doménech’s recipes, although born of privation, could well find themselves on the menu of an upmarket restaurant today, such as his rose petals with milk and honey. Álvarez did not just compile the recipes. “We recreated them and shared them with friends and family,” she said. “Some dishes, although they were prepared from scraps, surprised us as they were real gems, others were not so great.” The recipes in the book span the period from the founding of the second republic in 1931 to the phasing out of ration cards in 1952. In between, starvation stalked the land, especially in areas that supported the losing republican side in the civil war. According to Miguel Ángel del Arco Blanco, a historian at the University of Granada, between 1939 and 1942 about 200,000 people died of starvation in Spain. While people in the countryside could to some extent subsist on olives and whatever they could grow, Álvarez said “the hunger in Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia was horrific”. “It may seem implausible,” she said. “But for far too long, food in the postwar period was far worse than during the war.” Produce previously fed to livestock such as beetroot and turnips found its way to the table while the shortage of protein meant pets, cats in particular, were at risk. “They were dangerous years for cats,” Álvarez said. “People used to put notices up in the hallway saying ‘please respect your neighbour’s cat’. But the cats lived on rats and were not good to eat.” Álvarez said that what she learned while researching the book was to make the most of every kind of produce, adding that the book was also a homage to the generation that lived through those grim years. “I think it’s important that everyone knows what our grandparents lived through because it marked them as a generation. They were incredibly strong.”

title: Ryanair warns air fares in Europe will jump next year if oil price stays high
summary: Budget carrier says airlines could go bust as it cuts passenger targets to reduce exposure to ‘unhedged winter oil’
text: Ryanair has warned that air fares in Europe will jump next year if the oil price remains high and that some airlines could go bust. The Irish budget carrier has cut its passenger target for the year to 31 March, down from 216 million customers to 214 million, to help reduce its exposure to “unhedged winter oil” during the unprofitable off season, with jet fuel currently trading at $140 (£104) a barrel. Ryanair expects passenger numbers between November and March to be broadly flat compared with the same period last year. The company said: “If high oil prices continue through to summer 2027, Ryanair believes short-haul air fares in Europe will increase materially to reflect higher oil prices, as some less well-hedged competitors will struggle to maintain capacity or even survive this coming winter season.” Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, touched $97.04 a barrel on Wednesday, the highest since late July, after renewed clashes between the US and Iran fuelled concerns over supply. It later eased back to just below $95. Ryanair expects the cut to its winter schedule to reduce its winter losses by €70m (£60m) to €100m. But, because it has hedged 80% of its jet fuel at $67 a barrel, it expects to record another profitable year, albeit below last year’s record profit after tax. The airline said it was on track to increase summer passenger numbers – between April and October – by more than 5% from 138 million to 145 million. Fares are drifting “modestly down” between August and September compared with last year, as flagged in July. The rival budget airline Wizz Air reported on Wednesday that its passenger numbers had grown by 25.9% last month compared with a year earlier, driven by a jump in flight capacity. Ryanair was forced to reassure travellers in July that its planes were safe after a passenger was saved from being sucked out of a window mid-flight. Ljubisa Karović was sucked out headfirst after an engine failure resulted in parts smashing an acrylic window during a flight from Thessaloniki in Greece to Memmingen near Munich in Germany. His wife, Svetlana Grković, saved her 61-year-old husband by holding on to his legs and managed to pull him back in with the help of two other passengers.

title: Global bond sell-off intensifies as US-Iran tensions stoke inflation fears
summary: UK borrowing costs driven up, adding to challenges facing John Healey as he prepares for first budget
text: The global government bond sell-off resumed on Wednesday, driving up the UK’s borrowing costs and exacerbating the challenges facing John Healey as he prepares his first budget. The yield – effectively the interest rate – on 10-year UK government bonds, or gilts, jumped to just below 5.3% in early trading: its highest level since mid-2008. Investors across major markets have been dumping bonds in recent days amid fears about inflation and spiralling deficits. Global inflation fears have intensified since the US and Iran began exchanging fire again at the weekend, pushing up the oil price and increasing expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates in the coming months. Higher bond yields progressively increase the cost of financing the government’s debt. UK analysts have warned that higher gilt yields since the start of the Iran war have potentially wiped out almost half of Healey’s headroom against the government’s fiscal rules. Economists at Deutsche Bank reckon the £26bn room for manoeuvre Rachel Reeves created at her spring forecast could be down to less than £14bn by the time of the 28 October budget. Healey would then have to decide whether to rebuild the margin for error with tax increases or spending cuts – alongside facing pressure to fund higher defence spending. Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, said: “Governments around the world are feeling the pressure from bond markets, but the situation is particularly acute for the UK, where Andy Burnham’s grand promises about reforming the economy are about to meet the cold reality of high debt levels and rocketing borrowing costs.” The Brent crude oil benchmark is currently hovering at about $95 a barrel amid renewed fighting in the Middle East. The US launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets overnight, prompting counterstrikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Gulf allies. The resumption of the sell-off in UK markets came after Asian stock markets fell sharply. In Tokyo the Nikkei 225 share index slumped by 2.85%. China’s CSI 300 lost 1.4%, while South Korea’s Kospi dropped by 3.3%. Investors have also been rattled in recent days by the US administration’s attempts to interfere in financial markets – including helping the Japanese to prop up the value of the yen and buying back more US government bonds, or treasuries, to rein in rising yields. Neither move appears to have been successful.

title: Britain is OK with public ownership, but only by foreign powers. Why?
summary: Arthur Downing, author of Power and the People: A History of British Energy, says all-encompassing rapid transition will need a mutualised system
text: Have you ever wondered why it is that most houses in the UK are reliant on gas boilers? Not what’s stopping more people from replacing them with heat pumps, but instead why and how the gas boiler became so ubiquitous in the first place? Arthur Downing, the author of the new book Power and the People: A History of British Energy, can tell you exactly why. “We only have boilers in our houses because of a state-owned enterprise that went into everybody’s home and installed natural gas-suitable appliances at no direct cost,” he says. The nationalised gas industry of the 1940s to the 1980s, which oversaw this huge project, was for three decades one of the “most dynamic, innovative, efficient industries in Britain”, Downing says. Yet few of us would use these terms to describe it as such now. Instead, Britain’s electricity and gas industries are “fragile, fragmented, comically complicated and hopelessly dependent on imported fossil fuels”, Downing writes. On top of that, as consumers, we are facing soaring energy bills amid a cost of living crisis. Unearthing how this happened, by exploring the history of Britain’s energy industry, is the subject of Downing’s book. It’s one he lives and breathes – by day, Downing works as the director of strategy at Octopus Energy, the UK’s largest supplier of energy, but the book itself is written in a personal capacity. Central to his argument is that this is a history a lot of us, even people working in the industry now, know little to nothing about. Yet it is instructive for the present, Downing argues, showing why we have the system we do – and, importantly, how we might change it for the better. This summer’s string of climate crisis-driven heatwaves makes his book feel even more urgent. Although the UK has reduced greenhouse gas emissions by 50% compared with 1990 levels, Downing explains: “The second half of the journey will be much harder than the first. All the low-hanging fruits have been picked, like deindustrialising and switching from coal to gas.” Yet debates about the energy system often happen behind closed doors, and part of his aim was to make it more intelligible. An economic historian by training and with encyclopaedic knowledge about energy, both shine through in the book, which charts how the crisis came into being. His argument is straightforward: ownership matters. “Who owned and controlled the means of making, moving, and selling energy shaped which technologies were developed, what infrastructure got built and the extent to which citizens and consumers benefited,” he writes. Between 1926 and 1979, for instance, state-owned enterprises built huge infrastructure – from hydroelectric plants to power stations inside mountains – faster and cheaper than Britain’s private sector companies today. The system has been privatised since the start of the 1980s, and despite the mess it’s currently in, the orthodoxy tends to still be that private is always better than public ownership – cheaper, more efficient and more creative. Downing does not agree. “I tend to view things from the perspective of political economy – the institutions, the ownership models, the organisations and the people make the system,” says Downing, who speaks with energising enthusiasm and expertise. “For me, the technology is interesting, but it is very strange to think of the [energy] system composed of inanimate objects, as if these things have agency and they don’t. They’re only there because of [human decisions].” Downing’s book charts four phases over the last 200 years, each given a chapter of its own. In the first phase, from the late 1880s to the 1920s, ownership of Britain’s energy system was overwhelmingly public and municipal. This meant that even where private companies were involved, they were highly local, embedded in regional networks, and with municipal authorities making the decisions about how to plan and coordinate the gas and electricity system. The second phase, 1920-1945, saw government become a major owner and operator of some energy infrastructure. The third, from 1945-1979, saw energy nearly completely nationalised. And the final, before the mess of the system we have today, was characterised by almost total privatisation between 1979 and 2010. Although 1,500 energy entities were brought into two state-owned enterprises after the second world war, nationalisation didn’t begin in the 1940s but rather started in that second phase. In fact, in 1926, it was the Conservative prime minister, Stanley Baldwin, who set up the Central Electricity Board (CEB) – a state-owned public corporation that built the first National Grid. Unlike now, this was done on time and at cost. Downing says the energy system we have now is a zombie – a “dysfunctional hybrid” of public and private. For example, it remains privately owned but feeds off state subsidies, meaning few benefits of either model but most of the costs in that it is expensive and inefficient. In February, Engie, the electric utility company in which the French government is the largest shareholder, bought UK Power Networks (UKPN), which owns and maintains electricity cables in the south and east of England, from a conglomerate. On that very day, Downing points out, 10-year bond borrowing rates of the French state went down and the stock value of Engie went up, meaning every French citizen got a bit richer. It didn’t play out the way the British media often claims – the bond markets didn’t blink and the government didn’t collapse. Downing suggests Andy Burnham’s early announcement of a VAT cut on energy bills was a good first move. But if he could ask Burnham to do anything else, what would it be? “Shift the focus from producers to consumers, from investors to citizens,” he says. This would include getting bills down by taking off levies, which are added to fund environmental and social programmes. But it would also mean looking at questions of ownership. “Public ownership was an extraordinary tool for building infrastructure at pace while delivering benefits for citizens,” Downing says. “It can be again.” Downing doesn’t want a return to a 1940s-style system. Instead, he advocates for a mutualised system, meaning neither nationalised nor privatised. “The old labels don’t fit,” he explains. “The principle is that energy should be built around mutually beneficial relationships between capital, citizens and the state, with ownership and decision-making spread out rather than concentrated.” What does that look like in practice? “Public corporations owning the networks and part of generation, councils and community schemes taking real ownership stakes in local infrastructure, and households owning solar, batteries and electric vehicles and being paid properly for the flexibility those provide. Citizens as owners of the system, not only customers of it.” The state would become even more involved in regulation, because regulatory institutions make the system more complex. For example, Ofgem is tasked with setting the price cap and assessing the components of bills but in many instances it doesn’t actually control the costs that are accruing. Markets would still be involved. Natural monopolies – in networks and onshore transmission, for instance – would be publicly owned, while markets would stay for retail, electrical vehicle charging, home solar and batteries. “Public ownership and markets are not opposites,” Downing says. “The Nordic countries introduced competition in [power] generation and retail shortly after Britain and kept extensive public ownership. China is running markets at huge scale within a publicly owned system. The US has the longest tradition of private ownership and some of the least competitive markets in the world.” To make such a change would require bold political intervention. Maybe the local aspect, which is a big part of Downing’s proposal, appeals to Burnham’s talk of devolution, nationalisation and reindustrialisation. Energy transitions are rare and protracted, usually taking around a century, Downing says, and if this were to happen, it would be the “first all-encompassing rapid energy transition in human history”. His book suggests it is possible. We just have to reject the British orthodoxy that says the state is useless in a way private companies never are. “We have a strange situation where we are OK with public ownership, just not by our own state,” he says. • Power and the People by Arthur Downing (Verso Books, £25). title: Almost half of world’s farmers poisoned by pesticides every year, experts find
summary: Study reveals that pesticide poisoning kills 11,000 people each year, with India accounting for nearly 60% of fatalities
text: Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a study has found. Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by Pesticide Action Network, found there to be an estimated 402-433m cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year. Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46% of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by south-east Asia and east Africa. The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in Burkina Faso in west Africa, where nearly 84% of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning. The study, published in the journal Frontiers in Public Health on Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60% of these in India. Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network India, said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored”. The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action”, including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides. The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8m tonnes used in 2023, a doubling since 1990. Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.” The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure. Génon Jensen, the executive director of the Health and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings – both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.” Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with growing evidence linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s. Parkinson’s disease is a progressive disorder in which parts of the brain become damaged over time, affecting movement and balance. The global burden of the disease is rising, with France, Germany and Italy all recognising it as an occupational disease for farmers. Farmers and farm workers are mainly exposed to pesticides during preparation and application, as well as when touching treated crops and contaminated equipment or clothing. Speaking at a webinar organised by Friends of the Earth Europe earlier this year, Rendert Algra said he believed his Parkinson’s disease was linked to the pesticides he had used when working at his family farm in the Netherlands. “Being the eldest son, I did all the spraying of pesticides in our fields for several years in a row,” he said. Despite being the most robust study to date, the report highlights that available information on pesticide poisoning is inadequate, with the authors calling for standardised surveillance and reporting protocols so that pesticide-related poisonings become reliable and comparable.

title: Badenoch v Burnham: new battle lines drawn as the leaders face off
summary: Badenoch, now flanked at PMQs by a mix of centrists and rightwing hawks, may be rethinking the gloves-off style used against Starmer
text: When Kemi Badenoch steps up to the dispatch box for prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, she will face a very different opponent. And while all eyes will be on Andy Burnham’s first PMQs, those in the Conservative ranks will be watching their own leader’s performance just as closely. Badenoch attempted to get out of the traps quickly this week, instigating a reshuffle of her frontbench like a conscientious head girl refilling her pencil case for the start of term. Out went the unassuming shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, replaced by the Thatcherite Andrew Griffith. He will lead a new economic unit alongside the City minister, Richard Fuller, and Claire Coutinho, who will replace Griffith as shadow business secretary and act as his deputy after her parental leave. Priti Patel was also sacked as shadow foreign secretary and replaced with the former Tory leadership candidate Tom Tugendhat. The attention-grabbing anti-migration MP Katie Lam replaced James Cleverly as the shadow communities secretary, after he resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor. The new shadow cabinet will quietly get its first ensemble outing on Wednesday, against the soundtrack of 403 excitable Labour MPs keen to show support for their own new leader. Badenoch’s performance will matter. “Kemi has to change tack because she’s facing different opposition,” said the Conservative peer and polling expert Robert Hayward. “Like the manager of any football team, you have to adjust to the people you’re playing against. Kemi and everyone in the party knows she will have to adapt.” In the final weeks of Keir Starmer’s premiership, Badenoch fully embraced her cage-fighter instincts, showing little mercy or grace towards the former prime minister even after he announced his resignation. But early indications suggest she understands that Burnham’s folksy Hovis advert charm may require a different approach. Before the start of recess she referred to him as “a pair of eyelashes and a black T-shirt”, only for Burnham to playfully counter, in a social media video, “it’s dark blue, actually”. “When your opponent is an unpopular prime minister who’s been there a while, you can afford to take the gloves off,” said the Conservative commenter Henry Hill. “But when they are new and in the first flush of their honeymoon, it requires a little more subtlety.” While that is a quality that has rarely been associated with the MP for North West Essex, advisers were likely to have told her to keep her powder dry and see how Burnham plays his hand, said the Conservative Home editor, Giles Dilnot. “Kemi has her own way of doing things, but she won’t necessarily have to land a knockout blow on day one.” Her reshuffle, argued Dilnot, was less a reaction to facing a very different type of leader than a move to make her party battle-ready should Burnham announce a snap election in 2027. “Everything has shifted on its axis,” he said. “She knows they have to be ready.” Bringing more recognisable figures into the cabinet, including her former rival Tugenhat – seen as one of the party’s surviving One Nation centrists, despite his hawkishness on foreign affairs – indicates that Badenoch’s summer purge of the Wets may have pragmatic limits. The addition of Damian Hinds, seen as more to the centre than his leader, as health secretary backs up the theory. “It gives lie to the accusation that she’s trying to lead a clique,” said Hayward. Some new faces suggest Badenoch is casting her net wider to find talent. The Scot Andrew Bowie at energy is likely to maintain the “drill, baby, drill” stance that helped the Conservatives win a byelection in Aberdeen South in June. Harriet Cross, the new Scotland secretary, is touted as a rising star. It also is a tacit recognition that, while Badenoch herself is polling relatively strongly – YouGov found her popularity has improved in recent months, with 38% of Britons now saying she is doing well – the “Keminaissance” has not translated into support for her party: polling remains dire and has fallen from 25% at the end of 2024 to 19% now. “Her personal polling has gone up, but it hasn’t lifted the party with it,” said Hill. “I think there’s an understanding that if there was a general election now, they would get absolutely hammered.” The reshuffle is not without risk. Griffith was a Treasury minister during Liz Truss’s mini-budget, and repeatedly defended it during the economic chaos that followed. Critics warn that Tugendhat’s hawkishness could lead the party into dangerous territory. Lam’s incendiary rhetoric may turn off as many voters as it attracts. But with conference season ahead and a Labour party flushed with the success of Burnham’s first summer, Badenoch had to show she was not only the right woman for the job, but that she had a feasible team to run the country, said Dilnot. “Last year was all about Kemi, and this year it has to be about the brand,” he said.

title: UK must end all trade with Israel, says co-founder of BDS movement
summary: Exclusive: sanctions against ministers and settler groups are ‘smoke and mirrors cop-out’ says Omar Barghouti
text: Britain’s legal and ethical obligation to stop a genocide in Gaza requires it to take bigger steps than halting trade with illegal Israeli settlements or imposing further sanctions, Omar Barghouti, the co-founder of the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement has said. He described sanctions against individual settler groups or extremist ministers as a “smoke and mirrors cop-out and distraction” from the UK’s legal obligation under international law to end all support for Israel, including arms exports, trade deals and academic relations that “may directly or indirectly enable Israel’s illegal occupation” of Gaza, the West Bank and East Jerusalem. The British foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised on Tuesday to introduce a “comprehensive reset” of the UK’s policy on Israel in the coming weeks. It has been reported that the UK is preparing to ban trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank and Miliband told the Commons the government was looking at how to stop British companies “financing, constructing or advertising new settlements”. Miliband has called plans for the E1 settlement, which would involve the construction of 3,400 houses through the heart of the West Bank, unacceptable and destructive, adding that, by cutting across the territory, critics say it will render a two-state solution impossible. Tenders for the settlements are due to be handed out, potentially irreversibly, days before the Israeli elections on 27 October. The Board of Deputies of British Jews and the Jewish Leadership Council have warned Miliband that a UK ban on trade with settlements may fuel antisemitism in the UK. A third group of British Jews, Yachad, also met Miliband to highlight “the growing concerns of many British Jews about the entrenchment of occupation and effective annexation of the West Bank”. Barghouti, an influential advocate for Palestinian rights for more than 20 years, said the litmus test for human rights law and the west still lay in Palestine. He said: “In July 2024, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) said Israel’s entire occupation of Gaza, and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, is illegal and amounts to a violation of the racial segregation and apartheid prohibitions under international law. “Dozens of UN human rights experts have said to fulfil those obligations a set of minimal steps are required: a full military embargo, export import, dual-use transfer and transit. “They also said you have to end all trade, diplomatic and economic relations and academic relations that enable Israel’s illegal occupation.” Barghouti added: “Further in January 2024, the ICJ said there is a plausible case of the violation of Palestinian rights under the Genocide Convention. “The ICJ decided there is a plausible risk of genocide that is sufficient to trigger third state responsibilities. But UK government lawyers seem to ignore that part of the ruling and say the court has not ruled on genocide. “But the genocide convention is very clear – where there is a risk, the obligation to prevent is triggered, and how do you prevent a genocide? You stop enabling it. You end all forms of complicity.” The Israeli embassy referred to the warning by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools.” He added: “The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.” Explaining why he regards UK sanctions as “totally performative”, Barghouti said: “They have no concrete effect in holding Israel to account or pressuring it to comply with international law.” He added: “Israel has de facto annexed the occupied Palestinian territory, making it near impossible [to] differentiate so-called settlement goods and services.” Pressed whether the BDS movement is trying to change the minds of Israelis through economic force, Barghouti insisted sanctions have to be legal and ethical. “They have to target the perpetrators, whether entities or individuals that are involved in crimes, especially international crimes. They are actually measures of accountability, not sanctions that simply say settlers shall not have vacations in London.” Despite South Africa feeling forced to return to the ICJ to point out Israel is not complying with court orders, he said he retained his faith in international law – for all its colonial origins – arguing it was not something engraved in stone, but dynamic. “Humanity has agency to evolve and expand international law. We in the BDS movement have been pushing the envelope of its interpretation.” Barghouti added: “So, in the BDS movement, we try to hold states, corporations and institutions accountable to end their own complicity in genocide rather than just wait for the messiah of international law to come and save us. “We definitely need international law, just as we need to maintain the ethical high ground. Both are necessary, but not sufficient. We need people power to achieve liberation. There is no other way.”

title: Wednesday briefing: ​What’s behind the global backlash against datacentres?
summary: In today’s newsletter: Communities from Scotland to India are pushing back against datacentres, warning they threaten energy supplies and the climate
text: Good morning. This summer, datacentres have become targets of resistance across the world. Ever since the arrival of ChatGPT, big tech has been lobbying for the creation of enormous new facilities. Many governments claim they’re essential in any country that wants to cash in on AI. Campaigners argue datacentres drain resources and exacerbate the climate crisis. The Scottish National Party has backed a moratorium on new developments; so has the Greens. The boom has been immense, and so has the backlash. Today’s newsletter explains why. At First Edition, we’re keen on pushing the boundaries of frontier technologies (no luddites here), so today we’re trying something new: we’ve produced a video to accompany this newsletter, and you can watch more on the Guardian’s Instagram page. Let us know what you think by replying to this email. How’s that for innovation? Before you do, here are the headlines. Five big stories UK politics | Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years. Nepal-Tibet | A week on from the flash flooding disaster, authorities are urging relatives of the thousands of missing and dead to provide blood samples. Middle East | The US has launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets, prompting counter strikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan and Iraq, fuelling concerns about a ⁠wider renewal of hostilities. Ukraine | Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv. US news | Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada. In depth: ‘We’re in an extremely anti-democratic moment with AI’ In August I attended a meeting of campaigners and councillors in the east London borough of Tower Hamlets, where the government has recently approved plans for a 5,200 sq metre datacentre on the site of an old brewery off Brick Lane. The meeting, held on a sunny Monday evening, went on for three hours, in a stifling hall so packed that organisers had to create an overflow room. It’s a testament to how divisive the subject has become. The new east London datacentre won’t be anywhere near as large as the “hyperscale” datacentres that power AI, which are typically 10,000 square feet or more. Neither is it the first to be built in the area (there are already three similarly sized developments nearby). But attenders I spoke with shared the same concerns as other campaign groups globally. They worried about the amount of energy the building will consume (5.2MW, according to a local campaign group, which is enough to power 15,000 homes), about its use of water (projections for this haven’t been released), and about the noise and heat it could emit. They have good reasons to be concerned. The IMF estimates that by 2030, datacentres will consume more energy than all but the world’s three largest state emitters (China, India and the United States). They are already driving up electricity prices: one analysis found that wholesale electricity prices rose 267% over five years in locations near datacentres in Virginia. And although the industry argues that technology in newer AI datacentres consume less water than older facilities, not even the Environment Agency knows how much water datacentres use. It’s one of many unknowns. Much of the anger here centres on how it’s been approved. Despite fierce opposition from local residents and Tower Hamlets council, which wants the site to be used for hundreds of homes, housing secretary Angela Rayner intervened, overruling the council to approve the application, citing its creation of 44 homes (only six of which will be socially rented) as a “significant” public benefit. “When you have Andy Burnham talking about devolution and democracy, this feels like a slap in the face,” Henna Khanom, a Tower Hamlets resident, told me. “To me, it feels like many of these are springing up in places where low-income, ethnic minority communities just don’t have the power to resist these changes.” This reflects a feature common to many of these battles: locals feel that datacentres are being forced on them against their will, with very little transparency or democratic oversight. *** How many datacentres exist? Globally, the number of “hyperscale” datacentres has nearly tripled since 2018. The UK had 52 datacentres in 2000, and today there are an estimated 520, roughly 48 of which are “hyperscale”, though it’s impossible to get exact figures, since nobody (not even the government) knows the total number that have been built. In the US, where local governments have signed NDAs with tech companies, information is shielded from scrutiny. In the EU, Microsoft and other American tech companies successfully lobbied to conceal the environmental impact of their developments. Secrecy is power, particularly when your industry devours massive amounts of energy, much of it powered by fossil fuels. Because developers can wait years for an electricity grid connection, many are now opting to build their own gas-fired power plants instead. In the UK, more than 100 datacentres intend to burn gas to generate their electricity. It’s possible that some may do this permanently. These are reasons you might expect more scrutiny of these developments, not less. “We’re in an extremely anti-democratic moment with AI,” the Guardian’s tech correspondent Aisha Down tells me. It’s no wonder, then, that so many protests are kicking off. Several weeks ago, police in Scotland warned one developer that public anger over these buildings was so great it now poses a security risk. *** Why does the government want more of them? The Starmer government tended to proselytise about the benefits of big tech. In documents outlining the UK’s AI strategy last year, it argued that datacentres were “the engines of the AI age”, and set out its plans to accelerate construction. So far, Burnham’s government seems to agree: last week, he rejected the Green party’s proposal for a moratorium on new developments, arguing this would “send investment and good jobs abroad”. Since the start of this year, the government has allowed datacentres to opt into Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects (NSIPS), where the secretary of state rather than local councils make planning decisions, enabling developers to bypass local scrutiny. Two of the first datacentres to opt into the NSIPs scheme are applying to build new private gas power stations to fire up their operations, which will together be responsible for more than 4.5m tonnes of carbon emissions. “Most people don’t want diesel generators running constantly near where they live,” Aisha says. “That sort of thing is upsetting to communities.” *** What are they good for? With all the recent attention on datacentres, it’s worth noting many have existed for years, quietly whirring away and processing information you need to send emails or read newsletters like this one. Clearly, we need some datacentres. The question is whether we need the “hyperscale” variety. There has been lots of noise among policymakers about the UK being an “AI maker, not an AI taker” that can’t afford to be left behind in the AI “race” or lose its AI “sovereignty.” But nobody seems to agree on exactly how datacentres achieves these vague aims. Will they rejuvenate post-industrial areas with shiny new jobs? Probably not. Will they help the UK “shape the AI revolution”? It’s hard to see precisely how, when US tech companies building many of the datacentres on UK soil retain control over infrastructure, IP and profits. “People in the highest echelons of power seem to be making policy based on AI Fomo and vibes,” Aisha says. We’ll return to this vibes-based strategy and the risky financing of the AI boom in future newsletters. For now, it’s clear these fights reflect a feeling that datacentres are something done to communities, regardless of whether they consent. The Burnham government hopes to reignite people’s faith in democracy by giving them more control. The battle over datacentres will be a major test of that commitment. What else we’ve been enjoying Having written about the True Love Waits Christian purity campaign in the 90s, I wasn’t overjoyed to see its latest iteration in Girls Gone Bible. Alaina Demopoulos explains why it makes sense for so many Gen Z women. Libby I spent a childhood summer in France convinced I could communicate (via hee-haws) with the donkey in a nearby field. Decades on, I feel vindicated by this episode of Science Weekly on human/whale interspecies dialogue. Michael If the notion of an on-demand scotch egg excites you as much as it does me, Joanna Partridge has written about farmers using vending machines to bring fresh milk and local produce to rural locations that lack nearby shops. Libby After learning yesterday about the US non-profit Leaving Maga which helps people step away from the far-right, I found these reflections from four former Trump voters to be particularly thoughtful. Michael As a former Scotland correspondent, I was interested to read First Edition alumnus Patrick Greenfield on how the SNP is setting up yet more constitutional fisticuffs with the UK government over supermarket price capping. Libby Sport Football | Manchester City have equalled the British transfer record with a £125m deal to sign midfielder Enzo Fernández from Chelsea. Tennis | The Wimbledon semi-finalist Arthur Fery lost 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 to Lorenzo Musetti while Elena Rybakina sailed into the second round with a 6-3, 6-2 success. Cricket | Maia Bouchier hit 104 to power England to victory in the first ODI against Ireland, as they won by six wickets in Leicester. The front pages “Brexit and Thatcher to blame for UK’s era of low growth, says PM”, is the Guardian’s front page headline today, while the Times has “Burnham lays blame on Brexit for UK’s woes”, the Mail writes “Britain’s problems? I blame Thatcher and Brexit, says Burnham”, and the Telegraph says “Markets turn on Burnham”. The i Paper leads with “Burnham pushes welfare cuts into 2027 – as he plans bolder devolution”, the Express says “Kemi: New PM wants to take us back to 70s” and Metro’s take is “historic battle”. Elsewhere, the FT splashes “Russia secretly helping Iran develop advanced supersonic cruise missiles”, and the Mirror writes “A fresh start versus Farage farce”. The treatment of 22-year-old Finn Joughin comes after a surge of settler violence against Palestinian people in the West Bank that has been widely condemned internationally and also by many prominent figures within Israel.
