title: Japan halves speed limit to 30km/h on all narrow city streets
summary: Speed limit dropped from 60km/h for around 70% of general roads in the hope of making narrow streets of crowded cities safer
text: Drivers on residential roads in Japan have been forced to take their foot off the accelerator, after the speed limit was slashed from 60km/h (37mph) to 30km/h in an attempt to reduce deaths and injuries among pedestrians on narrow urban streets. The new limit, which went into effect on Tuesday, applies to residential roads with no centre line or maximum speed signs, media reports said. Narrow roads with no centre lines or pavements are a common sight in crowded Japanese cities, with data indicating that children and older people are at particular risk of being involved in a fatal or serious accident. The measures apply to about 870,000km of roads that are less than 5.5 metres wide and do not have centre lines or median strips, according to the Mainichi Shimbun. They account for about 70% of the country’s general roads, the newspaper said. Authorities hopes the restrictions will address concerns that residential areas are not experiencing the same improvements in safety seen on larger roads. While the overall number of deaths in traffic accidents is in decline – falling to a record low of 2,457 last year – those involving children and older people on residential roads has remained steady at about 300 a year since 2021, and rose for the first time in three years in 2025, according to the national police agency. The introduction in 2011 of “zone 30” areas on a limited number of residential streets and along school routes resulted in a 30% reduction in fatalities and serious injuries, the Mainichi said. Police agency data show that the mortality rate among pedestrians is less than 1% in accidents involving vehicles traveling at or below 30km/h, with the rate rising to 2.7% at speeds of 30-40km/h, and to 17.4% at 50-60km/h. “We ask drivers to recognise that they need to take particular care on roads shared by vehicles, pedestrians and cyclists,” the police agency’s commissioner general, Yoshinobu Kusunoki, told reporters this week.

title: ‘I want to live’: the disabled people unable to go abroad because of care funding refusal
summary: Campaigners say care users face a postcode lottery for support overseas – despite no extra cost to taxpayer
text: Disabled people are being blocked from travelling abroad by NHS care boards and local councils that refuse to let them use their care funding outside the UK, the Guardian has learned. Campaigners warn of a “postcode lottery” in England where the right of a disabled person to travel overseas depends on where they live or the whim of local officials – even when there is no extra cost to the taxpayer. Disabled care users report having to abandon travel plans at the last minute, or go for years without a break, when authorities refuse to pay for their care abroad, even though they have agreed to meet all the travel expenses. The Guardian is aware of instances where individuals have had requests for care and support for overseas travel turned down by NHS officials – only to have the decision reversed when they threatened legal action. Lucy Robinson, 38, told the Guardian she had been prevented from attending international work events and going on a holiday because health officials in Oxfordshire had refused to allow her to use her care package abroad. Robinson, who is quadriplegic and has a team of 24-hour personal assistants, is often required to travel in her role as the president of the European Spinal Cord Injury Federation. She has received NHS support for some trips. She said the experience had caused huge stress: “Travel is one of the things that defines my life, in terms of most of the work I do, but also because I like travelling. My quality of life is based around that. I want to live, not just to exist.” The cases have led to calls for national guidance amid concerns there are no clear or consistent NHS or council-wide rules clarifying the right of disabled people to take their carers abroad. Their care packages typically provide them with personal assistants for help with dressing, movement and night support. Campaigners have emphasised this is not about “holidays on the NHS”. There is no extra cost for the health service or local authorities, which are already paying for the care. In almost all cases, the care recipient is expected to pay for their assistant’s expenses and arrange their insurance. “Refusing to pay for care and support abroad does not deliver any financial savings for the taxpayer,” said Carol Barraclough, the advocacy and support manager at the Spinal Injuries Association. “We’d like to see national guidance on this that is effective and clear on the rights of all disabled people to take their carers outside the UK.” Robinson said the Thames Valley NHS integrated care board (ICB) told her in April it had rejected her care request to attend a conference in Germany because “NHS funding responsibilities cease at the UK border”. As a result, she was forced to abandon planned work events in Norway and Albania. She was able to go to Germany only because her 69-year-old mother stepped in as her 24/7 carer. The care board made a rapid U-turn in June when Robinson threatened the health board with legal action, arguing it was acting unlawfully. It then agreed to fund her care overseas on condition she dropped plans for a judicial review. Analysis by the Guardian shows a wide variety of policies across councils and the NHS. Some are explicit that overseas care is possible, while some agree in principle but attach a string of conditions. Others say overseas travel is allowed only at the discretion of their officials. “There’s a postcode lottery in NHS care and support policy to allow recipients of funding to take their assistants with them outside the UK,” said Barraclough, who added she was aware of several cases where disabled individuals had been turned down for care abroad. Giselle Hoad, the founder of the Adult Social Care Warriors campaign group, said: “There’s a concern that cultural prejudice about disability – that we don’t have families, partners, or jobs – means the care system sometimes assumes disabled people should be satisfied with opportunities closer to home.” Disabled people in England can get care funding through two main sources: NHS continuing healthcare, which provides support for daily living for people with the highest needs, and social care paid for by local councils. Anne-Marie Irwin, a solicitor at Rook Irwin Sweeney who represented Robinson, said NHS care boards had a legal duty to meet a disabled person’s assessed needs. As long as the care user remains a resident of the ICB’s area this duty does not stop if they temporarily leave the UK. Thames Valley said it did not comment on individual cases. It added that where a patient requested temporary travel abroad an ICB “may consider if it’s appropriate to continue commissioning care to meet their assessed health needs while they are outside the country”. It said its decisions were informed by considerations of patient safety, practical care delivery factors and risk assessment and insurance issues. Local authorities hold a similar duty to ICBs, previous court judgments suggest. Chelsea Pettitt, 25, and her parents, have been in dispute with Lancashire council over her entitlement to care on holiday. Chelsea, who has cerebral palsy, quadriplegia and learning difficulties, wants to return to Spain where she had a week-long break in 2022 accompanied by two assistants. Like other twentysomethings, she loved the sun, the swimming, food and culture. “I felt like I belonged there,” she said. But her parents, Barbara and Alison Pettitt, said they were told by a social worker that she was no longer eligible for care abroad as she now lived in supported accommodation. Her care plan specifies two-to-one care for seven nights a year for trips outside Lancashire – but the council stipulates the care must be used by Chelsea to “maintain … important relationships” with her birth family and friends. A lack of national guidelines means the family is unsure where this leaves Chelsea’s right to choose whether – or where – to travel. All Chelsea can do is savour her memories of Spain. “She had an absolute blast,” said Barbara, “and she’d like to do it again.” The council said it did not object in principle to Chelsea using her care package on a holiday abroad and it was “working closely with the individual, their family and care provider to understand the issues that have been raised and support a positive resolution”. A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: “This government is committed to making sure all those who are eligible for NHS continuing healthcare receive the support they need to live independent and fulfilling lives. “Integrated care boards are responsible for planning a package of care that meets each individual’s needs. We expect them to fulfil this duty in line with national policy and legislation.” Additional research by George Francis Lee

title: British man deported from Sweden despite living there since childhood
summary: John Sellers, 34, who moved with his family to Sweden aged 10, has been ejected despite his recent marriage to a Swede
text: A 34-year-old British man who has lived in Sweden since he was 10 has been deported in the latest of a series of Brexit-induced catastrophes for UK citizens in the country. John Sellers was told to leave despite living in Sweden for 24 years, having been educated in the country and newly married to his Swedish partner, Caroline. “It is time people know how people are being treated here, and it is time to show what Brexit has caused,” he said, as he described his near seven-year struggle to remain in the country. “Quite frankly, we have been holding our tongues too long. I am very well aware that different countries have different rules on immigration, but none of this would have happened were it not for Brexit,” he said. His parents moved to Sweden from Essex under the free movement rights that came with the UK’s membership of the EU because they liked the education system and thought it was a “good place to bring up children”. His father died when he was 16, and his mother moved back to England after he started a college course to become a teacher. He was deported in January after three failed attempts to remain in the country and is still fighting to return to Gothenburg, where he was hoping to build a family with his new wife. “Whenever I come to England, I feel like a tourist. Sweden is my home,” Sellers said. “It is horrible. Not only do I feel like I’ve let down Caroline, I’ve let down my family, let down myself. I’ve been ripped from the love of my life, my other half. “The pain is … I wish people wouldn’t have to go through this kind of pain, because you’re not whole. You’re broken.” Hit with the cost of fighting deportation, and lack of work due to the deportation, he said he does not know how long it will be before he can physically hold his wife in his arms again. Caroline, who has chronic conditions including fibromyalgia and symptoms of long Covid, including chronic fatigue, is trying to get back on her feet to return to teaching, but the case has caused a huge level of stress and upset. She said: “It’s just horrible – the feeling of finally having someone to help you with things, someone to lean on and someone who is always there for you and then having to spend so much time, effort and money on fighting the government just to be able to continue that relationship. “There are so many things we want to do. We just want to spend our lives together, and it’s so hard having to fight for that, especially when I am not well to begin with.” Sweden’s migration minister, Johan Forssell, is poised to respond to Swedish MP Håkan Svenneling’s demand for a review of the approach to British residents in the country post-Brexit. Svenneling intervened last month after it emerged one of his constituents, 78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas, who has been in the country for 21 years, was told to leave. Thomas has until 7 September to leave, but her friends and supporters are pleading with Forssell to freeze removals and review a policy critics have said is not consistent with the Brexit withdrawal agreement. Another elderly British citizen, George Mason, who is in full-time dementia care, was told to leave the country in August but has won a stay of execution until 28 September while the migration authorities consider the “obstacles to enforcement”, his son said. The Guardian is aware of another British man detained by police on Tuesday and told he will be deported. Caroline Sellers said she and John decided to go to the media because it was important for politicians and officials in Brussels to see how Sweden’s interpretation of Brexit was “crushing people, crushing families” rather than protecting them, as politicians promised. Eurostat data shows that Sweden has the highest number of Brexit-related deportations of Britons of all EU member states. About 2,500 British nationals have been ordered to leave the country since Brexit, one-third of the entire number of removal orders issued across the 27-member bloc since Brexit in 2021. The problem centres on the Migration Agency’s apparent refusal to allow late applications from people who were not aware they had to formally apply to remain post-Brexit – a process used in only 12 other EU countries. Before, Brexit deportation of an EU national to another member state was only permitted in exceptional circumstances involving threats to national security. But in the post-Brexit scenario in Sweden, deportations of Britons have been ordered even when no crime is involved. The UK Foreign Office has expressed concern on multiple occasions about Sweden’s approach to late applications. It is understood that senior officials at the European Commission are also watching with interest. David Milstead, an activist with the Brits in Sweden group, wrote in the Guardian last month that complaints about the Swedish approach had first been made years ago. Part of the problem, he says, stems from the lack of communication to registered British people living in the country, causing missed deadline applications. He said the Sellers’ case was “yet another example of systemic failings in Sweden’s implementation of the withdrawal agreement”. He added: “There are welcome signs that the Swedish government is taking these problems more seriously, although it is too early to know what will follow. Any remedial action needs to come soon, because people are suffering now.” Sellers was aware that Brexit might affect his right to stay in the country and, without any communication from government authorities, he considered his best option was to apply for Swedish citizenship. This he did in September 2021, before the Brexit deadline of 31 December that year. Not only was his citizenship rejected, but two subsequent attempts to remain in the country under family rights in national migration laws via his partner, now his wife, were also turned down. The latest adjudication, after he appealed against the first decision to refuse him residency on the grounds of a family relationship with Caroline, whom he had yet to marry, was that they had “not lived together abroad for an extended period of time”. The migration court had noted that other evidence of a durable relationship was “insufficient”. The Sellers are now appealing for a review of the judgment with fresh evidence.

title: Specieswatch: Deciduous trees are marching north and ousting evergreens
summary: Northern landscapes could soon look different, as wildfires and storms disturb boreal forests
text: A warmer world is making high latitude forests more deciduous and less evergreen, research shows. Global heating has increased the likelihood of extreme events such as wildfires and storms and this warmer and less stable environment is favouring deciduous trees over evergreens. Boreal forest stretches for miles and miles across high northern latitudes, covering huge swathes of Canada, Russia, Alaska and Scandinavia. It makes up nearly a third of global forest area and is mainly made up of evergreen trees such as spruce and fir. But this landscape could change. Researchers used a vegetation model to investigate the likely impact of climate warming on boreal forest over the 21st and 22nd centuries. Their findings, published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Biogeosciences, show that after disturbances like wildfire and storms, deciduous trees establish more quickly and start to dominate. Rising temperatures also assist by extending the growing season and increasing nitrogen in the soil, both of which disproportionately benefit deciduous trees. Data from Alaska and Canada indicates this transition is already under way, with a shift towards more deciduous saplings in a number of areas, with implications for carbon, water and energy cycles in these regions. Evergreens will not disappear completely, but the model suggests they will no longer be the dominant tree in boreal regions.

title: ‘It smelled like dead people’: the plan to tackle England’s illegal waste problem
summary: Andy Burnham has announced a crackdown, but doubts remain over authorities’ ability to take on organised crime
text: “There were parents dropping their children off and then heaving from the smell,” says Liz Thompson, 45, who runs Blessings Nursery in Bradford, West Yorkshire. During the recent heatwaves, the smell from an illegal waste dump on Midland Road, just metres from the nursery, became so unbearable that staff had to keep the doors and windows shut and the children couldn’t play outside. “It smelled like dead people, like really bad rotten food. It was horrible,” she says. The smell, which lingered for weeks, started to impact Thompson’s business, with prospective parents put off from enrolling their children at the nursery. “It was embarrassing,” she says. The situation Thompson faced is far from a one-off. The Environment Agency received 10,238 reports of suspected waste crime in England in 2025. Yorkshire is a particular hotspot, with a new heatmap showing 1,068 reports in 2025, second only to the West Midlands, where a record 1,542 reports of waste crime were filed. These figures are probably underestimated, with just 27% of waste crimes thought to be reported. It’s a problem that particularly exercises the public and it’s striking that in one of his first moves as prime minister, Andy Burnham visited the Midland Road waste dump, declaring that the “days of making easy money out of waste are over”. The dump, which first came on to Bradford Council and the Environment Agency’s radar in June after reports of foul smells, had been building for months. HGVs had been entering the site in the dead of night and early hours, with a large excavator unloading and dumping thousands of tonnes of waste. “There are really clear signs that this is linked to organised criminality,” says the Environment Agency’s area environment manager, Ben Hocking. Waste crime is profitable for the criminals involved, but costly for the public; approximately 20% of the waste in circulation in England is managed illegally, at a cost to the economy of about £1bn a year. The clean-up is particularly expensive. Burnham has earmarked three illegal sites where waste needs to be removed: Power Station Road, on the Isle of Sheppey, Kent; Aymer Close, in Runnymede, Surrey; and Midland Road. But Hocking estimates the cost to the taxpayer of cleaning up the Midland Road site alone will be upwards of £250,000. The cost of cleaning up the Hoads Wood illegal waste dump in Kent came to £15m. “The aim is to recoup the costs through the courts, but whether that will be possible for this site remains uncertain,” says Hocking. Criminal investigations are still taking place. As part of Burnham’s plans to tackle waste crime, Tracy Brabin, the mayor of West Yorkshire, will be appointed to take a new region-led approach to the problem. “We are cracking down on the criminals behind it and giving the Environment Agency the tools it needs to go further and faster,” said the environment secretary, Angela Eagle. But just how well equipped mayoral authorities and the Environment Agency are to tackle organised criminality at this scale remains up for debate, with the House of Lords recently accusing the agency of “incompetence” when it comes to waste crime. “We could always do with more funding,” says Hocking, “but we’re also looking to be more effective with the people that we have. We are really looking to get a better intelligence picture of what’s happening and where.” With no set timeline for when the clean-up of the Midland Road waste dump will begin, one woman who works at a nearby youth centre but asked to remain anonymous worries that more hot weather could bring more devastating smells. “It was really hard for us to work,” she says. The centre had to cancel its youth cooking and exercise classes because the flies and smell made working unbearable. “Whoever did this wasn’t thinking about the local people and how it’s affecting them and their businesses,” she says. “It’s really unfair. Whoever dumped this waste needs to be held responsible.”

title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong pleads guilty in second national security case
summary: Wong, 29, is accused of urging foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades and other hostile measures against China
text: Joshua Wong, one of Hong Kong’s most prominent pro-democracy activists, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiring to seek foreign sanctions against Hong Kong and China, a national security charge that carries a maximum life sentence. Prosecutors have accused Wong, 29, of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China. The court heard that Wong had visited foreign countries and met foreign politicians to lobby for sanctions against Hong Kong and China. The prosecution said he had continued to call for sanctions on Hong Kong and China after the implementation of the national security law and that he had posted meetings on his social media accounts. Wong has been continuously imprisoned since November 2020. He has spent nearly six years in detention and had been due to be released in January 2027. In 2022 he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit subversion for his role in an unofficial primary election. In November 2024 he was sentenced to four years and eight months in prison. Wong waved at supporters as he entered the dock. He wore a blue shirt and black-rimmed glasses. He stood with his arms behind his back as he pleaded guilty to the charges. Wong is expected to be sentenced later. The offence is punishable by a prison term of three to 10 years, or up to life imprisonment if the offence is deemed to be “of a grave nature”. Pleading guilty could typically result in a reduced sentence. Outside Hong Kong’s high court, people queued overnight to secure a seat at Wednesday’s hearing. One supporter who attended the court criticised the proceedings. “Under a compromised judicial system with zero space for a fair trial, Wong’s plea is a forced reality,” they said, asking not to be named. “This is not justice, but Beijing’s absolute eradication of Hong Kong’s dissident voices.” In 2014, the then teenage Wong became the international face of the Umbrella Movement, when thousands of protesters occupied major roads across Hong Kong for 79 days demanding greater democracy. In October 2014 he appeared on the cover of a Time magazine under the headline: “The Face of Protest”. When protests erupted in 2019 over a proposed extradition bill, Wong was serving a prison sentence for his role in the 2014 demonstrations. He was released at the height of the movement and immediately joined calls for the bill to be withdrawn. In 2020 Beijing imposed a wide-ranging national security law on Hong Kong after a year of anti-government protests. The authorities said the law was needed to restore stability to the international financial hub. Critics say six years on the law is continuing to expand in scope. Wong is the only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under the law. Supporters say the prosecution heavily relied on his advocacy before the national security law was enacted and argue his case has been applied retroactively. “It’s obvious that the government wants to keep him behind bars for as long as they can, so as to isolate him and not to let him become a visible symbol of resistance.” said Frances Hui from the Committee for Freedom in Hong Kong Foundation. Wong’s case has attracted widespread condemnation from global rights organisations. “By stacking one charge after another against Joshua Wong, the authorities are ensuring that the democracy icon stays behind bars, silencing him and the Hong Kong pro-democracy movement he helped lead and inspire,” said Elaine Pearson, Asia director at Human Rights Watch. “Conflating promoting democracy and free speech with undermining national security is a favourite dodge for authoritarians. Beijing also likes blaming ‘hostile’, but unspecified foreign forces,” said Sophie Richardson, a longtime China rights advocate. On Tuesday the former Conservative leader Iain Duncan Smith urged the UK government to raise Wong’s case with Beijing, saying: “Enough is enough. It’s time to stop chasing peaceful protesters.” With Associated Press

title: Country diary: The rain has come, and suddenly the land looks (and smells) different | Nicola Chester
summary: Inkpen, Berkshire: From lurid yellow to a moorland brown; from the scent of fire smoke to sheep urine. It’s amazing what some rainfall can do
text: After an entire heat-baked summer without rain, the land looks strange and unlike itself. Fields, banks and grassy margins are the lurid yellow ochre of climate fiction – the mise en scène captured with eerie relevance in the recent BBC TV drama The Rapture. There are cracks so deep in Weaver’s Field that the farmer can push his arm in up to his elbow. Spots of bird’s-foot trefoil and sky-blue chicory (the latter on uncannily short stems) polka-dot the otherwise dead pasture. Sentinel field oaks seem unaffected, but shallow-rooted beech trees, familiar in giant caterpillar shapes on the downs, shed shrivelled brown leaves and a poor, early beechnut mast. Gnarly field maples are almost leafless, while sycamores bracket the green with their browning leaf-curl. Even in the keepered woods, laurel has wilted. For a week, skeins of black smoke drift from the field fires at Enham Alamein, from the eastern end of Greenham Common, and from the New Forest further south. But over the nearby border into Wiltshire, it is white smoke that veils Salisbury Plain all the way to Avebury. The Westbury White Horse, of Eric Ravilious’s 1939 painting, is on fire – or the down and iron age Bratton Camp next to it is. Probably carved from the chalk in the late 1600s, it is surrounded by an apocalyptic vision. The smell of smoke lingers long after a fire is out. Dad was a fireman who fought the New Forest conflagration in 1976, and Windsor Castle’s blaze in 1992. For me, the smell of burning evokes heightened awareness, comfort and safety, an olfactory memory of him coming home from work in damp, sooty uniform, and the alarm bell that rang in my childhood home whenever he was needed. The rain teases us for a few more days, as towering piles of cumulus sail north like galleons. When it comes, it darkens the down to an unfamiliar moorland brown. The heat rises again afterwards, and with it the strong scent of ammonia from sheep’s urine. The only thing to wet the ground all summer, it had remained undiluted and on the surface. Reanimated, mingled with damp dust and baked grass, it’s a heady, confusing new scent. • Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now at guardianbookshop.com

title: Climate Goals Missed, U.N. Says World Must Now Remove Carbon at Scale
summary: Carbon removal combined with emissions reduction is the only remaining pathway to avert catastrophic levels of warming, a new report warns.

title: Global heating will hit at least 1.8C, UN warns, and there are ‘no good outcomes’
summary: But scientists say the world could get back to 1.5C through deep, rapid emissions cuts and removing carbon from the atmosphere
text: Global heating will reach at least 1.8C under even the most optimistic future, well beyond the Paris agreement goal of 1.5C, according to a UN report that warns every fraction of temperature rise intensifies destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and island and coastal city submersion. The report by the Nairobi-based UN Environment Programme confirmed overshooting the 1.5C goal inscribed in the landmark Paris agreement of 2015 was now “unavoidable” and, despite some progress in addressing the human-caused climate crisis driven by burning fossil fuels, likely in the next few years. It said: “There are no good outcomes above 1.5C”. Heating of up to 3C above preindustrial levels could lead to glaciers losing more than a quarter of their mass by 2100, raising sea levels by up to 13cm. Global food production could decline by up to 14% by 2050 if there are not effective strategies to adapt. Human health, water supplies, nature, cities, infrastructure and economies could all be severely damaged. Some losses would be irreversible. Many communities may have to relocate or change their livelihoods. The report said the best hope for humanity to limit damage was to adopt an “overshoot, peak and decline” pathway that required immediate and sustained greenhouse gas emissions cuts combined with steps to remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. It described the goal of net zero emissions – increasingly politically contentious in some countries – as “an essential milestone that cannot be skipped” and stressed carbon dioxide removal through steps such as establishing vast new forests must occur alongside, not as an alternative to, deep cuts in fossil pollution. Crucially, the authors of the report, titled Limiting Overshoot, said the average global temperature could be returned to 1.5C this century only if heating stayed below about 1.8C. They warned nature’s capacity to store carbon was uncertain and would shrink the more the planet heats. The president of Palau, Surangel Whipps Jr – this week hosting regional leaders including Australia’s Anthony Albanese for a Pacific Islands Forum meeting focused on security and climate – said the report was “a fork in the road moment for the planet”. “It is hard to overstate the depth of emotion for those of us living on the frontline after having fought so hard to put the 1.5C limit at the heart of the Paris agreement,” Whipps said. “We need to see an urgent and unprecedented increase in political will and investment in a climate safe future. Nobody can read this report and conclude otherwise.” Vishal Prasad, from Pacific Island Students Fighting Climate Change, said the report was terrifying for young people from the Pacific. “The International Court of Justice has made it clear – keeping to 1.5C is not a choice, it is a legal obligation,” he said. “We are not asking for your goodwill. We are not begging you. We are telling you what international law requires of you. End fossil fuel expansion. Your corporate profits cannot be allowed to extinguish our future.” The UNEP executive director, Inger Andersen, said the future would “bring many unknowns”, but extreme heatwaves – such as those that smashed records and exacerbated wildfires and droughts this northern summer – were already proving climate impacts would “strike faster, hit harder and last longer”. “We have to act with urgency and determination. Every fraction of a degree avoided, every year by which overshoot is shortened, and every adaptation action taken will save lives, will protect ecosystems, and reduce economic losses,” she told reporters. Prof Debra Roberts, a report author and co-chair of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, said a key message was that “the rules of the game are now changing”. “Existing approaches are no longer fit for purpose,” she said. “I think, for me, that’s the clarion call. We now have to reconfigure our climate governance around dealing with an overshoot pathway.” She said that meant not just pollution cuts and carbon removal, but “bold adaptation” to protect infrastructure and livelihoods, help sustain political and social support for reducing emissions, and prevent resources being diverted to crisis response. Climate Analytics, a science and policy institute, applauded the report for clearly describing the problem, but said it did a poor job of “showing us that there is a way out”. Its chief executive, Bill Hare, said UNEP had barely mentioned the need to phase out fossil fuels or evidence showing “real zero” emissions was possible in many economic sectors by mid-century. The report’s authors cited earlier work that found limiting heating to about 1.8C required global emissions to be halved by 2035. They said existing national policies were projected to lead to at least 2.3C heating, but it would still be possible to limit stay below 2C if countries delivered on net zero emissions commitments by mid-century. Prof Richard Betts, from the University of Exeter and UK Met Office and another report author, said the flooding catastrophe caused by the collapse of rock and glacial ice in Nepal and China was a demonstration of why the world needed to limit overshoot and come back to 1.5C. “That specific event obviously is very complicated [but] we are committed to glacier loss,” he said. “We can stop them getting much worse by reducing emissions and limiting the amount of warming.”

title: USS Abraham Lincoln arrives at Thai port after gruelling 270 days at sea
summary: Ship has been plagued by reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health because of lengthy deployment
text: The USS Abraham Lincoln, a US aircraft carrier at the centre of a row over conditions on board after months at sea as part of Donald Trump’s war against Iran, has arrived off a Thai port. Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health on the vessel, including attempted suicides, have made headlines around the world, provoking criticism of the president’s actions in the Middle East. A heavy security presence was in force at Laem Chabang port near Pattaya, south of Bangkok, where the 5,000-strong crew of the USS Abraham Lincoln arrived on Wednesday morning after more than 270 days at sea. The huge nuclear-powered ship left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago. The resort city of Pattaya, a rest-and-recreation destination for US troops since the Vietnam war, has stepped up security as it prepares to welcome the sailors and Marines. The sailors will disembark in groups of approximately 50, according to police colonel Anek Srathongyoo, a superintendent of Pattaya city police station. Once a quiet fishing village, Pattaya was transformed into one of the most infamous red light districts in the world with the arrival of American troops using military bases in Thailand during the Vietnam war. At its peak, tens of thousands of US military personnel came through each year, said Pipatpong Fakfare, an associate professor specialising in tourism at Bangkok University. “In my opinion, it’s really the founding influence for the town. The US military turned a quiet fishing village into a global destination for an international nightlife and entertainment hub in about 15 years,” he said. Pattaya is now hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism. Although the American troops left by the mid-70s, the sex industry infrastructure continued to grow, with European tourists taking their place, and more recently waves of Chinese and Russian visitors, Pipatpong said. Sex work is illegal in Thailand, but authorities often turn a blind eye, said Pattarachit Gozzoli, a sociologist at Mahidol University in Bangkok. Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, has downplayed the city’s past, saying there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied it was linked to the US arrivals. Local police arrested 25 women for soliciting on the beachfront promenade a week before the ship arrived. The mayor said buses had been arranged to transport the sailors between the ship and Pattaya until the carrier departs on Sunday. Outside one bar, a sign said: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.” Poramase said in a Facebook post: “They come to relax. Our preparations will focus on safety and ensuring fair pricing, so we don’t take advantage of them.” He said they had been banned from water sports such as jetskis, and from taking advantage of Thailand’s lax cannabis laws, but encouraged them to enjoy the city’s many other attractions, from malls to religious sites.

title: As Nepal’s morgues fill, Parkrit hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother
summary: A week on from the flash flooding disaster, authorities are urging relatives of the thousands of missing and dead to provide blood samples
text: An army official calls out a name. A young woman stands, two pieces of identification in her hands. She fills out a form, takes another and moves to the back of the hospital to give a vial of blood. With so many people killed by Nepal’s floods, and hundreds of bodies being buried because the morgues are full, there is now a push to identify victims through DNA. The woman, Prakrit Gurung, 19, is hoping her DNA will be linked to her mother’s body. Her father’s has been found – her brother recognised his picture on a wall outside the hospital. At the government’s request, Gurung is one of dozens lining up on Tuesday morning. Earlier, an Australian citizen was one of the first 14 people to attend. He had flown over to be with his family – his brother, a Nepali citizen, is missing. Authorities are asking relatives abroad to have their DNA profiles sent over. Several Australian families have already had samples taken. “We are collecting the blood samples here, from their siblings, or direct relatives,” says Rameshwor Adhikari from the army. “People are coming from all over the valley to give blood, and from different places all over the country.” Adhikari adds: “It is a disaster. A natural calamity.” The first day they set up 37 people came through but numbers are growing – and the army brings out more shade tents for people to sit under. Adhikari wants as many people as possible to come forward. There are now more than 1,000 people confirmed dead and nearly 4,000 reported missing. As of Wednesday morning, 38 of them are Australians. In a statement this week, family members of 25 missing Australians called for more government support to “bring our friends and loved ones back home”. Nepali families from the worst-hit area, the upper Rasuwa district, have been campaigning for their government to do more to get boots and rescue equipment on the ground. It has been a week since the floods and contact has still not been established in some places along the Chinese border. Lhakpa Gha’s village, Timure, is one of them. Standing outside a Buddhist monastery on Tuesday afternoon, the 53-year-old says that if she talks, the tears will come. And as she lists her relatives who were washed away, they do. Her father, brother-in-law, son, daughter-in-law, their four-year-old daughter, her daughter and her sister’s brother. All seven, gone. Gha and her husband survived because they were in Kathmandu, looking after two of their grandchildren attending school here. “I lost my whole family,” she says through a translator. “We’ve lost everyone.” The monastery is housing about 200 people from the upper region who managed to survive – they were higher up on the mountain when the flood hit. Many watched as their loved ones were swept away, their towns flattened. “The army has not been able to reach the village,” Gha says. “They keep saying our village is high risk but we don’t understand. We are fighting with them. If it’s high risk, you need to act. But they have just said they can’t get in.” Her son and daughter were doctors in the village – they stayed in Timure so they could keep providing for the family. “We have nothing,” Gha says. “We depended on my son for money.” On Monday a UN report into the conditions in the country’s far north said it could take weeks to reach the upper areas – there are hardly any roads left in, and bridges have been washed away. If the army cannot get in, nor can the aid groups. Amy Sagitta Lefevre from Save the Children says: “Aid is definitely getting through, but to a point.” Speaking from the agency’s warehouse in Kathmandu, she says its teams have reached Rusawa by road. Aid they can’t get further is stored at the army barracks. “The challenging bit for rescue workers is the same challenging bit for aid organisations, because we have the same access issues as they do,” she says. Save the Children is getting kits up the valley that include makeshift tents, so people have somewhere to shelter. It’s also setting up mobile toilets. “On the ground we’re giving out non-food items,” Lefevre says, “which are blankets, ropes, tarpaulin sheets – because a lot of people are sleeping exposed to the elements, so just sheets in case they need to be protected from the rain.” Many of the shelters up the valley are overcrowded, so families are being sent farther afield. “We’re also giving out things like buckets, just so people can carry things or wash, if need be. “And then we have what we call dignity kits … they’re aimed at women, but specifically pregnant women – they have an extra sari, some of the mothers need clothes because they’re still wearing the same clothes they were wearing the day of the disaster.” About 2,600 children are expected to need medical treatment for “severe wasting” and more than 100 may have been separated from their parents. Lefevre says it’s impossible to put a timeline on anything. But recognising that the full recovery process could take over a year, Save the Children has set up a field office. Its workers are worried about the spread of disease, water contamination, overcrowded shelters and the potential, in the chaos of the recovery, for children to be trafficked. “This area of Nepal has historically been a hotbed for child trafficking of girls,” she says. “We’ve heard anecdotally that it may have lessened in recent years, but because of this disaster we are now very concerned about the fact that children or girls … could be trafficked.”

title: Relief as five Australians missing in Nepal-Tibet flood disaster found alive
summary: Several missing Australians have been found since Tuesday morning, bringing the total citizens unaccounted for to 38
text: A total of five Australians missing after devastating floods ravaged the Nepal-Tibet border last week have been found. Of the five Australians confirmed safe, one was found in Nepal, one in Tibet, and three outside the crisis-hit area. The total number still missing is 38. These Australians had not spoken to families and next of kin since the disaster struck seven days ago. There were “grave concerns” for the dozens of citizens still missing in the disaster, the minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, told the ABC on Wednesday morning. “There are real logistic issues, including communications to find out where people are,” she said. “For those families that are still waiting, those 38 individuals unaccounted for, we understand that it’s a really concerning time, and we’ll continue to do what we can to try and locate those people.” Earlier, the minister for the Pacific, Pat Conroy, told Radio National the government was “focused on establishing their whereabouts and supporting their families”. The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (Dfat) has received nearly 800 calls in relation to the floods, with 18 Australian personnel having travelled to Nepal to join staff on the ground. More humanitarian and disaster relief from Australia was due to arrive in Nepal on Wednesday afternoon. Another Australian, 25-year-old Cara Severino, was safely located last week. After an Australian in Tibet made contact with family and Dfat yesterday, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said the government was “incredibly thankful”. “It’s hard to imagine the sense of relief their loved ones must be feeling after what will have been an incredibly harrowing few days.” The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet. More than 4,400 people are missing. Wong said the government needed to “remain realistic” about the days ahead. “Communications remain difficult, infrastructure has been destroyed and many areas are still difficult to reach,” she said. “As each day passes, our grave concerns for those still unaccounted for inevitably grow. “Our thoughts remain firmly with all those waiting for news of family and friends, and with the search and rescue teams working in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.” Australia has sent a $8m assistance package for affected communities on the border between Nepal and the Chinese region of Tibet. Nepal has deployed nearly 20,000 security personnel to support search and rescue, and Chinese state media has reported that 2,141 emergency personnel have been deployed. • This story was amended on 2 September 2026. An earlier version misstated the number of people who had been found.

title: Germany blames Russia for drone attack at Leipzig airport
summary: Government says ‘dangerous behaviour’ is part of effort by Moscow to cause damage with hybrid attacks
text: The German government has blamed Russia for the drone attack on Leipzig airport last month, calling it “dangerous behaviour” and part of a systematic and concerted effort by Moscow to “cause great damage” through a large number of hybrid attacks. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, and the foreign minister, Johann Wadephul, ended weeks of speculation and the government’s hesitancy to blame Russia, saying in a brisk 10-minute briefing in Berlin that all indications were the Russian state had provided the knowhow and equipment for the planned attack and “low-level agents” were recruited to carry it out. A drone loaded with explosives was discovered at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane used to transport weapons to Ukraine. It failed to detonate but could have caused a catastrophe, authorities said. Russia will face a package of penalty measures, Wadephul said, adding that the German government saw “a need for appropriate and necessary action in this situation”. It would respond “to this hybrid attack in Leipzig with proportionate and measured, yet equally resolute, action”, he said. “We are not at war, but we are a daily target of hybrid warfare.” He added: “The dangerous behaviour of the Russian Federation is part of attempts at destabilisation, disinformation, threats, sabotage and aggression.” Berlin regretted the abysmal state of its relations with Moscow, he said. The EU expressed “full solidarity” with Germany over the attack, and Nato assured Berlin that it would defend its members. The French president, Emmanuel Macron, supported Germany’s move and the new round of European sanctions, saying: “These hybrid attacks are multiplying in Europe. They cannot go unanswered. “In the face of this escalation, we must be united, determined, and strengthen our support for Ukraine. France will continue to play its full part.” Giorgia Meloni, Italy’s prime minister, said: “The security of our allies is the security of us all. Attempts to intimidate us or to drive a wedge between allies will not succeed: hybrid actions against any one of us are a matter of concern for all of us, and will be met with a united response.” The Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, said: “Attacking a Ukrainian cargo plane on German soil was an egregious attempt by Russia to weaken our resolve and our collective defence – and it will fail. Our support for Ukraine in the face of Russia’s aggression is unshakeable.” The Russian president, Vladimir Putin, called the sanctions “another mistake,” suggesting the restrictions were aimed at currying favour with voters. “I think it’s another mistake, a serious one,” Putin said during a press conference broadcast by the Russian state news agency Tass. “And in my view it clearly runs counter to the interests of the German people.” The Russian ambassador had been summoned to the foreign ministry at that very moment to be informed of the consequences, Wadephul said. The Russian consulate in Bonn will be closed later this month, and Russian House, a sprawling cultural and science institute in the centre of Berlin, which is alleged to house Russian spies and to have been the launchpad for a number of hybrid attacks carried out in Germany over the past few years, is to be turned out of its rented building. A clampdown on Russia’s shadow fleet – illegal ships carrying Russian oil and other supplies in the Baltic and North seas – is also planned. Sweden and Finland track and disrupt the shadow fleet but Germany does not, so vessels regularly opt to sail via German waters in its foreign economic zones. New lists of people on a blacklist would be drawn up and tighter border controls of Russians entering Germany would be carried out, Wadephul said. Parallel to these moves, Berlin is also backing the European Commission’s 22nd package of sanctions, to cover a further 1,600 companies and organisations with a Russian connection. The government has previously said it does not intend to directly involve Nato by invoking article 4 of the alliance. However, its Nato and European partners were informed about the investigation and agreed on the planned consequences, Wadephul confirmed. The Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, promised “full solidarity” with Berlin. Rutte said Berlin had put forward clear evidence of Moscow’s role in the “hybrid attack” and welcomed the measures announced in response, while von der Leyen vowed to “keep the EU united despite these escalating and serious acts”. Tuesday’s announcement marks the first time the German government has concretely named Russia as responsible for the attack. It marks the lowest point in decades for relations between Russia and the EU’s largest member, which had already plunged after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. This weekend will see a critical election in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg Vorpommern, in which the war in Ukraine and relations with Russia have been a focal point. The far-right populist Alternative für Deutschland, which is pushing a pro-Russia agenda as it seeks to win an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt, has accused the government of double standards over its treatment of Russia. Urging the government to prove Russia’s involvement in the Leipzig incident earlier this week, it said the same rigour should be applied to investigations into the attack on the Nord Stream pipeline, for which Ukraine is alleged to have been responsible. The drone in the Leipzig incident was carrying 600g of explosives and was discovered in the security area of the airport close to Ukrainian Antonov cargo planes on the night of 4-5 August. The explosive device detonator appeared to have failed. A second drone was believed to have been part of the planned attack but investigators have since thrown doubt on that theory. Traces of the military explosive hexogen were found on the edge of the airport on 14 August along with a further drone, investigators confirmed. Had the devices exploded they could have caused a catastrophe, German officials said. The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who last week said whoever was behind the attack “will pay”, did not attend the briefing to the press and public on Tuesday. Konstantin von Notz, the Green party’s security policy expert and commissioner for intelligence oversight, criticised the government before the announcement for what he described as its failure to stand up to Putin in the face of the growing hybrid threat from Russia. “The federal government must finally stop being hesitant, reticent and timid. Things must be called by their name, and decisive action must be taken,” he said in an interview with the RND network. Even within his own Christian Democratic Union party, Merz has faced calls to be tougher towards Russia. On Tuesday, the party’s foreign policy expert, Roderich Kiesewetter, urged the chancellor to take a tougher line against Russia, accusing successive governments of exercising “extreme caution with regard to Russian state terrorism on German soil”. Citing sources in German intelligence, Bild Zeitung said direct connections had been made by investigators between other drone and explosives finds and incidents in Germany and across Europe, including in Romania, Italy, Poland, Bulgaria and the UK. A cache of weapons discovered recently in a Berlin forest are thought to be connected to Russian activities in Romania. Investigators in various countries are believed to be working in parallel with each other.

title: US and Iran exchange more airstrikes, fuelling fears of wider return to hostilities
summary: Attacks on Iran’s Revolutionary Guard and reprisals against US bases in Middle East quash hopes that flare-up last weekend was limited in nature
text: The US has launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets, prompting counter strikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Bahrain, Kuwait, Jordan and Iraq, and fuelling concerns about a ⁠wider renewal of hostilities. The US Marine Corps base Camp Titin in Jordan was targeted for an “intense ballistic missile attack”, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said early on Wednesday, according to Iranian news outlet Tasnim. The Jordanian army said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired from Iran, and did not confirm any injuries or hits on the US training camp located on the Gulf of Aqaba, near the borders with Israel and Saudi Arabia. Three other missiles landed in remote areas, it said. Missile and drone attacks were also reported in Kuwait, where the army said it was responding to Iranian hostilities. Agence France-Presse reporters in Bahrain heard alert sirens for airborne attacks go off early on Wednesday. The IRGC also claimed it struck a US base in Erbil, Iraq. US central command (CentCom) said it had completed a new wave of strikes that targeted the IRGC. It said the strikes were in response to attempted attacks on commercial shipping in the strait of Hormuz and against American service members. The Iranian Red Crescent said four people, including a child, were killed and more than 50 were wounded when shrapnel from a US missile attack hit a home where a wedding celebration was taking place in the city of Kuhestak. Asked if the US military had received any credible reports of civilian casualties, a US CentCom spokesperson, Capt Tim Hawkins, said “the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC”. Iran’s state broadcaster reported explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, on the northern side of the strait, and state-linked news agency Nour ‌News reported explosions in the port city of Bandar Abbas and in Chabahar, a port on the southern coast. Oil prices are already on the rise after an exchange of attacks by the US and Iran at the weekend, the first since July, and after reports that two tankers had been hit in the strait of Hormuz, the global oil supply waterway that Iran has effectively closed to shipping. Tehran warned ⁠that it would prevent oil being exported from the Gulf, despite a threat by Donald Trump to hit Iran “hard” in response to the Iranian strikes, and a warning from Scott Bessent, the US treasury secretary, that Washington was about to ⁠impose new sanctions. The six-month conflict had shifted into an economic standoff before the weekend strikes, in which US forces attacked Iran’s Larak Island on Sunday and Iran responded by launching missiles at two US airbases in Jordan. On Tuesday, Trump warned that if Iran retaliated against the US’s latest strikes, “they will be hit again at a much harder and higher level, but it will not be the biggest attack of them all, that is waiting in the wings and, when it is over, there will be very little left of the Islamic Republic of Iran”. The US president has in the past made threats that could amount to war crimes if carried out, including threatening to destroy critical civilian infrastructure, bomb Iran “back to the Stone Ages”, and an April threat that “a whole civilization will die tonight” if a peace deal wasn’t reached. In Iran, the Fars news agency quoted an IRGC spokesperson as saying the US “will regret its new attacks”. The IRGC later said it had begun a “regretful response to the aggressors”, state broadcaster IRIB reported. In its statement, the IRGC said that “in blind and desperate attacks”, the US had bombed several locations, including civilian areas. It described them as “attacks that tightened the blockade of the strait of Hormuz and strengthened the determination of the fighters to suppress the foreign forces interfering in the strait of Hormuz”. Recent pledges by both sides to respond to further attacks have highlighted how quickly a conflict that has increasingly been fought through sanctions, blockades and economic pressure could spill back into military action. Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, had said early on Tuesday that Tehran would reciprocate immediately if Washington honoured its commitments under a June memorandum of understanding (MOU) that was intended to halt the conflict. The MOU declared an end to fighting that has now killed thousands in Iran and Lebanon since US and Israeli strikes began on 28 February. But it also deferred many of the most difficult issues and paved the way for a broader 60-day negotiation period – which passed without further agreement. “I am stating clearly that if the US returns to its commitments under the ⁠memorandum of understanding, the Islamic Republic of Iran will immediately reciprocate,” Pezeshkian said in the Kyrgyz capital, Bishkek, at a summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, which includes Russia and China. But Iranian officials have shown no public sign of bowing to pressure. “If the enemy wants us not to export oil from the Persian Gulf, no one will be able to export oil,” Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker, was quoted as saying by Iranian media. If the US intensified its “siege”, he said Tehran would respond militarily. Esmaeil Baghaei, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson, told a press conference in Tehran that Washington was “addicted to making excessive demands and has mistaken negotiations for dictating terms”. “As long as they act in this manner, they will certainly get no result other than what they have achieved so far,” he added, warning that Tehran would “use all our capabilities, whether on the battlefield or through our diplomatic apparatus”. Reuters contributed reporting

title: Senator Ed Markey wins Massachusetts Democratic primary
summary: Incumbent, 80, beats back challenge from Seth Moulton, who argued Markey was too old to be effective at his job
text: Senator Ed Markey won the Democratic primary in Massachusetts on Tuesday, beating back a challenge from Seth Moulton, a congressman who tried to unseat him by arguing to voters his opponent was too old to be effective at his job. Massachusetts is heavily Democratic, making the senator favored to win a third full term in the November general election, where he faces the Republican nominee, John Deaton. The 80-year-old incumbent, according to the Associated Press, easily defeated his 47-year-old rival, at a moment when Democratic voters agonize over the age of some lawmakers, a concern that was amplified by Joe Biden’s disastrous re-election bid in 2024, and Kamala Harris’s subsequent failure to keep Donald Trump from returning to the White House. In primaries elsewhere in the country this year, Democratic voters unseated a handful of long-serving incumbents in favor of younger, progressive challengers who vowed to break from the party orthodoxy on issues like support for Israel. But the dynamics in Massachusetts were somewhat of a reversal, with Markey being a longtime advocate for progressive causes and Moulton, who was born after Markey was first elected to the House in 1976, staking out more moderate positions on certain issues. The senator is a champion of proposals to create a universal single-payer healthcare system and enact sweeping clean energy policies known as the “Green New Deal”, and had the backing of top congressional progressives, including the Vermont independent senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic senator Elizabeth Warren, also of Massachusetts. Moulton, who first won election to a north-eastern Massachusetts district in 2014, has not endorsed single-payer healthcare proposals, and shortly before Tuesday’s primary election apologized for saying that he did not want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete” – comments made after Trump beat Harris in the 2024 election in part by vowing to curb transgender rights. The question of when a lawmaker is too old to continue serving loomed large when the candidates met for a debate in August. “I think everyone watching this debate can see that I’m more energized than I’ve ever been before in my life. I am crisscrossing the state. I’m fighting for families,” the senator said. Moulton said his opponent had spent less time holding town halls and candidate forums, and pounced when the senator replied to a question about what AI tools he used by answering “whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad – whatever comes up”. “Senator, if you don’t even know what you’re using on your phone or your iPad, this is why we need a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies to make sure that they are safe,” Moulton said. In the days before the primary, polls showed Markey with a sizable lead over Moulton. In 2020, the senator had fended off a challenge from congressman Joe Kennedy III, a member of the state’s best-known political dynasty.

title: Ukraine war briefing: Russian sky full of our drones and not safe, Zelenskyy warns airlines
summary: Germany accuses Russia over Leipzig airport attack, citing solid evidence; Russian economy in risky ‘berserk mode’ says Putin development tsar. What we know on day 1,652
text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned airlines and passengers against using Russian airspace because it will be filled with Ukrainian drones for the duration of the war. “Today, we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who still uses Russia’s key airports: Russian airspace is becoming completely unsafe,” said Ukraine’s president. “Ukraine does not threaten civilian aviation as such – not a single civilian aircraft. There will simply be drones in Russia’s skies on a scale that has to be taken into account.” Vladimir Putin responded by calling Zelenskyy’s comments “a declaration of state terrorism”. Russia has started deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, Dan Sabbagh and Luke Harding write, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv. Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and surrounds. At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children. The railway has been a lifeline for Ukraine’s civilians in wartime, transporting millions and bringing world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham. The German government has concretely blamed Russia for the botched drone attack at Leipzig airport that unsuccessfully targeted a Ukrainian cargo plane, Kate Connolly writes from Berlin. Berlin said all indications were the Russian state provided the knowhow and equipment to “low-level agents” on the ground. Russia will face penalties – its consulate in Bonn will be closed, and Russian House, a purported cultural and science institute in Berlin, will be evicted after allegedly serving as a base for hybrid attacks and spying. A clampdown on Russia’s shadow fleet operations in German waters is planned. New blacklists of Russians would be drawn up and border controls tightened on Russians entering Germany, said the foreign minister, Johann Wadephul. The EU is preparing to toughen sanctions against Russia. The Russian wartime economy risks going “berserk”, Vladimir Putin’s ⁠international development envoy was quoted ⁠as saying on Tuesday. Boris Titov told business outlet RBC: “This is not an economy at all, it’s a kind of ‘berserk mode’ that can only exist for a ‌very limited time, and the necessity of which should be considered very carefully.” Titov’s ⁠comments echo a statement by Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, who argued that “killing a normal economy is equivalent to killing the whole country”. Andrei Klepach, the chief economist at the state development bank, lost his job last month after a public speech highlighting the economic challenges posed by the war. Ukraine ⁠damaged ⁠oil-processing units at ⁠Russia’s ⁠Novatek Ust-Luga ‌complex ‌in the Leningrad region during ‌an attack on Tuesday, ‌Kyiv’s military ⁠intelligence said. Key components of the oil refining facility and process equipment were damaged, said the GUR, and a major fire broke out. Russia attacked Ukraine’s Black Sea export infrastructure ⁠and a border crossing with Romania in the southern region of Odesa, Ukrainian officials said on Tuesday. Ukrainian state energy firm Naftogaz said Russia also damaged its Odesa combined heat ‌and power plant with missiles ‌and drones. Russia’s ⁠defence ⁠ministry said ⁠its forces struck ‌two ‌cargo ‌vessels in ‌the port of Pivdennyi, ⁠near Odesa, claiming they were carrying military goods. The claim could not be verified. David Petraeus has urged the UK to help lead a reinvention of Nato by adapting to a fundamental shift in warfare in the wake of the Ukraine war. The retired US army general and CIA ex-director told the House of Lords that Ukraine was the “defining military laboratory” of this century. Swift US technological advances in the defence sphere were not enough, Petraeus said, and nor was other nations simply purchasing better technology. He said Britain had shown “strategic clarity” after Russia’s full-scale invasion. “That now presents Britain with another opportunity: to become the first major western nation to organise its defence institutions around the new concept of warfare that Ukraine has been pioneering, and, in doing so, to help lead the transformation of Nato itself.” Russia’s presence at US-hosted G20 talks has caused unease among participants, the Canadian finance minister has said. Francois-Philippe Champagne said “it created discomfort, no doubt about that … The G7 has always been very united in our support for Ukraine and the Ukrainian people in the face of the illegal invasion and the suffering that we see.”

title: Federal judge tosses Trump lawsuit over trans athletes in California school sports
summary: Justice department cannot force state to ban trans girls from women’s sports, in major win for LGBTQ+ rights
text: A federal judge has dismissed the Trump administration’s lawsuit challenging California’s policy of allowing transgender youth to play on sports teams that match their gender, a major loss for Donald Trump and the Department of Justice. The justice department had been fighting for a year to force California to ban trans girls from women’s sports, with the president directly singling out one trans track and field athlete in online attacks and regularly mocking trans athletes in his speeches. Since 2013, California has allowed trans girls to play on girls’ teams in schools, an LGBTQ+-inclusive policy that affected a small fraction of the state’s youth. More than 20 states now have similar laws. California’s policy sparked minimal controversy for years until Republicans and anti-LGBTQ+ groups across the US made attacks on trans people a central part of their campaigns in recent election cycles. In July 2025, the Trump administration sued California, alleging that its trans-inclusive sports policies violated Title IX, the federal law prohibiting sex discrimination in schools. The lawsuit focused on five trans girls who played sports, accusing them of taking opportunities away from other girls. The justice department argued California was obligated to ban trans girls from girls’ teams while the state’s schools received federal funding. On Monday, US judge Cynthia Valenzuela issued a major victory for California and trans rights, with a final order dismissing the justice department’s suit and terminating the case. The judge argued that the US government failed to give notice to the state that its federal funding was contingent on schools banning trans girls from sports. The ruling noted the federal government has repeatedly shifted its guidelines on this issue over the last decade. Although Trump issued an executive order last year calling for trans girls to be blocked from girls’ sports, the judge said that order did not constitute clear notice to California that it would lose funding if it maintained trans-inclusive policies. The ruling came two months after the US supreme court’s conservative supermajority upheld Republican-backed laws in West Virginia and Idaho that barred trans girls from girls’ teams. Valenzuela noted the supreme court decision was narrow, with the justices concluding that those states could maintain their anti-trans laws, without saying every school must adopt similar restrictions. The supreme court’s ruling did not call for a national ban on trans youth athletes nor did it address the question of whether Title IX permits trans girls to play on girls’ teams. A justice department spokesperson said on Tuesday it was “evaluating our options for appeal”, writing in an email: “We are disappointed by the Court’s order and remain committed to enforcing President Trump’s agenda preventing boys from playing in girls’ sports.” The California Interscholastic Federation, which oversees school sports and was the target of the lawsuit, declined to comment. California officials noted last year that out of the state’s nearly 6 million students in the K-12 public school system, it was estimated that there were fewer than 10 trans student-athletes actively participating in sports. But youth targeted by the lawsuit and the Trump administration’s policy attacks have said the impact has been severe, with out trans students facing harassment at games and death threats. Rainbow Families Action, a California group supporting trans youth, celebrated the ruling, saying: “This lifts a significant shadow that has been hanging over the joyous and expanding success story of girls’ and women’s sports in California.” The group said the ruling sent a clear message that schools across the state must allow trans youth to continue playing on the teams that match their gender, noting school districts had been facing pressure over the last year to “defy California law and to pass illegal and harmful policies that comply in advance with [Trump’s] discriminatory executive orders that hurt transgender children”. Trevor Norcross, father of a trans youth athlete targeted by the justice department lawsuit, said the ruling was an “acknowledgment that the Trump administration has been overreaching since the beginning of his term”. He said he hoped the decision would help support trans youth athletes across the country: “While this is a great victory in California … the fight is not over in other states.”

title: US officials defend Venezuela oil deal amid questions over rebuilding plan
summary: Government talks up pact but Venezuelan opposition alarmed that democracy yet to return after Maduro exit
text: Trump administration officials on Tuesday defended a highly contentious deal giving the US control of a significant chunk of Venezuelan oil reserves, arguing that the sweeping agreement would help stabilize and rebuild democracy in the shattered South American country while giving Washington vital access to strategic crude reserves. Last week, Donald Trump announced a “groundbreaking” deal that would give the US “majority” control over 65bn barrels – roughly one-fifth – of Venezuela’s oil reserves. On Tuesday, US officials argued that the agreement would create a stable economic platform to restore Venezuelan democracy after nearly three decades of autocratic rule under former president Nicolás Maduro and his predecessor, Hugo Chávez. But the pact, forged after months of secret talks, has provoked outrage among Venezuela’s opposition, already furious that democracy has still to return to the country eight months after the removal of Maduro by US special forces. “They are inheriting a government that is generating revenue that can be used to rebuild that country,” a US official said during a conference call with journalists on Tuesday. According to a White House fact sheet released on Monday, the agreement granted the US-backed North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep) 100-year ‌rights over 17 oil fields in what it touted as “the biggest oil deal in world history”. On Tuesday, a US official said allowing Nabep, which is owned by the controversial Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, to take over several oil fields would provide capital to “ramp up production rapidly”. “That in turn will generate royalty revenue for the government – initially, the interim government for the time being – but ultimately for the republic, for the democratic elected government,” the official said. “We can hand over a more stable Venezuela. But no matter what, a democratically elected Venezuela is still going to face challenges after 20 somewhat years of the disaster of Chavismo [the leftist ideology promoted by Chávez] and Maduro after the country was dismantled from the inside out, and it needs to be rebuilt. “That’s going to take time. You don’t reverse 20 years of corruption, 20 years of kleptocracy, 20 years of no democracy, no freedom.” The justification for the takeover of 17 oil fields previously controlled by Chinese and Russian companies came as Trump met oil refinery executives to discuss ways of converting crude into petrol and lowering prices for motorists at the pumps. Chris Wright, the energy secretary, was due to fly to Caracas, the Venezuelan capital, on Tuesday to follow up last week’s deal, which Trump has hailed as “a historic transaction” to fill the US’s strategic oil reserves. The oil deal has been given added urgency by Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran last February, which has caused fuel prices to soar after the Iranian forces retaliated by closing the strait of Hormuz, previously a passageway for 20% of the world’s oil supplies. Petrol prices now average about $4.10 a gallon compared with under $3 before the war started. Increased petrol prices have filtered into the rest of the economy and led to significant drops in Trump’s popularity, with polls showing a majority of voters disapproving of his handling of the war and the economy. The economic outlook formed the backdrop to the oil deal with Venezuela, first announced last Friday. The agreement was backed by Venezuela’s national assembly – dominated by the ruling United Socialist party – on Tuesday after the country’s president, Delcy Rodríguez, defended it at the weekend. “The benefits are endless,” claimed Rodríguez, a former vice-president whom Trump backed after ordering Maduro’s capture. Opposition critics have complained that the Trump administration has made no attempt to promote a transformation to democracy or stage new elections since Maduro was detained by US forces and taken to New York to face criminal charges after a raid on his Caracas residence in January. Instead, the White House has chosen to work with Rodríguez, despite her past vocal hostility to the US and previous roles in anti-opposition crackdowns in a regime that Washington believes has stolen recent elections. The official said talks between the Venezuelan government and the opposition were set to resume later this month. “The last thing we want to see is a new democratic elected government inherit a country in crisis,” he said. Joseph Gedeon contributed reporting

title: Accused Charlie Kirk killer must stand trial and is eligible for death penalty, judge rules
summary: Suspect Tyler Robinson to be tried for aggravated murder, felony charge that carries death penalty sentence in Utah
text: A Utah judge ruled Tuesday that the man accused of killing Charlie Kirk must stand trial for aggravated murder, a felony charge that makes him eligible for the death penalty if convicted. After several hours of closing arguments in Provo, Utah, judge Tony Graf ruled there is sufficient evidence to try Tyler Robinson, 23, who has been charged with the murder of one of the US right’s most prominent figures. Robinson pleaded not guilty after Graf’s ruling. A trial date has yet to be set. A key factor in charging aggravated murder is whether the shooter knowingly created a risk of death to anyone else as he carried out the killing. Judge Graf said: “These circumstances support a reasonable inference that defendant was aware that other individuals were positioned near Mr Kirk when he fired.” Robinson’s attorneys had argued the shooting should not be a capital offense, as the shooter hit the “intended target” and did not put anyone else’s life at risk. Graf had the option to send the case to trial on a lesser charge of murder, which carries a minimum sentence of 15 years and a maximum of life in prison, said Steve Burton, director of the Utah Defense Attorney Association. Kirk was fatally shot while speaking during an event at Utah Valley University nearly a year ago. The proceedings began Tuesday morning with Graf moving to allow cameras in the courtroom during the hearing, despite objections from the defense, and ruling on how the prosecution’s exhibits will be displayed. The judge also warned the audience of people attending the hearing not to make comments or visible reactions while court was in session. Prosecutors have accused the former ‌electrical apprentice of firing the single shot that killed Kirk, 31, as he debated with students at the Utah Valley University campus in Orem on 10 September 2025. On Tuesday, the prosecution argued there is a “mountain of evidence that proves [Robinson] is the shooter” and showed video of Robinson on campus the day of the shooting. Tuesday’s proceedings follow a weeklong preliminary hearing in July that was attended by Kirk’s widow, Erika Kirk. She attended Tuesday’s session. During the preliminary hearing, prosecutors presented what they called “overwhelming” evidence, including test results that allegedly show Robinson’s DNA on ‌the murder weapon. Robinson’s lawyers questioned the prosecution’s DNA testing and said police failed to investigate evidence someone else might have carried out the killing.
