That argument could bolster the prosecution as it pursues the death penalty. Defense lawyers have said there is no evidence Robinson disagreed with Kirk’s political views. Kirk, the co-founder of Turning ‌Point USA, helped build support for Donald Trump among young voters and aided Republican voter turnout efforts. At a memorial following Kirk’s shooting, Erika Kirk, who became CEO and board chair of Turning Point USA after her husband’s death, said she forgave the alleged shooter. She has not commented on the death penalty charge.

title: Fund defence spending from tax rise on middle earners, thinktank tells Healey
summary: Resolution Foundation argues that UK’s internationally low ‘tax wedge’ must rise to pay for defence ambitions
text: The chancellor, John Healey, must be prepared to raise taxes for middle earners if he wants to fund significantly higher defence spending, the Resolution Foundation thinktank has said. Healey resigned from Keir Starmer’s government in June, protesting against what he argued was the then prime minister’s failure to adequately fund defence. But in his new post in No 11 Downing Street, Healey has made clear that he will wait until next year’s spending review before presenting a plan to meet Labour’s pledge of devoting 3.5% of GDP to defence by 2035. In a new report, entitled Thin End of the Wedge, economists at the Resolution Foundation suggest he will not be able to raise the £28bn a year it would take to meet that promise without asking average workers to pay more. They say that despite historically large tax rises since Labour came to power in 2024, amounting to £70bn a year, the “tax wedge” – taxes on earnings, minus benefits – remains low by international standards. “Despite recent increases, the UK still taxes average earners less than most of our international peers,” says the foundation’s chief economist, James Smith. The analysis shows that tax rises under Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, resulted in a 2.4 percentage point jump in the tax wedge last year – the largest for any country in the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Yet at 32.4% for a single earner on average pay, it remains below the average for the OECD and the G7 major economies, they say. When the economists looked at countries with higher public spending, they found these tended to ask their average workers to contribute more – instead of relying on business or wealth taxes, for example. “No other OECD rich country has a bigger state and a lower burden on average workers, so any politician promising both is not being realistic,” Smith said. “There is a strong case that any benefits of increased defence spending will be broadly shared, so the tax rises needed to find this should be too, including higher rates on middle earners.” The tax wedge on a worker paid the median salary, of £33,000 as at April last year, is also low by historic standards, they argue – and is still below the level before the global financial crisis in 2008. In Reeves’s two tax-raising budgets before she was sacked by Andy Burnham, the biggest revenue-raisers were employer national insurance contributions and fiscal drag – where income tax thresholds were left unchanged, so that more people end up paying higher rates. She was constrained by Labour’s pre-election promise not to increase the rates of income tax, VAT or employee national insurance – which Burnham has promised to stick to. As well as the longer-term defence pledge, Burnham’s government faces pressure to do more to cushion households against rising energy bills over the coming winter, and to beef up efforts to help unemployed young people into work. Healey will present his first budget on 28 October and needs to find approximately £1.4bn a year over the next three years to pay for Starmer’s defence investment plan – which Healey in his last job derided as inadequate.

title: British aid worker mistakenly identified as a survivor of Nepal-Tibet disaster
summary: More than 1,000 people confirmed dead and more than 4,000, including 36 British nationals, remain missing
text: A British aid worker was mistakenly identified by Nepalese authorities as a rescued survivor after returning to Kathmandu on a humanitarian aid flight. Alastair Chambers, a 45-year-old former Gloucester councillor, said he flew to Nepal last week to distribute sleeping bags, food and essentials to communities cut off by collapsed bridges. After spending several days in a village near the Trishuli river in central Nepal, Chambers returned by helicopter to the capital, where he was greeted by police officers asking for his details. “I gave them my details, just abiding by the rules, and they obviously thought that I’d been rescued,” Chambers told the Press Association. Chambers appeared on a list of 119 names released by local authorities on Tuesday. An army spokesperson then told reporters at a press conference that a British national was among those rescued. “I was contacted by about 15 different journalists in the last few hours, just asking how I was and how I’m feeling after being rescued, and I had to say: ‘Well sorry, I haven’t been rescued,’” Chambers told PA. Those rescued included 118 Nepali nationals – 44 women and 74 men. Thirty-six British nationals are missing, the Foreign Office minister, Stewart Wood, told the House of Lords on Tuesday. The figure had previously been put at 33. Chambers was fined £49,000 after pleading guilty in June 2022 to breeding and selling dogs without a licence. The 45-year-old, who was the leader of a group of community independents on Gloucester city council until 2024, is due to face trial in November after denying he used homophobic slurs against a bar owner and former council worker. At least 1,050 people have been confirmed dead in Nepal since Wednesday’s flash floods, while Chinese state media said 66 people had been killed in Tibet. More than 4,000 people are still missing. Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region. This included 330 foreign nationals, the Nepalese tourist board said in an update on Tuesday. Preliminary analysis of satellite imagery suggests the collapse of a glacier high in the Himalayas was the primary cause of the disaster. The collapse – so large it was initially recorded as a magnitude-4.4 earthquake – triggered a deadly torrent of water, mud and ice that tore along the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers on Wednesday. Crews have faced dangerous and difficult conditions while searching unstable terrain and flood debris. Search efforts are now focused on attempts to reach about 600 workers believed to be trapped inside tunnels at several hydropower stations in the region. “Massive work has been going on in the tunnel, all the tunnels,” the army spokesperson said on Tuesday. A rapid deployment rescue team from the UK arrived in Nepal on Saturday to provide support for Britons and their families as part of the government’s £5m commitment to support relief and recovery efforts. The Red Cross estimates that 93,000 people have been directly affected by the disaster. • This article was amended on 1 September 2026. Due to information provided, an earlier version said that a British man had been rescued after the deadly floods in Nepal. In fact, he was Alastair Chambers, a British aid worker, who had flown out to help last week.

title: Trump homeland security chief says ICE agents could be sent to polling places
summary: Markwayne Mullin says officers could be deployed ‘if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant’
text: The US homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, on Tuesday said that federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers could be deployed to polling sites across the country. Speaking to reporters in New York, Mullin said: “ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places. We’re there to enforce specific threats.” For months, Democrats and voting rights groups have warned that the Trump administration might attempt to deploy federal agents to polling locations in an effort to intimidate voters and depress turnout ahead of the November midterm elections. Although the White House has downplayed such suggestions, Donald Trump has declined to rule it out while continuing to sow doubt about the integrity of past – and future – US elections. “The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. That’s their job … if we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be.” Federal law prohibits military personnel or other “armed” agents from being “at any place where a general or special election is held”. In a separate statement to Politico, the homeland security department said: “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.” The Guardian has contacted the DHS for additional comment. Mullin’s latest comments follow statements he made in July, when he threatened to withhold federal aid from states that refused to comply with homeland security election directives as part of the administration’s crackdown on what it alleges is widespread voter fraud. “We will scrub all election records, looking for illegal aliens and those who are ineligible to vote, including those that somehow voted, yet they were deceased,” Mullin said earlier this summer, adding: “If states want the grant funding, to recap, they must secure the election.” Yet experts say the administration has failed to offer any proof for its claims of non-citizen voting. In one instance, the DHS officials claimed that there may have been as many as 16,000 non-citizens registered to vote in Nevada, but later admitted they could confirm that only 185 of those people were actually non-citizens, according to records obtained by the Guardian. Meanwhile, Dan Caine, chair of the joint chiefs of staff, recently wrote in a letter that the US military had no plans to deploy troops to polling sites during the upcoming November midterm elections. Caine’s letter came in response to a request for information from Senator Elissa Slotkin amid concerns that the Trump administration could send US military personnel to patrol polling sites. In his letter to Slotkin, Caine said: “The joint force has no plans to send federal military personnel or federalized members of the national guard to polling places during the 2026 elections.” He added that there were “no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material”.

title: Democrats warn of ‘hollowed out’ leadership after army chief resigns amid clashes with Hegseth
summary: Sudden departure of Daniel Driscoll comes after Pentagon chief removed senior officers and blocked promotions, prompting warnings of a leadership crisis
text: A senior Senate Democrat accused Pentagon secretary Pete Hegseth of having “hollowed out” the army’s senior ranks after its top civilian leader resigned after months of internal clashes with Hegseth. No official reason was given for army secretary Daniel Driscoll’s departure after 18 months on the job, while thousands of US soldiers are deployed in the Middle East. In a statement on Monday night, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said Driscoll had been “highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda”, citing his work on “readiness and lethality” and his role in Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Democrats and Republicans alike praised Driscoll’s leadership, and, in a statement, the Democratic senator Jack Reed, the ranking member on the Senate armed services committee, said he did “not welcome” Driscoll’s resignation. “It is far past time for President Trump to recognize the lasting harm that Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense,” Reed said. “In the Army alone, he has fired and blocked the promotions of dozens of senior officers without explanation, including Army Chief of Staff General Randy George and half of all four-star generals. “Secretary Hegseth is cultivating a culture where dissent is punished and competence is secondary to personal allegiance.” An army official told CBS News that Driscoll spoke with Trump about the “current state” of the army before submitting his resignation. NBC News, citing a source familiar with the matter, reported that in that conversation Driscoll raised concerns about the army’s transformation and readiness and about Hegseth’s blocking those efforts by firing the generals responsible for them. The public rupture traces back to April, when Hegseth forced out the army’s chief of staff, Gen Randy George, along with two other senior officers. George had worked with Driscoll on the army transformation initiative, an effort to shift the service toward drones and faster weapons acquisition based on lessons from the war in Ukraine. Driscoll later told Congress he considered George “a transformational leader” and said he went to George’s house the day he learned of the firing. Driscoll sought the help of JD Vance, a friend since law school, as tensions with Hegseth deteriorated, the Washington Post reported. Driscoll also told the Post then that he had no plans to leave his post. “I have no plans to depart or resign as the secretary of the army,” he said. Since George’s departure, the army has moved to scale back a drone unit he and Driscoll had championed, returning it to a conventional infantry role, CBS has reported. Hegseth also removed four army colonels from consideration for promotion to brigadier general, over objections from Driscoll and George. Driscoll’s exit adds to a string of senior departures under Hegseth, including navy secretary John Phelan, Southern Command chief Adm Alvin Holsey, and Gen Chris Donahue, who commanded US army forces in Europe and Africa. Sean Parnell, Hegseth’s chief spokesperson, had privately expressed interest in the army secretary post before it became vacant, the Hill has reported, and is among those reportedly under consideration to succeed Driscoll. “The Pentagon right now is in some cases rudderless, without leadership at the senior rungs of the uniform offices and even in the civilian offices,” Representative Jason Crow, a Democrat and former army ranger who serves on the House armed services committee, told reporters. “I’m gravely concerned about it.” Driscoll, an Iraq war veteran who worked in finance and technology before joining the administration, also served as a Trump-appointed negotiator in talks to end the Russian war on Ukraine. Neither the White House nor the Pentagon has said what Driscoll told Trump in their final conversation or how the president responded.

title: Cleveland police to get £2m extra to tackle serious crime in Middlesbrough
summary: Cash announced after horror car crash that killed two police officers and house fire in which woman and young girl died
text: Cleveland’s police force is to receive a £2m funding boost to tackle serious crime, after the home secretary said successive high-profile tragedies in the Middlesbrough area had led to a “sense of disquiet” in the community. Shabana Mahmood and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, paid tribute in parliament on Tuesday to police constables Matthew Blades and Tom Clough, who were killed when a Volkswagen Passat travelling on the wrong side of the A66 dual carriageway collided head-on with their marked response vehicle. Five young men travelling in the Passat, which had earlier been pursued by different police, also died in the 22 August incident. Cleveland police said the five occupants – Cole Worthy, 17, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, Michael Robert Cahill, 23, and Jakub Matusiak, 23 – may have had links to “serious organised criminal activity”. Officers from outside the area have been deployed to Cleveland after the crash. Mahmood told the House of Commons on Tuesday that she had given her “full backing” to the investigation, making the £2m pledge to fight “both serious crime and its causes”. The funding is separate to real-term budget increases for all police forces, which will see Cleveland police receive an additional £7m compared with last year, she said. The home secretary said Cleveland police were also investigating the house fire in Grangetown that killed Natalie McDonald, 34, and her niece Valentina Foster, 7, and injured four others on 26 August. Investigators were not treating the fire and the A66 crash – which occurred within a mile of each other – as connected, Mahmood said. “However, it has undoubtedly added to the sense of disquiet in a community already reeling from the earlier tragedy,” she said. “I recognise how unnerving it will have been for law-abiding citizens, both in the affected areas and beyond, to see a spate of incidents occurring in close proximity and quick succession.” Cleveland police and crime commissioner Matt Storey said the £2m funding boost would help deal with the immediate aftermath of the incidents, but would not address the “chronic underfunding” of the force. “A one-off payment is not a solution,” Storey said. “It fails to tackle the deep-rooted funding inequalities that continue to disadvantage the hard-working officers, staff and communities of Cleveland.” Storey said the force needed at least £20m every year to recruit 200 more police officers and strengthen efforts to crack down on serious organised crime. The funding announcement came after a 23-year-old man appeared in court on murder charges over the deaths of McDonald and Foster. Jaden Wright, of no fixed address, appeared before Teesside magistrates court on Tuesday for a hearing that lasted less than two minutes. Wright briefly greeted his solicitor as he was brought into the dock before he was remanded in custody to appear at Teesside crown court on Thursday. The court clerk outlined that he faces two murder charges, two counts of grievous bodily harm with intent and two charges of attempted grievous bodily harm with intent. The charges relate to the six people who were in the house, two of whom cannot be identified by the media due to their age. The clerk said Wright faced a separate charge of intentional strangulation over an incident said to have happened on the day before the fire. Cleveland police said on Friday that a 48-year-old woman was in the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle in a “critical but stable” condition after the fire, and a 27-year-old man was at James Cook university hospital in Middlesbrough receiving treatment. Two teenage girls were discharged after sustaining non-life-threatening injuries. Katie Smith, the senior investigating officer from Northumbria police, said: “This has been a truly tragic incident and my thoughts remain with the families of all those involved. “I would like to thank local residents for their support and patience during this complex investigation. Anyone who may still have information, or has any concerns, can still submit information using the major incident public portal.” Katie Nicholson, the chief crown prosecutor for CPS North East, said: “Our prosecutors have worked closely with Cleveland police to establish that there is sufficient evidence to bring this case to court. “We remind all concerned that proceedings against the defendant are active and he has the right to a fair trial. It is vital that there should be no reporting, commentary or sharing of information which could in anyway prejudice these proceedings.” A 31-year-old man who was also arrested in connection with the case was released without charge on Sunday.

text: A corporate vice-president at Bank of America was killed in a stabbing in New York City’s Times Square, the second-biggest US lending bank ⁠said on Tuesday about a ⁠random incident that took place in broad daylight in the bustling heart of Manhattan. The incident had brought the streets of the crowded area to a halt on Monday as emergency vehicles swarmed between the skyscrapers. The ⁠deceased was Erin Piacenti, 32, according to the New York City police department (NYPD). Bank of America confirmed the loss of a staff member. Piacenti was a vice-⁠president in the bank’s business selection and conflicts unit, according to her LinkedIn profile. “We are shocked and deeply saddened by the tragic loss of our colleague. She was a valued teammate who will be greatly missed. ‌Our hearts go out to her ‌family and all of her loved ones,” the US banking company said in a statement on Tuesday. Bank of America’s Manhattan office ‌is located a stone’s throw from Times Square, at One Bryant Park. Piacenti had earned a law degree from Fordham Law School, graduating in 2021 alongside her husband, Frank, according to the school. Fordham Law said in a statement it was heartbroken by her death. An unnamed 68-year-old man also suffered stab wounds in the attack and was in stable condition, the NYPD said in a statement. Jessica Tisch, the NYPD’s commissioner, said Monday afternoon’s attack near West 42nd Street and Seventh Avenue, appeared to be random and unprovoked. The NYPD said when officers arrived on the scene they found Pamela Cisneros, a 49-year-old woman, who was brandishing two large knives and advanced toward ‌officers, who used a stun gun but were unable to persuade her to drop the weapons. Officers shot Cisneros and she was later pronounced dead. Tisch said Cisneros had a documented mental health history. Matthew Koder, Bank of America’s president of global corporate and investment banking, described Piacenti as a “cherished teammate and friend” in an internal memo seen by Reuters. “Erin was a valued member of the Business Selection and Conflicts team, having joined the bank 18 months ago,” Koder wrote. “Her loss is being felt deeply by many.” Koder said that Bank of America’s security teams were “fully engaged in supporting the police investigation here, and in addressing the ongoing safety and security of our offices and teammates”. Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Deported Milo Yiannopoulos says he is ‘ashamed’ of support for Trump
summary: British far-right pundit breaks silence on ICE arrest and deportation and says he was ‘really, really terrified’
text: Milo Yiannopoulos, the British far-right commentator who was arrested last week by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers in Louisiana and deported to the United Kingdom, has broken his silence about the experience, saying that “for the first time I know what it feels like to be really, really terrified”. Yiannopoulos on Tuesday appeared on Piers Morgan Uncensored, a YouTube show presented by Piers Morgan, the British broadcaster and media personality. Yiannopoulos, 41, described the experience in the US as “humiliating and disorientating”, “physically degrading” and “frightening”. He also said that he was “ashamed” of his previous support for Donald Trump, who has pursued an agenda of mass deportation throughout his second presidency. “I didn’t really understand the physical reality of how institutionalized the brutality is in America,” he said. “It’s like everybody that’s arrested is an MS-13 gang member, and it hurts a lot more than it looks like on television.” His remarks came just days after he was deported from the US, after being arrested on Thursday by ICE officers at the New Orleans airport. In a statement last week, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), the parent agency of ICE, said Yiannopoulos had “legally entered the country” in May 2019, but “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”. Yiannopoulos was an early supporter of Trump before Trump first became US president in 2016. He is a former editor of Breitbart News and later worked to help the rapper Ye, formerly known as Kanye West, explore a presidential run in 2024. The homeland security department said Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”. In the Piers Morgan interview, Yiannopoulos disputed the government’s account and denied previously overstaying a visa. He said he is married to an American, and claimed he held a green card that he was “renewing on a two-year basis”. The Guardian has contacted homeland security and the White House for comment on Yiannopoulos’s remarks. Yiannopoulos also said that while he was detained, “no one would tell me anything” – a common complaint from people held in ICE custody. “I don’t think I’ve ever been frightened like that before,” he told Morgan. “I think maybe in the past I’ve been a little bit blasé when people talked about their trauma, a little bit cavalier when people talked about stuff kind of lingering with them, but I get it now … I wouldn’t wish it on anyone.” Last year, in posts on social media, Yiannopoulos had been supportive of Trump’s crackdown on immigration. In one post, he wrote: “There is one concrete thing we must insist on this administration delivering. It matters a lot more than debts measured in imaginary money. We have got to deport millions and millions and millions of people. Without that, nothing else matters.” In another post, Yiannopoulos said that California “needs ICE checkpoints at supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersections and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”. During Tuesday’s interview, Yiannopoulos said of his past support for Trump: “If I had any clue that anything remotely like this was even possible, I would never have gotten involved in supporting Trump in the first place and I’m very ashamed that I did.”

title: Democratic contender Abdul El-Sayed hits back at JD Vance over ‘evil’ taunt
summary: Michigan Senate candidate accuses vice-president of ‘dog whistle’ and says Republican policies are true evil
text: Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic US Senate candidate in Michigan, has hit back at JD Vance’s onslaught against him, saying it is “evil” to deprive people of healthcare and affordable groceries. The Republican vice-president, in a Monday speech that railed against undocumented immigrants, cast El-Sayed as representative of “terrible evil” and as someone who fights for “one group at the expense of others”. El-Sayed, who would become the first Muslim US senator if he wins in November, accused Vance of a “dog whistle” at the Islamophobic attacks he has faced throughout his campaign. While Vance did not directly invoke El-Sayed’s religion during his speech in Sterling Heights, Michigan, the vice-president warned: “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil. And on the rise in the United States of America today.” El-Sayed retorted in a statement: “Evil is ripping healthcare away from working people in exchange for tax breaks for billionaires. Evil is making people pay more for groceries and gas while pushing for trade wars and actual war. Evil is dividing people for your own gain. Evil is selling out your morals for a little bit of power.” In his speech, Vance repeatedly claimed that El-Sayed prioritized his ethnic group over others, and called attention to comments El-Sayed made after the attack on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan, earlier this year, where a man rammed a truck filled with gas and fireworks into a synagogue with families inside. As part of his initial response to the attack, El-Sayed noted the attacker had lost family members in an airstrike in Lebanon, saying “hurt people hurt people”. El-Sayed recently said he “made a mistake” and should have issued a statement that solely condemned the attack. Vance said in his speech: “When you have people who start to say my ethnic group deserves something and yours doesn’t, or that ethnic group is good and this other ethnic group is bad, that is how you erode the very foundations of commonality and common citizenship that we need to continue to have the United States be the most powerful and prosperous nation anywhere in the world.” Vance also told El-Sayed to “keep my wife’s name the hell out of your mouth, because she’s way out of your league”. The jab was in response to comments El-Sayed had made about Vance’s family, after the vice-president said in an Ohio speech he would struggle to go back in time and explain the modern Democratic party to his late grandfather, whom he called “Papaw”. In those remarks, Vance baselessly accused El-Sayed of wanting to impose sharia law. After Vance’s comments about Papaw, El- Sayed wrote on X: “So do we think JD is taking [his wife] Usha with him back in time to meet Papaw, or no?” Rightwing commentators called the post racist, and said it was out of bounds to bring up spouses. Usha Vance, who is Indian American, told Fox News that although she had not met her husband’s grandparents, she said Vance’s family was loving to her, and she believed his grandparents would have been loving toward her as well. El-Sayed told CNN on Monday night he would “rather not talk about spouses at all”. But he said he brought up Usha Vance because JD Vance’s political philosophy relies on an idea that some people are “more American” than others. He asked why Vance would invoke his grandfather unless it was to hark back to a time when people like El-Sayed were “less than normal” in American politics. Last month, Trump posted a photo of El-Sayed and his wife alongside one of Trump and his wife, which El-Sayed said was an attempt “to highlight the fact that my wife wears a hijab, as if to make an argument that that’s somehow less American”. Trump used El-Sayed’s full name, which Republicans have done to call attention to his ethnicity and religion, and wrote “two VERY DIFFERENT America’s [sic]”. El-Sayed told CNN: “I believe in an America where any of us – me, his wife, any of us with different color skin or who pray different ways – can be just as American as JD and his Papaw, but he’s not making that argument. “He [Vance] likes to dog-whistle about these things, but when you actually call him out on it, he acts like he would never bring anything like that into our political conversation, despite him and his boss doing that every single day.” The escalating attacks come as Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee, seeks to appeal to moderate Democrats and Jewish Americans following a bruising primary that saw El-Sayed narrowly defeat the pro-Israel congresswoman Haley Stevens. In closing his speech, Vance called on Michigan voters to “reject” El-Sayed, saying he “defends literal terrorism”. Vance urged people to vote for Rogers. “I’m asking you to send the crazy people to the curb, send a message to the elected leadership of the Democratic party that if you want us to vote for you, you’ve got to stop sending us crazy people to represent your party,” Vance said. El-Sayed referred to Vance and Rogers as “sock puppets from Ohio and Florida”, a reference to Vance’s home state and Rogers’ residence in Florida. He said: “We understand what’s at stake, and Michiganders will show you at the ballot box this November when we send Mike Rogers packing.”

title: Peekaboo island: the floating forest confounding nature watchers in western Canada
summary: A 150-metre-long island appeared from nowhere on Williston Lake, British Columbia; vanished, then reappeared 20 miles away
text: A thickly forested island appeared mysteriously on a western Canadian lake. Nearly 150 metres (500 feet) long and 75 metres (250 feet) wide, the land mass took local people and experts by surprise. It wasn’t on any maps or navigation charts. One boater approached and took a video of the island, capturing nearly 100 trees undulating in the chop of the lake. And then, within days, it disappeared. On Monday, the island made its second appearance – nearly 20 miles from its location earlier in August – in stunning aquatic displacement that has left residents wondering how an entire island can seem to simply vanish. The mystery has unfolded in the middle of Williston Lake, a long and narrow reservoir created after the W.A.C Bennett dam flooded the region in the early 1970s. At nearly 1,700 sq km (650 sqmiles) it is the largest body of freshwater in the westernmost province. Bob Gammer, a spokesperson for BC Hydro, the government-owned utility that operates the reservoir and dam, said the island was “quite something and rather unbelievable” when he first saw the images. “In the days of AI, you really needed another form of verification or evidence like a corroborating eyewitness account,” he said. “And soon, we got that.” Satellite imagery confirmed the island was in fact real, and floating in the main body of the reservoir, roughly 60 miles west of the dam. BC Hydro believes the island is the result of years of trees and plants growing largely undisturbed on the woody debris along sheltered sections of the reservoir’s shoreline. Similar islands have shown up across the globe, including Wisconsin’s famed Forty Acre Bog. The giant, floating island on Lake Chippewa is knitted together by peat, mud, roots and trees. Measuring roughly 12,000 sq metres (14,000 sq yards) in size, the British Columbia island is also bursting with life: birds and small animals are living among the mix of coniferous and broadleaf trees. Observers suspect the root system in the water hides some of the lake’s best fish. Gammer likened the growing conditions to hydroponics and said: “Well-fed trees growing on a decaying food source with lots of water … they could grow pretty quick.” The reservoir, he added, is higher than it has been in 14 years, as a result of high winter snowpacks and consistent summer rains that have raised water levels in the Peace River and the lake. “Suddenly, there are all of the right conditions to potentially lift this kind of little island from where it was, and bring it out into open water,” he said. Between sightings, the island may have drifted to shore. Its seeming disappearance “doesn’t mean it’s gone to the bottom of the reservoir”, Gammer previously told CBC. “It may have returned to a more sheltered area along the shoreline.” BC Hydro doesn’t know how old the trees on the island are, but with the right conditions the forest could “just stay there for years” and grow. Local people speculated the trees could be decades old. “It’s not like they’re just a bunch of little shrubs. This is an island with larger trees and it’s something you really have to wrap your mind around,” said Grammar. “It’s not an everyday thing. This is really really unusual.” Rocky Avery, a friend of the boater and a longtime resident of the area who first posted the clip to social media to warn others about a possible hazard, said he would “totally jump on that island if I could”. “It’s probably a bit shaky on the outer sections, but with those huge trees in the centre, I imagine someone could walk on it,” he said. Gammer cautioned boaters from attempting to become the first to set foot on it, warning that video shows trees moving back and forth on a “delicate, thin layer of logs”, adding it is “very unsafe” and “very unstable”. Avery’s social media posts about the island prompted a flurry of excitement and a seemingly inescapable nod to the current political situation in Canada. Recently, the US president, Donald Trump, chose to rename Lake Ontario after trade talks collapsed between the two countries. The announcement has prompted anger, frustration and mockery from the Canadian public. “I’m surprised Trump hasn’t named [the island] and claimed it,” commented one user on Avery’s post.

title: Tucson police investigate deadly shooting outside gay bar as hate crime
summary: Two people shot dead and suspect later died in hospital after shooting in parking lot of Venture-N bar
text: Authorities in Tucson, Arizona, are investigating a shooting outside a gay bar that left three people dead as a possible hate crime. The shooting occurred shortly after midnight on Monday in the parking lot of Venture-N, according to Tucson police. The suspect, identified by police as 44-year-old Ousman Ceesay, allegedly killed 42-year-old Vincent Anthony Siqueiros and 33-year-old Cameron Davis Capara. Tucson police said Ceesay, who had suffered gunshot wounds, later died after being transported to a local hospital. In a news release, Tucson police said: “Initial evidence suggests that the suspect confronted the victims in the parking lot of the business. “After confronting Mr Siqueiros and Mr Capara, the suspect shot them. There is no known active threat to the community. The suspect was in possession of a note with several LGBTQIA+ associated businesses written on it. “The Tucson police department is currently investigating this homicide as a hate crime. The investigation remains active and ongoing.” Tucson police chief Monica Prieto said in a statement: “We recognize this incident may cause fear and pain within our community. Tucson is, and always has been, a diverse community where people of different backgrounds, identities and experiences call this city home. We are committed to ensuring every member of our community feels safe, valued and welcomed.” Speaking to the Tucson Sentinel, Tucson resident Peter Loya, who frequents Venture-N, said he was acquainted with Siqueiros, whom he had known for approximately 20 years, and Capara, who was newer to the bar. Describing Siqueiros, Loya said: “He’s always just been a thoughtful, considerate person, always looking for the best in people. You could always have fun with him.” Drew Fellows, a friend of Capara, described him as a “revolutionary” photographer who was “always with a people-first mentality”. “He always fought for and believed in a better future, for himself, for his community and, most importantly, for everybody,” Fellows told the Tucson Sentinel. Tucson mayor Regina Romero called the shooting “a direct and devastating attack on our LGBTQ+ community, another senseless act of gun violence”. “This tragedy serves as yet another painful reminder that homophobia is still rampant in our country. We must implement smarter policies to prevent mass shootings and keep our communities safe. Easy access to firearms and Arizona’s weak gun safety laws continue to put all of us at risk,” Romero added. In June 2016, 49 people were killed and 58 others were injured in a mass shooting at Pulse, a gay nightclub in Orlando, Florida, making it the second-deadliest mass shooting in US history. A 2020 study published in the peer-reviewed journal Science Advances found that LGBTQ+ people in the US are 2.7 times more likely to be victims of violent crime than cisgender, heterosexual people.

title: Pentagon official overseeing military AI sold millions worth of stock in AI firm
summary: Exclusive: financial disclosures from Emil Michael – who also reaped millions from xAI stock earlier this year – show he sold his Perplexity stock for up to $25m
text: The top Pentagon official overseeing military artificial intelligence policy, who reaped profits earlier this year of up to $24m selling his private investment in Elon Musk’s AI company, has now sold his holdings in another AI company for between $5m and $25m, according to records seen by the Guardian. (Federal financial records show ranges of dollar values rather than specific figures.) Earlier this year, the Guardian disclosed that the official, Emil Michael, had profited handsomely from his investment in Musk’s xAI in January, with a gain of 400% to 4,800%. Michael’s latest financial disclosures show that in June, he sold off his shares in Perplexity, an AI-powered search engine. Recent reports have said Perplexity is looking for a financial valuation of $30bn. The records don’t reveal whether he made a profit on the sale because of the large dollar range listed in his disclosures. The Lever reported in March that Michael had the holdings in Perplexity. His financial disclosure filings from 2025 also show that he had received a personal loan from Perplexity a year earlier, of $250,000 to $500,000, at an interest rate of 4.57%. He also joined a Perplexity advisory board, but his disclosures said he stepped down upon entering federal service. Some of his Perplexity stock was vested and some was unvested, and in his ethics agreement he pledged not to make a profit off the unvested stock. It is not clear from the disclosures what stock he sold. Perplexity announced a contract with the US government’s general services administration in November of last year, though records do not show specific ties to the Pentagon. “He should have sold all interest in the company before he started working,” said ethics expert Richard Painter, a former lawyer at the White House under George W Bush. “That’s the way we would have done it back when I was working for [a] president.” A Pentagon spokesperson said Michael and other defense officials “are in full compliance with ethics laws and regulations. Any claims otherwise are false.” The spokesperson said the department has “a rigorous, multi-layered ethics framework”. Painter said Michael’s ownership in an AI company would not be a violation of law but would have raised questions because of appearances: “Most administrations would have said get out of that stock before you start that job.” Michael’s lucrative trading while at the Pentagon isn’t limited to AI companies. His latest disclosure also shows he has now realized gains of at least 473% selling holdings he owned in a separate non-public company. According to the records, Michael sold holdings in Brex LLC in April for at least $5m. Brex, a financial software company, is backed by Peter Thiel and was acquired by Capitol One that month. Michael had been a consultant at the firm. Though the firm was privately held and stock prices were not available, Michael’s holdings jumped during his time in government: he reported in March 2025 that his Brex holdings were worth just a maximum of $750,000. Michael’s profit in the Brex sale could have been as large as $24m or as little as $4.25m. Brex, unlike Musk’s xAI, does not appear to do any reported work with the US government. Michael was the face of the department’s war against AI company Anthropic. He is a frequent guest on podcasts, including on the tech podcast called – and the episode on which he appeared in December, was sponsored by Brex while Michael was still an investor in the company. It was called “Misunderstood Power: Emil Michael on the Truth about DOW and Defense Tech”. Michael was chief business officer at Uber from 2014 to 2017. BuzzFeed News reported in 2014 that Michael had privately floated digging up dirt on critical journalists, though Michael said the comment, at what he thought was an off-the-record dinner, didn’t reflect his views.

title: Republican calls Leon Black and David Copperfield co-conspirators of Epstein
summary: Outgoing congressman Thomas Massie urges justice department to launch immediate investigation
text: An outgoing Republican congressman accused the billionaire Leon Black and David Copperfield, the illusionist, of being co-conspirators of the late accused sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein, and repeated a call for the Department of Justice to launch an immediate investigation into the men, among others. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican who recently lost his primary to a challenger backed by Donald Trump, named several friends and associates of Epstein on the floor of the House in his bid to “shame” the Department of Justice to investigate a group of men and one woman who Massie called “perpetrators” of Epstein’s crimes. He also noted that, nearly one year after Trump signed the Epstein Transparency Act, which led to the release of millions of so-called “Epstein files”, millions more have yet to be publicly disclosed. “The government continues to withhold over three million files” Massie said on Monday. “That’s why we’ve introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, to bring the fight to the state courts, accountability to the Department of Justice and closure for survivors. “We want perpetrators of these crimes to be investigated and prosecuted” he added. Massie called the individuals “co-conspirators” on his Instagram account. Black, the New York private equity investor who paid Epstein tens of millions of dollars in fees, is separately facing a threat of being held in contempt of Congress because of an ongoing standoff over demands that he appear to testify before the House oversight committee later this week, on 3 September. Black has not yet confirmed his appearance before the committee, according to a person familiar with the matter. Black’s spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the scheduled hearing or Massie’s comments. Black has described his work for Epstein as tax and estate-planning services. In a previous statement before the oversight committee in June, Black wrote of his relationship with Epstein: “I did not know about this nefarious activity until Epstein was charged with trafficking in July 2019.” But Black acknowledged that he did know about Epstein pleading guilty in “2008 to state charges relating to prostitution involving a minor”. The chairman of the House oversight committee, the Republican James Comer, has previously said he would hold Black in contempt if he did not fully cooperate with his panel’s ongoing investigation into Epstein, including by handing over subpoenaed documents. Susan Estrich, Black’s lawyer, has rejected Comer’s assertions that Black has not been cooperative and has said that Black was being targeted in a “political witch-hunt”. Epstein’s former lawyer, Alan Dershowitz, has also not yet confirmed his appearance before the oversight committee, according to a person familiar with the matter. Dershowitz’s appearance was scheduled to take place on Wednesday. Dershowitz told the Guardian on Tuesday that he was “working on a date”. FBI agents investigating Copperfield in 2007 said that “a clear connection” existed between the famous illusionist and Epstein, according to documents released by the Department of Justice earlier this year. Copperfield’s lawyers have previously denied he was friends with Epstein. Lawyers for the illusionist did not respond to a request for comment on Massie’s comments, accusing Copperfield of being an Epstein co-conspirator. In a post on X on Tuesday morning, Massie said that he, along with Representatives Ro Khanna and Teresa Leger Fernández had launched a “discharge petition to collect 218 signatures” to force a vote on the new Act. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Additional reporting by Anna Betts

title: Farage faces questions over his claim of second standards investigation
summary: Reform leader said inquiry had been widened but watchdog is not believed to have decided whether to do so
text: Nigel Farage is facing questions about why he claimed his finances were the subject of a second standards investigation, as he was sworn in again as Clacton’s MP. The Reform UK leader said when he resigned in July that the standards system had become a “political tool” because “yet another standards investigation is under way” into his finances. He argued he wanted the people of Clacton to be the judge of his actions, rather than “the establishment”, after revelations in the Sunday Times that his friend and convicted fraudster George Cottrell had paid for social media work, accommodation and security before the 2024 election. However, it is understood the parliamentary standards commissioner had not launched another investigation or widened the scope of the existing one at that point. The commissioner is believed still not to have decided whether to widen the inquiry as recently as two weeks ago, when it was reopened as Farage was returned as MP for Clacton with an increased majority. The commissioner launched his first investigation in May into Farage’s £5m gift from the Thailand-based donor Christopher Harborne before the 2024 election, which was not declared on the MPs’ register of interests and was first revealed by the Guardian. Initially Farage said the money was given to pay for his security, then he described it as a reward for campaigning for Brexit. At least two complaints were then submitted in July about Farage’s funding by Cottrell. Farage called a byelection on 7 July and the initial investigation was paused. However, Westminster sources said the standards commissioner was assessing information. There is no official confirmation that he has widened his inquiry to include the Cottrell donations, and the commissioner’s list of investigations currently only includes the one launched in May. The sources said the commissioner wanted to see further evidence that Farage had broken the rules in relation to donations from Cottrell in the year before the 2024 election, including his payments for social media work. Farage has maintained the videos were personal and likened his public role before that election to the work of an influencer. However, a number of the videos were political in nature, campaigning on immigration issues. Critics say these should be declared under rules that say donations related to politics must be registered in the 12 months before an MP is elected. The standards commissioner declined to comment on the status of the investigation into Farage and whether any decision had been made on widening the inquiry. If there is no second investigation nor a widened scope, it is possible the first investigation into Farage could conclude sooner than expected. The Times reported in July that the Reform leader would be interviewed within weeks but the byelection paused the process. In relation to the investigation, Alex Burghart, the shadow chancellor of the duchy of Lancaster, said: “The questions surrounding Nigel Farage’s £5m gift from Christopher Harborne and the donations from George Cottrell simply aren’t going away. “Farage has already tried to run away with his farcical byelection in Clacton, but he can no longer hide from these questions. He needs to come clean … The public deserves answers and Farage can’t keep hiding.” If the standards commissioner finds a breach of the rules, and the separate standards committee of MPs recommends a sanction of more than 10 days of suspension from parliament, Farage could end up facing a second byelection. As he was sworn in again on Tuesday, Farage told GB News that he planned to spend less time in parliament and would be leaving more Westminster work to [the Reform deputy leader] “Richard Tice and the gang” while he goes on a tour of the country. Farage will set his priorities for the year ahead when he gives his speech at the Reform party conference at the end of this week, where he is expected to attempt to draw a line under the focus on his finances.

title: Burnham blames Brexit and Thatcher for ‘wrong turns’ in first Commons speech as PM
summary: The prime minister said Britain needed to be brutally honest about the mistakes of the last 40 years of UK politics
text: Andy Burnham has blamed Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for a decade of low growth in the UK, arguing that Britain needs to be brutally honest about having taken “a series of wrong turns” in the last 40 years. In his first Commons appearance since he took over as prime minister about six weeks ago, Burnham told MPs he wanted to build a new sense of optimism so “we can make this next decade better than the last”. The British people wanted “much more substantial change” on the big issues facing the country, he said. “That is what I will bring. Britain is not where any of us would wish it to be. Things are not working as they should.” The UK economy has taken a 6% hit from the effects of Brexit, according to economists’ analysis of internal Bank of England data on thousands of British companies since the referendum a decade ago. Shortly before Burnham’s Commons address, Keir Starmer, his predecessor, announced he would stand down as an MP, saying he wanted to focus on international affairs, triggering a tricky first byelection test for Burnham in a seat where the Greens fancy their chances. The cabinet was told on Tuesday that the government will have three key priorities: cutting costs of essentials like childcare and mortgages; the regeneration of communities; and greater public control of water, housing and energy. Burnham’s deputy, Louise Haigh, will lead task forces on each of those issues, the Guardian understands. He told his ministers they must be “relentless” in fulfilling his priorities. His plans are set against a tough economic backdrop. The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists, and economists warn mortgage rates could go up this autumn. In his Commons statement, the prime minister also: Hinted that he would commit to spending 3% of GDP on defence by 2030, saying he had appointed John Healey as his chancellor “precisely because” of his position on military spending. Signalled he is open to renationalising the water industry – saying he is looking at “all possible solutions”, as the sector is a “leaking monument” to the failures of privatisation. Opened the door to looking again at electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto. “I do believe there needs to be a mandate to make that change. There are different views in this house, but I believe we will need to get a consensus at the next election. And if there is that consensus, then a change can be made in the next parliament.” Announced he would attend the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey and continue pursuing green energy – but that he would be “pragmatic” on supply, amid expectations he will approve the Jackdaw gasfield. “The mistake is saying it’s got to be one or the other for political purposes. The truth is, it’s going to have to be both.” Flanked by Healey and Haigh, Burnham suggested to MPs the Brexit vote had been a response to “a series of wrong turns” made by Britain in the 1980s onwards, that were then compounded by leaving the EU. The prime minister, whose Makerfield constituency voted for Brexit, has previously argued it would be a mistake to rerun the referendum – but has said that he wants the UK to rejoin in his lifetime. He suggested the next UK-EU reset summit could take place in November. “Political power was centralised, economic power privatised, the country de-industrialised. Austerity followed, hollowing out councils and depriving them of the agency to act to reverse any of this,” he said during a three-hour stint in the Commons. “And then Brexit compounded the damage, ushering in a decade of low growth and stalled regeneration. Change begins with honesty … Unless we are blunt about what went wrong, we won’t turn things around. “Far from taking back control, the combination of these policies took control out of the hands of communities up and down Britain for 40 years. Too many places have been drifting.” He added: “The government I lead will be relentless in giving people and places what they were promised 10 years ago: ownership and control, and from that control over their destiny comes change and growth.” The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, accused the prime minister of “living in the past” over his attacks on Thatcher – who was in power from 1979 to 1990 – and four decades of neoliberalism. “The year is 2026 but the prime minister said everything has gone wrong since the 1980s, still complaining about Margaret Thatcher. He is talking about a woman who became prime minister before I was born. He is living in the past and he wants to take us back to the 1970s.” In the statement, Burnham paid tribute to Starmer, saying he had created a platform for Britain to be fixed, “and we will use it well”. Just hours earlier, his predecessor announced he would be standing down as MP for Holborn and St Pancras, despite saying in July he planned to stay on until the next election. “It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country,” he said. “I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs, including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world.” Starmer’s seat, long seen as a safe Labour hold, is likely to be targeted by the Greens, potentially for party leader Zack Polanski, who is a London Assembly member. “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” a Green spokesperson said. Just as the Makerfield byelection was seen as a proof of concept for whether Burnham could beat Reform, so the north London seat will test his progressive credentials. Labour will choose its candidate to replace Starmer next Wednesday under an accelerated selection timetable. Burnham’s first taskforce will be charged with finding bold solutions to tackling “everyday rip-offs”. The cost of living taskforce will look at parking charges, subscription traps and cowboy builders, as well as long-term fixed pressures like mortgages, food costs and childcare. The second will assess the affordability and practicalities of the state taking over failing essential services. Burnham believes that greater state control of essential services is the surest way to economic growth, avoiding the potential for ineffective profiteering by privatised services. Government sources said that Haigh, the first secretary of state, wanted to look beyond sectors such as transport and explore serious opportunities for greater state control in areas like energy and housing – if it would bring down ordinary people’s costs. The third taskforce will explore more radical ideas to revive crumbling high streets and impoverished districts, such as potential legislative options on houses in multiple occupation, as well as devolving powers to mayors and councils to help them regenerate local high streets.

title: Ed Miliband promises ‘comprehensive reset’ of UK policy toward Israel
summary: Foreign secretary tells MPs he will try to stop illegal settlements carving up the West Bank
text: Ed Miliband has promised to “reset” Britain’s policy on Israel, saying he will try to stop British companies helping build settlements in the West Bank. Speaking to the Commons for the first time as foreign secretary, Miliband said he would set out measures to prevent UK involvement in projects such as the illegal E1 plan, which critics say would split the West Bank in half. Tuesday’s comments came after Israel issued tenders for around a third of the 3,400 homes planned for the project. Miliband called the settlement “the crossing of a red line”. He said: “It cuts through the heart of the West Bank and risks making a Palestinian state unviable. This government will not acquiesce in the destruction of the two-state solution. We will act, and I will set out a comprehensive set of measures in the coming weeks. “I want a comprehensive reset of our approach on these issues because it is necessary, it is high time.” Ministers have been under pressure for weeks to place tighter sanctions on Israel, specifically in relation to the E1 plan. Last month, Israel invited companies to bid for contracts to build 1,200 homes for the project between East Jerusalem and the settlement of Ma’ale Adumim. A group of former British diplomats called on the government in May to threaten action against any companies bidding to build any illegal settlement “designed to divide the West Bank in two and destroy Palestine’s viability”. They warned that E1 was part of Israel’s “systemic West Bank annexation”. Other governments have condemned the project. The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz – usually one of Israel’s staunchest defenders – called it a “big mistake”. The UK joined a group of 20 other countries, including France, Germany and Italy, as well as the European Union, to issue a joint statement calling E1 “unacceptable”. The statement said: “The E1 settlement will undermine the prospect of the two-state solution by driving a wedge through the West Bank and harming the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian territories.” Miliband said: “We need to look, and we are looking indeed, at our wider economic relationship with the occupied territories and the different tools we have to tackle it. “I want to be very clear: we do not want British companies financing, constructing, or advertising new settlements. The work we are now undertaking is how we can stop that. And as I say, I’ll have more to say soon.” Ministers are under pressure to go further and ban trade in goods and services with people or organisations linked to illegal settlements. James Naish, the Labour MP for Rushcliffe in Nottinghamshire, said: “Does the foreign secretary accept that this pace of expansion shows that current UK measures are failing to change Israeli government behaviour, and that a trade ban is now the necessary next step?” Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, indicated this could be included in the government’s measures. He said: “We have absolutely condemned the settler violence, the settler terrorism that we have seen, absolutely our condemnation of the proposals for E1 and all illegal settlements, and indeed we have joined other countries around the world in condemning this proposal and been very, very clear with the government of Israel that this must stop. “The prime minister has been very clear that we need to do more, including looking at further sanctions, both those involved in the violence in Gaza, but also looking at measures to ban trade in goods with illegal settlements.” The Israeli embassy to London responded by referring to previous comments by Gideon Sa’ar, Israel’s foreign minister, who said: “If Britain acts against the state of Israel, the state of Israel will act against Britain. We have the tools. The period is over when people act against the state of Israel and the state of Israel doesn’t respond.”

title: House passes funding bill to avoid shutdown before midterms
summary: Continuing resolution to approve government spending until 11 December passes 370-48 and will now go to Trump
text: The US House of Representatives on Tuesday approved legislation to prevent a government shutdown through the midterms, as both parties opted to defuse a volatile dispute before the November elections that will decide the balance of power in Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency. A continuing resolution (CR) authorizing government spending until 11 December passed the House by a 370-48 vote, with only 19 Republicans and 29 Democrats in opposition. Had it not passed, lawmakers would have had until the end of September to approve new funding or face a government shutdown. The measure, which keeps federal spending at their current levels until the CR expires, now heads to Trump’s desk, after the Senate approved it last month by an overwhelming margin. In July, the House passed its own CR that would have authorized government spending until 4 December, but most Democrats rejected it for funding immigration enforcement agencies without including new guardrails on their conduct that they had demanded, and the Senate never took it up. The relatively uneventful end to the annual government funding debate comes as lawmakers step up their campaigning before the 3 November elections, in which most forecasters believe Democratic candidates have an edge in retaking the majority in the House of Representatives. There are mounting signs that the minority may also be able to regain control of the Senate by winning seats in at least three states that voted for Trump two years ago, as the president struggles with approval ratings driven lower by persistent inflation and the war with Iran. In the run-up to the vote, top House Democrats said they were ready to support the Senate measure, noting it included policy tweaks that the party supported. Among those was a delay until 11 December on a new rule by the White House office of management and budget that Democrats feared would allow the Trump administration to cancel grants at any time for any reason. “Given that the objectives that we had were met, I think that there’s going to be broad bipartisan support,” Pete Aguilar, the Democratic caucus chair, told reporters before the vote. Tensions flared among House Democrats later on Tuesday, when representatives Jared Golden of Maine and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington unexpectedly joined Republicans to help House speaker Mike Johnson pass a procedural rule governing debate on a suite of GOP-backed bills. The Democrats’ votes effectively salvaged Johnson’s agenda in the face of a conservative revolt that risked tanking Republicans’ legislative priorities. While Golden, who is retiring at the end of his term, and Gluesenkamp Perez, who is running for re-election in a district Trump won in 2024, often buck their party, the move was highly unusual and prompted a sharp rebuke from Democratic leadership. In a joint statement, Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, whip Katherine Clark and Aguilar said the two lawmakers had “blindside[d] the entire House Democratic Caucus” and called their actions a “significant breach of trust”. “It is an action that necessitates a serious response, and we have asked the Committee on Caucus Rules to take this up in short order,” they said. Passage of the rule paved the way on Tuesday for a vote on a resolution denouncing socialism in “all its forms”, which passed the divided chamber with the support of Republicans and eight Democrats. Tuesday’s floor action was a reminder of the deep divisions within the Democratic ranks after losing control of both houses of Congress in the 2024 elections. Without power in Congress, they have used the Senate’s filibuster to force the government closed and push the Republican majority into compromising over their preferred policies. Last year, Senate Democrats instigated a government shutdown by refusing to vote for any spending bill that did not extend subsidies for Affordable Care Act health plans. That led to the longest funding lapse in US history, but ultimately no agreement to keep the cost offsets going after the shutdown ended 43 days later. Some government agencies shut down again briefly earlier this year after Democrats held up a funding bill for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in protest of the killings by federal agents of two US citizens in Minneapolis during an intensive immigration enforcement drive. While an agreement was reached to resolve that blockade, the two parties did not agree on funding the DHS for weeks, as Democrats held out for reforms to immigration enforcement operations. A bipartisan agreement was reached to fund the department operations exclusive of the agencies involved in Trump’s mass deportation push; then Republicans passed a party-line bill that allocated funding to Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Customs and Border Protection for the duration of Trump’s presidency, with no reforms to immigration enforcement.
