title: Five held by police after newborn baby dies from stab wounds in Sheffield
summary: Officers responded to reports concerning safety of baby girl at property in Wincobank area of the city
text: Five people are being held on suspicion of murder after a newborn baby died from stab wounds in Sheffield on Sunday. Police officers found the girl at a property in Holywell Heights, in the Wincobank area of Sheffield, while responding to reports concerning her safety just before 6am on Sunday. She was pronounced dead at the scene. Seven people were arrested on suspicion of murder. Two have since been bailed. A postmortem examination found the girl had died from stab wounds, police said on Tuesday. DCI Tom Woodward of South Yorkshire police said first responders, paramedics and detectives now leading the murder investigation had been profoundly affected by the baby’s death. “We recognise this is deeply distressing for those who would have loved to have a chance to love this baby girl, for the emergency services who responded and for the community who will inevitably be shocked by this incident,” Woodward said. “Our commitment to this little girl is unwavering. “We will confront every difficult and distressing challenge and pursue every line of inquiry with determination and care to secure justice for her.” Woodward said the investigation was fast-moving and asked the community to “avoid speculating around the circumstances of this tragic incident”. “We know the local community will hold her in their thoughts and support us as we work through this complex investigation,” he said. Five murder suspects remain in custody after police were granted a warrant for further detention, a force spokesperson said on Tuesday. A 26-year-old and a 37-year-old have been released on bail. Specialist search officers will remain in the Holywell Heights area as the investigation continues. South Yorkshire police said anyone with information about the case should contact them online or call 101, quoting incident number 993 on 30 August 2026. People can also report information to the independent charity Crimestoppers.

title: One last Starmer U-turn and it’s over to Andy ‘less policy, more vibes’ Burnham | John Crace
summary: What former PM could resist upstaging the new one hours before his first dispatch box appearance in 16 years?
text: No good deed goes unpunished. Or any deed for that matter. It was only a few weeks ago that Keir Starmer was insisting he would remain an MP until the next general election. So we should all probably have guessed that he would be off at the earliest opportunity. U-turns were a distinguishing feature of his two years in office. And what former prime minister could resist upstaging the new one hours before his first appearance at the government dispatch box for 16 years? Especially when the new one had been plotting his downfall for at least a year. It’s what everyone would have wanted. Right? Not that Starmer was framing his decision in these terms. This wasn’t a simple matter of revenge. Or a need to still feel relevant. These were the last things on his mind. Keir has only ever wanted what was best for Andy. But he now had his own life to think about. And why tell the world about it on a bank holiday weekend when nobody is paying attention to the news, when you can wait till the first day of the new parliamentary session and grab the headlines? Keir said in his statement that he had really meant it when he said he would remain MP for Holborn and St Pancras, but it had only latterly dawned on him that this would be incompatible with his ambitions to be a player on the international stage. Please spare us from another Tony Blair. There again, Keir is unlikely to be invited on to Donald Trump’s Board of Peace. He should use that as his calling card. In truth though, Keir had never seemed that interested in representing his constituents or serving as a backbencher. He’s not like Theresa May, who remained, sad and alone, on the backbenches for years after being removed by her fellow Tory MPs. Nor does he have the inclination to follow the example of Rishi Sunak and turn up to work every couple of months or so. Perhaps he is more in need of the money that might come from leaving the Commons. And for a prime minister, Starmer had always seemed curiously uninterested in politics. So much so that you wondered why he had ever become a politician. It probably just felt like a normal career progression. Meanwhile, Burnham could probably live with being pushed down the news agenda for the day. He had mixed feelings about Keir’s decision. In the long run, life would probably be easier without Starmer around to cause trouble, but the downside was a potentially tricky byelection. Especially if Zack Polanski chose to stand for the Greens. And never forgetting an almost obligatory appearance from Count Binface. But this would all be for another day. Right now he had a Commons statement on the government’s direction to negotiate. First, it was a time to be gracious. After saying he would be following his predecessors in reaffirming his commitment to Ukraine, Burnham spent the first few minutes of his speech praising Keir. He had given a lifetime of service, had created a platform for change and had made the Labour party electable again. You could almost believe he was sorry to see him go. Then we got to the heart of the matter. Less policy, more positive vibes. Andy hadn’t come to the Commons to pick a fight with the opposition. Rather he hoped they would listen to him, realise he was right and then work with him. It was a big ask – especially with Kemi Badenoch as leader of the opposition, and so disinhibited she can pick a fight with herself – but probably worth a go. Just on the off-chance. Andy wasn’t going to give in to point scoring without at least attempting to offer a hand of friendship. We ran through a wishlist. The climate crisis. Surely no one was going to argue with that, not after the emergency in Nepal and the hottest summer on record? You could sense Kemi longing to intervene, to say that net zero was a con. It took all her self-control not to make an idiot of herself. Burnham began. Small boat crossings down: tick. More prison places for the right kinds of prisoner: fingers crossed. Defence: that would be sorted later, somehow. The cost of living: we need to be honest that the country has been in decline since 1980. “I will be relentless about achieving change and growth,” he said. First he had taken Manchester, now he takes the UK. A Britain that would work for all of us. A desire to keep upbeat. The country had had enough of being told it was falling apart. Let the good times roll. Ish. We can make the next decade better than the last, he concluded. That suddenly didn’t feel quite so comforting. I mean, the next 10 years can hardly be worse than the shitshow of the last 10 years. Can it? Can it? Please. We need some reason to get out of bed each morning. As for Kemi, let’s also be generous. She did at least try to sound as if she had listened and would work at doing better to find common ground. Though she couldn’t do this without sounding vaguely patronising. As if Burnham was some sort of ingenu who had been parachuted into Westminster without a clue as to what he was doing, and she was the old lag who had seen it all before. “I’ll be gentle,” she said, as if Andy was a halfwit, before going on to say that almost everything he had said was totally wrong. The decline in small boat crossings was just a coincidence. Margaret Thatcher had taken office before she had been born, so therefore anything Thatcher had done was totally irrelevant. Kemi thinks the world began with her birth and will end with her death. The narcissist’s fantasy. She promised to help when it was in the national interest, but the national interest would only be served if she was in charge. Andy tried to let her down gently. He was here to help too. Kemi had gone to Rome and fantasised that Giorgia Meloni had told her not to do a deal with Reform. He would happily have saved her the air fare and told her the same thing. Then he took her by surprise – by pointing out she had just picked a shadow chancellor who had been the author of Liz Truss’s mini-budget. Kemi looked a little shell-shocked. She is going to have to up her game before tomorrow’s prime minister’s questions.

title: ‘I think he’s sensible’: constituents on Keir Starmer stepping down as MP
summary: Few regrets voiced in Holborn and St Pancras over decision despite former PM having had ‘rough time of it’
text: In Keir Starmer’s north London constituency, full of pretty pubs and elegant townhouses, few tears were being shed at the news of his departure as its MP. One man nursing a pint outside a pub in Kentish Town simply remarked “good” when informed his MP had quit. He added: “I thought he was very nice before he became prime minister; I met him a few times. But he messed the country up and screwed over pensioners.” Annie, a 30-year-old doctor having a coffee and pastry on a bench near the tube station, said: “I think everyone here wanted him to leave. He’s had a rough time of it, sure, but we have all had enough of him.” Dominic Ford, a 75-year-old pensioner reading a book outside the Parakeet pub, was more sympathetic. “I think he’s sensible. It would have been tough for him to sit behind the new prime minister,” he said. “He’s a very nice, honest guy, and he was very visible around here. We used to see him going to the Arsenal with his son. He was a good local MP, and very honest. I felt very sorry for him when he resigned as prime minister.” On a quiet street among rows of pastel-coloured terrace houses is the Pineapple, Starmer’s favourite pub. It is out of the way of the high street, and the former prime minister is frequently seen there drinking a pint. He may have become tired of his pub visits being documented in various newspapers, because when the Guardian visited and asked regulars what they thought about him stepping down, the bar staff firmly said that questions about Starmer were not allowed. Perhaps this commitment to discretion is why he has referred to the pub as his “church” and “the best pub in land”. Starmer announced his departure as prime minister in June after several unpopular choices including making Peter Mandelson, a friend of Jeffrey Epstein, ambassador to the US. On Tuesday, Starmer told the Camden New Journal he wanted to focus on international affairs and “pass the baton to a successor”. Starmer had previously said he would seek to serve out his term as a backbench MP, and his decision to quit will spark a byelection. The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, is understood to be considering a run for the seat. Laura Hyland, a 67-year-old artist, said she was pleased Starmer was stepping down and that she welcomed the prospect of a byelection. “He gave very little support for Palestine, and I hope Andy Burnham will be more supportive. Arresting people for holding signs saying ‘I support Palestine Action’ was disgraceful.” Anita, 52, was doing her shopping on the high street. She also welcomed Starmer standing down, and said: “I can’t stand him. He was completely useless and I am glad he stood down.” The former prime ministers Rishi Sunak and Theresa May both committed to serving out a term as an MP for their constituencies after losing a general election. Sunak is still representing his North Yorkshire constituency, now Richmond and Northallerton, two years after Starmer taunted him about whether he would be moving to California to work in tech. Lewis Galloway, 43, who works in marketing, said he would have liked to see the same from Starmer. “It’s a shame that he’s standing down,” he said. “There was something nice about Theresa May and Rishi Sunak when they stood down and still worked for their constituents from the backbenches. It is a real shame to lose him from this form of public service so prematurely.”

title: Who is John Ternus, Apple’s new CEO?
summary: Hardware engineering executive succeeding Tim Cook is a longtime Apple insider, indicating company will continue strategy that has led to record profits
text: Tim Cook stepped down as CEO of Apple on 31 August. John Ternus, a longtime company veteran, succeeded him the next day as the company’s new chief executive. Cook has transitioned to the role of executive chairman of Apple’s board of directors. Ternus, a hardware engineering executive, is a tenured Apple insider, and his ascension indicates the company will stay the course that has led to record profits under Cook’s leadership. Apple’s yearly profit now tops $100bn, the company is worth about $4.5tn, and it has notched record revenue from its iPhones this year, boosted by renewed demand in China. “I am profoundly grateful for this opportunity to carry Apple’s mission forward,” Ternus said in a company press release when Cook announced his retirement. “Having spent almost my entire career at Apple, I have been lucky to have worked under Steve Jobs and to have had Tim Cook as my mentor. It has been a privilege to help shape the products and experiences that have changed so much of how we interact with the world and with one another.” Cook praised his successor as having “the mind of an engineer, the soul of an innovator, and the heart to lead with integrity and with honor”. Ternus started at Apple in 2001 and assumed the role of vice-president of hardware engineering in 2013, then head of the department in 2021, responsible for the physical components that make up Apple products. Among his notable achievements are the development and launch of Apple’s proprietary silicon chips for its Mac line of computers, which saw sales soar after swapping out Intel chips in 2020, according to the Wall Street Journal. New products that debuted under Ternus’s leadership of the hardware division include the Apple Watch and the AirPods line of headphones, both of which grew into major lines of business for Apple, and the Vision Pro headset, which did not. The Journal described Ternus as “an affable mechanical engineer” with a management style closer to the calm Cook than to the inspiring but volatile Steve Jobs. The replacement in his role will be Johny Srouji, who previously worked as Apple’s senior vice-president of hardware. Cook, who joined Apple in 1998 and succeeded Jobs as CEO in 2011, had been engaged in planning his succession for the better part of a year, the New York Times reported in January, after the CEO told the company’s board and senior leaders that he wanted to work less. Ternus had been a favorite for replacing Cook, the newspaper reported. Ternus, a California native, received his bachelor’s degree in mechanical engineering from the University of Pennsylvania, where he joined the varsity swim team. After graduating in 1997, he briefly worked at Virtual Research Systems, a virtual reality startup. Even as Ternus may lead Apple along a similar route that Cook took to lucrative success, he will face pressure to catch up with the iPhone maker’s Silicon Valley peers on artificial intelligence, where it has lagged even while leading in consumer hardware. He inherits a perceived lack of name-brand consumer AI offerings and a promise to revamp of the Siri virtual assistant with Google’s Gemini AI.

title: Nepal-Tibet flood deaths pass 1,000 as police ask relatives for DNA to identify victims
summary: Relatives of missing tourists asked for blood samples and photos, as efforts continue to rescue trapped hydropower workers
text: Nepali rescuers have built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue hundreds of trapped workers, as the death toll passed 1,000 nearly ⁠a week after devastating floods left a trail of destruction across the country’s towns and valleys. About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts. The prime ⁠minister, Balendra Shah, said more than 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines had been restored in some areas. “Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones and property,” Shah said. Six days after the catastrophe struck the Himalayan border region, 4,400 people were still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist identification efforts. In a statement posted to social media, Nepal police on Monday asked relatives of those missing to “provide a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the Nepal police hospital in Kathmandu, or the nearest district police office. Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada. Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”. In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues. At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled. Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims. “Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.” She was waiting for her two other siblings, who live in the UK, to arrive on Tuesday so they could all try to get up to the village. She said she wanted to contact her grandmother or sister-in-law, who she thinks both survived the flood because their house is further up the mountain. Their village was still in a blackout, and making contact was impossible. “I can’t go there; the situation is very bad,” she said. “I can’t go up there alone. I am not sure if we’ll be able to get them.” The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse that sent a deluge of ice, rock and mud through Nepal’s border region with China, posing a massive challenge for the country’s six-month-old government. The region is vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events such as intense monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change. In a late-night social media post, Shah said aid worth more than $42m had poured into the country, but that Nepalis were reeling. “The government understands the immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to ‌support them through this suffering and help ‌them return to normal life through rehabilitation,” the prime minister said. Shah also said that 279 workers had so far been rescued from hydropower projects, where authorities estimated close to 1,000 people had been trapped. Days after the disaster, hope was rapidly diminishing that any of those trapped in a series of tunnels could be alive. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel. Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People’s Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side. The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state broadcaster said on Monday. Shah said the catastrophic event signalled the growing risks that the Himalayan region faces. “The region must therefore remain vigilant. The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change,” he wrote in his post.

title: Russia targets Ukraine’s rail network as war enters deadly new phase
summary: Six employees killed on Tuesday after Moscow escalates attacks on infrastructure and Ukrainian capital
text: Russia has opened a deadly new phase in its war against Ukraine by deliberately targeting the country’s railway network, with six employees killed on Tuesday in the latest strikes on Kyiv. Ukraine’s state-owned railway company, Ukrzaliznytsia, said its workers died when a ballistic missile plunged into a locomotive depot. The Russians hit other railway facilities, it added, during a massive bombardment of Kyiv and the Kyiv region. At least 12 people died, with a dozen wounded, including three children. “An unbearably difficult night for the entire railway family. Railway staff have been working at the scene since early this morning. The attack has caused significant damage. Rescue workers are still putting out a number of fires,” said Ukrzaliznytsia’s chair, Oleksandr Pertsovsky. The grim strike took place as Russia escalated its attacks on the Ukrainian capital. It has carried out continuous raids for six days, beginning last week, in an attempt to disrupt daily life and demoralise the city’s inhabitants. The onslaught took place hours before Ukrainian children began a new school year. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion, 58 railway staff have been killed and at least 318 injured. One wounded railway employee, Volodymyr, was taken to hospital on Tuesday, with people urged to donate blood if they were B positive – his group. “Our colleagues are by his side,” Ukrzaliznytsia said, adding it would support victims’ families. Ukraine’s railway network is Europe’s third largest, with 15,000 miles (24,000km) of track. It has been a lifeline for the country’s wartime civilians, transporting four million people and an estimated 120,000 pets. It has brought world leaders to Kyiv, including Joe Biden and Andy Burnham, who arrived last week on an overnight service from Poland. Serhii Leshchenko, a member of Ukrzaliznytsia’s supervisory board, described the railway as the “backbone of Ukraine’s economy”. It was the main logistical supplier for the country’s army and industry, and every week transported 600,000 people, he told the Guardian. With 170,000 workers, it was also Ukraine’s biggest company. For these reasons Russia was trying to destroy railways, he added. In the first year of the war it attacked bridges, which could be easily replaced. Next, it targeted rails and electricity substations. Ukraine then switched to using diesel engines. This year, Russia started “direct attacks on civilian locomotives”, he said – an insidious tactic, at a time when Ukraine is short of air defences. Several drivers have been killed and locomotives targeted inside depots. Leshchenko said that if a Shahed drone came within 50km of a train, it had to be evacuated, and could only continue once the threat has passed. So far this year Russia has hit the network more than 1,500 times – a higher figure than in the whole of 2025. Overall, 249 carriages and 492 locomotives have been damaged. Once known for their punctuality, trains now suffer regular delays, sometimes lasting as long as 12 to 15 hours. Amid air raid sirens, passengers are forced to disembark and take cover, including during winter. Writing on Facebook, the Ukrainian journalist Tetiana Zaiets described how she hid in April when Russian drones flew overhead. “It was hell. The train stopped at night somewhere in central Ukraine. I don’t even know the name of the town. Half asleep, I just heard the conductor say ‘evacuation’. We took only our personal belongings and valuables with us. It was raining outside. Thank you to the conductors for handing out blankets,” she posted. She added: “That’s how we held out for two hours. While kamikaze drones were buzzing overhead, we crawled under a goods wagon. The last carriage in the train was full of children. They were being taken back from hospital. They were crying in their sleep. I thought I’d ended up in some sort of horror film. But no, this is our life.” Since the incident, Zaiets said she was too frightened to travel by train. “Until the war is over, I won’t be using it,” she said, stressing she respected Ukraine’s “courageous” railway workers. Last week, an enemy drone hit a train in the Odesa region with 600 people on board, including 15 children. “The train was stopped, we were kicked out. We heard explosions, everything was burning. It was scary,” one passenger, Andriy, told the website Suspline. Another passenger, Eva, said she was evacuated twice, and “dropped off in a field”. “We sat there and heard something flying. Then we saw a drone very close by.” She managed to collect her belongings and was eventually picked up by a bus, she said. Leshchenko admitted the Russian strikes were hurting Ukraine’s economy and had slowed the export of grain from its under-fire Black Sea ports. He said Kyiv needed air defences from western partners, so it could protects its trains from marauding missiles and drones. “If the whole country is under attack, they will attack railways for sure,” he said. Up until this year more than 90% of Ukrainian trains arrived on time. This was in part down to the fact engines never go especially fast, rolling at 55mph. Carriages are clean and comfortable: the best way of getting around a vast country. Stewards look after night train customers and bring them morning tea in filigree holders. There is a trolley on day trains, and patchy wifi. On international services, border guards scrutinise male passengers, while dogs roam up and down corridors. Since the invasion, men between 18 and 60 have been forbidden from leaving the country, with some exemptions. On trains from Kyiv to Przemyśl, a railway hub in eastern Poland, most travellers are women. Since 2022 about six million people have departed abroad, many exiting by train. In recent days Russia has launched over 1,500 drones at Ukraine, 800 of them jet-fuel models, which are harder to shoot down. In the past, Moscow would send a swarm of drones a couple of times a week, usually at night. Now the attacks continue without a pause, with one or two drones dispatched every hour, paralysing ordinary life. Air raid sirens in Kyiv are non-stop. Pertsovsky, Ukrzaliznytsia’s boss, described the loss of his employees on Tuesday as “terrible”. “We are in touch with their loved ones. Everyone is with them to get through this extremely difficult time. The night is bitter with impossibility,” he wrote.

title: ICE holds man with stage 4 cancer in detention despite permanent US residency
summary: ICE spokesperson says Loreto Javar failed to disclose criminal conviction in Philippines when he applied for visa
text: A 76-year-old man holding permanent US residency and grappling with stage four prostate cancer is reportedly being held in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention in Tacoma, Washington. Federal immigration officials detained Loreto Javar during his US citizenship interview in Tukwila, Washington, in June. Javar, a Filipino national, moved to the US in 1995 and has lived in the country with his wife and daughter ever since. According to court documents reviewed by the Seattle Times and reported on by the outlet on Monday, federal officials allege that Javar was involved in an altercation in the Philippines in the 1970s that left one person dead. Javar told officials at the time of his arrest in June that he had served about three years in jail in the Philippines before being released on parole, according to the documents cited by the Seattle Times. Javar, a retired hotel worker, has renewed his permanent residency – or green card – several times without issue since moving to the US more than 30 years ago, including most recently in December, his daughter, Daisy Javar, told the outlet. Loreto Javar applied for US citizenship in November 2025 and has no criminal history in the country, Daisy Javar added. Although her father had never told his family about his conviction before his detention by ICE, she said: “He’s been following all the rules, paying his taxes, everything.” In a statement to the Seattle Times, an ICE spokesperson said Javar was arrested because he had failed to disclose a criminal conviction in the Philippines when he originally applied for a visa to move to the US in 1995 and join his father, who was already living in the country as a US citizen. The ICE spokesperson said Javar’s disclosure would have made him ineligible to enter the US at the time of his original application, adding, “He is therefore ineligible to remain in the United States now,” the Seattle Times reported. According to Daisy Javar, her father obtained police clearance from the Philippines’ National Bureau of Investigation as part of the process of securing his US visa at the time, the outlet also reported. The Guardian has reached out to ICE for comment. Javar as of Tuesday was being held at the Northwest ICE processing center in Tacoma, Washington. He was diagnosed with advanced prostate cancer in January and is prescribed two oral medications, as well as other medications for conditions including high blood pressure, the Seattle Times reported. Speaking to the outlet, Daisy Javar said her father’s meals were often delivered late, with lunch sometimes not served until 6pm and dinner at midnight. She said the delays have complicated his medication schedule. Meanwhile, an online petition organized by the Filipino migrant advocacy group Tanggol Migrante Movement calling for Javar’s release said: “Before his detention, [he] was actively receiving treatment for his Stage 4 Prostate Cancer, but since being taken into ICE custody, that course of treatment has been interrupted. “So far, he has missed two oncology appointments that occur on the 4th of every month and has recently developed a blood clot in his stomach. The appointments are crucial to conduct bloodwork and adjust his medication to prevent his cancer from further developing.” The petition added: “Furthermore, the Seattle Philippine Consulate has yet to provide concrete support despite promising [Javar] that they would help … The Philippine government and their overseas extension, the Seattle Philippine consulate, repeatedly fails to protect their nationals when they face detention, exploitation, abuse, or deportation.” According to the petition, the Philippines consulate visited Javar and “promised to help him and provide him with $300 for his commissary, but they have yet to fulfill that promise”. The Guardian has contacted the Philippine embassy and consulate general in Washington DC and Seattle, respectively. Donald Trump’s administration has been pursuing a campaign of mass deportation throughout his second presidency. The president and his allies said the campaign would mainly target “violent criminals” and the “worst of the worst”. But a Guardian analysis of government records has found that the vast majority of people who entered deportation proceedings for the first during the first year of Trump’s second presidency had no criminal conviction. A poll taken by PBS News, National Public Radio and Marist after immigration agents’ killings of US citizens Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minneapolis in January determined Americans largely disapproved of ICE. Nearly two-thirds of those surveyed – 62% – said they believed ICE had gone too far in enforcing the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, the pollsters said.

title: Private equity keeps picking off London-listed firms – and Westminster barely notices | Nils Pratley
summary: Bodycote is the latest FTSE 250 industrial company set to fall to an overseas bidder, despite the government’s talk of ‘reindustrialising’
text: The UK is in the business of “reindustrialising”, says the prime minister. If we are, an increasing portion of the activity will be under foreign ownership. Tuesday brought yet another overseas private equity swoop on a FTSE 250 industrial firm. This time it’s the Macclesfield-based Bodycote, which describes itself as “the world’s largest service provider of heat treatment and specialist metallurgical technologies” – think, for example, processes and coatings to toughen jet engine blades. The buyer is the US buyout firm Veritas for £1.65bn or 940p a share, or £1.85bn including debt. Unless, that is, the rival bidder, CVC, a European private equity firm, comes back for another bite, which the market clearly thinks is a possibility because Bodycote’s shares closed at 955p. The shame is that one cannot call 940p a stunning price. The valuation “does not appear particularly generous on a take-out basis”, said an analyst at the investment bank RBC, noting that it’s only 25% above the pre-bid level and the implied earnings valuation is merely in line with Bodycote’s 10-year average. Indeed, nine-tenths of the “reasons for recommendation” section of Bodycote’s announcement sounded like an argument for doing the opposite. The passage started by saying how well the medium-term “optimise, perform, grow” strategy adopted in late 2024 was going. The plan was designed to find efficiencies and shift towards the expanding aerospace and defence sectors in pursuit of enviable financial metrics, including 20%-plus operating margins and a return on capital employed of 15 to 20% through the cycle. Good progress has been made, say the directors. On the way, there has been enough spare cash for £120m of share buy-backs while maintaining a 38-year record of growing or maintaining the dividend. And the board is “confident in the ongoing execution” of the strategy, with “the majority of remaining improvements under Bodycote’s control”. It was only in the last sentence that the company also said it was “mindful of increasing structural challenges in certain automotive and industrial markets together with macroeconomic uncertainties which create meaningful risk to delivery of Bodycote’s medium term financial targets”. In other words, everything is going splendidly apart from a couple of risks – the sectoral one that the strategy is addressing, and the vague “macroeconomic uncertainty” that is a normal state of affairs for most companies. As a reason for accepting a bid at a mere 25% premium, it’s not terribly convincing. In Bodycote’s defence, one might say the takeover price could yet improve if CVC, which said it was considering its position, comes back. More depressingly, one suspects Bodycote simply lives in that unloved sub-£5bn capitalisation part of the stock market that suffers from lack of attention and lack of regular inward capital flows. It is harder to fight for independence if the unspoken market pressure is to accept a bid for the sake of certainty. The mini-tragedy in this case is that there was a wake-up call of sorts for investors when Apollo, yet another US private equity outfit, expressed an interest in bidding at 885p in the spring before walking away. The net result, though, is that Bodycote’s 54 years of London stock market life will come to an end one way or another. The company joins a long list of departees this year, which on Tuesday alone also took in telecoms company Gamma Communications for £1.1bn and the Scottish energy firm Capricorn for £292m. Bodycote can still prosper under private equity ownership, of course. But a leading UK-based global specialist in its field, with 130 sites across 22 countries and 4,000 employees, is yet another bad one for the London market to lose. The remedies for this rate of exodus have been trawled over in this column many times – and none are easy. But the process surely starts with recognition among politicians that “selling the family silver” – the title of a recent Peel Hunt report that calculated 150-plus bids for UK companies with a market value of more than £100m since the start of 2023 – may not be in the UK’s long-term economic interests. As ever, there was barely a squeak out of Westminster.

title: Swinney sticks with pledge to cap prices on basic foods in Scotland
summary: First minister sets out his government’s agenda and defends policy described by industry groups as a ‘potty gimmick’
text: John Swinney insisted on Tuesday he still planned to introduce a legally binding price cap on bread, milk and other essential food items in Scotland despite fierce opposition from farming and business groups. Unveiling the Scottish National party’s programme for government – the equivalent to the king’s speech – the first minister said he wanted to give “families greater peace of mind at a time of rising prices”. Swinney also announced commitments to restructure local government and NHS boards, introduce a misogyny bill to crack down on violence against women and girls, and set a £2 price limit on bus fares in the west of Scotland. He confirmed his government would pilot a minimum income for artists. But the proposals to limit essential food and drink prices have faced intense criticism from industry groups, which have described the policy as “unnecessary” and a “potty gimmick”. On Monday, 23 food, drink and farming organisations published an open letter arguing that markets were already working to deliver the best possible prices and a cap could increase the cost of household goods. “Scots benefit from western Europe’s most affordable grocery and food supply market,” the letter read. “A statutory cap would not address the root causes of elevated food prices: rising production, refrigeration, and distribution costs. Supply chain shocks after Covid and conflicts in Ukraine and Iran have pushed up fertiliser, fuel and energy costs.” The SNP committed to introducing price controls by the end of the year in a manifesto published before Holyrood elections in May, framing the scheme as a health measure. Similar initiatives have been implemented in Hungary and Croatia and the UK government encouraged supermarkets to consider voluntary price caps on foodstuffs in May. The Scottish government did not specify which essentials would be covered by the law in a consultation paper published on Tuesday, although Swinney has said that between 20 and 50 products would be included, such as rice, cheese and eggs. Any limit would cover only retailers that make more than half of their annual turnover from groceries, have more than 250 employees and make more than £250m a year. “It is our ambition, and intention, to put more money in families’ pockets, building on what is already the most generous cost of living support package anywhere in the UK,” Swinney told Holyrood on Tuesday. “Today we have also begun a formal consultation on the legislation that will introduce a legal price ceiling on a basket of essential food items, giving families greater peace of mind at a time of rising prices.” There is uncertainty over whether any price cap on food and drink essentials would even be legal. The Scottish government is planning to introduce the policy under devolved health powers. But critics say it would clash with post-Brexit internal UK market rules to stop regulatory divergence between England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Scotland is facing growing pressure on its finances. The Scottish government estimated last year that there would be a near-£5bn gap in its finances by the end of the decade, with experts warning that difficult choices await over how to fund healthcare, schools and other parts of the public sector. In his five-year programme for government, Swinney announced a major change to the structure of NHS Scotland, reducing the number of health boards from 14 to two. He described the shake-up as “the most significant structural reform of our NHS in the devolution era”.

title: A national commission on voting reform is essential | Letters
summary: Letters: Sandy Martin and Joan Ruddock respond to an article on changes to the voting system
text: Your report (Labour MPs will push Burnham to back voting reform in first 100 days, 25 August) says: “The UK last rejected electoral reform in 2011 after a referendum [on] whether to change to an alternative vote system.” Many people do not realise that the referendum was not about a proportional electoral system. While the alternative vote is the best way to elect a single person, it really doesn’t work for a government. That referendum was primarily a popularity contest for Nick Clegg, and it is no surprise that he was rejected, predominantly by people who were not aware of the actual terms of the referendum. A national commission, taking evidence from people across the country, followed by a general election that includes a manifesto commitment to changing the system, will be a far more reliable and accurate representation of the views of the British people than a referendum is ever likely to be. Sandy Martin Chair, Labour Campaign for Electoral Reform • The amendment to the representation of the people bill on which you report is not the only thing to which the government will have to reply. By law they will have to respond to a parliamentary petition, initiated by me, which calls for the setting up of a national commission in line with the all-party parliamentary group’s proposal. The petition states that it should be an independent, time limited, expert-led review to build consensus for changing the electoral system for parliament. Already more than 25,000 people have signed – twice the number required to trigger a government response. It is eagerly awaited. Joan Ruddock Former Labour MP and minister • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Don’t dismiss ‘Woke 1.0’ – young people’s activism should be encouraged | Letter
summary: Letter: Far from being crazy, the grandchildren of the radical ‘permissive’ generation are using their voices to fight for progress, as we taught them to do, writes Paul McGilchrist
text: I can’t help feeling that Nesrine Malik’s critique of “Woke 1.0” was more nuanced and focused than the published responses suggest (Letters, 24 August). Yes, it could be puritanical, dogmatic and wrong-headed at times, but to dismiss it on these grounds is to ignore Malik’s entreaty not to “trivialise and dismiss movements that resonated globally, and which had safety, dignity and equal opportunity at their heart”. Far from being “crazy”, so called “Woke 1.0” was the roar of the grandchildren of the radical “permissive” generation – on both sides of the Atlantic – using voices they were always encouraged to believe could change the world. They were schooled in human rights like no others before them, and inducted into activism through historical precedent, armed only with just cause and integrity. They were unashamed to wear conviction on their sleeves and prepared to face the inevitable backlash as readily as their often-celebrated countercultural forebears. Malik argues, persuasively and correctly, that how we “frame” this activism conditions how we appreciate its aims. And it has been comprehensively framed by rightwing reactionaries making space for the recrudescence of attitudes and proclivities which an older progressive generation fought tooth and nail to bury. Paul McGilchrist Cromer, Norfolk • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: UK entrepreneur makes £500,000 political donation to Restore Britain
summary: Simon Galbraith says Rupert Lowe’s party can ‘spark a British renaissance’ if it gets into power
text: The hard-right Restore Britain party has got its first major donation of £500,000 from an IT entrepreneur in a sign it may continue to pose a threat to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. Rupert Lowe, an MP who left Reform UK before starting his own party, announced on Tuesday that the British businessman Simon Galbraith had contributed two donations of £250,000 this year. Galbraith said his company Cade Hill Investments had given the money as he believes that “most British people sense Britain’s decline”. “There is a centralised, bloated and incompetent state which is increasingly undemocratic, British institutions are unfocused on what they should be for and our democracy doesn’t represent the interests and opinions of many,” he said in a statement. “Things are worse than most people realise, but the opportunity is much greater than everyone thinks too. If Restore win power, I think it will spark a British renaissance.” The sum is small compared with the millions given to Farage’s party by the crypto billionaires Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo, as well as further millions pledged by the Iranian-born billionaire Sasan Ghandehari. However, Restore Britain’s ability to raise a substantial sum from a private donor will improve its potential to challenge Reform UK from the right in targeted areas. The party has previously said it will field a candidate against Farage if he faces a second bylection in Clacton after the standards investigation into his finances is concluded. However, Lowe also offered an olive branch to Farage in August suggesting the parties could put aside their differences and work together on “mass deportation” of illegal migrants “including women and children”, tougher rules on legal migration, a ban on halal and kosher slaughter, the burqa, cousin marriage and sharia courts, and a referendum on the death penalty. He also called for the exclusion of former Tory ministers from any future cabinet. In response, Farage suggested Lowe was not making a credible “offer” and accused him of “screaming” and “threatening” colleagues when he was in the party ranks. Announcing Restore’s new donation, Lowe said: “I am delighted to announce that British entrepreneur Simon Galbraith has chosen to support Restore Britain, starting with two separate donations totalling £500,000 to our party – I would like to sincerely thank Simon on behalf of our party and our membership.”

title: Edouard Balladur obituary
summary: French prime minister beaten to the presidency by his former ally Jacques Chirac at the 1995 election
text: For many months before the 1995 French presidential election, Édouard Balladur, the incumbent prime minister, seemed certain of victory. Opinion polls consistently gave him a lead over his conservative rival Jacques Chirac, and the main leftwing candidate. But, as other politicians have discovered, polls can be misleading and voters change their minds. When the ballot papers were counted it was Chirac who won and succeeded François Mitterrand as president. The defeat of Balladur, who has died aged 97, was due partly to his lack of appeal to young voters, a consequence of his public image which, somewhat unfairly, was that of an aloof aristocrat. When he first became a minister, the satirical weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaîné dubbed him “his courteous self-importance” and Le Monde’s cartoonist Plantu depicted him as a bewigged 18th-century nobleman being carried around in a sedan chair. His manner and style – three-piece English tailored suits, dislike (figuratively and literally) of getting his hands dirty and obvious distaste for close personal contact – did not play well in the context of a presidential contest. There was nothing aristocratic in Balladur’s background, however, about which he maintained a certain mystery. He was born in Smyrna, now Izmir, in Turkey, the youngest of the six children of Pierre Balladur, the manager of a local branch of an Ottoman bank, and Émilie (nee Latour). His parents became naturalised French citizens in 1932 and the family moved to France when Édouard was six, settling in Marseille, where he went to school at the Lycée Thiers. Balladur began studies in law at Aix-Marseille University, then continued them at the Institute of Political Sciences (Sciences-Po) in Paris, living for a while in the Roman Catholic hostel where years earlier Mitterrand had resided. A bout of tuberculosis temporarily interrupted his studies; once cured he completed his military service in Algeria, which was then a French colony, two years before the war of independence, when tensions were high. On his return to Paris, he was accepted into the École Nationale d’Administration (ENA), then the nursery of France’s political, business and technocratic elite. He began his career with the Conseil d’État and the former state broadcasting organisation ORTF but caught the eye of Georges Pompidou, Charles de Gaulle’s prime minister, and became his adviser in 1964. This gave him a ringside seat during the student riots and civil unrest of 1968, and the negotiations that eventually got the country back to work after a national strike. In 1969, Pompidou succeeded De Gaulle at the Élysée, and Balladur went with him, becoming secretary general of the presidency. After Pompidou’s death in 1974, a leading industrialist took Balladur under his wing, and he ran two subsidiaries of a major company, making useful contacts in business. For many years he enjoyed a plum sinecure as president of the company operating the Mont Blanc tunnel. In 1980, he returned to politics. Chirac, who had walked out of his job as President Valéry Giscard d’Estaing’s prime minister in 1976 to found the conservative RPR party and pursue his own presidential ambitions, sacked two of his closest advisers and invited Balladur to replace them. Chirac’s first presidential bid the following year failed (though it sank Giscard), but five years later the conservative right recaptured the Assemblée Nationale, and Chirac was appointed prime minister after negotiations with the socialist Mitterrand in which Balladur played a key role. In this, the first “cohabitation” (in which the president and the government are of different political families), Balladur was appointed minister of finance, economy and privatisation. He was a powerful minister, but was in office for only two years. In 1988, Chirac made a second presidential bid and lost again. The re-elected Mitterrand called a general election, and the Socialists were able to form a minority government. Balladur returned to the world of business, where he now cut a more substantial figure after his experience in government, and set about establishing networks of friends and contacts. It was clear that the Socialist-led government was heading for defeat in the 1993 general election. Chirac, as the leader of the right, was the obvious choice as prime minister after a conservative victory. But he had been so bruised by his experience as prime minister under Mitterrand’s presidency during the first cohabitation that he was not eager to repeat the experience. Balladur emerged as the clear favourite for the role, acceptable to both Mitterrand and the right. It was evident at the time that Chirac saw Balladur as a proxy for himself. One of his closest allies even suggested Balladur might make weekly visits to Chirac in the Paris city hall, where he reigned as mayor, to brief him on government business. But Balladur established himself as his own man. The second cohabitation, unlike the first, was a courteous affair. The public took to the new prime minister, and seemed to appreciate the absence of confrontation between Mitterrand and Balladur. Balladur had never been one of the barons of Gaullism or Chirac’s version of neo-Gaullism, and his instincts appeared to favour Christian democracy on the German model more than the national populism of the likes of Charles Pasqua or Philippe Séguin. There was no shortage of crises – over reform of immigration laws, a strike at Air France that saw clashes between workers and police, the minimum wage for young school leavers, funding for church schools and the plight of French fishermen. Abroad, there were some serious questions over France’s role in the genocide in Rwanda. But Balladur avoided taking on protesters, preferring discreet withdrawal when it appeared there was strong opposition. He was credited with a success in the talks on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (Gatt) in 1993. It rapidly emerged that, far from being a surrogate for Chirac, Balladur was a man with views and, more importantly, ambitions of his own. Month after month, polls showed strong public support for him. Relations with Chirac and his allies deteriorated in spite of occasional public and unconvincing displays of unity. It is not clear when he decided to stand for the presidency, but he formally declared his intention in early 1995. Much of the centre-right and two significant RPR figures – Pasqua and the future president Nicolas Sarkozy – rallied to him. But Chirac had found an issue on which to campaign: the “social fracture” in French society. In the slightly improbable role of the outsider castigating the technocratic elites, Chirac struck a chord, particularly with the young. Balladur’s efforts to reach out to the people, including climbing on tables at public meetings, to much general derision, were less successful. His opinion-poll lead melted, and in the first round of voting Lionel Jospin, the socialist candidate, came top with 23% of the vote, followed by Chirac with a little under 21% and Balladur at 18.5%. Chirac won the run-off. The new president was not the man to forgive what he regarded as treason, and in the new government there was no place for Balladur, who, however, retained political ambitions. When it became clear that Jean Tiberi, Chirac’s successor as mayor of Paris, was tainted beyond political redemption by scandal, Balladur, after some hesitation, declared his candidacy. If he had hoped for help from Chirac, he was disappointed. Tiberi and Balladur split the centre right vote, allowing Bertrand Delanoé to become in 2001 the first leftwing mayor of the city since the Paris Commune 130 years earlier. Balladur continued to serve as an MP until 2007. In later years, questions began to be asked about the financing of his 1995 presidential campaign. The allegations centred on the sale of submarines to Pakistan and possible bribes, commissions and kickbacks. In 2002, a bomb in Karachi killed 14 people, 11 of them French employees of the national shipbuilders. Al-Qaida was initially suspected, but later it was suggested that on taking office Chirac had stopped the payment of kickbacks to middlemen and the bombing had been an act of revenge or intimidation. There were reports that some of the money had found its way into Balladur’s campaign funds. Certainly, claims that the huge sums of cash in large-denomination notes paid into campaign accounts were the product of the sale of T-shirts did not convince everyone. Several members of his entourage were investigated and charged by magistrates looking into alleged misappropriation of public funds in what became known as the “Karachi affair”. In 2017, Balladur himself was charged with funnelling kickbacks on state arms deals with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, alongside the former defence minister François Léotard. In 2021, the court of justice of the Republic ruled that there was no evidence that Balladur had personally ordered payments linked to the contract, nor sufficient proof to establish the origins of his campaign financing, and he was acquitted of all charges. Léotard was found guilty, and given a suspended prison sentence and a fine. Balladur’s wife, Marie-Josèphe (nee Delacour), whom he married in 1957, died last year. They had four sons, Pierre, Jerome, Henry and Romain. • Édouard Balladur, politician, born 2 May 1929; died 31 August 2026 • Stephen Jessel died in 2025

title: US lawmakers demand investigation into Trump administration’s secret surveillance of Americans
summary: Exclusive: Two congressmembers respond to revelations of government snooping on journalists, non-profits and unions
text: Two congressional Democrats asked a government watchdog on Tuesday to investigate the Trump administration’s use of an obscure law to secretly collect records on journalists, non-profits and unions without judicial oversight. The request from the Oregon senator Ron Wyden and the representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington seen by the Guardian comes amid mounting scrutiny over the way the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) recently used its power to issue administrative summonses related to customs matters to make extraordinary unilateral demands for information. They sent their request to the government accountability office (GAO), the non-partisan congressional watchdog. The Guardian reported this week that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), the investigative arm of the DHS, has used the summonses to secretly obtain six months’ worth of telephone records for Georgia Fort, a Minneapolis journalist. In one particularly stunning episode, it issued an administrative summons to Google requesting information on the YouTube accounts of Fort and Don Lemon after a judge had twice rejected a search warrant application for the information, telling the government Fort and Lemon needed to have a chance to contest the request. HSI sought the records after federal prosecutors charged Fort and Lemon with civil rights crimes in connection with a protest at a Saint Paul, Minnestoa, church in January that they were covering. Both have pleaded not guilty. The DHS has used administrative summonses to successfully obtain financial information on labor unions and Venmo transactions for a non-profit group. The DHS has also issued a slew of administrative subpoenas to tech giants such as Meta, X and Reddit to try to unmask anonymous DHS critics. Wyden and Jayapal asked the GAO to investigate the way that the DHS was using the summonses outside of customs matters. It also asked the GAO to investigate language in each summons requesting that the recipients of the summons not notify the user of its existence because it would “impede the investigation and thereby interfere with the enforcement of federal law”. Privacy experts say that language is not legally binding and the companies can ignore it. “Crucially, the recipients of these subpoenas – often third-party companies and service providers – maintain a First Amendment right to notify their customers of the demand, allowing the actual targets of the subpoenas the opportunity to assert their own legal rights or challenge the demand in court,” they added. “We request an audit of HSI’s use of non-disclosure language in immigration subpoenas and customs summonses, as well as the circumstances under which HSI has used customs summonses unrelated to import violations or customs duties.” A GAO spokesperson confirmed the office received the request and was examining it. Wyden and Jayapal also raised concerns about how the Department of Justice and the US Drug Enforcement Administration have used language in subpoenas that pressure companies into keeping a request subpoena private when, in many cases, the law does not prevent notifying the customer about the inquiry. “Although large technology firms with sophisticated counsel sometimes ignore these extra-legal requests, many other businesses in heavily-regulated sectors – such as telecommunications, pharmaceuticals, automotive manufacturing, and banking – often comply out of fear of regulatory retaliation,” they wrote. “Indeed, companies like AT&T and CVS have explicitly cited these extra-legal government demands to Congress to justify their failure to notify customers when their private records are turned over to the government.” Wyden and Jayapal also asked the GAO to identify any changes the DHS made to its policies around administrative summonses after a 2017 DHS inspector general report found they were being used improperly. Wyden and Jayapal additionally asked the judicial conference, the group that oversees policies for the federal courts, to amend the template for a grand jury or trial subpoena to make it clear that recipients are allowed to disclose their existence unless there is a court order prohibiting that. “These steps will help ensure that agencies do not abuse their subpoena authorities at the expense of privacy and free speech rights,” they wrote.

title: Judge strikes down New York law that forced climate polluters to pay damages
summary: State cannot enforce policy requiring oil firms to pay $75bn over 25 years for climate mitigation and adaptation
text: A federal judge has struck down a landmark New York law that forces major polluters to pay climate damages. In her Monday ruling, Brenda Sannes, chief judge of the US district court for the northern district of New York, sided with Republican-led states and oil interests in saying the state cannot enforce its “climate superfund” law, signed by Kathy Hochul, the governor, in December 2024. The policy required big oil companies to pay $75bn over 25 years for projects to help New York pay for climate mitigation and adaptation. Sannes’s 63-page decision said the law was “unusual and sweeping”. It relied on the second circuit’s 2021 decision in City of New York v Chevron, a case in which New York sued oil companies arguing they should pay climate damages. “This decision rests on contested precedent from a fundamentally different case, and Attorney General Tish James must appeal immediately,” said Cassidy DiPaola, communications director for Make Polluters Pay, which supports climate superfund policies. Donald Trump’s justice department argued in support of the lawsuit against the New York policy at a hearing last month. It has also filed its own litigation against it in the southern district of New York; that suit is still pending. Republicans praised Sannes’s decision. “This is a major victory in the fight against liberal states, trying to balance their budgets on the backs of our hard-working men and women in the coal, oil and gas industries,” said JB McCuskey, attorney general of West Virginia, whose office led the challenge against the New York law. Hochul has not yet confirmed if they will appeal the decision. The office is reviewing the decision to “determine possible next steps”, said Ken Lovett, senior communications adviser on energy and environment for Hochul. Vermont, the only other state to have passed a climate superfund law, is facing a parallel legal challenge. Similar bills proposed in other states have not been passed into law. “The fossil fuel industry would like nothing more than for one district court ruling in New York to scare lawmakers across the country into backing down, but this decision doesn’t bind other states or stop them from passing their own laws,” said DiPaola. “If allowed to stand, some of the richest corporations in history get to walk away from $75bn they owe New Yorkers. The floods will still come, roads will still wash out and communities will still need billions to protect themselves.”

title: Is flying a shark drone a boring job? Possibly – until suddenly it isn’t
summary: Taha Kafil-Hussain flies a drone above Coogee beach. Mostly he zooms in on seaweed or turtles – but occasionally he spots a shark and clears the water
text: “Hey Taha, what’s the visibility like?” shouts a man with a towel slung over his shoulder. “Uh, nice,” says Surf Life Saving New South Wales drone operator Taha Kafil-Hussain. “Good?” the man asks. “Very good,” Kafil-Hussain assures him. Thanking him, the early morning swimmer turns and heads down the steps to Coogee beach. Kafil-Hussain, who Guardian Australia has joined on his early morning shark surveillance flight, says: “When they’re local, they just want to see what the weather, what the water looks like, [if there’s] anything scary.” The 22-year-old has been flying drones for SLS NSW for four years, but only at Coogee beach for a matter of weeks. Before a shark attack on 34-year-old Sydney teacher and mother Leah Stewart in June, drone surveillance was not permitted at Coogee because it lies directly under the flight path from Sydney airport’s east-west runway. In an interview with 60 Minutes broadcast on Sunday, Stewart described the horror encounter with a four-metre white shark, after which her left arm was amputated, as “like fighting a dinosaur”. The attack, one of a series of high-profile incidents in Sydney in the past 12 months, has prompted the state government to massively ramp up its shark mitigation program. Under a $34m initiative by the state government which rolled out on 1 July, 38 of Sydney’s ocean beaches, including Coogee, now receive dawn-to-dusk drone monitoring year round. Seventy NSW beaches in total are part of the dawn-to-dusk program, while others will benefit from increased surveillance throughout the summer and school holidays. From Tuesday, surveillance hours increased, running from 6.15am to 5pm each day for the start of spring, as daylight increases. When Guardian Australia meets Kafil-Hussain in mid-winter, he arrives at 6.30am to throw up a marquee, before checking a radio to determine which direction the planes are flying in (drone surveillance at Coogee has been allowed with special permission from the airport). Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Not long after, the drone takes off in a whir of plastic from a miniature landing pad, rising 60 metres into the air before heading out to sea. During each 20-minute flight, Kafil-Hussain rakes the bay in sections from left to right, backwards and forwards, leaving a chequerboard pattern on his control screen. He says he’s looking for “anything moving in a different way than normal”. “Anything moving against the flow of water, anything that looks a little bit long – anything alive, really.” He pauses when he thinks he’s spotted something, to zoom in. “Looks like seaweed,” he says. University of Sydney shark policy expert and associate professor Christopher Pepin-Neff agrees that “drones are the best technology that we have at the moment”. But they say there are “important caveats that we need to give to the public”. “On days that are windy, if the shark is too small, the drone operator is not going to be able to see a shark if it’s there. “I’m slightly nervous that, in the absence of [a] large public education campaign, we have the possibility that we’re going to scare the shit out of people,” says Pepin-Neff. With more drone surveillance comes more regular shark sightings. The NSW government says there have been more 750 sightings and more than 200 intervention actions by Surf Life Saving NSW since 1 July. Shark listening stations are now tracking 1,698 white sharks, 938 tiger sharks and 374 bull sharks – the “target sharks” which are most frequently involved in serious shark bites. Kafil-Hussain says he has seen more bull and tiger sharks than whites, and has raised the alarm a few times, most recently for a bronze whaler – involved in rare attacks – which he initially thought was a target shark. If it’s early and he’s on his own, raising the alarm means making the call to clear the water himself – otherwise he shares what he has seen with lifeguards and they make the decision, with the time from spotting a hazard to fully clearing the water about two or three minutes. The SLS drones have a speaker attached to them, allowing him to communicate directly with surfers and swimmers. It’s a technology familiar to followers of the Instagram account Drone Shark App, run by Jason Iggleden, who has been using a drone since 2018 to surveil beaches including Bondi, Tamarama and Bronte. Videos on the account show an enormous seal barrel-rolling through the water and a swirling vortex of Australian salmon, while in another a whale lingers beneath a kayaker in Tamarama. “I just had a bit of a vision to help … with getting people out of water with sharks, and just showing them the beauty of what’s out there,” he said. The licensed and insured drone flyer, who continues to work independently, now passes on any sightings to SLS NSW. He is a firm believer in the drone surveillance, saying the ability to spot target sharks grows with experience. “I don’t think you really need to consider much more than drones, to be honest,” he says. Pepin-Neff is supportive of other non-lethal technologies, such as SMART drum lines. They say a trial of new artificial intelligence detection software on drones will take the pressure off humans to discern between more and less dangerous sharks. But their message on controversial measures such as shark nets, here to stay on NSW beaches, and culling, is unequivocal: “They do not work.” ‘Not a perfect solution’ Kafil-Hussain, who drives each day from his home in Parramatta, has now flown drones at most Sydney beaches, from Palm beach in the north to Cronulla in the south. Every beach is different – he sees turtles, dolphins, the occasional whale. Coogee is home to a wobbegong, a low-swimming carpet shark which does not hunt humans but can attack if threatened. “He’s not around. He’ll pop out eventually,” says Kafil-Hussain. When Guardian Australia visits the beach, arriving before sunrise, it is already heaving with eastern suburbs dog walkers, swim clubs and surfers. Just weeks after the attack on Stewart, Kafil-Hussain says numbers at the beach have only been growing. Pepin-Neff says the drone program will “restore confidence” ahead of a busy summer, but there is “no silver bullet”. “Drones are a great tool but they’re not a perfect solution.” Pepin-Neff swims at fully enclosed beaches, like Marrinawi Cove in Barangaroo, but their advice for those that swim at unenclosed beaches is: “Swim between the flags.” “The ocean is the wild and we need to treat the beach like the bush.”
