title: College football coach famed for Netflix show fired after calling officials ‘idiots’
summary: Buddy Stephens, who was featured on Last Chance U, publicly criticized his school and league hierarchy
text: A college football coach who rose to prominence in a Netflix documentary series about student athletes trying to make the big time on their final opportunity has been fired after publicly calling officials “idiots” for changing the structure of the league in which his team competed. Buddy Stephens, the coach in question, starred in the first two seasons of the gritty reality show Last Chance U that chronicled the struggles endured by football players at East Mississippi Community College (EMCC) as they juggled academics, challenging home lives and their full-contact sport in their efforts to reach the NFL. The show, which ran for five seasons between 2016 and 2020 while eventually covering programs other than EMCC, was a ratings success – with Stephens and his players coming close to a national championship appearance in the years they were featured. EMCC on Monday announced that Stephens had been let go from his position as head coach that he held for 18 years, days after he appeared at the college football program’s media day and criticized his school along with the hierarchy of the league in which it competes: the Mississippi Association of Community Colleges Conference. “They’re idiots,” Stephens said in comments reported by the Dispatch, a local newspaper, about a restructuring adding an additional game to each team’s schedule and altering the structure of the league’s play-offs. “It’s not a very well thought-out process,” he remarked. “It was really ‘junkified’, the way they decided they were going to do it and there wasn’t a lot of real thought. I was very surprised at how it came out because there were actual people who have doctorates that came up with this.” The changes, Stephens said, were made because some colleges were trying to avoid spending money on travel to play-off games and were concocting a scenario in which they were much more likely to become a host. A statement by EMCC on Monday did not mention Stephens, who won five national titles for the college from 2011 to 2018, all during seasons in which the program was not part of Last Chance U. It also did not provide a reason for why Preston Rice, the college’s associate head coach and offensive coordinator, had been appointed interim head coach “for the remainder of the season”. However, in comments in a post to the college’s Facebook page on Monday night, the EMCC president, Scott Alsobrooks, clearly alluded to Stephens, saying his institution “strongly disavows the remarks published in a recent article”. “While the college supports open and constructive dialogue, personal attacks have no place in that discourse and are contrary to the standards we uphold within our college community,” Alsobrooks said. Alsobrooks also wrote: “These comments are inconsistent with the college’s core values and standards of professionalism, respect, and civility and do not reflect the views, mission, or expectations of EMCC.” The college, he wrote, “sincerely apologizes for the concerns raised by these comments and remains committed to fostering a respectful, professional, and collegial environment for all”. Stephens, who led the college to a 27 August season opening win at Southwest Mississippi Community College, did not immediately comment on his dismissal publicly. During his tenure at EMCC, several players went on to achieve success in the NFL. They include Jarran Reed, defensive tackle for the Seattle Seahawks; Dakota Allen, a linebacker who played four seasons in the professional ranks for various teams; and Za’Darius Smith, defensive end for the Atlanta Falcons.

title: Mark Carney tells US to ‘start being serious’ amid escalating trade war
summary: Canadian PM is set to retaliate against tariffs levied by Donald Trump and criticized US officials over insults
text: Mark Carney has rebuked Donald Trump’s administration and urged officials in Washington to “start being serious” amid escalating trade tensions between the US and Canada. Days before Canada is due to retaliate against Trump’s sweeping tariffs with its own duties on US goods, the Canadian prime minister criticized US officials for insulting his country. “It is beneath their office,” he said. “When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions” about trade, Carney said. Trump signed an executive order last week directing the US federal government to rename Lake Ontario as Lake America – a move that has been rejected by Canadians. The US president’s most senior trade negotiator has meanwhile downplayed the potentially disastrous effects of a US trade war with Canada, declaring the spat to be “more their emergency than ours”. The US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, argued that Canada was more vulnerable after the breakdown in talks set the stage for sweeping tariffs between the two neighbors, telling Politico: “There are no negotiations happening on trade right now.” The comment comes just more than a week after US-Canada trade talks imploded. The US levied 50% tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods. Canada, the US’s second-largest trading partner, announced it would impose retaliatory tariffs on $20bn of American goods starting on 8 September. Now, US residents are poised to feel extreme pressure from Trump’s tariffs and Canada’s retaliatory measures, including on day-to-day items. Greer appeared to blame the escalating trade war on Canadian officials, telling Politico: “It’s not clear Canada wants a deal. “If Canada believes that prohibiting and banning American goods and services is appropriate, then obviously that’s something that the United States should consider as well.” Unacceptable asks from Canada included lighter taxes on heavy-duty trucks, according to Greer, who said such requests torpedoed the trade talks. Canadian officials, on the other hand, attributed the collapsed negotiations to a White House disagreement over who was directing trade talks. Mark Carney, the country’s prime minister, also said that American negotiators saw the French language in Canada as an “irritant”, but added: “In Quebec, these are rights.” Trump, for his part, has argued in recent weeks that Canada “wants the benefits” of being a US state, without being one – a preoccupation of the US president – as he lashed out at the country’s leaders. “They have also charged our great farmers, for many years, massive amounts of tariffs,” claimed Trump. “No more!!!” Greer suggested that negotiations broke down after a misunderstanding around what was, and wasn’t, on the table. “Was that political? I don’t know,” he told Politico. “Was it economic? … I’m not sure how much economic sense it makes because the choice is not between the current tariffs and … you know, duty-free trade. Like, that is that. Those weren’t the options.”

title: Full-blown adulthood: does it actually start at 50?
summary: According to a new survey, that’s the age when people feel most confident and in control of their lives. In other words, they no longer have a chairdrobe ...
text: Name: 50 (and thriving). Age: You can work this one out. Appearance: Cool, calm and collected. Also, very tidy. Don’t you mean frazzled? Come on, wouldn’t you say you’re more together now than you were at 20, or even 30? Who says I’m not still in my 20s? Why are we comparing ages anyway? A new survey has found that 50 is the age at which Brits feel “most confident and in control of their lives”. And what source do we have to thank for this? British Gas commissioned the survey of 2,000 British adults. Getting the boiler serviced is one way to feel like a grownup, I suppose. The survey found that recycling, putting clothes away and knowing when bin day is were widely-agreed-upon indicators that someone had “got it together”. What’s wrong with a chairdrobe? It’s a perfectly workable system! It’s a pile of clothes, is what it is. Respondents also said that having a litter-free car, spare batteries to hand and washing up after a dinner party, instead of leaving it till the next day, were signs of adulthood. I knew I was right to buy that bulk pack of triple As. It’s when you’ve got a spare CR2032 battery that you know you’re really nailing it. These do seem somewhat low or arbitrary bars for having your life together. Oh, so you want to hold people to owning a car, or buying a house, or becoming a parent? Not in this economy. True. But surely there are more meaningful markers of maturity than making your bed, or drinking two litres of water a day? As if you do either every day. You’re right, though: the top-rated sign you’ve got your life under control was making regular savings. Surely it’s what’s on the inside that counts for adulthood, not what’s in your bank account. The next top indicators were enjoying your own company, admitting when you’re wrong and saying no to things you don’t want to do. OK, those are way tougher than knowing when bin day is. It does get confusing around the bank holidays … You’re telling me that you have to be 50 to be on top of all this? That’s the average age respondents felt most in control of their lives. But 30% said they felt nowhere near being sorted, while 56% thought no one ever really is. Didn’t we only just discover that the brain doesn’t reach adulthood until age 32, anyway? Yes, that was a Cambridge University finding last year, and probably more credible than this consumer research. So, if you think about it, by 50 you’ve only been a grownup for 18 years. Long enough to know to make your bed. Do say: “Actually, drinking two litres of water a day is excessive for most people.” Don’t say: “Is it bin day?”

title: Summer of 2026 was UK’s hottest on record, Met Office says
summary: Meteorologists say mean average temperature of 16.5C was made 130 times more likely by climate crisis
text: This year’s summer was the UK’s hottest on record, according to provisional data, and the Met Office said the season’s mean temperature was made 130 times more likely by the climate crisis. Record-breaking and back-to-back heatwaves have scorched much of Europe. In England, temperatures peaked at 38.1C (100.1F) at Kew Gardens in London on 13 August, and June had already been confirmed as the country’s hottest since records began in 1884. Scientists have said these heatwaves are only possible because of the climate crisis driven by burning fossil fuels. The Met Office said an average mean UK temperature of 16.5C made this summer provisionally the warmest on record as well as the warmest season in a series going back to 1884. England, Wales and Northern Ireland broke their respective mean temperature records for summer while Scotland recorded its joint sixth hottest summer. This is the second year in a row that temperature records have been broken, with 2025 and 2026 both the warmest UK summers since records began. The infamous summer of 1976 is now the seventh warmest on record in terms of mean temperature. Katie White, the minister for climate transition, said it was a “brutal reminder that we’re not waiting for climate change to arrive in Britain, we’re living in the middle of it. With kids too hot to sleep, families worrying about older relatives, farmers watching fields dry out, and firefighters and our armed forces battling wildfires, we’ve all woken up to a reality none of us wants for the people and places we love.” England is on track to record its highest ever number of heat-related deaths this summer. The UK Health Security Agency announced on 30 July that an estimated 2,877 people had died in the May and June heatwaves alone. A study conducted by Met Office scientists showed this summer’s record-breaking heat was made about 130 times more likely because of human-induced climate change. The Met Office’s climate projections indicate that UK summers will continue to become hotter. The Met Office’s head of climate attribution, Dr Mark McCarthy, said: “The summer of 2026 has been remarkable and is an example of the extremes we can expect to see more frequently as a consequence of human-induced climate change.” Education, health services and transport all suffered in the heat, with many schools closed and hospital appointments cancelled. Across Europe, extreme heat has been linked to at least 35,000 excess deaths over the summer. The hot weather has been coupled with extreme and persistent drought and severe wildfires. England had its driest July on record with only 6.5mm of rainfall, which was 10% of its long-term meteorological average for the month and less than half of the previous record low of 13.4mm set in 1911. A wildfire near the Sizewell nuclear plant in Suffolk caused “total devastation” to a protected landscape, and in Stourbridge 19 homes were destroyed after multiple fires spread across the West Midlands. In his first Commons address as prime minister on Tuesday, Andy Burnham referenced the devastating Nepal-Tibet floods and said: “This is what the climate crisis looks like. We have just ourselves experienced what is likely to have been the hottest summer on record. This government will meet the climate challenge, and I can confirm to the house that I will attend Cop31 in Turkey in November.” On Wednesday, the Conservative party is due to present a 10-minute rule motion to parliament to repeal the Climate Change Act 2008. This act was a landmark piece of legislation which enshrined the UK’s legally binding net zero target into law. Alasdair Johnstone from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit said the act was designed to reduce short-term political expediency and to keep successive UK governments on track to cut emissions. “The science is very clear that reaching net zero emissions is the only way to stop baking in ever higher temperatures, the likes of which have put the UK on track for its worst harvest on record, pushing up food prices and threatening the basics of our food security,” he said. Dr James Pope, a Met Office climate scientist, said: “This summer will also be remembered for how dry it has been, particularly in the south in July. Looking at climate projections for rainfall, this summer fits closely to what we would expect an average summer to look like in the UK under 3C of global warming, as we expect summers to become both hotter and drier in the future.” Dr Amy Doherty, who leads the Met Office’s National Climate Information Centre, said: “The conditions we’ve seen this summer have broken UK climate records once again. These records are now breaking with increasing frequency, reflecting the influence of human-induced climate change on the temperatures we’re experiencing in the UK. “Particularly notable is how much we’ve exceeded the previous summer mean temperature record [16.1C), set just last year. The figures also knock the infamous summer of 1976 down to seventh for average summer mean temperature, with the top five warmest summers all occurring since 2003.”

title: ‘Not perfectly aligned’ with human values: Anthropic admits security failures behind AI hacking incidents
summary: US owner of Claude chatbot previously said its models had hacked three organisations during testing
text: The US startup behind the Claude chatbot has admitted a series of hacking incidents involving its models reflected a “failure of operational security” and said it has tightened its testing procedures. Anthropic revealed in July that its models had accessed the open internet three times and gained unauthorised access to the systems of three organisations. In a new blogpost on the incidents, the company admitted its technology was “not perfectly aligned” with human values and goals. Anthropic said the models had been deliberately tested without cybersecurity safeguards, and that they had been able to reach the open internet – the AI testing equivalent of leaving the front door open – due to a misunderstanding with an external testing company. As a result, the company said it had initially paused internal and external cybersecurity testing of models to introduce a tighter safety regime. “We had been largely relying on a single layer of defense … where we needed several,” said Anthropic. The startup has now put in place extra measures including: an alert system for when a model attempts to break out of a testing environment or gains internet access; walling off its riskiest test environments more effectively; and requiring external testing companies to commit to a set of safety standards, including making explicit instructions to models during testing – such as “you should not access the internet”. Anthropic said in July that three unnamed organisations had been hacked by three of its models after a “misunderstanding” with the company’s testing partner, a firm called Irregular, that resulted in the models gaining internet access. Following the implementation of new measures, Anthropic said it had resumed internal and external cybersecurity tests. Like OpenAI, which revealed a testing safety breach in the same month, Anthropic said it had paused some high-risk reinforcement learning – a trial-and-error development technique where AIs are rewarded for working out how to carry out a specific task. In its latest blogpost, Anthropic said it had found that defective training setups were “disproportionately large contributors” to misaligned behaviour, the term for when an AI fails to adhere to – or “align” with – human values like not committing harm. The startup said it had found two alignment failures in the testing incidents: “motivated reasoning”, where despite finding evidence they might be connected to the internet, they may still have adhered to the “belief” they were in a simulated environment and thus not breaching their test lab; and a “recklessness” factor where the models were willing to take harmful action on the internet to pursue the narrow goal of passing a cybersecurity test. Anthropic said it was tackling a phenomenon in AI development known as “reward-hacking”. This is where a model finds ways to game its training process and earn “rewards” without completing a task – an unsanctioned shortcut. However, Anthropic said, the testing incidents showed it still had some way to go despite trying to limit reward-hacking. “As evidenced by the incidents … our process isn’t perfect and our models are not perfectly aligned,” the company said. Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey, said Anthropic has admitted “its factory was running faster than its quality control”. He added: “Two things outran Anthropic’s controls this spring – the training pipeline and the security. The incidents are what that gap looks like from the outside.” The company, which is preparing for a stock market flotation that could value the business at $2tn (£1.47tn), reiterated its call for coordinated action between government and industry on pacing industry development. “We believe the world would benefit if the industry adopted a lawful, verifiable, effective mechanism for coordinated pacing as soon as possible,” Anthropic said. The blogpost added: “The July incidents have stressed that the urgency of improving our cybersecurity defenses is even higher than we previously believed.” As well as the similar breach at OpenAI, the Anthropic incidents followed an episode at the UK’s AI Security Institute, which reported in August that OpenAI and Anthropic models had carried out a hacking campaign against real people during a cybersecurity test. The Guardian also revealed last month that incidents of AIs escaping users’ control have hit a new high, almost doubling in July compared with the previous month to more than 300.

title: Russia kills at least 12 on sixth night of drone attacks on Kyiv
summary: Zelenskyy says Moscow is capitalising on shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors to lower morale in capital
text: At least 12 people have been killed in and around Kyiv overnight as Ukraine’s capital endured a sixth consecutive night of Russian drone and missile attacks aimed at shattering infrastructure and lowering the morale of the city. Eight of the dead were reported killed in Kyiv, including seven at a railway depot on the city’s left bank, and four were killed in Boryspil, to the east of the city, in a wave of strikes at about 2.30am after hours of air alerts. A further four people were killed in other parts of Ukraine, regional officials said, in 28 waves of attacks that included a strike on a border crossing point with Romania on the Danube at Orlivka. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, said “a significant number of jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles were used in the attack” and that Russia was taking advantage of a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors. In a morning post on social media, Zelenskyy said: “Russia always plans its strikes specifically to cause as much destruction to people’s lives as possible, and it succeeds only when air defence capabilities are insufficient.” Kyiv and the surrounding towns and villages have come under sustained attack in the past few days. Thirty-eight people were killed after a Russian drone struck an ammunition store in Myla, 15 miles west of Kyiv, on Thursday, the hit causing hours of secondary explosions and damaging nearby homes. Ukraine’s air force said Russia had attacked 28 locations, focusing on the cities of Kyiv and Odesa and their surroundings. Air defences shot down five Iskander ballistic missiles, two Banderol and five Kalibr cruise missiles and 187 out of 218 drones. Officials no longer reveal the total numbers of missiles fired. Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, the chief executive of Ukrainian Railways, said six of the seven people killed in and around the depot were employees of the network. Another rail worker was hospitalised, he added. Kyiv has been chronically short of air defence systems since the supply of Patriot interceptors dried up. The Patriots are the only weapon that can effectively stop high-speed Russian ballistic missiles, made at the rate of about 60 a month. Lockheed Martin, the US company that makes the most capable Pac-3 interceptors, produces about 600 a year, but US military supplies have been depleted during the US war with Iran. Ukraine is trying to secure a stockpile of about 300 for the winter, paid for by European allies, in a supply deal agreed with the US. Moscow appears to be trying to take advantage of an absence of air defence capability before winter, in an escalation of a conflict nearly deadlocked on the frontline. Ukraine has been responding by attacking oil refineries, warehouses and other military facilities deep inside Russia, aiming to hurt the country’s economy. Ukraine’s GUR military intelligence said it had attacked an oil refinery at the Baltic port of Ust-Luga, about 550 miles (885km) from its border. Russian officials said a civilian was killed in the border Belgorod region in an attack. Russia captured 35 square miles (56 sq km) of Ukraine’s territory during August, analysis by the AFP news agency concluded. It was Moscow’s largest advance since February but still much lower than the 150 square mile a month average of 2025. There remains little serious diplomatic effort to end the war, although on Monday India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, urged Vladimir Putin to end the war in public remarks at a bilateral meeting in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. “Every day that the war continues, humanity is, in effect, set back a step, while every step towards peace gives all of humanity real hope for peace. We need to move from endless war to an end to the war,” Modi ⁠said. Putin appeared impatient, tapping his feet as he listened. “Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path,” he replied.

title: AI chatbot helps teach online-only psychology classes at Macquarie University
summary: University’s move is part of trend that critics within academia say will lead to further staff cuts and loss of ‘everything that makes the job worth doing’
text: An Australian university has offered students classes with an AI chatbot and minimal human interaction in two subjects, as institutions give the technology more teaching responsibilities. Macquarie University’s Virtual Peer is part of each week’s learning in two mandatory psychology units, programmed to ask students questions and guide them through scenario-based exercises. The university said the AI activities were optional and only “supplement” the “core learning” of online readings, quizzes and videos. However, neither the core nor the AI activities are mandatory. Students are assessed on separate research tasks and exams. Both subjects had in-person classes in the first semester of this year, but were online-only for the second semester. The university said in-person classes would return in 2027 in alternate semesters so students could pick the format that suited their circumstances. Previously the online versions of the subjects included optional weekly tutorials with paid academics via Zoom. Material is now taught only by Virtual Peer and other online activities and videos. One student, who asked to remain anonymous, said they felt “short-changed” after issues with their degree structure forced them to enrol in the online option. “Instead of a group discussion or a tutor teaching you, it’s a class activity done with a robot,” the student said. “I feel like I’m teaching this robot how to take jobs away from my teachers.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Macquarie said the tool was designed in partnership with educators to support, not replace, them. Professors who used Virtual Peer uploaded the information it uses and checked it, the university said, making it more tailored than general-purpose AI tools. Experts say that could make the tool potentially less prone to “hallucination”, or inventing content without evidence. Macquarie can also monitor student conversations on the service, according to the university. The subjects still have paid tutors who run optional, unstructured Zoom feedback sessions each week. One introductory-level subject has six sessions a week for its 400 students, while the other final-year subject has 10 sessions a week for its 700 students – or roughly one class for every 70 students. Students who want to speak to a human for feedback are encouraged to attend. Macquarie said attendance at these was variable and rose around assessment due dates. Each individual psychology subject costs $2,174 for Australian students with commonwealth supported places in 2026. A three-year undergraduate degree now costs over $50,000. Virtual Peer was also used for learning activities in other subjects but was not available in all classes, Macquarie said. Its use has accelerated, answering close to 80,000 student questions in all of 2025 but nearly as many in just the first half of 2026, most of which were administrative questions. The university said staff and students overwhelmingly found the tool valuable or recommended its use when surveyed. Backlash to AI teaching grows Macquarie has been one of a handful of Australian universities to systematically incorporate AI into teaching, alongside the University of Melbourne and the University of Sydney, as the technology attracts growing student use – and backlash. Meena Jha, an associate professor at Central Queensland University, said she had not previously heard of any universities simultaneously cutting in-person teaching and introducing AI chatbots in her research into AI in higher education. “Students require that human touch … [and] engagement will be a very big issue if we replace everything with virtual tutors,” said Jha, who is also the head of CQU’s pedagogy and technology cluster. CQU is piloting its homegrown AI tool, named “Birdy”, as a “service/support tool” in 24 units. Jha has gone further, building an AI avatar in her likeness, named Neena Chatbot, to answer her students’ questions. “You have to give a bit of time for people to try it, use it, see value in it, and in doing so you need to guide them how they can use it,” Jha said. The University of Sydney has positioned itself as a leader in the field, with hundreds of academics using its education-focused generative AI platform, “Cogniti”, for chatbots and scenario exercises. It has shared Cogniti with other institutions in Australia, New Zealand and the Netherlands. The university in late August released a discussion paper that envisions futures where AI takes on even greater responsibilities, delivering personalised teaching for each student in each unit, while staff-student contact hours decline. A university spokesperson said Sydney was only supporting staff to use technology to improve student experience. “Human judgment, accountability and relationships are essential to everything we do, and can never be replaced by technology,” the spokesperson said. “This isn’t a cost-saving measure in any way.” Peter Chen, president of the university’s national tertiary education union (NTEU) branch, said the paper had added to growing staff concern about their future at the university as funding shortfalls left fewer academics to run bigger classes. “For some staff, they’re afraid they’re going to lose their jobs,” Chen said. “For other staff, the concern is that everything that makes the job worth doing will be lost … and they will be there simply to take the blame when things go wrong. The university’s staff plan to go on strike on Wednesday, fighting for AI protections and other support against growing workloads and job insecurity. Chen said the union would not accept a deal that did not address AI. The university said it would continue to engage in bargaining but Wednesday’s strike was “premature”. AI’s rapid evolution meant it should be governed at the university’s discretion through policy, rather than set in a three-year enterprise agreement, its spokesperson said. But Dr Alison Barnes, national president of the NTEU and a Macquarie academic, said staff across the sector would fight for workplace agreements that address AI. “University staff are being hammered by a workload crisis, but simply papering over those cracks with piecemeal AI rollouts could actually create even more damaging issues,” Barnes said. • The headline and text of this article were amended on 2 September 2026 to clarify the role of Virtual Peer in the relevant courses.

title: New system for screening mail-in ballots risks denying entire batches, says whistleblower
summary: US senator says that project, a key part of Trump’s voting restrictions, is ‘perilously rushed and potentially unlawful’
text: A new system to screen millions of mail-in ballots for this November’s US midterm elections was thrown together so hastily, and tested so little, that a single scanning glitch could see entire batches of ballots turned away, a whistleblower has told Congress. The project – a key part of Donald Trump’s new restrictions on voting – is “perilously rushed and potentially unlawful”, according to the US senator Richard Blumenthal, who disclosed the warning in a letter to David Steiner, the postmaster general, on Tuesday. Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the US Senate’s permanent subcommittee on investigations, said the account he had received made clear the US Postal Service “lacks the technical or operational capability” to roll it out safely before ballots go out to voters. The system stems from a March executive order by Trump tightening federal control over mail-in voting, directing USPS to check ballots against a federally approved voter list before sending them – a break from its usual role of simply delivering whatever is handed over by states. Courts have blocked and unblocked parts of the order repeatedly since, amid lawsuits arguing it oversteps into territory the constitution leaves to states. USPS calls the result the “Federal Ballot Mail Portal”. Officials upload voter and barcode data in advance; clerks then scan a sample of arriving ballots – 15 to 400, depending on batch size – against that list. According to the whistleblower’s disclosure, the system runs on a “zero percent failure rate”: one mismatched scan rejects the entire batch, even if it holds tens of thousands of ballots. USPS was contacted for comment. Engineers had roughly three months, including a court-ordered pause, for work the whistleblower says would normally take close to a year. The full system was not even assembled for testing until about 24 August, the disclosure says, leaving only a handful of working days to catch problems before launch. By the final week, officials were reportedly calling the effort “a shit show”, and one worker who raised concerns about the lack of testing time was told simply: “We cannot fail.” About a third of voters cast ballots by mail in 2024. The whistleblower’s prediction of mass disruption remains unconfirmed – the system had not gone live as of this week. “The whistleblower’s allegations make clear that USPS lacks the technical or operational capability needed to effectively implement the EO’s [executive order’s] provisions in a way that safeguards every citizen’s right to vote in the upcoming midterm elections,” Blumenthal wrote. “Despite this, the Trump Administration appears intent on USPS moving forward with its flawed plans, no matter the chaos they may create.” Blumenthal’s letter also alleges USPS kept building the portal under active court orders to stop, including one issued on 27 August that remains in force. “USPS should have ceased all work on the Portal on June 25, 2026,” he wrote. Blumenthal has given USPS until 4 September to answer questions, including who ordered the work to begin and resume, and until 8 September to hand over internal records. USPS has not disclosed an expected rejection rate, which the whistleblower says was withheld because it would expose how shaky the rollout is. The representative Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House oversight committee, said his panel had received similar reports. “This new secret tracking system at the US Postal Service is faulty, untested, and threatens to totally disrupt ballot delivery for millions of American citizens,” Garcia said, calling the policy an “unconstitutional and dangerous power grab”.

title: Norway’s new king swears oath of allegiance with daughter at his side
summary: Haakon VIII promises to uphold 1814 constitution but his queen misses ceremony because of post-surgery ‘complications’
text: King Haakon VIII swore an oath of allegiance before Norway’s parliament on Tuesday in the first major stage in the passing of the crown since the death of his father after 35 years on the throne. Wearing a ceremonial uniform, Haakon, who became king when Harald V died on Friday, promised to uphold Norway’s 1814 constitution with his 22-year-old daughter, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, by his side. “I promise and swear that I will govern the kingdom of Norway in accordance with its constitution and laws, so help me God, the almighty and omniscient,” the 53-year-old king pledged to cabinet ministers and MPs in the main chamber of the 169-seat parliament. Haakon’s wife, Mette-Marit, 53, was unable to attend the 17-minute ceremony because of complications after a lung transplant in June. Her doctors said such complications were not uncommon. Are Holm, a pulmonologist at Oslo university hospital, said the queen had had “complications on some occasions with the operation, including today. As a result, she must be put under observation throughout the day today.” Harald, whose funeral will be held in Oslo on 9 September, with heads of state from around the world invited to attend, was widely appreciated in Norway for his warmth, unassuming lifestyle and dedication to preserving national unity. Tens ⁠of thousands of Norwegians have flocked to the royal palace to lay flowers, drawings, candles and flags. A poll for the public broadcaster NRK found the monarchy’s popularity had risen over the past few months. The first survey since Harald’s death at the age of 89 found that about 72% of Norwegians supported the monarchy, compared with 54% in May. In February, while the royal family was mired in a succession of scandals, support for the institution fell to 60%. Mette-Marit has faced strong criticism for her association with Jeffrey Epstein, while her son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, is appealing against a four-year sentence for two rape convictions. Responding to Haakon’s oath, Masud Gharahkhani, the parliament’s president, who arrived in Norway as a child refugee from Iran, said Harald had personified “the values that underpin our liberal democracy”, including compassion. There will be no formal coronation of the new king and queen because Norway abolished the ceremony more than a century ago but Haakon may, like his father and grandfather, choose to have his accession consecrated at Trondheim’s Nidaros Cathedral. Harald, who will be buried in the royal mausoleum at the Akershus Fortress in Oslo, died while being treated in hospital for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells.

title: Dyson launches £420 toothbrush that films ‘live cleaning footage’ inside your mouth
summary: James Dyson says ‘complete dental system’ will also include toothpaste and mouth rinse that each cost £8.50
text: It is the live stream you never wanted to see but may find impossible to resist: rolling footage beamed live from inside your mouth while you are cleaning your teeth. Dyson, the home appliance maker that made its name inventing bagless vacuums and bladeless fans, has turned its attention to oral hygiene with a £420 all-singing, all-dancing toothbrush that can clean, floss and even spray tiny jets of mouthwash. In simpler times, a handle and bristles were enough, but the Dyson toothbrush, which took six years and the brainpower of 661 engineers to develop, has a “100k pixel macro lens camera” and an “anti-gravity (mouthwash) tank” on board. The camera functions as a “high-quality endoscope”, according to the company, enabling users to “see what their dentist sees”. The brusher can watch “live cleaning footage” on the MyDyson app and get feedback on their cleaning regime. On Tuesday, James Dyson, the company’s founder and chief engineer, launched the hi-tech toothbrush at an event in Paris. Engineers and scientists at the company – which despite the billionaire inventor’s support for Brexit moved its corporate base to Singapore in 2019 – had “spent well over a decade understanding oral care regimes and how nasties build up in the mouth”, Dyson explained. The rigorous process included developing a “proxy plaque” so it could test plaque removal accurately. Flossing was an “awkward and time-consuming chore” and “few of us do it even though we know we should”, he said. “Our research has shown that people consistently miss the areas where plaque forms: the gaps between teeth.” And while you will be familiar with the process of moving a toothbrush up and down with your hand, Dyson explained that by “combining a camera, machine learning, precision fluid dynamics, advanced brushing technologies, connectivity and wifi” the toothbrush offered an “entirely new way to keep your mouth healthy”. When the camera detects gaps between teeth, the jet on the stem releases a burst of mouth rinse to remove plaque as you brush, while the brush head cleans along the gum line and lifts surface stains. The brush claims to remove “up to 72% more plaque than market leading electric toothbrushes”. No dental routine would be complete without toothpaste, and Dyson’s claims to be a “complete dental system” with a non-foaming toothpaste and mouth rinse (so as not to obscure the camera lens) that each cost £8.50. Dyson is entering a crowded market as there are already dozens of ultra-advanced toothbrushes, including smart models with apps, that promise everything from plaque and stain removal to tongue cleaning. The Phillips Sonicare DiamondClean, for example, which is available in Boots and John Lewis, comes with a £600 price tag. If you don’t have a big toothbrush budget, the good news is that the British Dental Association (BDA) says you don’t need one. You just need to follow your dentist’s advice and brush twice a day. Eddie Crouch, the BDA’s chair, said: “Patients shouldn’t be lulled into thinking the latest gizmos will solve all their oral health problems. Big brands with high price tags are no substitute for a proper routine.”

title: UK long-term borrowing costs could halve chancellor’s budget headroom
summary: Yield on 30-year gilts highest since 1998 as rout triggered by global factors underlines tricky backdrop John Healey faces
text: The chancellor’s headroom against Labour’s fiscal rules could be almost halved at his first budget if the current global bond sell-off persists into the autumn, economists say. The UK’s long-term borrowing costs jumped to their highest level since early 1998 on Tuesday as investors dumped government bonds, betting on higher inflation. The yield – in effect the interest rate – on 30-year UK government bonds, known as gilts, hit 5.89% at one point as London markets caught up with a sell-off that swept Japan and the US on Monday, a bank holiday in the UK. Ten-year gilt yields were around 5.25%, their highest level since the 2008 global financial crisis. Higher yields progressively increase the cost of financing the government’s debt. If sustained, these would pass through to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR)’s forecasts for John Healey’s 28 October budget. Deutsche Bank’s chief UK economist, Sanjay Raja, said that based on Tuesday’s yields, Healey’s headroom against the current budget rule would fall from £26bn at Rachel Reeves’s spring forecast to £13.8bn before covering any additional spending plans. Almost all of the deterioration results from higher government interest costs. The OBR’s March forecast had gilt yields at 5.1% for this year. Gilt yields eased back a bit later on Tuesday – to 5.85% for the 30-year and 5.21% for the 10-year – but they are still well above the predicted level. Raja suggested Healey would be likely to try to maintain headroom of at least £10bn to assuage market concerns about the government’s commitment to balancing the books. “£10bn to me is the floor. In a perfect world you would want to keep 15,” he said. In addition to global forces, Raja said higher-than-expected growth in the UK in the first half of the year had also contributed to rising yields. “There are some good reasons,” he said. The current budget rule is the promise that the government will match day-to-day spending with receipts and only borrow for longer-term projects. Tuesday’s market moves underline the tricky global backdrop facing Andy Burnham’s government as he returns to Westminster promising to help consumers with the cost of living. The OBR takes market expectations of future gilt yields during a two-week reference period in to account in its forecasts. It does not announce these dates in advance, but Raja suggested judging by the timing in previous years, the current tumultuous period may be included in its budget projections. The bond sell-off was driven primarily by international factors. Japanese 10-year yields hit their highest level since the 1990s over expectations that the Bank of Japan would have to raise interest rates to control inflation. Investors also appeared to be responding partly to higher oil prices, which were up 3.8% at nearly $94 a barrel after renewed hostilities between the US and Iran. Higher energy costs drive up inflation, potentially forcing central banks to respond. As well as fretting about future price rises, bond investors also appear to be concerned about runaway deficits in the US, where the Trump administration has cut taxes and is having to hand back much of the revenue from swingeing trade tariffs. The chief economist at the consultancy Capital Economics, Neil Shearing, said: “It’s been a perfect storm for the bond markets: we’ve had these fiscal concerns that have pushed up the long end of the curve, and now that’s being compounded by upward energy price pressure, pushing up interest rate expectations in the short term – and if you’re sitting in the Treasury, none of that is good news.” Finance ministers and central bankers from the G20 major economies concluded their meeting in North Carolina to discuss the state of the global economy on Tuesday. The US and Japan took the rare step of intervening jointly in global foreign exchange markets in August in an attempt to prop up the yen, but the Japanese currency subsequently resumed its slide. Expectations of higher interest rates were also piqued by a speech on Friday by the Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, in which he said the US central bank would still have “work to do” if inflation did not return to target. Before Warsh’s intervention, markets were betting on about a one-third probability of an increase in US rates in September, but that has risen to 70%.

title: Four Maga defectors on what led them to walk away: ‘I’d been addicted to fear and rage’
summary: Ex-Maga supporters unpack their role in bolstering Trump’s platform and share what brought them to the Leaving Maga non-profit support network
text: Since Donald Trump’s first presidential campaign a decade ago, “Make America Great Again” (Maga) has evolved from a slogan into an identity, one that claims to center conservative, “America first” values and relies on lies and conspiracy theories to stay afloat. And while Maga has survived impeachments, indictments and a lost election, some devotees are walking away – and doing so loudly. Rich Logis, a former Trump campaign volunteer, left Maga in 2022, publishing a public apology to help others see that it was OK to challenge the movement. The overwhelming response led him to found the non-profit Leaving Maga, a network of support groups and meetups for people to unpack their role in bolstering Trump’s platform. Logis said he doesn’t persuade people to leave; he just gives them a place to land when they do. The group’s billboard campaign, now running in 27 states, is built around a simple message: “Having doubts? You are not alone.” Thousands of people have since found the organization and connected with others who have left through group chats and in-person meet-ups. When they pull away from Maga, many are left reckoning with their childhoods, their value systems, their relationships and faith, Logis said. They question why they were vulnerable to hateful rhetoric and sought a place to belong. They also face criticism from all sides. Maga dismisses them as sellouts and traitors for leaving, while some on the left argue that people who once amplified conspiracy theories – and harmed vulnerable communities in the process – don’t deserve a second act. But Leaving Maga wants to be a bridge when people are ready to finally step away. “There are a lot of us out there doing this work, and it keeps growing because it’s a safe place,” said Steven Francisci, who turned to Leaving Maga in 2024. “That’s what people really need: to feel safe enough to ask questions.” Below, four people share what it’s like to publicly leave Maga. ‘When you lack empathy, you let the so-called red flags go’ Steven Francisci, Virginia My Italian American dad was a huge Fox News person and Trump supporter. Growing up, I already had a lot of unhealthy beliefs around race, identity and LGBTQ+ issues. I didn’t really have a place where I felt like I belonged, and that creates the environment where you’re led toward whoever will accept you. When I joined the military, I found people who reminded me of friends and family back home. I grew up in New York City, and after 9/11, I became Islamophobic. Around that same time, I moved down to the Bible belt, and after being raised Catholic, I became an evangelical. In 2015, I almost died in a motorcycle accident. I had a traumatic brain injury, and every bone in my face was broken. My daughter was eight days old. I was already really unhealthy, my marriage was struggling and in 2016 I had a suicide attempt. Even after all that, I still voted for Trump. He had this tough-guy, business-mobster image, and I hadn’t yet reckoned with everything coming out about his past. When you lack compassion and empathy, you let the so-called red flags go, because it doesn’t seem that bad. By 2020, I’d bought my Maga hat and was advocating for his re-election. After getting divorced from my second wife and remarrying [again], I started getting into trauma-informed therapy. I started asking questions, and I spent years diving into stuff to find answers, doing self-reflection and questioning beliefs I’d inherited from childhood. I think that’s an important part of this conversation: the mental health of our country. There’s a real lack of empathy here. Getting away from Maga and Trump did not happen overnight. It was slowly, slowly, slowly, and then all of a sudden I was like: “Oh my God, this guy is a freaking psychopath.” I couldn’t see it until I could see myself more clearly. By 2024, I had real momentum out of Maga, and I voted for Kamala Harris. I joined my local Democratic committee and even considered running for my school board. I wasn’t outspoken when my dad was alive because I wanted to stay connected to him. I felt that if I went too liberal, he might have just said: “Screw yourself.” But after he died, I felt more free to explore who I wanted to be. My mom voted for Trump three times. My partner voted for Trump three times, too. Since I’ve changed, neither of them can stand him any more. I’ve educated them both on how he’s manipulative, how he’s controlling, and I’ve shown them the contradictions and the history. When you give people enough facts, at some point, it’s hard not to pause and say: “Wait a minute, maybe I was wrong.” ‘I was so deep in what I can only call a religious psychosis’ Stephania Messina, Michigan After having my third son, I had severe postpartum depression, though I wasn’t really aware of it at the time. I turned to faith and got “saved”. I was struggling with the overwhelm of three kids and working. I can see now that what I was really struggling with was the patriarchy. Our labor wasn’t evenly divided. I had no vocabulary for any of that, so I turned to the church instead. I remember thinking: I don’t need to work. I don’t need to worry about how I’m going to afford these kids, because God’s going to figure it out. If I’m obedient, if I surrender to the leadership of my husband, then God is going to bless me. I took that 100% seriously. I was a tradwife, because that’s where they want to keep you. They don’t want you knowing about politics. It wasn’t my job to vote or to know who to vote for. I was just supposed to submit to my husband and do what he thought was necessary. I never wore a red hat. I never went to a Trump rally. My Maga was “Make America Godly Again.” My loyalty wasn’t to Trump. My loyalty was to God and the church. I was told: “Don’t even look at leftwing media, because it’s demonic.” I was so deep in what I can only call a religious psychosis. Covid is what really broke it. I’m a respiratory therapist, and I watched Trump say masks work, then masks don’t work. My own pastor preached that the lockdowns were a demonic deep-state attempt to keep people out of church. Then in March 2021, my oldest son’s father died in a motorcycle accident. He wasn’t a Christian. At the funeral, the pastor’s wife told my son it was a blessing in disguise that he’d grow up without a non-Christian influence. After that, I was done. I was afraid to speak out, because I thought everyone would hate me. But it wasn’t until my perspective became more progressive that I felt like my empathy came back. I’d been forced into this highly controlled way of thinking, and it doesn’t just come right back. I don’t care how long it takes. I will be deconstructing the rest of my life. ‘I’d been complicit in dividing this country’ Rich Logis, Florida I grew up in a quintessential middle-class household in New York. My parents were as apolitical as could be. To my knowledge, they never even voted. It was really in college when I started to develop my own political sensibilities, and I spent many years voting for third-party candidates. By 2015, I was a registered independent. I felt that elected officials cared mostly about their donors and the wealthy and the powerful, and that democracy had failed a lot of people. When Trump came on the scene, I was enticed by his outsider status. I gravitated to the burn-it-all-down ethos of his campaign, because I felt the way to save democracy was to tear it all down and start anew. I didn’t just vote for him. I worked on the campaign. I wrote part of the call script. I recruited Bernie Sanders voters to switch. After 2016, I got deeper and deeper into the Maga community. I became an aspiring pundit, with bylines at Fox News and the Federalist, producing my own podcast. I had probably every hat available from Trump’s 2020 campaign. I don’t call Maga a cult. I refer to it as a community. It’s where people find belonging, camaraderie, a shared sense of trying to make the country great again and a shared enemy. I had a second family in Maga, and, as embarrassed as I am to admit it, that second family sometimes took precedence over my own blood family. I realized after I left that I’d been addicted to fear and rage, addicted to a belief in a “they” coming for my rights, my children, my guns. That addiction was affirmed and reinforced by the media I consumed. The beliefs in Maga are based on lies, falsehoods and conspiracy theories, even if the people who hold them don’t see it that way. The first accelerant to my leaving wasn’t Trump. It was Ron DeSantis platforming Covid anti-vaxxers in 2021, after he’d previously supported the vaccine. It shocked and confused me enough that I started diversifying my news sources – the Times, NPR, the Washington Post – and I slowly began to realize how much of what I’d believed was false. The final straw was the Uvalde school shooting, on 24 May 2022. As a gun owner, I found the predictable response – calling for more guns – offensive. I quietly left Maga that day. Three months later, I published a mea culpa, apologizing to anyone I might have hurt with my words and rhetoric. I genuinely thought no one would care. It turned out people did. That’s how Leaving Maga was born. I had to reckon with the fact that I’d been complicit in dividing this country and amplifying conspiracy theories that caused real suffering. So much of this work is about making amends. There are really two steps to leaving: you have to renounce and repudiate the lies, not just distance yourself from the president, and then you have to actively build back up, rather than tear down. ‘I thought the most I could do in life was be a mom and a wife’ Carter Brown, Georgia I was born into an evangelical Christian home, very strict. I wasn’t allowed to play with Barbies, couldn’t have my nails painted for church. I was also spanked. I don’t have a lot of memories from childhood, and I now suspect that’s from complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD). I wrote a book in kindergarten, and at the end it said: “When Carter grows up, she wants to be a mom.” I’m neurodivergent, with undiagnosed learning disabilities, and I just thought the most I could do in life was be a mom and a wife. I was like: “OK, God designed me to be that.” I went to college to be a kindergarten teacher, because I truly thought that’s all I could do. In 2016, I was actually in rehab, getting out of an opiate addiction, so I didn’t end up voting. But my family, who had just saved me and paid for that rehab, was telling me Trump was who we needed to save the country, who Christians needed. In 2019, I learned about Save the Children and QAnon, and I fell for it hook, line and sinker. It was under the guise of helping children. Conspiracy theories got me. My main fracture in all this was when I realized I could read the Bible differently than the way I was told to read it. I found this Harvard study that said being spanked and being sexually assaulted trigger a similar response in the brain. And I was someone who has been sexually assaulted. I was like: “My God would not create the brain to feel the effects of [being sexually assaulted], and then also want that to be the same form of discipline that was implemented in the Bible.” That was the domino that knocked everything else down: hell, purity culture, all of it. Then in January 2025, someone who knew I was into conspiracy theories sent me a video making a factual, historical case that hell isn’t real. I watched it, and the house of cards fell for me. That led to a few months of a really deep depression, an identity collapse. I had to accept that changing meant risking my husband, my family, my friends, everything I’d ever known. But I realized I had to do what was best for me in order to be best for everybody else, because living an inauthentic life has ripple effects on the people around you.

title: High winds during El Niño could be deadly for England’s stressed trees, say experts
summary: Head of tree collections at Kew ‘very worried about this autumn’ as hot, dry summer has caused brittleness
text: High winds associated with El Niño could cause widespread mortality among tree species already weakened by a prolonged period of extreme heat and drought, experts have warned. This summer much of Europe has been scorched by a series of record-breaking climate crisis-induced heatwaves. The impact is notable across much of England’s countryside, where once green land has turned brown, and many trees are undergoing “early autumn” – wilting and losing their leaves early – to cope with extreme heat. Kevin Martin, head of tree collections at Kew Gardens, said to cope with these extreme conditions, trees had not grown as they normally would, and had become less flexible and more brittle. “If we see the extreme winds that are predicted this year because of El Niño, we’re going to see potentially large impacts on trees,” he said. The UK’s Met Office has said the El Niño event developing over the Pacific Ocean is likely to be the strongest for more than a century, with increased rainfall and storms forecast to hit the UK this autumn. El Niño is a natural phenomena that has been made worse by global heating. Martin said this extreme weather could lead to root death, where dry weather followed by heavy rain can undermine the structure of the soil. “We could then start to see some trees actually fail at the root plate. I’m really worried about this autumn,” he said. This year’s weather has been so extreme that Martin thinks some species could be lost completely from certain landscapes. “We may lose species like the silver birch, the common beech and oak from landscapes where we’re used to seeing them,” he said. While the impact is widespread, the heat is disproportionately affecting the oldest trees, with experts warning that England’s ancient oaks are dying in the hot and dry weather. Martin said that what made 2026 so unprecedented was the spring heatwave, when temperatures reached 35C, making it the hottest May ever recorded. “The whole growing season this year has been under stress, I don’t think we’ve ever experienced environmental impact like this before,” he said. Simon Richmond, a technical officer at the Arboricultural Association, said trees were extremely resilient organisms, able to adapt to one-off years of extreme weather. However, he said the “danger that we face now is the likelihood with climate change of this being a prolonged pattern of weather”. After the 2022 heatwave, Kew Gardens lost more than 400 trees due to heat and drought. Martin thinks the impact of the 2026 heatwave could be much worse. He predicts that at Kew and across the south-east, there will be a “significant amount of mortality”. “From what I can see from the landscape here at Kew, we’re going to see a lot more mortality than what we saw in 2022 because a lot of trees that just got through 2022 are not going to make it through this year.” However, he said the full impact of this year’s extreme weather would not be known for the next two to three years. Marcus Lindner, a principal scientist at the European Forest Institute, said that several years of extreme weather could push certain species over the edge, with almost all tree species at risk from the changing climate. “Species that are normally drought-tolerant are adapted to a certain level of drought stress, but if we have continuous and repeated drought these trees will at some point not be comfortable with that any more,” he said.

title: MapQuest app reaches No 1 on US Apple list after defying Trump’s Lake Ontario order
summary: Navigating app surpasses Google and Apple Maps on top-downloaded US chart after posting ‘we’re not changing it’
text: A pioneering online mapping app that defied Donald Trump by refusing to rename Lake Ontario has become the most in-demand navigation tool in the US. MapQuest, which was openly dismissive of the president’s 27 August executive order directing federal agencies to refer to the smallest of the Great Lakes as “Lake America” amid a trade spat with Canada, leapfrogged rivals Google Maps and Apple Maps to top the most-downloaded list, as first reported by TechCrunch. The app held the No 1 spot on Apple’s App Store as of Tuesday morning, the Guardian confirmed. Google quickly capitulated to Trump’s demand, showing Lake America to US customers, while Apple is reportedly mulling a decision under pressure from the White House to make the same change. But MapQuest, a 30-year-old company that bills itself as “the OG” (original) of the internet mapping era, appears to have been rewarded for standing firm. TechCrunch said the app’s downloads had “soared” in recent days to become the fourth most popular of all apps in the US, excluding games – and to lead the Apple app store’s navigation chart, with Google at No 2. In Canada, meanwhile, MapQuest was the second-most downloaded app overall by Sunday night. It comes as polls show Trump’s efforts at renaming the lake found favor with only 14% of Americans, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday. And that survey found only slightly more, 20%, approved of higher tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on Canadian goods, with 57% opposed. MapQuest’s general manager, Doug Berger, said in a statement that usage of its app was running at about 50 times its usual rate. As a bit of fun, he said, the company was also offering subscribers the chance to generate their own name for the lake. That was courtesy of a tool it first introduced after Trump rebranded the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” among US federal government agencies in 2025 – to which Google also acquiesced in the American market. Berger said in a statement: “We took the same approach we did with the Gulf of Mexico: be part of the conversation, and give people an app that keeps the names they’re familiar with. “Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app.” MapQuest has maintained its defiance, and some might say mockery, of Trump’s Lake Ontario order since an original “We’re not changing it” post on social media on 27 August. The following day, in an all-capital letter post similar in style and language to those favored by the president, it wrote: “Our maps are big and beautiful. People come up to us and say we’ll get them places. And we do!” It also responded to a poster who expressed surprise that MapQuest still existed and was not “in the same grave” as RadioShack, the once prominent US technology and electronics company that went through two bankruptcies and shuttered its retail locations a decade ago. “Understandable but the other OG, @RadioShackUSA, is still here too,” MapQuest replied, noting its continued existence as an e-commerce operation. On Tuesday morning, Apple Maps continued to show the body of water spanning the US-Canada border as Lake Ontario, despite the insistence on Monday of Doug Burgum, Trump’s interior secretary, that he was “confident” it would soon show Lake America after the president contacted the company directly. On Google, its map for US users reflects the change – but remains Lake Ontario, a name it has had for about 400 years, for users in the rest of the world. Elsewhere, protests continue to escalate. A giant “Lake Ontario – Now and Always” sign in English and French was erected over the weekend near Grimsby, Ontario. Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, told ABC News: “No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.” On Monday, three Democratic US representatives, Tim Kennedy and Joe Morelle of New York, and Debbie Dingell of Michigan, introduced legislation called the Hands Off Our Great Lakes act, seeking to block the Republican president’s federal order to rename the lake, and prevent future changes.

title: Raise the Colours member denies murder of man in Staffordshire
summary: Billy Allison, 36, pleads not guilty to charge over Matthew O’Gara’s death after incident outside Lichfield bar
text: A man accused of murdering a businessman outside a bar in Staffordshire has pleaded not guilty. Billy Allison, 36, a member of the flag-raising group Raise the Colours, appeared at Stafford crown court on Tuesday and entered not guilty pleas to the murder of Matthew O’Gara and to causing grievous bodily harm with intent to a second person. Allison, of Shirley in Solihull, West Midlands, appeared via video link from HMP Dovegate. Officers were called to the Ricco & Loren bar on Market Street in Lichfield at 11.25pm on 24 May after receiving reports two men had been punched, Staffordshire police previously said in a statement. O’Gara, who was the director of the Plough pub in the nearby village of Huddlesford, sustained serious injuries and died in hospital two days later. The second man also attended hospital and was later discharged. Judge Mukherjee told Allison on Tuesday that he would stand trial in October and it would probably last for about 10 days. “I have adjourned your case for trial to the 28th of October,” he said. Lichfield rugby club paid tribute to O’Gara after his death, describing him as “a friend of the club and a very generous and valued sponsor”. Its post said: “From everyone at the club we would like to offer our deepest condolences to all of Matt’s family, friends, colleagues and the wider Plough family.” The Plough pub closed its doors in the immediate aftermath to give family and staff “the time, privacy and respect they need”, according to the post on Facebook.

title: Los Angeles villa that was hub for German exiles fleeing Nazis reopens after narrow wildfire escape
summary: Spectacular Villa Aurora, which was nearly destroyed in last year’s fires, leading the recovery as Pacific Palisades emerges from a dark chapter
text: A hillside villa that served as a cultural hub for German writers and artists fleeing the Nazis and narrowly escaped destruction in last year’s Los Angeles wildfires reopened its doors to the public this weekend, marking the latest milestone in the city’s slow recovery from one of the darkest chapters in its history. Hundreds of friends of the Villa Aurora, a 1920s Spanish Mediterranean house that has taken on a second life as a cultural center with a fierce commitment to artistic freedom, international dialogue and democracy, crowded into the house on Sunday to mark the resumption of speaker events and artistic residencies. They applauded the return of several art works rescued while the hillsides were still ablaze in January 2025, including an 18th-century Hebrew scroll of the Book of Esther and several busts and paintings, and they applauded again for city firefighters who managed to stop the flames right at the property edge. “Villa Aurora is returning at a time when solidarity, dialogue and mutual support within the community are of particular importance,” the villa’s director, Claudia Gordon said. She recognized the thousands of neighbors in Pacific Palisades who lost their homes. And she acknowledged the continuing impact of the fires, as victims and city officials complain of inadequate insurance payouts and the Trump administration’s refusal to release about $15bn in federal aid. To anti-Nazi German exiles including Thomas Mann, Bertolt Brecht and Lion Feuchtwanger, the novelist who purchased the Villa Aurora in 1943 and turned it into a cultural gathering point, Pacific Palisades became known as “Weimar-by-the-Sea”. The exiles were outspoken in their opposition to Hitler’s regime and, later, to the anti-communist witch-hunts in the United States that affected many of them directly. Although nobody at the reopening mentioned Donald Trump’s name, both Gordon and the leadership of the nearby Mann house – which is also now a cultural center and also narrowly survived the fires – emphasized the importance of the villa as a symbol of refuge, freedom of the arts, freedom of speech and defense of democracy. The burn scars are still plainly visible from Villa Aurora’s balcony. In the garden, now being rebuilt and replanted, the scorched stump of a eucalyptus tree indicates how close the flames came – and how unpredictable the pattern of fire damage proved to be. Several neighboring houses were destroyed outright. Nineteen months on, the heart of Pacific Palisades is one large construction site, with some houses already reconstructed and reoccupied and others still being rebuilt. The Palisades Village, a shopping center belonging to former mayoral candidate Rick Caruso, reopened two weeks ago, with some tenants from before the fires returning and other local businesses whose buildings did not survive moving in. Other restaurants and businesses have announced that they too will reopen shortly – in many cases in different Palisades locations from the ones they occupied before. However, roughly three-quarters of Palisades fire survivors were still displaced as of late July, according to a report by the non-profit Department of Angels, with many of them struggling with debt and inadequate insurance payouts even as sources of financial assistance have fallen away. In Altadena, where the Eaton fire ravaged a community in the inland foothills of the San Gabriel mountains, about two-thirds of fire survivors are yet to return home. City officials and other experts expect full recovery to take as long as five years. Villa Aurora’s own survival relied on support from many others including the German government and other cultural institutions in Los Angeles. In the days after the fire, staff of the Wende Museum, which curates artefacts from dissident movements including anti-communists in cold war-era Germany and Poland, won permission to cross police lines to rescue art work and verify whether the building was still intact. Christine Rank, the Wende museum’s director of collections, described how she and a small team were given just an hour to gather what they could. “We brought boxes and blankets, but we also ended up using sheets and trash cans, whatever we could find to transport the material,” she said. Among the artefacts was a portrait of Feuchtwanger’s wife, Marta, whose unveiling was the centerpiece of Sunday’s reopening. Danijel Skrelja from the German consul general’s office in LA exclaimed: “This house is coming alive.”

title: US public libraries at ‘breaking point’ amid ideological attacks, report finds
summary: PEN America study details verbal and physical threats to librarians, funding cuts and proliferation of book bans
text: Public libraries in the US are “at breaking point” because of an onslaught of political interference, harassment and ideological censorship, a new report published on Tuesday said. Book bans, cancelled story hours, attacks on librarians, funding cuts and the undoing of libraries’ independent governance are examined by the free expression advocacy group PEN America in its study called Out of Circulation: Expanding Censorship in Public Libraries. “Public libraries can be a foundational democratic institution only if they can speak to everyone and only if librarians’ curation decisions can occur free from partisan pressure or restriction,” the report, compiled by PEN America’s Freedom to Read Project, said. “However, ongoing political and public pressures are challenging these very principles. Public libraries nationwide are reaching a breaking point.” The 16-page document relates countless episodes and incidents across the US to support its assertion. They include verbal and physical attacks on librarians, disproportionate targeting of literature featuring LGBTQ+ people, a proliferation of bans on books dealing with gender identity and sexuality, and instances of politically appointed officials installed to override the policies of democratically elected library boards. In one prominent example, the conservative activist and former collegiate swimmer Riley Gaines was last year appointed to a library board in Sumner county, Tennessee, which repeatedly voted down a proposal by its chair to remove material she deemed “inappropriate or sexually-explicit, including anything with transgender themes”. Gaines, an anti-transgender voice who has taken rightwing positions on other issues, including supporting Donald Trump’s often violent immigration crackdown, immediately used social media to brand such books “filth”, and to denounce her new colleagues for “ignoring” Tennessee’s ban on state funding for “woke gender ideology”. The report points to an Idaho law passed in March that allows city councils to hire and fire library directors, discretion previously granted to appointed library boards; and efforts in Alabama that would have allowed local governments to remove library board members at will, and without cause. Another trend highlighted by the PEN America report is attacks on drag shows at, or promoted by public libraries. It chronicles bomb threats, protests and a physical assault on a librarian that caused the cancellation of events or story times at libraries in New York, Massachusetts and Nevada. The group said it had also tracked almost 23,000 book bans in school libraries since 2021, and an expansion to the point where 51% of all book bans attempted nationwide, documented by the American Library Association, came in public libraries. Among the materials banned, in a ruling later overturned by a Texas appeals court, were so-called “butt and fart” books objected to by some parents for their depictions of the human body and, in one case, a description of puberty. Despite the court’s ruling that public schools and libraries could not ban books just because they disagreed with their content, a branch head librarian in Llano county, Suzette Baker, was fired for insubordination when she refused to remove books on a list handed to her by her boss. Kasey Meehan, PEN America’s Freedom to Read director, said such “censorship” efforts reflected a growing, politically driven trend to control what is available to readers, and the ideas that are allowed to be represented. “Local libraries nationwide have long been safe havens for the freedom to read and finding joy and comfort in books,” she said. “Increasingly, they are censorship battlegrounds. When libraries become targets, communities suffer. The consequences extend to authors whose books are taken off shelves and readers who are denied access to stories and information.” PEN America said it had followed “how a movement to censor wide-ranging literature in public schools, especially stories with LGBTQ+ characters and characters of color, has evolved over the past five years, snowballing from coordinated attacks led by groups like Moms for Liberty to state and federal legislation that curtails the right to read”. Philomena Polefrone, senior manager of the Freedom to Read project, said: “The same arguments that have inflamed censorship in schools are also eroding public libraries. These attacks rob library users of vital public services, access to books, and an affirmation that they have a place in their community. “But wherever we see efforts to destabilize these vital public institutions, we also see communities organizing to protect their right to read, standing alongside their public librarians, and resisting funding threats from politically motivated decision-makers.” Evidence of a backlash came in Florida’s primary elections this month, when numerous Moms for Liberty candidates lost seats or failed to win their races, and the conservative group lost its majority on the Sarasota school board. • This article was amended on 2 September 2026. Sumner county, Tennessee, had been misspelled as Sumter county.
