title: Conservatives split from Silicon Valley allies as datacenter backlash grows
summary: Tech companies have underestimated the opposition to energy-hungry datacenters – and experts predict the pushback will intensify
text: Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m your host, Blake Montgomery, listening to Dolly Parton in the wake of her death. I was lucky enough to see her in concert a decade ago in California, in the same arena where Google now hosts its annual I/O conference. It’s been a long time, and all my iPhone 4 photos are so blurry you can barely tell it’s a musical performance, but my memory is clear enough to compensate. She told many stories about her childhood, which led into a trio of fabulous songs: My Tennessee Mountain Home, Applejack and Dr Robert F Thomas. They’re still my favorites. Tech dissection: datacenters divide Silicon Valley from US conservatives (except Trump) Silicon Valley has underestimated the backlash to datacenters in the US by a country mile. That opposition has now achieved substantial political momentum: it’s blocking proposed projects, nixing tax and power incentives, tilting the balance of the upcoming US elections. The backlash has even led US conservatives – politicians and constituents – to split from wealthy allies in Silicon Valley. The opposition to datacenters in the US has become so widespread that it is crossing partisan lines. Several prominent US conservatives, including the governors of Texas and Florida, have condemned datacenters’ enormous electricity usage. Both states’ governors hew closely to Trump on the majority of issues, but both have implemented restrictions on datacenters’ access to their states’ power grids. All of the candidates in the race to become Ohio’s next governor, including a member of Trump’s own administration, have called for restrictions on new datacenters. Meanwhile, the liberal governor of New York has implemented a yearlong moratorium on new hyper-scale datacenters. Read more: The datacenter backlash is bringing the entire political spectrum together – against big tech billionaires How did the tech giants’ leaders set themselves up so disastrously? AI CEOs have “failed miserably” to endear the public to their cause, noted Chamath Palihapitiya, a venture capitalist and co-host of the Silicon Valley podcast All In, on X. Executives such as Sam Altman and Dario Amodei have focused their attention on Trump, legislators and other power players in their bids for huge investments. It turns out the public, uncourted by AI executives, also has a say in whether the technology deserves so many public resources. Communities across the country are bristling at the emergence of the behemoths in their backyards. They’re raising questions about their impact on the environment, and the effect on their utility bills. But there’s more. Datacenters have become a stand-in for grievances against technology companies – harms to children, the feeling of too-rapid societal change with no opt-out, the loss of control over our attention, the extreme concentration of political and economic power in the hands of a few inhumane men – and the tide of that resentment is rising. “I’m not anti-datacenter. I’m anti-the people who run datacenters,” Benny Johnson, a popular rightwing commentator on social media, said in response to Palihapitiya, adding: “I have critical policymakers on my live show daily. The Governor of Texas was on yesterday. I’ve received ZERO effort from anyone in the tech industry to even try to explain datacenters …” Read more: One of east coast’s largest datacenters accused of ‘violating federal law’ Palihapitiya argues the backlash will grow. “Data centers have unfortunately become THE symbolic representation of the asymmetric upside for a very narrow tech elite and a class that are untrustworthy. Inasmuch, the safer bet may be that the pushback and resistance grows …” he wrote. The technorati on X seem to have recently woken up to the new hostile political reality, and over the weekend spilled some ink bristling at it. Many rejected the backlash as myopic, shallow and short-lived. “Any politician opposed to data centers is unqualified to hold public office,” Gavin Baker, an influential venture capitalist, tweeted on Saturday. On Monday, Donald Trump weighed in. “Let data reign,” he wrote on Truth Social Truth Social users answered the president’s post en masse and with uncharacteristic rage. As these battles reach a boil in the US, they’re heating up in other parts of the world. Scotland and Australia are seeing their own backlashes unite bitter political foes in opposition to datacenters, fueled by the widespread perception of Silicon Valley as an extractive, neocolonial force. Monday was Tim Cook’s last day as Apple CEO Siri, where does Apple go next? – podcast Apple’s Tim Cook leaves behind complicated legacy on privacy Fifteen years after Steve Jobs, Tim Cook leaves a dramatically different Apple Who is John Ternus, Apple’s next CEO? AI and medicine ‘Superhuman’ AI tool spots heart disease in less than 2 seconds Doctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warns AI can detect heart disease in women using mammograms, study suggests AI on the job: answering your questions about artificial intelligence in the workplace We’re trying something new! As part of our year-long Reworked series of stories on AI and work, editor Danielle Abril will answer readers’ questions about the changing workplace. You can ask a question for future editions by emailing us at techscape.us@theguardian.com. *** This week, readers ask: what skills do I need to learn to stay employable as more companies adopt AI? For workers whose jobs may be affected by AI, the takeaways from several studies all point to a somewhat counterintuitive answer: yes, you should familiarize yourself with generative AI tools. But at least as important: sharpen your human skills. Judgment, adaptability, analytical thinking and leadership all may become differentiators as AI gets embedded in work. Ask yourself: can you critically judge AI’s output? Can you quickly adapt to change? Can you problem-solve and delegate tasks efficiently to humans and AI? “Learn to work with AI in your field, while continuing to build the human and domain skills that help you apply it well,” said Elena Magrini, head of global research for labor market intelligence firm Lightcast.io. The tasks that employers are adding to AI-exposed jobs often rely on human skills such as empathy, judgment and creativity, according to PwC’s 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer report, which is based on 1bn job ads from six continents. Junior roles are now more likely to require traditionally senior skills like emotional intelligence and leadership, the report stated. In LinkedIn’s 2026 Skills on the Rise report, based on skills members added to their profiles along with those held by recent hires, in-demand skills included team management, cross-functional collaboration and mentorship, as well as prompt engineering and AI business strategy. One way to start developing experience in leadership and problem solving is at your own company. Work with your boss to find internal training and mentorship programs. And consider volunteering for tasks that may allow you to boost your weaker skills like leading a cross-functional project that requires you to delegate and communicate often. Beyond your employer, companies such as LinkedIn and Coursera offer free online courses for soft and technical skills and OpenAI and Anthropic provide educational materials on how to use AI. *** Ask us about AI and work! Email techscape.us@theguardian.com with your questions, and we’ll answer them in future editions of the newsletter. title: ‘Demonic oppression’ and ‘girly convos’: the podcast wooing young women back to Christianity
summary: Girls Gone Bible is on tour in the US, touting a regressive ideal of femininity through discussions of abstinence and mental health struggles
text: At first glance, the crowd gathering outside a music venue in Red Bank, New Jersey, could have passed for a group of sorority rush hopefuls – or Ella Langley fans on their way to the country star’s show. Most of them were under the age of 30. They wore cowboy boots, maxi sundresses and soft, bouncy blowouts, scrolling on their phones outside the doors as they waited for friends to arrive. But one accessory gave them away: the Bibles they toted. These women were there to pray. Specifically, they were there to see the Girls Gone Bible tour. Hosted by two “Bible-thumping bombshells” (per the Daily Mail), the Girls Gone Bible podcast is often sold as the conservative woman’s answer to Alex Cooper’s secular, sexual Call Her Daddy franchise. The hosts have “girly convo[s]” about some of the same issues you might hear on Call Her Daddy: dating dos and don’ts, going sober-curious, or battling insecurities. But Cooper never invited an Eastern Orthodox priest on to explain why the Greek church “makes manly men” or blamed the attention economy on Satan himself. Since debuting in 2023, Girls Gone Bible has become a brand all its own, with more than 1 million followers on Instagram and ranking 42nd for the religion and spirituality genre on Spotify. Its Revival tour began in April, bringing evenings of music, prayer and religious testimony to the east coast, as well as Alabama, Tennessee and California. Girls Gone Bible hosts Angela Halili, 30, and Arielle Reitsma, 36, call themselves “two imperfect girls serving an absolutely perfect God”, though neither grew up very religious or married into the faith. In fact, neither host is married, earning them relatability points among listeners who are still stuck in the dating scene. Both are relatively new Christians who spent their early careers as working actors in Los Angeles, a city usually depicted by conservatives as a den of sin. To that point: Reitsma played a character called “Slutty Girl” in the jukebox musical film Rock of Ages; Halili once appeared in a Marilyn Manson music video. Both converted in moments of personal crisis. Halili told the Christian publication Relevant that her anxiety and alcoholism stemmed from the pressures of working in the industry, and she first “met” God in 2019 when she started praying to help her through an anxiety attack. Reitsma, meanwhile, walked into a church “on a whim” after a rough breakup and “found peace like [she’d] never known”. The success of the podcast led to guest stints on Fox News segments about gen Z seeking faith. They opened Donald Trump’s “victory rally” the day before his 2025 inauguration with a prayer that included the lines “in the life of President Donald Trump, as it is in heaven” and “President Trump … we declare that no weapon formed against you will prosper.” This association with the ascendant Christian right, of course, makes them Maga figures. But unlike podcasters in the conservative-aligned womanosphere who regularly toe the party line when it comes to topics such as immigration, abortion or birth control, Halili and Reitsma prefer a more lobotomized hang. Speaking softly, with matching vocal fry, they dispense vague platitudes about “healing” and soothe listeners with promises they are not alone in their struggles. They stay away from explicitly political messages in the same way that a pastor’s wife would not want to offend a congregant while making small talk during a post-service coffee hour. It’s easy to fall into the Girls Gone Bible universe. Episode titles promise juicy discussions of topics that matter to young women: “Codependency and People-Pleasing”, “Overcoming an Eating Disorder”, “Honest Convo About Anxiety”. The hosts remind listeners that they are still figuring all of this out, too. It’s a welcoming space. Kelsey Hanson Woodruff, a scholar of American religious history and postdoctoral fellow at Wesleyan University, said that this come-as-you-are branding has deep roots in evangelism. “Evangelical Christians love a conversion story,” Woodruff said. “It can provide a lot of credibility to someone’s authentic Christian experience.” “They’re not shoving their opinions down people’s throats like some of these other podcasts [such as] Andrew Tate and all that stuff,” Alicia Reicis, a 30-year-old stay-at-home mom told me before the show. The hosts’ everygirl approachability belies their mission to woo women back into a faith that increasingly preaches their oppression. Adult women under 30 are rejecting organized religion at record rates; a study released this April found that 40% of female respondents claimed no affiliation – up from 29% in 2013. This is probably due in part to the very visible rise of Christian nationalism tied to Trump’s administration. (The secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth, brought a pastor who does not believe in a woman’s right to vote to speak at the Pentagon; the health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, has invoked terms like “spiritual warfare” and “malevolent forces” in speeches.) Despite this, Girls Gone Bible has found success with women who seem able to compartmentalize. Every woman I spoke to at the show declined to talk politics, or how they feel about the hosts supporting Trump. “I don’t really have a full opinion on that,” Reicis told me before politely excusing herself. Outside the venue, Genesis Gesualdo texted her friend who was running late. Gesualdo, 33, works at a salvage yard, which she called “a man’s job”. She told me that she had converted to Christianity less than a week ago because she felt she had strayed from a more modest lifestyle. “I wasn’t walking with him [Jesus], I didn’t obey him,” she said. “The way I dressed was provocative.” Gesualdo came to the event wearing a floor-length floral skirt. She said she was looking forward to “rejoicing”. I couldn’t know the political leanings of every person in attendance. Yes, there were a lot of women sporting what’s become known as “Republican face” – heavy makeup, plumped lips, fake tans – but there were others I would not feel comfortable pegging as such. I lost track counting the number of full-arm tattoo sleeves I saw; I watched a young woman hit her vape while waiting in the concessions line. I wondered if these fans – maybe new converts themselves – would soon find themselves evolving into what the hosts consider to be “godly” women: conservative in appearance, faith and political ideology. “One of the tactics of the Christian right is to narrow the definition of what it means to be a Christian,” Woodruff said. “[Girls Gone Bible] may not talk directly about policies, but they may put forth a certain definition of what it means to be a Christian woman, which is inherently political.” *** Girls Gone Bible touts a regressive ideal of femininity, encouraging women to be “modest” and abstain from sex before marriage, which Halili once called “demonic oppression”. Harsh, but both women often insist that they’re not trying to shame anyone for prior transgressions – after all, both have pasts of their own. And their audience is perhaps already comfortable with the idea of celibacy. More young women, religious or not, are going “boy sober”, as voluntary abstinence is sometimes called on social media, due to their dismal dating pool and past bad experiences with men. In fact, Girls Gone Bible’s message about dating gets very close to pop feminism. “It’s been genuinely the greatest joy of my life to enter into complete purity,” Halili said on a recent episode taped after she returned from a trip to Miami, a party city synonymous with bikinis and bottle service. “Living a life where I’m not seeking that sort of validation from men, for men to think that I am hot or to think that I’m sexy.” At the New Jersey tour stop, Halili continued preaching girl power. “Marriage isn’t the reward,” she said, as groups of friends cheered and nodded along from their seats. Then she veered back: “Jesus’s presence in your marriage is the reward.” Melissa, a 58-year-old woman grabbing a drink at an Italian restaurant before the show, told me that she wanted to bring her son in hopes of finding him “a Christian girl”. He couldn’t make it; she brought her hairdresser instead. Two college friends, Grace Colucci and Taylor Garvey, might have been just who Melissa was looking for in a potential set-up. Both are 22, and first encountered Girls Gone Bible through TikTok clips. Colucci has never had a boyfriend, but she still appreciates the hosts’ dating advice. “They just make [abstinence] so normalized,” Colucci said. “It’s very inspirational and it makes you feel good.” But Colucci and Garvey were most interested in what Halili and Reitsma say about their mental health struggles. Halili has spoken extensively about living with OCD and disordered eating; for Reitsma, it was suicidal ideation. Colucci listens to their podcasts on stress and burnout. “What they go through is similar to us, and they’re good at [talking about it] in a way that’s fun and easy to learn from. It’s not too heavy.” At the top of the show, Halili and Reitsma led a group singalong of worship music. When the pianist riffed that the “power in the name” of Jesus is “stronger than depression”, the crowd burst into the loudest cheers I heard all night. It makes sense that members of the most depressed and isolated generation in history would gravitate toward this subject matter. In her book Esther’s Army: The Christian Women Who Power the American Right, sociologist Katie Gaddini calls this audience “a post-pandemic female populace eager to hear ‘the truth’”. A recent Pew survey found that 44% of 18- to 29-year-olds listen to “religious audio programs”, which they overwhelmingly digest as podcasts (as opposed to radio programs). Thirty-nine per cent of Americans of all ages who consume this content say they listen for “life advice or guidance”. A young woman who posted on the subreddit r/Christianity seeking recommendations for podcasts geared toward “girls in their 20s” received this answer from another user: “Girls Gone Bible may not be the most theologically deep but they are a good starting place … Treat them [like] a source of relatability (a lot of their topics are highly relatable).” Evangelicals have long touted the Bible as a cure for mental anguish, and many pastors view depression as a spiritual attack. Reitsma told the audience she “met Jesus on the bathroom floor” during a time in which “everything in the world was telling me to end [her] life”. She explained needing “healing beyond what medication can fix”, meaning antidepressants. She quickly added, “there’s nothing wrong with medications,” but this felt like a concession. In general, the hosts speak of burnout without addressing the economic forces behind their generation’s collective exhaustion and despair. They detail their mental health struggles, but fall short of interrogating the institutional roadblocks women face when they do try to get help. The intended takeaway: Jesus alone will cure you. The night ended with Halili praying for “sexual sinners” (that’s anyone who has sex outside of marriage) and women struggling with infertility. Reitsma hugged audience members who lined up at the foot of the stage. Women cried, holding up their Bibles. Some wore newly purchased tour merch, sweatshirts with phrases such as “Keep the Faith” and “Thank You Jesus.” They would bring home a sense of validation: they were not alone in their pain. The tour has two more stops remaining, both in Florida in September, but there was something about the New Jersey show that especially delighted the hosts: it wasn’t happening in the Bible belt, or even a red state. “I feel such a hunger in here tonight,” Halili said. “It must be the east coast in ya.” Clearly, they believe their message is spreading.

title: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election
summary: Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago
text: The year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s congressional elections against its leftwing president, João Goulart, as a way of countering the supposed communist threat sweeping a region the US considered its back yard. Historians say that in the lead-up to the vote, the CIA and the Department of State secretly channelled millions of dollars to opposition candidates and a group tasked with spreading rightwing propaganda and stirring up unrest. “There was a very heavy-handed intervention here by the US government,” said Chico Rubens Paiva, a political activist whose congressman grandfather Rubens Paiva investigated Washington’s meddling during a 1963 parliamentary inquiry into the conspiracy. More than six decades later, Paiva, whose grandfather was murdered by the US-backed dictatorship that seized power in 1964, is among those who fear history is repeating itself on the eve of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election. October’s vote will pit the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Donald Trump ally who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a military coup. Polls suggest a tight race and Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have been accused of trying to tip the scales in Bolsonaro’s favour by launching an overt campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure against Lula. The US measures include imposing 25% tariffs on most Brazilian imports and designating Brazil’s biggest crime groups – Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s First Command of the Capital – as foreign terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials suspect this is partly designed to boost Bolsonaro by making Lula look soft on crime. In July, Lula said two Trump officials had been denied entry visas because they planned “to meddle in Brazil’s elections”. Brazilian officials believe the pair, who reportedly planned to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, intended to sow doubt about the reliability of Brazil’s internationally respected voting system – something the Bolsonaros have sought to do repeatedly. Soon after, the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington was revoked. Celso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist and podcast pundit, voiced bewilderment that US interference – which he considered the election’s most urgent theme – was not getting more coverage in mainstream media. “The greatest superpower in human history is explicitly backing a candidate in our election and is strangling the Brazilian economy in order to help him [win],” Barros claimed. “We cannot pretend that this isn’t happening and treat this like a normal election … the Brazilian economy is under attack.” Trump’s tactics have echoes of Washington’s cold war-era attempt to manipulate Brazilian politics in the lead-up to the 1964 coup, which ushered in two decades of authoritarian rule in which hundreds of people were killed or disappeared. Back then, the CIA helped finance the Brazilian Institute for Democratic Action, which, according to the historians Lilia Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, illegally poured money into the campaigns of hundreds of lawmakers and eight gubernatorial candidates. “The objective was strategic: to create a strong opposition in congress, block government initiatives and prepare the way for a coup d’état,” Schwarcz and Starling argued in their book Brazil: A Biography. Another US-funded group, the Research and Social Studies Institute, was used to disrupt Goulart’s government by bankrolling anti-communist propaganda and anti-government protests. James N Green, a Brown University historian who has written a book about the period, said: “The intention [was] getting rid of Goulart [and] opening the door to the military coming to power.” Green sees parallels between Trump’s use of tariffs to sabotage Lula’s campaign and how in the early 60s Washington sought to enfeeble Goulart’s government by funding his opponents and cutting off loans. Then, as now, the US government was “bent on doing everything possible to weaken the government” in Brazil. But Barros sees one key difference between the two US gambits. “[The 1962 campaign] was done covertly, precisely because the CIA knew there would be real public anger in Brazil if people knew the US was bankrolling candidates. So they did it secretly,” he said. “Today, this is being done openly – and on an incomparably larger scale.” The Department of State rejected claims the US was seeking to meddle in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” an official said in a statement. “We respect the Brazilian people and whatever government that they choose freely through free and fair elections in Brazil. We’ve respected and dealt with governments from both sides of the spectrum in Brazil, and had very successful relationships with them.” Last year Trump was accused of meddling in the politics of neighbouring Argentina after he threw his weight behind its rightwing president, Javier Milei, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Milei recently attended Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch in Brazil, using his speech to lambaste Lula as a “thief”. Green believes two strategic objectives lie behind the Brazilian pressure campaign being waged by Trump and by Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, who has made toppling Cuba’s communist government a personal project. Firstly, it is designed to weaken and delegitimise Lula’s government, making it harder for Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, to challenge the US economic asphyxiation campaign against Cuba. Secondly, it is about “neutralising” leftwing forces in Latin America more generally and boosting the right in the hope of helping to elect even more Trump-aligned leaders. Since 2023, a succession of radical rightwing populists have won power in Argentina and Chile, Costa Rica and Colombia. In reference to Trump’s tangerine complexion, this has been nicknamed Latin America’s “orange wave”. Paiva, 38, believes US interference is intended to have a similar effect to the abduction of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro – strengthening “American dominance” in a region it considers a US sphere of influence. Maduro’s removal in January allowed the US to impose a pliant successor, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has started opening up the South American country to US oil and mining firms. Paiva believes Bolsonaro’s election will “serve the same purpose: putting people into power who will serve their interests”. He fears that as election day draws near, US social media companies could enter the fray, potentially giving Bolsonaro another lift. “Any kind of change to the algorithm has a brutal impact in the way information reaches people,” warned Paiva, who is running for a seat in congress in the election for the centre-left Brazilian Socialist party. He highlighted “the scary lurch the Silicon Valley bros” had taken into Trump’s camp during his second term. Barros is convinced the US aims to help elect Flávio Bolsonaro, “because Flávio will give them everything they want”, he said. “Flávio will make a rare earths deal no other president would. Flávio will let American big techs do whatever they like in Brazil. Flávio will reduce economic relations with China as much as he can.” He noted that Bolsonaro supporters attended rallies carrying US flags. Barros believes the campaign’s real driving force is not Trump but Rubio, who hopes to bolster a possible 2028 presidential run by showing voters he has “delivered the whole of Latin America to American interests”. “The fact is, this is an election between Lula and Marco Rubio,” Barros said.

title: Keir Starmer to stand down as MP to focus on world affairs
summary: Former PM says it is right time to go, which will trigger byelection that Greens’ Zack Polanski could target
text: Keir Starmer is to quit as the MP for Holborn and St Pancras, saying it is the right time for him to leave the Commons. Starmer, who resigned as prime minister in July, told the Camden New Journal he wanted to focus on international affairs and “pass the baton to a successor”. Starmer had previously said he would seek to serve out his term as a backbench MP, and his decision to quit will spark a byelection. The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, is understood to be considering a run for the central London seat. Starmer told the paper: “It has been a huge honour and privilege to represent the best constituency in the country and to have taken over from Frank Dobson, who was such a great constituency MP and a member of the last Labour government. “I will now focus on other things and that will be international affairs including defence, security, trade and technology in a fast-changing world. I will also continue, as I have done for a long time now with others, work on combating violence against women and girls.” Starmer’s seat, long seen as a safe Labour hold, is likely to be targeted by the Greens, potentially for Polanski who is a London assembly member. “Zack has always made it clear he would like to be a London MP. London has been his home for over 20 years,” a Green party spokesperson said. The independent leftwing candidate Andrew Feinstein was Starmer’s closest challenger at the last election. Feinstein, who had been close to Jeremy Corbyn, was then involved in Your Party but resigned amid disagreements over party finances. Starmer told the New Journal he had decided over the summer that he wanted to focus on international work and that meant he had to step down as an MP. “I think once you’ve been prime minister, it’s important to answer the question: what are you going to do next? Having decided I’m going to concentrate on international affairs, I think it’s right to step down,” he said. Starmer said he was proud of his work in the constituency since 2015 as well as his achievements as prime minister. “I want to thank all of those I was privileged to work with in the constituency on issues that matter hugely: affordable housing, first-class education and the work we did on knife crime through the Camden youth support, which was really, really important,” he said. He said his local party “always had my back”, adding: “They have been resolute in their support for me, firstly in becoming an MP and then becoming the leader of Labour party and then as prime minister.” The Conservative party chair, Kevin Hollinrake, said it was “fitting that his final act as a member of parliament is yet another U-turn having pledged to stay on. The decision to stand down will mean a costly byelection for taxpayers at a time when Andy Burnham and John Healey are plotting tax rises on hard-working families across the country.”

title: Forest Service chief faces scrutiny over logging ties as Trump plans to scrap protections
summary: Rollback of ‘roadless rule’ expected to benefit companies US Forest Service chief, Tom Schultz, previously lobbied for
text: Donald Trump this month announced plans to rescind a landmark rule that has protected old-growth forests in the US for 25 years. If finalized, the rollback is expected to benefit the companies that Tom Schultz, chief of the US Forest Service, represented in his previous roles as a timber industry lobbyist and executive, according to research by consumer advocacy non-profit Public Citizen. The Roadless Area Conservation Rule, more commonly known as the “roadless rule”, was adopted in 2001 to limit development in roughly 45m acres of national forest. Industry interests and Republican representatives have long lobbied for the rule’s rescission, which would open up those swaths of untouched land to road construction, drilling and logging. In a statement, Schultz described the move as “the best way to restore the balance, reduce wildfire risk, and secure the long-term health of our forests and neighboring communities”. But studies suggest it could put 400 threatened and endangered species at risk and imperil ecosystems. Industry interests will be the main beneficiaries of the change, advocates fear. In an emailed statement, a Forest Service spokesperson, who did not provide their name, noted that Schultz had also held positions in Idaho and Montana government. “Chief Schultz’s appointment reflects the administration’s recognition that the Forest Service’s current challenges require leadership with broad federal land management experience, not just internal tenure,” the person said. Schultz is the first-ever Forest Service chief who did not previously work within the agency itself. Before Trump tapped him for the job, he served as president of the Federal Forest Resource Coalition, a trade association representing companies that purchase timber from the federal government, and was also vice-president of resources and government affairs at Idaho Forest Group, a major lumber manufacturer. He is one of dozens of former extractive industry insiders Trump has placed in key environmental positions. Energy secretary Chris Wright was CEO of fracking company Liberty Energy, while interior official Tyler Hassen was an oil executive. Forty-three former fossil-fuel employees and 29 former corporate executives held administration positions, an October analysis from Public Citizen and corporate watchdog Revolving Door Project found. Schultz has long been critical of the roadless rule. As it was being considered in 2000, he said: “It’s going to be very difficult to actually generate revenue from state trust lands that could be encompassed within a roadless designation.” The American Forest Resource Council (AFRC), a timber industry trade association on the west coast that includes the Idaho Forest Group, has recently directly advocated for the rescission of the roadless rule. In comments to the federal government last year, the lobbying group said the “one-size-fits-all” policy unnecessarily prevents “active forest management” – intentionally thinning forests through practices including logging – which it says is the best way to mitigate wildfire risk. Since his appointment, Schultz has echoed these calls. “Active forest management is not an option. It’s essential,” he said in the announcement of the proposal to rescind the roadless rule, which also referred to the policy as “one-size-fits-all”. “Active forest management is central to the Forest Service’s multi-use mission – not an industry agenda,” the Forest Service spokesperson said. In a statement, Nick Smith, spokesperson for the AFRC, said: “There is broad bipartisan support for increasing forest health treatments – thinning, prescribed fire, and even logging – to reduce the size and severity of wildfires and make forests more resilient to climate change.” A recent analysis of the Forest Service’s own data found that wildfires were nearly three times as likely to start near roads, raising questions about the administration’s claim that expanding road access will reduce wildfire risk, said Lois Parshley, climate research director at Public Citizen. “But from the industry’s perspective, it will also open up new possibilities for logging,” she said. Asked about Parshley’s concern, the Forest Service spokesperson said that repealing the roadless rule “allows safer use and maintenance of existing roads that first responders have long said they need to reach fires quickly”. “Forest‑treatment science is clear: thinning plus prescribed fire reduces wildfire severity by more than 60% – and up to 72% compared to untreated areas,” they said. “Access enables treatment; without access, prevention and response suffer. Gates and seasonal closures can be used to manage public traffic while preserving routes that firefighters and forest managers may need.” The AFRC’s comments say that “strategically placed and maintained roads are essential for safe and effective wildfire response”, and that in “nearly every major wildfire over the past 15–20 years”, the Forest Service has identified a lack of road access as a key barrier to effective response, Parshley said. That argument also appears in Schultz’s rationale for repealing the rule, she noted. In the administration’s announcement, he said the roadless rule “has frustrated land managers and served as a barrier to action – prohibiting road construction, which has limited wildfire suppression and active forest management”. Smith of the AFRC said that “millions of roadless acres have burned across the west since the rule’s adoption in 2001.” “Federal lands are far more likely to burn than private lands, which typically have far more roads,” he said. “According to the congressional budget office, a wildfire on federal land is on average five times the size of one on nonfederal land nearby.” Critics dispute the logic that the roadless rule is good for wildfire management, arguing that roads can increase the risk of human-caused fires. Since Schultz came into the Forest Service in February 2025, the American Forest Resource Council has spent more than $210,000 advocating to expand harvesting in national forests, lobbying records show. Meanwhile, the Idaho Forest Group increased its spending on lobbying in 2026 and reported advocating to support “efforts to advance forest management”, including with the agency now run by its former executive, Parshley found. Smith of the AFRC claimed that “the amount of money AFRC spends lobbying Congress and federal agencies in support of policies to improve the health of federal forests and nearby rural communities is dwarfed in comparison to the many anti-forestry NGOs.” Idaho is exempt from the roadless rule; it has its own regulations on roadless areas developed with the federal government. But the proposal to kill the roadless rule is just one industry-backed change to forestry that the Trump administration has put forth. As the head of the Federal Forest Resource Coalition, Schultz in July 2022 delivered testimony before Congress in which he suggested roadless areas were limiting the industry, saying: “nearly half of the National Forest System [is] off limits to management.” Though he did not call to overturn the policy specifically, he advocated allowing states to manage more Forest Service timber sales, expanding exemptions from environmental review processes, and changing stewardship contracting rules to support logging and wood-processing infrastructure. The Trump administration has since adopted or advanced each of those proposals, Parshley found in a report earlier this year. And Schultz has directly helped implement them, she found. For instance, in December 2025 he personally signed an agreement with Idaho’s governor to double federal timber sales from the state’s national forests. “That directly benefits his former employer the Idaho Forest Group”, she said. Idaho Forest Group has been contacted for comment. Under Schultz, the Forest Service has ramped up timber sales. In June, he told senators that the agency had exceeded its timber-sale target. He has also overseen a historic and widely criticized structural reorganization of his agency, moving the agency’s headquarters from the nation’s capital to Salt Lake City, eliminating regional offices and staff and shifting authority over forests to states. Schultz has made it clear that he aims to weaken regulations. In April, he told Congress that he is “trying to cut through regulation”. In a company earnings call after Schultz was confirmed, lumber company PotlatchDeltic CEO Eric Cremers confirmed that industry executives maintain direct familiarity with Schultz in his new role, saying: “We know the new Forest Service chief.” “It’s pretty clear that the industry was excited by their reactions to Schultz’s nomination and then confirmation,” said Parshley.

title: First Thing: Duane Keith Davis found guilty of 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur
summary: Jury took about three hours to reach verdict in case that relied heavily on confessions from the defendant. Plus, the woman who lived with and loved Freddie Mercury as her fiance
text: Good morning. A Las Vegas jury has found the former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane Keith Davis guilty of the murder of Tupac Shakur, bringing the case to a close nearly 30 years after the rapper was gunned down. The jury took about three hours to reach a guilty verdict in a case that relied heavily on multiple confessions from Davis himself. The 63-year-old, who was accused of instigating the deadly shooting but not pulling the trigger himself, had spent years telling investigators and interviewers alike of his direct involvement before he was arrested in 2023. Who was Tupac Shakur? Shakur was born in 1971 in East Harlem, New York, and rose to fame in the early 90s with lyrics that doubled as a sharp commentary on social injustice including systemic racism and police brutality. He was 25 when he died, is regarded among the greatest rappers to ever live, and continues to be celebrated around the world years after his life was cut short. How have his family reacted to the trial? “We’ve been waiting 30 years to grieve properly,” Zayd Akinyela, Shakur’s cousin, told reporters outside the courtroom when the trial was under way. “A lot of people don’t get to grieve until they understand what happened to their loved one and how it happened.” Why have authorities been so heavily criticised over the case? Las Vegas police faced criticism that they had bungled the investigation and failed to pursue crucial leads, including from a member of Shakur’s entourage who claimed he could identify the shooters. That witness died weeks later in a separate shooting. Rescue attempts continue in areas devastated by flash floods in Nepal and Tibet with 1,000 dead The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to more than 1,000. More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border. Rescue efforts have been complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and bad weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India and China are sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access. The swollen Trishuli River has continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern. US army secretary Dan Driscoll resigns over reported friction with Pete Hegseth The army secretary, Dan Driscoll, has handed his resignation to Donald Trump, the White House said Monday, becoming the latest high-profile figure to depart the defense department. The resignation comes after months of turmoil at the defense department, from leak investigations and budget issues to the ousting of several senior officials including the army chief of staff, Randy George, in April. In June, the army commander of forces in Europe and Africa, Gen Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down. What role had Driscoll been playing? An Iraq war veteran, tech investor and former adviser to JD Vance, Driscoll was tapped for the unusual role of key negotiator to try to end the war between Russia and Ukraine. He was also a major force behind trying to cut the red tape for military contractors to quickly develop more drones and counter-drone capabilities as warfare rapidly changes around the world. Teen charged with murder for recording San Diego mosque shooting live stream A 17-year-old North Carolina girl who recorded a live stream of a shooting that killed three people at a San Diego mosque and disseminated the attackers’ white-supremacist writings has been charged with murder by aiding and abetting, a district attorney said. The Forsyth county district attorney Jim O’Neill said the girl, whose name was not mentioned during the news conference, was arrested last week. On Monday a grand jury indicted her on three counts of murder and one count of conspiracy. Under North Carolina law, the aiding and abetting charges carry the same penalties as if the girl had committed the attack herself, O’Neill said. In other news … A divided US supreme court has permitted Donald Trump to continue building his controversial $400m White House ballroom despite legal challenges, raising the likelihood it will be completed. New York City police shot and killed a woman after she stabbed two people, one of them fatally, in Times Square, an act authorities described as “random and unprovoked”. The US military has no plans to send troops to midterm polling sites, the highest‑ranking US military officer has said. US health officials have excluded two measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania from their counts. RFK Jr, the health secretary, has suggested the deaths were “fabricated” while the CDC said it was reviewing them. The Tennessee Volunteers will be honoring Dolly Parton with a helmet sticker this season, the college football team’s head coach, Josh Heupel, announced. Stat of the day: US trade regulator and 22 states accuse Amazon of taking $20bn with secret surcharges The US’s main trade regulator and 22 states have sued Amazon, alleging the online retailer “secretly and systematically overcharged” advertisers, leading to higher costs for customers on items such as groceries and other essential goods. Amazon described it as a “misguided lawsuit” with which it “strongly disagrees”. Culture Pick: Ridiculed Olympic B-girl gets the last laugh … and it’s a total joy She spent the biggest moment of her career at the Paris Olympics thrashing around like a toddler having a tantrum – then went viral globally. Now, a Netflix film reveals how the much-mocked breakdancer Raygun got over it. Don’t miss this: Mary Austin on her best friend and the love of her life, Freddie Mercury Freddie was loud, flamboyant, confident, supremely camp and gay. Mary was quiet, inhibited, diffident and strictly heterosexual. Simon Hattenstone speaks to the late Queen singer’s former fiance about their life together. … or this: Can we stop AI from deceiving us? We are used to the idea that our fellow humans may intentionally mislead or manipulate us, but the idea that machines can now do the same is deeply unsettling, as Snigdha Poonam’s long read explores. Climate check: How intense rains in the Grand Canyon turned into a deadly disaster Scientists have long warned that the climate crisis will create stronger extremes and destructive shifts between wet and dry conditions, and the flash flooding in the Arizona tourist destination, which killed at least two people, was likely triggered by compounding climate factors such as local drought, recent wildfires and warming in the Pacific Ocean. title: London Stock Exchange to lose three more firms after takeover offers
summary: Latest purchases take value of deals to leave capital’s stock market this year past $100bn
text: Three more London-listed companies are set to be taken over as the value of deals removing firms from the capital’s under-pressure stock market so far this year passes $100bn (£74bn). On Tuesday, Bodycote, the FTSE 250 industrials group that has been listed on the London Stock Exchange since 1972, agreed a £1.84bn takeover by the US private equity group Veritas. The Macclesfield-based company, which offers services including heat treatment for manufacturing, metal joining and protective metallic coatings, had been the subject of a bidding war involving the rival European buyout group CVC. Shares in Bodycote soared 4.5%, making it the second biggest riser in the FTSE 250, after CVC indicated that it might make a counteroffer. “CVC is considering its position and a further announcement will be made when appropriate,” the company said. “Bodycote shareholders are strongly advised to take no action in response to the Veritas offer in the meantime.” Veritas said Bodycote’s prospects would be better served by being taken out of public markets. “As a private company under Veritas’s ownership, Bodycote will benefit from enhanced flexibility and long-term perspective to support continued investment in the business and pursue targeted organic and inorganic growth opportunities,” the US group said. Meanwhile, the telecoms company Gamma Communications recommended a £1.1bn offer from the UK private equity company Epiris, days after confirming it was in possible takeover talks with the European buyout company Waterland. Epiris first indicated its interest in a potential takeover in June. On Tuesday it said: “The additional flexibility that comes from a private company environment will enable Gamma to invest further and focus on sustainably improving the growth of its business over the long term.” Separately, the Scottish energy company Capricorn is set to end its 38 years on the FTSE all-share index after striking a deal with its Norwegian rival DNO for $396m. Capricorn had recommended an offer from Genel Energy, but the company switched its recommendation after receiving a higher offer from DNO. The takeovers put further pressure on the LSE, which has been hit by an exodus of companies this year in deals totalling almost $110bn, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. “Overseas acquirers continue to feast on the UK market like hungry customers at an all-you-can-eat buffet,” said Russ Mould, the investment director at AJ Bell. “While some investors may be toasting the payoff they receive from the wave of mergers and acquisitions, the longer-term implications are potentially bleak. These deals mean a further dilution of the breadth and quality of a UK market which is struggling to attract new companies to replace the ones which are being acquired.” The flurry of dealmaking includes easyJet’s £5.7bn takeover by the US private equity company Apollo, the warehouse landlord Segro’s £14bn takeover by its US rival Prologis, and the sale of ITV’s broadcasting and streaming business to Sky’s owner, Comcast, for £1.6bn. Earlier this year the historic British asset management group Schroders agreed a £9.9bn takeover by a US investor. Other deals include the £10bn takeover of the lab testing group Intertek by a consortium led by the Swedish private equity company EQT in June. Beazley, the specialist insurer with clients including Lloyds of London, agreed an £8bn deal to be acquired by its larger rival Zurich in February.

title: House Republicans ramp up labor union investigations before midterms
summary: Inquiries come after conservative thinktanks claim unions are using member dues to support Democratic causes
text: House Republicans are investigating several US labor unions based on claims from far-right non-profits alleging union dues are being used for illegal political funding. Republicans on the House’s education and workforce committee opened the investigation this summer after multiple reports from the conservative thinktanks targeted unions and their spending, claiming that unions are using member dues to support Democratic causes. While unions are allowed to advocate for political causes, they are prohibited from using union dues to directly fund specific candidates or political action committees (Pacs). Union members can voluntarily donate to labor unions’ political action committees. The unions under investigation include the American Federation of Teachers (AFT), United Auto Workers, United Steelworkers, Smart Transportation Division (Smart-TD), Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and Trainmen (BLET), and the Brotherhood of Maintenance of Way Employees Division (BMWED). The allegations come from research reports by the American Accountability Foundation (AAF), a “dark money” non-profit that counts Project 2025 architect the Heritage Foundation as a donor, and the Freedom Foundation, a conservative thinktank whose chair once protested against Labor Day, claiming: “I can’t think of a problem in society that can’t be traced in some way back to the abuses of organized labor.” Among the AAF’s allegations against labor unions are that the BLET supported a lawsuit filed by the UAW to halt the Trump administration’s attempt to end collective bargaining. It also highlighted the BLET’s criticism of Project 2025, which advocates for several policies that would weaken labor unions and collective bargaining rights. “The industrial unions the [House] committee is investigating have become glorified political arms of the Democrat Party,” said Tom Jones, president of the American Accountability Foundation in a statement. “When these unions care more about their friends in Congress than their members in the factories and railroads, it becomes clear they’re not serving the working men and women of America!” In a statement, a spokesperson for United Steelworkers said the group is “working diligently on fully addressing the committee’s request”. “Our union values transparency and annually reports our spending with the Department of Labor,” the spokesperson said. As a part of their union investigations, House Republicans are also investigating AFT president Randi Weingarten after the Freedom Foundation claimed, using speculation around the union’s annual financial filing, that union member dues funded her 2025 book, Why Fascists Fear Teachers: Public Education and the Future of Democracy. “Perhaps Weingarten’s next book should be entitled, Why Teachers Fear Teachers Unions,” the analysis claimed. In a letter responding to the allegations, Michael Bromwich, an attorney representing Weingarten and the AFT, called the Freedom Foundation’s report “a partisan attack masquerading as investigative journalism”. “Its claims are premised on factual inaccuracies, misleading characterizations, and a willful disregard for the complete record,” Bromwich wrote. “The documents produced to the House committee refute these allegations and demonstrate that the book project was lawfully and ethically undertaken to advance AFT’s mission, with appropriate oversight and transparent financial arrangements.” The Freedom Foundation and House Republicans on the investigating committee did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The House investigations follow reports that the Trump administration conducted surveillance of labor unions in Minnesota during a mass anti-immigration enforcement operation earlier this year, including the CWA and the SEIU. Cathy Creighton, director of Cornell University’s School of Industrial and Labor Relations Buffalo Co-Lab, said that union finances are strictly controlled, with disclosure requirements on how money is spent – which is how the conservative groups got the information for their reports. Most union members vote Democrat, because the party “has a platform that supports the labor movement, the right to organize [and] the right to bargain”, Creighton said. “The labor movement is allowed to spend money on political actions, and they do,” she said, noting that the motivation behind the reports seemed political. “The Trump administration has been trying to eliminate bargaining rights and unions, full stop.” A 2024 poll by Gallup found that 62% of Americans say the Democratic party best serves the interest of union members compared with 27% who said the same about the Republican party. US labor unions have historically supported Democrats over Republicans since Franklin Delano Roosevelt’s administration passed the National Labor Relations Act in 1935. But Republican presidents, up until Ronald Reagan in the 1980s, refrained from taking hostile positions toward labor unions and collective bargaining. In 1976, Republican Gerald Ford’s presidential campaign stated “free collective bargaining remains the best way to insure that American workers receive a fair price for their labors”. But under Reagan, the Republican party began to emphasize so-called “right to work” laws over collective bargaining and adopted more hostile, pro-business stances toward labor unions. Under Trump’s second term, he issued an executive order to rescind collective bargaining rights from more than 1 million federal workers and made cuts to federal agencies tasked with enforcing labor laws.

title: Progressive Ed Markey, 80, faces generational test in Massachusetts Senate primary
summary: Markey, looking to clinch another Senate term, leads younger rival Seth Moulton in blue state’s primary poll
text: Democrats have spent the summer ousting long-serving incumbents in primaries across the country. On Tuesday, Massachusetts voters will decide whether that generational revolt extends to the 80-year-old Ed Markey, whose younger Democratic rival has argued that the incumbent is simply too old to serve another term. But the Senate primary in this heavily Democratic state flips a central dynamic of previous contests, where youthful progressive insurgents have targeted – and in several cases, toppled – older incumbents they derided as avatars of an outmoded cautious establishment. In something of a role reversal, it is the long-serving Markey who is positioned as the voice of the progressive left, while 47-year-old Seth Moulton, a member of the House of Representatives, has moved some of his more moderate positions closer to those of his older rival in an effort to win over a younger voting cohort. Polls indicate that Markey – who was first elected to Congress in 1976, before Moulton was born – is poised to confound concerns over his age by winning election for a third full term, at the end of which he would be 86. Markey’s leftwing credentials have been burnished by endorsements from other high-profile progressives, including Bernie Sanders, the leftwing independent senator from Vermont, and Elizabeth Warren, his fellow Massachusetts senator. In a recent televised debate, Markey, who became a senator in a 2013 special election to replace John Kerry, when he resigned to become US secretary of state, attempted to tackle the age issue head on. “I think everyone watching this debate can see that I’m more energized than I’ve ever been before in my life. I am crisscrossing the state. I’m fighting for families,” the senator said. “Congressman Moulton has a hard time keeping up with me in the course of this campaign.” Moulton – a former marine who later ran a private health company after military service in Iraq – called for age limits to serve in Congress and contrasted Markey’s campaign performance with his own. “I’ve done over 50 town halls. You’ve done a couple,” he told Markey. “You’ve missed three candidate forums just in the past week. It’s a lot of work to represent this entire state.” But it was when the debate turned to technology and the candidates’ personal use of artificial intelligence that the age question appeared to sharpen. Asked whether the senator used AI platforms such as ChatGPT in his work, Markey replied that he uses “whatever is inside of my iPhone and my iPad – whatever comes up”. Moulton seized on that response as evidence that the incumbent did not fully understand the latest technology and how it was poised to transform every sector of society. “Senator,” he said, “if you don’t even know what you’re using on your phone or your iPad, this is why we need a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies to make sure that they are safe.” Moulton, who entered the House of Representatives in 2015, has embraced more moderate positions than Markey, namely on healthcare – on which he stopped short of advocating the single-payer system advocated by his opponent – and on transgender athletes. He apologized at a recent debate for previously saying in the fallout of Kamala Harris’s loss to Trump in 2024 that he did not want his daughters “getting run over on a playing field by a male or formerly male athlete”. He has said he would not vote for the Democrats’ current leader in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, if elected. Schumer, 75, has been portrayed as a symbol of what critics say is an out-of-touch and ageing establishment leadership that has left younger and left-leaning voters disenchanted. In blue Massachusetts, the Democratic primary often decides who wins office. An Emerson College Polling survey released on Sunday, suggested voters are willing to look past Markey’s age. In the survey, Markey led Moulton 60% to 33%, a dramatic increase from its May poll, when the senator held a five-point edge over the congressman. “If these numbers hold, this race will mirror Markey’s successful ‘peak-late’ approach to winning in 2020,” Spencer Kimball, executive director of Emerson College Polling, said, referring to the senator’s defeat of then congressman Joe Kennedy III, a scion of the state’s best-known political dynasty. Despite Kennedy’s youth – he was 39 at the time – young progressives rallied behind Markey, painting the incumbent as the leader most willing to take on the party’s establishment. Markey’s re-election would contradict the trend of a growing backlash against elderly leaders that critics have labelled a gerontocracy. Joe Biden was forced to drop his presidential re-election bid in 2024 amid concerns over his mental acuity after a disastrous presidential election debate in Atlanta against Donald Trump. Trump, who won the subsequent election against Biden’s replacement, Kamala Harris, is himself 80 and has been the subject of increasing age-related concerns about his health and ability to serve. Mitch McConnell, 84, the former Republican Senate majority leader, has been absent from Congress for months following a fall and hospitalization that has fueled fevered speculation about his health. On the campaign trail, Markey sought to cast his age as experience. “I’ve been standing up to the bosses for a long time, so I know no one gives it to you,” he says in one of his most prominent ads, featuring Warren and Sanders. “We have to fight for it.”
