title: Life after Maga: the group offering an ‘exit ramp’ for rightwingers questioning Trumpism
summary: The non-profit Leaving Maga is built on the premise that abandoning the Trump-built movement is like fighting a disease or breaking an addiction
text: Stephania Messina kept birthing boys. In the Quiverfull conservative Christian church she belonged to outside Detroit, Michigan, that made her a community celebrity. Your quiver, as the church taught it, is your womb, meant to be filled with as many arrows – a metaphor for children – as you can shoot unto the Lord. She shot five. “They treated me like I was Mother Mary, like I was this gift to the church,” she said. But while she was quickly pushed into leading worship and Bible study groups for women and children, she wasn’t permitted to talk about politics. “It wasn’t my job to vote or to know who to vote for. I was just supposed to submit to my husband and do what he thought was necessary,” Messina said. “I was being indoctrinated into Christian nationalism.” Messina quit her job, yielded to household voting, and took on home schooling and homesteading in a farmhouse, as part of an early 2010s precursor to the “Make America healthy again” (Maha) movement. When Donald Trump launched his first presidential campaign, he was suddenly “God’s chosen one” in the church, she said. Though Messina was never a “red-hat wearing” Maga supporter, she didn’t start questioning the movement until the early days of the Covid pandemic. Trained as a respiratory therapist, she watched Trump reverse course daily – from claiming the Covid vaccine was good to questioning its effectiveness. Meanwhile, her pastor preached that Covid lockdowns were a “demonic deep-state attempt to keep people out of church”. After a few other instances left her with doubts, she expanded her news sources beyond the church’s approved media, and then, she said: “The dam broke.” She sought mental health support and began to understand her years inside Maga as what she calls “a religious psychosis” built on fear, isolation and control. When she finally turned away from the church in 2021, she was cast as an outsider but felt the need to proclaim her Maga exit on social media: “I started speaking out to spread awareness. I was in so deep.” She felt alone. A few years later, she connected with the group Leaving Maga. “Leaving Maga is about normalizing leaving,” said Messina. “And it’s especially important now, since I think the Maga [bubble] is bursting.” Many Americans, like Messina, have drifted away from Trump in the past decade, but have done so quietly. Leaving Maga offers an exit ramp from Trump’s rightwing movement that has reshaped the Republican party and platformed political extremism. Launched in 2024, the movement turned non-profit is built on the premise that abandoning the Maga identity – and the community surrounding it – functions less like changing one’s mind and more like leaving a high-control religious group, fighting a disease or breaking an addiction. It requires not just rejecting a set of beliefs but rebuilding an entire structure of belonging and identity. Leaving Maga has touched thousands, operating on multiple fronts: weekly support meetings for the friends and family of people still inside Maga, monthly in-person meet-ups for those who have already left, a nationwide billboard campaign built around invitation rather than confrontation and a budding media literacy program meant to help people recognize disinformation. The goal isn’t to start or win a debate – it’s to give people somewhere to land once they’re ready to leave on their own. “There are more people than ever who are in Maga who are starting to have doubts and confusion,” said Rich Logis, who founded the group. “We’re trying to counter the toxicity of the Maga community by providing an exit ramp and a community where people can become what I call ‘a born-again human being’ and can reclaim their individuality, their empathy and their agency.” How Leaving Maga works Logis was drawn to Trump’s “burn it all down” energy in 2016, voting for him that year and in 2020. He spent nearly a decade as one of Maga’s most committed foot soldiers, writing part of the campaign’s call script for the first presidential election, helping register new voters for Trump, donating money and appearing on Fox News as a Maga pundit. But his decisive break from the movement came after the Uvalde school shooting in 2022 – he could no longer square his own values with the response he knew was coming from Trump supporters. Months after the Texas shooting that claimed the lives of 19 children and two teachers, Logis published a public apology online for supporting Trump and hurting people with his actions and rhetoric. The response was overwhelming – people commended him and criticized him – leading him to start the movement. He figured others had also left Maga and wanted to repair the damage they caused. “I had to go through a reckoning and acknowledge to myself that I had been culpable and complicit in assisting the president in dividing our country and amplifying conspiracy theories that resulted in unnecessary death, suffering and trauma,” Logis said. He built Leaving Maga the way he poured into Maga years prior – by writing countless online posts, speaking out on social media and reaching out to others. On any given day, Logis is on Instagram Live explaining how and why he left and how others can do the same. Maga leaders have defined the movement as one that calls for economic nationalism, secure borders, “America first” foreign policy and traditional conservative values, said Laura K Field, a political theorist and author of the book Furious Minds: The Making of the Maga New Right. “But an element of Maga that gets underestimated is its community-building dimension,” she said. “There’s a kind of appeal – a fascist and contrarian element, a deep religiosity to it – that unifies different parts of Maga, including the ordinary voters who aren’t DC beltway types, the elites, the high-powered Catholic intellectuals, or those in the manosphere, for example.” Logis was one of those people who saw Maga as a community more than a political ideology. “I think that it’s where people find vindication and validation,” he said. “It’s where they feel seen and heard and respected and appreciated.” But the glue holding the community together was “lies and falsehoods” and an “addiction to fear and rage” fueled by misinformation and disinformation, he said. “[In Maga], I had a dangerous belief in a ‘they’. A ‘they’ who were trying to abridge my rights and indoctrinate my children and take my guns and replace white people with brown people and foreigners.” Logis argues that leaving Maga requires more than distancing yourself from the president; you have to actively renounce Maga’s underlying conspiracy theories and also commit to building democracy that understands “we as Americans agree on important issues more than we disagree.” Logis and Messina describe leaving as a project of rebuilding empathy that Maga has deliberately suppressed. “As I began to listen to the people I had been told not to – the feminists, the people who they called ‘race baiters’, trans creators – my empathy came back,” Messina said. Logis put it similarly: leaving means you “no longer need to dehumanize and vilify and demonize those with whom we once disagreed”. They also don’t try to change the minds of Maga supporters. The idea is to let those who are already questioning it know there is support on the other side. “It is my philosophy that I do not engage in debates with people who are in Maga,” Logis said. “I don’t try to bombard and inundate people with facts and with policy.” Instead, he and other representatives for the organization spread the word through Instagram live streams and TikToks that receive thousands of likes. They go on cable news programs to speak out against the movement that once dominated their lives. One of the most effective methods is billboarding. Nearly 40 billboards have gone up in 27 states this year, with a simple message: “Having doubts? You’re not alone.” Logis said more than half a million visited the group’s website last year, and just as many have visited so far this year. Through the website, people can sign up for a newsletter that shares testimonies about people’s journeys out of Maga, access a guide on how to talk to family members and friends still engaged in Trumpism and join online group chats and monthly meet-ups with others who have left. Carter Brown, a former self-proclaimed tradwife who voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, said Leaving Maga had helped her realize she needed to do more than just speak out online after leaving; she needed to help rebuild. “It has taken deconstructing my religion and the dogma of western theology and realizing that I wasn’t even living like Jesus,” Brown said. She has changed her views on women’s rights, LGBTQ+ rights, capitalism and immigration. Brown said she now votes according to her new beliefs, volunteers with groups she harmed with her votes and has conversations with people she harmed. She also seeks friendship with people who have different lived experiences than her own. Leaving Maga is growing, Logis said, as polls show Trump’s increasing unpopularity. In recent months, Logis has spoken with people who left after being fired during “department of government efficiency” (Doge) cuts. Others have been turned off by Trump’s broken promises on foreign policy and rising costs. Messina said the people she had met in Leaving Maga came from all kinds of backgrounds. “We got into Maga for different reasons and got out for different reasons,” said Messina. “This is a space to learn other people’s stories and reckon with our own. Though the right knew how to capture us in its algorithms, I feel like the tide is turning.” How the group supports friends and family of Maga supporters Leaving Maga’s weekly online support group isn’t for people in Maga – it’s for the people who love them. That includes spouses, adult children, parents, siblings, friends and extended family who have watched someone close to them become “not the person who they once were”, said facilitator Julianna Forlano. Forlano, a therapist, has worked with families of people with narcissistic personality disorder and in addiction recovery, and said the ruptures she sees every week aren’t really about ideology. “What’s happening in families and in marriages, and between mothers and daughters and fathers and sons has to do with behavior,” she said. Forlano and her group borrow a framework used in addiction and recovery circles, treating the psychological grip of constant fear-based media and conspiracies like a disease. The mechanism is neurobiological, she said: people who consume a steady diet of fear narratives become fearful in general, adopt a “with us or against us” mentality and start treating loved ones as threats. “The mind is functioning as a dopamine seeker,” she said, craving the next piece of alarming news the way an addicted brain craves its next hit. Forlano is careful to note that holding certain political beliefs doesn’t make someone diseased; the compulsive, threat-seeking pattern layered on top of those beliefs is what the group tries to address. The stories members share reflect how the rupture disrupts daily life. One member married into a Latino family with her parents’ blessing, only to watch those same parents tell guests to “speak English” at her child’s birthday party and use slurs about mixed-race people; she has since decided her parents can no longer be part of their lives. Forlano said even conversations that start out ordinary can snap into political conflict without warning. “You could say something as simple as: ‘The tomatoes in my garden aren’t growing,’ and that person will respond by saying: ‘Well, climate change is a hoax,’” she said. Instead of encouraging members to cut ties, or to keep engaging in the kind of fact-based debate Forlano believes is useless, the group teaches patience and creates a space for members to see they aren’t alone. Members are coached to “hold the door open”, staying present in case a loved one ever starts to notice cracks in what they have been told, without continuing to push, argue or send articles that only further entrench the divide. The first step, Forlano said, was admitting that everything they have already tried hasn’t worked and to stop warring. Conflict often de-escalates once one party stops pushing back, she said. From there, the work isn’t about holding out hope that loved ones will turn on Trump and the movement he built; it’s about grief – mourning the relationship as it was, finding solidarity with others living through the same struggle and rebuilding a sense of self. Members stay in touch through group chats between sessions, trading techniques and support in real time. “The supportive nature of the community has been healing,” Forlano said. “It helps people find their footing again.” What life after Maga looks like Coming out on “the other side” is different for each person leaving Maga. Logis now supports Democrats. Messina has gone further. “I consider myself a democratic socialist now 100%,” she said. “I’m a member of the DSA. So is my son.” She has become an outspoken supporter of Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, and describes watching her husband and her 20-year-old son’s friend group all turn decisively against Trump within the past two years. But that doesn’t mean everyone in her family has left Maga. Her mother, 64, voted for Trump twice and still struggles to fully let go of messaging that casts Democrats as enemies. However, Messina has slowly had influence. She has talked to her mom about misogyny, intersectionality and the privilege that white women in Maga wield. “Now we’re working on Islamophobia because she can’t say Abdul El-Sayed without cringing because of these deeply ingrained biases,” Messina said. Their arguments used to end in screaming matches, but Messina has learned, slowly, not to cut her mother off. “Cutting them off completely just furthers the divides,” she said. The group continues to grapple with questions about forgiveness and grace. How much grace does the rest of the country owe people who spent years amplifying conspiracy theories before denouncing Maga? Logis said Leaving Maga regularly receives hostile messages from people who see forgiveness as unearned. Logis understands the anger, he said, but argues that a movement built entirely around punishing defection offers no incentive for anyone else to leave. “I am not asking anyone to like me. I’m not even asking for forgiveness,” said Messina. “I just hope that you’ll take what I have to say and believe it because I don’t have anything to gain except to hope that we can make a change.” • This story was amended on 1 September 2026. A previous version quoted Julianna Forlano as saying the mind functions as a “dope” seeker; in fact, Forlano said the mind functions as a “dopamine” seeker.

title: From milk to sausage rolls: how vending machines could help tackle UK ‘food deserts’
summary: Selling direct to public helps squeezed farmers control prices and improves access to food in rural areas
text: Fizzy drinks, packets of crisps and bars of chocolate: for decades, vending machines were known as a place to grab a quick snack. Now one family of farmers is trying to change that by bringing vending machines offering fresh milk and local produce – including scotch eggs, sausage rolls and brownies – to villages and other rural locations. Mark James, 70, and his sons Sam, 39, and Jacob, 36, first trialled vending machines as a way of selling their milk directly to consumers, giving themselves more control over the price they receive. “For the first time ever, we’re price makers rather than price takers,” Mark says. “If we weren’t doing [the vending machine business], we’d have to think about giving up milk.” Just under a third (30%) of the 4,500 litres of milk produced each day by the family’s herd of 130 dairy cows at Bodenham in Herefordshire is sold at their 17 Whole Moo World vending machines, located across Herefordshire and the neighbouring counties of Gloucestershire, Worcestershire and Shropshire. The remaining 70% is sold to a local milk processor. When Whole Moo World took off, Jacob and Sam branched out into retailing cakes, sandwiches and other treats made by small local producers from vending machines. Their business, Tuckshop, now has 22 sites, mostly alongside the milk machines, and also allows them to sell empty glass bottles for milk. Jacob says farmers are “waking up” to the advantages of selling directly to consumers, even if they do not have a suitable location or the funds needed to build their own farm shop. He believes vending machines could be the answer for villages and small rural communities at risk of becoming “food deserts”, where lower-income households struggle to find fresh healthy food amid closures of local shops and poor public transport. They also promise a more profitable way for squeezed farmers to reach customers directly and avoid expensive fees for intermediaries. Dairy producers in Britain and beyond have suffered in recent years from a boom and bust price cycle, where the price of milk, a globally traded commodity, has been extremely volatile. Strong global demand for dairy has usually led to farmers increasing their herd size and upping production, followed by oversupply and a crash in the milk price. Farmgate milk prices began to tumble again earlier this year, Mark says. “In August last year we were paid 44p a litre, and ever since the beginning of February it’s been down at 30p a litre.” For many dairy farmers, including the Jameses, this price does not cover the cost of production. Margins in the industry have always been tight and UK supermarkets have traditionally used low milk prices to tempt shoppers through the door, and the milk processing sector is dominated by three main players – Arla, Müller and First Milk. British supermarkets are currently charging between £1.20 and £1.30 for a two-pint, or 1.1-litre, bottle of milk. Whole Moo World customers pay £1.50 for a litre of the family’s unhomogenised milk – where the cream has not been separated from the milk during processing – delivered into a refillable glass bottle, which customers can buy once in the vending machines and wash and reuse. A litre of milkshake – with flavours including chocolate, strawberry, banana and specials such as mint choc and blueberry muffin – costs £2.90. Mark James says customers are prepared to pay a small premium for milk that, he says, tastes creamier and is more environmentally friendly thanks to the use of glass bottles. This is the Jameses’ second stint as dairy farmers. Mark took over his parents’ farm but quit milk production during the 2015 crisis, when low wholesale prices made it impossible to remain profitable. The family subsequently diversified their business, farming beef cattle and opening holiday lets, but the rolling banks of their land did not make it particularly suited to growing arable crops. The younger generation of the James family only supported a return to milk production if they ran the business differently. “It is only through doing this [the vending machines] that I have any interest in being a dairy farmer,” Sam says. It is not just the machines that make a difference: the mixed herd of dairy cows are milked by robots at a time of each cow’s choosing, freeing the family from 4am alarms and the labour-intensive nature of traditional milk production. On the day the Guardian visited one vending machine located next to the Primrose Vale pick-your-own and farm shop on the outskirts of Cheltenham, there was a steady flow of customers who arrived to fill up their glass bottles from the machines. “Our big issue is how to break the habit of [customers] picking milk up in a supermarket, and that is the difficulty because this means that someone is going to make a special trip to come here,” Mark says. For this, finding the right location is vital. Placing the vending machines next to a farm shop has mutual benefits for both businesses, says Jon Henley, one of the managers at Primrose Vale. “The machines seem to be bringing customers in 24/7, and then they see our strawberries and come back for the pick-your-own or the charging points [for electric vehicles]. It can also be helpful in winter when there isn’t much seasonal picking.” The machines are also a novelty for children. “We come to pick berries and then get milk. The machine is fun for little ones,” says Emma Coulter, buying a bottle of milk with help from her three-year-old daughter, Bonnie. Sam Carter-Campbell, who admits to treating himself to a strawberry milkshake as he drives around Gloucestershire for his job as an electrician, says: “I feel like I’m their best customer as I’m at the machine every day. I occasionally have a brownie, too, but sometimes I look and think, ‘I’d better not.’” One customer, who gave her name as Vicky, describes the machines as a good idea, provided they are installed in the right places in pretty villages and do not become an “eyesore”. The technology that powers vending machines has made significant advances in recent years, according to David Llewellyn, the chief executive of the Vending and Automated Retail Association. “It’s no longer just a standalone mechanical machine, which you don’t have any control over. Now with cashless payments, telemetry and connected equipment, you can see what’s happening, what needs replenishing and it will maintain a range of different temperatures,” he says. Machines stocked with fresh local produce have been available for consumers in France and Italy for some time, adds Llewellyn, while there is one machine for every 35 people in Japan. That compares with one for every 169 in the UK, where most are coffee and hot beverage outlets, usually found in factories and other workplaces. Although the James family can now monitor their machines remotely, they still refill them with milk themselves, travelling to locations within a 30-mile radius of their farm. They plan to keep expanding and may have to take on staff to support the business. “There is a new site we are looking at at the moment, a village of a couple of thousand people, where we think we could provide basic food like milk, eggs, cheese and sandwiches,” Jacob says. “We can do that fairly quickly. The place would support a a farm shop, but vending is much cheaper to install and run.”

title: UK house prices rise for first time since April, says Nationwide
summary: Average price of home rose 0.2% month on month in August to £275,465 as market awaits interest rate vote
text: UK house prices increased for the first time in four months in August, according to a leading index, as buyers and sellers remained in a “holding pattern” before an expected increase in interest rates later this year. The average price of a British home rose 0.2% month on month in August to £275,465, the first increase since April, according to Nationwide. Analysts had forecast a 0.1% rise. The increase follows a three-month decline in prices after Nationwide revised a month-on-month 0.1% rise in July to a fall of 0.1%. Ian Futcher, a financial planner at Quilter, said the UK housing market was awaiting the outcome of the next vote by the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee on 17 September on whether to raise the base rate of interest from its current 3.75%. “Over recent months, expectations for interest rates have been driven by the stop-start nature of the conflict in the Middle East,” Futcher said. “That leaves the housing market in something of a holding pattern ahead of the next interest rate decision. “While a hold remains the most likely outcome, it is becoming increasingly difficult to call with confidence. For borrowers, the key message is that rates may not have peaked. Until that uncertainty lifts, buyer confidence is likely to remain subdued.” After three months of falling prices, the average UK property remains valued more than £3,000 less than the £278,880 Nationwide estimated in April. On an annual basis, house prices were up 1.6% on the same month last year, ahead of the 1.4% year-on-year increase in July. However, that was below economists’ forecast of a 2% annual increase. Markets do not expect the MPC to raise rates this month but are pricing in a 0.25% increase by December. Robert Gardner, the chief economist at Nationwide, said the latest increase in the energy price cap, which will result in bills hitting a three-year high this winter, had not yet affected buying and selling activity. “While the latest energy price shock poses inflation risks, there have been encouraging signs that it is not feeding through to underlying price pressures,” he said. “Underlying affordability is improving as house price growth remains well below earnings growth, although some of these gains have been offset by higher mortgage rates. Nevertheless, this suggests that activity should regain momentum in the quarters ahead, providing the energy shock wanes and confidence returns.” On Tuesday, the Bank of England released data showing that the number of mortgage approvals made to homebuyers fell to its lowest level in more than two years in July. In July 56,053 mortgages were approved for house purchases, the lowest monthly figure since January 2024, when there were 56,032 approvals. There were 58,215 mortgage approvals made to homebuyers in June and over the past six months monthly mortgage approvals for house purchases have averaged about 60,800.

title: Trump suggests he is reviewing US support for UK over Falkland Islands
summary: Comments signal president prepared to use dispute to push UK to raise defence spending and Nato contributions
text: Donald Trump has suggested he is reconsidering US support for Britain’s sovereignty over the Falkland Islands, in a move likely to strain the “special relationship” between Washington and London. “I always review every position – that’s just one of many,” the US president told reporters in the White House, in response to a question about whether he was reviewing the US’s position over the South Atlantic islands, an archipelago whose status has long been disputed by Argentina, which claims sovereignty. Officially, the US takes a neutral position on who has rightful sovereignty over the islands, which Britain first claimed in the late 17th century and has held almost continually since 1833. In practice, it recognizes British administration over the territory, which was the subject of an Argentinian invasion and subsequent military conflict with Britain in 1982. Trump’s remarks were the clearest sign yet that the administration is prepared to use the dispute as leverage to pressure the government of the new British prime minister, Andy Burnham, to raise defence spending and contributions to Nato. A spokesperson for Burnham said on Tuesday that the UK’s position on the Falkands was “crystal clear”. “The Falkland islanders are British with a right to determine their own future. The islanders have expressed their wish to remain a British overseas territory, and our commitment to them is unwavering,” he said. “The prime minister was clear on his first day in office that we’ll meet our international commitments to our allies on defence spending, and he hasn’t wavered from that.” Trump’s comments came after an unnamed US official told the Telegraph last week that Washington could change its position over the islands if Britain failed to meet its defence spending commitments. That followed reports that John Healey, the UK chancellor, was preparing to drop Britain’s prior commitment to devote 3% of its GDP to defence spending by 2030 when he delivers his first budget on 28 October. Trump has made a priority of pressuring the US’s allies into boosting defence budgets and raising their Nato contributions during both his presidencies, accusing other countries of “freeloading”. At a summit in The Hague last year, allies committed to spending 5% of GDP on defence and security-related expenditures by 2035. Speculation about a US switch of allegiance over the islands has been swirling for months. In April, a leaked Pentagon email suggested reviewing Britain’s claim in response to its lack of support for Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. A switch of US position would represent a psychological blow to Britain’s sovereignty over the Falklands. After Argentina invaded the islands in 1982, the decision by Margaret Thatcher’s government to dispatch a naval taskforce that eventually resulted in their recovery was bolstered by staunch diplomatic support from Ronald Reagan, who came down on Britain’s side, even though Washington was also an ally of the Argentinian ruling military junta. A total of 649 Argentinian and 255 British personnel died in fighting before Argentina’s forces surrendered in June 1982. The episode played a central role in cementing the bond between Thatcher and Reagan, who were political allies and ideological kindred spirits. In recent times, Trump has become close to Argentina’s populist president, Javier Milei, who attended his second inauguration in January last year. Last year, Trump authorized a $20bn financial lifeline to Argentina to help it navigate a financial crisis, but made the funds contingent on Milei’s party winning subsequent congressional elections. Milei’s La Libertad Avanza party duly won the election, confounding pollsters’ forecasts. Trump later authorized the importation of Argentinian beef in an effort to reduce US grocery prices. Milei has vocally supported Argentina’s claim to the islands. In a 2013 poll, 1,513 out of 1,517 Falklands residents who cast a ballot said they wanted the territory remain a part of the UK. Feelings over the islands surfaced after Argentina’s 2-1 victory over England in the semi-final of the World Cup in July, when celebrating Argentinian players unfurled a banner reading “Las Malvinas son Argentinas” – the Falklands are Argentinian. The Argentinian football association was subsequently fined $235,000 by Fifa for violating its rules on non-sporting demonstrations.

title: Thai resort prepares to host USS Abraham Lincoln sailors after more than 270 days at sea
summary: Security stepped up in Pattaya before arrival of thousands of sailors and marines whose deployment was extended due to US war in Iran
text: Authorities in the Thai resort city of Pattaya have stepped up security as they prepare to welcome thousands of sailors and marines from the USS Abraham Lincoln who have spent more than 270 consecutive days at sea. “About 600 officials will provide security and other necessary assistance,” the provincial governor, Narit Niramaiwong, told AFP. The nuclear-powered aircraft carrier sailed past Singapore over the weekend on its way back to the US after a lengthy deployment in the Middle East as part of the US war against Iran. It left California in November 2025 for duty in the South China Sea and was rerouted to the Middle East before the US-Israeli attacks on Iran that began six months ago. Reports of deteriorating living conditions and poor mental health onboard, including attempted suicides, have made headlines in the US and provoked criticism of Donald Trump’s war against Iran. Pattaya’s mayor, Poramase Ngampiches, said the carrier would dock just after midnight on Wednesday (about 5pm GMT on Tuesday) at Laem Chabang port. About 40 buses have been laid on to transport the sailors to Pattaya and back in staggered groups before the carrier departs on Sunday. After meeting US officials on Monday, Poramase said service members would be banned from certain recreational activities such as parasailing and cannabis use. Medical cannabis was legalised in Thailand in 2022 and dispensaries have become common in Thai cities. Once a sleepy fishing village, Pattaya was transformed by the Vietnam war in the 1960s, when US soldiers on leave began coming for rest and recreation. The city has since become hugely popular with foreign tourists, known for its beaches and a nightlife scene that has long drawn scrutiny over sex tourism. Poramase told AFP there had been a recent crackdown on sex workers but denied this was linked to the US arrivals. Government officials are warning local businesses not to overcharge US sailors, and Poramase said there would be a greater police presence in popular areas along Pattaya beach and Walking Street. The city’s police chief, Anek Srathongyoo, said law enforcements agencies had been ordered to step up security measures to prevent undesirable situations. He said that if any US service members broke Thai law, they would be prosecuted accordingly. Local business owners feeling the tourism slump from the Iran war are eager for the new arrivals. A banner hung over a local bar near a beach read: “Welcome all US military personnel. Thank you for your service.” Bualuang Ponok, a bar employee, said she had seen US service members during past visits but she did not expect many from this crew. “They said 5,000 people will come here but how many will reach us?” she said. Earlier in August, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington relieved the long-deployed Lincoln in the Middle East. The Lincoln, one of the US navy’s largest warships, was part of American efforts in the Iran war, which flared back up over the weekend for the first time in a month. The deployment included a record-setting uninterrupted time at sea of more than 270 days. Trump downplayed concerns over conditions onboard and said the deployment was “not nearly long enough”. Thai officials have said the Lincoln will return to the US after its port call in Thailand. Associated Press and Agence France-Press contributed reporting

title: Shaun the Sheep hailed on latest list of storm names
summary: Meteorologists release list of monikers for potential storms this season after 40,000 suggestions from public
text: From a five-year-old weather enthusiast to a beloved animated sheep, the inspiration for the list of storm names for this autumn and winter is wide and varied. Austen, Boelo and Chloe will be the first named storms of this winter, meteorologists have revealed, after more than 40,000 suggestions were submitted by the public. The UK’s Met Office, in partnership with Ireland’s Met Éireann and the Dutch national weather forecasting service KNMI, released the list for the 2026-27 season on Monday. People submitted names in honour of a much-loved labrador puppy, meteorological pioneers and Shaun the Sheep, from the animation Wallace and Gromit. The Met Office said the purpose of naming storms was serious as it helped people take notice, prepare and stay safe in severe weather. The organisations have been naming storms since 2015, with the list running from early September to the following August. It coincides with the start of meteorological autumn, when the likelihood of low-pressure systems and the potential for storms severe enough to be named increases. In the last year, four names were used from the list, reaching the letter D with Storm Dave on 1 April, although the UK was also affected by a further three storms named by other European meteorological services: Benjamin, Claudia and Goretti. The third name in this year’s list, Chloe, was selected by the Met Office after being put forward more than 120 times, including by the mother of a five-year weather enthusiast who is “fascinated by the weather” but can also “create a storm by herself” when she is tired. The name Finn was suggested for a two-year-old boy described by his family as “wild and a force to be reckoned with”, while Ivy was nominated in honour of a nine-month-old labrador puppy affectionately known as “the absolute destructor”. Shaun also joins the list after a public vote that was run as part of a collaboration with the British animation studio Aardman, which is behind Wallace and Gromit. Holly Clements, the Met Office head of warnings and guidance, said: “For more than a decade, storm naming has helped us communicate the risks from severe weather more effectively. A named storm provides a clear focus for forecasts and warnings, helping more people understand the potential impacts and take action to protect themselves, their families and their property.” Storms are given a name when they are deemed to have the potential to have a medium or high impact in the UK, Ireland or the Netherlands. Wind is the primary focus, although additional issues such as rain or snow are also considered. This year’s names, and the countries they came from, are: Austen Ireland Boelo (Boo-loh) Netherlands Chloe UK Dano (Dah-noh) Netherlands Evelyn Ireland Finn UK Gwendolyn Netherlands Heather Ireland Ivy UK Jade Netherlands Kilian Ireland Laoise (Lee-sha) Ireland Miriam Ireland Nicola UK Olaf Netherlands Phelim Ireland Ruban UK Shaun UK Theo UK Vesna (Vehs-nuh) Netherlands Wende (Vhen-duh) Netherlands

title: Boss of City regulator accused of threatening consumer group over £9.1bn car loan scheme
summary: FCA chief, Nikhil Rathi, warned of ‘adverse consequences’ if challenge made to settlement, court filings allege
text: The boss of the UK’s financial regulator is accused of threatening a consumer group with “adverse consequences” if it blocked a £9.1bn compensation scheme meant to settle the motor finance scandal. Legal documents reviewed by the Guardian said the alleged comments by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) chief executive, Nikhil Rathi, amounted to “an inappropriate intervention by a public official”. The threat is said to have taken place during a Microsoft Teams call with the directors of Consumer Voice (CV) on 27 April, hours before the deadline to file legal challenges against the FCA’s proposed redress scheme for those missold car loans. Rathi warned that the City regulator would be “unable to collaborate” with Consumer Voice if it took legal action, “suggesting adverse consequences for CV’s future engagement with the FCA and adverse press briefings against it”, the filings said. “The implication was clear: the FCA’s willingness to engage constructively with CV was contingent on CV not challenging the scheme, and would give way to hostility if it did,” the documents claimed. Up until that point, the FCA had treated Consumer Voice as a “trusted expert consumer body”, the filings said. But once the group decided to challenge the scheme, “the FCA changed its position … now the FCA seeks to denigrate CV’s activities and motives in bringing this application”. Rathi also allegedly claimed that their potential legal challenge was the “biggest risk to the scheme” and that plans to get money to millions of victims by this Christmas would fail if directors followed through with their plans. The filings say it was not disclosed that three specialist lenders were also planning to challenge the scheme, only that the FCA had been “engaging with the banks”, who, over the previous weekend, decided not to challenge the payout plan. The episode marks a fresh controversy in the long-running saga surrounding mis-sold UK car loans, which prompted a contentious intervention by former chancellor Rachel Reeves last year, following intense lobbying by big banks. Lenders have been arguing that a large compensation bill would risk spooking investors and causing long-lasting economic damage to the UK. The documents were filed at the UK’s upper tribunal, as part of the wider legal challenge against the terms of the FCA’s compensation scheme. Consumer Voice and the specialist lenders – Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes-Benz Financial Services and Crédit Agricole Auto Finance – are challenging the scheme on different grounds. Consumer Voice, founded by former Which? staffers Nikki Stopford and Alex Neill in 2023, is the only group arguing for bigger compensation for drivers who were overcharged as a result of lenders paying out commission to car dealerships between 2007 and 2024. They say the scheme is low-balling consumers – offering average payouts of £830 per mis-sold loan – and is putting the interests of profit-making lenders, who fear big bills, ahead of the interests of consumers it is meant to protect. The FCA has since tried to get the claim by Consumer Voice thrown out of court by alleging that its co-founders have not been transparent about their funding and potential conflicts of interest. Last month, legal documents lodged by the regulator suggested Consumer Voice was not being honest about its business model and relationship with its lawyers at Courmacs Legal. Both firms, “operate for profit in the sphere of claims management”, the FCA said, adding that Courmacs had previously hired Consumer Voice to conduct consumer research on its behalf. The consumer group “therefore has commercial incentives of its own”. Consumer Voice says it partners with law firms with an aim to help consumers “get back money they’re owed from rule-breaking companies”. It has promoted claims against the likes of Amazon, Facebook, Mastercard, Apple iCloud, and Sony PlayStation, and makes money by doing communications work for law firms to raise awareness of their claims. It also receives a commission when its members join one of the law firms’ cases, according to its website. Courmacs, based in Blackburn, says it is providing pro bono services in the case against the FCA. Ultimately, larger payouts for consumers will boost Courmacs’ earnings, with the firm taking up to 30% of client settlements. A spokesperson for the FCA said “we don’t recognise the way this conversation has been characterised”, adding that officials had spoken to a range of parties, including lenders and claims firms ahead of the deadline. “It was important to explain the implications for consumers and that we would defend the scheme robustly as the best way of getting compensation paid,” the FCA said. “We were also clear that we would be upfront with consumers about why expected compensation would be delayed.” The FCA also said they did not know about the other challenges by specialist lenders until after the call. The regulator added that its staff had continued to engage with Consumer Voice since the call. That included discussions on how to best handle settlement offers that lenders might make outside of the official compensation scheme. “We will respond fully to Consumer Voice and Courmacs Legal in our court filings.” Consumer Voice co-founder Alex Neill said: “We remain resolute and confident in our challenge on behalf of millions of consumers who are being short-changed by the redress scheme.”

title: Shein shares slide on fast-fashion retailer’s stock market debut
summary: Hong Kong flotation at $26bn by firm once valued at $100bn follows failure to list in US and UK
text: Shares in the fast-fashion brand Shein slumped by as much as 10% as the China-founded company made its long-anticipated trading debut on the Hong Kong stock exchange. The Singapore-headquartered company, once valued at almost $100bn (£74bn), went public on Tuesday pricing shares at HK$48.56, valuing the business at just over $26bn. However, minutes after the flotation, which raised HK$13.6bn, the stock fell as much as 10%, pushing the online retailer’s valuation below $25bn. Shein’s share price recovered most of its early trading plunge, closing at HK$48.50, just 0.12% down on its opening price. “Let global consumers enjoy the sound of fashion,” said Leigh Gui, Shein’s chief financial officer, after a gong was struck to mark the start of trading. The lacklustre launch as a publicly listed company comes after one of the longest-awaited initial public offerings in recent years, after plans to list in New York were blocked by regulators over forced labour concerns. Shein also considered a £50bn flotation in London but faced similar questions about its supply chain from campaigners, MPs and investors. Nevertheless, the company has still floated as one of the world’s biggest listed fashion groups, with a valuation around the same as the Swedish retailer H&M. The Zara owner, Inditex, has a market capitalisation of about $213bn. Shein reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world at the time. The plunge in its value since has been driven by regulatory changes around the world that threaten its business model of shipping goods in small packages out of China to take advantage of tax breaks on low-value imported goods. The company swung to a loss of $99m in the first three months of this year, compared with a net income of $395m the year before, after the US removed its “de minimis” import duty exemption on small packages, hitting its sales in the country. The EU is also cracking down on the loophole, introducing a €3 (£2.56) duty on small parcels imported from outside the trading bloc in June, and intends to phase it out, while the UK has said it will do the same by October 2028. On Tuesday, France began imposing penalties on some fast-fashion items to curb the surge in sales of cheap products sold by retailers such as Shein and its Chinese rival Temu. Paris passed a fast-fashion law in June to address concerns about overproduction, with the penalties calculated using a formula that factors in the number of products sold, their prices and repairability. The penalties, which are set to increase in 2030, range from €0.25 for a pair of boxer shorts or socks to €12 for a coat, with the amount capped at 50% of the product’s pre-tax sales price. China’s commerce ministry has called the French law discriminatory and a trade barrier and said it could be in violation of World Trade Organization principles. Shein, founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at about the start of 2022, a move viewed by analysts as designed to avoid increasing scrutiny of Chinese companies. After forced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.

title: Almost half of terrorism arrests in Great Britain since 9/11 have been in past year
summary: Increase coincides with proscription of Palestine Action last year which has led to thousands of arrests for allegedly supporting the protest group
text: Almost half of all terrorism arrests in Great Britain since the 9/11 attacks on the twin towers in 2001 have come in the past year, official data shows. There have been 6,539 arrests for terror-related activity in Great Britain since the 2001 attacks and 3,021 of those arrests were in the year ending 31 March 2026, according to the Home Office. The increase coincides with the proscription of Palestine Action, which came into effect on 5 July last year and has led to thousands of arrests of people for allegedly supporting the direct action protest group, the first such group to be banned under the Terrorism Act. The ban, which has been criticised by UN experts, NGOs, a former director of public prosecutions and a former director of the security services, is the subject of a continuing legal challenge, which will next be heard at the UK supreme court on 4 November. Ruth Ehrlich, the director of external relations at Liberty, which intervened in the legal challenge, said: “The staggering increase in arrests over the past year is the clearest indicator that the UK’s counter-terror laws are not fit for purpose. “The government’s current definition of terrorism is so wide-ranging it captures behaviour most people would never consider terrorism. When it’s not clear what counts as terrorism, public trust collapses and without trust, counter-terror laws simply won’t work. “This data underscores the urgent need to update the current definition of terrorism to enable current and future governments to uphold their duty to safeguard the public whilst protecting people’s rights and preventing overreach.” The proscription led to a mass civil disobedience campaign with most of those arrested at demonstrations organised by Defend Our Juries (DOJ), where they held up placards saying: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.” Terrorism-related arrests were up 1,434% in the year ending 31 March compared with the previous 12 months. There was also a 3,761% increase in women and girls arrested and a 2,306% increase in arrests of those aged 30 and over. Earlier, this year, Raj Chada, the head of criminal defence at the law firm Hodge Jones and Allen, said: “The most common terrorist in the UK at present is a pensioner at a silent vigil holding a placard.” DOJ says the number of arrests relating to support for Palestine Action, which targets UK entities it claims to be complicit in Israeli genocide against Palestinians, has since risen to more than 3,600, which would be over half of the arrests since 9/11. About 2,500 people have been charged under section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which prohibits showing support for a terrorism group and carries a maximum sentence of six months in prison. DOJ says at least 50 people have been charged under section 12, which concerns inviting support for a banned group, must be heard by a jury and carries a maximum sentence of 14 years. A DOJ spokesperson said: “These shocking statistics expose the true nature of how the British government uses terror laws. Since July 2025, thousands of peaceful protesters have been arrested under the Terrorism Act for quietly expressing opposition to genocide and standing with those who have taken direct action against it. By doing this, the government has shown that they are not using these laws to protect the public – rather to silence those who speak and act against genocide.” In June, four Palestine Action activists became the first defendants convicted of property damage whose offending – during a 2024 raid on a factory near Bristol owned by the Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit – was deemed by a judge post-conviction to have a “terrorist connection”. A Home Office spokesperson said: “Showing support for a proscribed organisation is against the law. Decisions to arrest are operational matters for the police and are taken on the basis of the facts and circumstances of each case.”

title: Solar cuts ‘at least £400 from bills in even the cloudiest British areas’
summary: Savings grow as energy prices in Great Britain rise and cost of panel installation falls, analysis finds
text: Households in Great Britain’s cloudiest regions could still save more than £400 a year on their energy bills by installing rooftop solar panels, research has found. Rising wholesale energy prices mean the potential savings from a home solar panel system have climbed in recent years, as the cost of installation has continued to fall, leading to increased demand. An analysis carried out for the Guardian has found that in areas with the fewest sunny days, solar panels could bring annual savings of about £450 a year on the average household electricity bill. In areas with the brightest skies, this figure could climb to more than £600. The findings, provided by the UK solar firm Recharge Renewable, show that households in southern Scotland could save on average £440 a year, based on the estimated solar generation in Glasgow over a year, while homes in the north-west of England could save £463, based on the generation likely in Manchester. In southern England, where brighter weather means more solar generation, savings on bills could climb to between £571 and £618 a year for households in Brighton and Southampton, respectively, according to the figures. The potential savings have increased in recent years as conflict in Ukraine and the Middle East have compounded Britain’s rising electricity prices, leading to a boom in rooftop solar installations. Large-scale installations have also climbed under the Labour government, which has set a target to triple the UK’s solar farms by 2030. A Guardian analysis of the government’s official figures revealed there were more new solar power installations in the first half of this year than in any six-month period since 2011, the year the UK built its first large-scale solar farm, in Cornwall. Most of the new solar panels recorded are on household rooftops, with these smaller solar installations making up slightly less than a third of the country’s total solar power capacity. The increase in capacity allowed solar power to supply 14.4% of Great Britain’s electricity in July, more than in any previous month, after some parts of the UK recorded almost twice the average sunshine hours for the time of year. The rise was due to the summer heatwaves, made more severe by the climate crisis, which has triggered drought and record temperatures across Europe. Recharge Renewable, a Somerset-based solar provider, warned that households hoping to save on their energy bills from solar panels need to pay attention to the set-up of each rooftop system as well as the regional potential. “Even in cloudier parts of Britain, a typical 4kW system can still be worth around £450 a year in electricity used at home under the current price cap,” a spokesperson said. “The catch is that this is the value of the units displaced, not a finished bill, and a north-facing or shaded roof will not match a modelled south-facing array. Households should compare any regional headline with their own annual use, then look at whether a battery or more daytime demand would keep more of that generation on site.” The company’s analysis used the typical electricity output from a standard, south-facing 4kW rooftop solar system, and data for the average energy use of the typical household. These figures were then adjusted for each of Great Britain’s 14 regions, using satellite imagery to measure the different levels of annual sunshine across big cities and accounting for varying electricity rates. The calculations do not include the use of a battery and assume that each household uses only 50% of the electricity generated over a year. This means that bill payers who use more solar power while working from home, for example, or by timing appliances to run during daylight hours, could make even greater savings. However, a typical 4kW solar system costs about £7,000 after the government removed VAT for solar upgrades. This puts the upfront cost out of reach of many families and has prompted calls for the government to step in to help make rooftop solar more affordable for people on lower incomes. Plug-in solar panels went on sale in the UK for the first time last week, allowing households unable to use rooftop set-ups to generate power from their balconies.

title: Tuesday briefing: Scotland has promised on violence against women – can it deliver?
summary: In today’s newsletter: First minister John Swinney has pledged to put an end to violence against women and girls. But can he turn ambitious laws into real change?
text: Good morning. Violence against women and girls, in all its myriad forms – physical and mental, blatant and insidious – is a global challenge. It reaches back through millennia and, lately, it has been turbo-charged by technology, which offers abusers new ways to shame, harass and monitor victims. What would it take to eradicate it? Scotland’s first minister John Swinney wants to find out. Today, he will set out his programme for government (the Holyrood equivalent of the King’s speech), and Swinney surprised many when he pledged to put ending violence against women at the heart of his government’s ambitions for the coming year and beyond. But haven’t we been here before? Scotland has produced a raft of radical strategies, as well as legislation hailed as the international gold standard on domestic violence. So what hasn’t changed? For today’s newsletter, I spoke to equalities campaigner Talat Yaqoob, who co-chaired the Scottish government’s National Advisory Council on Women and Girls after four years until last month. I asked her what government – and societal – action constitutes meaningful change, and what other countries can learn from Scotland. But first, the headlines. Five big stories Nepal-Tibet | Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, who are thought to be trapped in underground areas in Nepal, after the devastating flash floods. Iran | The new US sanctions campaign is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars. UK | The British Museum privately hosted Palantir founder Peter Thiel in a private viewing of the Bayeux tapestry, the Guardian understands. Slavery | Countries are legally obliged to consider reparations for the transatlantic slave tried, and address the legacy racial discrimination, a UN committee has said. US news | A Las Vegas jury has found former South Side Compton Crips gang leader Duane Keith Davis guilty of the murder of Tupac Shakur, bringing the case to a close nearly 30 years after the famous rapper was gunned down. In depth: Why Scotland’s pioneering laws aren’t enough We’ll find out later today the detail of the measures John Swinney is proposing, but the SNP leader’s preliminary talk has been big: pledging his personal leadership, acknowledging that alongside resources to protect those most at risk of violence right now, his government needs to address underlying economic inequalities – and hinting at the need for focused prevention when he says that lasting change requires all of society to play our part. The context for Swinney’s vow is bleak: a steady increase in misogyny and violence against women and girls across the world. In Scotland, both domestic abuse and sexual crimes are on the rise – crimes recorded by Police Scotland including rape and attempted rape, sexual assault and communicating indecently were up 10% last year and are now at their highest level since 1971. Rape Crisis Scotland has pointed out that these figures reflect a significant rise in historic offences and that, despite the best efforts of Reform in Scotland to link them with immigration, the vast majority are perpetrated by people known to the victim. Moreover, as Yaqoob tells me, technological advances have “enabled an entirely new field of violence against women and girls – deepfakes, ‘revenge porn’, online coercion and control of women through things like GPS tracking” – while the now-quotidian misogyny of the manosphere is saturating playgrounds and classrooms. A survey of Scottish secondary school boys last year found a third believed that girls who wear revealing clothing were “asking for trouble”, while a third of female teaching staff, in a separate study, reported sexist abuse from children as young as eight years old. “We also know that when there is recession, when there is poverty, there is a rise of the far right, there’s a rise of anger, and women are often the victims of that anger,” Yaqoob says. The Guardian’s own research last year found that two out of every five people arrested after participating in the 2024 summer riots had been previously reported to the police for domestic abuse. Recession hits funding too: many services are on their knees, according to campaigners, while the post-pandemic court backlog and ongoing crisis in the legal aid system continues to deny victims access to justice. *** Haven’t we been here before? When I returned to Scotland to report for the Guardian just over a decade ago, there was a new female first minister, Nicola Sturgeon, one of three women heading the main political parties at Holyrood, and you could taste the change in the air. This visibility of women in top jobs – necessary, of course, but never sufficient – was accompanied by a raft of ambitious strategies and bills. Equally Safe, launched in 2014, was a plan across central and local governments to act together on tackling gender-based violence. The National Advisory Council on Women and Girls, established by Sturgeon in 2017, brought forward radical proposals to offer two months of paid paternity leave and establish a world-leading process for complainants of sexual violence. In 2018, the Scottish parliament passed legislation to criminalise coercive control for the first time, hailed by international experts at the time as “the gold standard”, and three years later added further powers with domestic abuse prevention orders. There’s been funding for sexual violence prevention programmes in schools and universities, and a national advocacy service to support victims as they navigate the justice system. And, in 2025, a landmark justice reform bill abolished the Scottish verdict of “not proven” – a global legal anomaly thought to be a key factor in the country’s significantly lower convictions rate for rape and sexual assault. These offer a useful case study of what Yaqoob describes as “the implementation gap”. While the 2018 Act was undoubtedly radical, campaigners say it hasn’t achieved its full potential because the institutional change demanded of police and prosecutors – including the training of officers and shifting of mindset over charging decisions – hasn’t happened. Only 4% of domestic abuse crimes were prosecuted under the new legislation last year. Meanwhile, many of the 2021 powers are gathering dust because poor drafting has rendered them too difficult to implement. “There is a theme here,” says Yaqoob. “There’s no shortage of inspiring rhetoric and in some cases good strategy and legislation. What there isn’t is the priority and resources when it leaves the desk of the Scottish government and that means a lack of tangible change in women’s lives.” *** What needs to happen now? Removing this block between declaration and delivery doesn’t have to be onerous, Yaqood argues. Partly it’s about making gender equality a priority across the public sector. “Gender equality is always on the periphery of interventions. Until it’s at the centre, you can have as many big commitments as you want, but it will not make a difference enough to women and girls’ lives”. And placing gender equality at the centre is the beginning of the systemic change demanded of the police and prosecution service, as well as resourcing the tailored, often grassroots, projects that can make a difference in schools and communities – especially those designed by and for men – like the Many Good Men project which takes the conversation into football clubs. “We don’t have to reinvent the wheel,” says Yaqoob. “There are years of well-evidenced practice that we need to scale up.” Credit where it’s due: Police Scotland has done some very decent work in recent years with Don’t Be That Guy – a campaign that has young men talking directly to their peers about problematic behaviour. But the force has struggled to take on misogyny and racism within its own ranks. In recent years in Scotland, the discussion around violence against women has been dominated by arguments around women-only spaces – the UK’s most influential gender critical group, For Women Scotland, is based in Edinburgh – and unfounded claims that Scotland’s asylum population is responsible for an increase in sexual violence. Yaqoob is clear: “Anyone who tries to position themselves as protectors of women and girls, but does not have an agenda that is focused on tackling poverty, putting money back into communities for women and girls, or the need for consent and sexuality education in schools, is selling you a lie.” (For more, that broader agenda of tackling gender inequality in all its forms is the subject of a new book of essays, co-edited by Yaqoob.) *** The solution is global – and also local A global problem demands, in part at least, a global solution. As I’ve written in previous First Editions, change at street levels demands that all of us engage in small acts of solidarity. Yaqoob puts it this way: “Whether you’re calling out misogynistic language in the pub or you’re the leader of a local council allocating resources, there are so many different facets of society where people need to take more responsibility for the space they occupy.” So much of this conversation applies beyond Scotland, but back at Holyrood it’s fair to say that, while there’s a bit of eye-rolling as yet another male politician “discovers” violence against women and some head-scratching over precisely what reforms he intends to unveil, there’s also wary optimism to hear this focus at the beginning of the SNP government’s five year term. As one campaigner told me yesterday: “This is an opportunity to kick the door down for bigger changes”. What else we’ve been enjoying Rebecca Solnit is on form in this column lambasting Donald Trump’s plan to “sell off” chunks of Yosemite national park. “The US is being sold for parts or just handed over to the oligarchy,” she writes. Charlie Lindlar, newsletters team I found Ben Quinn’s acute analysis of what’s gone wrong for Reform this summer a useful primer ahead of their party conference later this week. Libby I loved this perceptive piece from Tanya Aldred on the short shelf life of football shirts. For more from Tanya on the intersection of climate change and sport, sign up to The Hotspot. Charlie The story of how Jackson Pollock’s masterwork Blue Poles became Australia’s most controversial painting takes in Gough Whitlam, the Shah of Iran and Paul Hogan – and Guardian Australia’s political editor, Tom McIlroy, tells it brilliantly in this Full Story podcast. Libby Our Laura Snapes’s music coverage is indispensable, yet not even her Taylor Swift opus can compete with this vital piece against the term “picky bits”. “It’s the Boaty McBoatface of dinner time,” she correctly argues, “exposing our once-repressed nation’s surprisingly twee core and total disregard for shame”. Charlie Sport Football | Argentina’s Lionel Messi announced his retirement from international football, following his father’s death and the World Cup defeat by Spain. Tennis | Carlos Alcaraz beat Roman Safiullin 6-4, 6-4, 6-4 in the first round of the US Open in his first match since April. Football | Bukayo Saka scored the only goal of the game as Arsenal held off a much-improved Aston Villa to make it two wins from two in the Premier League. The front pages “Public control of utilities is key to growth – Burnham”, is the Guardian’s front page today. The Times leads with “Healey: I’ll prove I’m no hypocrite on defence”, the Telegraph writes “SAS chief: Army witch hunts put UK at risk”, and the Mail has “Kemi gets Tories battle ready with ruthless reshuffle”. The i Paper’s splash is “Killer kitchen dust: victims’ loved one to receive higher compensation”, the FT says “Crunch warning for consultants as clients harness AI to cut IT spending”. The Express has “Million OAPs hit with top-rate tax bills”, and the Sun’s headline is “Prem’s £10m crypto cash frozen”. The Mirror leads with “Maxwell to beg Trump for freedom”, and Metro’s front page is “Dad’s gift of life”. Today in Focus War of words: my language lessons in Ukraine For Charlotte Higgins, the Guardian’s chief culture writer, visiting Ukraine and meeting the artists, novelists and poets under fire changed her life. “It was even before I went home that I decided I needed to learn some Ukrainian,” she tells Helen Pidd. She talks about why she was inspired to learn Ukrainian and what it taught her about its people. Cartoon of the day | Ben Jennings The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad Rachel Aroesti has always loved podcasts, especially the kind that can be described as ‘Two Men Talking (In Excessive Detail About Their Lives)“. Initially drawn to them for their humour, she began to find them hugely comforting – sometimes falling asleep listening to Adam and Joe’s BBC 6 Music show. But, as her consumption increased, she became aware that she used podcasts as a psychological crutch, to prevent being alone with her thoughts. After a silent, tech-free train ride across the East Anglian countryside, Aroesti felt she was undergoing a mental reboot. Her mind flooded with ideas, plans, insights and reflections at a speed and intensity she had not experienced for years. Nowadays, she savors silence and boredom, and has successfully reduced her listening by at least 80%. “I’ve given my mind permission to wander – both productively and pointlessly – again,” she writes. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.
