In his opinion, Roberts wrote that the construction is a “likely infringement of the legislature’s power of the purse and authority to regulate federal property in the District of Columbia to continue”, and says the majority’s ruling “is no victory for the separation of powers”. “The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds – President’s Park – in the District of Columbia. Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the executive’s construction of it,” the chief writes. He also disagreed that the potential injuries to Hoagland are insufficient for the historic trust to sue, saying she was “deeply committed to the preservation of such historic American buildings” through her work with the association. “Hoagland’s injury suffices for standing,” Roberts wrote, likening the impact of the White House’s transformation on her to how “an environmentalist can sustain a concrete, particularized aesthetic injury from the extinction of a particular animal or the transformation of a particular forest or river that he regularly enjoys”.

title: North Carolina teenager dies from rare brain-eating amoeba infection
summary: Naegleria fowleri is commonly found in warm freshwater, and if it enters through the nose, can cause brain damage
text: A North Carolina teenager has died after contracting a rare and often fatal brain-eating amoeba. The state’s health department (NCDHHS) confirmed the boy’s death on Monday, saying: “NCDHHS has been informed that the teen who developed a rare illness, caused by Naegleria fowleri died on Aug. 31, 2026. We extend our condolences to the family, friends and community impacted by this loss.” Last Thursday, NCDHHS reported that the boy had contracted a rare illness caused by the single-cell organism commonly found in warm freshwater. The teenager – whose mother, Monica Mendoza, identified him as Moises Ponce Mendoza in an online fundraiser – was described earlier by the NCDHHS in its statement as “critically ill and receiving medical care”. A Facebook post from a user who identified himself as a close relative of Ponce – also said that the teen had died by Monday. In the online fundraiser, Mendoza described her son in Spanish as a “young man full of life currently fighting for his life in the hospital – in a coma”, adding that his illness started with severe headaches. She said she initially took Moises to a Burlington hospital for severe symptoms on 21 August – but they were sent home after a doctor briefly examined him. His condition quickly worsened and Mendoza said she rushed him to the University of North Carolina hospital’s emergency department at 7am the next day. Doctors there found he had an infection caused by Naegleria fowleri, which she described as “an extremely rare amoeba that can enter through the nose, reach the brain, and cause inflammation, infection, and brain damage”. “From that moment on, our lives changed completely,” Mendoza added. “Moises is in a coma, and doctors are doing everything possible to fight this illness and give him a chance to pull through.” Pictures posted online showed Moises intubated in a hospital bed and receiving intravenous fluids. The Guardian has contacted Mendoza for additional comment. Naegleria fowleri is often found in warm ponds, lakes and rivers. It is not found in saltwater or in properly maintained and chlorinated pools, the NCDHHS said. The amoeba is harmless if swallowed – but is often deadly if contaminated water enters the nose and reaches the brain, such as while diving in water, water-skiing or engaging in similar activities. Naegleria fowleri can cause an infection known as primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM), according to the US Centers of Disease Control (CDC). Its symptoms can include severe headaches, fever, nausea and vomiting, followed by stiff neck, seizures and coma, with the illness often progressing rapidly and causing death within about five days. Fewer than 10 cases are typically reported in the US each year, usually during prolonged periods of hot weather when freshwater temperatures rise, the NCDHHS warned. The CDC says more than 97% of people who contract PAM die from the infection. Health officials advise swimmers to keep their heads above water in warm freshwater, use nose clips or hold their noses shut when entering the water, and avoid diving or jumping in. They also recommend avoiding submerging the head in hot springs or thermal waters and disturbing sediment in shallow, warm freshwater. Ponce’s story gained attention after an eight-year-old Louisiana girl died after contracting a Naegleria fowleri infection. Lillian Smart may have been infected while she was swimming in Louisiana’s Lake Claiborne, the Louisiana health department said. The girl died on 23 August, eight days after she was hospitalized. As the climate crisis continues to alter environmental conditions, scientists warn that Naegleria fowleri is being detected in parts of the US where it has not traditionally been found, with the amoeba appearing to expand from southern states into the midwest. “It likes warm surface waters during the summer in the northern latitudes,” Charles Gerba, a University of Arizona microbiologist, told the Guardian in 2022.

title: US military has no plans to send troops to midterm polling sites, Dan Caine says
summary: Letter from chair of joint chiefs of staff addresses concerns over Trump officials using military to interfere with vote
text: The highest‑ranking US military officer says there are no plans to deploy troops to polling places during the November midterm elections – responding to Senator Elissa Slotkin’s request for information amid concerns about whether the Trump administration might send service members to election sites. In a letter obtained by the Guardian, first reported by the Associated Press, Gen Dan Caine, chair of the joint chiefs of staff, told Slotkin “the Joint Force has no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections”. He added that there were also “no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election‑related material”. Slotkin – a Democrat who serves on the Senate armed services and homeland security committees – sought confirmation from Caine and the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, after Donald Trump urged Republicans to “nationalize” elections and said he had not ruled out sending guard members or immigration enforcement agents to the polls. In his letter, Caine added: “I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections.” Slotkin’s office had not yet received a reply from Hegseth, said Sonja Thrasher, her press secretary. The senator had asked both men to respond by 28 August. Anxiety among Democrats that the Trump administration could try to meddle in the midterm elections has grown, particularly after the president deployed federal agents in Democratic-led states over the objections of local leaders. Slotkin told the AP earlier in August that Trump had been laying the groundwork to claim the elections were stolen. She noted that Trump contemplated using the military to seize voting machines after his loss in 2020 and had deployed the national guard to cities against the wishes of Democratic leaders. He also deployed active-duty marines to Los Angeles during his immigration crackdown in 2025. Federal law prohibits the deployment of armed federal forces to election locations unless “necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States”. If any element of the military were to get involved, it would probably be the national guard under state control. Susie Wiles, the White House chief of staff, denied in a Vanity Fair interview last year that Trump would use the military to suppress voting in the midterms. The Pentagon did not immediately respond to an email from the Guardian asking for the status of Hegseth’s response to Slotkin. Slotkin asked Hegseth during an April congressional hearing if he would follow orders to seize ballots. Hegseth called the question a “gotcha hypothetical”, but said: “I’ve never been ordered to do anything illegal, and I won’t.” In 2020, Gen Mark Milley, then chair of the joint chiefs of staff, responded to a similar letter from Slotkin, a congresswoman at the time. “I believe deeply in the principle of an apolitical U.S. military,” Milley wrote. “In the event of a dispute over some aspect of the elections, by law U.S. courts and the U.S. Congress are required to resolve any disputes, not the U.S. military.”

title: US health officials exclude measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania from counts
summary: RFK Jr, the health secretary, has suggested the deaths were ‘fabricated’ while the CDC claimed it was reviewing them
text: Top US health officials and government agencies are currently not including the two recent measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania in their counts. “This is highly unusual,” said Debra Houry, former chief medical officer of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). She noted that this did not happen with the three deaths reported from measles in Texas and New Mexico last year. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), gave the wrong number of measles deaths in a recent interview with Fox News. “In 10 years, there have been three measles deaths in America,” he said, comparing that with deaths from “food-induced illness” – a category the CDC does not appear to track. “The media and certain demagogue politicians are constantly trying to scare us about infectious disease,” Kennedy said, adding that he was attempting to “redirect attention and resource [sic] to the thing that’s really killing Americans, which are foodborne diseases”. There were three deaths associated with measles in the US last year, the first deaths from the virus in a decade. But Pennsylvania also reported two measles-related deaths in August, including at least one newborn who died soon after birth. Kennedy has suggested that these two deaths were “fabricated”. The CDC has also stopped short of reporting deaths from measles in 2026. The agency posted a note on Friday saying it was delaying its weekly update, keeping the number at zero. On Sunday, the measles landing page appears to have been updated twice, with the two deaths first reported and then replaced with an asterisk. The CDC will not include the two deaths reported by Pennsylvania “while CDC reviews additional information regarding the circumstances and causes of death”, an explanatory note reads. The agency added that “available information does not establish whether measles caused or contributed to the deaths or whether the individuals died from other causes while infected with measles”. This is not how deaths reported by states to the CDC are typically handled. The deaths in Texas and New Mexico last year, for instance, were reported by the two states and included in the CDC’s national tally. Usually, “states notify CDC of reportable cases on things such as measles. CDC does not review or adjudicate these cases unless a state asked for additional assistance”, Houry said. The unusual approach will probably affect the agency’s relationship with the states that report to it. “CDC and states usually work collaboratively together,” Houry said. “This will undermine that relationship.” The CDC has not clarified what information it is seeking about these cases and why this data was not acceptable. The agency is “working to determine what actually occurred”, according to a post on X sent by an HHS spokesperson in response to the Guardian’s inquiries. “The communication coming from CDC’s official channel on Friday was political and not focused on what should be done during an outbreak,” Houry said. An Amish couple in Lancaster county interviewed by the Atlantic said their newborn son died immediately after birth. The mother was severely ill with measles and went into labor one month early. The baby was born with a pulse, but was not breathing; paramedics were unable to resuscitate him. The mother said she was concerned about rising measles cases, but she was unable to get vaccinated because she was pregnant. The US has recently fallen below the threshold to keep measles outbreaks in check, which would protect vulnerable infants, pregnant people and others at particular risk of measles. The father said he had received a voicemail asking him to get in touch with Kennedy, but he had not responded. In 2021, Kennedy, then the leader of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, praised the Amish of Lancaster county for not vaccinating their children. Though the Amish do not have any formal religious objection to vaccines, they are frequently disconnected from the healthcare system. While Kennedy said he was attempting to focus on foodborne illnesses, he did not appear to comment on two deaths from the cyclospora outbreak that sickened more than 17,000 Americans this summer, instead saying only that the outbreak was “under control”. Foodborne illnesses also often fall under the umbrella of infectious disease.

title: US trade regulator and 22 states accuse Amazon of taking $20bn with secret surcharges
summary: FTC alleges in lawsuit that online retailer ‘secretly and systematically overcharged’ advertisers for years
text: The US’s main trade regulator and 22 states sued Amazon on Monday, alleging the online retailer “secretly and systematically overcharged” advertisers on Amazon.com. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) said these practices led to higher costs for customers on items like groceries and other essential goods that are sold on Amazon. “Amazon has millions of advertising customers who were misled into paying significantly higher prices. These higher costs were largely passed on to American consumers,” said Andrew Ferguson, the FTC chair. The agency accused the company of taking in more than $20bn from “hidden surcharges”, in what it deems an “ad-rigging scheme”. Amazon’s advertising business has grown significantly in recent years, becoming the third-largest online advertising marketplace after Google and Meta. The FTC says Amazon generates more than $68bn in ad revenue on its website. The lawsuit alleges that 1.2 million advertising customers were overcharged since 2019, including more than 500,000 small and medium-sized businesses. An Amazon spokesperson pointed the Guardian to a blogpost the company published in response to the legal action, which calls the legal action a “misguided lawsuit”. “Amazon strongly disagrees,” the post reads. The government’s case hinges on Amazon’s advertising auction system, called “second-price auctions”, that lets the winning bidder pay only slightly more than the second-highest bid. Regulators allege that with this system, Amazon could secretly raise the second-highest bids with a higher “shill” bid of its own. “We believe Amazon manipulated its ad auctions to inflate what sellers had to pay, adding billions of dollars in costs that ultimately get passed on to customers with higher prices,” said Jeff Jackson, the attorney general for North Carolina, one of the states involved in the suit. The suit alleges Amazon tested how much it could increase the amount it charges without advertisers flinching. Internal documents show one manager allegedly describing the company’s pricing strategy as “hoping that advertisers don’t notice and decrease bids or ad spend”. Amazon denied these allegations and said the company gave “customers the lowest prices every day across the widest selection of products”. “After reviewing approximately 1.5 million pages spanning six years, the FTC leans on a handful of simplified communications to allege a companywide effort to deceive,” Amazon wrote in its blogpost. “That is patently false.” Rob Bonta, the attorney general for California, noted in a press conference that the lawsuit arises from a partnership between conservative states, liberal ones and the federal government. He said this lawsuit was focusing on Amazon’s alleged unlawful activities and its deception around those practices. “Amazon’s price inflation is illegal, plain and simple,” Bonta said. “This is a massive corporation. They can be wildly successful and also follow the law.” The federal agency and states are asking the court to bar Amazon from continuing the allegedly deceptive advertising practices, along with paying civil penalties and refunding advertisers.

title: Conservative reshuffle: who’s who in Kemi Badenoch’s top team?
summary: From a darling of the Tory right to a moderate former army officer, we profile the key players
text: Kemi Badenoch has kicked off the return to parliament with a reshuffle of her top team in order to take on Andy Burnham and Reform UK. She has made sweeping changes to the shadow cabinet and ruthlessly axed her shadow chancellor. Here is a run-down of the new characters sitting across from Labour on the opposition frontbench. Andrew Griffith Griffith, the MP for Arundel and South Downs, replaces Mel Stride as shadow chancellor, a role he has reportedly long coveted. He is loyal to Badenoch and was one of her first backers for leader in 2024. Previously the chief financial officer and chief operating officer of Sky and the chair of Just Eat, he entered parliament as an ally of Boris Johnson after allowing the former prime minister to use his £9.5m townhouse as his leadership campaign HQ in 2019. He later became Johnson’s business adviser in government before running for election later that year. Griffith was a backer of Liz Truss for leader and as her treasury minister was partially responsible for the disastrous mini-budget which caused economic chaos. He continued to defend the budget and said the market turmoil was linked to global events. He was spotted last year at the launch of a climate denial group with Truss and Nigel Farage. Of his attendance, he said: “In any year, I attend hundreds of external events with business organisations and thinktanks, none of which automatically imply my endorsement.” He also recently spoke at a hard-right Cpac event organised by Truss. Claire Coutinho Widely tipped as one of the party’s rising stars, Coutinho made a fierce opponent to Ed Miliband when he was energy secretary and she shadowed his brief. A cabinet minister in Rishi Sunak’s government, she has been shifted to Badenoch’s economic unit and made shadow business secretary. Before parliament she was an investment banker at Merrill Lynch and KPMG, and has recently been holding the Labour government’s feet to the fire over rising energy bills. Colleagues describe her as forensic, she delights in doing her own research about what she terms “the hidden cost of net zero” and has spoken up in parliament for whistleblowers at the national energy systems operator. She became the first person to represent a political party at PMQs while pregnant earlier this year. Julia Lopez, the MP for Hornchurch and Upminster, will cover for her until the new year while she is on maternity leave. Coutinho is a keen cook in her spare time and once appeared on Nigella Lawson’s cooking gameshow The Taste. Tom Tugendhat Badenoch has made a show of purging the more “woke” MPs from the party, banning those who believe in pursuing net zero from standing at the next election for example, so the choice of the moderate Tugendhat as shadow foreign secretary surprised some. He replaces Priti Patel, who was sacked from the shadow cabinet. Tugendhat has experience in foreign affairs and previously served in the cabinet as security minister from September 2022 to July 2024. A former British army officer, he served in Afghanistan and Iraq. A remainer, he has also said he does not support leaving the European convention on human rights, which puts him at loggerheads with Badenoch. Tugendhat stood as the moderate option in the Tory party leadership contest in 2022, but was beaten by a long way by Truss. He tried and lost again against Badenoch when Sunak stood down in 2024. He was banned from driving for six months in 2022 for using his mobile phone at the wheel. Katie Lam A darling of the Tory right, Lam was only elected in 2024. She has been given the role of shadow housing and communities minister, and is likely to relish being Angela Rayner’s opposite number. She is a former special adviser to Johnson, and she worked on Sunak’s first leadership bid. Outside politics she worked at the PR company Portland Communications and the AI company Faculty. She has sometimes been tipped as a potential defector to Reform after saying many immigrants should “go home” and supporting the policy of revoking indefinite leave to remain. Her comments on immigration have gone further than official Conservative policy at some points. Lam has written five musicals, including an adaptation of The Railway Children. Other changes and those staying on Chris Philp remains shadow home secretary. He supported Badenoch’s successful leadership campaign and has held the role since she became party leader. James Cartlidge stays on as shadow defence secretary, a position he has held since Sunak appointed him to the role in 2024. Andrew Bowie takes up Coutinho’s previous role as energy secretary. The shadow health secretary, Stuart Andrew, quit the frontbench to “focus on constituency work”, and Damian Hinds assumes his brief.

title: Turkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disaster
summary: TCG Isin expected to play vital role in locating Filo Jet’s voyage data recorder 514 metres below surface
text: A deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus as Turkey joins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast. The TCG Isin will join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia. Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedy had claimed eight lives, increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20. A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot. International sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials. Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday, Tufan Erhürman, the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”. The Isin, capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing. The ship is expected to play a vital role in recovering the ferry’s voyage data recorder, or black box, now viewed as key in deciphering the cause of a maritime disaster not seen since the breakaway territory declared independence in 1983. Turkish Cypriot officials told the Guardian it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned. The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court. It remained unclear whether those still missing had been trapped on board. “Nobody is saying it publicly, but the hope of any survivors being found at this point is very slim,” one official confided. “Those who weren’t rescued very likely didn’t find a lifejacket. We believe many were elderly people and mothers with babies and young kids.” In testimony – and video footage – that emerged on Monday, panic-stricken passengers could be seen desperately looking for lifejackets and screaming before the double-hulled ferry flipped over. One mother, Ayten Biçer, described feeling her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as the ferry capsized and sank in a matter of minutes. “She was saying, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go,” she sobbed. Two of Biçer’s other children are among the 20 still missing. The captain of the ferry and seven crew members were detained on Monday as judicial authorities launched an inquiry into the tragedy amid claims they had been among the first to abandon ship. Appearing before a local magistrate, the crew attributed the disaster to the bow of the catamaran-style ferry breaking apart in turbulent seas. But eyewitness accounts contradicted that version of events, with passengers telling officials that appeals to turn back to port had fallen on deaf ears as the ferry began to take on water. Ünal Üstel, the territory’s prime minister, told reporters the Filo Jet was lying on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres and that he foresaw the Turkish salvage ship “reaching [it] tomorrow afternoon”. Boats, helicopters, aircraft and other search and rescue teams had joined the operation, he said, adding that search efforts were continuing “on a 24-hour basis”. Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when a coup aimed at union with Greece – engineered by the military junta then in power in Athens – prompted Turkey to invade and seize the island’s northern third. Ever since, as many as 45,000 mainland Turkish troops have been stationed in the north. In 1983, the territory unilaterally declared independence, but in the absence of a settlement, decades of international isolation have ensued.

title: Kalshi bans ex-congressman George Santos from prediction platform for life
summary: Santos was accused of profiting from bets tied to his attendance at Trump’s State of the Union address
text: George Santos, the former Republican congressman whose political career collapsed under a mountain of lies, has become the first person ever handed a lifetime ban by the prediction-market platform Kalshi. The company announced the permanent suspension on Monday, along with a $71,356 fine, after federal regulators accused Santos of profiting from bets tied to his own attendance at Donald Trump’s State of the Union address earlier this year. A Kalshi spokeswoman said Santos’s refusal to cooperate fully with the platform’s internal investigation was what pushed the penalty from temporary to permanent. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) alleges that Santos exploited stormy weather forecasts that threatened to disrupt his travel to Washington in February. According to the agency, he bought Kalshi contracts betting he would miss the speech, then posted social media updates suggesting he planned to attend after all, driving up the value of contracts he held on the opposite outcome and allowing him to cash out at a profit. Regulators concluded he had improperly traded on an event whose outcome he had some power to influence himself. Santos responded on X, thanking Kalshi for the ban. “Let’s see how much longer you guys are around for,” he said. Santos was expelled from the House in December 2023 after the ethics committee found substantial evidence he had defrauded donors, lied about his finances and fabricated much of his biography. He later pleaded guilty to federal wire fraud and identity theft charges and was sentenced to more than seven years in prison, serving less than three months before Trump commuted the sentence. Santos agreed in July to pay more than $35,000 to settle the CFTC’s case, without admitting wrongdoing, according to his attorney. That settlement also barred him from trading on any platform for three years, a far lighter penalty than the lifetime ban Kalshi has now added on top. The disgraced representative was not the only person disciplined by Kalshi on Monday. Laurie Buckhout, a Trump-endorsed Republican congressional candidate in North Carolina, was banned for three years and fined $2,590 after wagering under $1,000 on her own campaign, calling it a mistake she moved to fix as soon as she noticed it. The former Planet Fitness president Ben Midgley was banned for three years and fined $5,434.30 over bets on his unsuccessful bid in Maine’s Republican gubernatorial primary, and Diamond Resorts founder Stephen Cloobeck received a three-year ban and roughly $31,770 fine for wagering around $10,000 on his own abandoned run for California governor. The action follows a separate CFTC penalty last week against Gabriel Perez, a White House teleprompter operator accused of trading on inside information, who agreed to pay $65,000 and forfeit more than $107,000 in winnings. The ban arrives as Santos has been working to rebuild his public profile and finances. He is set to appear this month on the latest season of Fox’s endurance competition “Special Forces: World’s Toughest Test”, and has been supplementing his income through paid video shout-outs on Cameo, whose price has reportedly dropped from $300 to $100 as he works to pay down campaign debts once estimated above $800,000. He has said he does not plan to seek public office again for at least a decade.

title: More public control is the way to grow UK economy, Burnham to tell MPs
summary: Exclusive: Prime minister wants to ‘bring back hope’ by tackling cost of living as MPs call for electoral reform
text: Andy Burnham will drive home his pledge to bring more essential services back into public control, telling MPs in the Commons on Tuesday that it will be the only way to improve growth across the country. Burnham will address the house for the first time in 16 years from the frontbench, and six weeks since he became prime minister, after spending the summer recess announcing a slew of policies that will now be put before MPs. He will use the statement to put public control of services at the heart of his priorities for the coming months, sources told the Guardian, saying he would make the case that it would unlock investment, jobs and growth. Burnham will say that the cost of everyday services to family budgets is holding back the economy and promise a plan to regain control of the costs. A No 10 source said: “Andy is optimistic about our country’s future. He has a clear plan for how we turn things round. He is determined we make this the moment we bring back hope.” The prime minister will face an early test of his commitment to public control as he mulls legislation to make it easier to bring struggling utilities such as Thames Water under government ownership. The Guardian reported last week Burnham was considering laws to make it easier to put companies into insolvency proceedings and then take control of them afterwards. He will also face crunch decisions on possible changes to the immigration bill to exempt carers, as well as pressure from MPs to back moves towards electoral reform. A quasi-judicial decision on whether to allow more North Sea drilling is also expected soon: a highly divisive issue within the party. Burnham will tell MPs that he wants to “bring back hope” in politics and pledge to work constructively with opposition parties. On Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, sacked her shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel, promoting Andrew Griffith in Stride’s place in the hope of making further inroads in attacking Burnham’s economic approach. Patel is replaced by Tom Tugendhat. Burnham will give a scathing analysis of how privatised services have done little for the public, saying that utilities and transport have not been run in the public interest and are neither reliable nor affordable. He will point to action already being taken to bring more bus routes under public control, including through a partnership between No 10 North and the West Midlands Combined Authority. The Liverpool City Region will start taking control of bus services from next weekend. Burnham has promised a 10-year project to take public control of utilities which is expected to be a major focus of his next few months in power. Allies have said the prime minister is “completely committed” to putting utilities such as energy and water companies into public control, and is looking at every option. As well as setting out key priorities for his first months in office, Burnham will face a two-hour grilling from MPs about policies announced over the summer – including a cut to VAT on energy bills, £2 bus fares, the scrapping of digital ID, a major expansion of devolution and a plan for a national care service. Opposition MPs are expected to ask tough questions on how the pledges will be funded as well as how Burnham expects to fill a £4.7bn gap in the defence investment plan left by his predecessor, Keir Starmer. On Tuesday, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, will also present the government’s plans to cut the number of prisoners eligible for early release, including the killers of PC Andrew Harper. Though the decision will see most of those convicted of manslaughter remain in prison to serve longer sentences, it has also raised alarm that the number of prison places may reach crisis point faster. Later in the week, Burnham will face Badenoch for his first prime minister’s questions and will also need to navigate the growing number of Labour MPs who are heaping pressure on him to toughen up the representation of the people bill which returns to the Commons this week. Nearly 100 MPs have called on Burnham to back a commission on electoral reform, given the prime minister has previously been a vociferous supporter of changing the voting system. MPs have also been angered by the decision to drop any cap on party donations, after pressure from trade unions, despite the prime minister having previously backed a cap of £500,000. The Liberal Democrats said on Monday they would put their full backing behind an amendment from the Labour MP Alex Sobel that calls for a commission on electoral reform to be established within 100 days. The party’s leader, Ed Davey, said it was a chance for Burnham to prove he was different to Starmer. “Reform stand to benefit from our terrible voting system and could manipulate it all the way to No 10,” he said. Davey added: “Keir Starmer never would have agreed to a national commission. He failed to grasp that it is our role as progressives to fix the broken system the Conservatives created. The only question now is: what kind of politician is Andy Burnham? Is he willing to do the right thing?” Reform will host its party conference this week in Birmingham, with Farage speaking on Friday. In the latest poll from More in Common, Labour hold a four-point lead over Reform, with the Tories a point behind. The latest Opinium poll found that Burnham’s net approval rating had increased over the last fortnight by three points.

title: Andrew Griffith and Tom Tugendhat join Badenoch’s top team in Tory reshuffle
summary: Conservative leader sacks shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel
text: Kemi Badenoch sacked her shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, and the shadow foreign secretary, Priti Patel, in a sweeping Conservative reshuffle on Monday, replacing Stride with Andrew Griffith, and Patel with Tom Tugendhat. Stride, who had been shadow chancellor since Badenoch became leader, was widely seen among Tories as failing to make an impression at a time when Labour had been under pressure over the economy. Griffith, who was previously a high-profile businessman, moves from the shadow business brief, where he will be replaced by Claire Coutinho, the former shadow energy secretary. A senior Conservative source described Griffith, the former chief operating officer of Sky and chair of Just Eat, as “a no-nonsense, pro-growth shadow chancellor with real business experience”. “Kemi is changing the way the Conservative party approaches economic policy and creating a new economic leadership team for the next phase, focused on growth, higher living standards and fiscal credibility,” the source said. Badenoch paid tribute to Stride but confirmed in a statement that he would return to the backbenches. “He helped us steady the ship, rebuild economic credibility and become an effective opposition, and I am genuinely grateful for his contribution,” she said, calling him “exceptionally loyal, and I will always be grateful to him for the work he has done”. Stride said he would continue to back Badenoch’s leadership. “The Conservative party must continue to champion an approach which is both radical and deliverable … The Conservatives have a good story to tell on this now, and one that I know will continue to grow stronger and stronger under Kemi’s leadership,” he said. Badenoch has also sacked Stuart Andrew, the shadow health secretary, who said in a post on X he would be returning to the backbenches. Tugendhat, a former security minister, was a leadership candidate who had previously declined to join the shadow cabinet. Katie Lam, the hardline anti-migration MP who has been a key media voice for the Conservatives, will replace James Cleverly as shadow communities secretary, after he resigned from the shadow cabinet to run for London mayor. Tugendhat, who has been outspoken on China and Iran since returning to the backbenches, said: “We’re facing the most dangerous moment in a generation. Too often, the government has responded with weakness. As shadow foreign secretary, I’ll ensure Britain chooses strength again.” Patel announced on Sunday night that she would be leaving as shadow foreign secretary but said she would take on an “international role” with the party to build ties with other rightwing parties across the world. In a statement, Patel said she also wanted to spend more time in her Essex constituency. “I’m pleased to continue supporting Kemi and the Conservative party in a new role strengthening our relationships with fellow conservatives and centre-right parties around the world,” she said. “At a time of profound global uncertainty, when our values and freedoms are under threat, conservatives must work more closely together.” Coutinho will go on maternity leave shortly and will be covered by Julia Lopez, who had shadowed the now abolished science, innovation and technology department. Helen Grant, the shadow solicitor general, has also asked to leave the shadow frontbench. Cleverly, who announced his run for London mayor on Sunday, denied he had quit the shadow cabinet following a shift to the right under Badenoch’s leadership. “I am going to put forward a classic Conservative case to be the mayor of London, and it’s about enterprise, it’s about opportunity,” Cleverly told Times Radio. Cleverly, who lost the Conservative leadership race to Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has moved to the right as support for Nigel Farage’s rightwing Reform UK has grown. But the appointment of Tugendhat as shadow foreign secretary would bring a key voice from the party’s more centrist One Nation grouping into the fold, though Tugendhat is hawkish on foreign affairs. Badenoch has kept Chris Philp as shadow home secretary and James Cartlidge as shadow defence secretary. Joy Morrissey will be the new shadow minister for women and equalities, and Harriet Cross, another MP from the 2024 intake, is expected to become the new shadow Scotland secretary. Damian Hinds replaces Andrew as shadow health secretary and Andrew Bowie, who was key to the Tories recent byelection win in Aberdeen, will be shadow energy secretary.

title: Congressional nominee Brad Lander heckled over Israel stance at New York protest
summary: Lander screamed at and verbally abused as he protested against Hindu nationalist rally in Madison Square Garden
text: The New York Democratic congressional nominee Brad Lander was screamed at and verbally abused by protesters over his stance on Israel as he protested against a Hindu nationalist politician speaking outside Madison Square Garden. As Lander attended a demonstration on Saturday against the event, organized by the Hindu nationalist RSS movement and where Mohan Bhagwat, leader of Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh was speaking, he was confronted by several protesters demanding that he leave the rally. “We don’t want no Zionists here. Get the fuck out!” one man yelled at Lander in a video circulating online. “You say you’re a liberal but we know how you act.” Another shouted: “You’re a Zionist, we don’t need you. We don’t need your help!” Other protesters welcomed Lander’s presence at the event and defended him against the heckling. “Thank you for coming, thank you for standing in solidarity with us,” one man told Lander, shaking his hand. Lander, who is Jewish and an outspoken critic of the Israeli government, describes himself as a liberal Zionist – stating that he believes in the vision of Israel as a safe, Jewish home, but argues that it cannot ever be a true democracy while it continues to occupy Palestinian land and deny Palestinians their human rights and freedom. He condemns Israel’s continued occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, supported the restriction of US military aid to Israel, and believes that Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks amounts to genocide. An ally of the New York City mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and a former comptroller for the city, Lander is the progressive candidate for the US House of Representatives New York’s 10th congressional district. His critical approach to Israel was a key factor in his thumping primary victory in June against fellow Jew and Zionist Dan Goldman, a prominent supporter of Israel. Lander appeared undeterred by the abuse and determined to remain at the rally, to which he had been invited, on Saturday. In one exchange, he calmly responded, “Bring it on,” when a protester wearing a face mask and sunglasses shouted in his face that he was a “Zionist ball sack”. Addressing the incident in a video message on X on Monday, Lander said: “The event was dedicated to standing up against the persecution of religious minorities in India. I was honored to be invited and glad to participate. “I won’t stop joining rallies against hate – in India, in Israel and Palestine, or in New York City – because of a couple of loud numbskulls.” Lander went on: “I was proud to attend. As a Jewish New Yorker, I protest when I believe people are perverting Judaism to justify ethnic cleansing and exclusion, and I feel solidarity for Muslims who are doing the same.” He reiterated his critical stance on Israel’s actions in Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon, and noted that he gets “criticized frequently by centrist and rightwing Jews. And as someone who nonetheless believes in the vision and the possibility of a Jewish and democratic Israel, alongside a free Palestine, once decades of occupation and apartheid end, I get criticized by leftwingers who oppose Zionism.” He stressed the importance of people coming together, even when they don’t always agree on everything. “A few loud numbskulls must not deter us from building multi-faith, multi-racial coalitions for justice,” he said. He also thanked the Hindu and Muslim groups that had leapt to his defense on Sunday. The Indian American Muslim Council said on X: “The individuals responsible were not part of IAMC or our coalition and did not speak for us. Our fight … requires building strong coalitions, respecting differences, and working together wherever we share common ground. Insulting or silencing allies undermines that work and is unacceptable. We offer Brad Lander our sincere apologies for the treatment he received.” Hindus for Human Rights said on X: “Brad Lander is a Jewish leader who has vocally disavowed the genocide in Palestine and is a rare progressive voice against the RSS. Multiple organizations invited Brad to the protest as a longtime ally who understands the majority’s role in combating hate in their communities.” The confrontations Lander experienced are telling of tensions within the United States over Israel. Public opinion in the US has shifted against the country over its actions in Gaza in a historic way, while a wave of progressive candidates have swept to victory amid pro-Palestinian sentiment and criticism of the Israeli government. The incident has also tapped into an aspect of the debate where the lines between anti-Zionism and antisemitism are often blurred, with some commentary on social media suggesting that people hurled abuse at Lander because he is Jewish. But in a video shared on Substack, the liberal commentator Peter Beinart argued that the people harassing Lander “are rude, obnoxious, self-righteous, they’re really kind of acting like assholes. But they’re not saying anything antisemitic.” Highlighting that the protesters explicitly took issue with Lander’s self-declared Zionism, not his Jewishness, Beinart added: “The term antisemite should be reserved for clear cases in which people have an animus towards Jews as Jews.”

title: Police appeal after unidentified woman’s body found in Liverpool park
summary: Body of victim thought to be in her 70s found in bin bag in walled garden area of Stanley Park on Friday
text: Police in Liverpool have urged members of the public to come forward with information after the body of an unknown woman believed to be in her 70s was found in a black bin bag in a popular park. Merseyside police were contacted by a passerby who had found the woman’s body in Stanley Park, in the Anfield area of Liverpool, at about 5.25pm on Friday 28 August. The body was found in a black bin bag in the walled garden area of the park. It is believed that it may have lain there undiscovered for a number of weeks. “A postmortem took place on Saturday 29 August, the result of which has been withheld for investigation reasons,” Det Supt Rachel Wilson said at a press conference on Monday. “Our team have since been carrying out extensive enquiries to identify the woman, but we have so far been unable to do so.” Wilson said forensic work continued, adding: “We’re carrying out house-to-house, CCTV and other enquiries as a matter of urgency, but of course the methodical nature of such work can mean it takes time.” Officers believe the woman was in her 70s. She was described as white, about 1.57 metres (5ft 2in) tall, of small build, and with strawberry-blond hair. She was found wearing a pink Nike T-shirt. “Missing people reports in Merseyside and elsewhere have been checked but, so far, these have not resulted in an identification,” Wilson said. “Sometimes people go missing without those close to them realising, through holidays being planned or simple misunderstandings, and so we may not have received a report of any concerns. “While we do not want to worry people unnecessarily, it is vital that we follow every possible lead, both to rule people out and ultimately to identify the woman, notify her next of kin and apprehend the offender.” Describing the murder as a “shocking crime”, Wilson said police were “doing all we can to identify the person or persons responsible and bring them to justice”. Stanley Park separates the Anfield and Goodison Park football stadiums, which are respectively home to Liverpool FC and Everton Women. Assistant chief constable Andy Ryan said he understood “how unnerving” the discovery and the heightened police presence would be for local people, adding: “This is the exact reason that we are so determined to get answers as soon as we possibly can.” He described the park as “a very busy and popular green space, especially in the recent warm summer weeks”. “It is visited by dog walkers and families, as well as people walking and exercising,” he said. “It is quite possible that one or more of these visitors may have seen something suspicious recently and not reported it at the time.” “I want to reiterate Rachel’s appeal,” Ryan added. “If anyone recognises the description of this woman or you have any concerns whatsoever about someone you may know and haven’t seen or heard from recently, please tell us as a matter of urgency.” Potential witnesses are urged to contact Merseyside police via social media or to call 101, quoting reference number 26000706383. Reports can also be made anonymously by calling Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

title: Trump attacks datacenter backlash, claiming communities pushing back risk becoming ‘backwards and poor’
summary: Three-quarters of Americans said in a recent poll that they oppose datacenters being built next to their homes
text: Donald Trump has criticized communities pushing back against datacenter projects across the US amid a growing backlash, warning those that reject them risk becoming “backwards and poor”. As controversy surrounding local datacenter plans continues to swirl around election campaigns nationwide ahead of November’s midterm elections, the US president declared Americans “will only have yourselves to blame” if they are canceled. Bipartisan opposition to datacenter expansion has intensified across the US, particularly in states with ample land, low-cost power and generous tax incentives, as local communities raise concerns over environmental impacts, soaring utility costs and noise pollution. According to a recent poll, three-quarters of Americans said they would oppose a datacenter being built next to their homes, while more than six in 10 Americans said they would strongly oppose such a proposal. In a Truth Social post on Monday, Trump wrote: “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign. “The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them. If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame. China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement. Actually, they can’t believe it is happening!” Responding to Trump’s statement on Monday, JD Vance told reporters that datacenters were an “important part of the AI economy”, adding: “When people build them, they have to build the power plants along with the datacenters. I think probably 99% of the backlash to datacenters has come in areas where building a datacenter means higher utility and higher electricity for the people on the ground. “I think what these companies have to do is take advantage of some of the federal deregulatory efforts that we’ve undertaken,” the US vice-president added. “If you build a datacenter, you should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out. And if that is happening, I don’t think the datacenters are that controversial. It’s when the utility bills get so much higher that’s when it’s a real problem.” However, several users replied to Trump’s post on his own Truth Social platform, voicing their concerns about datacenters. “Mr. President: Think about farm land and about water resources, and a man as intelligent as you will see that the absolute position you are taking is flawed,” one user wrote. “What use is being rich if you cannot get access to water and food?” As opposition to datacenters grows, the research group Data Center Watch found that grassroots groups blocked or delayed at least 75 datacenter projects worth approximately $130bn in the first three months of 2026. Monterey Park, a small city east of Los Angeles, is among the local communities that have pushed back against datacenters and won. Other communities successful in their resistance include Prince William county, Virginia, as well as Wake county, North Carolina. Environmental groups have also weighed in, with a coalition of more than 230 organizations urging members of Congress last year to halt the development of new datacenters amid the climate crisis, worsening droughts in already water-stressed areas, and rising electricity bills.

title: Trump threatens further action as US and Iran exchange fire in new flare-up
summary: Washington says it acted after observing Iran was planning to deploy fresh mines in strait of Hormuz
text: The US and Iran have exchanged fire for the first time in a month, with missiles and drones fired at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, and Iran targeting US military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates in response. The US president, Donald Trump, on Monday threatened further action. The US is trying to prise open Tehran’s grip on shipping going through the strait, which before the war accounted for a fifth of the world’s seaborne energy supply. Washington claimed that Iranian control over the waterway had been loosened by repeated US attacks on Iranian missile launchers and radars. US Central Command said it acted late on Sunday, launching the first strikes on Iran since July, after it detected the Iranians were planning to deploy fresh mines in the strait. Last week Trump claimed the US navy had cleared the strait of mines for the first time since the conflict started on 28 February, a claim the Iranians rejected as lies. In response to the US attack, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”. The UAE defence ministry said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters. Trump responded to the Iranian reprisals by telling Fox News: “We’re going to hit them hard. There will be a response.” The US president called Iran “officially a failed nation without an airforce, a navy or a currency”, adding that inflation was at 300% and its leaders were incapable of representing their country. The White House last week signalled that Trump was shelving military measures in favour of a campaign to destroy the Iranian economy by enforcing sanctions. Iranian state TV claimed the military exchanges escalated on Sunday after a tanker caught fire when hitting two Iranian naval mines while attempting to pass through the southern side of the strait close to Oman. Officials later said Iran had targeted three ships trying to navigate the southern route that Tehran says is unauthorised. The IRGC warned that other ships violating ⁠its rules would face the same fate and said compliance with its regulations ‌for passage through the strait was mandatory. However, the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, told Pakistan’s prime minister, Shehbaz Sharif, in a bilateral meeting on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Kyrgyzstan on Monday that continuing the war was not in Iran’s interest, adding he was still ready to implement the memorandum of understanding with the US that Pakistan had mediated in June. The Iranian currency was under renewed pressure on Monday and the inflationary impact of its rapid depreciation is causing growing concern to MPs. Iran and Oman last week reached a verbal agreement on a new single temporary route for shipping through the strait in which Oman retains controls on shipping in Omani waters. One western diplomat familiar with the talks said the message had got through to Washington that this bilateral agreement would not be enough for Iran to open the strait and that to do so would at least require the US to end its blockade of Iranian oil exports, something Trump is not currently prepared to do. “There are many in Iran determined to torment Trump right up to the end of his presidency,” the western diplomat said. “We are stuck.” He said some oil was getting through but not very much. The latest fighting broke out late on Sunday with the US claiming it attacked Larak Island in the strait. A US official said: “I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.” The IRGC said the US attack had killed three soldiers and wounded two citizens. Iran’s Mehr news agency quoted the IRGC as saying its air defences shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, causing it to crash ‌into Gulf waters. The US said all missiles fired towards US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact. The White House claim that the US now controls the strait and ships are free to navigate its waters is heavily contested. Tanker Trackers, an independent tracking agency, said on Sunday: “Past seven days daily average of crude oil exports via the strait of Hormuz was 3.8m barrels per day. During the formal ceasefire period (which in effect only lasted for 25 days), it was 9.8m.” The agency said Iranian crude exports had been at zero for some time. A meeting of G20 finance ministers in the US is likely to lead to a clash over American demands that more countries impose sanctions on Iran or face punitive action by Washington. The German finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, who is facing difficult regional elections, is to urge the US to bring the conflict to a diplomatic end, pointing to the war’s inflationary impact. The US treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, echoing Trump, claimed on Monday the resumed exchanges of fire showed Iran was “lashing out” because the fresh sanctions were taking a heavy toll on its already battered economy. “They’re taking it very seriously ... they’re in shock at the state of their ‌economy,” Bessent told reporters at the G20 finance ministers ‌meeting in North Carolina. “I would think that they are lashing out kinetically because they are losing economically.” China, a key Iranian customer for its oil, has said it opposes the new US sanctions campaign. In Kyrgyzstan, Pezeshkian will be looking for concrete assurances from the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, that he will not allow the US to spread economic chaos through Iran.

title: Head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite thinktank quits over unpaid wages
summary: Frank Furedi announces resignation with immediate effect after organisation’s staff ‘not paid in July or August’
text: The head of Viktor Orbán’s favourite Brussels thinktank has quit, citing unpaid wages since the change of government in Hungary. The sociology professor Frank Furedi said he was resigning as the executive director of MCC Brussels with “immediate effect” on Monday over “persistent failure to provide the contractually agreed funds”. A spokesperson for MCC Brussels confirmed Furedi’s resignation and said no one working for the organisation in the EU capital had been paid in July or August. MCC Brussels launched in late 2022 with a self-styled mission to shake up political debate in the EU capital, although critics said it defended Orbán’s illiberal rule in Hungary while using a well-funded position to attack civil society groups. It was an ostensibly independent offshoot of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium Foundation in Budapest, a training ground for Orbán’s Fidesz party that was lavishly funded by his rightwing nationalist government. The future of MCC Brussels was thrown into doubt when Péter Magyar won a landslide election victory in April pledging to crack down on corruption in Hungary, which numerous independent organisations said had proliferated during Orbán’s 16 years in power. Soon after his victory, Magyar promised to end state financing for MCC Budapest and to investigate a large transfer of state assets to the organisation, which he described as a crime. Furedi has previously dismissed Magyar’s claims of a criminal transfer of assets to MCC Budapest as “bullshit”, while MCC Brussels said it condemned corruption by all politicians. In a letter to the senior leadership of MCC Budapest seen by the Guardian, Furedi wrote: “Without the contractually agreed resources, our colleagues cannot function and are facing serious economic hardship. We have been placed in a situation where our individual reputations and the integrity of our intellectual mission are systematically undermined.” The failure to provide funds, Furedi said, meant MCC Brussels had effectively ceased operations and was unable to pay suppliers or meet conditions under Belgian insolvency law. Furedi said he intended to ensure, “along with like-minded individuals, the work and intellectual legacy of our institution will continue to flourish in another form”, without elaborating on future plans. The letter was first reported by Politico. MCC Budapest did not immediately respond to a request for comment. MCC Budapest has also seen change at the top following the election of the new government. The MCC board was previously led by Viktor Orbán’s chief of staff, Balázs Orbán, who is no relation to the former prime minister. Balázs Orbán, now an MP for the Fidesz party, announced he was standing down as chair in June. The MCC Brussels spokesperson said after Furedi’s resignation and a round of lay-offs in June and July, MCC Brussels was down to 12 staff and three research fellows. Before the cuts it had employed 25 people and was one of the best-funded thinktanks in Brussels.

title: James Clyburn says supporting Clarence Thomas for supreme court ‘was mistake’
summary: Congressman says Thomas abandoned his principles to become an extremist, hard-right member of bench
text: The senior Democratic congressman James Clyburn said his decision to support Clarence Thomas for a US supreme court seat “was a mistake” and called for the expansion of the nation’s highest legal panel to 13 justices. Clyburn, of South Carolina, spoke up for Thomas at his fiery 1991 confirmation hearings, calling him “a personal and professional friend” who would use their shared experiences lifting minorities and advancing civil rights to become a respected and accomplished jurist. Instead, Clyburn told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, Thomas abandoned his principles to become an extremist, hard-right member of a bench that has delivered some stunning legal reversals in recent years, including the overturning of federal protections for abortion and ending affirmative action in higher education. Asked by host Kristen Welker if he regretted standing up for Thomas, Clyburn replied: “I have made mistakes in my life, and that’s one that I made. And I will own up to that mistake. “I had no idea that Clarence Thomas would rebel the way he has against his own background and experiences. He was raised by his grandfather, and he has shown very little sensitivity to the environment his grandfather grew up down in Pin Point, Georgia.” Before joining Congress in 1993, Clyburn was South Carolina’s human affairs commissioner for 18 years beginning in 1974. He said Thomas’s tenure as chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission from 1982 until 1990, a time in which it vigorously pursued anti-discrimination legal actions, had assured him that Thomas “believed in precedents, the law”. He told Welker: “I had faith and confidence in the fact that his background and experiences would instruct him in his professionalism, especially sitting on the bench. I thought, sure, that he would be here upholding those precedents set down in 1954 in the Brown v Board of Education decision” that declared racial segregation in public schools was illegal. But Thomas, whose later years on the bench have been mired in allegations of corruption, turned his back on civil rights, Clyburn suggested, notably in the 2024 decision on ideological grounds that ruled affirmative action in college admissions unconstitutional. “That was a mistake on my part,” Clyburn said of his past support for Thomas. “And I own up to it.” Clyburn spoke as the prospect of increasing the number of US supreme court justices, a popular rallying cry for sections of the Democratic party as it attempts to retake the House in November’s midterms, returned to public discourse. Former Democratic vice-president Kamala Harris in July called for the expansion of the bench from nine to 13, a proposal Clyburn said he would support. “Thirteen is a pretty good number,” he said. “A baker’s dozen would be a good number to have on the court. “And I would hope we would get people on the court who will follow the constitutional underpinnings of this great nation of ours. I had hoped that Clarence Thomas would follow the underpinnings of that constitution of ours, but he has not done so. “In fact, he’s decided to go all the way from an angry leftist, to a very angry rightist.” Clyburn, however, said Democrats’ immediate priorities after November should not be either supreme court expansion or impeachment of Donald Trump for what would be a third time across his two presidencies. “If the Democrats were to take back the House, and I feel confident that we will, our first order of business ought to be developing an accessible and affordable campaign effort that will yield what I will call making this country, its greatness, accessible and affordable for all of its citizens,” he said.

title: How to tackle the climate impact of datacentres | Letters
summary: Letters: Datacentres should generate their own power and control their emissions, writes Richard Lamming, while Michael McClelland says we should reduce our digital communication. Plus a letter from Malcolm Fraser
text: The case of future datacentres demanding more electricity than the entire United Kingdom (Two planned datacentres will have higher UK carbon emissions than ExxonMobil, analysis finds, 25 August) is an example of corporates transferring their problems to society and the electorate. This must not be allowed to happen. One solution would be to make each datacentre responsible for generating all its own electricity and for reducing its CO2 emissions to zero. These installations will have vast areas of roofing and car parks that could be covered in solar panels, space for wind generation and battery storage, and for emissions scrubbers. If the corporate response is that this is not possible, that is their problem, not ours. Perhaps some innovation is called for. Richard Lamming Shaldon, Devon • You report on the cost of a proposed new “hyperscale” datacentre in Havering, east London, in terms of its likely carbon footprint (Proposed London datacentre ‘incompatible’ with net zero with 1m-tonne carbon footprint, 21 August) – though the article doesn’t mention the huge use of water, which seems ironic in a period of drought. Locals and others are quite rightly up in arms about this and indeed many other datacentres that have been built or are under development. Nevertheless, we should all consider our own culpability here. Datacentres exist because we want to send, receive and store digital communications. Understandable enough, but a huge quantity of digital data is either junk or unnecessary. Research suggests that if each person in this country sent one less “thank-you” email a day, there would be an annual saving of more than 16,000 tonnes of CO2. We can all contribute to reducing and managing the problem. A structure of small charges by the government for digital communications would deter us all from generating junk. We pay to post letters, why not for digital communication? Michael McClelland Devizes, Wiltshire • If AI is so clever, it should be required to design itself datacentres that do not command all our water and energy before we let its oligarchs build. Malcolm Fraser Edinburgh • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Thriving lichen-loving moth is an exception to the rule | Letter
summary: Letters: Mark R Shaw says airborne pollutants have caused a massive decline in insect numbers, in response to a Country Diary
text: Nigel Brown’s understandable joy in finding a rosy footman in his moth trap (Country diary, 25 August) ends with “an important ecological message” that the substantial elimination of airborne sulphur dioxide pollution, which was devastating to the lichens and algae on which caterpillars of footman moths largely feed, has allowed recovery and even geographical spread. However, what might be a more realistic message is that the balance has changed in our major airborne pollutants since the 1990s, from sulphur dioxide to nitrogen oxides (a byproduct of internal combustion engines, among others), and this has benefited lichens and algae, which thrive under the current regime – and hence also footman moths as a special case. But environmental pollution from a host of sources is undoubtedly contributing in an ever more disastrous way to the widespread and massive declines in the numbers of most groups of moths and indeed other insects in today’s Britain. It’s OK for footman moths, but they are not a good model. Mark R Shaw Edinburgh • Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? Please email us your letter and it will be considered for publication in our letters section.

title: Longing for the season of mellow fruitfulness | Brief letters
summary: Brief letters: Autumn pleasures | Solar gain | Meghan and Harry | Rowing knowledge | Eye test | Bad mood
text: Regarding Emma Brockes’s Digested Week (Is there anything sadder than the end of summer?, 28 August), the end of summer is the beginning of autumn – the best season of the year. Trees changing colour making woodlands look so beautiful, with autumn crocuses underneath. Gentle weather for walking the dog. Harvesting apples and pears, and planting bulbs for spring. Enjoying the later months of this year and looking to the beginning of the next. Fiona Cruickshank Enfield, London • Following your article on plug-in solar panels (Plug-in solar: could a low-cost panel cut your bills?, 21 August), my only thought is exactly how long will they be hanging on the new owners’ balcony railings or garden walls before they go walkies? Highly portable and highly stealable. Ralph Jones Rochester, Kent • Regarding nominative determinism among letter writers (Letters, 30 August), I’m sure I have got valuable wisdom to impart on the return of Meghan and Harry. Catherine Williams Worksop, Nottinghamshire • I’m afraid I know very little about rowing. Adrian Cox Whitley Bay, Tyne and Wear • I regularly visit castles to test my eyesight. Tom Barnard Dunkeld, Perthshire • The wave of correspondence concerning appropriate names has gone too far and has made me rather ill-tempered. title: Pentagon plays down report of Hegseth regularly overruling military advice
summary: Response seeks to discredit Washington Post story that four generals and admirals advised against prolonging Iran war
text: Pete Hegseth regularly receives formal objections from senior commanders and proceeds anyway, the Pentagon’s top spokesman has said, as he tried to discredit a Washington Post report that four generals and admirals had advised against prolonging the war in Iran. “Of course, we demand candid military advice,” Sean Parnell wrote on X, formerly Twitter. “Non-concurs are standard. The Secretary sees them constantly. That’s how you run a real military.” Parnell was responding to the Post’s account of four four-star commanders who had lodged formal “non-concurs” against a plan to keep more than 50,000 US troops in the Middle East through September, with some deployments potentially running into 2027. In dismissing the story, Parnell did not dispute that the objections had been filed, or that Hegseth fields such dissent on an ongoing basis. “Publishing highly classified assessments from the Secretary’s orders book is a crime,” he wrote. “It’s a betrayal of the force. And much of what they’re publishing is inaccurate … We are in great shape around the world. This story isn’t about readiness. It’s TDS and PDS – they hate President Trump and Secretary Hegseth more than they love America.” It was unclear which parts of the story the Pentagon deems to be inaccurate. A community note attached to the X post noted that, while leaking classified material is illegal for government employees, the US supreme court ruled in 1971 that the first amendment protects the press’s right to publish classified information of public interest. The non-concurs described by the Post were in the 14 August edition of the secretary of defense orders book, a classified document typically produced twice a month that tracks the availability and deployment of US forces worldwide. They reportedly came from Adm Daryl Caudle, chief of naval operations; Gen Alexus Grynkewich, head of US European Command; Gen Francis L Donovan, chief of US Southern Command; and Adm Samuel Paparo, chief of US Indo-Pacific Command. The army and air force are said to have concurred with extending their deployments, but warned of significant risks. Caudle told Hegseth the navy could not sustain its current level of commitment because no end date for the operation had been set, according to the Post, which cited people familiar with the assessment. Paparo objected to the continued demand for an aircraft carrier strike group and destroyers. The European and Southern Command chiefs said shifting ships and surveillance aircraft to Central Command was already degrading their ability to fulfill homeland-defense obligations. In a statement to the Post issued before publication, Parnell used calmer language, saying troop-commitment decisions were “based on the current threat assessment, strategic priorities established by the President, and the advice” of military leadership. He said the department does not discuss “internal operational processes” or specific non-concurrences. Dan Lamothe, the Post reporter who broke the story, wrote on X that “independent journalism is not a crime” and that such reporting was necessary when officials withhold details about a war funded by taxpayers. The exchange came days after US and Iranian forces traded fire for the first time in roughly a month, and six weeks after Hegseth told senators the war had cost an estimated $37.5bn, including projected costs through September. Still, Donald Trump on Monday morning in effect said the war was won. “Iran is officially a Failed Nation. IT IS DEAD!” the president wrote on Truth Social. “They have no Navy, they have no Air Force, they have no currency, they are not paying their soldiers or police, Inflation is at 300%, and their leadership is in total disarray and incapable of properly representing the country.” He accused Iran’s government of killing more than 100,000 protesters and said its leaders “must be tried for war crimes against humanity”. Neither Trump nor Parnell explained how that squares with what four of the Pentagon’s own commanders had put in writing: that they can’t sustain the war effort as ordered.

title: ‘Superhuman’ AI tool spots heart disease in less than 2 seconds
summary: Technology trained on millions of routine ECGs could fast-track high-risk patients for treatment
text: Doctors have developed a “superhuman” AI tool that can spot heart disease in less than two seconds. The groundbreaking technology has been trained on millions of patients and works by extracting more information from a routine electrocardiogram (ECG) than the human eye can typically see. The traditional ECG, which records electrical activity in the heart, including the rate and rhythm, has been a vital medical tool in diagnosing heart attacks and abnormal heart rhythms for a century. But it cannot detect heart disease. That requires an echocardiogram, a type of ultrasound scan, which patients often have to wait months for. Now a team have developed an AI tool that can spot signs of heart failure and heart valve disease – two of the most common forms of heart disease – from ECG results in “the blink of an eye”. Details of the breakthrough, which could boost early diagnosis of heart disease, were presented to thousands of delegates at the European Society of Cardiology annual congress in Munich, the world’s largest heart conference. Early diagnosis is vital for heart failure and heart valve disease, enabling those who need lifesaving medicines to be spotted sooner, before they become dangerously unwell. The development is being seen as potentially significant, because ECGs are one of the most common tests in medicine, with about a billion performed worldwide each year. In a trial involving 67,000 patients in the US, the AI tool was able to identify up to 81% of those who had heart failure, and up to 90% of those with heart valve disease. Dr Sonya Babu-Narayan, a consultant cardiologist and clinical director of the British Heart Foundation (BHF), which funded the trial, said: “It is exciting to see that AI can now deliver a read-out from an ECG in what feels like the blink of an eye. “Technology like the AI ECG in this research, which has the potential to identify high-risk patients early, will not detect everyone with a heart condition. But it could be a solution to help fast-track the patients who are most likely to have a heart abnormality. When it comes to the heart, earlier diagnosis and treatment saves and improves lives.” The tech cannot be used on its own to definitively diagnose or rule out heart failure or heart valve disease, but it gives a very strong indication someone may have them. Someone judged as highly likely to have either could be sent rapidly for an echocardiogram, rather than wait months on the standard waiting lists. That could mean a quicker diagnosis which would enable them to start treatment earlier. Prof Fu Siong Ng, a professor of cardiology at Imperial College London, said: “Patients can often wait several months for a heart ultrasound scan after being referred for one by their doctor. “This makes it exciting that our technology could identify patients most at risk of heart failure and heart valve disease, so they could be prioritised for scans faster and more urgently.” The aim of the tool is to speed up diagnosis of those suspected to have heart failure or heart valve disease. But Ng said it could also prove lifesaving by spotting signs of the conditions in people who may have undergone an ECG for different reasons. “Another potential application of this AI model is to opportunistically diagnose heart failure and heart valve disease in whom these conditions are not suspected,” he said. “The AI model could be run on all ECGs done in a hospital to flag those at highest risk of these diseases, so that they can be diagnosed earlier.” Dr Ahmed El-Medany, a BHF clinical research fellow, who led the Imperial College London analysis, described the tool as a “superhuman AI” and said the next challenge would be to design handheld AI-led ECG readers for healthcare professionals to use. Delegates in Munich also heard how AI-based analysis of facial videos could rapidly and accurately detect undiagnosed high blood pressure and type 2 diabetes. Researchers at the University of Tokyo and the Institute of Science Tokyo said AI analysis of five-second facial videos could hep improve diagnosis. Millions of people who have high blood pressure or type 2 diabetes do not know they have the conditions.

title: Nepal rescuers race to reach hundreds feared trapped in hydropower tunnels
summary: Workers thought to be stuck in underground areas at 11 sites after last week’s devastating flash floods
text: Rescue teams are working to reach more than 900 missing hydropower workers, hundreds of whom are feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of 12 hydropower projects in Nepal after the devastating flash floods, the ⁠country’s disaster management authority has said.
