The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris on Wednesday last week has risen to 939 people, with 16 more dead reported in Tibet. More than 4,400 are missing on the two sides of the border. About 500 of the missing hydropower workers at projects damaged by the flooding in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts are thought to be trapped in tunnels built to control the flow of water. As rescue efforts drag on, experts fear the chances of finding survivors in tunnels are diminishing as oxygen levels fall. Some workers called for help when flooding started on Wednesday and those who had managed to escape tunnels said many of their colleagues were still trapped, said Mohan Kumar Dangi, the president of the Nepal Independent Power Producers’ Association. Rescue efforts have been complicated by difficult terrain, persistently high flood waters and difficult weather. With more than 40 bridges destroyed, rescuers are relying on helicopters, while India and China are sending prefabricated truss bridges to help restore access. The swollen Trishuli River has also continued to change course unpredictably, making planning a challenge. Areas that were dry one day are flooded the next, and further floods are a constant concern. Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, that were swept down the mountains by the torrent, have been buried in shallow graves after DNA testing on the plains ⁠of the Himalayan region. Nepali officials said on Monday that the focus was on reaching the 933 people missing from ‌hydropower plants. “A large amount of debris has been deposited and that is posing us a big challenge to open the tunnels,” the Nepal army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet told Reuters. About 250 people were rescued from the Upper Trishuli hydroelectric project over the weekend, and army engineers began blasting operations at the site to rescue another 42 workers thought be missing. The damage to hydropower infrastructure is estimated to have taken 700 megawatts out of service, about 10% of the country’s power capacity. Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams ⁠showed earth-moving equipment shovelling mud to try to reach the tunnels. Ashish Gurung, who normally works as a guide, was among the rescuers. “There is just mud everywhere,” he said. “Inside the tunnel it was worse. It’s so difficult to move, the mud is so deep.” His team was trying to access the Chilime hydropower plant in Rasuwa, one of the worst-hit areas. At least eight people are believed missing there, and an Indian team is working alongside the Nepali army using pumps and excavators to locate them. The Nepali prime minister, Balendra Shah, said rescue efforts were “challenging due to adverse weather, difficult terrain and ongoing risks.” Gurung said mountaineers were improvising by using planks of wood to check the depth of the mud, before using them as makeshift bridges along with a system of ropes to keep themselves safe. “Walking in it is very difficult, at one point it was up to our chests,” he said. “We got close to the first station, about 130 metres in. Inside that far … it looked like it was just bodies.” The hydropower company had given his team a map and it looked as if there was a chance people in the tunnels could have survived. “They have a safe area inside,” he said. “Some of them could potentially be alive. I am hoping they are alive.” The Red Cross estimates that more than 93,000 people have been affected by the disaster, heightening fears that the climate crisis is destabilising the geology of mountain and polar regions. Shah said the flood was an “unprecedented and devastating natural disaster” and that it was difficult to compile a complete assessment of the damage. “Despite the adverse weather, difficult terrain and continuing risks, we are moving forward with determination to save the lives of our citizens,” he said in a Facebook post late on Sunday. Almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations alongside civilian workers and volunteers, he said. Whole communities had been destroyed by the flooding, leaving families homeless in heavy rain. “There are no roads, they have all been washed away, and many areas are just not accessible,” said a police officer coordinating rescue efforts in Nuwakot district. “It is very difficult for my men. The area is still flooded, and elsewhere it is all marshland.” Nepal’s disaster agency said on Monday it had counted 903 deaths, with 4,793 people, including 592 foreigners, missing. Chinese authorities had reported 16 deaths and 546 people missing as of Sunday. State media said 261 of the missing were foreigners, including more than 100 Nepalis. Among those missing are more than 30 British nationals. On Saturday, a rapid deployment team from the UK arrived in Nepal to support Britons and their families. The UK government has given a £5m support package to assist Nepal in its disaster response. Amid the soaring toll of death and missing was some hope. On Monday, rescuers pulled a six-year-old girl out of mud after hearing crying. “Her body was trapped in mud, but her head was outside,” the Nepali armed police spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki told Agence France-Presse. China’s state-run CCTV said Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220m yuan (£24m) to support relief efforts and had been airdropping equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers, while its soldiers used life-detection equipment to look for the missing. Nepal has said it does not need foreign help in general search and rescue operations, but it has leaned on its neighbours, India and China, for their expertise in tunnel rescues. Rescue operations have been suspended several times since Friday because of bad weather and concerns that a lake formed across the Nepal-China border by the disaster could trigger fresh flooding after it began overflowing into Nepal’s rivers. The weather was good on Monday, however, and rescue ⁠work picked up pace, said Narendra Pariyar, the district administrator of Rasuwa, one of the two hardest-hit districts. In the holy town of Devighat on the banks of the Trishuli, residents walked around the shells of what had once been homes, trying to salvage their belongings from the debris. The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, CCTV reported, saying it was a “new and prominent feature of cryosphere ‌disasters” on the Tibetan plateau. Two Nepali officials said China had not shared much information on glacier risks and water levels after a meeting to strengthen cooperation earlier this year, and they feared that could hamper future disaster preparedness. China’s foreign ministry said Beijing had continuously provided Nepal with meteorological and hydrological data and will continue to “strongly support” Nepal’s disaster relief efforts and safeguard the two countries’ common interests. With Reuters and Agence France-Presse

title: Cisco probably violated Middle Eastern and Muslim employees’ civil rights, US agency finds
summary: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission finds ‘reasonable cause to believe’ tech firm subjected workers who spoke up about Palestine to hostile work environment
text: The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the agency tasked with enforcing federal anti-discrimination laws, has found that Cisco, the global tech company, probably violated the civil rights of Middle Eastern, Muslim and other company employees. The determination, reached earlier this summer and first reported by Politico Pro, is believed to be the first by the federal agency finding a major company at fault in connection to pro-Palestinian advocacy that swept campuses and workplaces in recent years. Complaints filed by employees in December 2024 detailed how, following the 7 October 2023 attacks in Israel, a Cisco internal communications platform was filled with racist and Islamophobic messages, which escalated after more than 1,700 employees signed a public letter challenging the tech giant’s ties to the Israeli government. The posts celebrated the killings of Palestinian civilians, called them animals, and targeted individual Cisco employees who had spoken up for Palestinian rights. Margaret Ly, local director of the EEOC’s San Jose office, wrote in a 9 June letter that following an investigation the office determined that “there is reasonable cause to believe that [Cisco] subjected a class of individuals to a hostile work environment based on their national origin (Middle Eastern), religion (Muslim), and/or their association with Muslim and/or Middle Eastern individuals, in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964”. A spokesperson for Cisco wrote in a statement to the Guardian that the company “disagree[d]” with the EEOC’s determination. “Cisco thoroughly investigated all concerns and took appropriate action,” the spokesperson said. The EEOC did not respond to a request for comment. The employees also filed grievances with the National Labor Relations Board and the California labor commissioner. Both remain under review. Christopher Ho, a director at Legal Aid at Work, which represents the Cisco employees who filed complaints, told the Guardian that the company “at best failed to take their harassment seriously and, through its inaction, sent the implicit message that its pro-Palestinian employees were unworthy of protection”. “This is a massive multinational corporation with all the resources in the world and they couldn’t get it right,” he added. “Thankfully the EEOC did.” Anti-Arab and anti-Muslim rhetoric was left unmoderated on Connected Jewish Network, an internal forum open to all Cisco employees, following the Hamas attacks. But the rhetoric turned to abuse and harassment directed at Cisco workers following an April 2024 open letter coordinated by “Bridge to Humanity”, or B2H, a group of mostly Palestinian, Arab and Muslim employees, which called on Cisco to disclose and end its business dealings with the Israeli military, adhere to its own human rights policy and protect those who had signed the letter from retaliation. According to the American Friends Service Committee, which tracks global companies’ connections to Israel’s actions in Gaza, Cisco provides hardware and communications capacity to the Israeli military’s central datacenter. Cisco treated the letter as a “form of harassment”, according to the complaints filed with the EEOC and three former employees who spoke with the Guardian on condition of anonymity out of fear of being doxed. In an internal email, Cisco said the letter was “under review” and removed it from an internal website where workers could sign on to it. Many of the employees who led efforts to challenge the company’s ties to Israel have since been terminated, laid off or forced out of the company, the former workers said. Several commenters on internal platforms equated support for Palestinians with antisemitism. One commented on a report about two members of a Palestinian family killed in Jerusalem, writing: “I for one am extremely grateful.” One person wrote that those who had signed the letter denouncing Cisco’s ties to Israel should “just up and quit (not just quit Cisco, but quit living and make this world a better place for all)”. Another wrote that he had exported a roster of signatories, to which another replied, “I’m sure those who have signed aren’t very happy that [redacted] now has their names in Excel.” Employees repeatedly flagged the posts to the company, expressing concerns that the list could be used to dox them and warning of the possible consequences for employees traveling to Palestine or whose families were based there. The company did nothing to address their concerns, the former workers said. Cisco only responded two months after they produced a 76-page report detailing racist and hateful posts, noting it had removed some comments it had deemed to be “inappropriate”, according to internal communications reviewed by the Guardian. While the EEOC issued its determination in June, mediation with Cisco led by the agency “didn’t go anywhere”, Ho said, and employees are currently considering next steps, including collective and individual litigation. “Of course we still hope that Cisco will come to the table,” Ho added. “These are people who were once proud to work there.” An employee who recently left the company said that colleagues who still worked there had felt “vindicated” by the EEOC findings, but that many remained fearful of speaking up. Cisco is one of several tech companies that have faced backlash from employees over their business ties to the Israeli government. A group of Cisco shareholders also called on the company to commission an independent human rights assessment, according to a June letter reviewed by the Guardian. “As long-term investors, we believe effective oversight of human rights risks is increasingly important to protecting shareholder value,” they wrote.

title: Kyiv suffers hours of daytime air raids as Russia deploys new jet-powered drones
summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy says about 800 Shahed drones fired into Ukraine in four days in effort to ‘wear down’ country
text: Kyiv is enduring hours of daytime air raids and air raid warnings as Russia has fired 800 jet-powered drones into Ukraine in four days, using the faster weapons to sustain prolonged waves of attacks The new-model Shahed drones have a cruising speed of 200mph to 250mph , about double the 115mph achieved by the piston-engine version and beyond the speed of Ukraine’s cheap interceptors, making them harder to stop. Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, said on Sunday that the jet-powered models now accounted for more than half the drones used by Russia to attack and “wear down” the country. “There were almost 1,500 drones of all types in these four days alone – about 800 of them jet-powered,” the president said. Ukraine was currently relying on combat aircraft to shoot them down, he added. A Geran-4, the latest jet-powered model, struck an ammunition dump at Myla, a village 15 miles west of Kyiv on Thursday. Thirty-eight people were killed as the strike unleashed hours of secondary explosions in one of the deadliest single attacks of the war, destroying warehouses and damaging nearby homes. Russia has also made heavy use of the drones in waves of daytime attacks in the past five days, leading to hours of air alerts, particularly in Kyiv. Eight air raid alerts sounded in Kyiv by lunchtime on Monday. Daytime attacks, although far from unknown, were uncommon previously, prompting some businesses to halt operations until the alert had passed, and leaving residents with the decision of whether to remain indoors, seek shelter, or ignore the warnings entirely. Close drone threats also force emergency services to leave an attack site, potentially worsening the impact of any fire caused by a hit, as happened when a food storage facility was struck in Boryspil, to the east of Kyiv, earlier this month. Kremlin forces have attacked warehouses around Kyiv in the past month, in retaliation to a Ukrainian campaign targeting the Wildberries and Ozon distribution chains inside Russia. The attacks have led to food shortages in the shops, but a Ukrainian official urged people not to panic. Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy on defence technology, urged people “do not give in to rumours, misinformation, and panic” and said that companies were rebuilding supply chains in response to the attacks. “We will not die of hunger,” he wrote in a social media posting. Shahed drones, with a distinctive delta wing, were originally designed in Iran, and the technology transferred to Russia. The jet Shahed, the 238, was first unveiled by Iran in autumn 2023, and appeared in Ukraine shortly after. It was not until spring that Russia began to manufacture and deploy its latest jet-powered variant – the Geran-4 – in numbers. Russia now makes more jet-powered drones than the original piston-engined variants, in two models, the delta winged Geran-4 and the Geran-5, which looks like a missile with wings. Beskrestnov said that at least 2,500 of the jet drones had been launched into Ukraine during August, up from 1,500 the month before. Production date stamps found on the bodywork suggest they are being fired within days after being made at a factory in Yelabuga, he added. Ukraine had successfully devised a range of low-cost ground-launched interceptors fast enough to eliminate a piston-engined Shahed, raising interception rates to above 90%. Over the weekend, the president said that level had to be maintained into the autumn. Engineers are now racing to make faster interceptor drones able to knock out jet-powered Shaheds, though details are scant. “Four companies have developed the relevant interceptor drones, and one company has the most successful technology,” Zelenskky said.

title: Letter: Michael Meadowcroft obituary
summary: Ruth Péchèr writes: Consistent with his values of liberty, equality and community my father, Michael Meadowcroft,  observed after my daughter’s death ‘not all individuals conform to some universal template’
text: The obituary of the Liberal politician Michael Meadowcroft – my father – noted the premature death of my daughter Esther in 2022. She lived with complex and multiple learning difficulties and intractable epilepsy. While there were seizure-free periods, much of her life was stolen by the rare disease GAMT. Sadly this was not diagnosed until she was 30. She died a fortnight later; our persistent requests to start treatment during this time proved fruitless. Society struggled to include Esther. She was loud in quiet places and would rarely sit down, even when everyone else around her did. Nonetheless, she brought out the best in people. Consistent with his values of liberty, equality and community, Michael observed after her death that “not all individuals conform to some universal template … human society has to accept every Esther as a full member of it”.

title: Burnham’s bumpy ride ahead: PM’s in-tray full of dilemmas as parliament returns
summary: Labour leader faces tough decisions on issues such as North Sea drilling, electoral reform and defence spending
text: After a relatively cheery summer in which he announced a range of eye-catching cost of living policies, Andy Burnham may find his return to parliament this week to be a rude awakening. While the new prime minister has enjoyed some success in the polls, he is faced with many of the same problems that stymied Keir Starmer and has some difficult and unpopular choices to make. North Sea oil and gas The Rosebank oilfield and the Jackdaw gasfield have been in limbo for a year after a court case ruled the consent given to drill by the previous Conservative government was unlawful. Now, it is in the hands of the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, to make the quasi-judicial decision to allow the drilling to start. Burnham has promised to take a “pragmatic” approach to North Sea oil and gas as the unions complain about job losses caused by Labour’s manifesto promise to end all oil and gas licences and the Iran crisis tightens supply of gas around the globe. It has been reported Burnham will direct his energy secretary to approve the Jackdaw gasfield. Industry estimates suggest the Jackdaw gasfield could supply roughly 6% of the UK’s future gas output. But this will not impact bills, as gas is sold on a global market. He is said to be less sure about allowing Rosebank, which the former energy secretary Ed Miliband, who is now foreign secretary, referred to as “climate vandalism”. He faces a revolt from left-of-centre Labour MPs and the Green party’s outspoken leader, Zack Polanski, will undoubtedly make hay out of the decision. It is also a difficult choice to make after a summer of record-breaking heat, exacerbated by climate breakdown. Face-to-face with Donald Trump Burnham is due to meet Donald Trump in September at the UN general assembly in New York City. It may be hard to break the ice; when he was mayor of Manchester, he previously referred to Trump as “poisonous” and said he would not be welcome in the city. The US president has disparagingly referred to Burnham as the “mayor of a town”. But the pair may get along. They had a friendly phone conversation, with Burnham saying : “We had a good phone call on my first day in office and looking forward to meeting in person.” Commenting on the call, Trump said approvingly: “He said he’s going to open up North Sea oil. If he does that, you’re going to be a wealthy country.” Rather than oil and gas, Burnham will be hoping to discuss the war in Ukraine with the president. He recently met Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv and promised to drum up more international support for the country. Donations and electoral reform One of his most pressing challenges is the electoral reform bill, which returns to parliament this week. Burnham has previously backed a cap on individual donations as low as £500,000 to stop the mega-rich influencing UK politics. But now he has reportedly dropped this cap altogether after being lobbied by the unions. The measure would have been a key tool in stopping Reform, which relies on a few wealthy donors. Another issue that will crop up in this bill is electoral reform, which Burnham has also previously backed. Nearly 100 Labour MPs are supporting an amendment which asks the prime minister to set up a commission on electoral reform in the first 100 days of his government. The Liberal Democrats will also take the opportunity to pressure Burnham on this. Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, said: “If Andy Burnham fails to change the political system as PM he will be remembered as another Starmer but with a decent social media team.” Labour conference A natural showman, Burnham might be looking forward to his first Labour conference as prime minister. The event, happening at the end of September, will demonstrate how good he is at bringing together members. He will also hope to avoid any votes that show the members have a different view to the government. Starmer struggled last year after a successful motion that labeled Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, a definition he did not accept. Immigration This will be a big one for Burnham as he tries to combat Reform, who have made immigration their main campaigning point. The numbers are trending down, with net migration at its lowest since the Covid-19 pandemic, and the number of asylum seekers in hotels has halved in a year. The immigration and asylum bill coming up this autumn will give Reform and the Conservatives a chance to cause mischief, with amendments and accusations that Burnham is not taking the issue seriously enough. Burnham also faces a battle with his own MPs after backing changes to tighten the asylum system, which some on the left have called cruel. The budget Burnham and the chancellor, John Healey, are in a sticky situation when it comes to the budget. The prime minister has already committed to tax cuts for pubs and a cap on bus ticket prices, but he has also said he will follow former chancellor Rachel Reeves’ fiscal rules on borrowing. The new government is also committed to the manifesto pledge not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT – which caused Starmer’s government to become unpopular with pensioners, farmers and businesses, as ministers enacted a tax raid on those sectors instead. Additionally, the fiscal headroom is likely to have been significantly shrunk by the economic turmoil caused by the Iran war and rises in borrowing costs and inflation. How the sums will add up remains to be seen. Tax rises are widely expected. Welfare Starmer faced huge rebellions after his attempts to cut the welfare bill and kicked the can down the road by commissioning the minister Stephen Timms to review the system. That report will be out in the autumn, meaning choices will have to be made. Will there be cuts to the personal independence payment (Pip), which disability campaigners railed against? Burnham will have to balance the needs of the most vulnerable in society with pressures to cut spending. Also due this autumn is the Alan Milburn’s review on the 1 million young people in the UK who are out of work, education, or training. Defence spending Healey finds himself in an interesting position on the budget amid expectations he will shelve his own target of spending 3% of Britain’s GDP on defence by 2030. This is a decision over which he resigned as defence secretarywhen Starmer made it. Choices will have to be made on how to properly fund the military at a time of dire finances. International partners including Trump will be watching any decision closely. Bills Energy bills are due to go up by 4% in October as the Iran war pushes prices to a three-year high. There could be another rise in January if international tensions are not soothed by then. Will Burnham feel obliged to step in? The cost of living has been one of his main focuses. But the energy support system designed by the former prime minister Liz Truss in 2022 cost tens of billions and added to the national debt. He will want to avoid such an outcome. Thames Water Burnham promised in his first speech as prime minister to “build a new economy where we put life’s essentials back under stronger public control to make them affordable to you again”. And what is more essential for life than water? The beleaguered Thames Water is due to run out of money this autumn, with its creditors wanting the government to agree a takeover deal before they open their wallet again. The public wants Thames to be nationalised, and Burnham said he wanted to do so before he became prime minister. But the Treasury is concerned about the potential cost of a legal battle if creditors challenge any government decision to tip the company into administration in order to take it over. Burnham will have to break the stalemate and make a choice very soon, and sources say he is considering ripping up insolvency laws to make the transition to nationalisation easier and less expensive.

title: Border area between Nepal and China where 33 Australians are missing still almost entirely cut off
summary: Majority of missing Australians were near Gyirong Port minutes before impact. Rescuers say the area is now destroyed, covered in metres of silt and debris
text: It has been almost a week since the catastrophic floods in Nepal and not even a vehicle can get into the area where the majority of missing Australians were last heard from. Gyirong Port, the border area between Nepal and China, was the first to be hit. Images from Chinese rescue teams who have managed to get in by helicopter or hiking show the area has been completely flattened. The immigration building, the power lines, everything, just wiped away. News that phone connectivity to the area was back on spread quickly on Monday around the families of lost Australians who have come to Kathmandu to wait. In WhatsApp groups and over Facebook, they shared any updates they had. One family member, who did not want to be named, told the Guardian she had been trying to ring her husband all morning after she heard the phone line was back up. He did not answer. “The embassies aren’t helping,” she said. The total number of Australians missing in the disaster rose to 43 on Monday, and at least 33 of them were understood to be near Gyirong Port just before the impact. The 15 Australians with the Himalaya Glacier Company, 11 travelling with the Isha Foundation, six from Kailash Journeys and one from Kathmandu Holiday Tours and Travel were all near the border – many of them arrived at the immigration building just 10 minutes before the flood hit. Sujan Wasti, the head of Kailash Journeys’ Nepal operations, said the last he heard from the group was at 7.30 am, when the guide touched base to say they were coming back. They were scheduled to land in Kathmandu on Thursday, with many of them flying home from the capital. “In the area, the rescue has been done,” he said. “Now, it will just be about collecting the bodies and bringing them [home].” Since last Wednesday, Wasti has sent teams up the Trishuli River to look for any signs of the missing trekkers. They have twice flown over the border by helicopter, and have visited local hospitals to see if anyone has shown up. “We are searching every place we can, but still we have not found anyone,” he said. “There is still no sign of them. “Along the border, it was only dead bodies. If they are alive, it will be a miracle.” China is coordinating the search and rescue effort in the area. As of Monday morning, crews reopening the highway towards the port on the Tibet side had 1.15km left of road to clear and reconstruct. Since Friday, no one except rescue crews has been able to access the area – some have hiked for 10 hours to get in, before rappelling down into the valley. Others, when the weather allowed, were helicoptered in. Akhilesh Surjan, a humanitarian, emergency and disaster management expert at Charles Darwin University, said one of “the sensitive questions” has become how far everyone keeps the hope alive. “The rescue experts consider the first 72 hours to be very critical,” he says. “Because after the first 72 hours, that is three days, the chance of finding survivors drops sharply.” Despite this, he said surviving after three days “is not uncommon”. In Japan after the 2011 earthquake, two people were found alive after nine days. “Survival usually depends on whether the person has access to the trapped air pockets, protection from extreme weather, no severe internal bleeding or pressure injuries,” he said. He said there were possibilities for survival – that people had been swept downstream and were stranded, or had been lucky enough to shelter in a place that wasn’t completely destroyed. Getting into Gyirong Port is not the only challenge. The thick layer of mud and pools of water have made it difficult to use life-detection devices accurately, teams have reported. Instead, rescuers are calling out as they look for survivors. Rain is forecast for the next two days, which will further complicate and slow efforts. There is also the threat of another flood or landslide. A team analysing hazards around the area on Monday found “high-risk geological disaster points”. Surjan said rescue teams would be analysing the landscape to determine where people may have moved to, but it was a dangerous job. In Nepal, at least 85 rescuers, including police and army officers, are now missing. “Continuing rainfall and river flow and the poor visibility for choppers or helicopters, communication failure of the first few days, and the limited ability to get heavy rescue equipment into the area will make it harder,” Surjan said. Three days after the disaster, the first team of Chinese rescue workers were able to reach the border crossing complex. They were the first on the ground and said everything had been destroyed. “There was no road … it was all virgin forest and sheer cliffs,” rescue worker Zou Mingqi told Chinese state media. At the border complex, “as far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins”. The Isha Foundation has sent volunteers to Kathmandu and Tibet to help families and find any updates they can. Their loved ones were standing inside the immigration centre and were about to cross the border when the disaster hit. On Sunday, the foundation sent families a message, asking them to “expect the worst”. “We have been informed that the valley at the Gyirong port is covered with significant debris, probably as much as [13-15 metres] of silt and debris,” it said. “The local experts who know the terrain well have told our on-ground team that it is very unlikely that anyone could have possibly survived the force of the flood. The mix of debris and water rose very high, probably as high as [45 metres] with immense force, completely wiping out the whole building complex. “We wish with all our hearts that we could offer you something more hopeful. Everything our teams have seen, and everything those closest to the site have shared with us, has led us to expect the worst.”

title: Germany poised to identify suspect in Leipzig drone attack on Ukrainian plane
summary: Berlin expected to outline response to incident this month widely speculated to have been coordinated by Russia
text: The German government is imminently expected to announce who it believes was behind a suspected drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane earlier this month and to outline its response to the incident in coordination with its European and Nato partners. The chancellor, Friedrich Merz, told the public broadcaster ARD in an interview on Sunday evening: “We are in the process of concluding the investigations; we have reached a broad agreement within the federal government on how we will respond, and we will make this clear in the coming days. It won’t take much longer.” The government has so far declined to say officially who it thinks was behind the attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport on 4 August. There has been widespread speculation that it was coordinated by Moscow. A drone containing explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used to transport military supplies. The drone was apparently intended to land on the wings of the aircraft, which was filled with kerosene, but the explosive device did not detonate, according to a report last week referencing the investigation. About 20 minutes after the discovery of the first drone, a second drone possibly collided with a DHL cargo plane, which had to abort its landing manoeuvre and was diverted. Days later, a third drone was found in a field in a municipality that directly borders the western edge of Leipzig airport. Forensic technicians from the federal criminal police office found residues of a substance that initial assessments indicated could have been the highly explosive substance hexogen. This explosive also failed to detonate but according to media reports, the investigators’ report stated: “The perpetrators may have had a far larger attack in mind than previously known to the public.” Moscow has denied involvement. Merz indicated that the information the government was due to release was being closely communicated with Berlin’s partners, and any response would also be carried out in cooperation with them. “It will be a response from Germany, but our partners in the European Union and Nato will not be taken by surprise,” he said. It has been speculated in Berlin that meetings this week of EU defence and foreign affairs ministers in Wicklow, Ireland, could be used to make the announcement. Last week Merz stopped short of naming a suspect but said: “They will pay for this.” He underscored the necessity for a decisive response due to the lengths he said those behind the Leipzig plot and other acts of sabotage had been prepared to go. “Attackers are increasingly ruthlessly accepting even serious property damage, and even injuries and deaths,” he said. The daily Die Welt and the news website Politico have reported, citing sources, that the government will blame Russia for the attack and that its retaliatory measures are likely to include a new, extensive package of sanctions coordinated with Brussels to hinder it financially, as well as more forceful measures against Russia’s shadow fleet, the Russian ships illegally transporting oil. The closure of Russian House, an institution representing Russia’s cultural interests that has a large presence in the centre of Berlin, is also said to be on the cards. In return, Russia would be expected to close Germany’s cultural body in Russia, the Goethe Institute. The political dimensions of the government’s response are potentially considerable owing to the timing. A heated election campaign in eastern German states culminates in a vote this Sunday in which the anti-immigrant, populist AfD is expected to do well. The debate over relations with Russia and whether and how Germany should continue to support Ukraine are playing an important role in the campaign. The AfD’s foreign policy spokesperson, Markus Frohnmaier, said he believed “without a doubt” Germany faced hybrid threats but said he would not speculate over who was behind them, calling on the government to “first establish transparency and provide information about the current state of knowledge”.

title: A pediatrician is running for Senate. Can doctors change the political debate over health and science?
summary: After Lindsey Graham’s death, Democrat Annie Andrews finds herself in a closely watched race as she seeks to flip his Republican seat
text: Annie Andrews was a dark horse Democrat challenging a five-term Republican in the US Senate when 314 Action, a political action fund devoted to electing scientists and doctors, first backed her. Now, after the unexpected death of Senator Lindsey Graham, Andrews finds herself in a closely watched race. Donald Trump persuaded South Carolina voters last week to select Graham’s sister, Darline, as the new Republican candidate. They will face off in November in an election still heavily favored to keep the seat in Republican hands in the conservative state. Andrews, a pediatrician for 20 years, has made public health and science a central part of her campaign, highlighting the importance of vaccines as measles spread through South Carolina – and so have the other candidates supported by 314 Action. Last year, 314 laid out an ambitious goal: elect at least 100 doctors to state and federal office by 2030. The group had an initial fundraising target of $25m, which it reached in August, to help establish Democratic doctors in state legislatures, governorships, and federal offices – “building that pipeline of talent to higher office”, said Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action. Headlines in 2026 have been dominated by outbreaks of infectious diseases and foodborne illnesses, the biggest cuts to Medicaid in its history, the gutting of scientific research, immigration raids in hospitals, and more, making health and science salient issues in the US midterm elections. Doctors and experts are “on the frontlines of this”, Andrews said. “I don’t think there’s ever been a more important time to elect scientists and medical doctors to all levels of our government.” In the 2018 midterm elections, record numbers of people – nearly 200 – with backgrounds in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (Stem) ran for House and Senate seats. But only about 12% of the candidates won, according to research by Matthew Motta, assistant professor at Boston University’s School of Public Health. “So to say that you want to get 100 physicians to not just run but to actually be elected to public office is quite a tall order,” he said. Endorsement and financial support from 314 Action do increase the likelihood that Stem candidates will win, according to his research. But the goal of 100 wins in the next four years is ambitious, Motta said. In fact, candidates with Stem backgrounds were less likely to win than non-Stem peers in 2018, according to an analysis co-authored by Meredith Conroy, political science professor at California State University, San Bernardino. They probably didn’t lose because of their science background, Conroy said, adding: “I just don’t think it was a salient enough identity at the time to suggest it made or broke their campaign.” But recent events are changing that, making health and science a top-of-mind concern for voters, Conroy and Motta pointed out. “It’s really important then, if we want to defend science from politicized attacks on its daily operation, that those who actually do science and who do medicine are elected to Congress,” Motta said. State-level leadership on health will also be key as national health agencies falter and as states consider restrictive laws on issues like vaccination and reproductive health, Motta said. Josh Green, the governor of Hawaii and an emergency physician, is the only doctor-governor in the United States right now. But he wants to feel less alone. “We want to create a bench of people” who are better-qualified and could be appointed to positions like these, Green said. He is mentoring candidates through 314 on how to engage with constituents and “how to message in a way that political people have to master”. There are 20 physicians in the House and Senate right now, but only six of the House representatives are Democrats, and there are no Democratic doctors in the Senate. Running for office takes deep pockets, which means doctors who are already wealthy – a group that tends to skew conservative – are more likely to be elected. Some of these doctors, like Rand Paul, have contributed to misinformation on vaccines and other health issues. That partisan divide is increasingly evident when it comes to health, Motta noted: “Just because somebody has a scientific background does not necessarily mean that they’re going to fight for science.” Yet electing more physicians could help repair trust in science, Naughton said, as “most people do trust their physicians and they bring a lot of credibility.” Doctor-politicians aren’t just important for opposing harmful laws or misinformation, Naughton added. They also have a fact-based approach to problem solving. Scientists and doctors frequently go into debt for their education, making it difficult for them to leave their fields for politics, Green pointed out. He was only able to do it because he qualified for student loan forgiveness through the National Health Service Corps. “Had I had $300,000 or $400,000 of debt, like a lot of my colleagues from medical school, I could never have run for the state house. There’s no way,” he said. “If we can seed their campaigns with enough money to get off the ground,” Green said of new candidates, “they’ll stand a chance.” When Barbara Bollier, an anesthesiologist and a Republican-turned-Democratic state lawmaker in Kansas, decided to run for the Senate in 2020, she knew the odds were long. Kansas hadn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Even though Bollier lost that race, she still feels victorious. “I moved the ball down the field,” she said. She received more votes than any Democrat in the history of the state, she said, and when the next big health issue arose in Kansas, the state shocked the country by voting to protect abortion rights. There’s a persistent belief that medicine and science are above politics, Naughton said, pointing out “that approach has failed us … We need folks to go beyond just signing polite letters and waiting to be tapped as scientific advisers, and actually step up and claim the seat at the table.” And the stakes are high: “The hard truth of it is, people are going to die if we don’t follow science,” Green said. Running for office “was not something I ever, in a million years, thought I would be doing with my life”, Andrews said. At the age of four, she told her preschool teacher she would be a doctor one day, and she never wavered from that plan. But “it became clear to me that the most effective and efficient way to solve the problems my patients and their families were facing was through politics, by changing who actually has the power, by electing people who inherently care about America’s children,” she said. It would take decades to counter the misinformation and damage from officials currently in power, Andrews said. But she is in it for the long haul. “I’m just so happy to be a part of this movement of physicians all across the country raising their hands, stepping up to run for office,” she said.

title: BT on track for estimated £2bn windfall from selling old copper amid AI boom
summary: Telecoms company to benefit from soaring prices for recycled metal recovered from full-fibre broadband rollout
text: BT is on track for an estimated £2bn-plus windfall over the next decade from selling off old copper cabling, as it cashes in on soaring prices amid the AI market frenzy and switches the UK’s network to full-fibre broadband. Copper is one of the main beneficiaries of the “electrification of everything”, essential for the rapid growth of AI datacentres, electronics and the fast-growing renewable energy industry. The metal hit its highest-ever closing price of $14,294 a metric tonne on Friday, close to the record intraday high of $14,500 reached earlier this year amid global shortage fears. BT has a recycling deal with EMR, the UK’s largest cable granulation company, and has now received £99m upfront for thousands of tonnes of surplus stripped copper. It is the second such payment received by the telecoms company, which is rolling out full-fibre broadband to 30m homes by the end of the decade through its Openreach subsidiary, after £105m in 2024. The forward sale agreements, which are understood to cover the delivery of about 20,000 tonnes of copper over a four-year period each, do not include any revenue BT makes each year if it chooses to sell recycled copper on the spot market. BT recovered a record nearly 10,000 tonnes in the year to the end of March, almost three times the amount it managed in the year to the end of March 2024, and a total of 22,347 tonnes since the telecoms company began stripping and selling the cabling in 2023. The record haul, which is 63% more than the 5,600 tonnes reported in BT’s 2025 results, comes at a time of soaring prices which could handsomely benefit BT. In the year that BT reported its first copper haul the average price for the metal was about $8,500 a tonne. “We recovered even more copper cabling,” said Mike McTighe, the chair of Openreach, acknowledging the potential financial benefit of the market surge, in BT’s latest annual report. “Removing 9,147 tonnes from our network for recycling at a time when global demand has never been higher.” Howeer, the jump in value has also made the metal a target of thieves across Britain’s telephone network, railways and even windfarms. Openreach has said it expects to be able to recover up to 200,000 tonnes, with telecoms cabling producing high-grade recycled copper, as the programme runs through the 2030s in line with moving customers on to full-fibre connections. While the precise details of BT’s contract with EMR, which initially runs until 2028, are not known, the market value of the copper it expects to be able to extract had previously been estimated at £1.5bn. However, the soaring price of copper and a future supply crunch – the rating agency S&P Global expects demand to grow from 25m metric tonnes now to about 50m by 2035 – means at current market prices BT’s entire copper tonnage could be valued at £2bn-plus. “Copper has become one of the most strategic materials in the modern economy,” said Abby Chicken, the head of sustainability at Openreach. “As we connect the nation to more reliable full fibre, we’re able to retire parts of the legacy network that are no longer needed. “Recovering and recycling that copper is the right thing to do. It reduces waste, supports the UK’s energy transition towards renewables and helps keep a critical resource in circulation at a time when growing demand is putting pressure on global supply chains.” Amid the soaring prices, Openreach has acted to prevent copper theft. Last year, thieves struck in St Neots, Cambridgeshire, twice in a month, resulting in nearly a mile of underground cables being damaged. In 2024, Openreach suffered copper thefts in the New Forest, affecting 128 premises, and County Tyrone, Northern Ireland, leaving hundreds of homes and businesses with connectivity issues. Openreach is using a wide range of anti-theft measures including coating miles of underground cables with a synthetic DNA and UV tracer, called SelectaDNA. This is widely used across the Openreach network and the tracer easily transfers to hands and clothing. Openreach reported a 30% fall in copper phone and broadband cable theft in 2024, which it attributed to the deployment of the new technology. • This article was amended on 29 September 2026. An earlier version said that the SelectaDNA technology cannot be applied to cables that are already underground.

title: British family pleads with French authorities to release body of relative who died in Channel
summary: Jasmeet Wadhwa, who fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan, lost his life while trying to reach UK in April
text: A British family is pleading with French authorities to release the body of a relative that officials have held for five months after he died in the Channel in April. Jasmeet Wadhwa, 32, died while attempting to reach the UK on a dinghy on 1 April with his mother, Harbans Kaur Wadhwa, after they fled Taliban persecution in Afghanistan in January. They endured a difficult two-month journey under the control of people smugglers before reaching northern France in mid-March. A man from Sudan, Nagmeldin Adam, 33, died on the same boat. Eight others were rescued, including Harbans Kaur Wadhwa. Adam’s journey from Sudan involved detention in Libya for an extended period and many attempts to cross the Mediterranean to Europe. He finally reached France in December 2025. At least 16 people have died trying to cross the Channel from France to the UK so far this year, with the latest reported death on Saturday in a similar part of the French coast to where the two men lost their lives in April. Relatives of the two men took part in a demonstration on Monday outside the courthouse in Dunkirk in protest against the French authorities’ refusal to release the bodies. Wadhwa’s relatives travelled from the UK to France to participate. Many who lose their lives trying to cross the Channel are never publicly identified and it is rare to see family members stage a protest of this kind. Neither the French interior ministry nor the part of the French police in charge of the bodies responded to questions from the Guardian about why there had been a delay in releasing the two men’s bodies. Ivnit Singh Wadwa, Wadhwa’s cousin, travelled from his home in west London for the protest. “We shouldn’t have to fight to say goodbye,” said Wadwa. “We are very upset with the French judicial system. Our family is waiting for Jasmeet’s body so we can lay him to rest.” After witnessing the loss of her son on the dinghy, Harbans Kaur Wadhwa made an application to the Home Office to come to the UK legally under the “one in, one out” scheme. This scheme forcibly returns one person to France who has arrived in the UK on a small boat in exchange for accepting another who has applied legally to come to the UK from northern France. She was hoping to join her family in the UK who have offered to accommodate and support her. But the Home Office rejected the application for not meeting the requirements, saying that the identity document submitted was not satisfactory. Afghans generally have an identity document known as a Tazkira. A Home Office spokesperson said: “We are deeply saddened to hear about a death in French waters. “Every death in the Channel is a tragedy and a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting vulnerable people for profit. We will continue working relentlessly with the French and our partners overseas to prevent these perilous journeys.” In an appeal for the release of Jasmeet’s body, the family wrote on social media: “A son. A brother. A life not forgotten. Help us bring Jasmeet back to his family. This is not about politics. It’s about a grieving mother being able to see her son one final time, it’s about a family being able to mourn.”

title: Georgia police officer put on leave after family’s pet donkey killed during search
summary: Donkey named HeeHaw was shot and killed as authorities reportedly looked on property in search of a missing person
text: A police officer in the US state of Georgia was placed on leave after a family’s pet baby donkey was shot and killed during an early-morning search on their property. The animal’s owner, Hannah Israel, said officers were at her pasture without notification or permission at about 12.45am on Sunday, reportedly looking for a missing person when they encountered the small male donkey named HeeHaw. According to a Facebook post by Israel, HeeHaw emerged braying at the presence of strangers at Elsberry farm in Rockmart – and was shot dead by an officer who claimed he felt under threat. Jamie Newsome, the Cedartown, Georgia, police department chief, told local media that an officer had been placed on leave and that an inquiry was under way. But a social media backlash by Monday morning was growing over the absence of any official statement or confirmation from the city or police department. Meanwhile, an online fundraising appeal launched by Israel to support legal action over HeeHaw’s killing quickly surpassed $35,000. “They claimed he ran up to them braying and they thought they were in danger and shot and killed him after trying to taze him,” Israel wrote in her Facebook post, which featured a photograph of her kneeling by the fallen donkey. “HeeHaw was raised in the house and did petting zoos [and] never knew a stranger. And was shot and killed in his own pasture for doing what donkeys do. Alerting to a stranger. There is no way this is legal. “We are heartbroken. He was my son.” The only official statement as of Monday was from the Polk county, Georgia, sheriff’s office, which said its officers were not involved. But the agency said that law enforcement personnel from the separate police departments of Polk county and Cedartown were. “We extend our sincere condolences to the family and everyone affected by this unfortunate incident,” the sheriff’s office said in a statement. “We understand the concern and sadness surrounding what occurred.” The Polk county police department, Cedartown’s municipal government and its police department did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In her post, Israel said HeeHaw was bottle-raised and maintained he was killed in his own pasture by “trespassing” cops. Coosa Valley News reported in an online article that Newsome said members of his department’s command staff had opened an investigation into the shooting – and that the officer involved, who was not identified, had been placed on administrative leave while the investigation into the case progressed.

title: Iran’s economy in crisis as US launches new sanctions campaign
summary: Trump’s Operation Economic Outcast is expected to push many Iranians into deeper poverty as food inflation soars
text: For many Iranians, the new US sanctions campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast, seems superfluous given the grim economic situation in their country. Iranians are facing runaway food inflation, closed petrol stations and a seemingly never-ending depreciation of the nation’s currency caused by a lack of foreign exchange reserves. Vegetable oil in Iran in August cost 383% more than a year ago. The price of eggs rose by 294%, chicken by 177% and red meat by 148%. The cratering economy leaves the country’s political class on edge as they try to prevent economic conditions leading to social chaos. In truth, long before Donald Trump’s latest sanctions push, Iran’s economy had become a parallel battlefield in which the country’s economic commanders were struggling to maintain control. On 23 August, the US dollar reached roughly 2m rials on Iran’s open market, a new record. Three days later, Iran’s statistical centre announced that year-on-year inflation in August reached 84.4%; the rolling annual average rate was about 65%. As purchasing power in Iran collapses, households are buying fewer goods. Diets are changing, clothes are being patched up and repaired rather than replaced, and medicine is in short supply, though it can be found on the hidden market. According to the Mehr news agency, demand for red meat fell by 50% in April 2026 compared with the same period last year. There has also been a leap in the consumption of potatoes, leading to shortages. Basic goods like eggs are now unaffordable to middle- and working-class families, Golshan Fathi, an Iranian feminist, recently said. “They don’t understand that people can no longer afford even a normal life.” Mohsen Zavaar, a biomedical engineer, said: “For part of the population, the issue is no longer buying a house or a car; the issue is cutting out meat, reducing food quality, postponing medical treatment, and scraping by until the end of the month.” Frustrated by the inability of officials to tackle the problems, he added: “The people don’t want miracles – they want decisions.” The crisis has spread beyond food and clothes. Long lines of cars stretched through parts of Tehran and the north-eastern Iranian city of Mashhad on Tuesday and Wednesday as motorists queued for fuel, with some lines blocking entire streets. Many petrol stations, including some of the largest, were closed. Officials blamed isolated panic buying caused by rumours of a government-planned price increase, or Israeli bombs that destroyed two of Tehran’s three main oil depots. Inside the government, anxious discussions have been under way for weeks about increasing the price of oil to reduce costly subsidies, but the political class know from past experience that there could be significant pushback. A sudden overnight petrol price rise of 50% in November 2019 sparked week-long violent protests. Public anger has been exacerbated by an admission that vested interests in the government made it hard to tackle fuel smuggling. Saqab Esfahani, deputy to Iran’s president, said: “Both political factions in the country are involved in fuel smuggling, and if I were to shut down their operations, they would break my windows.” Masoud Pezeshkian, Iran’s president, has been urged to investigate the remarks. However, transparency over the economic conditions in Iran is likely to decrease. Fatemeh Mohajerani, a spokesperson for the Iranian government, said recently that future poverty statistics would only be published with the permission of the country’s supreme national security council, making the decline in living standards akin to a classified state secret. Iran’s leaders now cast the home front as part of the war against America. Hojatoleslam Taeb, the new head of the Basij paramilitary force and a close ally of Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, recently delivered a speech that conjured up an image of resistance against market forces distorted by US sanctions. As part of this war, he said it was necessary to reduce petrol consumption by as much as 10% to reduce the need for expensive imports. Avoiding unnecessary travel would be an act of patriotism, he implied. But these patriotic appeals increasingly have an air of desperation as the economic crisis becomes worse. Mohsen Rezaei, the new, more hardline secretary of the supreme national security council, said: “I advise young people to start producing the products they and society need in their homes, just as they gather in public spaces.” Mohammad Taheri, editor of the economics magazine Tejarat Farda, said the advice reminded him of Mao’s “backyard steel furnaces” during the Great Leap Forward. Mao encouraged people to produce their own steel, with disastrous effect. Amirhossein Hashemi-Javid, an energy expert, said Iran’s true economic crisis was its inability to export oil due to the US blockade. “The channels for selling Iranian oil are drying up. “Oil that cannot reach customers from the well provides no revenue for the Iranian economy; it is simply barrels that incur increasing production, storage and risk costs every day,” he said. At some point, the Iranian government will have to decide if it might achieve more through diplomacy than through continued confrontation. Only six months on from starting a war, after Trump promised protesters in January that help was on its way, the only commodity the US is now offering Iranians is deeper poverty.

title: Smelling test: children need education in sniffing aromas, scientist says
summary: Exclusive: Dr Will Tullett says better understanding of scents can improve wellbeing and perception of the world
text: Children need a better education in sniffing aromas, a leading historian of smells has said, noting it may improve their wellbeing and help them understand the world around them. Dr Will Tullett, of the University of York, said pollution had been found to impair people’s olfactory abilities, while many objects and substances today – from margarines to car interiors and even our own homes – were stripped of their original smells and “reodourised” with synthetic scents. “There is an open question about what the proliferation of those kinds of synthetic scents in our daily lives does to our ability to discriminate between different smells,” he said. As a result, Tullett said, there was a need for olfactory education. “I would love a world where at primary and secondary school people are taught to engage their noses,” he said, adding that training could also be done at home. He said one approach would be to encourage people to smell more items. “The more we smell, the more we enlarge the vocabulary through which we can describe other things,” he said, noting that sommeliers took a similar approach. “They’ll go to marketplaces and they’ll walk around and they’ll smell everything. And then what they’re doing is expanding their range of reference points. And then I think it’s being able to compare and contrast and think about what are the similarities between different smells.” Tullett said thinking about smells could also help us to understand ourselves, such as why we find some odours comforting, and could provide useful information about the world. “A classic example here is food safety and food sustainability – smelling as to whether something is fresh or not and whether you need to bin it, rather than relying solely on a use by date, for example,” he said. And there could be other benefits. “Lots of studies have shown that smells and our ability to enjoy them are crucially linked to our sense of wellbeing and that those who suffer from forms of smell loss, often the result of that is depression and anxiety and various other kinds of symptoms.” But while people may benefit from a greater olfactory education, Tullett pushed back against the idea that people’s sense of smell was underappreciated, noting that when asked, people often recounted vivid memories associated with particular aromas. “You get this sense from people that actually they want to tell you about the role that smell played in their lives, and that they do know that smell is important. It’s just that they’re not necessarily given the opportunity, or equipped with the language, or even given a sense of confidence that they can talk about it,” he said. Tullett, whose book Sniff: A History of Smells is to be published on 8 September, said a common misconception was that the past was a smellier place. “The past didn’t stink any more or less than the present. It just smelled different,” he said. “And I think that’s important. Because it gets the heart of one of the key problems with how we all approach smell, which is smell is so often used to mark difference.” Tullett said smells were still used to discriminate, from landlords refusing to let properties to people of particular ethnicities because of a belief about food aromas, to a proposed bill in the Commons that could have criminalised rough sleepers for “excessive” smells. Tullett said it was important to question why we considered a smell pleasant or not, how those associations may have arisen, and what others may make of it. “We should be both more self-aware of our attitudes to odours, but also more empathetic towards other people’s olfactory preferences,” he said. “Rather [than] instinctively using smell to build divides, a thoughtful sniff can help us get to know ourselves and others better.” He said smells were often particular to certain times, contexts and places, and he suggested 21st-century Britain would be associated with the aromas of hand sanitiser, wildfires and water pollution. “A wood fire is a nostalgic smell for many people,” he said. “But the smell of burning vegetation and wood will increasingly become not a nostalgic smell, I think, but a fearful smell.”

title: Anthropic sued over alleged theft of ‘tens of thousands’ of songs
summary: AI company faces multibillion dollar lawsuit over misuse of copyrighted songs to train Claude models
text: All AI wants for Christmas is a vast back catalogue of songs without paying for it, according to a multibillion-dollar lawsuit against the startup behind the Claude chatbot. Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell, music publishers who manage the copyright of songs on behalf of songwriters and composers, are seeking damages for alleged misuse of “tens of thousands” of copyrighted works by Anthropic. The compositions include Mariah Carey’s All I Want for Christmas is You, Ain’t No Mountain High Enough, originally performed by Marvin Gaye and Tammi Terrell, and Survivor’s Eye of the Tiger. The plaintiffs claim they are victims of “one of the largest and most blatant ongoing thefts of intellectual property in history”. The lawsuit, filed in a California court, targets Anthropic and its chief executive, Dario Amodei, as well as co-founder Benjamin Mann. It alleges the defendants breached copyright law by “torrenting, scraping and downloading” lyrics from copyrighted works to train its family of Claude AI models – as well as reproducing those lyrics in responses to users’ prompts. It claims that Mann and Anthropic downloaded at least 7m copies of books from pirate websites, including the lyrics and sheet music to songs such as Bon Jovi’s Livin’ on a Prayer and Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah. The figures are from a recent copyright case against Anthropic brought by US authors which the company settled for $1.5bn. The lawsuit, filed on 28 August, was first reported by trade publication Music Business Worldwide. Other songs allegedly having their copyright infringed included Mark Ronson’s Uptown Funk and Katy Perry’s California Gurls. It also claims that Anthropic acquired copies of songs in other ways including scraping lyrics from legal sites like Musixmatch and LyricFind, and datasets on archive sites such as Common Crawl. In another section of the claim, the publishers allege that Anthropic stripped identifying information from songs while processing the texts, which denied copyright owners “valuable attribution” to their work. “Defendants specifically elected to harvest unauthorized copies of Music Publishers’ works so that they would not have to pay Music Publishers a licensing fee to use their works in AI training and development,” said the plaintiffs. The music publishers are seeking damages that could run into billions of dollars, based on a claim of up to $150,000 per infringed piece of work and $25,000 for each removal or alteration of identifying data. The suit implies at least 20,000 works are involved in the suit, referring to the unlawful copying of “tens of thousands of Music Publishers’ copyrighted musical compositions”. Ed Newton-Rex, a UK-based composer and campaigner for protecting artists’ copyright, said he was “not surprised” that rights holders were defending themselves against a company with a “history of downloading and training their AI models on huge libraries”. Alongside the authors’ lawsuit, Anthropic has also faced claims from Universal Music Group and Concord Music Group. In a separate case this month, AI music generator Suno lost a copyright infringement case against German licensing agency GEMA, which alleged illegal use of songs including Boney M’s Daddy Cool to train its technology. A spokesperson for Anthropic, which is preparing for a stockmarket listing that could value the company at $2tn, said: “We disagree with the publishers’ claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court.”

title: Can Reform UK recover from its summer horribilis?
summary: Clacton, funding, internal divisions – party prepares for annual conference next week after a season of missteps
text: Senior Reform UK figures like to boast that the summer time – and parliament’s longest recess – is when the party makes hay. Supposedly, it is when Nigel Farage and co can muscle in on the news cycle with provocative statements and new policies, painting “establishment” opponents as workshy layabouts. Last year’s summer break came with an added opportunity, which the rightwing populist party eagerly grasped, in the form of protests against hotels housing asylum seekers. As Labour and the Tories tempered their language, Farage eagerly weighed in, warning of the prospect of “civil disobedience on a vast scale”. Yet as August comes to an end, and with Reform preparing for its annual conference in Birmingham later this week, the party might look back on summer 2026 as a damp squib, or worse. While almost weekly Reform press conferences have taken place and new policies have been rolled out – Robert Jenrick has been particularly busy with promises to slash the benefits bill and scrap supposed “red tape” for businesses – there has been no repeat of last summer’s unrest in England, aside from disturbances in the Norfolk market town of Thetford. There have also been missteps of Reform’s own making, not least the hint of internal divisions related to the noisy pronouncements of its home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf. Farage was eventually forced to reprimand him for calling Ben Wallace, a former Conservative defence secretary and veteran, a “traitor”. Divisions also surfaced around the suspension of Tim Montgomerie, a high-profile activist who defected from the Conservatives. However, perhaps the biggest error was Farage’s decision to spark a byelection in Clacton in an attempt to neutralise the pressure he was under over questions about an undeclared £5m payment by the Reform megadonor Christopher Harborne. Farage himself scaled back press events amid scrutiny after the payment was first revealed by the Guardian. Though he cruised to victory over his closest challenger – Count Binface – the need to get the vote out meant Farage was pinned down in a corner of Essex for six weeks, rather than being free to roam the UK at will and entice media coverage in a way his lieutenants fail to. The prospect of a “people versus the establishment” battle which Farage so clearly craved did not materialise when other main parties ignored the contest, while a parliamentary standards investigation into the payment has once again started after it was only paused during the byelection. Opponents have taken note. “You could say that Reform are quite good at tactics but bad at strategy, and with Clacton he made a strategic mistake because it bound him to one part of the country for six weeks,” said Giles Dilnot, the editor of ConservativeHome and a former political adviser who covered Farage for years for the BBC. “He made that decision in anger and you never make good strategic decisions when you are angry. Then he had to take a break because of the understandable toll the byelection and all that went before it this year would have taken.” Dilnot suggested two other issues that will have caused worries in Reform ranks. First, despite Reform consistently attacking the Tories, signs of a knockout blow do not seem to have materialised. Second, the centralised way in which Farage has always run his political projects may now be taking a toll. “Over the 15 years it’s always the case he is both the biggest asset and biggest weakness of any party he has led. Everything is centralised, he falls out with people and voters can also be very polarised,” said Dilnot. Recent polls have indicated that the surge in support for Reform has stalled, with the party failing to break out beyond core supporters and signs that Farage himself might even be a drag on its further growth. A poll released last week by More in Common put the party at 23% – four percentage points behind Labour and Reform’s worst performance in 18 months. Labour also now leads Reform for the first time since the general election in Ipsos polling – 28% to 25%. Nearly two-thirds of the public (65%) do not believe Farage is ready to be prime minister, according to Ipsos, while nearly three-quarters backed continuing the standards investigation even before the Clacton result. Aside from struggling to shake off questions about the £5m, there was yet another reminder last week of another drag – namely Reform having to look over its shoulder at the siren call to its voters from Rupert Lowe’s hard-right Restore Britain party. The latter was a factor in a much-watched byelection last Thursday on Dover district council, where Reform had swept the board during Kent local elections last year, but where Farage’s party was narrowly pipped by the Greens after Restore polled 10%. Nonsense, say Reform sources, pointing to new policies and attention-grabbing moves by councils such as Kent, which announced plans to “protect” communities from immigrants. “We’re coming out of this summer with a plethora of policies, our councils are getting on with it and at conference there will be more headlines, a proper fringe discussing ideas and a business engagement programme which is a major step up from last year,” said one. Reform says it will use the conference at the Birmingham NEC to set out the first 100 days of what a government led by it would do. One of the biggest questions will be whether any dissent emerges.

title: The London office, the empty boxes and the £1bn tax loophole
summary: Exclusive: How a court case over an unoccupied office block could end a widely used tax avoidance scheme
text: From the outside, the seven-storey building at 2 America Square looks like any other office block in the heart of London’s financial district. Located about half a mile from Tower Bridge, one might expect it to be a hive of commercial activity, teeming with employees holding important meetings. However, much of the property is home not to staff vying for their next bonus, but to stacks of nondescript black boxes arranged in neat lines. The building, leased by a Virgin Islands-based company called 48th Street Holdings Ltd, has found itself at the centre of a court case that has finally signalled the end of a tax avoidance scheme believed to have cost local authorities more than £1bn. For almost two decades, companies in England have been exploiting a legal loophole to avoid paying business rates on unoccupied commercial buildings. The controversial practice dates back to 2008, when the last Labour government changed business rates rules. This meant occupiers of vacant buildings no longer qualified for a 50% discount on the levy. However, they were entitled to claim a three-month rate holiday at the end of each tenancy – and the “box shifting” scheme was born. With commercial property owners facing higher bills, a lucrative “rate mitigation” industry emerged. Historically, this typically involved boxes being moved into the empty space at the end of the three months and back out after just six weeks. The building then became unoccupied again and the clock was reset, allowing the owner to claim another three-month rate-free period. This cycle continued, designed to cut the rates owed by up to 67%, until a new long-term tenant could be found. It has been costing one London council an estimated £35m a year since the pandemic, when the number of claims for empty property relief doubled. However, last month a landmark ruling by three court of appeal judges looks to have sounded the death knell for box shifting. They ruled that the scheme “cannot amount to beneficial occupation”. The case was brought by the City of London Corporation against 48th Street Holding Ltd and a second company, Principled Offsite Logistics Ltd (POLL), which provides “rate mitigation” services. 48th Street paid £27.6m for a lease on the office block in 2019 before it brought in POLL to save £111,475.30 in rates across a series of three-month periods in 2022 and 2023. POLL describes itself as “the largest and most reliable” provider of “empty business rates mitigation” in the UK and is jointly owned by a Labour councillor from North Hertfordshire. It claimed by 2021 to have already saved its clients “£500m” in rates and that “every council in the UK now totally recognises Principled as being robust in every way”. That bold claim followed a significant high court win in 2018, when POLL defeated a challenge from Trafford council. The judge in that case accepted that “the purpose of the occupation is not to store goods; it is, so to speak, to plant the occupier’s flag” and that “the motive … is rates avoidance for the landlord”, but added “the morality of that is neither here nor there”. When the case against POLL and 48th Street came before the high court last year, Charles Bagot KC, sitting as a deputy high court judge, also ruled against the City of London. “I agree with POLL that if legislation produces clear tramlines and someone organises themselves to fall within them, then it is not for the court to get involved in moral judgments,” he said. “If the government does not like the position, it can amend it.” He concluded that “the RMS [rate mitigation scheme] is effective”. However, last month the court of appeal overturned that decision, with Lady Justice Falk ruling: “In my judgment, ‘occupation’ for, in effect, the sake of it, and which has no use, value or benefit other than rate saving, does not amount to occupation for the purpose of the statutory scheme.” A City of London Corporation spokesperson said: “We welcome the court of appeal’s decision, which represents a significant victory for local authorities across England. “This landmark ruling closes one of the most widely used tax avoidance schemes in the country and helps safeguard revenues that support essential public services. “We are proud that the City of London Corporation has led the way nationally in pursuing this case. “For more than a decade, councils across the country have seen hundreds of millions of pounds of public revenue lost through artificial business rates avoidance schemes and we believe the decision restores fairness, protects money that funds vital local services, and provides greater certainty for councils, ratepayers and property owners alike.” A government spokesperson said: “We recognise concerns about the misuse of Empty Property Relief, which exists to support genuine property owners between tenants. “Business rates avoidance is unacceptable and we are taking the necessary action to address this, and make sure that businesses are paying the tax they owe.” It is unclear what action the government is planning, but there are calls for a general anti-avoidance rule to control the rate mitigation industry. POLL is not the only business offering box shifting. The same scheme was even used by Public Health England at its future headquarters in Harlow in 2018. The resulting £2.5m dispute with Harlow district council ended up in the high court, where PHE won. It remains to be seen how councils and their rate mitigation opponents will respond. One rating expert said that the total cost to councils of box shifting could have topped £1.5bn, and some of that money should now be reclaimed as a deterrent. Under the terms of POLL’s contracts with clients, its success fees are refundable in the event the scheme fails. The latest accounts show it has just over £500,000 in net assets. POLL did not respond to a request for comment and its website went down this week, replaced with a message which read: “This account has been suspended”.
