The company’s founder, Steven Dawson, died in 2024 and the POLL was acquired in a management buyout by two of its own executives. One of them is a Labour councillor, Sarah Lucas, who, according to her LinkedIn profile, has been POLL’s director of finance since 2018. Lucas was elected to North Hertfordshire council in 2024, two months after she took 50% ownership of POLL, and she serves as vice-chair of the council’s finance, audit and risk committee. The Guardian understands that POLL’s application for permission to appeal to the supreme court was refused by the court of appeal this week but an option remains for it to apply to the supreme court directly. The rules on empty property relief changed in 2024 and buildings now need to be occupied for 13 weeks instead of six in order for the three-month holiday to apply. According to one recent judgment, this makes box shifting schemes “less attractive but still effective”. There are still a range of variants of rates mitigation on offer. One involves placing Bluetooth boxes in the offices to broadcast adverts. Another uses charitable exhibitions to claim not only empty property relief but also the extra rates relief available for charities. Some schemes install snail or mushroom farms to claim agricultural reliefs, while others involve opening faith rooms to cut rates.

title: Rise of Chicken Shop Date highlights how YouTube turned the tables on TV
summary: Amelia Dimoldenberg says publicists ignored her interview show for years but she can now be picky over A-list guests
text: Just a decade ago, Amelia Dimoldenberg found it impossible to drum up any mainstream celebrities to come on her mock date YouTube show, in which she chats awkwardly with guests over chicken and chips. Even persuading a local actor connected with her London youth club to come on took years of prodding. Managers of A-listers with movies or albums to push instead battled to claim a spot on the hallowed cushions of the primetime TV chatshow sofa. Yet after those early years of rejection, Dimoldenberg has said that she has reached a watershed moment. Such is the influence of her Chicken Shop Date show, she says it now ranks alongside Graham Norton’s chatshow or BBC Radio 1 for celebrities seeking media cut-through. “When I started the show in 2014, no publicist and no manager would let their talent come on a YouTube show – that was just insane,” she told the Edinburgh TV festival. “I would be banging down the doors, it was just so challenging. Now it’s so fascinating because it’s the opposite. “If your publicist is coming to you and you’ve got a movie out, or you’ve got an album rollout campaign, now I do think one of the first things up there on the list of things to do would be to come on Chicken Shop Date. “That has always been the ambition – my ambition – to make it as important as going on Graham Norton or going on Greg James, Radio 1, for example. So I’ve achieved that goal.” Dimoldenberg’s rise is a prime example of how digital platforms have radically reshaped the media world, with viewers across all ages switching to YouTube, especially under-35s. Dimoldenberg has shared the ketchup with Ed Sheeran, Charli xcx and Jennifer Lawrence, although Lawrence got Dimoldenberg’s name wrong. Even Paul McCartney turned up for a date in a vegan chicken shop this year, declining Dimoldenberg’s suggestion that he adopt a pet otter. Dimoldenberg initially focused on interviewing figures from the UK rap and grime scene when she launched Chicken Shop Date in 2014. She secured her first big name, the actor Daniel Kaluuya, because he was a fan of the show. Her interviews have repeatedly gone viral since then, thanks to Louis Theroux rapping or the chemistry between Dimoldenberg and the actor Andrew Garfield. “I didn’t realise fully how much the audience would catch on to how obsessed he is with me,” she said. She is increasingly picky over guests and rejects anyone who wants to be on the show only as part of a “press run” publicising their latest project. It marks a shift in the media hierarchy and underlines YouTube’s muscle. The platform’s rise has become so all-consuming in the TV world that Pedro Pina, YouTube’s head for Europe, the Middle East and Africa, was invited to give the keynote MacTaggart lecture at the Edinburgh TV festival last week, the industry’s most important get-together of the year. Pina used the speech to insist YouTube was “not the villain” about to destroy the TV industry, though he made clear the age of monopoly for TV networks was over. Sure enough, the temptation of having total creative control – as well as scooping up the ads, sponsors and brand deals that can follow – is now enticing more established media names to try their luck on YouTube. The presenter Holly Willoughby launched her YouTube channel over the summer, amassing 22,000 subscribers so far. Amol Rajan will finish as a presenter of BBC Radio 4’s Today programme this week and launch a YouTube show, The Amol Rajan Connection. The road from TV personality to YouTuber is already well established in the US. Yet in a media world that continues to converge, Dimoldenberg is moving in the other direction, seeking success in conventional movies and television. She is writing a teen drama for the BBC, similar to the show Skins, which ran for seven series on E4. She is also writing a Hollywood romcom, in which she will star as a journalist who finds romance with a celebrity after interviewing them. Other than the chicken, it is a plot that sounds close to home. “It’s a character that I’ve been playing half my life, so I feel like I know it very well,” she said. “It’s definitely just an exaggeration of who I am.”

title: ‘Who knows what they’re taking?’: people risk the gray market for the newest weight-loss drug
summary: Retatrutide, not yet approved by the FDA, is the latest wonder drug to shed pounds despite warnings from doctors
text: About two years ago, Henry, who is 6ft 3in, weighed 210lb, which meant he was only slightly overweight, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention body mass index. Still, the thirtysomething who lives in the Pacific north-west had hypertension, sleep apnea and body image issues, so he started taking the weight-loss drug Ozempic. While he dropped pounds, he experienced constipation, a common side-effect, so he wanted to try retatrutide, another peptide which not only targets GLP-1 but two other hormone receptors as well. He had read about it in the news and on Reddit forums. The problem is, the US Food and Drug Administration has not approved the drug, so Henry bought it online from sellers in China. Henry, who did not want his last name used, is among a growing number of people dissatisfied with the revolutionary weight-loss drugs that can be obtained legally with a prescription and have instead turned to the gray market to purchase retatrutide, which is manufactured by the pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly and is being studied in clinical trials. Physicians see the drug as a promising potential solution for people struggling with obesity, but strongly warn patients that they are seriously risking their health by using it without oversight from doctors and government regulators. Yet these warnings often go unheeded. “All of these medications should be monitored and prescribed in a medical situation where the doctor or the clinic is partnering with the patient on a complete plan” including “monitoring their lab [work], their vital signs, their response”, said Dr David Shafer, a plastic surgeon in New York who takes the drug. “It’s really the self-prescribing and unknown usage that is leading to a lot of the problems.” Retatrutide could work well in helping people lose weight – and potentially have other health benefits – because whereas Ozempic targets one receptor, and tirzepatide, sold as Mounjaro and Zepbound, targets GLP-1 and the receptor GIP, the newer drug is a “triple agonist”, meaning it targets those two receptors and glucagon, which speeds up the body’s metabolism and helps it break down fat cells for energy. In an 80-week clinical trial, patients with severe obesity and heart disease taking the highest weekly doses of ⁠retatrutide achieved an average weight loss of 22%, or 55lb, according to Eli Lilly. “The more natural gut hormones that you upregulate, the more weight loss we see,” said Dr Caroline Messer, an endocrinologist in New York. If a patient were to ask Messer whether she recommends the drug, she would say: “Wholeheartedly – but not through the gray market. Just wait till it hits the market.” Patients, in fact, ask Messer about retatrutide about five times daily, she said. Most of them “have maxed out on Zepbound and still are not at their target weight, but it’s also people who enjoy being at the cutting edge of things”, she said. A Reddit group dedicated to the drug gets more than 179,000 visits each week. The demand for the drug is “concerning because of the way it’s been popularized through podcasts and politicians, not through doctor-patient relationships”, said Dan Burke, a former division chief of the US Food and Drug Administration office of criminal investigations. In August, Eli Lilly announced it would provide a limited number of patients access to the drug before the FDA approves it, Reuters reported. But Messer said that while the process is supposed to help patients “who are desperate” to try the drug, it is “just so unbelievably difficult” to qualify for special access that it could take years to obtain it, by which time the FDA will probably have already approved it. “It pits the patient against the doctor because now the patient thinks that we are not doing everything we can to get them the medication, where it’s really actually just this super-onerous process,” Messer said. As such, patients are finding other ways to obtain the drug. The Reddit group features a “beginner’s guide” to getting it through the gray market and encourages people to “find communities (not on Reddit)”, “get tapped in” and “vet vet vet like your money depends on it”. The guide also provides instructions on dosing and warns people not to use the product if it comes in a prefilled pen. Eli Lilly recently filed lawsuits against six companies that allegedly sold the drug, including Lone Star Peptide, which is based in Texas and markets the drug for “research use only”, and Aesthetic Envy Cosmetic Centers, a med-spa in Sacramento, California. A person who answered the phone at Lone Star Peptide declined to comment. Aesthetic Envy did not respond to a request. “Illegal drugs made outside of a regulated, inspected supply chain are more likely to contain bacteria and other harmful contaminants and impurities. Consumers have no way to know whether these products are safe or effective,” a lawsuit states. Messer argues that obtaining the drug through the gray market is potentially dangerous because patients do not know how much of the drug the product contains or its purity. In June, the Victoria state government in Australia reported six cases of acute liver toxicity among patients who consumed a product labeled as retatrutide. “This is something that you are injecting, and you don’t know where it’s being made,” Messer said. Despite warnings from physicians and government agencies, patients are still buying the drug on the gray market – and at least sometimes getting their desired results. “The ones who have plateaued on tirzepatide [Zepbound] are starting to lose weight again, so losing an additional 20 to 30lb,” Messer said. Henry has not told his doctor he is taking retatrutide because he did not want documentation of it, he said. But he has lost 30lb since starting on it and is “doing good”, even though his skin has become extra sensitive, a common side-effect of the drug. “For the first time in my entire life, I feel like I am in control of my body,” said Henry, who also now drinks less alcohol. Shafer, the plastic surgeon, said that even if people are not obtaining retatrutide from a prescription, they should disclose their use of it to their provider. “The doctors are not the police, and they are not going to turn you in for buying something online,” Shafer said. “The doctor and the patient can partner together to formulate the best plan.” Shafer said he started taking a GLP-1 agonist because he wanted to lose about 20lb for health and aesthetic reasons. He then started taking retatrutide because his weight loss had plateaued, and also because he expected to someday prescribe it to patients and wanted to see how it worked. He obtained it from a compounding pharmacy, which prepares medications on site. He said it not only helped him lose weight but improved his muscle tone and reduced his blood pressure, which had been slightly elevated. Shafer argues that the FDA should expedite its review of it. “I don’t think it’s something that should take 10 years for them to do studies on,” Shafer said. “Then you’re going to have all these other people that are doing it anyway off the black market, and who knows what it is they are taking.”

title: Cross-party talks needed to tackle climate crisis, say Lib Dems
summary: Andy Burnham urged to seek consensus over response to extreme heat and forthcoming ‘super El Niño’
text: Andy Burnham should call a cross-party meeting to discuss the UK’s response to worsening extreme weather, including the forthcoming ‘super El Niño’, the Liberal Democrats have said. The prime minister chaired a Cobra emergency meeting on the drought earlier this month but there has been little from the government on the wider threats posed by five successive heatwaves since May and expected global issues with food shortages and inflation. Pippa Heylings, the Lib Dem spokesperson for energy security and net zero, said: “Andy Burnham has shown he is able to commit to talking about things people care about, which is good. But there’s been a baffling silence from him on extreme heat. What we have heard so far has been underwhelming. Banning disposable barbecues is good, but we need to see more.” Heylings and Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, wrote to Burnham a fortnight ago, proposing a meeting of the UK’s party leaders “to discuss the long-term measures needed to protect our country from climate impacts and build resilience to the extreme weather we are already experiencing”. They say they have not had a response. Heylings contrasted Burnham’s reluctance to address the climate crisis with his prioritising of social care, on which he has called for cross-party support: “We want the same approach [to the climate].” She said even the leaders of Reform and the Conservatives, both of whom have vowed to scrap net zero and downplayed the climate crisis, should be able to join in an effort to protect the UK. “I think there is not a single MP who would not want to show their constituents they were trying to prepare us [for the impacts of extreme weather],” she said. The forthcoming El Niño could bring more serious problems, Heylings said. “The scale of this Super El Niño is unprecedented and will have impacts here in the UK exacerbating our extreme weather particularly with more intense flooding and storms over the autumn and winter. We’re looking at a double whammy.” Any cross-party approach should not be limited to discussing preparedness for extreme weather, she said. “The key question is how do we stop it worsening?” Clive Lewis, the Labour MP for Norwich South, backed the Lib Dem call for a cross-party meeting. “It’s the kind of politics we need,” he said. “We may disagree on how we do it and how far we go, but political cooperation like this is the start of consensus building, something any radical transition has to build across both political parties and society, especially if they’re to take on those vested interests that want the status quo to continue.” But Jon Pearce, the Labour MP for High Peak in Derbyshire, warned it was unlikely a meeting would happen. “The idea the Conservatives and Reform UK would be willing to face up to the risks we face is for the birds,” he said. “The Conservatives and Reform UK have ripped up the political consensus on tackling climate change as they compete to see who can most downplay the need for action. “They are refusing to see what is right in front of their eyes: wildfires, drought, pressure on water supplies and farmers facing growing challenges on food production. There should be political consensus on a matter of such national importance but sadly there is not.” In the past few years, Reform and the Conservatives have broken sharply with the consensus on the need for climate action, despite polls consistently showing a large majority of voters support the idea. A spokesperson for the Conservatives said: “We wouldn’t speculate on hypothetical talks to which we have not been invited.” The Reform party did not respond to a request for comment. Hannah Spencer, a Green party MP, said: “The climate crisis should be a priority across every sector of the economy and every government department. Greens have led this agenda for decades and welcome the consistently strong support shown by voters for all parties for bold climate action.” A spokesperson for the government said: “The UK continues to be a world leader in tackling the climate crisis, accelerating the transition to clean power, and acting to protect people and places from the impacts of climate change that are already being felt across the country. “We are working to adapt to the changing climate through our work with the National Drought Group, building nine new reservoirs across the country and investing at least £10.5bn by March 2036 to construct new flood and coastal erosion schemes, as extreme weather becomes more frequent.”

title: ‘Revenge of the Rust belt’: Starbucks film-maker on Baristas vs Billionaires
summary: Director Mark Mori followed coffee chain workers’ struggle to unionize: ‘These young kids are so inspirational’
text: As the food service industry was pushed on to the frontlines of the Covid-19 pandemic in 2021, workers at Starbucks stores in the Buffalo region of New York went public to announce their union-organizing campaign. Their efforts, and Starbucks’ responses, have culminated in one of the most expansive union-organizing campaigns – and one of the most aggressive union-busting campaigns – in modern US history. In the new documentary film Baristas vs Billionaires, Starbucks workers in Buffalo recount their experiences with the billionaire Howard Schultz descending on the city to attempt to quell the unionization efforts. Narrated by the actor Susan Sarandon, with Alec Baldwin serving as a contributing producer, the film was directed and written by Mark Mori, who received an Academy Award nomination in 1991 for the documentary Building Bombs and received an Emmy award for a 2001 documentary on the Kent State shootings. “Even though the Starbucks workers’ fight for a living wage was so public, I had no idea of the twists and turns and heartbreak connected to their struggle,” said Sarandon. In an interview with the Guardian, Mori said his former background as a steelworker and a union member with the United Steelworkers – and in political activism – had informed his decision to take on the project. He began reading about the union drive at Starbucks and spoke with a friend who would shoot the film for him. “We just went out and started interviewing baristas,” Mori said. “To me, I looked at it as the beginning of a long upsurge in the labor movement. I looked at this as we were in the 1930s, the 21st-century version of that.” Mori sees the Starbucks union-organizing drive as a counter to the drastic decline of the manufacturing industry in the US midwest in recent decades that has decimated the working class. “I call it the revenge of the Rust belt. Many of these kids are the children or grandchildren of the steelworkers from Bethlehem Steel in Buffalo, the grain silos in Buffalo, all of these factories across the Rust belt that were shut down. Their parents and grandparents lost their pensions, lost their homes, and these kids don’t see any future,” said Mori. “These young kids are so inspirational, and they’re showing one way to deal with what’s going on, and there are many other ways. But the real number one thing about this is these young people taking matters into their own hands and inspiring other people to stand up against these billionaires.” He explained the Starbucks workers who led the union-organizing drive reminded him of Vietnam war activists in the 1960s and 70s. “This is part of what some refer to as a wealth gap,” he added. “These kids can’t make enough money to pay off their student loans, to get married, to buy a house, to have children, They’re so brave and articulate in what they’re doing. I’m of an older generation, I was in the anti-Vietnam war movement. They reminded me very much of that.” The film is currently only available via scheduled screenings, though a distribution deal is in the works. The film comes as tensions between Starbucks and the union continue to escalate. Starbucks Workers United launched a boycott on 25 August against Starbucks over the company’s failure to reach a first contract with the union. More than 700 Starbucks stores have won union elections since 2021. The union is pushing for a $17-an-hour minimum wage, improved staffing and scheduling, and workplace protections, and for Starbucks to resolve the unfair labor practice charges. Administrative law judges and the National Labor Relations Board found Starbucks committed more than 500 labor law violations, and hundreds of unfair labor practice charges at the agency are still unresolved. A spokesperson for Starbucks did not directly comment on the movie or the union’s boycott. “Starbucks has competitive pay, industry-leading benefits, and meaningful opportunities to grow a career,” the spokesperson said in an email. “People love working at Starbucks which is why we have the lowest turnover in the industry and why more than 1 million people every year apply to wear the green apron. As we have always been, we’re committed to engaging in productive bargaining.”

title: In a town in the heart of the US, Israeli settler violence in West Bank hits close to home
summary: War on Gaza and violence in West Bank is playing out in the streets of Toledo, Ohio, where the Arab American community has flourished
text: From his office outside Toledo, Ohio, Thamin Tim Ridi opens his phone to livestream the scene outside the besieged house of his brother, Loui, thousands of miles away in the occupied West Bank. This month, with his property at risk of being destroyed by Israeli settlers, Loui traveled from Ohio to his ancestral home in Qusra, south of Nablus, where his mother and other family members have been living in constant fear of attack. In Qusra, settlers have besieged a number of Palestinian properties and homes, preventing members of the Ridi family from leaving, as their food and water supplies dwindled. The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, took to X on 13 August to describe the settlers’ actions as those of “terrorists”. While the Trump administration has offered broad support to Israel and its illegal settlement building over the years, recent comments from JD Vance, the vice-president, and Donald Trump himself indicate a change of tone. Regardless, for Loui’s extended family in Ohio, it’s created a world of concern. “This building has been taken by settlers; that one up there by the soldiers,” Ridi said, pointing at the outline of buildings further up the hill from his brother’s home that are barely visible on his phone. “I’m extremely worried about them,” he said, his eyes fixed on the security camera footage that’s coming through his phone. One of the first things Loui did upon arriving at his home in Qusra, said Ridi, was plant an American flag on his property. For decades, the war in the Middle East had been a distant headline, something that appeared briefly on the evening news, for residents of Toledo in north-west Ohio. But decades of migration to small cities in the American heartland, combined with the war on Gaza and recent rise in settler violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, are bringing the conflict into the streets and homes of places such as Toledo. Last October, five people were arrested in downtown Toledo for protesting outside the office of Jon Husted, an Ohio Republican senator, who at the time had voted to send aid to Israel. “There’s been demonstrations, petitions and the city council passed a resolution calling for a ceasefire not long after October 7 [2023]. There’s a palpable difference of opinion regarding what Israel is doing and that the US is funding it,” said Mike Ferner, a US navy veteran and one of those arrested in Toledo. Ferner said he began speaking out against America’s support for Israel after the war on Gaza began. “It just comes to a point where you have to ask: is this what I want my country paying for?” Israel’s military assault has largely destroyed the Gaza Strip and killed more than 76,000 people while being condemned by a United Nations body as a genocide. It has prompted Ferner to travel to New York City and organize a 40-day fast in front of the United Nations building last year. “We made our point as best we could that this is something dreadful and the US has got no business participating in it,” he says. Ferner’s position is illustrative of a widening gap between American public opinion and the US government’s support for Israel. While Americans broadly supported Israel in the past, a Pew Research Center poll released in April found that six in 10 participants had an unfavorable view of the country – an increase of 7% in just a year. The reason is partly explained by mounting anger with the actions of pro-Israel groups such as American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac), which have spent billions of dollars over a period of decades helping to elect American politicians who are supportive of Israel. This year, many of its high-profile candidates have been defeated in primary elections, despite an outlay of tens of millions of dollars. Arab American communities have grown particularly in the midwest, where job opportunities and a comparatively affordable cost of living have attracted many immigrants to start out. Aside from English and Spanish, Arabic is the most popular primary language spoken in Ohio. Drawn to the region’s growing manufacturing industry in the early 20th century, Toledo once had its own “Little Syria” district, located in the Old North End neighborhood. “Since the late 1800s, people would come here, work at Cooper Tire and then retire back in Lebanon; my great-grandparents did that, everyone did it,” says Nabil Shaheen, who as a child emigrated from Lebanon with his mother, brother and sister in 1979, and also worked in manufacturing. “There are at least 300 families from Sultan Yacub [Shaheen’s village in Lebanon] here. We even have a Sultan Yacub club, which for every occasion we meet there.” Today, he and his family run a sign manufacturing company west of downtown Toledo. “This used to be a church, then it was empty, and we came in. There’s a variety of [Arab American] businesses that are contributing to the city of Toledo,” he says from his office, which has wall-to-wall paraphernalia of the Cincinnati Bengals NFL team. Today, many Arab Americans in the area have moved to suburban Sylvania west of Toledo, where eastern Orthodox churches, a mosque and an Islamic school have opened in recent decades. In these communities, away from the conflict, dialogue between Arab and Jewish Americans has flourished. “As a Jewish community, we believe deeply in the importance of a shared society: one grounded in respect for diversity, the dignity and rights of every individual,” says Roy Büchler of the Jewish Federation of Greater Toledo. “Loui [Ridi] and his brother have built successful businesses, created jobs, paid taxes, supported numerous philanthropic causes, and worked to build bridges among people of different backgrounds throughout our community.” However, the federation declined to comment on the settler violence. Founded in 1999, the Ridi family’s chain of supermarkets, car washes and gas stations stretch out across north-west Ohio, Michigan and Indiana after several of the brothers came to the US to attend university during the 1990s. The company, which employs hundreds of people, forms the cornerstone of Toledo’s bustling Palestinian American community and donates hundreds of thousands of dollars every year to charities and non-profits. Ridi said he typically visits Qusra three times a year, taking his children, but the war on Gaza and violence in the occupied West Bank have made that harder in recent years. Still, he is not without hope for change. “I was so surprised by [US ambassador] Huckabee’s comments, calling the settlers Israeli terrorists,” he said. “Maybe something is changing.”

title: French high schools rush to put Macron’s phone ban into force
summary: Unions say ban will take time to enact, while president also wants under-15s social media ban as key legacy
text: French high schools are rushing to put in place a ban on mobile phones this week as Emmanuel Macron pushes for children to spend less time in front of screens. Education unions warned that banning mobile phone use in lycées – where children are aged 15 to 18 – would be hard to implement quickly. Macron approved the high school phone ban this month after another measure he had hoped would be a key legacy, his proposed social media ban for under-15s, was knocked back as unconstitutional. The text of the social media ban is being rewritten in the hope it can be pushed it through before Macron leaves office in May. France has already banned children from using mobile phones in primary schools and in middle schools, or collèges, which are attended between the ages of 11 and 15. The government’s focus is now on banning mobile phone use among older teenagers at school from September, as it argues that too much screen time is harming children’s development. In order to enforce the hurriedly signed-off ban, high schools must amend their rules – a lengthy process – and many schools have said they will struggle to implement the measure swiftly. “It’s impossible to put this in place from scratch from 1 September,” said Jérôme Fournier, the national secretary of the SE-Unsa trade union. “Schools will need to change their internal regulations and that requires a full consultation process and a vote, and for high school students to be consulted. So we need time for everyone to meet and work on this.” Fournier said a key challenge was that high school students were often obliged to rely on school smartphone apps to find out even the most basic information for the school day, such as timetables, room changes and homework. “Some even have to use apps on their phones as a badge to enter the canteen to eat lunch or to borrow books from the school library,” he said. Fournier said high schools often hosted students for higher education courses or apprenticeships, some of whom were aged 20 and needed to use their phones for their work. He said the key issue for each high school was to decide where exactly to enforce the ban, whether across the whole school, including corridors, or with exceptions such as in the playground. He said teenagers could be tempted to leave the school grounds in order to use their phones on the street outside, which could have implications for security and road safety. Fournier said students should be consulted on the process rather than being treated as children. “These older teenagers are pre-adults – some in their final school year are going to vote in the upcoming presidential election,” he said. Macron’s office has said he has no plans to give up on his push to bar under-15s from social media platforms such as TikTok and Snapchat, and the government is working redraft the law. France’s constitutional council recently struck down the first version of the law after concerns that its definition of social media was not specific enough. This meant a host of sites not generally considered social media but that allowed commentary or communication could be banned, amounting to a “disproportionate restriction” on freedom of expression. The constitutional council also raised concerns about the privacy implications of putting in place an age-verification system for all users. Valère Ndior, a law professor at the University of Western Brittany, said it was no surprise to legal experts that the law in its current form had been knocked back, and it would be a challenge to rewrite it. “For the moment, as a legal practitioner, I can’t see how it’s possible to strike a balance between European law and French constitutional law,” he said.

title: Desperate rescue attempts continue in Nepal to reach people thought to be trapped | First Thing
summary: Death toll from unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud ​and debris now stands at more than 900. Plus, was it a mistake to take away Pluto’s planet status?
text: Good morning. Rescue teams are working to reach hundreds of people feared trapped in the tunnels and underground areas of half a dozen hydropower projects in Nepal as more than 900 workers were reported missing after the devastating flash floods. The death toll from the ⁠unprecedented deluge of ice, rock, mud and debris that crashed through valleys of Nepal on Wednesday last week has risen to 903 people, with 16 reported dead on the Tibet side of the border. More than 4,000 are missing in Nepal, with another 500 in Tibet. Hundreds of bodies, many unidentified, have been buried in shallow graves. How large is the rescue operation? Nepal’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said almost 21,000 security personnel were involved in the rescue operations, besides civilian workers and volunteers. China’s state-run CCTV reported that Beijing had mobilised more than 2,100 rescue workers. The Red Cross has ‌estimated that more than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, which China and some experts linked to the effects of the climate crisis. Why has the disaster sparked a racism row in Australia? A slew of racist social media comments have been made towards missing Australians. Most of them were on pilgrimages, including to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Mainstream media outlets including News Corp, Channel 7, Channel 10 and Nine have been hit with highly offensive and discriminatory comments on Facebook articles identifying the missing Australians. US strikes Iranian launchers in strait of Hormuz, sparking reprisal attack on airbases in Jordan and UAE Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates after the US attacked Iranian rocket launchers in the strait of Hormuz, the first such hostilities in a month. The last known ‌US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks. The latest exchange of fire was sparked late on Sunday by a US attack on the island of Larak in the strait. Iran’s ⁠Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) said the US attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and would be met with “punishment” from ‌Tehran. What has Donald Trump claimed US forces are doing? Hours after the attacks, the US president, Donald Trump, claimed in a social media post that Iran’s energy hub of Kharg Island was being “blown to smithereens” but gave no further details. The White House and ⁠the US defense department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Attacking Kharg, which handled 90% of ⁠Iran’s oil exports before the war, would severely disrupt the Islamic republic’s energy trade and put huge pressure on its economy. Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates Donald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel at the weekend over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the Ontario premier erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting an AI video depicting him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA. The Wendat Nation grand chief, Pierre Picard, called Trump’s move an attempt to erase Indigenous history. “I want to tell him that it is unacceptable for us, as a nation, to have a president who can eradicate our history, our culture and our identity,” Picard said. Trump ‘border czar’ denies Milo Yiannopoulos was deported quickly to spare him from ICE detention The White House “border czar”, Tom Homan, denied on Sunday that deporting the British far-right commentator Milo Yiannopoulos just a day after being arrested by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) amounted to preferential treatment. Homan said it was his understanding Yiannopoulos, 41, had overstayed what he believed to be a visitor visa, had not appeared at an immigration hearing and was issued a final order of removal on 22 July. He added: “He had his due process, ordered removed by a federal judge, and ICE removed him. It’s that simple.” In other news … Donald Trump ⁠said NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker should face “rebuke or punishment” from the FCC after she described the success record of political candidates whom the president had endorsed as “mixed”. Ghislaine Maxwell has virtually run out of legal routes to overturn her conviction for her involvement in Jeffrey Epstein’s abuse of girls and young women, experts say, bar a presidential pardon. At least eight people have died off the coast of Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus after a ferry capsized. Nearly 20 people are still missing. The Trump administration is shuttering ⁠two of the three US Department of Agriculture research projects studying cyclospora after the foodborne parasite has ⁠sickened tens of thousands of Americans during the summer. Michigan’s Democratic US senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed apologized to the state’s Jewish Democratic Caucus for comments he made after an attack on a synagogue in March, which he tied to Israel’s actions in the Middle East. Stat of the day: Discount gas stations praised by Trump sold $4m of stolen fuel, lawsuit claims Mansfield Oil Company of Gainesville is suing KRSM and its president, Syed Kazmi, for allegedly picking up nearly $4m of fuel and not paying for it. KRSM sold some of the fuel to stations that are part of the Freedom Fuel Network, promoted by the Trump administration when drivers were facing higher oil prices amid the war with Iran.
