title: Morocco not to blame for Ceuta border breach, says Spanish PM
summary: Pedro Sánchez says two countries cooperating and accuses Israel and Russia of spreading fake news about migration
text: Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has said there is no evidence to suggest the Moroccan government was behind last month’s massive border crossing into Ceuta but accused Israel and Russia of spreading disinformation. As many as 141 people are thought to have died trying to enter the Spanish enclave at the end of July. The influx of about 70,000 men, women and children unleashed a political crisis, a humanitarian emergency and reignited tensions within the EU over immigration. Despite speculation that Rabat may have engineered the mass crossing as a means of showing its displeasure at Spain’s rapprochement with Algeria, Sánchez said there was nothing to indicate the involvement of the Moroccan authorities. “There’s no information from any intelligence agency that raises doubts over the involvement of Moroccan authorities,” he told Cadena Ser radio on Monday. “Cooperation with Morocco is frankly positive. I’d like to stress that we need to be aware that this crisis can be resolved only through cooperation – and not through a lack of trust in Morocco, which would only further aggravate the already complex situation we have in Ceuta.” Sánchez said fake news had been pumped out on social media accounts “associated with Russia, Israel and the international far right that always use migration to attack not just Spain but also Europe”. The accusation drew a furious response from Israel. The country’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, called it a “brazen lie”, adding: “Continuing to spread defamatory lies will not distract from Sánchez’s disgraceful failure to manage his country’s affairs.” The ⁠Kremlin rejected allegations ⁠that Russia was connected to ⁠the Ceuta migration crisis, the ⁠RBC daily reported ‌on ‌Monday. Sánchez repeated his assertion that the influx was due to the activities of “criminal gangs” who had used disinformation to falsely claim that a ruling by Spain’s supreme court meant that no one who entered Ceuta by swimming could be deported back to Morocco. Although the overwhelming majority of the migrants crossed back into Morocco weeks ago, at least 5,000 people, including 1,200 minors, are still on the streets of Ceuta. Their continuing presence has led to clashes between some Ceuta residents and police, while some of the migrants have had their belongings burned while sleeping rough on beaches. On Saturday, four Moroccan migrants were arrested for throwing stones at Spanish soldiers. Sánchez said there would soon be “sufficient capacity” to accommodate all those still in the enclave. Spain’s conservative People’s party has accused the government of failing to protect the people of Ceuta. “It did nothing to avoid the invasion on 30 July and it’s doing nothing to stop the public order crisis that’s getting worse every day,” the PP’s leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said last week. Santiago Abascal, the leader of the far-right Vox party, has described events in Ceuta as “an invasion and an act of war promoted by Morocco and allowed by Sánchez, who is incapable of responding because he is subservient to Morocco”.

title: US man says ‘hold tight’ to loved ones after wife and toddler killed by lightning
summary: Kameron Glasgow of Florida honors wife Kenya and daughter Kennedi at local vigil after last week’s tragedy
text: A Florida man whose wife and toddler daughter were killed by a lightning strike while he was near them recently has implored people to “hold … tight” to their loved ones. Kameron Glasgow made that arresting remark to local media at a weekend gathering honoring the memories of his wife, Kenya, and two-year-old daughter Kennedi after they died on 23 August from an exceedingly rare cause. As Glasgow put it to the news station WSVN, Kenya and Kennedi were in the driveway of a family member’s house in Margate, a small city in the Miami metropolitan area, when a lightning bolt hit them. Kenya, 31, and Kennedi were taken to separate hospitals, but each died shortly after arriving, authorities have said. Kameron told the WSVN that he was mere feet away from the strike and experienced some of its effects – while Kennedi’s twin sister, Kensli, was inside their family’s parked car close by and was uninjured. The widower later said to the outlet that it was the “worst feeling in the world … to turn around and see your wife and your daughter” mortally injured. “I just lost my best friend,” Kameron subsequently wrote in part on social media. “My daughter [Kensli] just lost her best friend [Kennedi].” On Saturday, neighbors, friends and other loved ones of the Glasgows attended a candelight memorial for Kenya and Kennedi at Margate elementary school. Kameron spoke with WSVN at the event and discussed how he believed Kensli’s young age was probably helping her cope with the grim reality that she was now playing alone – without her twin sister’s company – in the aftermath of Kennedi’s death. He also remembered Kenya as uniquely loving. “Words can’t describe her – like it doesn’t matter if she knows you her entire life, 10 days, five minutes, she’s going to love you all the same, and she’s always going to make sure you’re OK before … herself,” Kameron said to the channel. “Guys, if you have someone like that in your life, hold them tight because they are one in a million.” The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has calculated that there are about 37m lightning strikes in the US annually. However, an individual’s chances of being struck by lightning are extremely remote – with the CDC estimating those odds at less than one in a million. And the CDC says that almost 90% of all lightning strike victims survive. Nonetheless, the National Weather Service (NWS) warns that lightning can strike up to 25 miles (40km) away from a storm, including in places where it’s not raining at the time. The NWS advises people to go indoors if they can hear thunder because it indicates they are close enough to be struck by lightning. Kameron expressed his gratitude on social media for his community’s support, saying it left his, Kensli’s and their family’s metaphorical cups “overflowing”. He also wrote: “Hug your people tight and tell them you love them.”

title: As US-Canada tensions flare, who’s calling the shots in Trump’s trade team?
summary: US trade representative Jamieson Greer has a level-headed reputation but commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and White House adviser Peter Navarro also have key roles
text: Having reportedly read Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables, in French, during a military tour of duty in Iraq, Jamieson Greer considered himself an unlikely target for accusations of francophobia. But Donald Trump’s US trade representative, hitherto one of the president’s less high-profile cabinet members, found himself in that uncomfortable position amid the acrimonious collapse of bilateral trade talks with Canada that now threatens to degenerate into an all-out trade war between the two close trading partners whose economies are tightly intertwined. An apparent pending deal between Washington and Ottawa aimed at avoiding damaging tit-for-tat tariffs broke down at the last minute, with Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, claiming his country had come “under attack” from the US. Among the multiple and complex points of disagreement was a Canadian accusation that US negotiators had pressed for a weakening of legal protections for the French language, which is most heavily spoken in the province of Quebec. Canadian provisions include legislation that mandates streaming and online video companies to invest in and promote Canadian content and promote the French language. Carney cast US objections to such regulations as a deal-breaker, and said they amounted to “threats to French language and culture”. For Greer, a fluent French speaker who once served as a Mormon missionary in Belgium, France and Luxembourg, the charge was too much. “I speak French, too,” he told CNBC, dismissing the claims as “a funny, fake story”. “My kids speak French,” he said. “One of my kids was born in Paris. So I like the Québécois, and I like that they speak French. What we don’t like is a situation where Canada, the federal government, forces American tech companies to take their earnings and give a percentage to their competitors in Canada.” The controversy may be the closest glimpse the public will see of Greer being rattled. By Thursday, in what was being being seen by some Canadian officials as a potential olive branch, he was peddling a softer line on the language issue. “President Trump, myself and the US government recognizes the importance and sensitivity of the French language in Canada,” he told CBC, the Canadian broadcaster. “We know that this is quite sensitive and quite important, and we actually champion the use of French.” The impact was undermined hours later, however, when Trump publicly signed a retributive executive order supposedly changing the name of Lake Ontario – one of the Great Lakes which has shores on both countries – to Lake America. Petty as the act was, it seemed to graphically illustrate the limited freedom of manoeuvre held by anyone representing a president so preoccupied with trade. And Greer is not the only official seeking to steer the president’s aggressive agenda on trade – raising questions over who is really in control. Moving the goalposts Those who have met and worked with Greer describe the 46-year-old – who served as a military lawyer in Iraq, where he is reported to have read Hugo’s classic novel between bombardments – as a model of calm and expertise. “I have high respect for him. He been pretty creative in terms of trying to thread the needle with other countries as he tries to promote Trump’s trade policies,” said Wendy Cutler, a former US trade representative’s negotiator who has met Greer several times. “From a professional viewpoint, he’s extremely impressive. His reputation as being very level-headed, a very calm demeanor, and not someone who loses his temper or who grandstands.” It is not known if Greer retained his sang-froid in private as the talks with Canada unravelled, just days after Trump himself publicly declared a deal was at hand. According to reports, the agreement was derailed after Howard Lutnick, the US commerce secretary, objected to the scale of proposed tariffs reductions on imports of Canadian steel, aluminium and cars, sectors falling under his responsibility after Trump declared them areas of national security under the 1962 Trade Expansion Act. Carney, explaining why Canada decided to abandon the talks, pointed to disunity among the US negotiators. The White House has denied claims of division between Greer and Lutnick, but seasoned commentators are skeptical. “Lutnick viewed all this as his turf, and here is Greer, who is the designated guy to be effectively the trade minister, if you think about it in the context of other countries, conducting the negotiations,” said William Reinsch, a senior adviser to the Center for Strategic and International Studies and a former undersecretary for commerce. “It appears Greer was willing to go farther than Lutnick was. “From the Canadian point of view, this was a disagreement that developed late in the day and led the Canadians to believe that the United States was moving the goalposts.” Cutler, who served Republican and Democratic administrations during a 27-year stint as a US trade negotiator, said tensions within negotiating teams were not unprecedented, but were normally ironed out before talks reached the critical stage. “I think the challenge under this administration is that you have Greer in charge of the trade portfolio, but Lutnick’s in charge of section 232 investigations [restricting foreign import on national security grounds] and that’s where a lot of the sensitive issues are,” said Cutler, now vice-president of the Asia Society Policy Institute. ‘Trump whisperer’ Greer cut his trade negotiating teeth as chief of staff to Robert Lighthizer, US trade representative in Trump’s first presidency, who played the leading role in renegotiating Washington’s economic ties with Mexico and Canada, and the former North America Free Trade Agreement (Nafta), which was replaced with the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) in 2020. He was chosen for the position when Lighthizer apparently indicated he did not wish to be considered for the post a second time. “Greer plays the same role that Lighthizer played,” said Reinsch, who noted, however, that Greer lacked his former boss’s intimate understanding of Congress. “He figures out legal ways to do what Trump wants to do, and to get as much of Trump’s objectives accomplished as is possible within the framework that he has to operate in,” added Reinsch. “So that allows him to come back to Trump on occasion and say, ‘there’s a better way to get what you want than what you’ve employed so far.” Another complicating element may be Peter Navarro, the president’s senior counsellor for trade and manufacturing. He is reckoned by analysts to be a “Trump whisperer” on Canada, despite a belief that his influence has been marginalized compared with the first Trump presidency, when it was widely joked, according to Reinsch, that Lighthizer was reluctant to travel outside Washington for fear that Navarro would persuade the president to adopt impractical trade policies in his absence. Navarro, who went to jail for contempt of Congress after refusing to comply with a subpoena from the committee investigating the 6 January 2021 insurrection, vented in an appearance on the C-Span network last week. Asked to respond to an article in the Guardian by the Canadian writer Jen Gerson, who wrote that US retaliation should be taken as a warning by other western allies, Navarro said: “Madam, your country screws us. You’re in bed with the Chinese and playing games with us. “Look in the mirror at your tariffs codes. You are the problem.” Blame game Navarro has voiced concern that Canada has allowed the import of nearly 50,000 Chinese-manufactured electric vehicles under a most favoured nation agreement, which he fears will ultimately end up crossing the border to be sold in the US. “Navarro’s worried that the whole USMCA negotiation is really about how do we prevent Canada and Mexico from being a backdoor to Chinese stuff,” Reinsch said. “He would probably have argued last week that the deal wasn’t any good because it wouldn’t shut down Chinese imports in the United States.” Yet the focus on Trump’s advisers cannot obscure the president’s own fixation with tariffs. Carney referred to agreements being “signed in pencil”, suggesting that Trump would try to change terms even after the details had been hammered out. “The larger Canadian objection was not due to interagency American disagreement,” Reinsch said. “Trump has very strong fixed views on trade. He thinks tariffs are good. So if you’re going to blame somebody, don’t blame Lutnick or Greer. Blame Trump, because I’m quite confident he had the last word on this.” Regardless of where blame is apportioned, the consequences of Carney’s defiance will reverberate beyond Canada, analysts say, as other countries forced to confront Trump’s threats of tariffs reassess and recalibrate how they should respond. “Other countries are watching the developments with Canada very closely,” said Cutler. “Some of our other trading partners have expressed similar frustrations [to the Canadians] to me privately, and so we could be at a turning point. “It is possible that what we’re experiencing with Canada now spreads to other countries.”

title: First US military attacks on Iran in a month prompt retaliation
summary: US attacks Iranian rocket launchers on island in strait of Hormuz and Tehran targets US bases in Jordan and UAE
text: The US has reverted to military attacks on Iran for the first time in a month, firing missiles and drones at Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, prompting the Iranian military to attack US military bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. US Central Command said it acted late on Sunday after it detected the Iranians planning to fire fresh mines into the strait. Last week Donald Trump claimed the US navy had cleared the strait of mines for the first time since the conflict started on 28 February, a claim the Iranians rejected as lies. Iranian state TV later reported that a tanker had caught fire after hitting two naval mines while attempting to pass through the southern side of the strait close to Oman. It ‌did not identify the vessel or provide information about its crew. The Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned that other ships violating ⁠its rules would face the same fate and said compliance with its regulations ‌for passage through the strait was mandatory. The last known ‌US strikes on Iran were in late July, but there has been little sign of hard diplomatic progress apart from claims that Oman and Iran had reached agreement on a single permitted navigation route through the strait. Iran has set preconditions before the agreed route is opened, and the US has not stated its position on the route. The latest fighting broke out late on Sunday with a US attack on Larak Island in the strait. A US official said: “I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. Islamic ⁠Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz.” The IRGC said the US attack killed or wounded several soldiers and citizens and would be met with “punishment” from ‌Tehran, Iranian state media reported. At least two Iranians were killed and two injured, initial reports said. One IRGC navy officer was announced killed. The Mehr news agency quoted the IRGC as saying its air defences shot down a US MQ-9 drone over the strait, causing it to crash ‌into Gulf waters. In response to the US attack, the IRGC “targeted technical infrastructure, maintenance facilities and enemy fighter jet positions at the US-operated King Hussein and al-Azraq airbases in Jordan” with ballistic missiles, causing “heavy damage”, according to state TV. On Sunday night, Reuters reported a US source as saying all incoming missiles on US forces in Jordan had been intercepted with no significant impact so far. The UAE ministry of defence said it intercepted a drone over its territorial waters. The White House claim that the US now controls the strait and ships are free to navigate its waters without fear of Iranian reprisals is heavily contested. Tanker Trackers, an independent tracking agency, said on Sunday: “Past seven days daily average of crude oil exports via the strait of Hormuz was 3.8m barrels per day. During the formal ceasefire period (which in effect only lasted for 25 days), it was 9.8mbpd.” The agency said Iranian crude exports had been at zero for some time. A G20 finance ministers meeting in the US is likely to lead to a clash over US demands that more countries impose sanctions on Iran or face punitive action by the US. The German finance minister, Lars Klingbeil, facing difficult regional elections, is to urge the US to bring the conflict to a diplomatic end, pointing to the war’s inflationary impact. The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, is attending a meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in Kyrgyzstan where he will hold talks with Chinese officials. China, a key Iranian customer for its oil, has said it opposes the new US sanctions campaign, and Pezeshkian will be looking for concrete Chinese investment to reduce the scale of the economic chaos inside Iran.

title: Uber driver takes TfL to court over ‘pain‘ caused by licence renewal delay
summary: Julius Mugabo launches landmark case as union says thousands in capital lost incomes due to ‘broken system’
text: An Uber driver who got into thousands of pounds of debt and feared losing his home due to delays in Transport for London renewing his licence to pick up passengers is taking on the organisation in the high court in the first challenge of its kind. Julius Mugabo, 55, has been an Uber driver licensed by TfL since 2016. Under the Private Hire Vehicles (London) Act 1998, all minicab drivers cannot work lawfully unless TfL has carried out checks on them and issued or renewed their licences. These licences must be renewed every three years. There are approximately 100,000 private hire drivers in London working through apps such as Uber and Bolt. According to freedom of information data obtained by the Conservatives, almost 18,000 of them have received “goodwill” payments of between £300 and £500 due to delays in renewing their licences. “Because of all the pain I have been through, I am bringing this legal challenge to help other drivers,” Mugabo told the Guardian. Mugabo had not experienced any problems until he made a routine renewal application at the end of last year. TfL repeatedly delayed processing his renewal application, asking him to provide supporting documentation he said he had already provided. “Even if TfL delay renewing licences, drivers like me still have to eat and pay bills. My licence expired at the end of March 2026. I only received my renewed licence recently after I started the legal action against TfL,” he said. “Because of their delays everything in my life was a mess. I owed HMRC £3,000 in tax but because I couldn’t pay my tax bill on time the bill has gone up to £20,000 because of the interest. We didn’t lose our home but I was under so much stress and pressure. The landlord threatened to evict us because I struggled to pay the rent.” The high court action against TfL alleges that the transport authority breached its legal duties by failing to process private hire vehicle licence renewals on time. In a ruling granting a full judicial review hearing, Mr Justice Sweeting said the delay “caused immediate and serious consequences for [Mugabo] and his family”. He added: “TfL accepts that the processing of the claimant’s application did not meet its usual standards.” The Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain (IWGB), which represents private hire drivers on apps such as Uber and Bolt, said it had many members affected by the TfL licence processing delays, and that some of drivers had fallen into debt, had lost their cars and faced eviction. It is supporting the high court challenge. Alex Marshall, the president of the IWGB, said: “As they celebrate this ruling bringing them closer to justice, the minicab drivers who keep London moving are sending TfL a clear message: they will not be taken for a ride. “The suffering TfL inflicted on its predominantly migrant private hire driver workforce speaks volumes about who this public institution values, and who it takes for granted. TfL could easily have acted at the earliest sign of crisis, as the first drivers lost their incomes through no fault of their own. Instead, it watched at least 17,000 others suffer the same fate. “By the time TfL finally acted, drivers had burned through their savings, lost their houses and fallen into debts they are still working longer hours to repay. Now, thanks to drivers’ tireless fighting and campaigning, TfL will have to answer for its failures in court. We will not stop until TfL has been forced to fix this broken system for good.” Ahmed Aydeed, of Deighton Pierce Glynn solicitors, who is representing Mugabo, said: “TfL regularly strips drivers of their livelihoods, by failing to provide renewal licences before the expiry of the previous licence. Any driver who continues to work while waiting for their renewal licence is liable for criminal prosecution. “No one should be stripped of their ability to feed their families and pay their bills, especially during this cost of living crisis. Any public authority that does this to working-class people is not fit for purpose,” he said. A TfL spokesperson said: “We are aware of the judicial review claim, which has been brought by one driver regarding the processing of his licence. We are awaiting the date of the hearing.”

title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Bank of England governor tells G20
summary: Andrew Bailey, in role as financial stability watchdog chief, warns advanced models risk destabilising system
text: The Bank of England’s governor, Andrew Bailey, has joined the throng of figures warning about the global risks posed by the most advanced artificial intelligence technology. In a two-page letter sent to international finance ministers and central bank governors as part of his role as chair of the international Financial Stability Board (FSB), Bailey said “frontier” AI models were “showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy and problem-solving abilities, as well as threat capabilities”. He said the models risked destabilising the “highly interconnected” global financial system via cyber-disruption that “can spread across jurisdictions”. Bailey wrote to G20 finance ministers and central bank governors before their meeting in North Carolina, US, this week: “Recent developments have also highlighted to me that many jurisdictions do not have the protocols in place to manage the development, release, and deployment of advanced frontier AI models, heightening risks for the financial sector and beyond”. His letter adds to alarm bells about AI that have been sounded by prominent technologists over the past few weeks – and mirrors his previous calls for international cooperation to tackle growing AI threats, when he told City bosses: “No country can seal itself off from the cross-border nature of systems that are prevalent today.” Last month, a letter signed by 1,367 researchers and engineers at frontier AI labs – mainly OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind – also shone a light on the concerns of the engineers working on the technology every day. It stated: “There is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems,” before going on to ask for the US government’s support for “an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development”. Earlier this month, it also emerged that OpenAI staff observed signs of rogue behaviour among its cutting-edge AI agents weeks before they escaped their training environment to launch an unprecedented hacking crusade that spread global alarm. Extending this theme into the world of financial policy, Bailey continued: “For the financial system, the most immediate concern is the potential impact of frontier AI on cyber-risk. Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber-risk, which could undermine market confidence system-wide, especially due to highly concentrated third-party service providers.” Bailey called on those tasked with safeguarding the world’s financial systems to prioritise “appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis”. The letter also noted Bailey’s concerns about the increased use of leverage in bond and equity markets, which he said was combining with high valuations in concentrated financial markets – particularly fuelled by investor optimism about the prospects of AI – in a way that could amplify a future market correction. “I remain concerned therefore that a large shock or combination of shocks could concurrently trigger multiple vulnerabilities,” Bailey wrote. Bailey has been governor of the Bank of England since March 2020, and previously headed both the Financial Conduct Authority and the Prudential Regulation Authority, the UK’s two main financial regulators. He was appointed chair of the FSB last year. The FSB, based in Basel, Switzerland, coordinates the work at international level of national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies in an effort to develop effective regulation and policies in the interest of financial stability.

title: Bhutan hosts first ‘conscious food summit’ amid threats to global supplies
summary: Organisers say people must revive spiritual relationship with food amid double threat of climate crisis and conflict
text: Mending the broken food system under the threat of climate-driven weather extremes will require more than economic fixes and intensive agriculture, according to the organisers of a pioneering summit this week, who say the world must revive its spiritual relationship with food. Delegates from more than 60 countries and the UN will gather for the next five days in Paro in the tiny Himalayan nation of Bhutan for the world’s first “conscious food summit”, which will bring together governments and farmers, mindfulness experts and yoga therapists. Tshering Tobgay, Bhutan’s prime minister, said: “Food lies at the intersection of many of the defining challenges of our time – hunger, poor nutrition, poverty, climate change, biodiversity loss, and increasingly food security is also being disrupted by conflict and geopolitical instability. Our central message is simple: transforming our food systems requires both inner and outer change.” Conscious eating is at the heart of these talks, which will promote regenerative practices and Indigenous knowledge. “Consciousness can cultivate compassion, empathy, resilience, creativity and a stronger connection with nature,” Tobgay said in an interview with the Guardian. “This does not mean choosing spirituality over science. It means recognising that our values and mindsets influence how science, policy, finance and technology are used.” The impacts of the climate crisis have been brought home close to Bhutan’s borders with the disaster in its near neighbour Nepal last week where a glacial collapse led to floods and landslides that killed hundreds. This year and next as the “super El Niño” hits, the World Food Programme has warned that 50 million people could be pushed close to starvation. Food shortages and higher prices for staples are likely around the world. It follows a summer in the northern hemisphere in which harvests have been devastated by drought, intense heat and wildfires. Jerry Spooner, of Regenerative Vanua, a Pacific NGO, said the threats would push global food systems to their limit. “As we face the growing impacts of climate change, a potential super El Niño, biodiversity loss and increasing global instability, it is becoming clear that our food systems are not resilient enough for the challenges ahead,” he said. “The opportunity in Bhutan is to move beyond discussing how we produce more food and instead focus on how we build food systems that regenerate ecosystems, strengthen communities, celebrate culture and improve our collective resilience.” Tobgay said people must articulate the values they wanted to see reflected in the way food is produced and consumed, instead of relying on businesses and governments to shape food choices. “Food systems are ultimately shaped by human choices, institutions, incentives, relationships and values,” he said. “So we must address root causes as well as symptoms.” Farmers and rural people were often at the mercy of markets and global forces. “Too often, policies are developed for these groups rather than with them,” Tobgay said. The summit will focus not on bombastic political speeches and promises but on fostering inner change, with the help of “spiritual masters” such as mindfulness practitioners. Food had become a commodity on world markets and was treated carelessly as a result, leading to waste and unhealthy eating, and those attitudes must be reversed, Tobgay said. “Outer change is agriculture, markets, finance, public policy and consumption,” he said. “Consciousness has value only if it influences our decisions and changes how we act. For example, a conscious approach to production would care for both the land and the farmer. It would regenerate soils, not deplete them. It would protect water. It would reduce pollution and deforestation and recognise the dignity and wellbeing of the people who produce the food that sustain us.” Tobgay begins each day at 5am with a bowl of porridge and a banana, eaten sitting by a small stream that runs near his house. “I listen to the birds that are up and about by that time, I listen to the stream and the water,” he said. Anyone could try conscious eating, he added. Many cultures have a tradition before meals of reflecting on the food, its provenance and preparation, and giving thanks. Reviving such practices would take almost no time but could, he hopes, be one of the first steps to a revolution in the way we treat the planet and each other.

title: Weather tracker: Warm Yellow Sea strengthens storms in South Korea
summary: More than 200mm of rain forecast in parts of South Korea, while parts of southern Europe to be 10C above average
text: South Korea’s prime minister, Han Seong-sook, met officials to prepare for heavy rain expected this week, with rainfall totals across central and northern parts of the country forecast to exceed 200mm in some areas. South Korea was battered by heavy rainfall earlier this month and some areas were particularly hard hit. Over the weekend further thunderstorms pushed into the region and these are expected to cause disruption through Monday. This heavy rain is caused by a series of severe thunderstorms that developed over the Yellow Sea, on the western side of South Korea, and will slowly push eastwards on Monday before easing on Tuesday. These storms have been strengthened by the very warm Yellow Sea, which now has a surface temperature of 29C, 4C above the climatological average. Thailand is also under a warning for heavy to very heavy rain as the country passes the middle of its monsoon season, which runs from May to October. In the Philippines, the province of Tarlac has been placed under a state of calamity due to prolonged heavy rain in August. Nearby in the north Pacific, which has had an active typhoon and tropical storm season so far and will continue to do so this week, several tropical systems have the potential to develop. Last week, Typhoon Bang-lang and Tropical Storm Etau developed very close to each other in the north-west Pacific and both travelled northwards, although neither made landfall. Another two systems near the Philippines and China have a medium to high chance of developing into a tropical cyclone. For this to happen, wind speeds need to reach 39mph (63km/h). Across in the eastern north Pacific, Karina has developed into a category 1 hurricane and is expected to head just to the north of Hawaii but is not forecast to make landfall. Tropical Storm Lowell is expected to strengthen into a hurricane on Tuesday before passing just to the south of Hawaii. As Europe reaches the end of its record-breaking meteorological summer, the hot weather is showing no signs of easing off for the start of September. The heat is expected to intensify again later this week across central and southern parts of Europe, with temperatures rising to 10C above the climatological average. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, temperatures could reach about 40C by the weekend, falling just shy of the country’s all-time temperature record of 43.1C, set in 2007.

title: ‘Breakthrough’ as Turkmenistan starts fixing ‘mindboggling’ methane mega-leaks
summary: Secretive state begins repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as worst country for leaks of potent greenhouse gas
text: Turkmenistan has started plugging the mega-leaks of methane that spew from its ageing oil and gas facilities, the latest UN data shows, in a move hailed as a breakthrough. Methane, also called natural or fossil gas, is a potent greenhouse gas. It traps 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide and causes 25% of global heating today. Stopping leaks can be quick and cheap and, because methane breaks down in the atmosphere far quicker than CO2, this has a rapid impact, with some experts calling it the climate “emergency brake”. The Guardian revealed in 2023 that Turkmenistan was the worst country for methane mega-leaks. Sources in Turkmenistan said this scrutiny was the “critical step” in leading the secretive and authoritarian government to engage with foreign partners. A “super-emitter” leak, the escape of tonnes of methane per hour from a single valve or pipeline, heats the planet more than the emissions from a million SUVs or an entire coal-fired power station. Turkmenistan had now stopped eight leaks by repairing corroded pipes, faulty wells and failing flares. The work was an “incredible first step”, said the UN, but much remained to be done. The UN Methane Alert and Response System (Mars) sent 192 alerts of methane plumes to Turkmenistan in the last year. The country had three of the six worst leaks detected in the world by Mars in last six months, and nine of the top 50. Turkmenistan responded to about 20% of the alerts with on-the-ground information about the leaks and potential plans to fix them. In contrast, the US was sent the second highest number of alerts – 138 – but responded to none and had fixed no leaks in the last year. Other nations that failed to respond to any alerts were Iran, Russia and China. The worst methane leak detected was an extraordinary leak in Mexico’s offshore oil and gas industry of 37 tonnes per hour, equivalent to the emissions of more than 7m SUVs. Mexico responded to all 23 Mars alerts in the last year, but had yet to complete a fix. The plugging of leaks in Turkmenistan was encouraging, said Meghan Demeter, the programme manager of Mars, which is part of the UN Environment Programme. “These mitigation cases are a proof point of what can be done with satellite data, especially in situations like Turkmenistan, where there are a lot of detections. We’re seeing that the pipeline of satellite data to mitigation action works, and it can work quite quickly.” “This is a breakthrough in terms of having real documented mitigation action,” she told the Guardian. “But it is not yet a breakthrough in the overall magnitude of emissions. Eight cases is an incredible first step, but there’s also a lot more sources in Turkmenistan that need to be addressed. We are in pretty constant communication and the response rate is growing month by month. We’re seeing steady progress.” In March 2023, the Guardian revealed Turkmenistan had the most super-emitting methane leaks in the world. It then revealed in May that the methane emissions alone from the nation’s two main fossil fuel fields caused more global heating in 2022 than the entire carbon emissions of the UK, which experts described as both “mind-boggling” and “infuriating”. The findings caused a furore in Turkmenistan, prompting the government to engage with the UN, the EU and other nations and institutions to try to end the leaks, according to sources in the capital, Ashgabat. In December 2023, Turkmenistan joined the global methane pledge, two years after it had launched. Turkmenistan has huge gas reserves and is a major supplier to China. Previously, leaks were ignored due to the enormous volumes on tap. But in November 2024, the first leak was fixed after a faulty well was repaired. The most recent repair, in March, was to a corroded pipeline. Turkmenistan’s ministry of foreign affairs and state companies Turkmenoil and Turkmengaz did not respond to a request for comment. The most recent Mars data shows Kazakhstan, another former Soviet republic with ageing oil and gas infrastructure, has stopped eight leaks. However, the overall number of leaks in Kazakhstan is smaller, with 38 Mars alerts in the last year. In total, Mars alerts have led to 43 leaks being sealed so far. Many have been straightforward fixes, with leaks plugged on the spot, while others required more planning and funding. One major leak now stemmed in Algeria had been running for almost 40 years, due to a faulty flare. Flares burn unwanted methane and turn it into CO2, a much less potent greenhouse gas. The previous US administration, under President Joe Biden, did engage with Mars and one small leak in New Mexico was fixed in 2024 after a pressure safety valve was repaired. But this engagement ended with the second presidency of Donald Trump. Last year, Trump called climate change “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world” at the UN general assembly. Mexico, Brazil and Argentina have 100% response rates to Mars alerts, while Libya and Azerbaijan have high response rates. “Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan are home to some of the world’s most significant methane hotspots and their response to satellite alerts is much-needed good news in the global effort to minimise methane pollution,” said Dan Grossman, the vice-president at the Environmental Defense Fund. “Stemming methane emissions from oil and gas operations is the quickest and most cost-effective method to reduce climate pollution available today,” he said. “Alerts only matter if they lead to action, and governments and industry must do a better job.” The UN secretary general, António Guterres, has called for all countries to respond to 80% of alerts. Demeter said: “We’re scaling up a lot in terms of the support that we can offer – knowledge building and technical support – and we are working alongside many partners. There are also a lot of requests for funding for direct mitigation.” The Mars system uses artificial intelligence to analyse data from more than a dozen satellites and detect potential leaks, which are then checked by two layers of review by analysts. Verified leaks are then notified to the relevant government or company. Responses are recorded if they report on-the-ground information and an intention to plug the leak. If a leak is reported as fixed, Mars monitors the site until the data shows emissions have ended before recording it as a success. • The Guardian’s climate forum 2026 On Tuesday 20 October, join Damian Carrington and our panel of experts, including Prof Andy Haines, Katie White MP, Asad Rehman, Shruti Suresh Gareth Thomas and Amy Fairman, for a hopeful and solutions-focused evening. title: Australians missing in Nepal targeted by ‘heartbreaking’ and ‘abhorrent’ racist slurs
summary: As families await news after the catastrophe, community members appeal for compassion in the face of hateful rhetoric
text: A slew of racist social media comments have been made towards Australians missing in the catastrophic Nepal-Tibet floods, prompting calls for greater accountability of major platforms to remove hateful rhetoric. On Monday, the total number of Australians missing after flash floods triggered by a massive glacier collapse in the Himalayas rose to 43, and the overall death toll was at least 810 people. Most of the missing Australians were on pilgrimages, including to Mount Kailash in Tibet, which is a sacred site for Hindus, Buddhists, Jains and followers of the Bon faith. Fourteen are Sydney-based members of the Australia Bharatha Brahmin Samaj community. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email As families and friends face an agonising wait to learn the fate of their loved ones, mainstream media outlets including News Corp, Channel 7, Channel 10 and Nine have been hit with highly offensive and discriminatory comments on Facebook articles identifying the missing Australians in Nepal. Some outlets, including Guardian Australia, have limited who can comment on posts about the missing tourists after receiving strings of racist replies on social media. One Daily Telegraph article received dozens of comments on Facebook from people claiming that missing citizens who were not white weren’t Australian, which were later deleted. One said: “Hoping we have new vacancies in Australia that Aussies can fill.” The outlet’s editor, Ben English, said the comments on the post were “abhorrent” and “have no place on our platforms”. “We are responsible for the comment threads on our pages and we take that responsibility seriously … But no automated filter reliably catches racism expressed in coded language,” he said. “Where we cannot actively moderate a thread on a sensitive story, we will close it – and we have moved to do that here.” The comments have also proliferated on X. One post by conservative commentator Kobie Thatcher, who wrote “Aussie family” in quotation marks alongside an image of an identified missing couple, was viewed 3.2m times. Associate Prof at QUT’s Digital Media Research Centre, Tim Graham, said hateful rhetoric had been increasing on social media platforms for the past decade. “The design architecture of these websites, the algorithms that they use to curate content and put it into feeds, rewards this kind of stuff,” he said. “It brings out the worst in people, but it also plays into the political economy of these platforms where rage bait, extreme content or borderline content … attracts so much attention.” He said platforms had the technical infrastructure and the resources to push back against harmful content, including generative AI models that could detect “nuanced content at scale”, but weren’t using it for moderation. “I really don’t understand why that can’t be applied in special circumstances to a really terrible humanitarian catastrophe like this,” he said. “It’s a bit mind-boggling.” The race discrimination commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, said he wasn’t surprised by the comments, which he connected to Australia’s current debate on migrants. “They’re saying, you don’t deserve to … be seen as Australian. And that’s amplified by the rhetoric of far-right populist parties,” he said. “We should be very concerned because it’s indicative of a real rise in white supremacy ideology … Words have consequences … It’s heartbreaking.” Sivaraman said racism was “profitable” for social media companies, and the notion they were attempting to stop hate speech on their platforms was “fanciful”. “This is just more evidence as to why we need a digital duty of care for all social media platforms that operate in Australia,” he said. Hindu Council of Australia vice-president Surinder Jain said it was “saddening” to see people making use of a tragedy to “express their displeasure with the government”. “I … ask them to show some dignity to those who have perished and the families of those who are mourning their loss: give them a fair go,” he told Guardian Australia. Australia’s Indian diaspora, which includes Hindus, has been the target of racist comments from far-right movements including March for Australia as immigration has emerged as a hot-button issue. Nepalese Australian Welfare Society president, Chiran Tiwari, said Australians needed to look past nationalities and have humanity. “It is very hurtful and the families who are impacted feel really, really bad,” he told Guardian Australia. “All of us are human.”

title: Monday briefing: Nepal and Tibet’s floods are a warning for the future
summary: In today’s newsletter: As rescuers search for survivors after catastrophic floods, the disaster offers a stark warning about the climate risks facing the region, and the world
text: Good morning. Over the weekend, rescue workers in Nepal and Tibet raced to find people who are still trapped in villages affected by catastrophic flash floods. As of this morning, the death toll stands at 903, and more than 4,000 people are missing. For those of you reading this in a place where life continues as usual, the scale of devastation is hard to fathom. In a matter of minutes, a torrent of mud and debris engulfed entire villages, snapped bridges and swept away people’s homes and families. Some survivors are marooned on top of buildings that rescue workers can’t reach. Others are trapped in tunnels beneath the ground. Many have no idea if their loved ones are still alive. The floods exemplify a wider threat. The delicate processes that have shaped our climate for centuries are unwinding at a terrifying pace. Scientists are still investigating the precise sequence of events that caused these floods, but as the planet heats up and glaciers melt, events like this will keep happening. The Guardian has been covering the floods extensively – you can read our visual guide to the disaster, and our latest report on it here. For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to our south Asia correspondent Hannah Ellis-Petersen, who is on the ground in Kathmandu. She’s been speaking to survivors and reporting on the rescue operation since Thursday. That’s after the headlines. Weekend roundup UK politics | PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain in prison after Andy Burnham announced changes to the early release scheme that will see anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, excluded from the scheme. Milo Yiannopoulos | Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US back to the UK by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in connection with what the agency said was expired authorisation to be in the country. US-Iran | Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month. Iceland | In a blow to Brussels, Iceland has held a referendum that has narrowly ⁠rejected ⁠the government’s proposal to hold ⁠accession talks with ⁠the EU. Nepal-Tibet disaster | A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing. In depth: An ‘absolute catastrophe’ At 8:37am on Wednesday morning, an enormous chunk of ice from a glacier in the Himalayas broke off and crashed on to a mountain near the border between Nepal and Tibet. It caused a fearsome avalanche of ice and rock, which surged downstream into the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, submerging villages and sweeping roads away. At first, the scale of damage was unclear. Nepal is prone to natural disasters, and many of the villages affected by these floods are extremely remote. Early satellite images of the region were obscured by thick clouds of dust, and scientists initially assumed that an earthquake must have caused the flood, rather than a glacier collapse. By Wednesday night, as more images and reports emerged, it became clear that the floods were an “absolute catastrophe,” Hannah says. On Thursday, she boarded a flight to Kathmandu, the capital city near the destruction. When Hannah arrived in Bidur, a small city two hours from Kathmandu, on Friday morning, most of its buildings had been destroyed, their carcasses exposed like matchsticks. A team of rescue workers in yellow hard hats were working to clear the roads. “There was a bank, an ATM machine, and a truck that was lying on its side,” she says. “Everything else was either submerged in mud, or mangled.” *** The race to save lives The Nepali army has been organising the rescue operation from a military base in Bidur. Large sections of the road that links Bidur to villages higher in the valley have been washed away, so rescues are happening by air, and the sound of helicopters is nearly constant. Every two to three minutes, a chopper lands, deposits survivors, and sets off again. The mud is so thick in some places that helicopters have struggled to land. Rasuwa, an area where entire villages were destroyed, was still inaccessible when I spoke to Hannah on Sunday afternoon. “The ground zero of the floods has still not been reached by journalists, and is only just being reached by the army,” she says. Hundreds, if not thousands, of people have been rescued, and hundreds of people are now waiting outside the army base in Bidur scanning lists of survivors posted on the walls. At hospitals in Kathmandu, health workers have put up photos of bodies that are so disfigured their families have struggled to identify them. Authorities have begun burying human remains because there isn’t enough mortuary space to prevent them from decomposing. “I’ve spoken to people who have up to 12 relatives who have gone missing,” says Hannah, who visited hospitals in Kathmandu on Saturday. “And there’s no phone signal in the more remote villages. So another big cause of suffering is this huge uncertainty.” *** Thousands still missing So far there are 4,247 people who are missing, according to Nepal’s disaster agency (592 of whom are foreigners, including 43 Australians, and 48 from the UK, including 15 reported missing in China). Among them are 933 workers from Nepal and neighbouring countries who were working on hydroelectric power projects along the river. These rely on vast tunnel systems that are built deep into the ground, and rescue teams have to dig through mud and bore through tunnel walls to extricate trapped workers. On Saturday, the Nepali army had a small breakthrough when it successfully inserted a pipe into a tunnel at a hydroelectric site in Trishuli, allowing air to be pumped into the tunnel. In the early hours this morning, rescue efforts were “intensified” at the site, with a team of 90 people deployed. The army is racing against time to rescue the living. “People are stuck in areas that have no drinking water, or access to food. They’re completely cut off,” Hannah says. The picture of devastation has emerged more quickly in Nepal than in Tibet, where the Chinese government retains a tight grip on information. On Friday, as the official death toll in Nepal rose to 538 people, China estimated that just five people had died in Tibet. The Chinese authorities have since revised their numbers, and estimate that at least 16 people are dead and 546 missing. *** The long road to recovery It will take months to clear away the mud, and some people will never find their relatives’ bodies. Some were pushed so far down the river that they have washed up in India. “People have lost everything,” says Hannah. “I saw one woman clutching a bottle of cooking oil, because it’s the only thing she had left.” Climate stories in the global south often struggle to break through, so it’s encouraging that these floods have been covered so widely. But when the news cycle has moved on, Nepal will be left with the enormous task of rebuilding. It estimates that cost could be between $4bn to $5bn, almost a tenth of its economy. “It’s getting increasingly difficult for Nepal to pick itself up,” Hannah tells me. In Kathmandu, buildings destroyed by the 2015 earthquake, which killed nearly 9,000 people, are still in ruins. The EU has committed €2m to Nepal to help with the floods, and Britain has committed £5m. There’s also been a lot of focus on the need for better early monitoring systems. All of this matters. But as Sunil Acharya, a climate policy specialist based in Kathmandu, wrote in this interesting Opinion column, it also obscures a more fundamental problem: systems to monitor these events were designed for yesterday’s risks, not today’s extremes. Nepal’s warning systems were destroyed before they could alert people near the source of the flood. Looming over all this is the fact that nations like Nepal, which has contributed a minuscule amount to historic greenhouse gas emissions, will suffer the worst effects of the climate crisis. It needs far more assistance to cope with the consequences of richer nations’ actions. And it needs those nations to rapidly cut their emissions, before the crisis gets worse.
